name: Java

topics.name: Introduction to Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Java is a high-level, object-oriented, platform-independent programming language.
  • You write code once in a .java file, the compiler turns it into bytecode, and the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) runs that bytecode on any operating system.
  • It is statically typed and class based.
  • The JVM checks the bytecode, interprets it, and then JIT-compiles (Just-In-Time compiles) the busy methods to native code.

2. Need of This Topic

  • You need to know what Java really is before writing bigger programs.
  • Learn the write, compile, run cycle and why one compiled file works on Windows, Linux and Mac.
  • Banks, college portals, railway booking, UPI backends and Android apps run on Java.
  • Every later topic, such as OOPs, collections and Spring, depends on these basics.
  • It also helps you understand JVM problems in production, such as OutOfMemoryError, long GC pauses and NoClassDefFoundError.

3. Advantages

  • Platform independent: one .class file runs anywhere a JVM exists (write once, run anywhere).
  • Simple and safe: no pointers, no manual memory free, and automatic garbage collection.
  • Huge library and ecosystem: Spring, Hibernate, Kafka, Maven, plus strong tooling such as JFR, jcmd and jstack.
  • Mature JIT and pluggable collectors (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah) bring long-running servers close to native speed.
  • Backward compatible, and a big job market for Java developers.

4. Disadvantages

  • More verbose than Python or Kotlin; even a small task needs a class and a main method.
  • Slower startup and warm-up, so less ideal for short-lived serverless functions.
  • Higher memory use because of object headers and metaspace, and GC pauses or tuning can hurt latency.
  • No low-level hardware control, and generics lose type information at runtime (type erasure).
  • Needs a JVM installed or bundled to run.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Java is the base for Spring Boot, microservices and Android development.
  • Interviews for backend roles start with core Java, class loading, JIT and memory areas.
  • Understanding the JVM helps you debug performance and memory problems and explain why the same jar behaves differently on two servers.

6. Basic Concepts

What is Java?

Java is a high-level, class-based, object-oriented programming language designed to have as few implementation dependencies as possible.

It was developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems (now owned by Oracle Corporation) and officially released in 1995.

In simple words: you write Java code once, and (thanks to the JVM) it can run on almost any device or operating system - Windows, Linux, macOS, and more - without changing the code.

Why is Java so widely used?

Because it is beginner-friendly, reliable, and works almost everywhere - from mobile apps and websites to large banking systems and enterprise servers.

Key Features of Java:

  • Platform Independent: Write Once, Run Anywhere (WORA)
  • Object-Oriented: Everything is designed around objects and classes
  • Simple and Easy to Learn: Clean syntax, no explicit pointers
  • Secure: No direct memory/pointer access, runs inside the JVM sandbox
  • Robust: Strong memory management and automatic garbage collection
  • Multi-threaded: Built-in support for concurrent programming
  • Architecture Neutral: Compiled bytecode is portable across platforms

Your First Java Program: "Hello, World!"

Every Java program starts execution from the main method. Below is the traditional first program every learner writes.

JDK, JRE, and JVM - the basics

These three terms are the foundation of how Java code runs, and every beginner should know the difference:

  • JDK (Java Development Kit): The complete toolkit for developers - includes the compiler, debugger, and everything needed to write and build Java programs.
  • JRE (Java Runtime Environment): The environment needed to run a Java program (it does not include development tools like the compiler).
  • JVM (Java Virtual Machine): The engine that actually reads and executes the compiled Java bytecode. This is what makes Java "Write Once, Run Anywhere".

How does a Java program actually run?

Here is the simple flow from writing code to seeing the output on screen:

  You write code          Compiler converts it        JVM executes it
  +----------------+       +------------------+       +------------------+
  |  HelloWorld    |       |  javac compiles  |       |  java command    |
  |  .java file    |  -->  |  .java to        |  -->  |  runs .class on  |  -->  Output on screen
  |  (source code) |       |  .class file     |       |  the JVM         |
  |                |       |  (bytecode)      |       |  (bytecode ->    |
  |                |       |                  |       |   machine code)  |
  +----------------+       +------------------+       +------------------+

Because the middle step produces platform-independent bytecode, the same .class file can run unchanged on any operating system that has a compatible JVM installed - this is exactly what "Write Once, Run Anywhere" means.

Fresher Notes

  • Compile once, run anywhere: javac turns your code into bytecode, and any JVM can run it.
  • Entry point: every program starts at public static void main(String[] args).
  • Strongly typed: every variable has a declared type, checked at compile time.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Pipeline: javac makes .class bytecode, then the JVM interprets it and JIT-compiles hot code to machine code.
  • Garbage collection: the JVM frees unused objects, so there is no manual free.
  • LTS releases (8, 11, 17, 21) are the ones most companies run in production.

8. Advanced Concepts

History of Java

1. Beginning (1991) - The Green Project

  • In 1991, James Gosling, Mike Sheridan, and Patrick Naughton at Sun Microsystems started a project called the Green Project.
  • Goal: Develop software for digital devices (TVs, set-top boxes, etc.).
  • The language was first called Oak (after an oak tree outside Gosling's office).

2. Rename to Java (1995)

  • Oak was already trademarked.
  • The team renamed it to Java, inspired by Java coffee (Gosling drank a lot of it).
  • In 1995, Sun officially released Java 1.0 with the slogan "Write Once, Run Anywhere" (WORA).

3. Java in the Internet Era (1990s - early 2000s)

  • Java gained popularity quickly because it was perfect for web applets and networked applications.
  • Many companies adopted it for enterprise-level applications (banking, telecom, etc.).

4. Ownership Changes

  • 2006 - Sun released Java as open-source under the GNU General Public License (GPL).
  • 2010 - Oracle Corporation acquired Sun Microsystems and became the official owner of Java.

5. Modern Java (2011 - Present)

  • Oracle introduced Java SE (Standard Edition), Java EE (Enterprise Edition), and Java ME (Micro Edition).
  • Java 8 (2014) was a turning point - introduced Lambdas, Streams, and functional programming features.
  • Java now follows a 6-month release cycle (new versions every March and September).
  • Latest versions focus on performance, cloud, modularity, and modern language features.

Summary

Java started in 1991 as Oak, was renamed to Java in 1995, and has evolved into one of the most widely used programming languages for web, enterprise, mobile, and cloud applications.

Design Goals of Java

Sun designed Java around a small set of explicit goals - these explain almost every design decision in the language:

Design GoalHow Java achieves it
SimpleNo pointers, no operator overloading, automatic garbage collection
Object-orientedEverything (except primitives) is modeled as a class/object
Portable / Architecture-neutralSource compiles to bytecode, not native machine code - runs on any JVM
RobustStrong compile-time type checking + runtime checks + automatic memory management
SecureNo direct memory access, bytecode verifier, classloader sandboxing, security manager
MultithreadedBuilt-in language and library support for concurrent execution
High performanceJust-In-Time (JIT) compilation converts hot bytecode to native machine code at runtime

Java vs C/C++ - Why Java Was a Big Shift

AspectC / C++Java
Compilation targetNative machine code (platform-specific)Bytecode (platform-independent, run by JVM)
Memory managementManual (malloc/free, new/delete)Automatic (Garbage Collector)
PointersExplicit pointer arithmetic allowedNo explicit pointers (references only)
Multiple inheritance (classes)Supported in C++ (diamond problem possible)Not supported for classes; achieved via interfaces
Platform dependencyMust recompile per platform"Write Once, Run Anywhere" via the JVM

WORA Internals: Source Code to Execution on Any Platform

"Write Once, Run Anywhere" is not magic - it works because the compiler never targets a specific CPU/OS. It always targets the JVM's bytecode instruction set, and each platform simply needs its own JVM implementation to translate that bytecode into native instructions.

                         HelloWorld.java  (source code - written once)
                                 |
                                 v
                         javac (Java Compiler)
                                 |
                                 v
                       HelloWorld.class  (platform-independent bytecode)
                                 |
              +------------------+------------------+
              |                  |                  |
              v                  v                  v
      JVM on Windows      JVM on Linux        JVM on macOS
              |                  |                  |
              v                  v                  v
      Windows native      Linux native        macOS native
      machine code        machine code        machine code
              |                  |                  |
              v                  v                  v
         Output runs        Output runs        Output runs
        (same result)      (same result)      (same result)

The only platform-specific piece is the JVM itself - Oracle/OpenJDK ship a separate JVM build for each OS, but the .class bytecode file never changes.

Java Architecture: JDK vs JRE vs JVM

These three nest inside one another - JDK is the largest, JVM is the innermost engine:

+------------------------------------------------------+
| JDK (Java Development Kit)                            |
|   compiler (javac), debugger, tools, docs             |
|                                                        |
|   +------------------------------------------------+ |
|   | JRE (Java Runtime Environment)                  | |
|   |   core libraries (java.lang, java.util, ...)    | |
|   |                                                  | |
|   |   +----------------------------------------+    | |
|   |   | JVM (Java Virtual Machine)               |    | |
|   |   |   loads, verifies & executes bytecode    |    | |
|   |   +----------------------------------------+    | |
|   +------------------------------------------------+ |
+------------------------------------------------------+
  • JDK (Java Development Kit): complete environment to develop, compile, and run Java applications.
  • JRE (Java Runtime Environment): the runtime environment needed to run Java applications (JVM + core libraries), without development tools.
  • JVM (Java Virtual Machine): the abstract machine that actually loads, verifies, and executes Java bytecode.

Compilation and Execution Process:

  1. Source code (.java) → Java Compiler (javac) → Bytecode (.class)
  2. Bytecode → JVM (Class Loader → Bytecode Verifier → Interpreter/JIT) → Machine Code → Execution

JVM Memory Areas:

  • Heap: Where all objects are allocated
  • Stack: Stores method call frames and local variables (one stack per thread)
  • Method Area: Class structures, method data, and constants
  • PC Register: Holds the address of the currently executing instruction (per thread)
  • Native Method Stack: Supports native (non-Java) method execution

Class Loading and Initialization Order in Action

When the JVM loads and initializes a class, static blocks run once (at class-loading time), then instance blocks and the constructor run every time an object is created - in that fixed order.

Senior Notes

  • One runtime, many languages: Kotlin, Scala and Groovy also run on the JVM and share its libraries.
  • Backward compatibility: old bytecode keeps running on new JVMs, which slows language change.
  • When to choose Java: large, long-lived systems that need tooling, speed and an ecosystem (Spring, Hibernate, Kafka).

9. Code for Each Concept

Code: Definition
Code: Advantages
Code: Definition
Code: Advantages

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax rules:

  • A class holds fields and methods.
  • Statements end with a semicolon, and blocks use braces.
  • Names are case sensitive.
  • Comments are //, /* */ and /** */ (Javadoc).

Naming rules:

  • Classes use PascalCase.
  • Methods and variables use camelCase.
  • Constants use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

When you run java Hello, these steps happen in order:

  1. The launcher creates the JVM.
  2. The bootstrap class loader loads the core classes.
  3. The application class loader loads Hello.
  4. The verifier checks the bytecode.
  5. The interpreter runs main.

Methods that run many times are compiled by the JIT (Just-In-Time compiler). It uses tricks such as inlining (copying a small method into its caller) and escape analysis (finding objects that never leave a method).

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • The file name does not match the public class.
  • The main method is missing static, or its signature is wrong. The code compiles but will not run.
  • Writing string instead of String, because Java is case sensitive.

Newer Java versions allow an instance main: a preview feature in Java 21, and standard from Java 25.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Startup and warm-up matter for short programs, because the JVM interprets first and compiles later. These tools reduce startup time:

  • AppCDS (Class Data Sharing): saves loaded classes in an archive.
  • GraalVM native image: compiles the app ahead of time.
  • CRaC: restores a saved, already warm process.

For benchmarks, warm up first and use JMH. Never trust one cold run.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: Java powers banking back ends, Android apps (via Kotlin/Java), big-data tools (Hadoop, Kafka, Spark), and e-commerce. A typical service is built with Maven or Gradle, packaged as a jar, run in a container, and monitored with JFR and Micrometer.

10. Examples

Real Time Examples

  • Banking: core banking systems of SBI, HDFC and ICICI process crores of transactions in Java.
  • IRCTC: the railway ticket booking backend handles lakhs of bookings using Java servers.
  • UPI and payment apps: settlement services on the server side are commonly Java based.
  • Android: apps like early WhatsApp and Flipkart were written in Java.
  • College and school portals: attendance, marks and fee systems.
  • E commerce: Amazon and Flipkart use Java microservices for orders and payments.

Real Time Examples

  • NPCI UPI switch: JVM services tuned with low pause collectors to keep response under 100 ms at crores of transactions a day.
  • Zerodha and Upstox order gateways: latency sensitive JVM tuning with pre warmed JIT paths.
  • Aadhaar authentication services: horizontally scaled JVM microservices behind load balancers.
  • Netflix and Amazon: thousands of JVM microservices with JFR based production profiling.
  • Kafka and Elasticsearch: infrastructure written in Java and Scala running on the JVM.

Interview tip: when asked why a service is slow only after deployment, mention JIT warm up, cold caches and class loading before blaming the code.

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Reading command-line arguments.

11. Quick Revision

  • Java compiles to bytecode, the JVM runs it.
  • Entry point: public static void main(String[] args).
  • Statically typed, object-oriented, garbage collected.
  • LTS versions in use: 8, 11, 17, 21.
  • Platform independence comes from bytecode plus a JVM per platform.

interviewQA: Who created Java, and when was it released?
James Gosling at Sun Microsystems; released as Java 1.0 in 1995 (originally started as the "Green Project" in 1991, named Oak)
What does "Write Once, Run Anywhere" mean?
Java source compiles to platform-independent bytecode (.class), which any JVM - on any OS - can execute, so the same compiled file runs everywhere without recompilation
Difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
JVM executes bytecode; JRE = JVM + core libraries needed to run apps; JDK = JRE + development tools (compiler, debugger) needed to build apps
Is Java purely interpreted?
No - the JVM interprets bytecode initially, then uses a JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler to convert frequently executed ("hot") bytecode into native machine code for speed
Why is Java considered "secure" compared to C/C++?
No explicit pointers/pointer arithmetic, bytecode is verified before execution, and code runs inside the JVM's managed, sandboxed environment
Why doesn't Java support multiple inheritance of classes?
To avoid the "diamond problem" ambiguity that C++ has with multiple class inheritance; Java achieves similar flexibility safely through interfaces
What are the main JVM memory areas?
Heap (objects), Stack (method frames/local variables, per thread), Method Area (class data/constants), PC Register (per-thread instruction pointer), Native Method Stack

topics.name: Getting Started with Java (Installation & Setup)

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Getting started means installing a JDK, setting JAVA_HOME and PATH, choosing an IDE, writing a .java file, compiling it with javac and running it with java.
  • At a professional level it means owning a reproducible toolchain: a pinned JDK version, a build tool (Maven or Gradle), locked dependencies and the same setup on your laptop, the CI server and the production container.

2. Need of This Topic

  • You cannot run even one line of Java without a correct setup, and most beginners lose hours on errors such as javac is not recognized, which is only a PATH problem.
  • You also learn the rule that a public class name must match the file name.
  • In real teams, works on my machine bugs are almost always JDK or classpath mismatches, and audited builds must be reproducible.

3. Advantages

  • Free and open: OpenJDK costs nothing and works on Windows, Linux and Mac; notepad plus a terminal is enough to learn.
  • One-time setup: once PATH and JAVA_HOME are set, every project uses them.
  • IDEs (IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, VS Code) give instant feedback and debugging; Maven and Gradle automate compiling and dependencies.
  • Reproducible builds with a pinned JDK, and javac --release lets one modern JDK build for older runtimes.
  • jlink and jpackage can ship a trimmed custom runtime and containers freeze the whole runtime.

4. Disadvantages

  • PATH and JAVA_HOME mistakes confuse beginners, and several JDKs on one machine can run the wrong javac.
  • Version mismatches cause UnsupportedClassVersionError; upgrading from JDK 8 to 17 breaks removed APIs.
  • Large download, and the two-step compile then run cycle feels slow compared to Python.
  • Vendor differences (Temurin, Corretto, Zulu, Oracle) and classpath ordering bugs where the first jar silently wins.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • A correct environment saves hours of debugging.
  • The same tools are used in real projects and CI pipelines.
  • You learn the compile, package and run cycle from the start and how to control the classpath yourself.

6. Basic Concepts

What You Need Before Writing Any Java Code

To write, compile, and run Java programs on your own machine, you need three things:

  • JDK (Java Development Kit) - includes the compiler (javac) and everything needed to build Java programs.
  • A place to configure the PATH environment variable, so your terminal can find java/javac from anywhere.
  • An IDE (Eclipse, IntelliJ IDEA, or VS Code) - optional for tiny programs, but the normal way real projects are built.

This topic walks through installing the JDK, verifying it, setting up an IDE, and running your first program.

1. Downloading and Installing the JDK

  • Download a JDK build from Oracle (oracle.com/java) or a free OpenJDK distribution (Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto) - any recent LTS version (17 or 21) is a safe default.
  • Run the installer for your OS (Windows .exe/.msi, macOS .dmg/.pkg, Linux via package manager e.g. apt install openjdk-21-jdk).
  • The installer places the JDK in a folder such as C:\Program Files\Java\jdk-21 (Windows) or /usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk (Linux).

2. Setting the PATH Environment Variable

The PATH variable tells your operating system where to look for executable commands. Adding the JDK's bin folder to PATH lets you type java/javac from any terminal location, not just from inside the JDK folder.

Windows:

  • Search "Environment Variables" in the Start menu -> Edit the system environment variables.
  • Under "System variables", edit Path, add a new entry pointing to the JDK's bin folder (e.g. C:\Program Files\Java\jdk-21\bin).
  • Optionally set a JAVA_HOME variable pointing to the JDK root folder (many build tools like Maven/Gradle expect this).

macOS / Linux (bash/zsh):

Add these lines to ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, or /etc/profile:
codeExamples:
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk
export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH

beginner.content:
3. Verifying the Installation

Open a fresh terminal/command prompt (PATH changes only apply to newly opened terminals) and check both tools:

4. Installing an IDE

While you can write Java in any text editor, an IDE gives you auto-complete, error highlighting, debugging, and project/build management:

  • Eclipse - download the installer from eclipse.org, choose "Eclipse IDE for Java Developers", and it auto-detects any JDK already on your PATH.
  • IntelliJ IDEA - Community Edition is free; widely used in industry.
  • VS Code - lightweight, needs the "Extension Pack for Java" installed from the Extensions marketplace.

None of these IDEs replace the JDK - they all still need a JDK installed to compile/run your code; the IDE just wraps javac/java with a friendlier interface.

5. Your First Program — Command Line

No IDE is required to compile and run Java - the two commands you'll use constantly are javac (compile) and java (run):

6. Your First Program — Inside Eclipse

  • File -> New -> Java Project -> give it a name -> Finish.
  • Right-click src -> New -> Class -> name it HelloWorld, check "public static void main" to auto-generate the method stub.
  • Write the System.out.println("Hello, World!"); line inside main.
  • Click the green Run button (or Run -> Run As -> Java Application) - Eclipse compiles and runs it automatically, showing output in the Console panel at the bottom.

Fresher Notes

  • Install a JDK (Temurin, Oracle, Corretto), then check with java -version and javac -version.
  • Set JAVA_HOME to the JDK folder and add its bin to PATH.
  • Pick an editor: an IDE (IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, VS Code) or just a text editor and the terminal.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Class and file name: a public class must match its file name (Hello.java contains public class Hello).
  • Build tools (Maven, Gradle) manage dependencies and builds; the IDE usually creates the project for you.
  • Common errors: javac is not recognized means a PATH problem; Could not find or load main class means a wrong class name or classpath.

8. Advanced Concepts

The Filename-Must-Match-Class-Name Rule

For a public top-level class, the .java file name must exactly match the class name (case-sensitive) - this is enforced by javac, not a mere convention.

What javac and java Actually Do

HelloWorld.java  --javac-->  HelloWorld.class (bytecode)
                                    |
                                  java
                                    |
                              JVM loads + runs it
                                    |
                            Native machine code (via JIT)

javac only compiles - it never executes anything, and it produces a .class file containing JVM bytecode, not native machine code. java starts a JVM instance, loads that .class file, and executes its main method - it does NOT need or accept a .class extension in the command (java HelloWorld, not java HelloWorld.class).

Common Setup Errors and Fixes

ErrorCauseFix
'java' is not recognized as an internal or external commandPATH doesn't include the JDK's bin folder, or terminal opened before PATH was updatedAdd JDK's bin to PATH, then open a brand-new terminal window
Error: Could not find or load main class HelloWorldRunning java from a different folder than the .class file, or a package mismatchcd into the folder containing the .class file, or use the classpath (-cp) flag
class X is public, should be declared in a file named X.javaFile name doesn't exactly match the public class nameRename the file (or the class) so they match exactly, including case
javac: command not found (but java works)A JRE-only install was used instead of a full JDK (JRE has no compiler)Install the JDK, not just the JRE

Multiple JDK Versions on One Machine

Professional setups often need several JDK versions side by side (e.g. Java 8 for a legacy project, Java 21 for a new one). Tools like SDKMAN! (macOS/Linux) or manually swapping JAVA_HOME/PATH entries (Windows) let you switch the active version per terminal session without reinstalling anything - IDEs also let you configure a different JDK per-project independent of the system default.

Senior Notes

  • Many JDKs: manage them with SDKMAN, jEnv or the Gradle/Maven toolchains feature.
  • Reproducible builds: CI should pin the JDK version.
  • Older targets: use --release 17 in javac to build for an older API level safely.

9. Code for Each Concept

Code: Definition
Code: Advantages
Code: Definition
Code: Advantages

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Tooling: javac, java, jar, javadoc, jshell (REPL), jcmd, jstack, jmap, jfr. jshell is ideal for trying snippets. Maven (pom.xml) and Gradle (build.gradle) add dependency management.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The launcher resolves the class path in order; -cp lists directories and jars separated by ; (Windows) or : (Unix). Packages map to folders, and -d tells javac where to write class files. Since JDK 9 the module path (-p) is separate from the class path.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: installing only a JRE, wrong JAVA_HOME with a trailing bin, mixing JDK versions between compile and run (UnsupportedClassVersionError), spaces in class paths, and committing IDE files. UnsupportedClassVersionError means the class was compiled for a newer Java than the runtime.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Build speed: use Gradle or Maven daemons, incremental compilation and the build cache; in CI cache the dependency folder. Locally, give the IDE enough memory, and keep tests fast.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world team setup: pin the JDK version in the build file (toolchain), commit the wrapper (mvnw or gradlew), and document one-command setup.

10. Examples

Real Time Examples

  • College lab: students install the JDK and set PATH before the first practical.
  • Fresher onboarding in Indian IT companies: day one is JDK, Maven and IDE setup.
  • Build servers: Jenkins pipelines set JAVA_HOME before running a Maven build.
  • Docker images: an eclipse-temurin base image already ships the JDK, so the setup is baked in.
  • Bank projects: teams often pin one exact JDK version so every developer builds the same bytecode.

Real Time Examples

  • Infosys and TCS delivery teams: a shared settings.xml and a pinned JDK so every developer and the CI agent build identically.
  • Bank release pipelines: the artifact is built once on a controlled JDK and the same jar moves through SIT, UAT and production.
  • Docker: a multi stage build compiles with a JDK image and runs on a smaller JRE image.
  • Migration projects: a JDK 8 to JDK 17 upgrade for a legacy insurance system, fixing removed APIs.

Interview tip: if asked how you would debug NoSuchMethodError in production, answer classpath shadowing first, then version mismatch between compile time and run time.

Practice Exercise 2

11. Quick Revision

  • Install a JDK, not only a JRE.
  • Check with java -version and javac -version.
  • Set JAVA_HOME and add bin to PATH.
  • Public class name must match the file name.
  • Compile: javac Hello.java, run: java Hello.

interviewQA: What's the difference between installing the JDK vs just the JRE?
The JRE can only run compiled Java programs; the JDK additionally includes javac and other tools needed to develop and compile Java code
Why doesn't "java is not recognized" go away right after editing PATH?
Already-open terminal windows keep their old environment snapshot - PATH changes only take effect in newly opened terminals/processes
Do you write the .class extension when running "java"?
No - java takes the class name only (java HelloWorld), never java HelloWorld.class
Why must the file name match the public class name?
It's enforced by the Java compiler itself so the class-loading mechanism can reliably locate a public class's bytecode by file name
What does JAVA_HOME point to?
The root installation folder of a specific JDK - many build tools (Maven, Gradle) and IDEs read it to know which JDK to use

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Java was created to be portable, simple and secure.
  • These traits are called Java buzzwords.
  • At an advanced level they are contracts enforced by the compiler and the JVM: static typing, a specified memory model, verified bytecode and a managed heap, with modern additions such as records, sealed types, pattern matching and virtual threads.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Knowing the features explains why Java is chosen over C or C++ for large systems: banks need security and robustness, mixed teams need platform independence and exam portals need multithreading.
  • It answers the most common interview question (name the features of Java) and helps you defend a technology choice, for example picking virtual threads or sealed types for a given requirement.

3. Advantages

  • Platform independent and portable: write once, run anywhere.
  • Secure: no pointer arithmetic, bytecode verification and a sandboxed runtime.
  • Robust: strong type checking, exception handling and garbage collection.
  • Built-in multithreading, networking and a rich standard library, with a specified memory model (volatile, final, happens-before).
  • Virtual threads (Java 21), records and sealed types give scalable concurrency and compiler-checked designs.

4. Disadvantages

  • Not purely object-oriented: the eight primitive types are not objects.
  • No operator overloading and no direct hardware access.
  • Slower startup and higher memory use than native code; garbage collection cannot be forced.
  • Type erasure, checked exceptions with lambdas, autoboxing traps and the subtle Java Memory Model need care.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • It is a basic interview question.
  • It helps you choose the right language and the right feature for a project.
  • Each feature maps to a later topic: OOP, threads, exceptions, collections.

6. Basic Concepts

Java has traits that make it a strong choice as a programming language. It is widely used in mobile development, chatbots and DevOps. Java was created to be portable, simple and secure. These traits are called Java Buzzwords.

The common features of Java are:

  1. Simple
  2. Object-Oriented
  3. Portable
  4. Platform independent
  5. Secured
  6. Robust
  7. Architecture neutral
  8. Interpreted (compiled, then interpreted)
  9. High Performance
  10. Multithreaded
  11. Distributed
  12. Dynamic

Below is a short, plain-language explanation of every feature, with a small runnable example where code can show it.

A Short History of Java

  • 1991 - The Green Project: James Gosling, Mike Sheridan and Patrick Naughton at Sun Microsystems started a project to build software for digital devices (TVs, set-top boxes). The language was first called Oak, after a tree outside Gosling's office.
  • 1995 - Renamed to Java: "Oak" was already trademarked, so the team renamed it Java (inspired by Java coffee). Sun released Java 1.0 with the slogan "Write Once, Run Anywhere" (WORA).
  • 1990s-2000s: Java exploded in popularity for web applets and networked/enterprise applications (banking, telecom).
  • 2006: Sun open-sourced Java under the GPL.
  • 2010: Oracle acquired Sun Microsystems and became Java's official owner.
  • 2014 - Java 8: A turning point release - Lambdas, Streams, and functional-programming features.
  • Today: Java follows a strict 6-month release cycle (new version every March and September), with recent releases focused on performance, cloud-readiness, modularity, and developer productivity.

One-line summary: Java started in 1991 as Oak, was renamed Java in 1995, and has evolved into one of the most widely used languages for web, enterprise, mobile, and cloud applications.

1. Simple

  • Java is very easy to learn, and its syntax is simple, clean and easy to understand.
  • Java syntax is based on C++ (so it is easier for programmers to learn it after C++).
  • Java removed many complicated and rarely-used features, for example, explicit pointers and operator overloading.
  • There is no need to remove unreferenced objects manually because Java has Automatic Garbage Collection.

2. Object-Oriented

  • Almost everything in Java is a class or an object. The eight primitive types (int, char, boolean and so on) are the exception, so Java is not 100% object-oriented.
  • Object-oriented means we build software from objects that hold both data and behaviour.
  • Object-oriented programming (OOP) gives simple rules that make software easier to build and maintain.

The basic concepts of OOP are:

  1. Object
  2. Class
  3. Inheritance
  4. Polymorphism
  5. Abstraction
  6. Encapsulation

3. Platform Independent

  • C and C++ compile to machine code for one platform. Java instead follows write once, run anywhere.
  • A platform is the hardware or software environment in which a program runs. Java provides a software-based platform that runs on top of the hardware platform.
  • The Java platform has 2 components: the Runtime Environment and the API (Application Programming Interface).
  • The compiler converts source code into bytecode. Bytecode runs on Windows, Linux, macOS and any other system that has a JVM. This is Write Once, Run Anywhere (WORA).

4. Secured

Java is well known for security. It makes it much harder to write code that damages memory or the system. Java is secure because of these points:

  • There is no explicit pointer.
  • Java programs run inside a virtual machine sandbox.
  • Classloader - loads Java classes into the JVM and keeps code from the local file system separate from code that came over the network.
  • Bytecode Verifier - checks code for illegal operations that could break access rights to objects.
  • Security Manager - decides what resources a class may use, such as the local disk. It is deprecated for removal since Java 17, so modern apps rely on containers and OS permissions instead.

Java gives these protections by default. Developers can add more with SSL, JAAS, cryptography and similar tools.

5. Robust

Robust means strong. Java is robust because of these points:

  • It has strong memory management.
  • It has no pointer arithmetic, which avoids a whole class of memory bugs.
  • Automatic garbage collection removes objects the program no longer uses.
  • It has exception handling and type checking at compile time.

6. Architecture-neutral

  • Java is architecture neutral because it has no implementation-dependent features. For example, the size of each primitive type is fixed.
  • C only guarantees that int is at least 16 bits. The real size depends on the compiler and CPU (2 bytes on old 16-bit compilers, 4 bytes on almost all modern ones).
  • In Java, int is always 4 bytes, on both 32-bit and 64-bit systems.

7. Portable

  • Java is portable because you can carry the same bytecode to any platform.
  • It needs no platform-specific changes to run, only a JVM.

8. High-performance

  • Java is faster than traditional interpreted languages because bytecode is close to native code and the JIT compiler turns hot code into machine code.
  • It can still be a little slower than fully compiled languages such as C or C++, mainly at startup.

9. Distributed

  • Java is distributed because it has built-in support for programs that run on many machines and talk over a network.
  • RMI (Remote Method Invocation) and EJB (Enterprise JavaBeans) are classic tools for this.
  • With them, a program can call methods on objects that live on another machine.

10. Multi-threaded

  • A thread is a small unit of work that runs at the same time as other threads. A Java program can do many tasks at once by using several threads.
  • Threads share one common memory area, so they use less memory than separate programs. Threads are important for multimedia, web applications and similar work.

11. Dynamic

  • Java loads classes on demand, when the program first needs them, not all at start.
  • It can call native C and C++ code through JNI (Java Native Interface).
  • The JIT compiler compiles hot code at run time, and the garbage collector manages memory automatically.

Fresher Notes

  • Main features: simple, object-oriented, platform independent, secure, robust, multithreaded, portable and high performance.
  • No pointers in the language; the garbage collector manages memory.
  • Rich standard library: collections, I/O, networking, concurrency and more.

topics.name: Difference between JVM, JDK, JRE

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) loads, verifies and executes bytecode.
  • The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) is the JVM plus the core class libraries needed to run a program, and the JDK (Java Development Kit) is the JRE plus development tools such as javac, javadoc, jar and jdb.
  • In short, JDK contains JRE and JRE contains JVM
  • The JVM itself is a specification with implementations such as HotSpot, OpenJ9 and GraalVM.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Developers need the JDK while end users and servers that only run a jar need just the runtime, so you must know what to install.
  • The error javac is not recognized appears when only a JRE is present.
  • Knowing the parts explains platform independence, the compile then run pipeline, and class loading and memory problems such as OutOfMemoryError Metaspace or UnsupportedClassVersionError.

3. Advantages

  • Clear separation of running and building programs; one JDK ships javac, jar, jshell and more.
  • The JVM hides the operating system (portability), verifies bytecode and frees memory with garbage collection.
  • Specification driven: swap HotSpot for OpenJ9 or GraalVM without code changes.
  • Pluggable collectors (Serial, G1, ZGC) and container awareness since JDK 10.
  • jlink and jpackage build minimal runtime images; JFR, jcmd and jstack give free observability.

4. Disadvantages

  • Three similar names confuse beginners about which package to install.
  • The JVM layer makes Java slower than natively compiled C; bytecode is portable but the JVM is platform specific.
  • Version mismatch: a class compiled on JDK 21 fails on a JDK 17 JVM; modern JDKs no longer ship a separate JRE.
  • Metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers live outside the heap and are easy to forget when sizing containers.
  • Tuning flags are many and class loader leaks can exhaust metaspace.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Helps diagnose version, classpath and class loading errors.
  • Needed to understand memory areas, heap sizing and garbage collection later.
  • Common interview topic, including how to shrink a large runtime image.

6. Basic Concepts

JVM, JRE, and JDK

In one line: JDK is used to develop Java programs, JRE is used to run them, and JVM is the engine inside the JRE that actually executes the bytecode.

1. What is JVM (Java Virtual Machine)?

  • JVM is an abstract machine. It is a specification that vendors implement, not a single file.
  • It provides a runtime environment in which Java bytecode can be executed.
  • It can also run other languages that compile down to Java bytecode.
  • JVMs exist for many platforms (Windows, Linux, macOS). This is what makes Java portable.

There are 3 notions of the JVM:

  • Specification: the document describing how a JVM should behave.
  • Implementation: an actual product, for example HotSpot.
  • Instance: the running process on your machine.

The JVM's main jobs

  • Loads code (via the Class Loader)
  • Verifies code (bytecode verification)
  • Executes code (interpreter + JIT)
  • Provides the runtime environment (memory areas, garbage collection)

2. What is JRE (Java Runtime Environment)?

  • JRE is used only for running Java applications. It cannot compile code.
  • Unlike the JVM specification, the JRE is a real, installable package.
  • It holds the JVM plus the libraries and supporting files the JVM needs (for example the java.lang and java.util classes).
  • In short: JRE = JVM + Libraries.

3. What is JDK (Java Development Kit)?

  • JDK is the complete kit used to develop Java applications. It is a real, installable package.
  • It contains JRE + development tools.
  • Key tools: launcher (java), compiler (javac), archiver (jar), documentation generator (javadoc).
  • In short: JDK = JRE + Development Tools (compiler, debugger and more).

How They Fit Together

JDK contains JRE, and JRE contains JVM. Each one is a superset of the one inside it:

JDK
Development Tools — javac, jar, javadoc
JRE
Libraries needed to run code
JVM
Executes bytecode
.java source flows down through javac → JRE libraries → the JVM core, where bytecode actually executes

Quick Comparison

AreaJVMJREJDK
Full FormJava Virtual MachineJava Runtime EnvironmentJava Development Kit
Made up ofClass loader + memory areas + execution engineJVM + LibrariesJRE + Development Tools
Used forExecuting bytecodeRunning Java applicationsDeveloping Java applications
Platform dependent?YesYesYes
  • JVM is platform-dependent; the bytecode it runs is platform-independent.
  • Java's "Write Once, Run Anywhere" is possible because of the JVM.

Compile & Run - What Actually Happens

Save your source as Hello.java, then run javac Hello.java. The compiler (part of the JDK) produces Hello.class containing Java Bytecode. Running java Hello starts the JVM (part of the JRE) and executes that bytecode.

Hello.java  (source code)
     |
     |  javac Hello.java   <- JDK compiler
     v
Hello.class  (bytecode)
     |
     |  java Hello         <- JRE starts the JVM
     v
   JVM executes the bytecode
     |
     v
Program Output

Fresher Notes

  • JVM runs bytecode; JRE = JVM + core libraries (run programs); JDK = JRE + tools like javac and jar (build programs).
  • Nesting: JDK contains JRE, and JRE contains JVM.
  • Platform: the JVM is platform specific, but bytecode is platform independent.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • JVM parts: a class loader subsystem, runtime data areas (heap, stack, metaspace) and an execution engine (interpreter, JIT, GC).
  • No separate JRE: since Java 11 Oracle does not ship one; use a JDK or build a trimmed runtime.
  • Small runtime: use jdeps to find the modules and jlink to build the image.

8. Advanced Concepts

Uses of JVM, JRE and JDK

  • JVM: runs and manages Java applications on any OS.
  • JRE: used by end users to run Java-based software (like desktop apps).
  • JDK: used by developers to write, compile and debug Java code.

You can query the running JVM at runtime using system properties and the Runtime class:

The Big Picture - JDK, JRE and JVM Together

This diagram shows what happens from writing a .java file to running the application.

                         JDK
                 Java Development Kit

   Development Tools
   |-- javac
   |-- javadoc
   |-- jar
   |-- jdb
   |-- javap
   |-- jlink
   `-- jpackage

   +---------------------------------------------+
   |                  Runtime                    |
   |   Java Runtime Libraries                     |
   |                                               |
   |   +---------------------------------------+   |
   |   |                 JVM                   |   |
   |   |         Java Virtual Machine          |   |
   |   |                                       |   |
   |   |  Class Loader                         |   |
   |   |  Runtime Memory                       |   |
   |   |  Execution Engine                     |   |
   |   |  JIT Compiler                         |   |
   |   |  Garbage Collector                    |   |
   |   +---------------------------------------+   |
   +---------------------------------------------+

Modern Java: Java 9 made the platform modular, and since Java 11 Oracle no longer ships a separate JRE. For Java 17/21, the layout is:

JDK
|-- JVM
|-- Java Runtime Libraries
`-- Development Tools

The term JRE still describes the runtime part of Java, but you normally install a JDK instead of a separate JRE.

JVM Architecture - Class Loader, Runtime Areas & Execution Engine

                    JVM
                     |
        +------------+------------+
        |            |            |
        v            v            v
 Class Loader   Runtime Data   Execution Engine
                   Areas
        |            |            |
        |            |       +----+----+
        |            |       |         |
        |            |       v         v
        |            | Interpreter    JIT
        |            |
        |            v
        |       Heap / Stack /
        |       Metaspace etc.
        |
        v
 Bytecode Verification

Class Loader Subsystem

Loads .class files into JVM memory before they can be executed. Modern Java uses several class loaders:

  • Bootstrap Class Loader - loads the core API classes (java.lang.*, java.util.*, java.io.*). It is implemented natively and has no parent.
  • Platform Class Loader - loads platform-level classes; it replaced the old "Extension Class Loader" in Java 9.
  • Application/System Class Loader - loads classes from the application classpath or module path (for example your com.example.* classes).
  • Custom Class Loaders - your own loaders (extend ClassLoader and override findClass()), for example to load from a network or an encrypted source.

Class loaders follow the parent delegation model: a loader first asks its parent, and loads the class itself only if the parent cannot find it. This stops application code from silently replacing core classes like java.lang.String.

Bytecode Verification

Before executing bytecode, the JVM checks its structure, type safety, valid instructions, stack consistency and access rules:

.class
  |
  v
Class Loading
  |
  v
Bytecode Verification
  |
  v
Preparation / Linking
  |
  v
Initialization
  |
  v
Execution

JVM Runtime Data Areas

JVM Runtime Data Areas
|
|-- Heap
|-- Java Stack
|-- PC Register
|-- Method Area
`-- Native Method Stack

Heap

Where Java objects are generally allocated. This area is shared across all threads, and the garbage collector manages objects living here.

Stack
  |
  | emp
  v
Heap
+------------------+
| Employee Object  |
|                  |
| id = 101         |
| name = "Pankaj"  |
+------------------+

Java Stack

Each thread has its own JVM stack; every method call creates a stack frame holding local variables and partial results.

Thread
  |
  v
Java Stack
+------------------+
| calculate()      |
| x = 10           |
| y = 20           |
+------------------+
| main()           |
| args             |
+------------------+

PC Register

Program Counter - each JVM thread has its own, tracking the address of the current bytecode instruction being executed.

Native Method Stack

Supports execution of native methods, e.g. through JNI (Java Native Interface), used when Java interacts with platform-specific native libraries.

Method Area / Metaspace

Stores class metadata (class structure, constants, static variables) and related runtime information. In modern HotSpot JVMs, this concept is implemented as Metaspace, which uses native memory rather than the traditional Java heap - unlike the old PermGen (pre-Java 8), which was a fixed-size heap region prone to OutOfMemoryError, Metaspace grows dynamically.

Execution Engine - Interpreter, JIT & Garbage Collector

Once classes are loaded and verified, the execution engine runs the bytecode:

Execution Engine
|
|-- Interpreter
|-- JIT Compiler
`-- Garbage Collection integration/runtime services

Interpreter

Executes bytecode instructions directly, letting code start running without waiting for the whole application to compile into native code.

JIT Compiler (Just-In-Time)

Improves performance by compiling frequently executed ("hot") bytecode into native machine code:

Method called once
      |
Interpreter may execute it

Method called thousands of times
      |
JIT identifies it as hot
      |
Compiles optimized native code
      |
Future executions become faster

Garbage Collector

Automatically reclaims memory for objects that are no longer reachable:

Object
  |
No reachable references
  |
Eligible for GC
  |
Garbage Collector
  |
Memory reclaimed

Modern JVMs provide multiple collectors depending on application needs: G1, ZGC, Shenandoah, Parallel GC, Serial GC.

JDK Development Tools

ToolPurpose
javacCompiles .java source into .class bytecode
javaStarts the JVM and runs a compiled application
jarCreates and manages Java Archive (.jar) files
javadocGenerates API documentation from source comments
javapInspects/disassembles compiled .class files
jlinkBuilds a custom runtime image with only required modules
jpackagePackages an app into a platform installer (.exe/.msi, .deb/.rpm, .pkg/.dmg)

javac and java

javac Employee.java     # Employee.java -> Employee.class (bytecode)
java Employee            # JVM starts -> loads class -> finds main() -> executes bytecode

jar

jar cf application.jar *

A JAR can contain .class files, resources, configuration and metadata. A Spring Boot application is commonly packaged as a JAR.

javap

Useful for inspecting compiled class files and learning how source becomes bytecode:

javap Employee.class
javap -c Employee.class   # shows bytecode instructions

jlink

Useful for creating smaller, purpose-built Java runtime distributions.

Complete Compilation & Execution Lifecycle

Step by step, from source code to CPU execution:

StepWhat happens
1. Source CodeHuman-readable Employee.java is written
2. Compilationjavac compiles it into Employee.class bytecode
3. Bytecode.class holds JVM bytecode, not CPU-specific machine code
4. JVM Startupjava Employee starts the JVM
5. Class LoadingEmployee.class is loaded via the class-loading subsystem
6. LinkingVerification, preparation, resolution
7. InitializationStatic initialization runs as required
8. main() ExecutionJVM invokes public static void main(String[] args)
9. Interpreter/JITBytecode executes; hot code gets JIT-compiled
10. Native ExecutionOptimized native instructions run on the CPU
Employee.java
     |

Employee.class
     |
    JVM

Interpreter / JIT
     |
Native Code
