The for loop is used to iterate and evaluate a block of code multiple times.

When to use: If the number of iterations is fixed, it is recommended to use a for loop.

Syntax:

for (initialization; condition; increment/decrement) {

  Statements;

}

2) While Loop

The while loop evaluates a condition BEFORE executing the loop body.

If the condition is true, the loop continues; otherwise, it stops.

When to use: If the number of iterations is not fixed, it is recommended to use a while loop.

Syntax:

Initialization;

while (condition) {

  Statements;

  Increment / Decrement;

}

3) Do While Loop

The do-while loop is similar to the while loop, but the condition is checked AFTER executing the loop body.

This guarantees that the loop body runs at least once, even if the condition is false right from the start.

When to use: If the number of iterations is not fixed and the loop must execute at least once (e.g. menu prompts).

Syntax:

Initialization;

do {

  Statements;

  Increment / Decrement;

} while (condition);

Proof: do-while runs its body even when the condition is false from the start

This is the single most important difference between while and do-while - it is a very common interview question.

4) Enhanced For-Each Loop

The for-each loop is a simplified way to iterate over arrays and collections, without needing an index variable or the loop's condition/increment.

Syntax:

for (Type element : arrayOrCollection) {

  Statements;

}
All In One Program (For, While, Do While, For-Each)

Fresher Notes

  • Pick the loop by the job: for when you can count, while when a condition decides, do-while when the body must run once.
  • Three parts of a for loop: initialization, condition and update, as in for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++).
  • break and continue: break leaves the loop and continue skips to the next iteration.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • for-each (for (String s : list)) avoids index errors, but it gives no index and you must not add or remove elements inside it.
  • Infinite loop: while (true) or for (;;); leave it with break or return.
  • Off-by-one: array indexes run from 0 to length - 1.

8. Advanced Concepts

for vs while vs do-while

All three loops repeat a block of code, but they differ in when the condition is checked and the minimum number of executions guaranteed.

LoopCondition checkedMinimum executionsTypical use case
forBefore each iteration0Fixed/known number of iterations
whileBefore each iteration0Unknown iteration count, condition-driven
do-whileAfter each iteration1Must run at least once (e.g. menu prompts)

do-while's "execute-then-check" flow

   +-------------------+
   |  Execute body     | <---+
   +-------------------+     |
            |                |
            v                |
     +-------------+         |
     | Check        |  true  |
     | condition?   |--------+
     +-------------+
            | false
            v
          Exit loop

for Loop Internals - Order of Evaluation

The for loop's three clauses run in a very specific order. Misunderstanding this order is a classic source of off-by-one bugs.

for (init; condition; update) { body }

Step 1: init         -> runs ONCE, before anything else
Step 2: condition     -> checked BEFORE every iteration
        |
        +-- false --> exit loop immediately
        |
        true
        v
Step 3: body          -> runs
Step 4: update        -> runs AFTER the body
        |
        +-- go back to Step 2 (condition)

init executes exactly once. condition is evaluated before every single pass, including the first. update runs only after a completed body execution, never before the very first check.

Nested Loops - Pattern Printing

A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. For every single iteration of the outer loop, the ENTIRE inner loop runs to completion. This is the classic mechanism behind pattern printing.

Nested Loops with Labeled break/continue

A plain break only exits the innermost loop. To exit an outer loop early from inside a nested loop, label the outer loop.

Enhanced for-each - Iterator Under the Hood

for (Type x : collection) is syntactic sugar. The compiler rewrites it to use the collection's Iterator internally.

for (String s : list) { ... }

   compiles roughly to

Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    String s = it.next();
    ...
}

Because it's really an Iterator underneath, modifying the list directly (e.g. list.remove(...)) while a for-each loop is iterating it throws ConcurrentModificationException. The safe fix is to remove through the iterator itself.

Infinite Loops & Loop-Invariant Code Motion

for(;;) and while(true) both create intentional infinite loops that rely on an internal break (or return) to exit safely. All three clauses of for(;;) are optional - an empty condition is treated as always true.

Performance note: if a loop bound is expensive to recompute (like list.size() on certain collections, or any method call), compute it once before the loop instead of on every iteration - this is called loop-invariant code motion. Modern JIT compilers often do this automatically for simple cases, but writing it explicitly keeps intent clear and helps in cases the JIT can't safely optimize.

Off-By-One and Other Loop Pitfalls

TrapWhat goes wrong
Off-by-one errorsUsing <= instead of < incorrectly, e.g. looping i <= array.length causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Modifying the loop variable in the bodyChanging i inside a for loop's body makes iteration count unpredictable
Bad increment directionwhile (i < 10) { i--; } never terminates - i moves away from the exit condition
while vs do-while first checkIf the condition is false initially, while never runs its body; do-while always runs it at least once

Senior Notes

  • Streams or loops: use streams (IntStream.range, filter, map) for transformations, and plain loops for early exit and hot code.
  • Hoisting: move work that does not change (method calls, list.size() on slow structures) out of the loop.
  • Safe removal: use an iterator, because removing inside for-each throws ConcurrentModificationException.

9. Code for Each Concept

Code: Definition
Code: Advantages
Code: Definition (Advanced)
Code: Advantages (Advanced)

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Choosing a loop style:

  • Classic for: when you need the index, a reverse walk or a step.
  • for-each: for reading every element.
  • while: for an unknown count, such as reading input or polling.
  • do-while: for menus and retries.
  • Labeled break/continue: for nested searches.
  • Iterator and ListIterator: for removal and insertion.
  • entrySet(): to walk a map.
  • IntStream.range and iterate: for functional pipelines.
  • Recursion: also repeats work, but costs stack frames.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Loops compile to conditional jumps, and the JIT then tunes them.

  • Bytecode: a for becomes init, a condition check, the body and an update, then a backward goto.
  • JIT: unrolls small loops, hoists invariants and removes bounds checks it can prove safe.
  • Vectorizing: simple array loops use SIMD, and counted loops with an int counter are optimized best.
  • For-each: over an array it is an index loop; over an Iterable it calls iterator(), hasNext() and next().

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and the fix for each:

  • Off-by-one: <= used instead of <.
  • Loop variable changed in the body: the count becomes hard to predict.
  • Infinite loop: the condition never changes, or continue skips the update in a while loop.
  • Changing a collection while iterating: use an iterator or removeIf.
  • LinkedList with get(i): each call walks the chain, so the loop is quadratic.
  • Floating-point counter: for (double d = 0; d != 1; d += 0.1) never ends, so use an integer counter.
  • Boxing: an Integer counter allocates on every pass.
  • Swallowed exceptions: an empty catch in the body hides real failures.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Algorithmic complexity (O(n) versus O(n^2)) matters far more than loop syntax. Replace nested searches with a HashSet or HashMap. Other tuning tips:

  • Small bodies: keep loop bodies small and free of allocation.
  • Hoisting: compute int n = list.size() or any costly call once.
  • Memory order: walk 2D arrays row by row.
  • Strings: use StringBuilder instead of repeated concatenation.
  • Numbers: use primitive loops or IntStream.
  • Branches: keep them few inside hot loops.
  • Parallel: use parallelStream only for independent, CPU-heavy work.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Loops that depend on an outside system must be bounded by a maximum number of attempts or a deadline. Typical real-world loops:

  • Batch processing: page through database rows in chunks until empty.
  • Retry: backoff with a maximum.
  • Stream reading: read until end of file.
  • Polling: check a job status with a timeout.
  • Event loops: games and servers.

10. Examples

Real Time Examples

  • College result sheet: one loop over sixty students, an inner loop over six subjects to compute totals.
  • Bank passbook printing: a while loop reading transactions until the end of the statement period.
  • ATM PIN entry: a do while loop that asks at least once and blocks the card after three wrong tries.
  • Swiggy cart total: an enhanced for over the cart items adding price into a running total.
  • Railway seat chart: nested loops over coaches and berths to print the layout.
  • Global example, a web crawler: a while loop that keeps pulling pages from a queue until the queue is empty.

Student tip: pick for when you can count, while when you cannot, do while when the body must run once, and enhanced for whenever you just want each element and no index.

Real Time Examples (Advanced)

  • End of day settlement in a bank: a nested loop over accounts and transactions was replaced with a HashMap index, cutting a four hour batch to eleven minutes.
  • N plus 1 in Hibernate: a loop calling a repository per row issued ten thousand queries. A single join fetch fixed it.
  • Kafka consumer poll loop: a while true that polls, processes and commits, with a volatile flag for a clean shutdown.
  • Telecom rating engine: a primitive long array walked sequentially rather than a List of Long, which removed most GC pressure.
  • Global example, log parsing: a stream over Files.lines with a filter, which keeps memory flat over a ten gigabyte file.
  • Retry with backoff: a bounded for loop with a growing sleep, never a while true, so a dead dependency cannot hang the thread forever.

Interview answers to keep ready

  • Why does the enhanced for not let you remove elements? Because the underlying iterator sees the modCount change and fails fast.
  • When is a stream slower than a loop? For small collections and cheap operations, because of pipeline setup and boxing.
  • What is on stack replacement? The JIT compiling a method whose loop is already running, and swapping the frame over to native code.
  • How do you break out of two loops? A labelled break, not a flag variable and not an exception.

Worked Example 1

Safe removal.

Worked Example 2

Nested loops: pattern.

Practice Exercise 1

The four loops.

Practice Exercise 2

Patterns: sum, factorial, table.

Golden rule: pick for when the iteration count is known up front, while when it depends on a condition evaluated before each pass, and do-while only when the body must run at least once regardless of the condition.

11. Quick Revision

  • for: known count; while: condition first; do-while: at least once.
  • for-each reads elements without an index.
  • Use Iterator.remove or removeIf to delete safely.
  • Watch the loop bounds: 0 to length - 1.
  • Avoid floating point loop counters.

interviewQA: Difference between while and do-while?
while checks the condition before the body (0+ runs); do-while checks it after the body (1+ runs guaranteed)
Can a for loop's clauses be omitted?
Yes - all three (init, condition, update) are optional; for(;;) is an intentional infinite loop
How does for-each work internally?
It is compiled to use the collection's Iterator (hasNext()/next()) behind the scenes; for arrays it uses a plain index-based loop
Why does removing from a List during for-each throw an exception?
Structural modification while an Iterator is active throws ConcurrentModificationException; use Iterator.remove() instead
How do you break out of a nested loop entirely?
Use a labeled break (e.g. break outer;) on the outer loop's label
What is loop-invariant code motion?
Moving computations that don't change across iterations (like a collection's size) outside the loop, so they run once instead of every pass
When would you prefer for over while?
When the number of iterations is known/fixed up front; while is preferred when iteration depends purely on a runtime condition

topics.name: Packages

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A package is a namespace that groups related classes and interfaces, mapped to a folder structure and declared with the package statement.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Large programs have thousands of classes.
  • Packages prevent name clashes, organize code and control access.

3. Advantages

  • Avoids naming conflicts.
  • Organizes code by feature or layer.
  • Works with access control (package-private).

4. Disadvantages

  • Wrong package or folder names cause class-not-found errors.
  • Cyclic dependencies between packages harm design.
  • Wildcard imports can hide name clashes.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Every real project uses packages.
  • Needed to understand imports, classpath and modules.
  • Spring component scanning depends on packages.

6. Basic Concepts

What is a Package?

A package is simply a folder that groups related classes and interfaces together - it's Java's way of organizing code.

Why do we need packages?

  • Organization - Imagine a project with thousands of classes all dumped in one place; finding and maintaining anything would be a nightmare. Packages group related classes into folders, just like folders on your computer.
  • Avoiding name collisions - Two different teams could each write a class called Employee. As long as they live in different packages (e.g. hr.Employee and payroll.Employee), there's no conflict.
  • Reusability - Common code can be packaged once and reused across many projects.
  • Access control - Packages work together with access specifiers to control which classes can see which other classes.

Types of packages:

  1. Built-in (predefined) packages - shipped with Java itself, e.g. java.lang, java.util, java.io.
  2. User-defined packages - packages we create ourselves for our own project.

Declaring a Package

To put a class inside a package, the package statement must be the very first line of the .java file (only comments may come before it).

Syntax:

package package_name;

Naming convention: package names are always written in lowercase, and by convention companies use their reversed domain name as the root.

Example: domain www.google.com ➝ package com.google

A deeper, real-world example: com.dell.smartwatch.android

  • com ➝ generic root, reversed from the company's domain
  • dell ➝ the company/client name
  • smartwatch ➝ the project name
  • android ➝ a module within that project (there could also be a "mobile" or "tab" module)

How Package Names Map to Folders

The package name is not just a label - it must exactly match the directory structure on disk. Dots in the package name become nested folders.

package com.company.project;

     maps to directory
            |
            v

src/
`-- com/
    `-- company/
        `-- project/
            `-- MyClass.java   (package com.company.project;)

The import Statement

When you want to use a class that lives in a different package, you must either import it or refer to it by its fully-qualified name. The import statement just saves you from typing the full package path every time.

Different ways to import:

import com.p1.Test;  // correct - imports one specific class

import com.p1.*;    // correct - imports every class in that package

import com.p1;      // wrong - you cannot import a package itself, only its classes

Note: This example needs two separate files placed in matching folders (com/p1/Test.java and com/p2/Pankaj.java) to actually compile and run - it will not run as a single file.

A Built-in Package Example: java.util.Scanner

Scanner lives in the built-in java.util package and is the easiest way to read user input (integers, doubles, strings, etc.) from the keyboard via System.in.

Common Scanner methods:

  • nextInt() - reads an int
  • nextDouble() - reads a double
  • next() - reads a single word (String)
  • nextLine() - reads an entire line (String)

Fresher Notes

  • Package: groups related classes and avoids name clashes. package com.acme.orders; must be the first statement.
  • Import: use import java.util.List; or import java.util.*;. java.lang is imported automatically.
  • Folders: package names map to folders, such as com/acme/orders.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Naming convention: reverse domain name in lowercase (com.company.project.module).
  • Static import: import static brings in static members such as Math.max.
  • Same simple name: use the fully qualified name for one of them (java.util.Date vs java.sql.Date).

8. Advanced Concepts

Package Declaration & Directory Structure (Deep Dive)

A package's name must exactly mirror the directory path the .java file lives in - the compiler and classloader rely on this mapping to find classes.

package com.javaschoollab.service;

         maps to directory
                |
                v

src/
`-- com/
    `-- javaschoollab/
        `-- service/
            `-- Employee.java   (package com.javaschoollab.service;)

The compiled .class file must live in the matching folder under the classpath root as well, or the classloader cannot find it.

Single-Type vs On-Demand Import & Naming Ambiguity

import com.p1.Test; imports exactly one type. import com.p1.*; is an on-demand import - it imports every visible top-level type in that package, but does not affect runtime performance (it's purely a compile-time convenience for the compiler to resolve names).

The real danger of wildcard imports is naming ambiguity: if two packages you import both contain a class with the same simple name, the compiler cannot pick one for you - you must use the fully-qualified name.

Access Control Across Packages

Default (package-private) access is invisible outside the declaring package - even to an unrelated class in a completely different package. protected access IS visible to subclasses even in other packages (through inheritance), though not to unrelated classes there. A private top-level class is not even legal Java - private is only allowed on nested/inner classes.

ModifierSame PackageDifferent Package (subclass)Different Package (unrelated)
defaultYesNoNo
protectedYesYes (via inheritance)No
publicYesYesYes

CLASSPATH and Class Lookup

The classpath is the set of root directories/JARs the JVM and compiler search when resolving package-qualified class names. To find a class in package com.p1, the classloader looks for com/p1/ClassName.class under each classpath root/JAR in turn, in order, and uses the first match it finds.

Static Imports

import static lets you reference a class's static members without prefixing the class name - handy for constants and utility methods, but overusing it can hurt readability.

Package-Private Top-Level Classes

A top-level class declared without public is package-private: it can only be used by other classes in the same package. This is a legitimate design choice - it lets you hide implementation-detail classes from consumers of your package while still exposing a public API class.

Senior Notes

  • Organize by feature (orders, payments) rather than by layer only, so related code changes together.
  • Avoid cycles: cyclic dependencies between packages hurt design; tools like ArchUnit and jdeps can enforce rules.
  • Modules: module-info.java adds strong encapsulation on top of packages.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Layout best practice: one top-level class per file, folders matching packages, a base package per module, sub-packages by feature (orders.api, orders.internal), tests in the same packages under src/test/java. package-info.java holds package docs and annotations. Split packages across modules are not allowed in JPMS.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

At run time a class is identified by its package, its simple name and its class loader. The compiler resolves a simple name in this order: local scope, class members, single-type imports, the same package, on-demand imports, then java.lang. Package-private access depends on the runtime package, so the same package name in two class loaders is two different runtime packages.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: package statement not matching the directory (class not found), unused wildcard imports hiding name clashes, circular dependencies between packages, the default (unnamed) package in real projects, and duplicate classes on the class path (the first one wins).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Large package graphs slow comprehension more than the JVM. Use jdeps to inspect dependencies and ArchUnit tests to forbid cycles and layer violations.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a Spring Boot app uses base package scanning. Placing the main class in the root package (com.acme) lets component scanning find everything below it.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Compile with packages.

Worked Example 2

Wildcard imports do not recurse.

Practice Exercise 1

Declaring and using a package.

Practice Exercise 2

Name clash and static import.

Sub-packages Are NOT Hierarchical for Access (Classic Interview Trap)

This is one of the most commonly misunderstood facts about Java packages: com.company.util and com.company.util.internal are treated as completely unrelated, independent packages by the compiler - even though the folder names look nested. Package-private members of one are NOT visible to the other just because the name looks like a "sub-package".
Rule of thumb: prefer explicit single-type imports for clarity in production code; reserve wildcard imports for quick scripts or when a class uses many types from the same package.

11. Quick Revision

  • package must be the first statement.
  • Names use reverse domain: com.acme.app.
  • import brings classes into scope; java.lang is automatic.
  • Folders must match package names.
  • Fully qualified names resolve clashes.

interviewQA: Can a .java file have multiple public classes?
No - at most one public top-level class per file
Must the file name match the public class name?
Yes - e.g. public class Employee must live in Employee.java
What if there's no explicit package declaration?
The class belongs to the default/unnamed package (not recommended for real projects)
Do you need to import java.lang.*?
No - java.lang (String, Object, Math, etc.) is auto-imported into every file
Does import com.p1.*; slow down the program?
No - imports are resolved at compile time only, zero runtime cost
Is com.a.b a sub-package of com.a?
No - Java has no true package hierarchy for access purposes; each package name is independent, they just happen to nest as folders
Can two classes with the same simple name coexist in a project?
Yes, as long as they are in different packages - packages exist precisely to avoid this kind of name collision
Can a top-level class be private?
No - only public or default (package-private); private/protected are only legal on nested classes

topics.name: Array in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • An array is a container object that holds a fixed number of values of the same type in contiguous memory.
  • Each element has an index starting at 0, the size is fixed at creation with new and read through the length field, and elements get default values (0, false, null).
  • Arrays are heap objects with a header and a length, so an array variable holds a reference
  • They are covariant, and a 2D array is an array of arrays that can be jagged.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Real data comes in groups such as marks of sixty students or twelve monthly sales figures, and an array keeps them under one name and lets you process them in a loop with constant-time access by index.
  • Arrays are the base of matrices, strings, ArrayList, StringBuilder and HashMap, and almost every coding interview starts with an array question, so understanding index bounds avoids ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

3. Advantages

  • Instant O(1) access by index and a cache-friendly contiguous layout.
  • Low memory overhead: a primitive array has no per-element header and can be vectorized by the JIT.
  • Type safe, simple, and supported by Arrays utilities (sort, parallelSort, fill, copyOf) and fast System.arraycopy.
  • Byte arrays map directly onto buffers, files and network I/O.

4. Disadvantages

  • Fixed size: growing needs a new array and a copy; insert and delete shift elements.
  • No add, remove or contains methods, and index errors appear only at run time.
  • Copying is shallow for object arrays; covariance can cause ArrayStoreException and generic arrays are not allowed.
  • Arrays inherit equals and hashCode from Object, and Arrays.asList is fixed size and backed by the array.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Foundation for algorithms and collections.
  • Heavily used in interviews (covariance, clone versus deep copy).
  • Understanding arrays explains how ArrayList grows and why presizing helps.

6. Basic Concepts

What is an Array?

An array is a collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory locations.

  • In Java, an array is itself an object.
  • Array size is fixed once created — it cannot grow or shrink at runtime.
  • Array elements are accessed using an index, starting from 0.

How Indices Map to Memory Slots

Think of an array as a row of numbered boxes. For int[] a = new int[5], the 5 boxes are indexed 0 through 4 (length - 1).

Index:   0     1     2     3     4
       +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
Value: | 10  | 20  | 30  | 40  | 50  |
       +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
a.length = 5   (valid indices: 0 to 4)

Declaring an Array

There are three equivalent ways to declare an array reference in Java:

  1. dataType[] arr; (preferred style)
  2. dataType []arr;
  3. dataType arr[]; (C-style, still valid)

Declaring alone does not create the array — it only creates a reference variable that currently points to nothing.

Creating & Filling an Array Element by Element

new int[5] allocates space for 5 integers (all default to 0), then each index is assigned individually.

Single-Line Initialization

Java also lets you declare and fill an array in one statement using an array literal.

Iterating with a for-each Loop

The for-each loop reads each element in order without needing an index variable — simpler when you don't need the index itself.

Array Length

arr.length is a field (no parentheses) that tells you how many elements the array holds. It is fixed for the lifetime of that array object.

2D Arrays — the Basics

A 2D array is stored as rows and columns (like a matrix). arr[row][col] accesses a single cell.

Passing an Array to a Method

Arrays can be passed to methods so the same logic can be reused on any array of that type.

Advantages & Disadvantages

Advantages

  • Random access — direct access to any element using its index (O(1))
  • Simple and memory-efficient for fixed-size data

Disadvantages

  • Fixed size — cannot grow or shrink dynamically
  • Can waste memory if the size is over-estimated
  • The Collections Framework (e.g. ArrayList) overcomes this limitation

Fresher Notes

  • Fixed size, one type: int[] a = new int[5]; or int[] a = {1, 2, 3};.
  • Index starts at 0; a.length gives the size (a field, not a method).
  • Bad index (negative or at least length) throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Default values: 0, 0.0, false, null. Arrays are objects stored on the heap.
  • 2D arrays are arrays of arrays, and rows can have different lengths (jagged).
  • Helpers: Arrays.toString, sort, fill, copyOf, equals, binarySearch, asList.

8. Advanced Concepts

Arrays Are Objects on the Heap

Even an array of primitives (like int[]) is a full-fledged object in Java, allocated on the heap. The array variable itself is just a reference.

Stack                    Heap
+-------+               +---------------------+
| arr   |-------------->| int[] object        |
+-------+               | length = 5           |
                         | [0,0,0,0,0]          |
                         +---------------------+

Default values on creation depend on the element type:

  • new int[5] -> all elements 0
  • new boolean[5] -> all elements false
  • new String[5] / any object array -> all elements null (an object array is NOT auto-populated with instances)

ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException — Edge Cases

The JVM throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException whenever an index is negative, equal to length, or greater than length - 1. A very common bug is using <= instead of < in the loop condition.

Rectangular vs Jagged 2D Arrays

A rectangular array has every row the same length. A jagged array is an "array of arrays" where each row can have a different length - useful when rows genuinely represent different-sized data.

Rectangular (3x3)          Jagged (rows differ)
[1 2 3]                    [1 2]
[4 5 6]                    [3 4 5]
[7 8 9]                    [6]

Array Covariance Gotcha — ArrayStoreException

Java arrays are covariant: String[] is assignable to Object[]. This compiles, but lets you write code that fails only at runtime when the actual array type doesn't match the stored value.

The Arrays Utility Class

java.util.Arrays provides most of the operations you'd otherwise hand-write: sorting, searching, comparing, printing, copying and filling.

Copying & Cloning an Array

System.arraycopy() copies a range from a source array into a destination array. clone() creates a new array object: for a single-dimensional array of primitives it copies the values, but for an array of objects or a multidimensional array it copies only the references (a shallow copy).

Anonymous Arrays & Returning Arrays from Methods

An anonymous array can be created and passed straight into a method call without ever assigning it to a variable — useful for one-off calls.

A method can also return an array, just like it returns any other object reference — the caller receives a reference to the array created inside the method.

An Array's Class Name at Runtime

Since an array is an object, calling getClass().getName() on it returns the JVM's internal type descriptor rather than something like "int[]" - [I means "array of int", [Ljava.lang.String; means "array of String", and an extra leading [ is added per extra dimension (e.g. [[I for int[][]).

Matrix Addition & Multiplication

2D arrays are the natural representation of a matrix. Addition just adds corresponding cells; multiplication takes the dot product of each row of the first matrix with each column of the second.

Fixed-Size Array vs ArrayList

AspectArrayArrayList
SizeFixed at creationGrows/shrinks dynamically
Element typePrimitives or objectsObjects only (autoboxed for primitives)
PerformanceFaster, less overheadSlightly slower due to resizing/boxing
APIMinimal (length, indexing)Rich (add, remove, contains, streams, etc.)
Multi-dimensionalNative supportNeeds nested collections

Rule of thumb: reach for a plain array when the size is fixed and known upfront (or you need raw primitive performance); reach for ArrayList/Collections when the size changes or you need the Collections Framework's utility methods.

Senior Notes

  • Covariance: Object[] o = new String[1] compiles but can throw ArrayStoreException at run time; generics are invariant.
  • Copies: clone() and Arrays.copyOf are shallow, so object elements are shared.
  • Choice: prefer collections for changing data; arrays suit fixed-size, performance-critical or primitive data.

9. Code for Each Concept

Code: Definition
Code: Advantages
Code: Definition (Advanced)
Code: Advantages (Advanced)

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Utilities: Arrays.sort (dual-pivot quicksort for primitives, TimSort for objects), parallelSort, Arrays.fill, setAll, mismatch, compare, asList (fixed-size view), stream, System.arraycopy. Varargs are arrays too.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

An array is an object with a length field and contiguous elements (references for object arrays, values for primitives). Bounds are checked on every access (the JIT removes redundant checks). Multidimensional arrays are arrays of references to arrays, so memory is not one contiguous block. Large arrays can be allocated directly in the old generation.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: off-by-one with length, using == or equals on arrays (use Arrays.equals), printing an array directly (type and hash), Arrays.asList on int[] (list of one array), modifying through Arrays.asList then adding, and shallow clone of 2D arrays.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Arrays give the best cache locality. Row-major traversal is faster than column-major for 2D arrays; avoid allocating in loops; reuse buffers; use System.arraycopy for bulk copies.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: image pixels, sensor buffers, lookup tables, dynamic programming tables, and fixed-size ring buffers.

10. Examples

Real Time Examples

  • Cinema seat booking: a two dimensional boolean array where row and column say whether a seat is taken.
  • College attendance register: a boolean array of sixty entries for one lecture, and a two dimensional one for a whole month.
  • Bank monthly statement: an array of transaction amounts used to compute the opening and closing balance.
  • Cricket scorecard: an int array of runs per over for the run rate graph.
  • ATM note counter: an array of note values and a matching array of counts.
  • Global example, image processing: a picture is a two dimensional array of pixel values.

Student tip: use an array when the size is known and fixed, and use an ArrayList when items get added and removed. Never forget that the last valid index is length minus one.

Real Time Examples (Advanced)

  • Market data tick store: parallel primitive arrays for timestamp, price and volume rather than one array of objects, which cut a heap from thirty gigabytes to four.
  • Telecom CDR rating: a long array of call durations processed with a vectorisable loop, giving several million records per second per core.
  • Netty and Kafka: byte arrays and direct ByteBuffers reused from a pool so the network path allocates nothing per message.
  • Aadhaar biometric matching: fixed size feature arrays compared with a tight loop, where range check elimination is what makes it fast enough.
  • Core banking end of day: Arrays.parallelSort on a settlement array, sorted once and then binary searched instead of re scanning.
  • Global example, image and video pipelines: pixel data in a flat int array with manual index maths, since a two dimensional array would scatter the rows.

Interview answers to keep ready

  • Why are arrays covariant but generics invariant? Arrays predate generics and needed to work with pre generic APIs. The price is ArrayStoreException.
  • Why can you not create a generic array? Erasure means the array cannot perform its store check, so the compiler forbids it.
  • Which is faster, a two dimensional array or a flat array? A flat array, because it is one contiguous block with no row pointer chase.
  • How does ArrayList grow? A new array is allocated at about 1.5 times the old capacity and the contents are copied with System.arraycopy.

Worked Example 1

Shallow copy trap.

Worked Example 2

ArrayStoreException.

Practice Exercise 1

Common array operations.

Practice Exercise 2

Jagged 2D array (Pascal triangle).

Interview Classic: Find the 3rd Largest Element

A common interview question with two solutions: a hand-written exchange sort and Arrays.sort(). Both sort the array and then read the element at index length - 3. The point of the question is usually "can you avoid writing your own sort?"

11. Quick Revision

  • Index from 0 to length - 1.
  • length is a field, not a method.
  • Default values: 0, false, null.
  • Arrays.sort, copyOf, toString, equals.
  • Array copy with clone is shallow.

interviewQA: What is an array?
A fixed-size, index-based object holding elements of the same type, stored contiguously
Why is array size fixed?
Memory is allocated as one contiguous block at creation time; resizing would require reallocating and copying the whole block
Array vs Collection
Array holds a fixed number of homogeneous elements (primitives allowed); Collections (List/Set/Map) grow dynamically and hold objects only
What is a jagged array?
An array of arrays where each row can have a different length
Array vs ArrayList
Array is fixed size and can store primitives directly; ArrayList is dynamically resizable but stores objects (autoboxed primitives)
What causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException?
Accessing an index < 0 or >= array.length
What is ArrayStoreException?
Runtime exception thrown when storing an incompatible type into a covariant array (e.g. an Integer into a String[] referenced as Object[])
arr.length vs str.length()
Array length is a field (no parentheses); String length is a method call

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Array programs are practice problems such as finding maximum, reversing, searching, sorting, removing duplicates and rotating.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Writing programs is how concepts become skills.
  • These problems appear in coding rounds for freshers.

3. Advantages

  • Builds problem solving and logic.
  • Teaches complexity thinking (O(n) vs O(n^2)).
  • Reusable patterns: two pointers, prefix sums, sliding window.

4. Disadvantages

  • Edge cases (empty, single element, negatives) are easy to forget.
  • Brute force solutions can be too slow.
  • Memorizing without understanding does not transfer.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Frequently asked in written tests.
  • Strengthens loops, conditions and indexing.
  • Prepares for data structures and algorithms.

6. Basic Concepts

Basic Array Operations

  1. Sum of array elements
  2. Maximum and minimum element in array
  3. Reverse an array
  4. Sort an array (Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, Insertion Sort)
  5. Find the second largest element in an array

Array Analysis & Combining Arrays

  1. Count the number of even and odd elements in an array
  2. Find the number of occurrences of a given element in an array
  3. Check if an array is a palindrome
  4. Merge two arrays
  5. Find the intersection of two arrays

Array Transformation Programs

  1. Find the union of two arrays
  2. Remove duplicates from an array
  3. Rotate an array to the left by a given number of positions
  4. Rotate an array to the right by a given number of positions
  5. Move all zeros to the end of the array

Advanced Beginner Array Programs

  1. Find the sum of two arrays
  2. Find the common elements in three sorted arrays
  3. Find the smallest and second smallest element in an array
  4. Find the kth smallest and largest element in an array
  5. Segregate even and odd numbers in an array

Fresher Notes

  • Typical programs: find max/min, sum and average, reverse, search, sort and remove duplicates.
  • Loop choice: use an index loop to change elements and for-each to only read them.
  • Empty array: always check length before taking max or min.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Subsequence & Sum Programs

  1. Find the equilibrium index of an array
  2. Find the maximum sum of a subarray (Kadane's algorithm)
  3. Find the longest increasing subsequence in an array
  4. Find the longest common subsequence between two arrays
  5. Find the missing number in a given array of size n containing numbers from 1 to n-1

Subarray & Pair Analysis

  1. Check if there are duplicate elements in an array within k distance from each other
  2. Find the length of the largest subarray with 0 sum
  3. Find the largest subarray with equal number of 0s and 1s
  4. Find the maximum product of two integers in an array
  5. Find the peak element in an array

Element Relationship Programs

  1. Find the maximum difference between two elements in an array such that larger element appears after the smaller element
  2. Find the element that appears more than n/2 times in an array (Majority Element)
  3. Find the next greater element for each element in an array
  4. Find the first repeating and first non-repeating element in an array
  5. Find the maximum sum of a subarray with at least k elements

Advanced Subarray Sum Programs

  1. Check if there is a subarray with sum equal to zero
  2. Find the sum of the minimum elements of all subarrays
  3. Find the maximum circular subarray sum
  4. Find the maximum sum of a subarray with exactly k elements
  5. Find the minimum difference between the sums of two subarrays of size n/2

Mid-Level Notes

  • Linear search is O(n); binary search needs sorted data and is O(log n).
  • In-place reverse: swap with two indexes moving in from both ends.
  • Two pointers and prefix sums solve many problems in O(n).

8. Advanced Concepts

Advanced Subarray Search Programs

  1. Check if a given array represents a Binary Search Tree or not
  2. Find the maximum length of a subarray with a given sum
  3. Find the minimum length of a subarray with a given sum
  4. Find the maximum length of a subarray with distinct elements
  5. Find the minimum length of a subarray with all elements of another array

Sliding Window & Hashing Programs

  1. Find the length of the smallest subarray with at least k distinct elements
  2. Find the longest subarray with the same element
  3. Find the longest subarray with alternating even and odd elements
  4. Find the longest subarray with a sum less than or equal to a given value
  5. Find the number of subarrays with a given sum

Two-Pointer & In-Place Techniques

  1. Find all pairs in a sorted array with a given sum (two-pointer technique, O(n))
  2. Rotate an array left using the 3-reversal trick (in-place, O(1) extra space)
  3. Find all duplicate elements in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (values in range 1..n)
  4. Trapping Rain Water - maximum water trapped between bars (two-pointer, O(n))
  5. Longest subarray of 1s after flipping at most k zeros (sliding window, O(n))

Senior Notes

  • Complexity and memory: in-place algorithms use O(1) extra space.
  • Streams vs loops: use streams for readability (IntStream.of(a).max()) and loops for hot paths.
  • Edge cases: empty, single element, duplicates, negative numbers, overflow.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Prefix sums answer range sums in O(1) after O(n) setup; sliding window finds the best fixed-size window; two sum on sorted data uses two pointers; hashing finds pairs in unsorted data in O(n). Choose the structure from constraints.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Core techniques: single pass accumulation, two pointers (sorted arrays, partitioning), sliding window (subarrays of fixed or variable length), prefix sums (range queries), and Kadane algorithm (maximum subarray). Each turns an O(n^2) brute force into O(n).

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: initializing max with 0 (wrong for negatives), not handling empty arrays, modifying while iterating indexes, integer overflow in sums (use long), and mid = (lo + hi) / 2 overflow (use lo + (hi - lo) / 2).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Big-O summary: scan O(n), binary search O(log n), sort O(n log n), nested loops O(n^2). For n = 10^6 an O(n^2) approach is far too slow; prefer hashing or sorting. Use primitive arrays for speed.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: finding the best stock profit in one pass, moving averages on sensor data, and top-k values.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Missing number with sum.

Worked Example 2

Rotate right by k.

Practice Exercise 1

Max, reverse and second largest.

Practice Exercise 2

Remove duplicates in a sorted array.

11. Quick Revision

  • Check for empty arrays first.
  • Max: running maximum; reverse: swap ends.
  • Binary search needs a sorted array.
  • Two pointers solve many problems in O(n).
  • Use long for large sums.

topics.name: String in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A String is an immutable object of java.lang.String that holds a sequence of characters
  • Every method that seems to change it returns a new String.
  • Literals created with double quotes go into the String pool (in the heap), so the same literal is stored once, while new always creates a fresh object.
  • Since Java 9 strings use compact storage (LATIN1 or UTF16) and the hash code is cached
  • StringBuilder and StringBuffer are the mutable alternatives.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Almost every input from a user, file, database or API is text, so Strings store and process names, messages and JSON with ready-made methods to compare, search, split and format.
  • Immutability makes String a safe key for HashMap and switch, but it also brings the famous == versus equals bug and slow concatenation in loops.
  • Interviews always include palindrome, reverse, anagram or character count questions.

3. Advantages

  • Immutability gives safe sharing, thread safety and security (a checked path cannot change afterward).
  • The String pool saves memory and compact strings halve memory for ASCII text.
  • Cached hash code makes String an ideal fast HashMap key.
  • Rich API (substring, split, replace, format, join) and optimized concatenation through invokedynamic.
  • String deduplication in G1 can shrink heaps without code changes.

4. Disadvantages

  • Every change creates a new object; concatenating in a loop creates garbage and is slow.
  • Using == compares references and gives the wrong answer silently.
  • Passwords in a String linger in memory, so char[] is safer.
  • split uses a regex, bad patterns can backtrack badly, and toUpperCase depends on the locale.
  • Strings take a large share of heap dumps, and intern can slow down at scale.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Text processing is everywhere.
  • Frequent interview topic (pool, immutability, StringBuilder, intern).
  • Needed for I/O, parsing, formatting and handling Unicode correctly.

6. Basic Concepts

What is a String?

A String is a class (java.lang.String) that represents a sequence of characters. It is one of the most commonly used types in Java for storing and manipulating text.

CharSequence Interface

  • Represents a readable sequence of characters.
  • Implemented by String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer.
  • Lets code treat all three uniformly wherever text is expected.

Creating a String — Literal

The simplest way: assign text in double quotes. Literals are stored in the String Constant Pool so identical values can be reused.

Creating a String — new String()

Using the new keyword always creates a brand-new object on the heap, even if an identical value already exists in the pool.

Strings Are Immutable

Once created, a String's content never changes. Any method that looks like it "modifies" a String (like concat()) actually returns a brand-new String object — the original stays untouched unless you reassign the reference.

length()

Returns the number of characters in the String.

charAt(index)

Returns the character at the given index (0-based).

substring(begin, end)

Extracts a portion of the String. begin is inclusive, end is exclusive.

indexOf()

Returns the position of the first occurrence of a character/substring, or -1 if not found.

toUpperCase() / toLowerCase()

Return a new String with all characters converted to upper- or lower-case.

== vs equals()

== compares references (are they the same object in memory?). equals() compares content (do they hold the same characters?). Always use equals() to compare String values.

concat()

Joins two Strings together and returns the combined result as a new String.

Fresher Notes

  • Immutable: a String is a sequence of characters that never changes; every change creates a new String.
  • String pool: literals are stored once, so "hi" == "hi" is true, but new String("hi") == "hi" is false.
  • Comparing: use equals or equalsIgnoreCase for content, never ==.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Common methods: length, charAt, substring, indexOf, contains, replace, split, trim, strip, toUpperCase, isBlank, repeat, join.
  • Many appends: use StringBuilder; StringBuffer is the synchronized legacy version.
  • Text blocks (Java 15) hold multi-line text: """...""".

8. Advanced Concepts

String Constant Pool — What Actually Happens in Memory

A string literal is looked up in the String Constant Pool (part of the heap since Java 7) before creating anything new. If an identical value already exists, the JVM reuses that object instead of allocating a new one. new String(...) always creates a fresh object on the heap, bypassing the pool.

String s1 = "pankaj";      String s3 = new String("pankaj");
String s2 = "pankaj";
                                      Heap
      String Pool                +-----------+
   +--------------+              | "pankaj"  |  <-- s3
   |  "pankaj"    | <--- s1      +-----------+
   +--------------+ <--- s2
      (one object, two references)      (separate object)

Why String Is Immutable — And What "Modifying" Actually Does

Once created, a String's internal character data never changes. Reasons Java made this design choice:

  • Security - passwords, DB URLs, file paths passed around as Strings can't be silently altered by any code holding a reference.
  • Thread safety - immutable objects are automatically safe to share across threads with no synchronization.
  • String Pool reuse - pooling only works because the JVM can guarantee a shared literal's value will never change under any reference.
  • Hashcode caching - String caches its hashCode() after first computation, safe only because the content can't change; this makes Strings very fast HashMap keys.

Every "mutating" call (concat, +=, replace, toUpperCase...) returns a new String object; if you don't reassign the reference, the original is untouched.

String Concatenation Performance — Why StringBuilder Wins in Loops

Every += on a String inside a loop discards the old object and allocates a brand-new one — for N iterations that's O(n²) total character copying. StringBuilder grows an internal mutable buffer instead, giving O(n) total work.

ClassMutableThread-safeTypical use
StringNoYes (immutable)Fixed/rarely-changing text
StringBuilderYesNoSingle-threaded loops, builders (fastest)
StringBufferYesYes (synchronized)Shared mutable buffer across threads (slower)

String Concatenation Techniques

Beyond +, Java offers several ways to build Strings: concat(), StringBuilder, String.format(), String.join(), and StringJoiner (useful for adding a delimiter between multiple pieces without extra bookkeeping).

String Coding Practice Programs

Frequently asked hands-on String programs:

  1. Count vowels / consonants in a string
  2. Check if a string is numeric
  3. Capitalize the first letter of each word (title case)
  4. Count words in a sentence
  5. Convert camelCase to snake_case, and back
  6. Remove special characters / punctuation from a string
  7. Count frequency of each character
  8. Check if two strings are anagrams
  9. Count uppercase letters, lowercase letters, and digits in one pass
  10. Remove duplicate characters while preserving order
  11. Reverse the words in a sentence (not the whole string)
  12. Extract only the digits / only the letters from a string
  13. Print all substrings of a string
  14. Convert a string to hexadecimal and back
  15. Convert a string to binary and back
  16. Pad a string with leading zeros to a fixed length
  17. Validate an email address / a 10-digit phone number with regex
  18. Find the longest word in a sentence
  19. Mask all digits of a card number except the last 4
  20. Find the first non-repeating character
  21. Find the longest palindromic substring
  22. Find the longest common prefix among an array of strings
  23. Find the longest common substring between two strings
  24. Check if two strings are rotations of each other
  25. Generate all permutations of a string
  26. Remove leading zeros from a numeric string
  27. Rotate a string left/right by N characters
<div class="bg-secondary p-2 rounded-md">

Senior Notes

  • Thread safety: immutability makes Strings safe to share, cacheable (hash code) and safe as map keys.
  • Interning: intern() adds a String to the pool; use it sparingly.
  • Unicode: Strings are UTF-16, so use codePoints() for characters outside the BMP (emoji).
  • Passwords: sensitive data belongs in char[], which you can wipe.

9. Code for Each Concept

Code: Definition
Code: Advantages
Code: Definition (Advanced)
Code: Advantages (Advanced)

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Rich API: formatted, chars(), codePoints(), lines(), strip, isBlank, repeat, translateEscapes, indent, transform, regex methods matches, replaceAll, split. Use String.valueOf, StringBuilder.insert/reverse/deleteCharAt, and Collectors.joining.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Internals: a String holds a byte[] value and a coder (Latin-1 or UTF-16, compact strings since Java 9), plus a cached hash. Literals are interned in the pool at class load; new String creates a separate heap object. String concatenation with + compiles to invokedynamic (StringConcatFactory) since Java 9.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: == for comparison, ignoring the result of immutable methods, concatenating in loops, split with regex special characters ("a.b".split(".") returns an empty array), substring index errors, case-sensitive comparison bugs, and charAt on emoji. Escape regex with Pattern.quote.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Performance: StringBuilder for loops (preallocate capacity), avoid regex in hot paths (precompile Pattern), reuse formatters, and use String.join. Compact strings halve memory for Latin-1 text. Huge strings should be streamed.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: building CSV and JSON lines, masking card numbers, validating emails, and normalizing user input safely.

10. Examples

Real Time Examples

  • Bank statement download: each row is a CSV String split into account, date, narration and amount.
  • Aadhaar masking: only the last four digits are shown, done with substring and a repeat of the letter X.
  • UPI id validation: checking that the text contains exactly one at sign and a known bank handle.
  • College portal login: the entered password is compared with equals, never with double equals.
  • SMS and email templates: a StringBuilder or String.format fills in the customer name and amount.
  • Global example, a REST API: the JSON body arrives as a String and is parsed into objects.

Student tip: use String for fixed text, StringBuilder when you build in a loop, always compare with equals, and remember that every String method returns a new String rather than changing the old one.

Real Time Examples (Advanced)

  • Core banking heap tuning: a heap dump showed forty percent of the heap in byte arrays behind Strings. Enabling G1 string deduplication and canonicalising branch codes reclaimed several gigabytes.
  • High volume file parser: replacing split with indexOf offsets and a reusable StringBuilder cut allocation per row from twelve objects to two.
  • Payments API outage: a validation regex with nested quantifiers hung request threads on a crafted VPA. The fix was a possessive quantifier plus an input length cap.
  • Customer name printing: names in Devanagari and Tamil broke a fixed width receipt until code point iteration replaced charAt.
  • Global example, a search index: tokens canonicalised through a bounded map instead of intern, so the pool never grew without limit.
  • Password handling: char arrays wiped after use, because a String password appeared in a support heap dump during an incident.

Interview answers to keep ready

  • Why is String immutable and final? For pool sharing, safe map keys, thread safety and security checks that cannot be defeated by later mutation.
  • What changed in Java 9 with compact strings? char array became byte array plus a coder flag, halving memory for LATIN1 text.
  • How does concatenation compile today? Constants are folded, and the rest goes through invokedynamic and StringConcatFactory.
  • StringBuilder or StringBuffer? StringBuilder unless the same instance is genuinely shared across threads, which it almost never should be.

Worked Example 1

Immutability.

Worked Example 2

Palindrome and reverse.

Practice Exercise 1

Pool vs heap.

Practice Exercise 2

Everyday methods.

Essential String Methods for Interviews

  • equals() - case-sensitive content comparison. equalsIgnoreCase() - same, but ignores case.
  • compareTo() - lexicographical comparison; returns 0 if equal, a negative number if this String is smaller than the other, and a positive number if it is larger.
  • substring(begin, end) - since Java 7 it returns a new independent copy of the characters. Before Java 7 it shared the original array, so a tiny substring could keep a huge String alive. That leak no longer exists.
  • split(regex) - splits on a regular expression, not a literal string. Characters like ., | and + need escaping (e.g. split("\\.") to split on a literal dot).
  • String.format() / printf() - C-style formatted output using %s, %d, %.2f placeholders.

Common Interview Traps

TrapWhat happensFix / takeaway
new String("x") == "x"false - different objectsAlways use .equals() for content comparison
Switching on a StringWorks via .equals()/hashCode() internally, but NullPointerException if the switch variable is nullNull-check before switching, or use a default case carefully
Modifying a String in a loop with +=Compiles and "works" but is O(n^2) - a new object every iterationUse StringBuilder inside loops
Palindrome check without reversing correctlyEasy to get off-by-one errors comparing manuallynew StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString().equals(s) is a clean one-liner
split(".") on a literal dotThe dot is a regex wildcard, so every character is a separator and the result is an empty arrayEscape it: split("\\.")

Less Common but Real Interview Methods

Beyond the everyday methods, the String API has a handful of methods that show up specifically in "have you actually read the Javadoc" interview rounds:

  • codePointAt(index) / codePointBefore(index) / codePointCount(begin, end) - work with Unicode code points instead of raw chars, needed for characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (e.g. emoji) that take 2 chars (a surrogate pair) to represent.
  • offsetByCodePoints(index, offset) - moves an index forward/back by a number of code points rather than chars - safe for surrogate pairs where index + 1 is not.
  • regionMatches(toffset, other, ooffset, len) - compares a slice of this string against a slice of another string without allocating a substring first; has a case-insensitive overload too.
  • getChars(srcBegin, srcEnd, dst, dstBegin) - copies characters directly into an existing char[], avoiding the extra array allocation that toCharArray() causes.
  • contentEquals(CharSequence) - compares a String's content against any CharSequence (including a live StringBuilder/StringBuffer) without first converting it with toString().
  • subSequence(begin, end) - the CharSequence-interface equivalent of substring(begin, end); on String they return equal content.
  • chars() / codePoints() - return an IntStream of char values / code points, letting you run Stream operations directly over a string's characters.
  • indent(n) (Java 12+) - adds (or, for negative n, strips) n spaces at the start of every line.
  • transform(Function) (Java 12+) - passes the whole string through a function and returns the function's result, useful for chaining a custom transformation into a fluent call.
  • formatted(Object... args) (Java 15+) - instance-method shortcut for String.format(this, args).

11. Quick Revision

  • Strings are immutable.
  • Compare with equals, not ==.
  • StringBuilder for many appends.
  • Literals are interned in the pool.
  • Use char[] for passwords.

interviewQA: Why is String immutable in Java?
Security, thread safety, String Pool reuse, and safe hashCode caching for use as HashMap keys
What is the String Constant Pool?
A special area (part of the heap since Java 7) where literal String values are stored and reused to save memory
== vs equals()
== compares references (object identity); equals() compares actual character content
StringBuffer vs StringBuilder
Both mutable; StringBuffer is synchronized (thread-safe, slower), StringBuilder is not (faster, single-threaded use)
How does the JVM handle the + operator on Strings?
Java 8 and older rewrote one + statement into a StringBuilder; Java 9 and later use invokedynamic. In both cases, += across loop iterations still creates a new String each time
What does intern() do?
Looks up the String's value in the pool and returns the pooled reference, adding it to the pool if not already present

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A constructor is a special member with the class name and no return type that initializes a new object when it is created with new.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Objects must start in a valid state.
  • Constructors guarantee required data is supplied and validated at creation.

3. Advantages

  • Guarantees initialization.
  • Can be overloaded for different ways to create objects.
  • Supports validation and immutable objects.

4. Disadvantages

  • Many parameters become hard to read (use builders).
  • Not inherited.
  • Calling overridable methods inside is risky.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Every object creation uses one.
  • Needed for inheritance, DI and immutability.
  • Common interview questions on default constructor and chaining.

6. Basic Concepts

A constructor in Java is a special block of code used to initialize objects when they are created.

It is automatically called when an instance of a class is created using the new keyword.

Key Characteristics

  • Same Name as Class: A constructor must have the exact same name as the class it belongs to.
  • No Return Type: It does not have a return type, not even void. Adding a return type makes it a regular method.
  • Automatic Invocation: Java calls it for you when the object is created.
  • Initialization Logic: It sets the starting values of the object's fields and does any set-up, so the object is valid from the start.

There are 2 types of constructor:

  1. Default constructor (no-argument constructor)
  2. Parameterized constructor (takes arguments)

Below is one small, runnable code + output for each:

1. Default Constructor (No-Argument Constructor)

A constructor that takes no arguments is a no-argument constructor. If you write no constructor at all, the compiler adds one for you; that one is the default constructor. Below, we write the no-argument constructor ourselves.

Proof: When you write NO constructor, the compiler silently inserts one

Here we have not written any constructor. The compiler adds a default one. Fields that nobody sets keep their default values (0 for int, false for boolean, null for objects).
Default values assigned by the compiler-generated constructor:

2. Parameterized Constructor

A constructor with arguments is called a parameterized constructor. It lets you set an object's fields to specific values at creation time.

Proof: once you write ANY constructor, the free default one disappears

The compiler adds a no-argument constructor only when the class declares none at all. Once you write one, new Example() no longer compiles.

Fresher Notes

  • Constructor: initializes a new object. It has the class name and no return type: public Student(String name) { this.name = name; }.
  • Default constructor: if you write none, the compiler adds a no-argument one; once you write one, it does not.
  • When it runs: every time you use new.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

What is the Use of a Constructor?

It runs code at object creation, mostly to set the starting values of the instance variables.

A constructor can be called in these ways:

  • new Employee(): creates an object (the usual way).
  • this(...): calls another constructor of the same class.
  • super(...): calls the parent class constructor.
  • Class.forName("com.test.Employee").getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(): reflection.

Constructor overloading: a class can have many constructors with the same name and different parameters.

Note

  • A constructor cannot be overridden, because constructors are not inherited. A subclass has its own constructors.
  • A private constructor is mostly used in the singleton design pattern.

1. What is a Constructor?

  • A constructor sets up the initial state of a new object.
  • Like a method, it holds statements, but they run once, when the object is created.

2. Is there a Copy Constructor in Java?

  • Java has no built-in copy constructor and does not generate one. You write your own: Student(Student other).
  • Other ways to copy an object: assign field values one by one, or use the clone() method of Object.

3. What is Constructor Chaining?

Calling one constructor from another is called constructor chaining. Use this(...) for the same class and super(...) for the parent class. When you create a child object, the parent constructor runs first, then the child constructor.

Rules:

  1. this(...) or super(...) must be the first statement of the constructor.
  2. Constructors cannot call each other in a loop (compile error).
  3. At least one constructor must not use this(...), so the chain can end.

4. Can a parent constructor call a child constructor?

No. Java has no way to call a subclass constructor from a superclass constructor.

5. What happens if you give a constructor a return type?

It is no longer a constructor. A member with a return type is a normal method, even if it has the class name. It compiles, but most tools warn about it.

6. What is a no-arg constructor?

A constructor without parameters is a no-arg constructor. The default constructor that the compiler adds is always a no-arg constructor.

7. How is a no-arg constructor different from the default constructor?

  • A no-arg constructor is any constructor without parameters, written by you or added by the compiler.
  • The default constructor is the one the compiler adds when the class has no constructor. It has no parameters and no throws clause.
  • In Object, its body is empty. In every other class, it just calls super().

8. What are private constructors and where are they used?

  • A constructor can have an access modifier like any method.
  • A private constructor can be called only inside its own class.
  • Uses: the Singleton pattern, static factory methods, and utility classes that must not be created.

9. When do we need constructor overloading?

  • When objects can be created in different ways, for example with or without optional values.
  • The compiler picks the constructor by the number and types of the arguments.

10. Are there destructors in Java?

  • No. The garbage collector frees memory, and you cannot predict when (or whether) an object is removed.
  • To release resources such as files, use try-with-resources and AutoCloseable.

11. Can we override a constructor?

  • No. Constructors are not inherited, and a constructor name must match its own class.
  • A subclass has its own constructors and can call the parent one with super(...).

12. Can a constructor be final?

  • No. final is not allowed on a constructor, because constructors are not inherited, so there is nothing to override.
  • A constructor can be private, for example in a Singleton.

13. How do you handle exceptions in constructors?

  • A constructor can use try-catch inside, or declare throws and let the caller handle it.
  • If a constructor throws, the object is not created, so throw early for invalid arguments.

14. Can a constructor call a method?

  • Yes. Avoid calling overridable methods, because the subclass fields are not ready yet.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Overloading: a class can have many constructors with different parameters, and they can be private (singleton, factory).
  • Chaining: use this(...) to call another constructor in the same class and super(...) to call the parent one. It must be the first statement.
  • Not inherited: constructors cannot be abstract, static or final.

8. Advanced Concepts

Default Constructor vs No-Arg Constructor You Write

The compiler adds a default constructor only when your class declares none at all. Once you write any constructor, even a parameterized one, the free default constructor is gone.

Constructor Overloading

A class can have several constructors with different parameter lists. The compiler picks the one that matches the arguments.

Object Initialization Order

When an object is created, Java runs things in a fixed order:

Class loading (once per class, first use only)
  |
  +-- Static variable initializers + static blocks (top to bottom)
        |
        v
Object creation (new)
  |
  +-- Parent class construction runs FIRST (implicit super())
  |     +-- Parent's instance initializer blocks + field initializers
  |     `-- Parent's constructor body
  |
  +-- Instance initializer blocks + field initializers (this class)
        |
        v
  Constructor body (this class)

What Modifiers Are (and Aren't) Allowed on a Constructor

Constructors are not inherited. Only access modifiers apply to them, never abstract, static, final or synchronized.

ModifierAllowed on constructor?Why
public / private / protected / defaultYesControls who can instantiate the class (e.g. private for Singleton)
abstractNoAn abstract member has no body, but a constructor must run initialization logic
staticNoConstructors build a specific instance; static means "belongs to the class", which is contradictory
finalNofinal prevents overriding, but constructors are never inherited/overridden in the first place
synchronizedNoNo other thread can see a partially-constructed object's reference yet, so there's nothing to synchronize against

Senior Notes

  • Validation: check arguments in constructors and keep objects valid from creation; prefer immutable objects with final fields.
  • Many parameters: use a builder or static factory methods.
  • Overridable calls: do not call them from constructors, because the subclass fields are not initialized yet.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Patterns: telescoping constructors, static factories (of, valueOf), builders, copy constructors, private constructors, records (canonical constructor with compact validation), dependency injection via constructor parameters, and enums (private constructors).

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

new C(args) allocates zeroed memory, sets the header, then runs the constructor bytecode <init>: it calls the super constructor first, then field initializers and instance blocks (copied into every constructor that calls super), then the body. Before the body finishes, this is only partly constructed, so publishing it (to another thread or a listener) is unsafe.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forgetting a no-arg constructor required by frameworks (JPA, Jackson), calling overridable methods, doing heavy I/O in constructors, shadowing fields (name = name; assigns the parameter to itself), and swallowing validation. Use this.name = name.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Object creation is cheap, but constructors that open connections or build big structures are not. Make them lazy or move work to factories, use object pools only for expensive resources (connections, threads), and rely on escape analysis for short-lived objects.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: Spring prefers constructor injection: dependencies are final and required, and the class is easy to test.

10. Examples
