Worked Example 2

Default constructor disappears.

Practice Exercise 1

Overloaded constructors and validation.

Practice Exercise 2

Static factory.

Common Interview Traps

TrapAnswer
Constructor vs MethodConstructor: no return type, same name as class, runs once at creation. Method: has a return type (or void), any name, callable anytime
Calling an overridable method from a constructorDangerous. The subclass version may run before the subclass fields are initialized
Private constructorsUsed for Singleton (blocks outside new) and static-only utility classes like Math

11. Quick Revision

  • Same name as class, no return type.
  • Default constructor only if none is written.
  • this(...) and super(...) must be first.
  • Constructors can be private (singleton, factories).
  • Validate arguments early.

topics.name: Constructor Chaining

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Constructor chaining is calling one constructor from another: this(...) within the same class or super(...) to the parent class.

2. Need of This Topic

  • It avoids duplicated initialization code and makes sure parent parts of an object are initialized before the child.

3. Advantages

  • Single place for initialization logic.
  • Parent state is always initialized first.
  • Keeps constructors short.

4. Disadvantages

  • Long chains are hard to trace.
  • Recursive this() calls fail to compile.
  • Order of initialization can surprise beginners.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Required to understand inheritance and object creation.
  • Appears in output-prediction questions.
  • Helps design clean constructors.

6. Basic Concepts

What is Constructor Chaining?

Constructor Chaining is the process of calling one constructor from another constructor.

  • It happens within the same class using this(), or between parent and child classes using super().
  • It exists so common initialization logic can live in one place instead of being copy-pasted into every constructor.

Why use Constructor Chaining?

  • Improves code reusability
  • Maintains a proper, predictable initialization sequence
  • Makes code clean and easy to maintain

Chaining Within the Same Class — this()

A constructor can call another constructor of the same class using this(...). This lets a simpler constructor delegate to a more complete one instead of repeating its logic.

Chaining to the Parent Class — super()

When chaining happens between a parent and a child class, we use super(...) to call the parent's constructor. The parent's constructor always finishes running before the child's constructor body executes.

If you don't write super() yourself, Java implicitly inserts a call to the parent's no-argument constructor as the first line.

Fresher Notes

  • Chaining is one constructor calling another: this(...) in the same class, super(...) in the parent.
  • First statement: the this(...) or super(...) call must be the first statement of the constructor.
  • Implicit call: if you do not write super(...), the compiler inserts super().

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Parent first: the parent constructor runs before the child body, so objects are built from the top of the hierarchy down.
  • Main constructor: chain to one "main" constructor so initialization logic lives in one place.
  • Recursion: circular this(...) calls cause a compile error.

8. Advanced Concepts

this() / super() Must Be the FIRST Statement

Whichever one you use, this() or super() must be the very first statement in the constructor. The compiler enforces this so a well-defined, single initialization path is guaranteed before any other code runs — no field can be touched before the object's "base" state exists.

Putting any statement before it is a compile-time error:

public class Employee {
    int id;

    Employee(int id) {
        System.out.println("Creating employee...");
        this(0);   // ERROR: call to this must be first statement in constructor
    }

    Employee() {
        this(-1);
    }
}

The fix is simply to move the chaining call to the top of the constructor body.

What Happens When NEITHER this() Nor super() Is Written

If a constructor doesn't start with this() or super(), the compiler silently inserts super() as the first statement — calling the parent's no-argument constructor.

But if the parent class has no no-arg constructor (only a parameterized one), the compiler can no longer insert a silent super() — you MUST call super(args) explicitly, or you get a compile-time error:

class Vehicle {
    Vehicle(String type) { ... }   // no no-arg constructor
}

class Car extends Vehicle {
    Car() { }   // ERROR: implicit super() needs Vehicle(), which doesn't exist
}

Fix — call the parameterized parent constructor explicitly:

Multi-Level Constructor Chaining (3 Classes Deep)

When a chain of subclasses is instantiated, constructor execution always runs top-down — grandparent first, then parent, then child — even though you call new on the child:

new Child()
     |
     v
Child()  --super()--> Parent()  --super()--> GrandParent()
                                                    |
                                          runs FIRST, prints first
                                                    |
                                         Parent() body runs next
                                                    |
                                          Child() body runs last

The Trap: Trying to Use Both this() and super() Together

Only ONE statement can occupy the "first line" of a constructor, and both this() and super() compete for that position. Allowing both would mean the object's fields could be initialized twice — once through the chained sibling constructor, and again through the parent constructor — breaking Java's guarantee that every object is initialized exactly once, in a well-defined order.

So the compiler flatly rejects this:

class Base {
    Base() { System.out.println("Base"); }
}

class Sub extends Base {
    Sub() {
        this(10);
    }
    Sub(int x) {
        this();       // ERROR: recursive constructor invocation
        super();      // ERROR: call to super must be first statement
        System.out.println(x);
    }
}

Exactly one constructor in the chain must be the "base case" that skips this() — that constructor is the one that eventually calls (or implicitly gets) super().

Senior Notes

  • Initialization order: static blocks run once per class. Then, for each object: parent field initializers and instance blocks, parent constructor, child field initializers and instance blocks, child constructor.
  • No no-arg parent: if the parent has no no-arg constructor, the child must call super(args) explicitly.
  • Newer Java: Java 22 added statements before super() as a preview feature (they must not use this). It is final in Java 25.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Design tips:

  • Put validation and the real initialization in one main constructor. Other constructors supply defaults through this(...).
  • Make parent constructors protected when only subclasses use them, and document what they expect.
  • Records chain through their canonical constructor.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The compiled constructor begins with an invokespecial call to either this.<init> or super.<init>.

  • Field initializers and instance blocks are copied in right after the super call.
  • They are copied only into constructors that call super, not into those that call this.
  • Class initialization (<clinit>) runs once, parent class first.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Circular this() calls (compile error).
  • Using child fields inside a parent constructor. They are not set yet.
  • Long chains that hide behavior. Keep chains short.
  • Forgetting the implicit super() when the parent has no no-arg constructor.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Deep hierarchies make construction expensive and fragile. Prefer composition and flat hierarchies; measure only if profiling shows allocation hot spots. Static initialization cost is paid once but may delay startup.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: framework base classes. A JPA entity needs a protected no-arg constructor, while the public constructor enforces required fields.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Explicit super needed.

Worked Example 2

Central constructor.

Practice Exercise 1

Chaining and order.

Practice Exercise 2

Initialization order.

11. Quick Revision

  • this(...) calls a constructor of the same class.
  • super(...) calls the parent constructor.
  • Must be the first statement.
  • Implicit super() is added if missing.
  • Order: parent first, then child.

interviewQA: What is constructor chaining?
Calling one constructor from another — within the same class via this(), or from a subclass to its parent via super()
Can this() and super() both be used in the same constructor?
No — only one "first statement" is allowed per constructor, so they are mutually exclusive
What happens if you write neither this() nor super()?
The compiler implicitly inserts super() (parent's no-arg constructor) as the first statement
What if the parent has no no-arg constructor?
The implicit super() insertion fails, causing a compile error — you must call super(args) explicitly
What happens if this() forms a cycle back to itself?
Compile-time error: "recursive constructor invocation" — there is no base case to stop it
In a 3-level inheritance chain, which constructor runs first?
The topmost (grandparent) constructor always finishes first; execution is top-down even though new is called on the child
Why must this()/super() be the first statement?
So the compiler can guarantee a single, well-defined initialization path before any other code touches the object

topics.name: Static Keyword

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • The static keyword makes a member belong to the class instead of any object: static variables, methods, blocks and nested classes.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Some data and behavior is shared by all objects (counters, constants, utilities) and needs no object to use.

3. Advantages

  • Memory shared by all instances.
  • Utility methods callable without objects.
  • Static blocks run one-time setup.

4. Disadvantages

  • Mutable static state is global state and hurts testing.
  • Static methods cannot use this.
  • Cannot be overridden, only hidden.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • main is static; constants use static final.
  • Needed for singletons and factories.
  • Common interview topic.

6. Basic Concepts

What is the Static Keyword?

  • The static keyword is used to create class-level members.
  • Static members belong to the class, not to individual objects.
  • Only one copy of a static member is ever created in memory - all objects share it.

Where can static be used?

  • Variable, method, block, and nested (inner) class.
  • Local variables and constructors can never be static.

Why use static?

  • Saves memory - no need to duplicate the same data per object.
  • Shares common data/behavior among all objects of a class.

Static Variable - Shared Across All Objects

A variable declared with static is also called a class variable. It is stored once (per class), and every object reads/writes that same copy - so if one object changes it, every other object sees the change.

Below, a Counter object increments the shared count field in its constructor every time a new object is created:

Static Method - Called Without Creating an Object

A method declared with static belongs to the class rather than to any object, so it can be called directly using the class name - no new keyword required.

Static Block - Runs Once When the Class Loads

A static block is a group of statements that run exactly once, automatically, just before the class is first actively used (first object creation, static method call, or non-constant static field read).

Class initialization is lazy. So for any class other than the one declaring main(), the static block runs after main() has already started. It is commonly used to set up static resources.

Why is main() Itself Static?

The JVM calls main() to start a program before any object of that class exists. An instance method can only be called on an object, and there is no object yet at startup. So main() must be static, and the JVM calls it directly on the class.

Fresher Notes

  • Class-level members: static members belong to the class, not to any object. They are shared by all instances and used as ClassName.member.
  • Uses: static variables (shared counters, constants), static methods (utilities like Math.max) and static blocks (one-time setup).
  • Static main: main is static so the JVM can call it without creating an object.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • No this: a static method cannot use this or access instance members directly.
  • Hiding: static methods are hidden, not overridden, in subclasses.
  • Constants and nesting: static final creates constants; a static nested class does not need an outer instance.

8. Advanced Concepts

Where Static Members Live in Memory

A static variable belongs to the class, not any single object - every instance reads and writes the same memory location. Class metadata (method code, field layout) lives in Metaspace (native memory, which replaced PermGen in JDK 8). The static field values are kept once per class on the Heap, in the class's Class object. Each object's own (non-static) fields are stored separately on the Heap.

JVM Memory Layout
+--------------------------------------------+
| Metaspace                                   |
|   Employee class metadata (methods, layout) |
+--------------------------------------------+
| Heap                                        |
|   Employee.class -> static employeeCount=3  |  ONE shared copy
|   e1 -> Employee { id: 1 }                  |
|   e2 -> Employee { id: 2 }                  |
|   e3 -> Employee { id: 3 }                  |  each object's own "id"
+--------------------------------------------+

Static Initialization Order: Class Loading vs Object Creation

Static blocks and static variables initialize once, in top-to-bottom order, when the class is first actively used - before that class's first object is constructed. Instance initializer blocks and constructors, by contrast, run every time a new object is created.

Multiple static blocks in the same class all run once, in the order they are written:

Static Methods Are Hidden, Not Overridden

True overriding is resolved using the object's runtime type (dynamic binding) - that is what makes polymorphism work for instance methods.

Static methods belong to the class, not to any object. So they are resolved using the reference's declared (compile-time) type instead. This is called method hiding, and it is NOT polymorphic.

Static Methods Cannot Touch Instance State Directly

A static method has no implicit this, so it cannot directly reference instance (non-static) fields or methods, and cannot use this/super. It can only call other static members directly, or reach instance members through an explicit object reference.

class Demo {
    int instanceField = 10;

    static void staticMethod() {
        // System.out.println(instanceField);
        // COMPILE ERROR: non-static field 'instanceField'
        // cannot be referenced from a static context
    }
}

The fix is either to make the field static too, or to access it via an object: new Demo().instanceField.

Static Nested Class vs Non-Static Inner Class

A static nested class behaves like a top-level class placed inside another for grouping. It does NOT need an instance of the outer class, and cannot access the outer class's instance members directly.

A non-static inner class is tied to an enclosing instance. It must be created through an outer object, and it CAN access the outer instance's fields and methods directly.

Historical Trivia: Running a Class Without main()

Before JDK 1.7, a class with no main() could still run. The logic went in a static block that ended with System.exit(0). The static block ran during class loading, before the JVM looked for main().

Since JDK 1.7, this trick no longer works. The JVM checks for public static void main(String[] args) upfront and refuses to run the class if it is missing.

Senior Notes

  • Global state: mutable static state hurts testing and thread safety. Prefer dependency injection.
  • Initialization: order matters. Class initialization is lazy and thread-safe, which is the basis of the holder idiom for singletons.
  • Utility classes: static imports and utility classes are fine for pure functions; avoid static for things with state or I/O.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Uses: constants, utility classes (private constructor, final class), factory methods, singletons (enum or holder), static nested classes (builders, entries), static imports, and counters. Static nested classes have no outer reference and avoid leaks, unlike inner classes.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Static fields live in the class mirror (in the heap since Java 8) and are initialized once during class initialization by <clinit>, which the JVM runs under a lock, making it thread-safe. Static methods use invokestatic (no receiver), so they cannot be overridden or use dynamic dispatch.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes: static collections that grow forever (memory leak), static SimpleDateFormat (not thread-safe), static state leaking between tests, calling instance code from a static context, and static references to large objects that keep them in memory. Use immutable statics and DateTimeFormatter (thread-safe).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Static final constants are inlined by the compiler, so changing one means recompiling the classes that use it. Static access is fast, but shared state causes contention across threads. Use LongAdder for hot counters.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a logger per class, application constants, and validation helpers. Avoid statics for services; inject them so tests can replace them.

10. Examples

Worked Example 2

Common Interview Traps

TrapExplanation
Static methods "override"Not real overriding - it's method hiding. The subclass's static method shadows the parent's; resolution is by reference type, not the runtime object, unlike true polymorphism
static import misuseOverusing import static makes code ambiguous about which class a method belongs to - readability suffers even though it compiles fine
Memory leaks via static fieldsA static field lives for the entire class lifetime (effectively the app's lifetime). A static List/Map that keeps growing and is never cleared holds references forever, preventing garbage collection
Static + inheritanceStatic members ARE inherited (accessible via subclass name) but are not polymorphic - calling a static method through a subclass reference still resolves at compile time based on the reference's declared type

Rule of thumb: use static for class-wide constants, helper methods that do not need object state, factory methods, and one-time initialization - never for anything that should vary per object.

11. Quick Revision

  • Static belongs to the class.
  • Static methods cannot access instance members directly.
  • Static block runs once at class load.
  • Hidden, not overridden.
  • Avoid mutable static state.

interviewQA: What is the purpose of the static keyword?
It marks a member (variable, method, or nested class) as belonging to the class itself rather than to instances - so it is shared among all instances of the class.
What is a static variable?
A class-level variable shared among all instances. It is initialized once, at class load time, and retains its value across all objects.
What is a static method?
A method that belongs to the class rather than any specific instance. It can be called without creating an object, and can only directly access other static members.
What is a static block?
A static initializer used to set up static variables. It runs once when the class is loaded into memory, before any object is created or static method is called.
Static block vs constructor - what's the difference?
A static block initializes static variables and runs once at class load. A constructor initializes instance variables and runs every time an object is created.
Can a class be static?
A top-level class cannot be static, but a nested class can - this is called a static nested class, and it does not need an instance of the outer class.
Why use the static keyword?
For memory management, utility/helper methods that need no object state, defining constants, and implementing patterns like Singleton.
Can static methods be overridden?
No - they belong to the class, not instances, so they cannot be overridden. A subclass can define a same-signature static method, but that only hides the parent's version.
Static method vs instance method?

A static method belongs to the class and needs no object to be called; it can only access static members. An instance method belongs to an object, needs an instance, and can access both static and instance members.
Can a static method access instance variables/methods?
Not directly - it has no this reference. It can only reach instance members through an explicit object reference.

topics.id: Input and Output Stream in Java
topics.name: Input and Output Stream in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Streams move data: InputStream and OutputStream handle bytes, Reader and Writer handle characters.
  • NIO adds Path and Files.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Programs read files, networks and keyboard input and write results.
  • Streams give a uniform way to do it.

3. Advantages

  • Uniform API for files, network and memory.
  • Buffered streams make I/O fast.
  • Decorator design lets you combine features.

4. Disadvantages

  • Forgetting to close streams leaks resources.
  • Checked IOException everywhere.
  • Wrong charset causes garbled text.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Needed for file processing and logging.
  • Foundation for serialization and networking.
  • Used in nearly every real application.

6. Basic Concepts

Input and Output Stream in Java

  • Java I/O (Input and Output) is used to read input and produce output.
  • Java uses the idea of a stream to move data in order, step by step.
  • The java.io package holds the classes for input and output.
  • File handling in Java is done with the Java I/O API.

What is a Stream?

  • A stream is a sequence of data.
  • In Java, a stream is made of bytes.
  • There are two kinds: byte streams (raw or binary data) and character streams (text). The difference is explained in the Expert Level section.

Below is one small, runnable code and output for each core building block:

1. Automatically Created Streams

Java creates three streams automatically and attaches them to the console:

  1. System.out - Standard Output Stream
  2. System.in - Standard Input Stream
  3. System.err - Standard Error Stream

2. OutputStream - writing data to a destination

  • OutputStream is used to write data to a destination.
  • The destination may be a file, array, device, or socket.
  • System.out itself is a PrintStream, which is an OutputStream.

3. InputStream - reading data from a source

  • InputStream is used to read data from a source.
  • The source may be a file, array, device, or socket.
  • System.in is an InputStream connected to the keyboard.

4. Reading Console Input with Scanner

The simplest way to read user input from the keyboard is Scanner wrapped around System.in. Since we can't take live keyboard input in a demo, this example reads from a fixed string source instead so the output is deterministic.

5. Write Data into a File using FileWriter

In this example, data is written into a file using the FileWriter class.

6. Read a File Line by Line using Scanner

Scanner can also be wrapped around a FileInputStream to read a file's contents line by line.
<div class="bg-secondary p-2 rounded-md">

Fresher Notes

  • Streams move data: InputStream and OutputStream handle bytes; Reader and Writer handle characters.
  • Standard streams: System.in, System.out and System.err.
  • Closing: always close streams, best with try-with-resources.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Common classes: FileInputStream, FileOutputStream, BufferedReader, BufferedWriter, PrintWriter.
  • Buffered wrappers read and write in chunks, which is much faster than byte by byte.
  • Charset: pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8 to avoid platform-dependent text.

8. Advanced Concepts

Byte Streams vs Character Streams

Java I/O splits into two parallel hierarchies:

Byte Streams (raw 8-bit data)                       Character Streams (Unicode text)
InputStream / OutputStream                          Reader / Writer
  |                                                 |
  +-- FileInputStream / FileOutputStream            +-- FileReader / FileWriter
  +-- BufferedInputStream / BufferedOutputStream    +-- BufferedReader / BufferedWriter
  +-- ObjectInputStream / ObjectOutputStream        +-- InputStreamReader / OutputStreamWriter
  +-- DataInputStream / DataOutputStream            +-- PrintWriter

Why do character streams exist at all? Byte streams move raw bytes with no notion of text encoding - reading a multi-byte UTF-8 character one byte at a time can split it incorrectly. Character streams (Reader/Writer) understand the platform/specified charset and decode bytes into proper Unicode chars, which is exactly what you want for text files.

InputStreamReader and OutputStreamWriter are the bridge classes that wrap a byte stream and expose it as a character stream (with a chosen charset).

Writing and Reading a File with try-with-resources

Modern Java I/O should always use try-with-resources so streams are closed automatically, even if an exception occurs mid-way:

Why Buffering Matters

An unbuffered FileReader/FileOutputStream can trigger a system call for every single byte or character read/written - each system call has real overhead (context switch into the OS kernel).

BufferedReader/BufferedWriter (and their byte-stream equivalents) wrap the underlying stream with an internal char[]/byte[] buffer (default 8KB). Reads/writes go against that in-memory array first, and the real system call only happens when the buffer fills up or is explicitly flushed - turning thousands of tiny I/O calls into a handful of large ones.

Unbuffered:  read() read() read() read() ...  -> many system calls
Buffered:    [fill 8KB buffer in one syscall] -> read() read() read() ... (from memory)

This is why you almost always wrap a raw FileReader/FileWriter in a Buffered* class in real applications.

try-with-resources & AutoCloseable

Any class implementing AutoCloseable (which includes every I/O stream) can be declared in a try-with-resources header. Multiple resources close automatically in the reverse of their declaration order:

Senior Notes

  • NIO: prefer java.nio.file.Files and Path, for example Files.readAllLines, Files.lines, Files.writeString, Files.copy.
  • Large files: read line by line; do not load the whole file into memory.
  • Decorator pattern: streams wrap other streams, as in new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(in)).

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

NIO.2 is the modern file API. Main pieces:

  • Path and Files.walk, Files.copy, Files.move, Files.newBufferedReader
  • WatchService to watch folders for changes
  • Memory-mapped files via FileChannel.map

Close streams from Files.lines and Files.walk, because they hold file handles.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The I/O classes use the decorator pattern: a base stream does the raw transfer, and wrappers add behavior.

  • Wrappers add buffering, decoding, object serialization or compression.
  • InputStreamReader bridges bytes to chars with a charset.
  • NIO adds channels, buffers and non-blocking selectors.
  • Files offers convenient high-level calls.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Not closing streams (handle leaks, unflushed data).
  • Reading with the platform default charset.
  • Loading huge files fully (OutOfMemoryError).
  • Ignoring the return value of read(byte[]), which can be less than the array size.
  • Mixing Scanner and BufferedReader on System.in.
  • Forgetting to flush.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

For throughput:

  • Use 8 KB or larger buffers and buffered wrappers.
  • Copy in bulk with in.transferTo(out).
  • Use memory-mapped files for random access.
  • Avoid per-byte calls on unbuffered streams.

Disk and network latency dominate, so batch the work.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: stream a large CSV line by line with a progress counter. Write results to a temp file, then move it into place so readers never see a half-written file.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Reading console input.

Worked Example 2

Append to a file.

Practice Exercise 1

Copy a file with try-with-resources.

Practice Exercise 2

Text with NIO.

Common Interview Traps

TrapExplanation
Forgetting to close streams (pre-Java 7)Causes file handle/resource leaks; try-with-resources (Java 7+) solves this automatically
read() returns int, not char-1 signals end-of-stream; a char type (0 to 65535) can't represent -1, so int is used
InputStreamReaderBridges a byte stream into a character stream using a specified/default charset
FileWriter without append flagOverwrites the file by default; use new FileWriter(path, true) to append
FlushingBuffered writers may hold data in memory until flush()/close() is called - always close (or use try-with-resources) or data may be lost

Rule of thumb: use character streams (Reader/Writer) for text, byte streams (InputStream/OutputStream) for binary data, always wrap with a Buffered* class for performance, and always use try-with-resources so resources close automatically.

11. Quick Revision

  • Bytes: InputStream/OutputStream; text: Reader/Writer.
  • Always close with try-with-resources.
  • Use buffering.
  • Specify UTF-8.
  • Prefer Files and Path in new code.

What is a stream in Java?
Difference between InputStream and OutputStream
What are System.in, System.out, and System.err?
Difference between FileInputStream and FileReader

topics.name: Scanner in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Scanner reads and parses input from the keyboard, files or strings: nextInt, nextDouble, next and nextLine.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Programs need user input.
  • Scanner is the simplest way for beginners to read it.

3. Advantages

  • Easy to use.
  • Parses numbers and words directly.
  • Works with files and strings too.

4. Disadvantages

  • Slow for large inputs.
  • nextLine after nextInt gives an empty line.
  • InputMismatchException on bad input.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • First tool for interactive programs and practice problems.
  • Teaches input validation.
  • Common bug area in tests.

6. Basic Concepts

What is Scanner?

Scanner is a class in java.util used to read input - most commonly from the keyboard (System.in), but also from a String or a File.

  • It breaks input into tokens using whitespace as the default delimiter and lets you read each token as a specific type (int, double, a whole line, etc.).
  • It saves you from parsing raw bytes or characters yourself.

Basic usage:

Reading Different Types

Scanner has a matching next...() method for each primitive type, plus next() for a single whitespace-delimited word and nextLine() for an entire line.

hasNext...() — Checking Before You Read

Calling nextInt() (or any next...()) when there's no more matching input throws NoSuchElementException. The hasNext...() family lets you check first - this is the standard pattern for reading an unknown number of values, e.g. in a loop.

Fresher Notes

  • Create it: Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in); reads and parses input from the keyboard, files or strings.
  • Common methods: nextInt, nextDouble, next, nextLine, hasNext, hasNextInt.
  • Closing: close it when done, but not if System.in is still needed elsewhere.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Newline pitfall: after nextInt() the newline stays in the buffer, so a following nextLine() returns an empty line. Call nextLine() once to consume it.
  • Word vs line: next() reads a word; nextLine() reads the whole line.
  • Bad input: avoid InputMismatchException by checking hasNextInt() first.

8. Advanced Concepts

The Classic Trap: nextInt() Followed by nextLine()

nextInt(), nextDouble(), etc. read only the token itself - they do NOT consume the trailing newline character left in the input buffer. A following nextLine() then immediately reads that leftover empty remainder instead of waiting for new input.

This is one of the most common beginner bugs with Scanner:

InputMismatchException

If the next token doesn't match the type you asked for, Scanner throws InputMismatchException - and critically, the bad token is NOT consumed, so it's still sitting there for the next read (which will fail again unless you skip it).

Custom Delimiters

By default Scanner splits on whitespace, but useDelimiter(regex) lets it tokenize on anything - useful for CSV-style input.

Scanner Sources: String, File, and try-with-resources

Scanner can wrap a String, a File/InputStream, or System.in - the same API works regardless of source. Since Scanner implements Closeable, wrapping it in try-with-resources guarantees it's closed even if reading throws.

Important: closing a Scanner wrapped around System.in also closes the underlying System.in stream - so if your program needs to read from the console again later, don't close a System.in-backed Scanner prematurely (typically you only close it once, right before the program ends).

Full Scanner Method Reference

Beyond nextInt()/nextDouble()/next()/nextLine(), Scanner has a matching read method for every other primitive type, plus support for arbitrary-precision numbers:

MethodReads
nextByte()a byte value
nextShort()a short value
nextInt()an int value
nextLong()a long value
nextFloat()a float value
nextDouble()a double value
nextBoolean()a boolean value
next()a single whitespace-delimited word
nextLine()an entire line of text
nextBigInteger()a java.math.BigInteger (arbitrary-precision whole number)
nextBigDecimal()a java.math.BigDecimal (arbitrary-precision decimal)

nextBigInteger()/nextBigDecimal() matter when a value is too large for long/double, or when you need exact decimal precision (e.g. financial calculations) instead of binary floating-point.

There's also no nextChar() - to read a single character, read a word with next() and take its first character with charAt(0).

Scanner vs BufferedReader

AspectScannerBufferedReader
ParsingBuilt-in per-type parsing (nextInt, nextDouble, ...)Reads raw text only - you parse it yourself (e.g. Integer.parseInt)
PerformanceSlower - regex-based tokenizing overheadFaster - simple buffered character reads
Ease of useSimpler for typed, tokenized inputSimpler for fast line-by-line raw text
Typical use caseSmall console programs, quick input parsingLarge files, performance-sensitive reading

For everyday console input and small programs, Scanner's convenience wins. For reading large files quickly, BufferedReader is the better choice.

Senior Notes

  • Speed: Scanner is slow for large input (it uses regex); use BufferedReader with StringTokenizer for competitive programming.
  • Sources and delimiters: it can read a File or String and split on custom delimiters, e.g. useDelimiter(",").
  • Locale: it affects number parsing; set Locale.US for consistent decimals.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Practical usage: menu-driven loops, parsing files with new Scanner(new File(...)), findInLine with regex, useLocale(Locale.US), and try-with-resources. For batch or large inputs prefer BufferedReader; for typed config files use a real parser.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Scanner wraps a Readable (stream, file, string), reads into a char buffer and uses a delimiter regex (whitespace by default) to cut tokens, then parses them with the locale's number rules. hasNextX methods peek without consuming. nextLine uses the line separator pattern, which is why it behaves differently from next.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: nextInt then nextLine, not validating input (InputMismatchException loops forever if the bad token is not consumed), closing Scanner(System.in) too early (closes System.in for the rest of the program), locale decimal commas, and using Scanner for performance critical input.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Scanner reading 10^6 integers can take several times longer than BufferedReader plus manual parsing because of regex and per-token objects. In contests use DataInputStream custom readers.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a small CLI that reads commands in a loop, validates each, and exits on quit. For production CLIs use a library (picocli) for arguments and help text.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

The newline trap.

Worked Example 2

Fast reader.

Practice Exercise 1

Validated integer input.

Practice Exercise 2

Scan a string with delimiters.

11. Quick Revision

  • next reads a word, nextLine a line.
  • Consume the newline after nextInt.
  • Use hasNextInt to validate.
  • BufferedReader is faster for big input.
  • Close the Scanner when done.

interviewQA: Why does nextLine() after nextInt() return an empty string?
nextInt() consumes only the number token, leaving the trailing newline in the buffer; the following nextLine() immediately reads that leftover empty remainder
How do you fix the nextInt()/nextLine() bug?
Call an extra sc.nextLine() right after nextInt() to consume the leftover newline before reading the next real line
What happens if the input doesn't match the requested type?
Scanner throws InputMismatchException, and the invalid token is NOT consumed - it stays for the next read
What is Scanner's default delimiter?
Whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) - changeable via useDelimiter(regex)
Is it safe to close a Scanner wrapped around System.in and then read again later?
No - closing it also closes System.in itself, so any later read attempt will fail
Scanner vs BufferedReader - which is faster?
BufferedReader, since Scanner's type parsing uses regex-based tokenizing that adds overhead

topics.name: Serialization in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Serialization converts an object to a byte stream and deserialization rebuilds it, using Serializable, ObjectOutputStream and ObjectInputStream.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Objects often need to be saved to disk, sent over a network or cached.
  • Serialization turns their state into transferable data.

3. Advantages

  • Easy persistence of object graphs.
  • Supports sessions and caching.
  • transient excludes sensitive fields.

4. Disadvantages

  • Security risk when deserializing untrusted data.
  • Class changes can break compatibility.
  • Slower and larger than JSON or Protobuf.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Needed in legacy and framework code.
  • Teaches object lifecycle and security.
  • Common interview topic (transient, serialVersionUID).

6. Basic Concepts

What is Serialization?

Serialization is the process of converting an object's state into a byte stream, so it can be saved to a file, sent over a network, or stored in a database.

Deserialization is the reverse process - reading that byte stream back and reconstructing the original object in memory.

Serialization in Java is implemented using ObjectOutputStream (to write) and ObjectInputStream (to read).

How to Implement Serialization

  • A class must implement the Serializable interface to allow its objects to be serialized.
  • Serializable is a marker interface - it has no methods to implement. It simply tells the JVM "objects of this class are allowed to be converted into a byte stream."
  • ObjectOutputStream is used for serialization (writing the object out).
  • ObjectInputStream is used for deserialization (reading the object back in).

Below, the Student class implements Serializable:

Serializing an Object (Object -> File)

Create the object, then write it out with ObjectOutputStream.writeObject().

Deserializing an Object (File -> Object)

Read the same file back with ObjectInputStream.readObject() and print the fields to prove the object's state came back intact.

Important Points to Remember

  • ObjectOutputStream and ObjectInputStream are used for serialization and deserialization respectively.
  • Static variables are not serialized, because they belong to the class, not to any single object instance.
  • If a superclass implements Serializable, all of its subclasses are serializable by default (the marker is inherited).
  • Every Serializable class has a version number called serialVersionUID, used to verify compatibility during deserialization.
  • Serialization/deserialization is platform-independent - you can serialize an object on one platform and deserialize it on a completely different one, since the byte stream format doesn't depend on the OS or JVM implementation.

Where Is Serialization Used?

  • Storing a list of objects (e.g. Student objects) to disk instead of writing custom parsing logic.
  • Sending Java objects as messages between processes (e.g. a chat application, or between JVMs over a network).
  • Caching computed objects, or sending them across RMI/distributed calls.

Fresher Notes

  • Serialization turns an object into a byte stream. Deserialization rebuilds it. The class must implement java.io.Serializable, a marker interface (it has no methods).
  • Use ObjectOutputStream.writeObject to write and ObjectInputStream.readObject to read.
  • transient and static fields are not serialized.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • serialVersionUID identifies the class version. Declare it yourself to avoid InvalidClassException after class changes.
  • Object graphs: every field must be serializable (or transient), else NotSerializableException.
  • Constructors of the serializable class do not run on deserialization. The first non-serializable parent needs a no-arg constructor.

8. Advanced Concepts

Object -> Byte Stream -> Object

Serializable is a marker interface - it declares no methods. It just tells the JVM "this class is allowed to be converted into a byte stream."

   Object (in memory)
        |
        | ObjectOutputStream.writeObject()
        v
   Byte Stream  ------->  File / Network / Byte Array
        |
        | ObjectInputStream.readObject()
        v
   Object (reconstructed)

Below, ByteArrayOutputStream/ByteArrayInputStream are used instead of real files, so the whole round-trip runs safely in memory.

serialVersionUID - Version Compatibility

Every Serializable class has a version number used to verify that the sender and receiver of a serialized object agree on the class structure.

If you don't declare it explicitly

The serialization runtime (ObjectStreamClass) derives one at (de)serialization time from the class structure - javac never emits a serialVersionUID. This is fragile: if you later add/remove a field and recompile, the auto-generated UID changes.

Old serialized object (UID = 1234)
        |
        | class structure changes, no explicit serialVersionUID
        v
New class version (UID = 5678, auto-generated)
        |
        | ois.readObject() on the OLD byte stream
        v
InvalidClassException: local class incompatible

Best practice: always declare private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L; explicitly, and only bump it deliberately when you intentionally break backward compatibility.

transient - Skipping Sensitive/Derived Fields

A transient field is excluded from serialization entirely. After deserialization, it comes back as its default value (null for objects, 0/false for primitives) - not the value it held before serialization.

Serialization and Inheritance

  • Static fields are never serialized - they belong to the class, not the object instance.
  • If a superclass implements Serializable, every subclass is automatically serializable too.
  • If a superclass is NOT serializable, its fields are not written out either. During deserialization, only that non-serializable superclass's no-arg constructor runs (via reflection) to initialize its part of the object - so its fields fall back to whatever that constructor sets, not their previous values.

Serializing Object Graphs

If a Serializable object holds a reference to another object, that referenced object must also implement Serializable - otherwise serialization fails at runtime with NotSerializableException, even though the outer class compiles fine.

Custom Serialization: writeObject / readObject

Sometimes the default field-by-field serialization isn't enough - for example, encrypting a value before it's written, or recomputing a derived field after reading. Declaring private writeObject/readObject methods lets a class hook into the process while still using the standard Serializable mechanism.
<div class="bg-secondary p-2 rounded-md">

Senior Notes

  • Security: native serialization allows deserialization attacks. Never read untrusted data. Use ObjectInputFilter or avoid it.
  • Alternatives: JSON, Protobuf or Avro are language neutral, versionable and safer for data exchange.
  • Customizing: use writeObject / readObject, writeReplace, readResolve (keeps singletons) or Externalizable.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

readResolve replaces the object just read, so a singleton stays a singleton. The other hooks are writeObject / readObject (encrypt or validate), writeReplace (serialization proxy, safe for immutable classes) and Externalizable (full control).

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

ObjectOutputStream writes a stream header, class descriptors (name, serialVersionUID, field metadata) and field values. It tracks objects it has already written, so cycles work. Deserialization allocates the object without calling its constructor (it runs the first non-serializable parent constructor), then fills the fields. Static and transient fields are skipped.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes: no serialVersionUID (the auto value changes when the class changes), serializing inner classes (they capture the outer object), non-serializable fields, and secrets not marked transient. Records use their canonical constructor; enums are always safe singletons. The fix for the first mistake is below.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Native serialization is slow and verbose compared to Protobuf, Kryo or JSON. For caches and RPC use schema-based formats. For large graphs, avoid serializing whole entity graphs (for example lazy relations).

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

HTTP sessions and distributed caches serialize objects, so session classes must be Serializable. In production, set a global deserialization filter.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Deserialization filter. Allow only your own package and reject the rest.

Worked Example 2

JSON instead.

Practice Exercise 1

Save and load an object.

Practice Exercise 2

Not serializable field.

Common Interview Traps

ClaimReality
Static fields get serializedNo - static fields belong to the class, not the instance, so they're skipped entirely
The constructor runs during deserializationNo - the object is rebuilt via reflection; only the FIRST non-serializable superclass's no-arg constructor runs
If a superclass is Serializable, subclasses are tooYes - Serializable is inherited automatically
transient fields keep their value after deserializationNo - they reset to the type's default value

Serializable vs Externalizable

AspectSerializableExternalizable
Methods to implementNone (marker interface)writeExternal() / readExternal()
Control over formatJVM-default, automaticFully manual, you decide exactly what's written
PerformanceSlower (uses reflection)Faster (explicit, no reflection overhead)
Public no-arg constructorNot requiredRequired - called during deserialization

Rule of thumb: use plain Serializable for everyday DTOs; reach for Externalizable only when you need precise control over the wire format or serialization performance is critical.

11. Quick Revision

  • Implement Serializable.
  • transient and static fields are skipped.
  • Declare serialVersionUID.
  • Never deserialize untrusted data.
  • Prefer JSON or Protobuf for APIs.

interviewQA: What is serialization and deserialization?
Serialization converts an object's state into a byte stream; deserialization reconstructs the object from that byte stream
Why is Serializable a marker interface?
It declares no methods - it just flags the class to the JVM as "safe to serialize", relying on reflection to do the actual work
What is the transient keyword used for?
To exclude a field from serialization; it comes back as the default value (null/0/false) after deserialization
Why aren't static variables serialized?
They belong to the class itself, not to any individual object instance, so there's no "object state" to save
What is serialVersionUID and why does it matter?
A version number that verifies the sender and receiver agree on the class structure; a mismatch throws InvalidClassException during deserialization

topics.name: Properties File in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A properties file stores configuration as key=value pairs and is loaded with java.util.Properties.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Settings such as database URLs and ports change per environment and should not be hard-coded.

3. Advantages

  • Externalized configuration without recompiling.
  • Simple text format.
  • Supported by Spring Boot and many libraries.

4. Disadvantages

  • Only flat string values.
  • No type safety.
  • Secrets must not be stored in plain files.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Real applications are configured, not hard-coded.
  • Prepares for Spring profiles.
  • Teaches resource loading from the classpath.

6. Basic Concepts

What is a Properties File?

A properties file is a simple configuration file - a plain text file with a .properties extension that stores data as key=value pairs.

  • It is used to externalize configuration (database URLs, credentials, app settings, language translations) so it can be changed without touching or recompiling the source code.
  • Values like usernames, passwords, or environment URLs change often. Hardcoding them in Java classes forces a rebuild for every change. A .properties file solves that.

Example - simple.properties

username=pankaj
password=pune

Format and Key Features

  • Each line represents one property, in the form key=value.
  • Comments start with # or !.
  • Commonly used for application configuration and internationalization (i18n) - storing separate translation files per language.

Example - config.properties

# Database configuration
db.url = jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/mydatabase
db.user = root
db.password = secret

# Application settings
app.name = MyApp
app.version = 1.0.0

Reading a Properties File with java.util.Properties

The java.util.Properties class loads key-value pairs from a file via load(), and reads them back with getProperty().

How It Works

  • Properties class - an instance of java.util.Properties holds the loaded key-value data in memory.
  • FileInputStream - opens the .properties file so it can be read.
  • load() method - reads all key=value lines from the stream into the Properties object.
  • getProperty() method - retrieves the value for a given key, returning null if the key does not exist.
  • try-with-resources - closes the InputStream automatically once reading is done, even if an exception occurs.

Fresher Notes

  • Format: a .properties file stores configuration as key=value lines, loaded with java.util.Properties.
  • Reading: use props.load(inputStream) and getProperty("key", "default").
  • Comments: lines starting with # or ! are ignored.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Class path: load with getResourceAsStream("/app.properties") so it works inside a jar.
  • String values: values are always Strings, so parse numbers and booleans yourself.
  • Saving and encoding: save with store(out, comments). load(InputStream) reads ISO-8859-1, so for non-ASCII text pass a UTF-8 InputStreamReader to load(Reader).

8. Advanced Concepts

getProperty() Overload With a Default Value

getProperty(String key) returns null if the key is missing, forcing a null check everywhere. getProperty(String key, String defaultValue) avoids that by supplying a fallback directly.

Writing / Updating a Properties File with store()

Properties is a subclass of Hashtable, so values can be set with setProperty() just like a map entry, then persisted back to disk with store().

Loading Properties From the Classpath

Reading via a hardcoded FileInputStream path breaks once the app is packaged into a JAR - the file is usually not at that filesystem path anymore. The standard fix is loading it as a classpath resource instead, using the class loader.

Senior Notes

  • Externalize environment-specific settings (URLs, secrets) from code. Spring Boot supports application.properties and profiles.
  • Secrets: never commit them; read them from environment variables or a vault.
  • Hierarchy: for nested config prefer YAML or typed config classes (@ConfigurationProperties).

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Layered configuration: defaults, file, environment, command line. ResourceBundle loads localized properties (messages_hi.properties). Spring Boot binds properties to typed beans with @ConfigurationProperties and supports relaxed names and profiles.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Properties extends Hashtable<Object,Object> and parses lines with key separators =, : or whitespace, supports line continuation with a trailing backslash and Unicode escapes \uXXXX. getProperty checks the defaults chain; stringPropertyNames returns keys of String type. Since Java 9, ResourceBundle reads its properties files as UTF-8, but Properties.load(InputStream) still uses ISO-8859-1.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: relative file paths that break in jars, ignoring missing files (NPE when getResourceAsStream returns null), storing secrets, forgetting trimming, parsing booleans or numbers without defaults, and editing files at run time without reload logic. Fail fast on missing required keys.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Loading config once at startup is cheap; reading files on every request is not. Cache parsed values, reload with a WatchService only if needed, and avoid synchronizing on Properties (it is a synchronized Hashtable).

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: Spring Boot externalized configuration with profiles and secrets from environment variables.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Environment override.

Worked Example 2

System properties.

Practice Exercise 1

Load from the class path.

Practice Exercise 2

Write properties.

11. Quick Revision

  • key=value, # for comments.
  • Load with getResourceAsStream.
  • getProperty(key, default).
  • Values are strings; parse them.
  • Keep secrets out of the repository.

interviewQA: Why use a properties file instead of hardcoding values?
It externalizes configuration so values (DB URLs, credentials, app settings) can change without recompiling the source code
Which class is used to read/write a properties file?
java.util.Properties
What does getProperty() return if the key does not exist?
null, unless the overload with a defaultValue is used, in which case it returns that default
What class does Properties extend?
java.util.Hashtable<Object,Object> - so it can also be used with the general Map/Hashtable API, though the String-based getProperty()/setProperty() methods are preferred
How do you comment a line in a .properties file?
Start the line with # or !
Why load properties from the classpath instead of a fixed file path?
A fixed filesystem path breaks once the app is packaged into a JAR; classpath loading (getResourceAsStream) works consistently in both the IDE and the packaged artifact
What is a common real-world use of properties files?
Internationalization (i18n) - separate .properties files per language/locale - and environment-specific configuration (dev/test/prod)

topics.name: Final Keyword

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Final prevents change: a final variable is assigned once, a final method cannot be overridden and a final class cannot be extended.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Constants, safe APIs and immutable objects rely on final to guarantee that something never changes.

3. Advantages

  • Clear constants.
  • Protects behavior from overriding.
  • Final fields are safely published to other threads.

4. Disadvantages

  • Final reference does not make the object immutable.
  • final classes cannot be mocked or extended easily.
  • Overuse adds noise.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used for constants and immutable classes.
  • Needed for lambdas (effectively final).
  • Common interview topic (final, finally, finalize).

6. Basic Concepts

  • final is a keyword in Java that can be applied to variables, methods, and classes.
  • In every case, final is used to restrict modification:
    • final variable: the value cannot be reassigned (acts like a constant).
    • final method: cannot be overridden by a subclass.
    • final class: cannot be extended/inherited at all.

Below is one small, runnable example (with proof) for each of the three uses.

1. Final Variable

  • A variable declared with final is called a final variable.
  • Once a value is assigned, it cannot be changed - final variables behave like constants.

Final Variable - Compile Time Error

  • Any attempt to reassign a final variable's value causes a compile-time error.

2. Final Method

  • A method declared with final is called a final method.
  • Final methods cannot be overridden by a subclass.

3. Final Class

  • A class declared with final cannot be extended/inherited at all.
  • String, Integer and every wrapper class are examples of final classes in the JDK.

Fresher Notes

  • Three uses: a final variable is assigned once, a final method cannot be overridden, a final class cannot be extended (like String).
  • Constants are written static final int MAX = 10;.
  • Final reference: it cannot point to another object, but the object itself can change.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Blank final fields must be set in the declaration, an initializer block or every constructor.
  • Final parameters and locals cannot be reassigned; lambdas can capture effectively final variables.
  • Do not confuse final with finally (try block) and finalize() (deprecated).

8. Advanced Concepts

final Applies to Three Things - Quick Recap

Applied toEffect
VariableValue can be assigned only once - acts as a constant
MethodCannot be overridden by any subclass (can still be overloaded)
ClassCannot be extended/inherited by any subclass

Blank Final Variable

  • A blank final variable is declared without an initializer.
  • It must be assigned exactly once, in an initializer block or in every constructor of the class.
  • If even one constructor path forgets to assign it, that is a compile-time error.

Final Reference vs Immutable Object

  • final on a reference variable only stops reassignment of that reference.
  • It does not make the object itself immutable - mutable fields can still change via setters.
  • emp = new Employee(); after a final assignment is a compile-time error, but emp.setName(...) works fine.

Final Parameters

  • A method parameter declared final cannot be reassigned inside the method body.
  • Used mainly for defensive coding: it signals (and enforces) that the parameter's value stays untouched.

Effectively Final - Why Lambdas & Anonymous Classes Need It

  • A local variable that is never reassigned after initialization is called effectively final, even without the final keyword.
  • Any local variable or parameter used inside a lambda or anonymous inner class must be final or effectively final.
  • Reason: the lambda may outlive the method call (for example, stored and run later). The compiler copies the value when the lambda is created, so it forbids capturing a variable that could still change.

final + static = True Constant

  • static alone means "one copy shared by the class"; final alone means "cannot be reassigned".
  • Combined, static final gives a single class-wide constant - the standard way to declare true constants in Java.
  • Convention: name constants in UPPER_CASE with underscores, e.g. MAX_USERS.

Final Class in the JDK - Why String/Wrapper Classes Are Final

  • String, Integer, and every wrapper class (Double, Boolean, etc.) are final.
  • Reasons: it locks in immutability, protects the String Pool from a mutable subclass changing behavior, and closes security holes (for example, a fake String subclass slipping past code that trusts String).

Performance: Does final Make Code Faster?

  • Common folklore says "final helps the JIT inline methods and speeds things up."
  • Reality: the JIT compiler can already inline non-final methods in most cases (using class hierarchy analysis). It only has to undo that work if a subclass later overrides the method.
  • final mainly helps the compiler and the developer reason about correctness. Any speed effect is usually negligible, so use final for design intent and safety, not as a performance trick.

final Is Not Allowed on Interface Methods

  • The Java Language Specification does not permit the final modifier on any interface method (abstract, default or static). It is a compile-time error.
  • Intuition: an abstract method has no body to protect, and a default method that could never be overridden would defeat the purpose of an interface as a flexible contract.
  • Related fact: any field declared in an interface is implicitly public static final, so interfaces hold only constants, never mutable state.

Senior Notes

  • Immutable classes use a final class, private final fields and no setters; the Java Memory Model (JMM) guarantees safe publication of final fields.
  • Compile-time constants (static final primitives and strings) are inlined into callers.
  • Design rule: declare classes final unless designed for extension (Effective Java).

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Use final for: constants (static final), fields set once, parameters you do not reassign, classes not designed for extension, and methods that must keep their behavior (template methods). For an immutable class use: a final class, private final fields, no setters, and defensive copies of mutable inputs and outputs.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The compiler checks that every final variable is assigned exactly once (definite assignment). Reflection can change final instance fields only in special cases, and it is blocked for records and hidden classes. The Java Memory Model adds a freeze at the end of a constructor, so other threads see final fields correctly without synchronization.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes: thinking final makes an object immutable, making everything final out of habit (noise), changing a constant in a library without recompiling its clients (constants are inlined), and marking methods final only to speed them up. Use final for intent.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

final has no direct speed effect; its value is correctness and thread safety. A new final local in each loop pass lets every lambda capture its own value.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: value objects, configuration holders and DTOs are final and immutable, which makes them safe to share across threads without locks. A record is implicitly final and has final fields.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Effectively final in lambdas.

Worked Example 2

Final method.

Practice Exercise 1

Final reference vs immutable object.

Practice Exercise 2

Blank final set in constructor.

11. Quick Revision

  • final variable: one assignment.
  • final method: no override.
  • final class: no subclass.
  • Final reference, mutable object is possible.
  • final vs finally vs finalize.

interviewQA: Difference between final, finally, finalize()?

final = keyword restricting modification (variable/method/class); finally = block that always runs after try/catch for cleanup; finalize() = deprecated Object method GC used to call before reclaiming memory - the three are unrelated
Can a final method be overloaded?
Yes - final only blocks overriding, not overloading in the same class
Can a final class have subclasses?
No - a final class can never be extended
What is a blank final variable?
A final variable declared without an initializer; it must be assigned exactly once in every constructor
Does final on a reference make the object immutable?
No - it only prevents reassigning the reference itself; the object's mutable fields can still change via its own methods
Why must lambdas/anonymous classes only use final or effectively final locals?

They may execute after the enclosing method returns, so the compiler captures the variable's value at creation time; allowing reassignment would create a mismatch between the captured value and the live variable
Why are String and wrapper classes final?
To preserve immutability, protect the String Pool, and prevent security exploits via malicious subclassing
Does final always improve performance?
Not meaningfully - modern JITs can already inline non-final methods; use final for correctness/design intent, not as a performance trick
Can an interface method be declared final?
No - never, for abstract, default, or static interface methods alike; it's a compile-time error in all three cases

topics.name: Wrapper Class

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Wrapper classes (Integer, Double, Boolean, Character and others) wrap primitives as objects, with autoboxing and unboxing between them.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Collections and generics work only with objects, so primitives need object versions with useful methods.

3. Advantages

  • Allow primitives in collections and generics.
  • Provide utility methods like parseInt and compare.
  • Can represent null (absent value).

4. Disadvantages

  • Boxing costs memory and time.
  • Unboxing null throws NullPointerException.
  • == on wrappers can mislead (cache).

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used daily with collections.
  • Frequent interview topic (cache, autoboxing).
  • Understanding the cost of boxing improves performance.

6. Basic Concepts

What is a Wrapper Class?

A Wrapper Class is a predefined class (in the java.lang package) that "wraps" a primitive data type inside an object. Every primitive type (int, double, boolean, etc.) has a matching wrapper class (Integer, Double, Boolean, etc.) that stores the same value, but as an object.

Why do we need Wrapper Classes?

Primitives are fast and lightweight, but plain values - they don't behave like objects. Wrapper classes exist to bridge that gap:

  1. Collections need objects - classes like ArrayList and HashMap can only store objects, never primitives directly.
  2. Object methods - wrapper objects support useful methods like toString(), equals(), and compareTo() that a bare primitive can't offer.
  3. Null is allowed - a wrapper variable can hold null to represent "no value", something a primitive can never do.
  4. Utility conversions - wrapper classes provide handy static methods like parseInt() to convert between Strings and numbers.

The 8 Wrapper Classes

Java has exactly 8 primitive types, and each one has exactly one matching wrapper class:

Primitive TypeWrapper Class
byteByte
shortShort
intInteger
longLong
floatFloat
doubleDouble
charCharacter
booleanBoolean

Autoboxing - Primitive to Object

Autoboxing is the automatic conversion of a primitive value into its wrapper object, done by the compiler. You don't have to write new Integer(...) yourself - simply assigning a primitive to a wrapper-typed variable is enough.

Unboxing - Object to Primitive

Unboxing is the reverse: automatically converting a wrapper object back into its primitive value. This happens whenever a wrapper object is assigned to (or used as) a primitive.

Useful Wrapper Methods

Wrapper classes ship with static helper methods that make conversions easy:

  1. parseInt(String) - converts a String into a primitive int.
  2. valueOf(...) - returns a wrapper object for a primitive or a String.
  3. toString() - returns the String representation of the wrapped value.

Fresher Notes

  • Wrapper classes wrap primitives as objects: Integer, Long, Double, Boolean, Character, Byte, Short, Float.
  • Autoboxing converts a primitive to its wrapper automatically, unboxing does the reverse: Integer x = 5; int y = x;.
  • Collections need objects: List<Integer>, not List<int>.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Useful methods: Integer.parseInt, valueOf, toString, compare, MAX_VALUE, Character.isDigit.
  • Compare with equals, not == (the Integer cache covers -128 to 127).
  • Null unboxing: unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException.

8. Advanced Concepts

Integer Caching (-128 to 127)

Java caches Integer objects for values from -128 to 127 (the IntegerCache). When autoboxing a value in that range, the same cached object is reused, so == comparison returns true. Outside that range, each autoboxed value creates a new heap object, so == returns false.

NullPointerException Risk from Unboxing

A wrapper variable can legally hold null. But the moment that null is unboxed - used inside an if condition, in arithmetic, or as a method argument expecting a primitive - Java throws a NullPointerException. This is one of the most common real-world wrapper bugs, especially with fields that were never initialized or values missing from a database/map.

Autoboxing/Unboxing Cost in Loops

Using Integer instead of int inside a tight loop causes a new wrapper object to be created on every autobox, adding allocation and garbage-collection overhead that a primitive int never incurs. Prefer primitives for counters/accumulators and only box when an API (like Collections) requires an object.

Wrapper Classes Are Immutable

Like String, wrapper objects can never change the value they hold once created. Reassigning a wrapper variable doesn't mutate the existing object - it points the reference at a brand-new object.

parseInt() vs valueOf() and NumberFormatException

Integer.parseInt(String) returns a primitive int. Integer.valueOf(String) returns a boxed Integer (using the cache when possible). Both throw NumberFormatException if the string isn't a valid number.

Radix-Based Parsing and MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE Constants

Numeric wrapper classes accept an optional radix (base) argument in parseInt()/valueOf(), useful for parsing binary, octal, or hex strings. Every numeric wrapper also ships MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE constants describing its representable range.

Senior Notes

  • Boxing in loops creates garbage and slows hot code; use primitives or primitive streams.
  • Immutable wrappers can be map keys; Integer.valueOf may reuse cached objects, new Integer is deprecated.
  • Overloads: be careful with list.remove(int) vs remove(Object).

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Utility methods: Integer.parseInt(s, radix), toHexString, bitCount, Integer.MAX_VALUE, Character.getNumericValue, Double.isNaN, Boolean.logicalAnd, Long.compareUnsigned, Integer.toUnsignedString. Primitive streams (IntStream) avoid boxing; OptionalInt avoids boxing for optionals.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Boxing calls Integer.valueOf(int), which returns cached instances for -128..127 (the upper bound is configurable with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax), otherwise allocates. Unboxing calls intValue(). Wrappers are immutable final classes extending Number (except Boolean and Character). A boxed Integer is about 16 bytes versus 4 for int.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: == on wrappers, NPE on unboxing, mixing types in a ternary (cond ? 1 : null unboxes to int and can NPE), Long vs Integer equals (different types are never equal), and boxing in generic code in hot loops. Use equals or compare.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Boxed collections cost memory and cache misses: a List<Integer> of one million items uses about 20 MB versus 4 MB for int[]. Use primitive arrays, IntStream, or libraries like Eclipse Collections and fastutil for numeric workloads.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: JSON and database mapping use wrappers to represent nullable numbers (a missing value is null, a zero is 0). Use Integer fields in entities for nullable columns and primitives for required ones.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Remove overload trap.

Worked Example 2

Parsing errors.

Practice Exercise 1

Boxing, parsing and caching.

Practice Exercise 2

Null unboxing.

Common Interview Traps

TrapWhy it happens
NullPointerException on unboxing null Integer in arithmeticInteger x = null; int y = x + 1; unboxes null, throws NPE
== vs .equals() for wrappers== compares references (only reliable inside the -128..127 cache); .equals() always compares values
Ternary autoboxing NPEMixing an int and an Integer in a ternary makes the result type int, so the Integer branch is unboxed. Only the branch actually chosen is evaluated, so the NPE happens only when the null wrapper is chosen. With flag = true the code below prints 1; set flag = false to see the NullPointerException

11. Quick Revision

  • Autoboxing: int to Integer automatically.
  • Integer cache: -128 to 127.
  • Use equals for wrappers.
  • Unboxing null causes NPE.
  • remove(int) vs remove(Object) on lists.

interviewQA: What are the 8 wrapper classes in Java?
Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character, Boolean
Why do we need wrapper classes if we have primitives?
Collections/generics only work with objects, wrapper objects support useful methods, and only wrappers can hold null
What is autoboxing vs unboxing?
Autoboxing = compiler auto-converts primitive to wrapper; unboxing = compiler auto-converts wrapper back to primitive
What is the Integer cache?
Integer.valueOf() (used implicitly by autoboxing) reuses cached objects for values -128 to 127, so == works there but not for larger values
Are wrapper objects mutable?
No, they are immutable, just like String - every "change" creates a new object
What causes NPE with wrappers?
Unboxing a null wrapper reference, e.g. using it in arithmetic, an if condition, or a ternary expression

topics.name: Methods in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A method is a named block of code with parameters and an optional return value, defined inside a class and called to perform an action.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Methods remove duplication and break big problems into small, testable steps.

3. Advantages

  • Reusability.
  • Modularity and readability.
  • Overloading gives flexible APIs.

4. Disadvantages

  • Too many parameters hurt readability.
  • Long methods are hard to test.
  • Overload resolution can be confusing.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • All behavior in Java lives in methods.
  • Needed to understand OOP and recursion.
  • Pass-by-value is a favorite interview question.

6. Basic Concepts

What is a Method?

A method is a named block of code that performs a specific task, defined inside a class. Methods exist so logic can be written once and reused via a simple call, instead of copy-pasting the same code everywhere.

Anatomy of a method:

Calling a Method

A method runs only when it's called - defining it doesn't execute anything by itself. Call it using objectName.methodName(arguments) for instance methods.

Parameters vs Arguments

  • Parameters are the variables listed in the method's definition (int a, int b).
  • Arguments are the actual values passed in when the method is called (5, 3).

People often use the two words interchangeably, but technically a parameter is the placeholder, an argument is the real value plugged into it.

void vs Value-Returning Methods

A method's return type says what kind of value it hands back to the caller - or void if it doesn't return anything at all.

Method Overloading

Java lets multiple methods share the same name in the same class, as long as their parameter lists differ (different number, type, or order of parameters). The compiler picks the right one based on the arguments you pass at the call site.

Fresher Notes

  • Syntax: returnType name(parameters) { ... }. Call it by name with arguments.
  • Return: void methods return nothing; others must return a value of the declared type.
  • Kinds: instance methods need an object; static methods are called on the class.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Overloading: same name, different parameter lists (type, number or order); the return type alone is not enough.
  • Pass by value: a primitive copies its value; an object variable copies its reference, so the object can change but the caller variable is never repointed.
  • Varargs: int... nums accepts any number of arguments.

8. Advanced Concepts

Pass-by-Value — Even for Objects

Java is strictly pass-by-value - always. For primitives, a copy of the value is passed. For objects, a copy of the reference (the address) is passed - not the object itself. This distinction is one of the most misunderstood/asked interview topics in Java.

Because the reference is copied, the method CAN mutate the object it points to (both copies point to the same heap object), but reassigning the parameter inside the method never affects the caller's original reference.

Overload Resolution — Which Method Actually Gets Picked

When multiple overloads could technically match, the compiler prefers, in order: (1) an exact type match, (2) a match via widening primitive conversion (e.g. int -> long), (3) a match via autoboxing (int -> Integer), (4) a match via varargs - varargs is always the last resort.

Return Type Alone Cannot Distinguish Overloads

Two methods with the same name and same parameter list, differing only by return type, do NOT compile as valid overloads - the compiler can't tell them apart from the call site alone.

Static vs Instance Methods

AspectInstance MethodStatic Method
Belongs toAn objectThe class itself
Called viaobjectRef.method()ClassName.method() (or unqualified within the same class)
Can access instance fields directly?YesNo - only static fields, unless given an object reference
Can be overridden?Yes (runtime polymorphism)No - can only be hidden, resolved at compile time

Senior Notes

  • Design: keep methods small with one purpose; name them with verbs; limit parameters (3 or fewer, otherwise pass an object).
  • Validation: check inputs early (Objects.requireNonNull, IllegalArgumentException).
  • Ambiguity: when two overloads fit equally well, the call fails to compile.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants
