Advanced forms: varargs, generic methods (<T> T first(List<T> l)), recursion, method references, default and static interface methods, private helper methods, synchronized methods, and covariant returns. Tail calls are not optimized by the JVM, so deep recursion can overflow the stack.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Each call creates a stack frame holding locals, the operand stack and a reference to the constant pool; arguments are copied into it (pass by value). Dispatch: invokestatic (static), invokespecial (constructors, private, super), invokevirtual (class instance methods, dynamic lookup), invokeinterface, and invokedynamic (lambdas). Overloads are chosen at compile time, overrides at run time.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: believing Java is pass by reference, swapping values with a method (cannot swap primitives), huge methods, unnecessary side effects, too many parameters, boolean flag parameters (split into two methods), ignoring return values, and unbounded recursion (StackOverflowError). Return results instead of mutating parameters.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Small methods are inlined by the JIT (default limit about 35 bytecodes for non-hot methods, 325 for hot), so splitting code for clarity rarely costs speed. Avoid allocation in tight loops and prefer iteration over deep recursion; memoize repeated work.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: service methods with guard clauses, clear names and small responsibilities; helpers extracted until each method reads like a sentence.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Ambiguity.

Worked Example 2

Early validation.

Practice Exercise 1

Overloading and varargs.

Practice Exercise 2

Pass by value.

11. Quick Revision

  • Signature: name + parameters.
  • Java is always pass by value.
  • Overloading: same name, different parameters.
  • Varargs accept many arguments.
  • Keep methods small and focused.

interviewQA: Can a method mutate an object passed into it?
Yes, since both the caller's and the parameter's references point to the same heap object - but reassigning the parameter itself never affects the caller's reference
Why can't two methods differ only by return type?
The compiler resolves which overload to call based on the arguments at the call site, not the expected return type, so an ambiguous case would be uncompilable

topics.name: Return Object from Method

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A method can return an object, for example a new instance, an existing reference or this for chaining.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Methods often produce complex results, not just numbers.
  • Returning objects allows factories, builders and fluent APIs.

3. Advantages

  • Enables factory methods and builders.
  • Method chaining gives readable code.
  • Records can return several values at once.

4. Disadvantages

  • Returning internal mutable objects breaks encapsulation.
  • Returning null causes NullPointerException.
  • Callers may modify shared objects by mistake.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Needed for real-world design patterns.
  • Teaches reference semantics.
  • Common in interview code reading.

6. Basic Concepts

  • In industry, methods usually return objects instead of primitive data types.
  • One method call can hand back several related values bundled together, so the caller does not juggle separate int and String returns.
  • This makes code more reusable and maintainable.

Basic Object Return

A method can return an object of its own class type, just like it can return an int or a String.

Printing a Returned Object (Without toString)

If toString() is not overridden, printing the object prints its default reference text: fully.qualified.ClassName@hashcode.

Printing a Returned Object (With toString)

Override toString() so the returned object prints something meaningful instead of a memory reference.

Getter-Style Method Returning an Object

Instead of returning a raw int id, a method can construct and return the whole object that owns that id - the caller then reads whichever field it needs.

Why This Matters: Bundling Multiple Values Into One Return

A Java method can only return one value. If a method needs to hand back an id, a name, and a city, you cannot return three separate primitives. Returning one object that carries all three fields is the standard fix.

Fresher Notes

  • Return type: a method can return an object: static Student create() { return new Student(); }. The return type is the class.
  • Reference: the caller gets a reference to the same object that was created or stored.
  • Chaining: return this to enable method chaining.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Encapsulation: returning internal mutable fields exposes your state; return a copy or an unmodifiable view.
  • No null: return an empty collection instead of null; use Optional for a possibly missing single value.
  • Factory methods return objects of a class or its subtypes (an interface return type).

8. Advanced Concepts

Returning a Newly Created Object (Factory-Style Method)

A method can construct an object on the heap and hand back a reference to it - the caller's variable simply points to that same heap object.

createEmployee()
      |
  new Employee()  -----> Heap: Employee{id=10, name="Pankaj"}
      |
   return emp            ^
      |                  |
   caller's "e" ---------+

Returning "this" for Method Chaining (Fluent API)

Returning this from an instance method lets calls be chained together - the pattern used by StringBuilder and most builder classes.

New Object Every Call vs a Shared/Cached Object

A factory method can either build a brand-new object every time it is called, or hand back a reference to the same cached/shared object (common in caches, flyweights, and singletons). The two behave very differently once the caller starts mutating what it got back.

Danger: Returning a Mutable Internal Reference

Returning a mutable field directly (like a List) leaks a live reference to your internal state - external code can silently modify it. The fix is a defensive copy.

Returning null vs Optional<T> (Java 8+)

Returning null to signal "no result" forces every caller to remember a null check, or risk a NullPointerException. Optional<T> makes the "may be absent" case explicit in the method signature.

Senior Notes

  • Interface types: return List, not ArrayList, to keep flexibility.
  • Multiple values: records and small immutable objects are ideal for returning several values.
  • Covariant return types let an override return a subtype.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Options for results: plain object, record, Optional<T>, a result type (sealed Success/Failure), exceptions for truly exceptional cases, and CompletableFuture<T> for async. Never return null for collections or arrays; return List.of().

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Returning an object returns a copy of the reference; both caller and callee see the same heap object. Escape analysis may avoid allocating objects that never escape the method. Fluent APIs return this (or a new immutable instance in "wither" style); factories return subtypes behind an interface.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: returning null (NullPointerException at the caller), exposing internal mutable state, returning Optional fields or Optional parameters (misuse), returning concrete types unnecessarily, and returning arrays that callers modify. Return copies or immutable views.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Allocation per call is cheap; the cost is garbage and pointer chasing. Return primitives where a value is enough, and reuse objects only for proven hot spots. Records are compact and JIT friendly.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a repository returns Optional for lookups, a service returns a DTO record, and a controller maps it to a response.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Optional return.

Worked Example 2

Leaking internal state.

Practice Exercise 1

Fluent builder.

Practice Exercise 2

Return a record.

11. Quick Revision

  • The return type is the class.
  • The caller gets a reference, not a copy.
  • return this enables chaining.
  • Return empty collections, not null.
  • Use Optional for absent values.

interviewQA: Why return an object instead of multiple primitives?
A method can only return one value; bundling related values into an object is the standard way to return "multiple" results
Returning a local primitive vs a local object
A primitive returns a copy of the value; an object returns a copy of the reference - the caller still points to the same heap object the method created
Returning an array vs a Collection
Both leak a mutable reference to internal state the same way - always consider a defensive copy or an unmodifiable wrapper
Covariant return types
An overriding method may narrow the return type to a subtype of the parent's declared return type (e.g. Animal reproduce() overridden to return Dog)
Returning "this" from a void-intent method
Only do this deliberately for fluent/builder APIs - it changes the method's contract from "do something" to "do something and let me chain"
null vs Optional as a return value
null forces every caller to remember a check; Optional makes "may be absent" part of the method's signature, which the compiler and IDE can nudge callers to handle

topics.id: Different way to return to the method in java.
topics.name: Different way to return to the method in java.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A method can end by a return statement, by throwing an exception or by reaching the end of a void method.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Understanding all exit paths helps you write correct control flow, especially with loops and try-finally.

3. Advantages

  • Guard clauses simplify logic.
  • Early return avoids deep nesting.
  • Exceptions signal failures clearly.

4. Disadvantages

  • Multiple returns can hide logic if overused.
  • return in finally overrides exceptions.
  • Missing return paths fail to compile.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Helps predict program output.
  • Important for exception handling topics.
  • Common interview trap questions.

6. Basic Concepts

Returning a Primitive Value

A method can return a primitive type (int, double, boolean, etc.) - the caller gets a copy of the value, not a reference.

Returning an Object

Instead of a primitive, a method can return a whole object - useful when the caller needs more than one related piece of data.

Returning an Array

A method can return an array when it needs to hand back a fixed-size group of values of the same type.

Returning Nothing - void

A method declared void returns no value at all. It can still use a bare return; (no value after it) to exit early.

Fresher Notes

  • Ways to end: a method ends by return (with or without a value), by throwing an exception, or by reaching the end of a void method.
  • Early exit: return; leaves a void method early.
  • Non-void rule: a method with a return type must return a value on every path.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Stop early: return from loops, switch cases and nested conditions.
  • Return types: primitives, objects, arrays, collections, lambdas or null.
  • Unreachable code: a statement after return does not compile.

8. Advanced Concepts

Returning a List / Collection

Just like an array, a method can return a List (or any Collection) so the caller can iterate over a variable number of results.

Returning Multiple Values from a Method

A Java method can only return one value - there is no native tuple/multi-return syntax. To hand back several related values at once, bundle them into a single object or array. The standard workarounds, from best to worst:

ApproachNotes
record (Java 16+)Cleanest - type-safe, immutable, auto toString/equals/hashCode
Small wrapper classSame idea pre-Java 16, more boilerplate
Array/List of ObjectType-unsafe, needs casting - avoid
Mutable holder / out-parameterPass an object in, mutate it - works but less idiomatic in Java

Returning "this" for Method Chaining (Fluent API)

An instance method can return this (the current object) instead of a new object - each call returns the same instance, letting calls be chained one after another. This is the pattern used by StringBuilder and most builder classes.

Returning a Functional Interface / Lambda

A method can return an instance of a functional interface (like Supplier<T>) - effectively returning "behavior" rather than a plain value. The caller decides when to actually invoke it.

Guard Clauses (Multiple Returns) vs Single Exit Point

Two competing styles for the same logic - both are valid, but readability differs:

  • Guard clauses - return early for invalid/edge cases, keeping the "happy path" unindented and easy to scan.
  • Single-return style - one return statement at the very end, using nested if/else to build the result.

Modern Java style generally favors guard clauses for validation-heavy methods.

"Returning" via Output Parameters (void methods)

A void method can still hand data back to the caller by mutating an object passed in - common with StringBuilder/collections, but should be used sparingly since it hides the "output" from the method signature.

Returning a Stream Instead of a Materialized List

A method can return a lazily-evaluated Stream<T> instead of fully building a List<T> up front - elements are only computed as the caller consumes them, which can save memory/work for large or infinite sequences.

Senior Notes

  • Guard clauses: several return points are fine when they avoid deep nesting.
  • try/finally: the finally block runs before the method really returns; a return inside it overrides the earlier result.
  • Lambdas: return the value of their expression, or use return in a block body.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Exits: normal return with value, early void return, exception, System.exit (never returns), infinite loops, and for lambdas the return of the functional method. Use guard clauses, Optional chaining, switch expressions with yield, and streams (findFirst) to express early outcomes.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

In bytecode a method ends with one of ireturn, areturn, return or by an exception propagating out. finally blocks are copied before every exit path. The JVM unwinds the frame and passes the result to the caller, or searches the exception table for a handler.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: return in finally, System.exit inside libraries, forgetting to return in a branch, and unreachable code after return/throw/break. Also, a catch that returns null hides failures; log or rethrow with context.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Exceptions are far slower than returns when thrown frequently (stack trace capture). For expected failures such as validation, return a result or boolean instead of throwing in hot paths.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: request handlers use guard clauses to return errors early (401, 400) and keep the happy path unindented.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

finally overrides.

Worked Example 2

Missing return.

Practice Exercise 1

Guard clauses.

Practice Exercise 2

Return from a lambda and from a loop.

11. Quick Revision

  • return; exits a void method.
  • Non-void methods must return on every path.
  • Code after return is unreachable.
  • finally runs before the method returns.
  • Lambdas return their expression value.

interviewQA: Can a Java method return more than one value?
Not directly - a method has exactly one return type. Bundle multiple values into an object, record, or array instead
Difference between returning a primitive and an object?
A primitive returns a copy of the value; an object returns a copy of the reference, so the caller still points to the same heap object
Is unreachable code after a return statement allowed?
No - any statement placed after an unconditional return in the same block is a compile-time error
What happens to return inside try + finally?
finally still runs before the method actually returns; a return inside finally silently overrides the try's return value
Is a bare return; valid in a void method?
Yes - it exits the method early with no value, same idea as a guard clause
Why return this from a method?
To support method chaining / fluent APIs (e.g. StringBuilder, builder classes) - each call returns the same object so calls can be linked together
Can a method return a lambda?
Yes - a method can return any functional interface type (e.g. Supplier, Function); the caller decides when to actually invoke it
Array vs Collection as a return type?
Both leak a mutable reference to internal state the same way - consider a defensive copy or an unmodifiable wrapper for either

topics.name: This and Super Keywords

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • This refers to the current object and super refers to the parent class part of it, for fields, methods and constructors.

2. Need of This Topic

  • They resolve name conflicts between parameters and fields and let child classes reuse parent behavior.

3. Advantages

  • Avoids ambiguity between fields and parameters.
  • Reuses parent methods and constructors.
  • Enables method chaining with return this.

4. Disadvantages

  • Cannot be used in static contexts.
  • Leaking this from a constructor is risky.
  • Field hiding with super.field is confusing.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Required for constructors and overriding.
  • Common interview topic.
  • Basis for inheritance understanding.

6. Basic Concepts

What are this and super?

  • this refers to the current object — the instance whose method or constructor is currently executing.
  • super refers to the parent class part of that same object — it gives access to parent members that the child class might hide or override.
  • Both keywords can be used with variables, methods, and constructors.

Both also have a constructor-chaining form — this() calls another constructor of the same class, and super() calls the parent's constructor. That behavior (including the "must be first statement" rule) is covered in depth in the Constructor Chaining topic — here we focus on this/super as everyday keywords for fields and methods.

this — Resolving a Field vs Parameter Name Clash

When a constructor (or method) parameter has the same name as an instance field, the parameter shadows the field inside that block. this.fieldName explicitly targets the instance field, so the assignment isn't just the parameter being assigned to itself.

this — Calling the Current Object's Own Method

Inside a class, this.methodName() calls a method on the current object. Writing just methodName() works identically — Java implicitly adds this — but it can be written explicitly for clarity.

super — Accessing a Field Hidden by the Child Class

When a child class declares a field with the same name as one in its parent, the child's field hides the parent's — both copies exist. super.fieldName reaches the parent's copy directly from inside the child.

super — Calling a Parent Method Overridden by the Child

When a child class overrides a parent method, calling it normally always runs the child's version. super.methodName() is how the child explicitly invokes the parent's original implementation.

Fresher Notes

  • Meaning: this refers to the current object; super refers to the parent class part of the object.
  • Name clash: use this.name = name to separate a field from a parameter with the same name.
  • Parent access: use super.method() to call the parent version and super(args) to call the parent constructor.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Constructor calls: this(...) calls another constructor of the same class; super(...) calls the parent constructor; both must be the first statement.
  • Static context: neither this nor super can be used there.
  • Passing and chaining: this can be passed as an argument or returned (return this) for chaining.

8. Advanced Concepts

this Cannot Be Used in a Static Context

this refers to the current instance — but a static method or block belongs to the class itself, not to any particular object, so there is no instance for this to refer to. Using this inside a static context is a compile-time error. This ties directly into the Static Keyword topic: static members are resolved at the class level, before (or even without) any object existing.

class Demo {
    int value = 10;

    static void show() {
        System.out.println(this.value);
        // COMPILE ERROR:
        // "non-static variable this cannot be referenced
        //  from a static context"
    }
}

The fix is to either drop static from the method, or access the value through an actual object reference instead of this.

super — Extending Behavior Instead of Replacing It

A very common override pattern: the child overrides a method, calls super.method() first (or last) to run the parent's original logic, and then adds its own extra behavior on top. This lets the child extend the parent's behavior instead of fully rewriting it — avoiding duplicated logic.

Field Hiding vs Method Overriding Through super

Fields in Java are not polymorphic — which field is accessed is decided by the reference type at compile time. Methods (unless static/private/final) ARE polymorphic — dynamic dispatch always picks the actual object's most-overridden version, even when accessed through a parent-typed reference. super inside a child class always reaches the parent's field directly, but super.method() is the only way to bypass dynamic dispatch and force the parent's implementation to run.

Reference type Parent p = new Child();

p.field   -> resolved by REFERENCE TYPE (Parent)   -> Parent's field
p.method()-> resolved by ACTUAL OBJECT TYPE (Child) -> Child's overridden method

Inside Child:
this.field   -> Child's own field
super.field  -> Parent's field (direct, unambiguous)
this.method()  -> dynamic dispatch -> Child's version
super.method() -> explicitly forces -> Parent's version

this — Passing the Current Object to Another Method

this can be passed as an argument so another object gets a reference back to the caller — common in listener/callback/helper registration patterns.

this vs super — Quick Comparison

thissuper
Refers to the current class objectRefers to the immediate parent class object
Used to access current class membersUsed to access parent class members hidden/overridden by the child
Can be used in any non-static contextCan only be used inside a subclass
Cannot be used in a static contextCannot be used in a static context
this() chains to another constructor of the same classsuper() chains to the parent class constructor

Senior Notes

  • Field hiding: super.field reaches a hidden parent field; avoid hiding fields in real designs.
  • Interfaces: Interface.super.method() picks one default method to resolve a diamond conflict.
  • Leaking this: registering this (for example as a listener) from a constructor can expose a half-built object.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Patterns: fluent setters returning this, copy constructors using this(...), template methods calling super then adding behavior, decorators calling super, interface default conflict resolution, and constructor delegation. super never refers to a separate parent object: there is only one object.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

this is local variable 0 in instance methods and holds the receiver reference; super.m() compiles to invokespecial on the parent method (bypassing dynamic dispatch), and super(...) invokes the parent <init>. Inner classes also hold Outer.this.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using this or super in static methods (compile error), expecting super.super, shadowing fields so that this.x and super.x differ, calling overridable methods via this in constructors, and passing this to other threads from a constructor.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

There is no runtime cost to this or super: they are plain references and invokespecial calls the JIT inlines. Excessive super chains hint at a deep hierarchy that should be replaced by composition.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: extending a framework class and calling super so the framework behavior is preserved, for example overriding a Servlet lifecycle method or a Spring callback.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Field shadowing.

Worked Example 2

Chaining with this.

Practice Exercise 1

this and super in practice.

Practice Exercise 2

Resolving default methods.

11. Quick Revision

  • this: current object.
  • super: parent members.
  • this(...) and super(...) are constructor calls and must be first.
  • Not allowed in static methods.
  • Interface.super.method() resolves default conflicts.

interviewQA: Why can't this/super be used in a static method?
Static methods belong to the class, not to any instance, so there is no current object for this/super to refer to — compile error
Does super.field always give the "right" value?
Yes — fields aren't polymorphic, so super.field is a direct, unambiguous lookup on the parent's own copy
Why does super.method() work differently from super.field?
Instance methods use dynamic dispatch (resolved by actual object type); super.method() is the explicit way to bypass that and force the parent's version
If Parent p = new Child(); what does p.field return?
Parent's field — field access is resolved by the reference type at compile time, not the actual object
If Parent p = new Child(); what does p.method() return (if overridden)?
Child's overridden method — method calls are resolved by the actual object type at runtime
Can this be reassigned, e.g. this = obj;?
No — this is a keyword, not a variable; reassigning it is a compile error
Where are the this()/super() constructor-chaining rules covered?
In depth in the Constructor Chaining topic — including the "must be the first statement" rule

topics.name: Classes and Objects

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A class is a blueprint that defines fields and methods
  • An object is an instance of a class created with new.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Real-world problems are modelled as things with data and behavior.
  • Classes and objects are the building blocks of object-oriented programs.

3. Advantages

  • Models real-world entities naturally.
  • Reusable and organized code.
  • Each object keeps its own state.

4. Disadvantages

  • Poor design leads to god classes.
  • Objects use more memory than plain data.
  • Shared references can cause unexpected changes.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Everything in Java is built from classes.
  • Needed for inheritance, polymorphism and frameworks.
  • Interviews start with class and object basics.

6. Basic Concepts

A class is a blueprint for creating objects. An object is an instance of a class.

Key Concepts

  • Class: template that defines properties and behaviors
  • Object: instance of a class
  • Fields: variables that hold the state
  • Methods: functions that define behavior
  • Constructor: special method that initializes objects

Fresher Notes

  • Class: a blueprint with fields (state) and methods (behavior). Object: an instance created with new.
  • Instance fields: each object has its own copy.
  • References: objects are accessed through references; null means no object.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Object is the parent class of all classes in Java. It is the topmost class and lives in the java.lang package.

Every class is directly or indirectly derived from Object. If a class does not extend any other class, it is a direct child of Object.

Methods of the Object class

  1. public final Class getClass()
  2. public int hashCode()
  3. public boolean equals(Object obj)
  4. protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException
  5. public String toString()
  6. public final void notify()
  7. public final void notifyAll()
  8. public final void wait()
  9. public final void wait(long timeout)
  10. public final void wait(long timeout, int nanos)
  11. protected void finalize() throws Throwable

1. public final Class getClass()

It returns the runtime class of the object (its metadata, such as the class name).

2. public int hashCode()

Every object has a hash code, an int derived by the JVM. It is NOT guaranteed unique: two distinct objects may legally share one, which is why hash buckets fall back to equals().

Hash-based collections such as HashMap use the hash code to pick the bucket where an object is stored.

Note: the default hashCode() is a native method (written in C or C++), so you cannot see its Java body.

3. public boolean equals(Object obj)

It compares the given object with this object. The default equals() in Object compares references (addresses), not field contents. Classes such as String override it to compare contents.

4. protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException

It creates and returns a copy (clone) of this object. The class must implement Cloneable.
In the second output line above we get ClassName@hash instead of the value. To fix this, override toString().

5. public String toString()

It returns the string representation of this object.

6. Thread and cleanup methods

public final void notify()

It wakes up a single thread that is waiting on this object's monitor.

public final void notifyAll()

It wakes up all threads that are waiting on this object's monitor.

public final void wait(long timeout) throws InterruptedException

It makes the current thread wait for the given milliseconds, or until another thread calls notify() or notifyAll().

public final void wait(long timeout, int nanos) throws InterruptedException

Same as above, with an extra nanosecond part in the timeout.

public final void wait() throws InterruptedException

It makes the current thread wait until another thread calls notify() or notifyAll().

protected void finalize() throws Throwable

The garbage collector used to call it before collecting the object. It is deprecated for removal since Java 18, so do not rely on it.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Stack and heap: a local reference lives on the stack and the object on the heap; several references can point to one object.
  • Reference copy: b = a copies the reference, not the object.
  • Garbage collection: an object becomes eligible when no references reach it.

8. Advanced Concepts

Class as a Blueprint, Object as an Instance

A class defines the shape of state and behaviour, but it doesn't occupy heap memory itself. Each new call creates an independent object on the heap with its own copy of the instance fields.

class Employee { int id; String name; }        (blueprint - no memory yet)

Stack                          Heap
------                         ----------------------
e1  ----------------------->   Employee Object #1
                                id = 101, name = "Pankaj"

e2  ----------------------->   Employee Object #2
                                id = 102, name = "Raghunath"

Two objects created from the same class never share instance state - changing e1.name has no effect on e2.name.

Object Creation — Step by Step

When new runs, four things happen in order:

new Employee()
      |
      v
1. Heap memory allocated for the object
      |
      v
2. Fields set to their default values (0, false, null...)
      |
      v
3. Instance initializer blocks run (top to bottom)
      |
      v
4. Constructor body runs
      |
      v
Reference returned to the caller

Because default values are assigned before the constructor body runs, a field read at the very start of the constructor already has its default - not garbage, and not yet whatever the constructor is about to set.

Anonymous Objects

An object created and used inline, without ever being assigned to a variable. Useful for one-off calls where you don't need to keep a reference around afterwards.

Object Identity vs Value Equality

Every object carries its own identity, independent of its field values. The default toString() prints ClassName@hexHashCode, and == compares references, not contents.

Two objects with identical field values are still two different objects unless you explicitly override equals() to compare by value.

Senior Notes

  • Class design: single responsibility, small public API and valid state from construction.
  • Value classes: override toString, equals and hashCode (or use record).
  • Composition over inheritance; keep objects immutable when possible.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Design principles: encapsulation, single responsibility, immutability, tell don't ask, composition over inheritance, equals/hashCode/toString for value types, and records for data carriers. Object identity (==) versus equality (equals); defensive copies at boundaries; clone alternatives (copy constructors).

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

An object has a header (mark word with hash and lock state, class pointer), then fields, padded to 8 bytes. new allocates in the young generation (a thread-local allocation buffer makes it fast), initializes fields to defaults, then runs the constructor. Each class has a class object and a method table used for virtual dispatch.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: public mutable fields, god classes, anemic models with logic scattered in services, forgetting equals/hashCode when using objects as keys, null references, and memory leaks from long-lived references (static maps, listeners). Remove listeners and bound caches.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Allocation is fast, but millions of short-lived objects increase GC work; keep objects small, avoid unnecessary wrappers, and reuse immutable constants. Use JFR allocation profiling to find hot spots, and values/inline classes (Project Valhalla) are coming for flat data.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world domain modelling: an Order aggregate owns its line items, enforces invariants (total, status transitions) in methods, and exposes read-only views.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Reference vs object.

Worked Example 2

Garbage eligibility.

Practice Exercise 1

Class with state and behavior.

Practice Exercise 2

Equality of objects.
Golden rule: the class exists once at compile/load time; objects are created (and destroyed by the GC) as many times as the program needs, each with its own independent state on the heap.

11. Quick Revision

  • Class = blueprint, object = instance.
  • Objects live on the heap; references point to them.
  • b = a copies the reference, not the object.
  • Unreferenced objects are garbage collected.
  • Override toString, equals and hashCode when needed.

interviewQA: Class vs Object, in one line each
Class = blueprint/template; Object = a concrete instance built from that blueprint
Do objects of the same class share instance fields?
No - each object has its own copy. Only static fields are shared across all instances
How is an object reference passed to a method?
The reference itself is passed by value (a copy of the reference), but both the original and the copy point to the same object on the heap - so mutating fields through either one is visible to both
Can you have a class with zero objects ever created?
Yes - e.g. a utility class with only static methods, which by convention is often given a private constructor

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Encapsulation bundles data and methods in a class and hides the data with private fields, exposing it through controlled public methods.

2. Need of This Topic

  • It protects objects from invalid changes and lets the internal design change without breaking users.

3. Advantages

  • Data protection and validation.
  • Flexibility to change internals.
  • Loose coupling between classes.

4. Disadvantages

  • More code (getters and setters) if done mechanically.
  • Slight overhead of method calls.
  • Can be bypassed by reflection.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • One of the four OOP pillars.
  • Basis of maintainable code.
  • Interview favorite.

6. Basic Concepts

  • Encapsulation in Java is a core Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) concept where the data (variables) and the code (methods) that operate on that data are bundled together as a single unit, which is typically a class.
  • This mechanism is also known as data hiding because it restricts direct access to the class's internal state.
  • The main idea is to hide the internal implementation details from the outside world and provide controlled access through well-defined public methods (getters and setters).

How to Achieve Encapsulation in Java

To implement encapsulation, you follow these steps:

  1. Declare variables as private: This prevents other classes from accessing the data directly. The variables are only accessible within their own class.
  2. Provide public getter and setter methods: These methods allow controlled, indirect access to the private variables.
  3. Getter methods (getXXX()) are used to retrieve the values of the variables.
  4. Setter methods (setXXX()) are used to modify the values of the variables and can include validation logic to ensure data integrity.

Below is one small, runnable code + output (proof) for every step:

Step 1: Declare variables as private

Proof: trying to touch the field directly from outside the class fails to compile.

Step 2: Provide a public getter method

The getter (getXXX()) is the only way to read the private field from outside the class.

Step 3: Provide a public setter method (with validation)

The setter (setXXX()) is the only way to change the private field, and can reject bad values.

Step 4: Putting it all together

Full Person class with private fields, getters, and setters — this is a complete encapsulated class.

Fresher Notes

  • Encapsulation bundles data and the methods that work on it, and hides the data: make fields private and expose public getters and setters.
  • Validation: a setter can reject bad values before assigning, so the object stays valid.
  • Read-only class: has getters but no setters.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

The binding of data into single entity called as "Encapsulation".

Example- Class is the entity which contains variables & methods.

Class Employee {

int salary;

void m5() {

statements ;

}

}

Through encapsulation, data is hidden and protected from access by outside non-member methods of a class.

Only member methods defined in a class will have access to the data.

A Java class is an example of encapsulation because class binds variables and methods together.

Key Concepts of Encapsulation:

1. Private Variables:

  • How: Declare class variables as private so they cannot be accessed directly from outside the class.
  • Why: This restricts external code from directly accessing and modifying the internal state of the

object, ensuring data integrity.

2. Public Getter and Setter Methods:

  • How: Provide public methods (getters and setters) to access and update the private variables.
  • Why: This allows controlled access to the internal state of the object. You can add logic to these

methods to validate data before it is changed.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Invariants: getters and setters are not the goal; the goal is to protect the rules of the object and hide the implementation.
  • Behavior over setters: expose account.deposit(100) instead of setBalance.
  • Mutable fields: return copies or unmodifiable views.

8. Advanced Concepts

Generally, variables of a class are declared as "private" whereas, methods of class are declared as "public".

This means that variables cannot be accessed from outside the class but methods can be accessed from anywhere outside the class.

  • To use variables from outside, we will have to take the help of methods.
  • Thus, encapsulation protects data of a class from members of another class.

Real Time Example:

Suppose you have an account in the bank. If your balance variable is declared as a public variable in

the bank software, your account balance will be known as public, In this case, anyone can know your

account balance. So, is it correct approach? Answer => is No.

So, they declare balance variable as private for making your account safe, so that anyone cannot see

your account balance.

The person who has to see his account balance, will have to access only private members through public

methods defined inside that class.

Thus, we can achieve security by utilizing the concept of data hiding. This is called Encapsulation in Java.

Why ?

Employee e1= new Employee();

e1.salary= 5000; // case 1

Employee e2= new Employee();

e2.salary= -3000; // case 2

In this example, case 1, we are passing the 5000 salary to the employee that is correct but in case 2 we are passing a salary of -3000, which is negative.

So salary cannot be negative.

Below is one small, runnable code + output (proof) for the valid case and the rejected case:
The Employee class (encapsulated salary field)
Case 1 — Proof: a valid, positive salary is accepted

Case 2 — Proof: a negative salary is rejected by the setter

The setter's validation (if (sal > 0)) silently defaults invalid input to 0 instead of

storing the negative value - this is the "why" of encapsulation in action.

Note-

Always keeps global variables private & allows others to assign values through public

methods. Below is a more complete example with 3 encapsulated fields (id, name, city) taking dynamic

values from user input.

Through encapsulation, data is hidden and protected from access by outside non-member methods

of a class.

Only member methods defined in a class will have access to the data.

A Java class is an example of encapsulation because class binds variables and methods together.

Generally, variables of a class are declared as "private" whereas, methods of class are declared as

"public".

This means that variables cannot be accessed from outside the class but methods can be

accessed from anywhere outside the class.

To use variables from outside, we will have to take the help of methods. Thus, encapsulation protects

data of a class from members of another class.

Benefits of Encapsulation:

  1. Control: Allows you to control how data is accessed and modified.
  2. Data Hiding: Protects the internal state of the object from outside access and misuse.
  3. Flexibility: Enables changes to the internal implementation without affecting external code.
  4. Maintainability: Simplifies code management and maintenance.
  5. Security: Enhances the security of data by restricting access to it.

Disadvantages of Encapsulation (In Short):

  1. Increased Complexity: Requires additional getter and setter methods.
  2. Performance Overhead: Extra method calls can slightly impact performance.
  3. Restricted Flexibility: Can make data access and modification harder.
  4. Testing Challenges: Private methods are harder to test directly.
  5. Verbose Code: More lines of code due to getter and setter methods can reduce readability.

1. What is encapsulation in Java?

o Encapsulation is the process of wrapping data (variables) and code (methods) together into a single

unit, typically a class. It is also known as data hiding because it restricts direct access to some of the

object's components.

2. How do you achieve encapsulation in Java?

o Encapsulation is achieved by:

Declaring the variables of a class as private.

Providing public getter and setter methods to modify and view the variable values.

3. What are the benefits of encapsulation?

o Encapsulation helps in:

Protecting the internal state of an object from unintended or harmful changes.

Improving modularity by keeping the data and methods that operate on the data together.

Enhancing maintainability and flexibility of the code.

4. What is the difference between encapsulation and abstraction?

o Encapsulation is about bundling the data and methods that operate on the data within a single unit

and restricting access to some of the object's components. Abstraction, on the other hand, is about

hiding the complex implementation details and showing only the essential features of the object.

5. Can you give an example of encapsulation in Java?

o Sure! Here's a simple example:

Java

public class Person {

private String name;

private int age;

public String getName() {

return name;

}

public void setName(String name) {

this.name = name;

}

In this example, the name and age variables are encapsulated within the Person class, and access to them

is controlled through getter and setter methods.

6. What is a tightly encapsulated class?

o A tightly encapsulated class is one where all the instance variables are declared as private and

accessed only through public getter and setter methods.

7. How does encapsulation improve code maintainability?

o Encapsulation improves maintainability by allowing changes to the internal implementation of a

class without affecting other parts of the code that use the class. This makes it easier to update and

manage the code.

8. What is the role of getter and setter methods in encapsulation?

o Getter and setter methods provide controlled access to the private variables of a class. They allow

you to read and modify the values of the variables while maintaining control over how the variables

are accessed and updated.

9. Can encapsulation be violated using reflection?

o Yes, encapsulation can be violated using Java Reflection API, which allows you to access private

fields and methods of a class. However, this should be avoided as it breaks the principles of

encapsulation and can lead to code that is difficult to maintain and debug.

10.Which design pattern is based on encapsulation in Java?

o The Singleton design pattern is based on encapsulation. It ensures that a class has only one instance

and provides a global point of access to it, encapsulating the instance creation logic.

Senior Notes

  • Changing internals: a field can become computed, or a list a set, without breaking callers.
  • Immutable objects are the strongest form: no setters, final fields, defensive copies.
  • JavaBeans naming (getX/setX) matters to frameworks such as JPA and Jackson; records give accessors without boilerplate.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Techniques: private final fields, validation in constructors, defensive copies on input and output (mutable types like Date, arrays, collections), package-private and nested classes for internals, the module system, immutable value objects, and the builder pattern. Frameworks need accessors or reflection: JPA can use field access, Jackson uses getters or record components.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Access modifiers are checked by the compiler and again by the JVM at run time, but its real purpose is protecting invariants: rules that must always hold for an object (balance is not negative, start is before end). All state changes go through methods that preserve the invariants, so the object is valid from construction until it is collected.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: generating getters and setters for every field (anemic model), returning mutable internals, setters that accept anything, public static mutable fields, and exposing entity objects directly from REST APIs (use DTOs). Also, reflection setAccessible(true) can break encapsulation unless modules restrict it.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Encapsulation lets you optimize internals without API changes: switch from a list to an array, add caching or lazy loading, or compute values on demand. Immutability enables sharing and safe caching and avoids defensive copying.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a banking Account class never exposes balance setters; transfers are methods that lock, check and update atomically.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Leaky encapsulation.

Worked Example 2

Record as immutable carrier.

Practice Exercise 1

Validated setter and behavior method.

Practice Exercise 2

Defensive copy.

11. Quick Revision

  • Private fields, public methods.
  • Validate in setters or constructors.
  • Return copies of mutable fields.
  • Immutability is the strongest form.
  • Expose behavior, not raw state.

topics.name: Inheritance in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Inheritance lets a class (child) reuse and extend another class (parent) using extends, modelling an is-a relationship.

2. Need of This Topic

  • It avoids code duplication and lets related classes share behavior and be treated through a common type.

3. Advantages

  • Code reuse.
  • Enables polymorphism.
  • Clear is-a hierarchies.

4. Disadvantages

  • Tight coupling between parent and child.
  • Fragile base class problem.
  • Deep hierarchies are hard to maintain.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Core OOP pillar.
  • Frameworks rely on extending base classes.
  • Interviews ask inheritance vs composition.

6. Basic Concepts

In Java, it is possible to inherit attributes and methods from one class to another.

We group the "inheritance concept" into two categories:

  • subclass (child) - the class that inherits from another class
  • superclass (parent) - the class being inherited from

To inherit from a class, use the extends keyword.

In the example below, the Car class (subclass) inherits the attributes and methods from the Vehicle class (superclass):

Fresher Notes

  • Inheritance lets a class (child, subclass) reuse the fields and methods of another (parent, superclass) using extends.
  • Is-a relationship: a Dog is an Animal.
  • Extend and override: a child can add new members and replace parent methods.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

  • Creating a new class by using the functionality of an existing class is called Inheritance.
  • It is a mechanism in which one class acquires the property of another class.
  • Inheritance means simply reusability.
  • It is called as - (IS Relationship)

Example :

IS Relationship

package com.javaschoollab.demo;

class Policy { // Policy = Super Class

}

class TermPolicy extends Policy { // TermPolicy = Sub Class wher TermPolicy is Policy

}

Note-

All the parent members are available in the child class, but only if both conditions below hold:

  • The access specifier allows it.
  • The child class does not redeclare the member.

UML Diagram

Parent -P // Where P = Parent Class & C is the Child Class

|

|

|

Child – C

Note-

Below are different names for super and sub class.

Super Class->Parent Class->Base Class-> Old Class

Sub Class-> Child Class-> Derived Class -> New Class

Note-

  1. Inherit a class by using the extends keyword.
  2. When we create an object of the subclass, the superclass part of the object is created too, because superclass members are inherited.
  3. We use inheritance for code reusability: we reuse the variables and methods of an existing class.
  4. We cannot extend a final class.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Single class inheritance: a class has one parent class but can implement many interfaces.
  • Private members exist in the child object but cannot be accessed directly. Constructors are not inherited; call the parent one with super(...).
  • @Override: use @Override so the compiler checks that you really override.

8. Advanced Concepts

When to use?

If we want to extends or increase of features of class then go for inheritance.

Advantages

  1. Modify the attributes / fields / variable in the existing class but this is not good option it will

increase the testing efforts for that class.

  1. Add the attributes / fields / variable in the new class, this is the good option we can also reduce

the testing efforts for this.

Why inheritance?

Suppose a class has the fields firstname, lastname, address, city and mobile number. Later we must add an email. What options do we have?

How the class will look like

package com.javaschoollab.demo;

class Parent {

String firstname;

String lastname;

String address;

String city;

String mobilenumber;

}

class Child extends Parent{

String email;

}

Note:

We cannot assign parent class to child class- it means

Child c=new Parent(); => Here we can't write new Parent();

All the members of super class will be directly inherited into sub class and they are eligible and depends

on access specifiers only.

Dynamic Dispatch

Assigning a child object to a parent reference is called upcasting. Dynamic (method) dispatch is the separate mechanism by which a call to an overridden method is resolved at RUNTIME using the object's actual type.

Example :

package com.javaschoollab.demo;

class X {

}

package com.javaschoollab.demo;

class Y extends X {

}

package com.javaschoollab.demo;

class Test {

public static void main(String[] args) {

X x = new Y(); // Here we are assigning the child reference new Y() to parent class as X.

}

}

Scenario 1

package com.javaschoollab.demo;

class X { // Super Class: X

int a = 10; // Initialization

int b = 20; // Initialization

void m1() {

System.out.println("Class X- m1() method");

}

void m2() {

System.out.println("Class X- m2() method");

}

}

package com.javaschoollab.demo;

class Y extends X { // Sub Class: Y

int b = 30; // Initialization

int c = 40; // Initialization

void m2() {

System.out.println("Class Y- m2() method");

}

void m3() {

System.out.println("Class Y- m3() method");

}

}

Below is one small, runnable proof for every scenario of accessing members through parent vs child references:

Scenario 1: Accessing members through a plain X reference

Only X's own members are visible - a=10, b=20, m1(), m2(). c and m3() (from Y) don't exist here.

Scenario 2: Accessing members through a plain Y reference

Y has all of X's inherited members plus its own b (shadowed), c, and m3(); m2() is overridden.

Scenario 3: Dynamic Dispatch — assigning a child object to a parent reference

Here a child object is assigned to a parent variable (X x = new Y();, upcasting).

The reference type (X) decides which fields are visible,

but the actual object type (Y) decides which overridden method runs (dynamic dispatch).

Scenario 4: Same as Scenario 3, done via assignment instead of declaration

Note: assigning x = y; after separate declarations behaves identically to

X x = new Y(); - both produce the exact same output as Scenario 3.

Scenario 5: Type casting a parent reference back to Y

Casting (Y) x gives back full access to Y's own members (b=30, c=40, m3()) — equivalent

to working with the object as a plain Y reference (same result as Scenario 2).

Scenario 6: Proof — a parent object CANNOT be assigned to a child reference

A Y reference must point to an actual Y (or subtype of Y) object. Assigning a plain X object to it

fails at compile time.

package com.javaschoollab.demo;

public class Parent {

int Dheeraj = 5000;

int Sheru = 6000;

void x1() {

System.out.println("Dheeraj From Parent Class");

}

void x2() {

System.out.println("Sheru From Parent Class");

}

}

package com.javaschoollab.demo;

public class Child extends Parent { // Step: 01

int Sheru = 10000;

int Omkar = 20000;

void x2() {

System.out.println("Sheru From Child Class");

}

void x3() {

System.out.println("Omkar From Child Class");

}

}

Below is one small, runnable proof for each access scenario between this Parent and Child:

Scenario 1: Parent Class Data Access

A plain Parent object only sees Parent's own members - Omkar and x3() (defined only in Child) are not visible.

Scenario 2: Child Class Data Access

Child inherits Dheeraj from Parent, shadows Sheru with its own value, adds Omkar, and overrides x2().

Scenario 3: Dynamic Dispatch — Parent reference pointing to a Child object

Field access (Dheeraj, Sheru) is resolved by the reference type (Parent), so

Parent's Sheru (6000) is used. Method calls are resolved by the actual object type

(Child), so the overridden x2() runs.

Scenario 4: Same as Scenario 3, done via assignment

Note: assigning p4 = c4; after separate declarations behaves identically to

Parent p3 = new Child(); - same output as Scenario 3.

Scenario 5: Type casting a Parent reference back to Child

Casting (Child) p5 restores full access to Child's own members - same result as Scenario 2.

Scenario 6: Proof — a Parent object CANNOT be assigned to a Child reference

A Child reference must point to an actual Child (or subtype) object. Assigning a plain Parent object

to it fails at compile time.

Senior Notes

  • Composition over inheritance: inheritance couples child to parent and can break when the parent changes (fragile base class).
  • Design for inheritance or prohibit it with final; document which methods subclasses may override.
  • Liskov substitution: a subclass must work wherever the parent is expected, with no surprises.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Guidelines (Effective Java): design and document for inheritance or forbid it; do not call overridable methods in constructors; prefer composition and forwarding (decorator); use interfaces plus default methods; make classes final by default; use protected sparingly; and prefer abstract skeleton classes for APIs. Inheritance of implementation breaks encapsulation.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

An object of a child class contains parent fields followed by child fields in one block of memory. Method calls use the virtual method table: each class has a vtable, a subclass overrides entries, and invokevirtual picks the entry for the actual class. Constructors run from the top class down; static members are inherited but hidden, not overridden.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: inheriting for code reuse when not is-a, fragile base classes, overriding equals asymmetrically, changing behavior that callers rely on (violating Liskov), forgetting @Override (accidental overload), and calling overridable methods from constructors. The fix for the counting set is composition with a forwarding wrapper.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Virtual calls cost a small indirection, but the JIT uses class hierarchy analysis and inline caches: a call site that sees one or two receiver types is inlined. Megamorphic call sites (many types) are slower, which can matter in hot loops.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: frameworks use abstract base classes (HttpServlet, JpaRepository adapters) with documented extension points, while your business logic uses composition and interfaces.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Square extends Rectangle problem.

Worked Example 2

Final prevents extension.

Practice Exercise 1

Extending and overriding.

Practice Exercise 2

Composition instead.

11. Quick Revision

  • extends for classes, single inheritance only.
  • Constructors are not inherited; use super(...).
  • Use @Override.
  • Prefer composition when not truly is-a.
  • Every class extends Object.

interviewQA: What is inheritance and which keyword achieves it?
A mechanism where a subclass acquires the fields/methods of a superclass, using the extends keyword
What is "dynamic dispatch"?
Resolving a call to an overridden method at runtime by the actual object type, not the reference type (e.g. X x = new Y(); x.m2() runs Y's m2). Field access is still resolved by the reference type
Are field accesses polymorphic in Java?
No - only method calls are polymorphic. Field access through a parent reference always uses the parent's own field, even if the child shadows it with the same name
Can a parent class object be assigned to a child class reference directly?
No - that's a compile-time error (incompatible types); you'd need an explicit cast, which itself throws ClassCastException at runtime if the object isn't actually an instance of the child class
Why can't you extend a final class?
final on a class explicitly forbids inheritance - the compiler rejects any attempt to subclass it
What determines which members are inherited?
The access specifier of each member in the superclass, and whether that member is redeclared (shadowed/overridden) in the subclass

topics.name: Inheritance Types

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Types of inheritance are single, multilevel and hierarchical for classes
  • Multiple and hybrid inheritance are achieved through interfaces.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Knowing the types explains how hierarchies are shaped and why Java avoids multiple class inheritance.

3. Advantages

  • Flexible modelling through interfaces.
  • Avoids the diamond problem for classes.
  • Sealed types limit hierarchies.

4. Disadvantages

  • No multiple class inheritance.
  • Deep multilevel chains are fragile.
  • Default method conflicts need manual resolution.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Frequent interview topic.
  • Helps design clean hierarchies.
  • Prepares for interfaces and abstract classes.

6. Basic Concepts

Java supports several "shapes" of inheritance between classes, depending on how many super classes and sub classes are involved. In this topic we cover each shape with a small runnable demo. (Overriding and dynamic dispatch are covered in the "Inheritance in Java" topic. Here we focus only on the class-hierarchy shapes.)

The shapes are:

  • Single Inheritance
  • Multilevel Inheritance
  • Hierarchical Inheritance
  • Multiple Inheritance (not supported via classes - covered in Expert Level)
  • Hybrid Inheritance (not supported via classes - covered in Expert Level)

1. Single Inheritance

One super class and exactly one sub class.

Insurance            (Super Class)
    |
    |  extends
    |
HealthInsurance      (Sub Class)

2. Multilevel Inheritance

A chain of inheritance: a class inherits from a class, which itself inherits from another class (A → B → C). Each level automatically gets everything from every level above it.

Account              (Grandparent)
    |
    |  extends
    |
CurrentAccount       (Parent)
    |
    |  extends
    |
SavingAccount        (Child)

3. Hierarchical Inheritance

One parent class is inherited by many sub classes independently. The sub classes do not know about each other and cannot see one another's members.

                Loan                (Parent)
        /        |        \
       /         |         \
 HomeLoan   PersonalLoan   CarLoan   (Children)

Quick Recap

TypeShapeExample
Single1 parent → 1 childInsurance → HealthInsurance
Multilevel1 parent → 1 child → 1 grandchild (chain)Account → CurrentAccount → SavingAccount
Hierarchical1 parent → many childrenLoan → HomeLoan, PersonalLoan, CarLoan

Java does NOT allow a class to extends two classes at the same time (Multiple Inheritance of classes), and therefore also disallows Hybrid Inheritance built purely out of classes. The Expert Level below explains exactly why, and how interfaces give you the same power safely.

Fresher Notes

  • Types: single (B extends A), multilevel (C extends B extends A), hierarchical (B and C extend A).
  • Multiple inheritance of classes is not allowed in Java; it is achieved with interfaces.
  • Hybrid is a mix and is also done with interfaces.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Diamond problem: this is why Java has no multiple class inheritance. Two parents may define the same member, so the choice is ambiguous.
  • Default conflicts: a class can use implements A, B. If both have the same default method, the class must override it and choose.
  • Root class: every class implicitly extends Object.

8. Advanced Concepts

Why Java Does NOT Support Multiple Inheritance (of Classes)

If a class could extend two classes that each declare the same method, the compiler would not know which version the sub class should inherit. This is the classic Diamond Problem:

class A { void m1() { ... } }
class B { void m1() { ... } }
class C extends A, B {   // NOT LEGAL JAVA
    // Which m1() does C inherit? A's or B's?
}

Both A and B provide their own m1(). If C could extend both, calling c.m1() would be ambiguous, because the compiler has no rule to pick a winner. Java's designers avoided this whole class of bugs by allowing a class to extend only one class.

The following would-be code is illegal and does not compile:

How Java Achieves Multiple Inheritance Safely - via Interfaces

A class can implements any number of interfaces. Before Java 8, interfaces only declared abstract methods with no body, so there was nothing to conflict. The implementing class always had to supply exactly one, unambiguous body. This gives Java "multiple inheritance of type" without the diamond problem.

Java 8 default methods bring the diamond problem back - and how it's resolved

Since Java 8, interfaces can have default methods with a body. This reintroduces the diamond problem: if two interfaces implemented by the same class declare the SAME default method, Java cannot silently pick one. It forces the implementing class to override the method and resolve the clash itself.

Hybrid Inheritance

Hybrid inheritance combines more than one of the above types in the same design (for example, hierarchical + multiple). Since it includes multiple inheritance, Java cannot support it with classes alone. It is easily achieved with a mix of class inheritance (extends) and interfaces (implements, for the "multiple" part):

        Vehicle (class)          Electric (interface)
             |                        |
             |  extends               |  implements
             |                        |
         Car (class) --------------------
             |
             |  extends
             |
         SportsCar (class)

Aggregation (HAS-A) - an alternative to Inheritance for code reuse

When there is no real IS-A relationship, prefer composing objects instead of inheriting. If a class holds a reference to another class as a field, that is Aggregation (HAS-A). It gives code reuse (via delegation) without forcing an inheritance hierarchy.

Types of Inheritance - Summary Table

TypeSupported via classes?Supported via interfaces?
SingleYesYes
MultilevelYesYes
HierarchicalYesYes
MultipleNo (diamond problem)Yes (class implements many interfaces)
HybridNo (contains multiple)Yes (class + several interfaces)
<div class='bg-secondary border border-primary p-2'>

Senior Notes

  • Shallow hierarchies: deep ones are hard to maintain. Prefer interfaces plus composition.
  • Sealed classes (Java 17) restrict which classes may extend a type.
  • Abstract base classes share code; interfaces define capabilities.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools for hierarchy design: sealed classes and interfaces (closed set of subtypes), records implementing interfaces, mixin style default methods, abstract skeletal implementations (AbstractList), marker interfaces, and generics bounds. Hierarchy shape: wide and shallow beats deep.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The JVM allows single class inheritance only, which keeps the object layout and method resolution simple and avoids ambiguity. Interfaces add multiple inheritance of type, and since Java 8 of behavior through default methods. Resolution rules: class wins over interface, more specific interface wins, otherwise the class must override explicitly.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forcing an is-a relation (Stack extends Vector), diamond default conflicts without override (compile error), deep multilevel chains, using inheritance only to share utility code, and exposing protected fields. Prefer delegation.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Deep hierarchies increase class loading and initialization chains and slow comprehension. Keep depth under about three levels, and prefer interfaces so implementations can vary without extending a base class.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: the collections framework uses interface hierarchy (Collection, List, Set), abstract skeletons (AbstractList) and concrete classes (ArrayList); you can add your own implementation by extending the skeleton.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Sealed hierarchy.

Worked Example 2

Object is the root.

Practice Exercise 1

Multilevel and hierarchical.

Practice Exercise 2

Multiple through interfaces.

11. Quick Revision

  • Single, multilevel, hierarchical via extends.
  • Multiple via implements.
  • Diamond problem avoided for classes.
  • Resolve default conflicts with X.super.m().
  • sealed restricts subclasses.

interviewQA: What are the types of inheritance in Java?
Single, Multilevel, and Hierarchical are directly supported via classes. Multiple and Hybrid are not supported via classes but are achievable via interfaces.
Why doesn't Java support multiple inheritance of classes?
To avoid the Diamond Problem - if two super classes declare the same method, the compiler has no unambiguous rule for which implementation the sub class should inherit.
How does Java achieve multiple-inheritance-like behavior?
A class can implement any number of interfaces (multiple inheritance of type). Prior to Java 8, interfaces had no method bodies, so there was nothing to conflict.
Do Java 8 default methods reintroduce the diamond problem?

Yes - if two implemented interfaces declare the same default method, the implementing class gets a compile error and MUST override that method itself to resolve the ambiguity (optionally calling Interface.super.method()).
What is hybrid inheritance and why isn't it supported via classes?

It's a combination of more than one inheritance type (e.g. hierarchical + multiple). Since it includes multiple inheritance as a sub-case, it inherits the same diamond-problem restriction and must be built using a mix of class extends + interface implements.
What is Aggregation and how does it relate to inheritance?
Aggregation is a HAS-A relationship (a class holds a reference to another class as a field). It's an alternative to inheritance for code reuse when no true IS-A relationship exists.

topics.name: Abstraction in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Abstraction hides implementation details and exposes only essential behavior, using abstract classes and interfaces.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Users of a class should know what it does, not how.
  • Abstraction allows implementations to change and be swapped.

3. Advantages

  • Reduces complexity.
  • Loose coupling and easy testing.
  • Supports multiple implementations.

4. Disadvantages

  • Too many layers add indirection.
  • Poor abstractions leak details.
  • Interfaces with one implementation can be noise.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Core OOP pillar.
  • Basis of Spring dependency injection.
  • Interviews ask abstract class vs interface.

6. Basic Concepts

Data abstraction means hiding the details and showing only the essential information to the user.

Java gives two tools for abstraction: abstract classes and interfaces (interfaces are covered below).

The abstract keyword is a non-access modifier. It is used on classes and methods:

  • Abstract class: a restricted class that cannot be used to create objects. To use it, another class must extend it.
  • Abstract method: a method with no body. It is declared in an abstract class (or an interface). The subclass provides the body.

Fresher Notes

  • Abstraction hides implementation details and shows only essential features. In Java it is done with abstract classes and interfaces.
  • An abstract class (abstract class Shape) cannot be instantiated and may have abstract methods (no body) and concrete methods.
  • A subclass must implement all abstract methods or itself be abstract.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Abstraction is hiding the internal details and showing only the important functions to the end user.

Real-life examples:

  1. Car: you use the steering wheel and pedals, not the engine internals.
  2. ATM machine.
  3. TV remote.
  4. Sending an SMS: you type the text and press send. You do not know how the message is delivered.

How to achieve abstraction in Java?

There are 2 ways:

  1. Abstract class (0 to 100% abstraction)
  2. Interface (up to 100% abstraction)

1. Abstract Class

  • An abstract class is declared with the abstract keyword.
  • It can contain abstract methods, concrete methods, both, or neither.
  • It can have constructors.
  • A class cannot extend more than one abstract class (no multiple inheritance with classes).

If a class declares an abstract method, the class itself must be abstract.

How to implement abstract methods?

Create a class that extends the abstract class and overrides every abstract method.

If the subclass does not want to override them, it must also be declared abstract.

2. Interface

  • Interface methods are public abstract by default.
  • Interface variables are public static final by default.
  • If you leave out public or abstract, the compiler adds them for you.
  • Design to interfaces: code against the interface and keep the implementation behind it.
  • An interface method with a body (without default, static or private) is a compile error.

All four methods below mean the same thing:

Does Java support multiple inheritance?

  • With classes: No. A class extends only one class.
  • With interfaces: Yes. A class can implement many interfaces, and an interface can extend many interfaces.

Combinations to try on your computer

  • interface extends interface
  • interface extends interface1 and interface2
  • class implements interface
  • class implements interface1 and interface2
  • class extends class implements interface
  • class extends class implements interface1 and interface2
<div class='bg-blue-200 p-3 '>

Mid-Level Notes

  • Abstract class: state, constructors, partial implementation, single inheritance. Interface: contract, multiple implementation, default and static methods.
  • Use an interface for capability (Comparable, Runnable) and an abstract class for shared base code.
  • Abstract methods cannot be private, static or final.

8. Advanced Concepts

1. Abstract Class

  • We cannot create an object of an abstract class.
  • To use its abstract methods, extend the class and override them.
  • A subclass that does not override every abstract method must also be declared abstract.
  • If any method in a class is abstract, the class must be declared abstract.

Advantages of Abstraction

  1. It reduces the complexity of viewing things.
  2. It avoids code duplication and increases reusability.
  3. It increases security, because only essential details are shown to the user.
  4. It improves maintainability and modularity: a big system splits into smaller parts.
  5. The user focuses on what an object does, not how it does it.
  6. We can change the internal implementation without affecting users, as long as the interface stays the same. For example, disk brakes and drum brakes work differently inside, but both are used through the same pedal.

Disadvantages of Abstraction

  1. It can make it harder to understand and debug how the system works, especially for people who do not know the layers.
  2. Used badly, it adds complexity and increases development time.
  3. Too many layers add indirection and can cost some performance.

2. Interface

  • In a company, senior engineers or team leads often design the interface. Developers then implement it with the business logic.
  • We cannot create an object of an interface.
  • An interface defines the methods. The implementing class provides the bodies.
  • Before Java 8, an interface could not have method bodies. Java 8 added default and static methods.
  • Java 9 added private methods in interfaces.
  • Java supports multiple inheritance through interfaces, but not through classes.
  • An interface does not have a constructor.

Why interface?

Suppose Amazon wants to add SBI bank payment code to its shopping cart, so customers can pay for their orders.

SBI could share its Transaction class directly. But then Amazon would see SBI database code and business logic, which is a security risk.

The solution: SBI publishes only an interface (Transactionid) and keeps the implementation (TransactionImpl) private. Amazon codes against the interface.

Both sides reach their goal: Amazon can pay, and SBI keeps its internals hidden.
<div class='bg-blue-200 p-2'>

Senior Notes

  • Program to abstractions (dependency inversion): depend on interfaces, inject implementations.
  • Template Method pattern: an abstract class defines the algorithm skeleton, subclasses fill in the steps.
  • Keep abstractions small and stable (interface segregation); avoid leaking implementation details through them.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Design: interface for roles and ports (Repository, PaymentGateway), abstract class for shared implementation with template methods, functional interfaces for single behaviors, sealed interfaces for closed hierarchies. Dependency inversion: high-level code owns the interface; low-level code implements it. Hexagonal architecture is built on this.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

An abstract class compiles to a normal class with the ACC_ABSTRACT flag; abstract methods have no code attribute. Interfaces compile to class files with ACC_INTERFACE; methods are public abstract unless default, static or private. The JVM resolves interface calls through invokeinterface (itable lookup, optimized by inline caches).

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: interfaces with one implementation created out of habit, huge fat interfaces (violating interface segregation), leaky abstractions that expose SQL or HTTP details, abstract classes used when an interface suffices, and default methods that hold state-dependent logic. Keep abstractions small and honest.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Interface calls through a polymorphic site cost a lookup that the JIT often removes. Abstraction is not a performance problem in practice; excessive layers are a maintenance problem. Measure before removing abstractions.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: JDBC is abstraction at work: your code uses Connection and PreparedStatement while drivers (MySQL, PostgreSQL) implement them.

10. Examples

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 2

11. Quick Revision

  • Abstract class: partial implementation, state.
  • Interface: contract, multiple implementation.
  • Cannot instantiate abstract classes.
  • Program to interfaces.
  • Template Method uses abstract steps.
