topics.name: Polymorphism in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Polymorphism means one interface with many forms: compile-time (overloading) and run-time (overriding).

2. Need of This Topic

  • It lets the same code work with different object types, removing if-else chains and making programs extensible.

3. Advantages

  • Extensible, open-closed design.
  • Cleaner code through common types.
  • Supports frameworks and plug-ins.

4. Disadvantages

  • Run-time dispatch hides which code runs.
  • Fields and static methods are not polymorphic.
  • Overload resolution rules can confuse.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Core OOP pillar.
  • Needed to understand interfaces and frameworks.
  • Very common interview topic.

6. Basic Concepts

One entity that behaves differently in different cases is called Polymorphism.

Real-life examples:

  • A light switch — the same switch turns lights on or off.
  • A person — an employee at office, a customer at a mall, a passenger on a bus, a student at school, a son at home.
  • A smartphone — one device that sends texts, makes calls, sends mail, and does video calls.

We achieve polymorphism in Java in 2 ways:

  1. Method Overloading — Compile Time Polymorphism / Early Binding / Static Binding
  2. Method Overriding — Runtime Polymorphism / Late Binding / Dynamic Binding

Below is one small, runnable code + output for each:

1. Method Overloading — same method name, different number of arguments

Rules: the method name must be the same; parameters must differ (in count, type, or order); return type and access specifier can be anything. No super/sub-class relationship is needed.
2. Method Overloading — same method name, different data type of arguments

3. Method Overriding — same method name, same arguments, but Parent/Child classes

Rules: the method name and parameters must be the same; return type must be the same (or covariant); access can be widened but not narrowed. This needs a super/sub-class relationship, unlike overloading.

4. Proof: Overloading is resolved at compile time, Overriding is resolved at runtime

With overloading, the compiler picks the version from the arguments you wrote. With overriding, even if the reference type is the parent class, the actual object's overridden method runs. This is decided at runtime (dynamic dispatch).

Fresher Notes

  • Polymorphism means one interface, many forms. Compile-time (overloading) and run-time (overriding).
  • Overloading: same method name, different parameters, resolved by the compiler.
  • Overriding: a subclass redefines a parent method; the JVM picks the version from the actual object type at run time.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Parent reference can hold a child object: Animal a = new Dog();; a.speak() runs Dog.speak.
  • Fields and static methods are not polymorphic (resolved by reference type).
  • Overriding rules: same signature, return type same or covariant, not less accessible, no broader checked exceptions.

8. Advanced Concepts

Why Overloading Is Compile-Time and Overriding Is Runtime

Overloading is resolved by the compiler. It looks only at the reference type and the argument types, so the JVM never needs to know the actual object.

Overriding is resolved at run time from the object's actual type (through the method table, called the vtable). So the same call site can run different code depending on which object is really there.

Overload Resolution Order: Exact Match → Widening → Autoboxing → Varargs

When several overloads could match a call, Java prefers them in this order. This is a classic interview trap.

  1. Exact type match.
  2. Widening primitive conversion (int → long → double).
  3. Autoboxing / unboxing.
  4. Varargs (last resort).

Access Modifier Rule: Can Widen, Cannot Narrow

An overriding method must have the same or wider access than the method it overrides, never narrower. protected can be widened to public, but public can never be narrowed to protected in a subclass.

Proof: static Methods Are Hidden, Not Overridden

A static method belongs to the class, not to an object, so it cannot take part in runtime polymorphism. Declaring the same static method in a subclass is called method hiding. The version that runs is chosen by the reference type at compile time, not by the object's actual type.

Proof: private and final Methods Cannot Be Overridden

private methods are not inherited, so a same-named method in the subclass is a brand-new, unrelated method, not an override. final methods forbid overriding, and the compiler enforces it.

Real-World Use: Runtime Polymorphism for Extensible Business Rules

A common pattern: define a method in a base type and override it in each concrete class. The calling code stays unchanged as new types are added. A new payment, interest or seat-tier type is just one new subclass.

Quick Comparison

AspectOverloadingOverriding
Also calledCompile-time / Static / Early BindingRuntime / Dynamic / Late Binding
Class relationshipNot required (same class)Required (subclass)
ParametersMust differMust be identical
Return typeCan be anythingSame or covariant
Access modifierCan be anythingSame or wider only
static methodsCan be overloadedCannot be overridden (only hidden)
private / final methodsCan be overloadedCannot be overridden

Senior Notes

  • Run-time dispatch uses the virtual method table (vtable); the JIT can inline monomorphic calls and guard with a class check.
  • Open/Closed principle: polymorphism removes if-else on type; add a new subclass instead of editing a switch.
  • Sealed types with pattern matching offer a closed-world alternative (exhaustive switch).

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Forms: subtype polymorphism (overriding), parametric polymorphism (generics), ad hoc polymorphism (overloading), and coercion (widening). Design patterns built on it: Strategy, State, Visitor, Command, Template Method. Double dispatch (Visitor) emulates multimethods.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Overloads are resolved by the compiler from the static types of the arguments (phases: exact/widening, boxing, varargs). Overrides use invokevirtual: the JVM looks up the method in the vtable of the receiver's actual class. Interface calls use itables. invokedynamic backs lambdas and string concatenation. Pattern matching on sealed types gives type-safe branching.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting overload resolution at run time (it uses the static type), overriding with a different parameter type (becomes an overload), narrowing access, hiding static methods, and relying on field polymorphism. Always use @Override.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Monomorphic and bimorphic call sites are inlined with a type guard; megamorphic ones fall back to vtable calls. In hot paths with many types, consider a switch on a type tag or sealed pattern matching.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a payment service chooses a gateway implementation at run time (strategy), and a plugin system loads implementations with ServiceLoader.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

Replace if-else with polymorphism.

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Overload vs override.

11. Quick Revision

  • Overloading: compile time; overriding: run time.
  • Parent reference can hold child object.
  • Fields are not polymorphic.
  • Use @Override.
  • Covariant return types are allowed.

interviewQA: What are the two types of polymorphism in Java?
Compile-time (method overloading) and runtime (method overriding)
Can return type alone distinguish two overloaded methods?
No - overloads must differ in parameter list (count/type/order); return type alone is not enough and causes a compile error
Why can't static methods be overridden?

Static methods are resolved at compile time by the reference type (method hiding), not at runtime by the object's actual type - overriding requires dynamic dispatch, which only applies to instance methods
Can a constructor be overridden?
No - constructors aren't inherited at all, so there's nothing to override (though they can be overloaded within the same class)
What is a covariant return type?
An overriding method may narrow its return type to a subtype of what the parent method declared (e.g. Animal reproduce() overridden to return Dog)

topics.name: Multitasking in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Multitasking is running several tasks at once: process-based (separate programs) or thread-based (threads inside one program).

2. Need of This Topic

  • Modern programs handle many users and I/O waits.
  • Doing tasks concurrently keeps them responsive and uses all CPU cores.

3. Advantages

  • Better CPU and I/O utilization.
  • Responsive applications.
  • Threads share memory cheaply.

4. Disadvantages

  • Shared data causes race conditions.
  • Debugging concurrency bugs is hard.
  • Too many threads waste resources.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Servers and apps must handle concurrent work.
  • Foundation for threads and executors.
  • Interview staple.

6. Basic Concepts

Multitasking in Java refers to the system's ability to run multiple tasks concurrently, primarily achieved through

Process-based multitasking (running different Java apps or OS apps simultaneously) and Thread-based multitasking (multithreading),

where a single Java program performs multiple tasks (threads) concurrently, sharing resources for better efficiency and responsiveness,

using java.lang.Thread and Runnable for implementation.

Multithreading is Java's key to efficient resource use, allowing tasks like UI updates and background processing to run in parallel

Types of Multitasking in Java

  1. Process-based Multitasking:
  • Definition: Running multiple independent programs (processes) at the same time, managed by the Operating System (OS).
  • Example: Using a web browser, media player, and code editor simultaneously.
  • Key Feature: Each process has its own memory space, providing isolation.
  1. Thread-based Multitasking (Multithreading):
  • Definition: Executing multiple threads (lightweight sub-processes) within a single Java program concurrently, within the same memory space.
  • Example: Formatting text while printing in a word processor, or a server handling multiple client requests.
  • Key Feature: Threads share resources, leading to faster execution and better CPU utilization for complex tasks.

How Java Actually Creates a New Process

Thread-based multitasking is built into the language via Thread/Runnable, but Java can also trigger true process-based multitasking - launching a brand-new OS process (with its own separate memory and its own JVM/executable) - using ProcessBuilder (or the older Runtime.exec()).

Fresher Notes

  • Multitasking is doing several tasks at the same time. Process-based multitasking runs separate programs; thread-based runs several threads inside one program.
  • Shared memory: threads of one process share memory, so they are lightweight and communicate easily (but need care).
  • Java support: thread-based multitasking uses Thread, Runnable and the executor framework.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Process of executing multiple tasks simultaneously. We use multitasking to utilize the CPU.

  • Multitasking is when a single CPU performs several tasks (program, process, task, threads) at the

same time. To perform multitasking, the CPU switches among these tasks very frequently so that

user can interact with each program simultaneously.

  • In a multitasking operating system, several users can share the system simultaneously. CPU rapidly

switches among the tasks, so a little time is needed to switch from one user to the next user. This

puts an impression on a user that entire computer system is dedicated to him.

  • When several users are sharing a multitasking operating system, CPU scheduling and

multiprogramming makes it possible for each user to have at least a small portion of Multitasking

OS and let each user have at least one program in the memory for execution.

Multitasking can be achieved in two ways:

  • Process-based Multitasking (Multiprocessing)
  • Thread-based Multitasking (Multithreading)

Example:

In online session, what are the different activities done by students as?

  • Listen the class
  • Taking running notes
  • Checking mobile

1. Process Based / Process Based Multitasking (Multiprocessing):

  • Executing several tasks simultaneously where each task is separate independent process such

as multitasking is called as Process Based.

Example

1: Typing java program into eclipse, also listening the audio songs, download a file from

internet.

  1. In this every activity is independent process here.

Example

2: Task manager, see the multiple process list. (Control+Shift+Esc key)

  • Cost of communication between the process is high.
  • Switching from one process to another requires some time for saving and loading registers, memory

maps, updating lists, etc.

  • Process is heavy weight components.
  • Each process has an own address in memory. In other words, each process allocates a separate

memory area.

2. Thread Based / Thread Based Multitasking (Multithreading):

  • Executing several tasks simultaneously where each task is separate part of same program called as

thread based.

Example-

suppose I have 1000 lines of code into java program and it will takes 4 hours to execute it

where first 500 line is executed after that remaining 500 lines is executed but there is no any

dependency between them so I can run that tasks simultaneously to minimize the execution time.

  • Thread shares the same address space.
  • Thread is light weight components.
  • Cost of communication between the thread is low.
Process-Based Multitasking Thread-Based Multitasking
This deals with "Big Picture" This deals with Details
These are Heavyweight tasks These are Lightweight tasks
Inter-process communication is expensive and limited Inter-thread communication is inexpensive
Context switching from one process to another is costly in terms of memory Context switching is low cost in terms of memory , because they run on the same address space
This is not under the control of Java This is controlled by Java

Mid-Level Notes

  • Concurrency means tasks make progress by interleaving; parallelism means tasks run at the same instant on multiple cores.
  • When to use threads: for I/O waiting (network, disk) and CPU parallelism, not for tiny tasks.
  • Scheduling: the OS scheduler decides which thread runs, so order is not guaranteed.

8. Advanced Concepts

Process-Based vs Thread-Based Multitasking: Memory Model

The fundamental difference between the two forms of multitasking is where the memory boundary is drawn. A process gets its own isolated address space from the OS; a thread lives inside an address space that is already shared with its sibling threads.

PROCESS-BASED MULTITASKING (Multiprocessing)
+------------------+   +------------------+   +------------------+
|   Process A      |   |   Process B      |   |   Process C      |
|  (e.g. browser)   |   |  (e.g. IDE)       |   |  (e.g. JVM)       |
|  own heap         |   |  own heap         |   |  own heap         |
|  own stack(s)      |   |  own stack(s)      |   |  own stack(s)      |
|  own file handles  |   |  own file handles  |   |  own file handles  |
+------------------+   +------------------+   +------------------+
        No shared memory - OS enforces isolation. Heavyweight
        context switch: save/restore full CPU register set,
        memory maps (page tables), open file tables, etc.

THREAD-BASED MULTITASKING (Multithreading) - inside ONE process
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    Single JVM Process                        |
|   +-----------+   +-----------+   +-----------+              |
|   | Thread-1  |   | Thread-2  |   | Thread-3  |              |
|   | own stack |   | own stack |   | own stack |              |
|   +-----------+   +-----------+   +-----------+              |
|                        |            /                        |
|                        |           /                         |
|          Shared Heap + Shared Static/Class data               |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
        Threads share heap & static memory. Lightweight context
        switch: only registers + program counter + own stack
        pointer need saving - no page table / memory map swap.
  • Process-based: each process (e.g. a browser, an IDE, a music player) has its own memory space - isolated, safe, but expensive to switch between and expensive to communicate across (needs IPC - pipes, sockets, shared memory files).
  • Thread-based: all threads of one Java program run inside the same process, so they automatically share the heap and static fields - no IPC needed, communication is as cheap as reading/writing a shared variable.

Proof: Multiple Threads, One Process, Shared Memory

The demo below starts 3 threads from a single main(). Each thread prints its own name (proving they are distinct threads) alongside a shared static counter (proving they all read/write the SAME memory, because they belong to the SAME process). If these were separate OS processes instead of threads, none of them could see or modify another's counter without explicit IPC.

Each thread still has its own private call stack and its own local variables - only the heap/static area is shared. The next demo proves both halves of that claim in one program: a local variable is independent per thread, while a static field is the same memory for every thread.

Why Threads Are Cheaper Than Processes

For an application that needs many concurrent units of work (a web server handling thousands of requests, for example), spinning up an OS process per task is far too expensive - threads are the practical choice. The table below compares the cost of a context switch in each model.

AspectProcess Context SwitchThread Context Switch
Memory map / page tableMust be swapped (TLB flush)Same for all threads - not touched
CPU cache effectCold cache after switch (different process' data)Cache often stays warmer - same process' data
Creation costHigh - OS allocates new address space, file tables, etc.Low - just a new stack + thread control block
Communication costHigh - needs IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory)Low - direct read/write of shared heap/static fields
Isolation / safetyStrong - one process crashing doesn't affect anotherWeaker - an unsynchronized thread can corrupt shared data of the whole process
Typical scaleTens to hundreds per machineThousands per single JVM process is feasible

This is exactly why a single Java application uses thread-based multitasking internally (via Thread/Runnable/ExecutorService) rather than spawning a new OS process for every concurrent task - the per-task overhead of a thread is a small fraction of the overhead of a process.

Concurrency vs Parallelism - It Depends on CPU Cores

Multitasking makes tasks appear to run at the same time, but whether they are truly simultaneous depends on the hardware:

  • Concurrency: multiple tasks make progress by being interleaved on a single CPU core - the OS/JVM rapidly switches between them, so no two instructions from different tasks execute at the exact same instant.
  • Parallelism: multiple tasks genuinely execute at the exact same instant, each on its own CPU core.

A multi-core machine running multiple threads gets both: parallelism across cores, and concurrency (interleaving) among any threads that outnumber the available cores.

Senior Notes

  • Pick the model: platform threads (OS), bounded thread pools, virtual threads (Java 21) for blocking I/O at scale, reactive for non-blocking pipelines.
  • Amdahl law: the serial fraction limits speedup, so adding cores helps only the parallel parts.
  • Pool sizing: size CPU pools near the core count and I/O pools by waiting ratio; measure.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Models: thread-per-task, bounded pools (newFixedThreadPool, ForkJoinPool with work stealing), asynchronous composition (CompletableFuture), reactive streams (Reactor, RxJava), actors, and structured concurrency (preview) to scope subtasks. Parallel streams use the common ForkJoinPool and suit CPU-bound pure functions on large data.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

A Java platform thread maps one-to-one to an OS thread with its own stack (about 1 MB reserved). The OS scheduler time-slices threads across cores; context switches save registers and invalidate caches, so too many threads waste time. Virtual threads (Java 21) are scheduled by the JVM on a small pool of carrier threads and park cheaply when blocked.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: creating a thread per request without limits (resource exhaustion), blocking inside a small pool (starvation), sharing the common pool for blocking I/O, ignoring exceptions in tasks (swallowed by Future), unbounded queues, and forgetting to shut down executors (JVM never exits). Name threads and use bounded queues with rejection policies.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Throughput depends on contention, not only thread count. Amdahl law: with 10% serial work the maximum speedup is 10x, however many cores you add. Measure with realistic load, watch context switches and CPU stalls, and use JFR (Java Flight Recorder) to find lock contention.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a web server handles each request on a worker or virtual thread, calls downstream services in parallel with CompletableFuture and applies timeouts, bulkheads and a bounded queue to protect itself.

10. Examples

11. Quick Revision

  • Process vs thread.
  • Concurrency vs parallelism.
  • Threads share the heap.
  • Size pools by workload type.
  • Amdahl law limits speedup.

The ability of a system to execute more than one task at the same time (or apparently at the same time)
What are the two types of multitasking?
Process-based multitasking (multiprocessing) and thread-based multitasking (multithreading)
What is the key memory difference between a process and a thread?
Each process has its own isolated memory space; threads of the same process share that process' heap and static memory
Why is a thread called "lightweight" compared to a process?
Creating/switching a thread doesn't require allocating a new address space or swapping memory maps - only a new stack and CPU register state are involved
Why is inter-thread communication cheaper than inter-process communication?
Threads already share memory, so they communicate via ordinary shared variables; processes are isolated and need OS-level IPC mechanisms (pipes, sockets, shared memory)
What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
Concurrency is multiple tasks making progress via interleaving (possibly on one core); parallelism is multiple tasks executing at literally the same instant on separate cores
How can you find out how many CPU cores are available to the JVM?
Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()
Does having more threads than CPU cores still help performance?

Yes for I/O-bound or blocking tasks, since idle threads (waiting on I/O) let the OS schedule other threads on the same core - though for pure CPU-bound work, threads beyond the core count add context-switch overhead without real parallel gain
Which classes does Java provide to implement thread-based multitasking?
java.lang.Thread and the java.lang.Runnable interface, plus higher-level utilities like ExecutorService

topics.name: Multithreading in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Multithreading is the ability of a Java program to run more than one thread inside a single process, created with Thread, Runnable, Callable and executors.
  • A thread is the smallest unit of work the CPU can schedule
  • Threads share the heap but each has its own stack and program counter.
  • At production level it also means understanding the Java Memory Model (happens-before rules) and the java.util.concurrent toolkit, with platform threads and, from Java 21, lightweight virtual threads.

2. Need of This Topic

  • It lets one program do several jobs together, so a slow task such as a file read or bank API call does not block everything behind it, and the application stays responsive while using all CPU cores.
  • Real frameworks such as Spring Boot and Tomcat are multithreaded, and high-throughput services need bounded pools, back pressure and safe shutdown instead of a thread per request.

3. Advantages

  • Faster execution: independent jobs run together and use multi-core CPUs better.
  • Responsive programs: the UI thread stays free during long background work.
  • Threads are cheaper than processes and failures stay isolated to one thread.
  • Tuned pools give high throughput and bounded resource use under traffic spikes.
  • CompletableFuture hides latency; virtual threads scale blocking IO code simply.
  • Built-in tools such as CountDownLatch, Semaphore and ConcurrentHashMap reduce hand-written locks.

4. Disadvantages

  • Race conditions and deadlocks (also livelock).
  • Bugs are non-deterministic and hard to test or debug.
  • Context-switch overhead and extra memory for each thread stack.
  • Thread pool starvation, false sharing and ThreadLocal leaks can hurt production systems.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • All server applications use threads.
  • Needed for executors, async and virtual threads.
  • Choose the right tool: ExecutorService for CPU work, CompletableFuture for pipelines, virtual threads for blocking IO.
  • Top interview topic (volatile, synchronized, atomics, pool sizing).

6. Basic Concepts

  • Multithreading in Java is a programming concept that allows multiple threads (smaller units of a process) to run concurrently within a single Java program.
  • Each thread represents a separate path of execution, enabling tasks to be performed simultaneously, which enhances the efficiency and responsiveness of applications.
  • Java provides built-in support for multithreading through the java.lang.Thread class and the Runnable interface, allowing developers to create and manage threads easily.
  • Multithreading is particularly useful for tasks that require parallel processing, such as handling user interfaces, performing background operations, or managing multiple client requests in server applications.

Process vs Thread

  • A process is a running program with its own separate memory space (heap, stack, code) allocated by the OS. Two processes cannot directly share memory.
  • A thread is a lightweight sub-unit of a process. All threads inside the same process share that process's memory and resources, but each thread still gets its own stack and program counter.
  • Because threads share memory with the process they belong to, creating a thread is much cheaper (faster, less memory) than creating a whole new process.

Every Java Program Already Has One Thread: main

  • The moment a Java program starts, the JVM automatically creates one thread called main to run the public static void main(String[] args) method.
  • Any additional threads you create in your program run alongside this main thread - that's what makes the program "multithreaded".

Single-Threaded vs Multithreaded Execution

  • In a single-threaded program, tasks run one after another - the next task only starts once the previous one fully finishes.
  • In a multithreaded program, independent tasks can run at (roughly) the same time, so the total time taken can be much less than running them one by one.

Creating a Thread - Quick First Example (extending Thread)

The simplest way to get a second thread running: extend Thread, override run() with the code you want to execute, then call start() (never call run() directly - that just runs it like a normal method on the current thread, with no new thread involved).

Creating a Thread - Quick First Example (implementing Runnable)

The alternative, generally preferred, approach: implement Runnable's single run() method, then hand that Runnable to a Thread object to actually run it. (The full comparison between the two approaches is covered later.)

Naming Threads and Running Several at Once

  • Every thread has a name - if you don't set one, the JVM auto-assigns something like Thread-0, Thread-1, etc.
  • Giving threads meaningful names (via the Thread(Runnable, String name) constructor or setName()) makes debugging and log-reading far easier once several threads are running together.

Daemon Threads vs User (Normal) Threads

  • By default, every thread you create is a user thread - the JVM keeps running as long as at least one user thread is still alive, even if main() has already finished.
  • A daemon thread is a background/service thread (e.g. garbage collection) that does NOT keep the JVM alive - once every user thread finishes, the JVM exits immediately, killing any daemon threads mid-execution without waiting for them.
  • Mark a thread as daemon with setDaemon(true) BEFORE calling start() (calling it after start() throws IllegalThreadStateException). Use daemon threads for background housekeeping work that should never block the application from shutting down.

Why Multithreading Matters - A Concrete Timing Comparison

The clearest way to see the benefit is to time independent, slow tasks run one-by-one versus run concurrently. When tasks don't depend on each other's results, running them on separate threads lets their waiting/working time overlap instead of stacking up.

Fresher Notes

  • Create a thread: extend Thread or (better) implement Runnable and pass it to new Thread(runnable).
  • start() vs run(): start() runs the task in a new thread. Calling run() directly runs it in the current thread.
  • Waiting: join() waits for a thread to finish. sleep(ms) pauses the current thread.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Process of executing multiple threads simultaneously.

  • Multithreading vs multitasking: multitasking runs several programs (processes) at the same time. Multithreading runs several threads of one program at the same time.
  • A thread is a basic unit of execution. It has its own program counter, registers and stack. It shares the code, data and open files of its process.
  • One process can have many threads. The CPU switches between them so fast that the user feels they all run together.

Benefits of Multithreading

  • Responsiveness: if one thread is busy or blocked, other threads keep the application alive, so the user does not sit idle.
  • Resource sharing: threads of one process share its code and data in the same address space.
  • Low cost: a new process needs its own memory and resources. A new thread of the same process needs no separate memory.

What is Thread?

  • A thread is a lightweight sub-process and the smallest unit of processing. It runs inside a larger process as a separate path of execution.
  • Threads are independent. If one thread throws an exception, the other threads are not affected. They use a shared memory area.

In the figure above, threads run inside a process and the CPU switches between them (context switching). An OS can run many processes, and each process can have many threads.

Note: Only one thread runs per CPU core at a time - on an N-core machine up to N threads execute in true parallel

How to Create a Thread?

There are 2 ways:

  1. By extending the Thread class
  2. By implementing the Runnable interface

1. By Extending the Thread Class

The Thread class has constructors and methods to create and control a thread. It extends Object and implements Runnable.

Constructors

  • Thread()
  • Thread(String name)
  • Thread(Runnable r)
  • Thread(Runnable r, String name)

Methods with Description

  1. public void run(): holds the action the thread performs.
  2. public void start(): starts the thread. The JVM then calls run() on it.
  3. public static void sleep(long ms): pauses the current thread for the given milliseconds. It is static, so t.sleep(100) still pauses the caller, not thread t.
  4. public void join(): waits for a thread to die.
  5. public void join(long ms): waits for a thread to die, for at most the given milliseconds.
  6. public int getPriority(): returns the priority of the thread.
  7. public void setPriority(int priority): changes the priority of the thread.
  8. public String getName(): returns the name of the thread.
  9. public void setName(String name): changes the name of the thread.
  10. public static Thread currentThread(): returns the thread that is running now.
  11. public long getId(): returns the id of the thread (deprecated since Java 19, use threadId()).
  12. public Thread.State getState(): returns the state of the thread.
  13. public boolean isAlive(): tests if the thread is alive.
  14. public static void yield(): hints that the current thread is willing to let other threads run.
  15. public void suspend(): suspends the thread (deprecated, unsafe).
  16. public void resume(): resumes a suspended thread (deprecated, unsafe).
  17. public void stop(): stops the thread (deprecated, unsafe; it throws UnsupportedOperationException in recent Java).
  18. public boolean isDaemon(): tests if the thread is a daemon thread.
  19. public void setDaemon(boolean b): marks the thread as daemon or user thread.
  20. public void interrupt(): interrupts the thread.
  21. public boolean isInterrupted(): tests if the thread has been interrupted.
  22. public static boolean interrupted(): tests if the current thread was interrupted, and clears the flag.

2. By Implementing the Runnable Interface

Any class whose instances are meant to run on a thread can implement Runnable. The interface has only one method, run().

Note

A class that only implements Runnable is not a thread. You must create a Thread object and pass your object to it, so that your run() method can execute.

When to use which?

  • Extend Thread: when your class does not need to extend any other class.
  • Implement Runnable: when your class already extends another class. Java has no multiple inheritance, so Runnable is the way to go.

Difference between Thread class and Runnable interface (Self assignment)

Sr.no Key Thread Runnable
1. Basic Thread is a class. It is used to create a thread Runnable is a functional interface which is used to create a thread
2. Method It has multiple methods including start() and run() It has only abstract method run()
3. Object Each thread creates a unique object and gets associated with it Multiple threads share the same objects.
4. Limitation Java has no multiple inheritance, so a class that extends Thread cannot extend any other class A class that implements Runnable can still extend another class

Advantages for Multithreading in Java

  • Not blocked: threads are independent, so users are not blocked and many operations run at the same time.
  • Failure isolation: an exception in one thread does not affect the others.

Key benefits:

  1. Improved performance: threads run concurrently and use multi-core processors well.
  2. Better resource use: while one thread waits for I/O, other threads keep the CPU busy.
  3. Responsive user interface: slow work runs in the background, so a GUI stays smooth.
  4. Simpler program structure: tasks like asynchronous I/O, periodic jobs and background processing become easier to organise.
  5. Scalability: a multithreaded program can use more CPU cores as they become available.
  6. Concurrency handling: a server can process many client requests at once.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Callable: Callable returns a value and can throw. Submit it with ExecutorService.submit to get a Future.
  • Daemon threads: setDaemon(true) threads do not keep the JVM alive. The JVM exits when only daemon threads remain.
  • Interrupts: on InterruptedException, either stop the work or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt().

8. Advanced Concepts

Thread vs Runnable — Which Should You Actually Use?

Both ways of creating a thread ultimately run the same JVM machinery, but they are not equally good choices for real code. The comparison below goes beyond the beginner-level list already covered earlier and focuses on WHY Runnable is the preferred approach in production code.

Aspect extends Thread implements Runnable
InheritanceUses up your one allowed superclass slotLeaves the superclass slot free - you can still extend another class
DesignCouples the "task" with the "thread mechanism"Decouples the task (what to run) from how it is run - the same Runnable can be handed to a Thread, an ExecutorService, or run directly
Object identityEvery task IS-A ThreadThe task HAS-A Thread (or no thread at all, e.g. inside a pool)
ReusabilityCannot share the same Thread object's task across multiple threadsThe same Runnable instance can be passed to multiple Thread objects or submitted to a pool
Fits Executor framework?Not directly - ExecutorService expects Runnable/CallableYes - Runnable is exactly what ExecutorService.submit() accepts
Industry recommendationAvoid unless you genuinely need to override other Thread methodsPreferred default

Rule of thumb: almost always implement Runnable (or Callable). Only extend Thread directly when you truly need to override its behavior (rare).

Thread Priority — A Hint, Not a Guarantee

Every thread has a priority between Thread.MIN_PRIORITY (1) and Thread.MAX_PRIORITY (10), with Thread.NORM_PRIORITY (5) as the default. You set it with setPriority(int) and read it with getPriority().

Critical interview point: thread priority is only a suggestion to the OS/JVM thread scheduler about relative importance - it is NOT a contract. The JVM specification does not guarantee that a higher-priority thread will run before, more often than, or instead of a lower-priority one. Actual scheduling behavior is platform-dependent (it can differ between Windows, Linux, and different JVM implementations). Never rely on priority for correctness - use it only as a soft performance hint, and use proper synchronization (join, locks, etc.) whenever ordering actually matters.

join() — Waiting for a Thread to Finish

By default, once you call start(), the calling thread does NOT wait for the new thread to complete - both proceed independently and their output can interleave unpredictably. join() makes the calling thread pause until the target thread finishes (or until an optional timeout elapses), which is how you get deterministic, ordered output when you actually need it.

Beyond Raw Threads: the ExecutorService / Thread Pool Approach

Manually creating a new Thread(...) for every task does not scale: unbounded thread creation exhausts memory and OS resources, and there is no easy way to reuse threads, queue excess work, or manage a shutdown sequence. Production Java code almost never calls new Thread().start() directly for application tasks - it uses the java.util.concurrent Executor framework, which manages a pool of reusable worker threads for you.

Manual Thread                      ExecutorService (thread pool)
--------------                     -----------------------------
new Thread(task).start()           executor.submit(task)
  |                                    |
  v                                    v
1 task  -> 1 brand-new OS thread    N tasks -> reused from a fixed
(created & destroyed every time)    pool of worker threads
  |                                    |
No built-in queueing,               Built-in task queue, thread reuse,
no lifecycle management             graceful shutdown() / awaitTermination()

Common factory methods on Executors: newFixedThreadPool(n), newSingleThreadExecutor(), newCachedThreadPool(), and (Java 21+) newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Always call shutdown() when done so pooled threads can terminate.

Senior Notes

  • Executors: prefer them over manual threads, and always shut them down (shutdown, awaitTermination).
  • Safe sharing: use immutability, confinement, locks, atomics or concurrent collections.
  • Virtual threads: from Java 21, one thread per task is cheap for blocking code.

9. Code for Each Concept

Code: Definition
Code: Advantages
Code: Definition (Advanced)
Code: Advantages (Advanced)

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Coordination utilities: CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, Semaphore, Phaser, Exchanger, BlockingQueue, ScheduledExecutorService, ForkJoinPool / RecursiveTask. Timeouts everywhere: future.get(timeout), tryLock(timeout).

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Thread.start() asks the JVM to create an OS thread (native call) that runs run(). The new thread has its own stack and program counter, and shares the heap. ThreadPoolExecutor keeps core threads alive, queues extra tasks, grows to the max size when the queue is full, then applies the rejection policy. Thread locals give per-thread state.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: calling run instead of start, ignoring InterruptedException, using Thread.stop (deprecated, and it throws in recent Java), non-daemon pool threads preventing exit, thread leaks, SimpleDateFormat shared across threads, unsafe publication, and ThreadLocal leaks in pools (always call remove). Also wrong: catching Exception and doing nothing inside tasks.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Thread creation costs about 50-100 microseconds and 1 MB of stack reservation; pools amortize this. Contended locks cause parking and context switches. Use fewer, longer-lived threads for CPU work, virtual threads for blocking, and avoid sharing mutable state.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a nightly job splits files across a fixed pool, collects results via futures, and reports failures with context; timeouts and interruption allow a clean shutdown.

10. Examples

Real Time Examples

  • IRCTC ticket booking: thousands of users book at 10 AM. The server gives each request its own thread so nobody waits for another person.
  • Bank cheque clearing: a nightly batch splits one lakh cheques among 10 threads so the job finishes before morning.
  • Paytm or PhonePe app: one thread shows the spinning loader while another thread waits for the UPI reply.
  • WhatsApp: one thread sends your message, another downloads photos, another keeps the chat list smooth.
  • College attendance app: a background thread syncs today attendance to the server while the teacher keeps marking students.
  • Global example: a web server such as Tomcat keeps a pool of 200 threads and gives one thread to each incoming HTTP request.

Real Time Examples (Advanced)

  • NPCI UPI switch: handles crores of transactions a day using bounded thread pools per stage and idempotent retries, so a duplicate request never debits twice.
  • Spring Boot on Tomcat: the container keeps a pool of worker threads. Setting server.tomcat.threads.max too high causes memory pressure, too low causes queueing.
  • Zomato or Swiggy order pipeline: when an order is placed, restaurant confirmation, rider assignment and payment capture run in parallel as CompletableFuture stages.
  • Kafka consumer group: each partition is handled by one thread so message order inside a partition is preserved while different partitions run in parallel.
  • Bank end of day batch: a Spring Batch job partitions accounts across threads. A shared AtomicLong holds the total and a CountDownLatch waits for all partitions.
  • Global example: Netflix uses bulkheads, one small pool per downstream service, so a slow recommendation service cannot exhaust the threads needed for video playback.

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1
