Practice Exercise 2

start vs run.

11. Quick Revision

  • start() creates a thread, run() does not.
  • Runnable vs Callable.
  • join waits for a thread.
  • Use executors, not raw threads.
  • Handle InterruptedException.

interviewQA: Why is implementing Runnable generally preferred over extending Thread?

Java allows only single inheritance, so extending Thread uses up your one superclass slot; Runnable also decouples the task from the threading mechanism, letting the same task run on a raw Thread, an ExecutorService, or directly
What happens if you call run() directly instead of start()?
It executes like a normal method call on the current thread - no new thread is created, and none of the JVM's thread-scheduling machinery is invoked
Can you call start() twice on the same Thread object?
No - it throws IllegalThreadStateException; a Thread instance can be started only once, ever
Does a higher thread priority guarantee that thread runs first?
No - priority is only a scheduling hint to the OS/JVM; actual behavior is platform-dependent and not guaranteed by the Java specification
What does join() do, and why is it needed?
It makes the calling thread block until the target thread finishes (or a timeout elapses) - needed whenever you require deterministic ordering between a spawned thread and the thread that started it
Why prefer ExecutorService over manually creating Thread objects?

Manually creating unbounded threads wastes memory/OS resources and has no reuse or queueing; ExecutorService manages a pool of reusable worker threads with built-in task queueing and graceful shutdown
What is the difference between Runnable and Callable in the Executor framework?
Runnable's run() returns void and cannot throw checked exceptions; Callable's call() returns a value (via Future) and can throw checked exceptions
What must you remember to do after submitting tasks to an ExecutorService?
Call shutdown() (or shutdownNow()) so the pool's worker threads are allowed to terminate once queued/running tasks complete - otherwise the JVM may not exit

topics.name: Life Cycle of Thread

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • The life cycle of a thread is the set of states it passes through from creation until it dies: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING and TERMINATED, defined in Thread.State.
  • You can read the current state with getState().
  • BLOCKED means waiting for a monitor lock, while WAITING means a call such as wait(), join() or LockSupport.park() without a timeout.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Knowing the states shows what a thread is really doing (ready, sleeping or stuck on a lock) and lets you tell a slow thread from a stuck one.
  • It explains why start() works only once and why calling run() directly is a mistake, and it gives the vocabulary of thread dumps used to diagnose hangs and deadlocks in production.

3. Advantages

  • Clear model of thread behavior and easy debugging with getState() and jstack.
  • Explains wait, notify, sleep and join, so code ordering becomes predictable.
  • Prevents wrong API use such as IllegalThreadStateException from restarting a thread.
  • Deadlock detection (ThreadMXBean) and graceful shutdown with interrupt() and awaitTermination().
  • Helps size pools: mostly WAITING on IO suggests more threads or virtual threads, RUNNABLE suggests more cores.

4. Disadvantages

  • States are JVM-level and can mislead (RUNNABLE may be blocked in native I/O).
  • getState() is only a snapshot, so never use it for program logic.
  • A terminated thread cannot restart, and suspend() and resume() are deprecated.
  • Thread dumps are point in time, cost a pause and are hard to read with many virtual threads.
  • Interrupt is cooperative: a swallowed InterruptedException keeps a thread waiting.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Frequent interview question (BLOCKED vs WAITING vs TIMED_WAITING).
  • Needed to read thread dumps and find contended locks.
  • Basis for synchronization topics and clean shutdown design.

6. Basic Concepts

What is a Thread "State"?

  • A thread does not run continuously from birth to death - at every moment it is in exactly one of a fixed set of states.
  • Java models this with the enum Thread.State, which has 6 values: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED.
  • You can check any thread's current state by calling thread.getState().

We will look at the 3 simplest states first - NEW, RUNNABLE, and TERMINATED - then go deeper into BLOCKED, WAITING, and TIMED_WAITING in the Expert section.

1. NEW State

  • A thread is in the NEW state right after it is created with new Thread(...), but before start() has been called.
  • In this state the thread exists as an object only - no thread of execution has actually started at the OS level yet.
new Thread(task)
      |
      v
  +-------+
  |  NEW  |   <-- object created, start() NOT called yet
  +-------+

2. RUNNABLE State

  • Once start() is called, the thread moves to RUNNABLE.
  • RUNNABLE means the thread is eligible to run - it may actually be executing on a CPU core right now, or it may just be waiting its turn from the thread scheduler. Java does not distinguish these two as separate states.
  +-------+  start()   +-----------+
  |  NEW  | ---------> | RUNNABLE  |   <-- eligible to run / running
  +-------+            +-----------+

3. TERMINATED State

  • A thread enters TERMINATED (also called "dead") once its run() method completes - either normally or by throwing an uncaught exception.
  • A terminated thread can never be started again; calling start() on it throws IllegalThreadStateException.
  +-----------+  run() returns   +------------+
  | RUNNABLE  | ---------------> | TERMINATED |   <-- dead, cannot restart
  +-----------+                  +------------+

Why does the life cycle matter?

  • A thread is "born" (NEW), gets "started" (RUNNABLE), may pause temporarily (BLOCKED / WAITING / TIMED_WAITING - covered in Expert level), and finally "dies" (TERMINATED).
  • Understanding these states helps you debug deadlocks, diagnose hung threads with a thread dump, and reason about concurrency correctly.

Fresher Notes

  • Thread states: NEW (created), RUNNABLE (running or ready), BLOCKED (waiting for a monitor lock), WAITING (wait/join without timeout), TIMED_WAITING (sleep, wait with timeout) and TERMINATED.
  • Reading state: thread.getState() returns the current state.
  • Terminated: a terminated thread cannot be started again.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Transitions: start() moves NEW to RUNNABLE; sleep gives TIMED_WAITING; synchronized contention gives BLOCKED; wait() and join() give WAITING.
  • Wake-up: notify/notifyAll wake waiting threads, which then compete for the lock.
  • Restart: calling start() twice throws IllegalThreadStateException.

8. Advanced Concepts

The Complete 6-State Life Cycle

Java's Thread.State enum has exactly 6 values. The full transition diagram:

                         start()
        +-------+ ---------------> +-----------+
        |  NEW  |                  | RUNNABLE  | <---------------------+
        +-------+                  +-----------+                      |
                                     |   |   |                         |
                    needs lock       |   |   | Thread.sleep(ms)        |
                    held by another  |   |   | wait(timeout)           |
                    thread           |   |   | join(timeout)           |
                       +-------------+   |   +----------------+        |
                       v                 |                    v        |
               +-----------+             |            +----------------+
               |  BLOCKED  |             |            | TIMED_WAITING  |
               +-----------+             |            +----------------+
                       |            Object.wait()             |        |
                       |            join()  (no timeout)       |        |
        lock acquired  |                 v                    | timeout|
        (notified/     |         +-----------+                | elapses|
         monitor free)  |         |  WAITING  |                |        |
                       |         +-----------+                |        |
                       |                 |                     |        |
                       +-----------------+---------------------+--------+
                                          |
                                          v  run() returns / exception
                                  +------------+
                                  | TERMINATED |
                                  +------------+
StateMeaningHow you get thereHow you leave
NEWThread object created, not startednew Thread(...)start()
RUNNABLEEligible to run (running or ready)start(), or resumed from a wait/block/sleepblocks, waits, sleeps, or finishes
BLOCKEDWaiting to acquire a monitor lock (synchronized)entering a synchronized block/method held by another threadlock becomes available
WAITINGWaiting indefinitely for another thread's actionObject.wait(), join() (no timeout), LockSupport.park()notify()/notifyAll(), target thread finishes, unpark()
TIMED_WAITINGWaiting for a bounded amount of timeThread.sleep(ms), wait(timeout), join(timeout)timeout elapses, or notified/finished early
TERMINATEDrun() has completed (dead)run() returns or throwsnone - final state

Demo 1: TIMED_WAITING via Thread.sleep()

A thread that calls Thread.sleep(ms) moves into TIMED_WAITING for the duration of the sleep. We inspect its state from the main thread while it is sleeping.

Demo 2: BLOCKED via synchronized lock contention

Two threads compete for the same object's monitor lock. The first thread to enter the synchronized block holds the lock and sleeps inside it; the second thread tries to enter the same block and is forced into BLOCKED until the first thread releases the lock.

Demo 3: WAITING via Object.wait() / notify()

A thread that calls wait() with no timeout goes into WAITING and stays there indefinitely - releasing the lock - until another thread calls notify() on the same object.

Reference Diagram

Historical Note - Deprecated States

Older Java versions exposed suspend() and resume() methods that put a thread into a "suspended" state and back. These are deprecated because suspend() can freeze a thread while it still holds a lock, causing deadlocks - modern code should never use them. Prefer wait()/notify(), Lock/Condition, or higher-level java.util.concurrent utilities instead.

Senior Notes

  • Thread dumps: use jstack or jcmd Thread.print to see states and diagnose deadlocks and contention.
  • Reading counts: many threads in BLOCKED means lock contention; many in WAITING on a pool queue means idle workers.
  • RUNNABLE caveat: it includes threads blocked in native I/O, which can mislead.

9. Code for Each Concept

Code: Definition
Code: Advantages
Code: Definition (Advanced)
Code: Advantages (Advanced)

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Diagnostics: jstack, jcmd Thread.print, ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads(), JFR thread events, and VisualVM. Interrupt protocol: interrupt sets a flag and wakes blocking calls with InterruptedException; code should check isInterrupted() in loops and exit cleanly. Virtual threads show as "VirtualThread" in dumps (use jcmd Thread.dump_to_file).

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Thread.State is a JVM-level view. RUNNABLE covers both running on a CPU and ready or blocked in native I/O. Transitions: NEW to RUNNABLE on start; RUNNABLE to BLOCKED when entering a contended synchronized block; to WAITING on Object.wait(), Thread.join(), LockSupport.park(); to TIMED_WAITING with timeouts; to TERMINATED when run ends or throws.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using Thread.stop/suspend (removed or unsafe), busy waiting instead of wait/park, assuming RUNNABLE means executing on a CPU, ignoring spurious wakeups (always loop on the condition around wait), and swallowing interrupts. Always call wait inside a while loop.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Context switches and lock convoys slow throughput. Look for many threads BLOCKED on the same monitor in dumps: shrink critical sections, use lock striping, concurrent data structures, or read/write locks.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a stuck service with all request threads WAITING on a connection pool shows pool exhaustion; fix by finding leaked connections (not closed) or sizing and timeouts.

10. Examples

Real Time Examples

  • ATM cash dispenser: the thread is RUNNABLE while counting notes, TIMED_WAITING while it waits 30 seconds for you to take the cash, and TERMINATED once the receipt prints.
  • IRCTC payment page: the booking thread goes to WAITING while it waits for the bank to confirm, then returns to RUNNABLE when the reply arrives.
  • College library counter: only one clerk desk is free, so the second student thread is BLOCKED until the first one leaves. That is exactly a lock.
  • Printer queue in an office: jobs sit in WAITING, one job moves to RUNNABLE, then TERMINATED when the page comes out.
  • Swiggy delivery app: a background sync thread is in TIMED_WAITING between two location updates, using Thread.sleep of 10 seconds.
  • Global example: a Tomcat worker thread that shows BLOCKED in a production thread dump usually means a slow database query is holding a lock.

Real Time Examples (Advanced)

  • Bank core banking hang at month end: the dump shows 190 of 200 Tomcat threads BLOCKED on one synchronized interest calculation method. The fix is a per account lock or an optimistic update.
  • UPI timeout storm: threads sit in TIMED_WAITING on a socket read because no read timeout was set. Setting a 2 second timeout moves them to TERMINATED and frees the pool.
  • Kafka consumer stuck: the poll thread is WAITING on a rebalance. A long max.poll.interval.ms keeps the partition unassigned and lag grows.
  • Spring Boot graceful shutdown: server.shutdown=graceful gives in flight requests time to reach TERMINATED before the container exits, so no order is lost.
  • Zomato image service: after moving to Java 21 virtual threads, threads that were TIMED_WAITING on IO no longer pin a platform thread, so 20000 concurrent uploads work with 8 carrier threads.
  • Global example: a connection pool leak shows as many threads WAITING on getConnection. The real bug is a missing close in a finally block far away in the code.

Worked Example 1

Restart error.

Worked Example 2

Thread dump.

Practice Exercise 1

Observing states.

Practice Exercise 2

BLOCKED state.

BLOCKED vs WAITING vs TIMED_WAITING - The Key Interview Distinction

These three states are the ones interviewers probe most, because they are easy to confuse:

  • BLOCKED - the thread wants to enter a synchronized block/method but another thread already holds that monitor lock. It is purely about lock contention; the thread did nothing to voluntarily wait.
  • WAITING - the thread voluntarily called Object.wait() (with no timeout) or Thread.join() (no timeout) and is waiting indefinitely for another thread to call notify()/notifyAll() or for the joined thread to finish. It has released the lock while waiting.
  • TIMED_WAITING - same idea as WAITING, but bounded by a timeout: Thread.sleep(ms), wait(timeout), or join(timeout). It resumes automatically once the timeout elapses even if nobody notifies it.
BLOCKEDWAITINGTIMED_WAITING
CauseLock held by someone elseVoluntary indefinite waitVoluntary bounded wait
Triggered byentering synchronized blockwait(), join() no-argsleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms)
Holds the monitor lock?Never acquired itReleased it while waitingsleep() keeps lock; wait(ms) releases it
Resumes onLock becomes freenotify()/notifyAll() or target finishesTimeout elapses OR notify/finish

11. Quick Revision

  • NEW to RUNNABLE on start().
  • BLOCKED waits for a monitor lock.
  • WAITING: wait/join; TIMED_WAITING: sleep.
  • sleep keeps locks, wait releases them.
  • Thread cannot be restarted.

interviewQA: How many thread states does Java define?
6 - NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED (java.lang.Thread.State)
Difference between BLOCKED and WAITING?
BLOCKED is involuntary - waiting for a lock held by another thread. WAITING is voluntary - the thread called wait()/join() with no timeout and released the lock
What moves a thread from TIMED_WAITING back to RUNNABLE?
Either the timeout elapses, or the thread is notified/interrupted/joined thread finishes early
Does RUNNABLE mean the thread is actually executing right now?
Not necessarily - RUNNABLE covers both "currently running on a core" and "ready and waiting for the scheduler's turn"; Java does not distinguish these
Can a TERMINATED thread be restarted with start()?
No - it throws IllegalThreadStateException; a Thread object can only be started once
Does Thread.sleep() release the object's monitor lock?
No - sleep() keeps any locks the thread holds; only wait() releases the lock while waiting
Why are suspend()/resume() deprecated?
suspend() can freeze a thread while it still holds a lock, leading to deadlocks - use wait()/notify() or java.util.concurrent instead

topics.name: Synchronization in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Synchronization controls access to shared data so only one thread at a time runs a critical section.
  • It is written with the synchronized keyword on a method or block, using the hidden monitor lock every object has, and sits on a scale with volatile, atomics, ReentrantLock and StampedLock.
  • The Java Memory Model guarantees that an unlock happens before the next lock of the same monitor, which makes writes visible.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Without it, concurrent updates corrupt data (race conditions) and threads may see stale values.
  • It makes read-modify-write steps atomic and visible, as needed for a shared bank balance, the last train seat or any shared counter, cache or map.
  • Choosing the cheapest correct tool, the right lock granularity and a fixed lock order keeps systems both correct and fast.

3. Advantages

  • Prevents race conditions and keeps shared data accurate.
  • Gives mutual exclusion and memory visibility with one keyword, built into the language.
  • Lock is released automatically on exceptions and is reentrant.
  • Cheap when uncontended, and supports wait and notify coordination.
  • Rich alternatives: atomics, ReadWriteLock, StampedLock, Semaphore, concurrent collections.

4. Disadvantages

  • Contention reduces parallel work; Amdahl law caps speedup.
  • Deadlock, livelock and lock convoy risk, especially with opposite lock order.
  • No timeout, no tryLock and not interruptible.
  • Easy to lock the wrong or a dangerous object (String literal, boxed Integer, this) or to use too wide a block.
  • In Java 21 blocking inside synchronized pins a virtual thread (fixed in Java 24).
  • Double-checked locking is broken without volatile.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Essential for correct multithreaded programs.
  • Most-asked concurrency topic (double-checked locking, volatile).
  • Basis for java.util.concurrent and for avoiding production hangs.

6. Basic Concepts

  • Synchronization controls how many threads can use a shared resource at one time.
  • When many threads use the same resource together, the results can become inconsistent.
  • Synchronization is necessary for reliable communication between threads.

Fresher Notes

  • Critical section: the code that only one thread may run at a time, marked with synchronized on a method or block.
  • Race condition: threads update shared data together and lose updates, for example count++.
  • Monitor lock: every object has one. A static synchronized method locks the class object.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Synchronization can be applied to methods and blocks only. It cannot be applied to variables or classes.

  • It is used when many threads reach the same resource at the same time.
  • The goal is that only one thread at a time uses that resource.

Why do we need it?

Two threads share one Account below. Each makes five withdrawals of 500.

In this example two threads run in random order. To make them use the account safely, mark makeWithdrawal as synchronized.

Note

A synchronized method gives mutual exclusion for each call. The lock is released at every method exit, so both threads compete again on each loop turn and the two names normally still interleave. Synchronization removes the corrupted balance, not the interleaving. To let one thread finish its whole loop first, hold the lock across the entire loop or join the first thread.

A possible output with synchronization (each withdrawal is complete before the next starts):

Output: using synchronization

Pankaj is going to withdraw=>
Pankaj complete withdrawal=>4500
bhande is going to withdraw=>
bhande complete withdrawal=>4000
Pankaj is going to withdraw=>
Pankaj complete withdrawal=>3500
...
bhande complete withdrawal=>0
Account is overdrawn...

A possible output without synchronization (both threads start before either finishes, so the balance and the order are mixed):

Output: without synchronization

Pankaj is going to withdraw=>
bhande is going to withdraw=>
bhande complete withdrawal=>4500
Pankaj complete withdrawal=>4000
...
bhande complete withdrawal=>0
Account is overdrawn...
Pankaj complete withdrawal=>500
Account is overdrawn...

Type 1: Synchronized method

  • A method declared synchronized is a synchronized method.
  • It locks the object while one thread runs it.
  • The thread gets the lock when it calls the method and releases it when the method ends.
synchronized void test() {
    // write code here
}

Type 2: Synchronized block

  • A synchronized block locks only the lines inside it.
  • If a method has 50 lines but only 5 touch shared data, put just those 5 in a block.
  • If you put the whole method body in the block, it works like a synchronized method.
  • The scope of a block is smaller than a method, so other threads wait less.
synchronized (objectReference) {
    // code block
}

Mid-Level Notes

  • Block vs method: synchronized (lock) { ... } locks less code than a whole method. Lock on a private final object.
  • volatile vs atomic: volatile gives visibility, not atomicity. AtomicInteger gives lock-free atomic updates.
  • Coordination: wait and notify work only inside synchronized code.

8. Advanced Concepts

The Race Condition Problem — Proof, Not Just Theory

A race condition happens when two or more threads read-modify-write a shared variable without coordination, and the operations interleave in a way that loses updates. count++ is NOT atomic - it is really 3 steps: read count, add 1, write count back. If two threads interleave between those steps, one thread's increment can be silently overwritten.

Below, two threads each increment a shared counter 100,000 times. The expected final value is 200000. Without synchronization, the actual value comes out less than 200000 almost every run (the exact number varies run to run - that unpredictability IS the bug).

The Fix — synchronized Method

Making the increment method synchronized forces both threads to acquire the same lock before entering it, so the read-modify-write sequence completes fully for one thread before the other can start. Now the result is deterministic and correct on every run.

The Intrinsic Lock (Monitor) — What "synchronized" Actually Acquires

  • Every object in Java has an associated intrinsic lock (also called a monitor lock), inherited from Object - you don't declare it, it's just there.
  • When a thread enters a synchronized method or block, it must first acquire the intrinsic lock of the object named in the synchronized(...) reference (or this, for a synchronized instance method).
  • Only one thread can hold a given object's lock at a time; every other thread trying to acquire the same lock is blocked until the holder exits the synchronized region (lock is released automatically, even if an exception is thrown).
  • This is why the lock reference matters: synchronizing on two different objects provides ZERO mutual exclusion between them - they are different locks entirely.
Thread A                    Object's Monitor Lock          Thread B
   |                              [ FREE ]                     |
   |-- synchronized(obj) ------->  ACQUIRED by A                |
   |   (critical section runs)                                  |-- synchronized(obj) --> BLOCKED (waits)
   |-- exits block, lock released -> [ FREE ] ------------------>|   ACQUIRED by B
   |                                                              |   (critical section runs)
   |                                                              |-- exits, lock released

Synchronized Method vs Synchronized Block

AspectSynchronized MethodSynchronized Block
Scope of lockEntire method bodyOnly the statements inside the block
Lock objectImplicit - this (instance method) or the Class object (static method)Explicit - you choose exactly which object to lock on
PerformanceCan be worse - blocks other threads even from non-critical, unrelated code inside the methodBetter - smaller critical section means less time other threads spend waiting
FlexibilityLow - all-or-nothingHigh - lock on a dedicated private lock object, and only around the lines that actually touch shared state

Why smaller critical sections win: anything a thread does while holding a lock blocks every other thread that needs the same lock. If a method does file I/O, logging, or heavy computation in addition to touching the shared variable, wrapping the WHOLE method in synchronized serializes all of that unnecessarily. A synchronized block lets you do the expensive/unrelated work outside the lock and only hold the lock for the few lines that read/write shared state.

The Static Synchronized Trap — Locks on the Class, Not the Instance

  • A synchronized instance method locks on this - i.e., the specific object the method is called on. Two threads calling the method on two DIFFERENT instances do NOT block each other.
  • A synchronized static method locks on the Class object itself (e.g. MyClass.class) - there is only ONE such lock per class, shared by ALL instances.
  • Common trap: engineers assume that because two threads use two different object references, they must be safe from blocking each other. If the method is static synchronized, that assumption is wrong - both threads share the exact same Class-level lock and WILL block each other, even though they never touch the same object.

Deadlock — When Two Locks Wait on Each Other Forever

A deadlock happens when Thread A holds Lock 1 and waits for Lock 2, while Thread B holds Lock 2 and waits for Lock 1. Neither can proceed, and neither ever will - the program hangs on those two threads permanently. Do not actually run the snippet below expecting it to finish - it is written to illustrate the hang, not to be executed to completion.

The Standard Fix — Consistent Lock Ordering

The classic remedy is to make every thread acquire multiple locks in the SAME global order (e.g. always lock1 before lock2, everywhere in the codebase). If both threads only ever request lock1 first, then lock2, a circular wait can never form.

ReentrantLock — A More Flexible Alternative to synchronized

java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock provides the same mutual-exclusion guarantee as synchronized, but with extra capabilities synchronized cannot offer:

  • tryLock() - attempt to acquire without blocking forever, optionally with a timeout.
  • lockInterruptibly() - a thread waiting for the lock can be interrupted.
  • Explicit, code-visible lock() / unlock() calls, instead of an implicit block scope - useful for non-block-structured locking.
  • Caveat: unlike synchronized, the lock is NOT released automatically - you must always unlock() in a finally block, or a thread that throws an exception will leave the lock held forever.

Senior Notes

  • Deadlock: threads wait for each other locks. Avoid it with a fixed lock order, tryLock with a timeout, or a smaller lock scope.
  • Higher-level tools: ConcurrentHashMap, AtomicLong, LongAdder, ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock, StampedLock.
  • Happens-before: the Java Memory Model rule that makes writes visible: unlock then lock, volatile write then read, thread start and join.

9. Code for Each Concept

Code: Definition
Code: Advantages
Code: Definition (Advanced)
Code: Advantages (Advanced)

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools you can choose from:

  • synchronized: the built-in monitor lock.
  • ReentrantLock: tryLock, fairness and conditions.
  • ReadWriteLock and StampedLock: many readers, optimistic reads.
  • Atomic* and LongAdder: lock-free updates with CAS.
  • VarHandle, concurrent collections, immutable objects, thread confinement, queues.

Lock striping splits one lock into many. ConcurrentHashMap locks per bin.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The Java Memory Model (JMM) defines visibility and ordering through happens-before edges:

  • Monitor unlock, then a later lock of the same monitor.
  • Volatile write, then a later read of that variable.
  • Thread start, then the actions of that thread.
  • Thread end, then a join that returns.
  • Final field freeze, after the constructor ends.

Without these edges the CPU and compiler may reorder or cache values, so another thread can see stale data. A monitor lock is reentrant. Internally it moves between thin and inflated states (biased locking was removed in recent JDKs).

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Locking on a String or boxed Integer (shared instances), on a mutable field, or on this in a public class (outsiders can lock it).
  • Forgetting to unlock() in finally.
  • Calling unknown code while holding a lock (it may cause a deadlock).
  • Double-checked locking without volatile.
  • Check-then-act on concurrent collections.
  • Assuming ++ on a volatile is atomic.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Lock contention is the usual bottleneck. To reduce it:

  • Shrink the locked scope and split locks.
  • Use LongAdder for counters (striped cells).
  • Use copy-on-write snapshots for read-heavy data.
  • Use optimistic reads.

False sharing (threads writing nearby memory on one cache line) also hurts. @Contended pads fields to avoid it.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

A bank transfer must lock two accounts without deadlock. Order the locks by account id.

10. Examples

Real Time Examples

  • Bank balance update: a debit from an ATM and a credit from NEFT must not overlap, so the account update method is synchronized.
  • IRCTC tatkal booking: the seat count must go down by exactly one per confirmed ticket, even with lakhs of clicks in the same second.
  • BookMyShow seat map: two users clicking seat A15 together must produce one booking and one polite error.
  • College exam form counter: a shared token number generator must never give the same token to two students.
  • Printer spooler in an office: only one job may write to the printer port at a time, otherwise pages get mixed.
  • Global example: an e commerce stock counter for a flash sale. Without a lock, more units get sold than exist in the warehouse.

Real Time Examples (Advanced)

  • NPCI style ledger: instead of one lock, the service takes a lock per account number and always in ascending account order, so a transfer from A to B and from B to A can never deadlock.
  • Flash sale stock counter: Flipkart Big Billion Days uses an atomic decrement or a database conditional update, not a Java monitor, because the stock lives outside one JVM.
  • Spring singleton bean: a bean field mutated by request threads needs a lock or must be made stateless. Most production bugs in Spring come from a mutable field in a singleton service.
  • In memory rate limiter: a Semaphore of 100 permits caps concurrent calls to a partner bank API, which is a form of synchronization without a monitor.
  • Read heavy config cache: a ReentrantReadWriteLock lets hundreds of reader threads work together and blocks them only during the rare refresh.
  • Global example: Kafka producer batching uses fine grained locks per partition buffer so different partitions never contend, which is the same striping idea.

Worked Example 1

Deadlock and ordered locking.

Worked Example 2

wait and notify.

Practice Exercise 1

Race condition and fix.

Practice Exercise 2

Atomic counter.

11. Quick Revision

  • synchronized: mutual exclusion + visibility.
  • volatile: visibility only.
  • Atomics use CAS.
  • Lock in a consistent order to avoid deadlock.
  • Prefer immutability and concurrent collections.

interviewQA: What is a race condition?
Two or more threads read-modify-write shared data without coordination, so interleaved execution loses or corrupts updates - the outcome depends on unpredictable thread timing
What lock does a synchronized instance method acquire?
The intrinsic/monitor lock of this - the specific object instance the method is called on
What lock does a synchronized static method acquire?
The intrinsic lock of the Class object (e.g. MyClass.class) - shared by ALL instances, not per-object
Why prefer a synchronized block over a synchronized method?
A block lets you shrink the critical section to only the lines that touch shared state, reducing the time other threads are blocked and improving throughput
What is a deadlock and what causes it?
Two or more threads are each waiting for a lock the other holds, forming a circular wait, so none can ever proceed; caused by acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent order across threads
How do you prevent deadlock?
Always acquire multiple locks in a fixed, consistent global order across the entire codebase, use lock timeouts (tryLock), or avoid holding more than one lock at a time where possible
Is synchronized reentrant?
Yes - a thread that already holds an object's lock can re-enter another synchronized method/block guarded by the same lock without blocking itself
What is the difference between synchronized and ReentrantLock?

ReentrantLock offers tryLock (non-blocking/timeout acquire), lockInterruptibly, and explicit unlock control, but requires manual unlock() in a finally block since it isn't released automatically like synchronized
Does synchronizing on two different objects prevent both threads from running concurrently?
No - synchronized only blocks threads competing for the SAME lock object; different lock objects provide no mutual exclusion between them at all
Can you synchronize a variable or a class declaration?
No - the synchronized keyword can only be applied to methods and blocks, never directly to variables or class declarations

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • This topic collects the most common multithreading interview questions with clear answers and code.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Multithreading is one of the most tested areas for Java roles.
  • Practising typical questions builds confidence.

3. Advantages

  • Covers frequent questions in one place.
  • Short answers plus code.
  • Good for last-minute revision.

4. Disadvantages

  • Memorized answers without understanding fail follow-up questions.
  • Cannot cover every scenario.
  • Real systems are more complex.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Prepares for interviews.
  • Reveals gaps in understanding.
  • Connects threads, locks and executors.

6. Basic Concepts

1. What is multithreading in Java?

  • Multithreading means running several threads at the same time to keep the CPU busy.
  • It lets one program do many operations concurrently.

2. How do you create a thread in Java?

There are two main ways.

  1. Extend the Thread class:
class MyThread extends Thread {
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Thread is running");
    }
}
MyThread t1 = new MyThread();
t1.start();
  1. Implement the Runnable interface:
class MyRunnable implements Runnable {
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Thread is running");
    }
}
Thread t1 = new Thread(new MyRunnable());
t1.start();

3. What is the difference between start() and run()?

  • start() creates a new thread and runs run() in that new thread.
  • Calling run() directly creates no thread. It runs in the current thread.

4. What are the states of a thread in Java?

  • New: the thread is created but not yet started.
  • Runnable: the thread is ready to run and waits for CPU time.
  • Blocked: the thread waits for a monitor lock.
  • Waiting: the thread waits indefinitely for another thread to act.
  • Timed Waiting: the thread waits for another thread for up to a given time.
  • Terminated: the thread has finished.

Fresher Notes

  • Common topics: thread vs process, Runnable vs Thread, start() vs run(), synchronization, volatile, deadlock, wait/notify, thread pools.
  • Thread states: know what each method does to them.
  • Coding tasks: be ready to write a small producer-consumer or a thread-safe counter.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

1. What is synchronization in Java?

  • Synchronization stops two or more threads from running a critical section (shared code) at the same time.
  • It prevents thread interference and memory consistency errors.

2. What is a deadlock in Java?

  • A deadlock is when two or more threads are blocked forever, each waiting for the other.
  • It usually happens when two threads need the same two locks in opposite order.

3. How can you avoid deadlock in Java?

  • Avoid nested locks.
  • Use a timeout while waiting for locks.
  • Use a lock ordering (lock hierarchy).

4. What is the difference between wait() and sleep()?

  • wait() releases the lock on the object and waits until another thread calls notify() or notifyAll() on it.
  • sleep() pauses the current thread for a given time but keeps the lock.

5. What is the volatile keyword in Java?

  • volatile marks a variable that different threads may change.
  • Every read comes from main memory, not from a thread-local cache.

6. What is the ThreadLocal class in Java?

  • ThreadLocal provides thread-local variables.
  • Each thread that uses such a variable gets its own independently initialized copy.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Race conditions: explain them, plus visibility problems and atomicity, with examples.
  • Toolbox: know java.util.concurrent: ExecutorService, Future, CompletableFuture, ConcurrentHashMap, CountDownLatch, Semaphore, locks.
  • Comparison: be able to compare synchronized, ReentrantLock and atomics.

8. Advanced Concepts

Synchronization & Locks

Every Java object has an intrinsic lock (also called a monitor). synchronized is built on this monitor. Knowing exactly what it locks is a favourite interview trap.

QuestionAnswer
What does the synchronized keyword actually lock?It acquires the intrinsic lock (monitor) of an object. For a synchronized instance method the lock is this. For a synchronized static method it is the Class object. For a synchronized(obj) block it is the object you pass in
Difference between synchronizing a method and a block?A synchronized method holds the lock for the whole method, always on a fixed object (this or Class). A synchronized block guards only the critical section and lets you choose ANY object as the lock. It is more fine-grained and usually faster
Can two threads run two different synchronized methods on the SAME object at the same time?No. Both methods use the same monitor (this), and only one thread can hold it at a time, whichever method it calls
Is a static synchronized method blocked by a synchronized instance method?No. The static method locks the Class object and the instance method locks this. They are different monitors, so both can run at the same time
Is synchronized reentrant in Java?Yes. A thread that already holds a monitor can take it again, for example by calling another synchronized method on the same object, without blocking itself

volatile - Visibility, Not Atomicity

QuestionAnswer
What guarantee does volatile actually give?Visibility. Every read of a volatile variable comes from main memory and every write goes to main memory at once, so all threads see the latest value. It also stops the compiler and JIT from reordering that variable's reads and writes
Does volatile make an operation atomic?No. count++ on a volatile int is still three steps (read, add, write). Two threads can read the same value before either writes, so an update is lost. volatile fixes stale reads, not compound operations
When is volatile enough on its own?When one thread writes (or writes do not depend on the previous value) and others only read. Example: a boolean stop flag that ends a worker loop
volatile vs synchronized: what is the trade-off?volatile is cheaper (no locking, no blocking) but covers visibility of one variable only. synchronized gives visibility AND atomicity for a whole critical section, but it blocks other threads

Deadlock & Race Conditions

QuestionAnswer
What are the 4 classic conditions for deadlock?Mutual exclusion (a resource is held by one thread only). Hold and wait (a thread holds one lock while waiting for another). No preemption (locks cannot be taken away by force). Circular wait (a cycle of threads, each waiting for the next one's lock)
How do you avoid deadlock in practice?Always take locks in the same global order. Use tryLock(timeout) from java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock instead of blocking forever. Keep nested locks few and short. Or use one coarser lock instead of several fine-grained ones
What is a race condition?A bug where the result depends on the timing of two or more threads that use shared mutable state without proper synchronization
Why does count++ lose updates under concurrency?It is three separate steps: read count, add 1, write it back. Threads can interleave between the steps, so two threads that read the same value overwrite each other's increment
How do you fix a lost-update race?Wrap the read-modify-write in a synchronized block or method, or use a lock-free class such as AtomicInteger, whose incrementAndGet() is atomic through CAS (compare-and-swap)

Thread Coordination - wait(), notify(), notifyAll()

QuestionAnswer
Why must wait() and notify() be called inside a synchronized block?They work on the object's monitor, so the thread must own it. wait() releases the monitor while the thread is parked. notify() and notifyAll() wake a waiter, which must still re-take the monitor before it continues. Calling them without the lock throws IllegalMonitorStateException
What exactly happens when a thread calls wait()?It releases the monitor and enters the WAITING state. It stays parked until another thread calls notify() or notifyAll() on the same object, it is interrupted, or the timeout given to wait(ms) ends
notify() vs notifyAll(): which one when?notify() wakes one arbitrary waiting thread. Use it only when all waiters are interchangeable. notifyAll() wakes every waiter, and each re-checks its condition. It is the safer default and avoids lost-wakeup bugs when waiters wait for different reasons
Why check the wait condition in a while loop, not an if?A thread can wake up spuriously, or be notified when the condition is not true yet (another thread got there first). The loop re-checks the condition and waits again if needed

Concurrency Utilities - What Modern Code Prefers

Hand-written synchronized, wait and notify code is error-prone: it is easy to deadlock or forget a notify. The java.util.concurrent package (added in Java 5) offers tested, higher-level building blocks that production code should use first.

QuestionAnswer
What does ExecutorService give you over creating Thread objects yourself?A managed, reusable pool of worker threads with task queuing, submit() and execute(), results through Future, and controlled shutdown. It avoids the cost and unbounded growth of one new thread per task
Why prefer ConcurrentHashMap over a synchronized HashMap?It locks only part of the map, so threads can read and write different bins at the same time. Java 7 used segment locks; Java 8 uses CAS plus synchronized on the bin head. This gives far better throughput than one global lock from Collections.synchronizedMap()
Why is AtomicInteger often faster than synchronized for a counter?It uses CAS (compare-and-swap), a lock-free hardware instruction. Threads never block on a monitor; they just retry if another thread changed the value first. Under contention this scales better than locking
What is the rule of thumb for choosing an approach?Use the highest-level tool that fits. First java.util.concurrent collections, atomics and executors. Then explicit Lock objects (for tryLock, fairness or several conditions). Raw synchronized, wait and notify come last

Senior Notes

  • Senior topics: the Java Memory Model, happens-before, false sharing, lock striping, work stealing, virtual threads, structured concurrency, backpressure.
  • Debugging: thread dumps, JFR, deadlock detection, race detectors, stress tests (jcstress).
  • Trade-offs: explain more than definitions, for example when to prefer immutability or message passing to locks.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Frequently asked implementations: producer-consumer (BlockingQueue or wait/notify), print odd-even with two threads, dining philosophers (lock ordering), thread-safe LRU cache, rate limiter (token bucket), read-write cache, parallel merge sort with ForkJoin, and a custom thread pool. Practice writing them from scratch.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Deep-dive answers: volatile prevents caching and reordering across the write-read pair but is not atomic for compound actions. synchronized gives atomicity plus visibility. CAS (compare-and-swap) retries until the expected value matches, enabling lock-free algorithms with ABA caveats (use AtomicStampedReference). ConcurrentHashMap uses CAS for empty bins and synchronized on the bin head otherwise.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Classic traps: Thread.sleep keeps locks while wait releases them; notify wakes one arbitrary waiter (use notifyAll or Conditions); join on yourself deadlocks; synchronized is reentrant; static synchronized and instance synchronized use different locks; finalize is not for cleanup; parallel streams with shared mutable state are wrong.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Senior-level trade-offs: throughput vs latency, fairness vs speed, locks vs lock-free, shared state vs message passing, thread pools sizing (Little law: threads = throughput x latency), and backpressure (bounded queues, rejection). Virtual threads change sizing: cap concurrency with semaphores to protect downstream resources, not threads.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world answer pattern: describe the problem, the unsafe version, the failure mode, the fix and how to verify (stress test, jcstress, thread dump, load test).

  • Explain volatile vs synchronized.
  • Describe deadlock and avoidance.

  • Know thread pools and CompletableFuture.

topics.name: Executor Framework in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • The Executor framework separates task submission from execution using thread pools: ExecutorService, Executors, Future and ScheduledExecutorService.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Creating a thread per task is expensive and unbounded.
  • Pools reuse threads and manage lifecycle and queues.

3. Advantages

  • Thread reuse and bounded resources.
  • Futures return results and exceptions.
  • Scheduling and shutdown support.

4. Disadvantages

  • Misconfigured pools cause starvation or memory growth.
  • Futures block on get.
  • Must be shut down.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Standard way to run concurrent tasks.
  • Base for Spring async and CompletableFuture.
  • Common interview topic.

6. Basic Concepts

Why Not Just Create Threads Manually?

Creating a raw Thread for every task (as covered in Multithreading) does not scale in real applications.

  • Thread creation is expensive — each OS-level thread costs memory (its own stack) and setup time.
  • There is no reuse — every new Thread(...) is thrown away after run() finishes.
  • There is no bounded control — nothing stops a program from spawning thousands of threads and crashing the JVM.

The Executor Framework (java.util.concurrent) solves this with a managed pool of reusable worker threads that tasks are submitted to.

ExecutorService and Thread Pools

ExecutorService is the main interface for submitting tasks to a thread pool. Instead of managing threads yourself, you hand work to the executor and it decides which pooled thread runs it.

  • Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) — a fixed number of reusable threads; extra tasks wait in a queue.
  • Executors.newCachedThreadPool() — creates threads as needed and reuses idle ones; can grow unbounded under load.
  • Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() — exactly one worker thread; tasks run one at a time, in order.

Runnable vs Callable<T>

  • Runnable — run() returns nothing and cannot throw a checked exception.
  • Callable<T> — call() returns a value of type T and is allowed to throw a checked exception.

Submitting a Callable gives you back a Future<T> — a handle you can use to retrieve that result once it's ready.

Fresher Notes

  • Core idea: submitting a task is separate from running it. Create an ExecutorService with Executors and submit Runnable or Callable tasks.
  • Common pools: newFixedThreadPool(n), newCachedThreadPool(), newSingleThreadExecutor(), newScheduledThreadPool(n), newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().
  • Cleanup: always call shutdown() when done.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Future: submit returns a Future; future.get() waits for the result and rethrows a task exception as ExecutionException.
  • Batches: invokeAll runs a list of tasks; invokeAny returns the first successful result.
  • Stopping: shutdown() stops accepting tasks and finishes queued ones; shutdownNow() interrupts running tasks.

8. Advanced Concepts

Future<T> — get(), isDone(), cancel()

A Future<T> represents the eventual result of an asynchronous task:

  • get() — blocks the calling thread until the result is available (or throws if the task failed).
  • get(timeout, unit) — blocks only up to a timeout, then throws TimeoutException.
  • isDone() — non-blocking check for whether the task has finished (normally, exceptionally, or by cancellation).
  • cancel(mayInterruptIfRunning) — attempts to cancel the task; returns false if it already completed.

Submitting Multiple Callables and Collecting Results

ExecutorService also offers invokeAll(...) to submit a batch of Callable tasks and block until all of them complete, returning a List<Future<T>> in the same order the tasks were submitted.

shutdown() vs shutdownNow() — Graceful vs Immediate

An ExecutorService's threads are non-daemon by default, so the JVM will not exit until the pool is explicitly shut down.

  • shutdown() — stops accepting new tasks, but lets already-submitted tasks finish (graceful).
  • shutdownNow() — attempts to stop all actively running tasks immediately (via interruption) and returns the list of tasks that were still waiting in the queue.
  • awaitTermination(timeout, unit) — blocks until either all tasks finish or the timeout elapses; commonly paired with shutdown() for a clean-and-bounded exit.
executor.shutdown();
if (!executor.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    executor.shutdownNow();   // force-stop if graceful shutdown took too long
}

Why the Unbounded Executors Factories Are Discouraged

Executors.newCachedThreadPool() and newFixedThreadPool() (via their default queue) can hide resource exhaustion: newCachedThreadPool() has an effectively unbounded thread count, and newFixedThreadPool() uses an unbounded work queue, so a burst of tasks can silently pile up memory instead of failing fast.

Modern guidance (Java's own documentation and Effective Java) recommends constructing ThreadPoolExecutor directly, with an explicit bounded queue and a rejection policy:

Senior Notes

  • Production pools: build them with ThreadPoolExecutor using a bounded queue, named threads, a rejection policy and metrics.
  • Overload risk: newCachedThreadPool and the unbounded queue in newFixedThreadPool can exhaust memory or threads under load.
  • Java 21: ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, so try-with-resources waits for tasks to finish.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Sizing and shutdown rules:

  • CPU-bound pool: about the number of cores (+1).
  • I/O-bound pool: about cores x (1 + wait time / compute time).
  • Virtual threads remove the need to size for I/O. Limit them with a Semaphore.
  • Shutdown steps: shutdown(), then awaitTermination, then shutdownNow().
  • Context: wrap tasks to copy MDC or trace context to the worker thread.
  • Results as they finish: use ExecutorCompletionService.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

For each new task, ThreadPoolExecutor follows these steps in order:

  1. Fewer than core threads exist: start a new thread.
  2. Otherwise: put the task in the queue.
  3. Queue full and fewer than max threads: start an extra thread.
  4. Otherwise: reject the task.
  • newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded queue, so the max size is never used.
  • newCachedThreadPool uses a SynchronousQueue, so threads grow without bound.
  • ForkJoinPool is different: each worker has its own deque and idle workers steal tasks.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • No shutdown: non-daemon pool threads keep the JVM alive.
  • Unbounded queues hide overload until memory runs out.
  • Starvation deadlock: a task waits for another task in the same pool.
  • Ignored Future: exceptions are lost when nobody calls get().
  • New pool per request: wastes threads. Create pools once and reuse them.
  • One tiny shared pool for unrelated work: no bulkheads.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning checklist:

  • Monitor: active count, queue size, completed tasks, rejections and task wait time.
  • Back-pressure: use a bounded queue and CallerRunsPolicy to slow producers.
  • Fewer pools: keep each pool for a clear purpose.
  • Metrics: publish them through Micrometer.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: separate bulkhead pools for payments and notifications so a slow email provider cannot starve payment processing.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Production-style pool.

Worked Example 2

Timeout on get.

Practice Exercise 1

Fixed pool with Futures.

Practice Exercise 2

Scheduled tasks.

11. Quick Revision

  • submit returns Future.
  • Always shutdown.
  • Use bounded queues and named threads.
  • Fixed pool for CPU, tune for I/O.
  • Rejection policies handle overload.

interviewQA: Why use ExecutorService instead of raw Thread?
It reuses a bounded pool of threads instead of creating an expensive new OS thread per task
Runnable vs Callable?
Runnable's run() returns nothing and can't throw checked exceptions; Callable's call() returns a value and can throw checked exceptions
What does Future.get() do?
Blocks the calling thread until the async task's result is available (or rethrows its exception)
shutdown() vs shutdownNow()?
shutdown() lets in-flight tasks finish and rejects new ones; shutdownNow() tries to interrupt running tasks immediately and returns unstarted ones
Why avoid Executors.newCachedThreadPool() in production?
Its thread count is effectively unbounded, so a task burst can exhaust memory/OS threads instead of failing fast
What does invokeAll() return?
A List<Future<T>> in submission order, after blocking until every submitted task has completed

topics.name: CompletableFuture in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • CompletableFuture is an asynchronous result you can chain and combine with thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine, allOf and exception handling.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Calling several slow services one after another wastes time.
  • CompletableFuture runs them in parallel and combines results without blocking threads.

3. Advantages

  • Non-blocking composition.
  • Built-in error handling and timeouts.
  • Parallel calls with allOf.

4. Disadvantages

  • Callback chains can be hard to read.
  • Easy to block the common pool by mistake.
  • Exceptions are wrapped in CompletionException.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used in microservice calls.
  • Modern alternative to Future.
  • Interview topic for async programming.

6. Basic Concepts

The Problem With Plain Future<T>

The Future returned by ExecutorService.submit() is very limited:

  • get() blocks. You cannot say "run this callback when the result arrives".
  • Futures cannot be chained. You cannot say "when this finishes, feed its result into another async step".
  • Futures cannot be combined. There is no built-in way to wait for two independent futures and merge their results.
  • A plain Future cannot be manually completed from outside the task that created it.

CompletableFuture<T> (Java 8+) fixes all of this. It implements Future<T> and adds many composition methods.

Starting an Async Computation — supplyAsync / runAsync

  • CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(Supplier<T>) runs a task asynchronously and completes with a result.
  • CompletableFuture.runAsync(Runnable) runs a task asynchronously with no result.

Both use the common ForkJoinPool by default. You can pass your own Executor as a second argument.

Chaining With thenApply / thenAccept / thenRun

  • thenApply(Function) transforms the result into a new value and returns a new CompletableFuture.
  • thenAccept(Consumer) consumes the result and returns nothing (CompletableFuture<Void>).
  • thenRun(Runnable) runs after completion and ignores the result.

Fresher Notes

  • Async result: CompletableFuture holds a result that arrives later. Start it with supplyAsync(() -> ...).
  • Chaining: use thenApply and thenAccept to run a step when the previous one finishes.
  • Errors: handle them with exceptionally or handle.
  • Waiting: join() or get() waits for the result.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • thenApply maps the result to a new value.
  • thenCompose flattens a step that returns another CompletableFuture.
  • thenCombine merges two independent futures.
  • allOf / anyOf: allOf waits for all futures; anyOf returns when the first one completes.
  • Executor: pass your own executor to async methods. The default is the common ForkJoinPool.

8. Advanced Concepts

Combining Two Independent Futures — thenCombine

thenCombine(otherFuture, BiFunction) waits for both futures to complete (they can run concurrently) and merges their results with the given function.

Exception Handling — exceptionally() and handle()

  • exceptionally(Function<Throwable,T>) supplies a fallback value only if the pipeline failed. It is skipped on success.
  • handle(BiFunction<T,Throwable,R>) runs on both success and failure. It gets the result and the exception, and one of them is null.

Waiting on Many Futures — allOf() and anyOf()

  • CompletableFuture.allOf(f1, f2, f3, ...) completes only when every given future completes. It returns CompletableFuture<Void>, so read the results from the original futures.
  • CompletableFuture.anyOf(f1, f2, f3, ...) completes as soon as any one of them completes, with that result.

join() vs get() — the Unchecked-Exception Difference

Both block until the result is ready. get() throws the checked ExecutionException and InterruptedException. join() throws an unchecked CompletionException instead.

That makes join() easier inside lambdas and streams (like the allOf example above), where checked exceptions cannot be thrown.

Senior Notes

  • Timeouts: add them with orTimeout and completeOnTimeout (Java 9+).
  • Common pool: never block inside it. Use a dedicated executor for blocking calls.
  • Wrapped errors: failures arrive as CompletionException. Unwrap with getCause().

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

More methods you will meet:

  • thenAcceptBoth consumes two results together.
  • applyToEither uses whichever of two futures finishes first.
  • whenComplete observes the result or error without changing it.
  • exceptionallyCompose recovers with another future (Java 12+).
  • completeAsync and failedFuture create or finish futures by hand (Java 9+).
  • new CompletableFuture<>() plus complete turns a callback API into a future.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

A CompletableFuture is a small state machine. It is pending, completed normally, or completed exceptionally. It also keeps a stack of dependent actions.

  • Each stage runs when its source completes.
  • thenApply runs in the thread that completed the source.
  • thenApplyAsync runs on an executor.
  • Exceptions travel down the chain as CompletionException until a stage handles them.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Calling get() inside an async chain. It blocks a pool thread.
  • Forgetting errors. A failed future stays silent if nobody calls join().
  • Running blocking calls on the common pool.
  • Thinking thenApply is async. It runs in the completing thread.
  • Losing thread context (MDC, security) when work moves to another thread.
  • Using allOf and forgetting to read the results from the original futures.
  • Using thenApply with a function that returns a future. Use thenCompose.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Each stage adds a little overhead and allocation.

  • This is fine for I/O composition and wasteful for tiny CPU steps.
  • Use a dedicated executor with a bounded size for blocking calls.
  • Set a timeout on every remote call and avoid unbounded fan-out.
  • For large pipelines, consider Reactor, or virtual threads with plain blocking code (often simpler).

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: aggregating a product page from three services in parallel with fallbacks, so one slow dependency does not fail the page.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Parallel calls with allOf.

Worked Example 2

thenCompose flatten.

Practice Exercise 1

Chaining and combining.

Practice Exercise 2

Errors and timeout.

11. Quick Revision

  • supplyAsync starts async work.
  • thenApply maps; thenCompose flattens.
  • exceptionally/handle for errors.
  • Use a custom executor for blocking calls.
  • orTimeout adds a deadline.

interviewQA: What problem does CompletableFuture solve over plain Future?
It adds non-blocking chaining, combining, exception handling, and manual completion - things plain Future can't do
supplyAsync vs runAsync?
supplyAsync runs a Supplier and produces a result; runAsync runs a Runnable and produces no result
thenApply vs thenAccept vs thenRun?
thenApply transforms and returns a value; thenAccept consumes the value and returns nothing; thenRun ignores the value entirely
How do you combine two independent async results?
thenCombine(other, BiFunction) - waits for both, merges their results
exceptionally() vs handle()?
exceptionally() only runs on failure to supply a fallback; handle() runs on both success and failure
get() vs join()?
get() throws checked ExecutionException/InterruptedException; join() throws an unchecked CompletionException, making it lambda-friendly

topics.name: Concurrent Collections in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, BlockingQueue and others) are thread-safe collections designed for high concurrency.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Plain collections break under concurrent modification, and synchronized wrappers scale poorly.

3. Advantages

  • Safe and scalable.
  • Atomic operations like merge and putIfAbsent.
  • No ConcurrentModificationException.

4. Disadvantages

  • Compound operations still need atomic methods.
  • CopyOnWrite is costly for frequent writes.
  • size is only an estimate.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used in caches and queues in production.
  • Interview favorite (ConcurrentHashMap internals).
  • Needed for correct concurrent code.

6. Basic Concepts

Why Plain Collections Aren't Thread-Safe

HashMap, ArrayList, and friends assume single-threaded access. Under concurrent modification they can corrupt internal state, throw ConcurrentModificationException during iteration, or even (for HashMap before Java 8) loop forever.

  • Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()) fixes this by wrapping every method in a single lock. That lock is held for the whole call, so all threads compete for it even for unrelated keys. It works, but scales poorly.
  • java.util.concurrent instead offers collections built from the ground up for concurrent access, with finer-grained (or lock-free) synchronization.

ConcurrentHashMap

ConcurrentHashMap lets many threads read and write at the same time without one map-wide lock:

  • Reads are largely lock-free.
  • Writes use fine-grained locking (per bucket in modern JDKs) instead of locking the whole map.
  • Iterators are weakly consistent. They never throw ConcurrentModificationException, but may or may not show updates made during iteration.
  • Unlike HashMap, it does not allow null keys or values (Hashtable rejects them too). This avoids the ambiguity between "no value" and "value is null" under concurrent access.

Fresher Notes

  • Thread-safe collections live in java.util.concurrent: ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentLinkedQueue and the BlockingQueue family.
  • No ConcurrentModificationException: iterators are weakly consistent or work on a snapshot.
  • Better scaling than Collections.synchronizedMap or Hashtable.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Atomic methods: ConcurrentHashMap offers putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent and merge. Null keys and values are not allowed.
  • Copy on write: CopyOnWriteArrayList copies the array on each write. It suits many reads and few writes (listeners).
  • Producer-consumer: BlockingQueue (ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue) uses put and take.

8. Advanced Concepts

CopyOnWriteArrayList — Read-Heavy, Rare-Write Lists

Every write (add/remove/set) creates a brand-new copy of the underlying array. Reads use the current snapshot with no locking at all.

  • Perfect for many readers, very few writers (for example, a list of event listeners).
  • Iterators work over a fixed snapshot, so they never throw ConcurrentModificationException. If the list changes mid-iteration, the iterator does not see that change.
  • Poor for write-heavy workloads, because every write is an O(n) array copy.

BlockingQueue — Producer-Consumer Made Easy

BlockingQueue<E> adds waiting to a normal queue. put() blocks while the queue is full, and take() blocks while it is empty. No manual wait()/notify() is needed.

  • ArrayBlockingQueue: fixed capacity, backed by an array.
  • LinkedBlockingQueue: optionally bounded, backed by linked nodes.

This makes it the natural building block for a producer-consumer pipeline.

ConcurrentSkipListMap — Sorted, Thread-Safe Access

When you need a concurrent map that stays sorted by key (like a thread-safe TreeMap), use ConcurrentSkipListMap. ConcurrentHashMap gives no ordering at all. It is built on a skip list and gives O(log n) navigation (firstKey(), ceilingKey()) with mostly lock-free access.

Quick Comparison

CollectionBest forKey trade-off
Collections.synchronizedMapQuick retrofits of legacy codeSingle coarse lock - poor concurrency
ConcurrentHashMapGeneral-purpose concurrent mapNo ordering; disallows null keys/values
CopyOnWriteArrayListMany readers, very few writersO(n) copy on every write
ArrayBlockingQueue / LinkedBlockingQueueProducer-consumer pipelinesBlocking put()/take() replace manual wait/notify
ConcurrentSkipListMapSorted concurrent accessO(log n) ops vs O(1)-ish for ConcurrentHashMap

Senior Notes

  • Compound operations across separate calls are still not atomic. Use the atomic methods, not get then put.
  • Other types: ConcurrentSkipListMap is a sorted concurrent map; ConcurrentLinkedDeque is a lock-free deque.
  • size() is only an estimate while other threads update the structure.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Choose by access pattern:

  • ConcurrentHashMap: general use.
  • ConcurrentSkipListMap / ConcurrentSkipListSet: sorted.
  • CopyOnWriteArrayList / CopyOnWriteArraySet: read-mostly.
  • ArrayBlockingQueue: bounded, gives back-pressure. LinkedBlockingQueue: optionally bounded.
  • PriorityBlockingQueue, DelayQueue (items released after a delay), LinkedTransferQueue, ConcurrentLinkedDeque.

ConcurrentHashMap also has bulk operations: forEach, search and reduce, each taking a parallelism threshold.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

ConcurrentHashMap (Java 8+) uses an array of bins: empty bins are filled with CAS, non-empty bins are locked on the head node, long bins become trees, and resizing is cooperative (threads help transfer). Reads are lock-free via volatile reads. CopyOnWriteArrayList swaps in a new array on writes under a lock. ConcurrentLinkedQueue is a lock-free Michael-Scott queue; LinkedBlockingQueue uses two locks (put and take).

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Compound check-then-act. Use atomic methods instead.
  • Expecting size() to be exact.
  • Storing null keys or values.
  • Keeping an iterator across updates.
  • Using CopyOnWriteArrayList for write-heavy data (O(n) copy per write).
  • Unbounded blocking queues (memory keeps growing).
  • Wrapping a ConcurrentHashMap in synchronized, which defeats its purpose.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

CopyOnWriteArrayList write cost grows with size, because all elements are copied. LongAdder and ConcurrentHashMap scale well with more threads. Queue choice affects latency: ArrayBlockingQueue uses one lock, LinkedBlockingQueue uses two, and the LMAX Disruptor library gives extreme throughput. Benchmark with JMH under realistic thread counts.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an in-memory session store, a rate limiter counting requests per user, and a work queue between request threads and a writer thread.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Check-then-act race.

Worked Example 2

Snapshot iteration.

Practice Exercise 1

Atomic updates in ConcurrentHashMap.

Practice Exercise 2

BlockingQueue pipeline.

11. Quick Revision

  • ConcurrentHashMap: no null keys or values.
  • Use merge, compute, putIfAbsent.
  • CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-mostly data.
  • BlockingQueue for producer-consumer.
  • Weakly consistent iterators.

interviewQA: Why not just use Collections.synchronizedMap everywhere?
It locks the entire map for every operation, so all threads contend for one lock even on unrelated keys - much worse throughput than ConcurrentHashMap
Does ConcurrentHashMap allow null keys/values?
No - unlike HashMap, this is disallowed to avoid ambiguity under concurrent access
Why doesn't CopyOnWriteArrayList throw ConcurrentModificationException?
Its iterator works over an immutable snapshot taken when iteration began, so concurrent writes never affect that iterator
When is CopyOnWriteArrayList a bad choice?
Write-heavy workloads - every write copies the entire backing array, which is O(n)
What does BlockingQueue's put()/take() replace?
Manual wait()/notify() coordination for producer-consumer patterns

topics.name: Locks in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Locks in java.util.concurrent.locks (ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock, StampedLock) offer more control than synchronized.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Some problems need timeouts, try-lock, fairness, multiple conditions or many readers with few writers.

3. Advantages

  • tryLock and timeouts.
  • Read-write separation.
  • Multiple Condition queues.

4. Disadvantages

  • Must unlock in finally.
  • More code than synchronized.
  • Easy to misuse.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Needed in advanced concurrency.
  • Interviews compare synchronized and ReentrantLock.
  • Used in many library internals.

6. Basic Concepts

Limitations of the synchronized Keyword

synchronized (covered in Synchronization) is simple but rigid:

  • You cannot try to acquire the lock with a timeout. A thread either waits forever or gets it immediately.
  • You cannot interrupt a thread that is blocked waiting to enter a synchronized block.
  • There is no fairness policy. The JVM does not guarantee waiting threads are served in arrival order.
  • Each monitor has only one implicit condition (via wait()/notify()). You cannot have separate wait-sets for different conditions.

java.util.concurrent.locks provides the Lock interface and its implementations to address exactly these gaps.

ReentrantLock — The Explicit Alternative to synchronized

ReentrantLock implements Lock and behaves like synchronized (a thread can re-acquire a lock it already holds, hence "reentrant") but with explicit control:

  • lock() acquires the lock, blocking if necessary.
  • unlock() releases it. It must be called in a finally block, because nothing releases the lock automatically as a synchronized block does.

Fresher Notes

  • Locks in java.util.concurrent.locks give more control than synchronized: ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock, StampedLock.
  • Always unlock in finally: lock.lock(); try { ... } finally { lock.unlock(); }.
  • tryLock() tries without blocking; tryLock(timeout, unit) waits a limited time.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Fairness, interrupts, conditions: ReentrantLock supports fair order, interruptible waits (lockInterruptibly) and many Condition objects.
  • Read-write lock: ReentrantReadWriteLock allows many readers or one writer.
  • Reentrant means the same thread can acquire the lock again; you must unlock the same number of times.

8. Advanced Concepts

tryLock() — Avoiding a Deadlock synchronized Cannot Avoid

tryLock() attempts to acquire the lock and returns false at once if it is unavailable, instead of blocking forever. tryLock(timeout, unit) waits only up to a limit. This lets a thread back off and retry instead of deadlocking, which plain synchronized cannot do.

Fairness, isLocked() and getHoldCount()

  • new ReentrantLock(true) enables a fair policy: the longest-waiting thread gets the lock first (slower, because of extra bookkeeping).
  • isLocked() reports whether any thread currently holds the lock.
  • getHoldCount() returns how many times the current thread has acquired the lock (it grows on each re-entry).

ReadWriteLock — Many Readers, One Writer

ReentrantReadWriteLock exposes two locks from one object: readLock() and writeLock().

  • Many threads can hold the read lock at the same time, as long as no thread holds the write lock.
  • The write lock is exclusive. While it is held, no other thread can hold the read or write lock.

This is a big win for read-heavy workloads. A single exclusive lock (like plain synchronized) forces even simple reads to take turns.

Condition — Multiple Wait-Sets Per Lock

A synchronized monitor gives you exactly one implicit wait-set (wait()/notify()). A Lock can create multiple Condition objects via newCondition(), each with its own wait-set. This helps when different events should wake different threads, for example a bounded buffer with a "not full" and a "not empty" condition.

Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();
Condition notFull  = lock.newCondition();
Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();
// producer awaits notFull, signals notEmpty
// consumer awaits notEmpty, signals notFull

Senior Notes

  • StampedLock offers optimistic reads (tryOptimisticRead and validate) for very read-heavy data but is not reentrant.
  • Prefer synchronized when it is enough: it is simpler and fine for most code. Use locks for advanced needs.
  • Keep critical sections short: avoid holding locks during I/O or while calling unknown code.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Patterns: lock ordering to avoid deadlock, tryLock with back-off, hand-over-hand locking, lock striping, condition queues (await/signal), read-write caches, and lock-free alternatives (atomics, VarHandle). In Java 21+, synchronized blocks can pin virtual threads (improved in later JDKs); ReentrantLock parks virtual threads cleanly.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Locks are built on AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS): an int state plus a FIFO wait queue of parked threads (LockSupport.park). ReentrantLock stores the owner and hold count; fair mode grants in arrival order (slower), non-fair allows barging (faster). ReentrantReadWriteLock packs reader and writer counts in the state. StampedLock uses a version stamp for optimistic reads.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: unlock outside finally, unlock without owning (IllegalMonitorStateException), lock in one method and unlock in another, awaiting a Condition without holding the lock, signaling instead of signalAll when several waiters have different predicates, ignoring the interrupt, and holding a lock while calling listeners (alien code).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Uncontended synchronized and ReentrantLock cost about the same; under contention, fairness hurts throughput (many context switches). StampedLock optimistic reads avoid writes to shared memory, which scales best for read-heavy workloads. Profile lock contention with JFR (jdk.JavaMonitorEnter, jdk.ThreadPark).

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a scheduler uses a ReentrantLock with two Conditions (notFull, notEmpty) for a bounded work queue, and a read-write lock for rarely changed configuration.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Forgetting unlock: wrong version, then the fix.

Worked Example 2

Optimistic read.

Practice Exercise 1

Lock with tryLock (inside a method that throws InterruptedException).

Practice Exercise 2

Condition for a bounded buffer.

11. Quick Revision

  • lock(); try { } finally { unlock(); }
  • tryLock avoids blocking forever.
  • ReadWriteLock for read-heavy data.
  • StampedLock: optimistic reads.
  • Lock in a fixed order.

interviewQA: Why use ReentrantLock instead of synchronized?
It supports tryLock() with timeout, interruptible waiting, fairness policies, and multiple Condition wait-sets - none of which synchronized offers
What must you always do after lock.lock()?
Wrap the critical section in try/finally and call unlock() in finally - there's no automatic release like a synchronized block gets
How does tryLock() help avoid deadlock?
It returns immediately (or after a timeout) instead of blocking forever, letting a thread back off and retry rather than wait indefinitely for a lock another thread holds
What does ReadWriteLock optimize for?
Read-heavy workloads - multiple readers can hold the read lock concurrently, while the write lock stays exclusive
What replaces wait()/notify() when using explicit locks?
Condition objects created via lock.newCondition(), which support multiple independent wait-sets per lock

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Exception handling deals with runtime errors using try, catch, finally and throw, so programs can recover or fail cleanly.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Real programs meet missing files, bad input and network failures.
  • Without handling, they crash with unhelpful errors.

3. Advantages

  • Separates error handling from normal logic.
  • Stack traces help debugging.
  • Resources are cleaned up with finally and try-with-resources.

4. Disadvantages

  • Overuse hides bugs.
  • Exceptions are slow when thrown often.
  • Checked exceptions add boilerplate.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Every real application handles errors.
