  • Interviews test try-catch-finally rules.
  • Needed for robust APIs.

6. Basic Concepts

An exception is an abnormal condition that occurs during the execution of a program and stops the normal flow of the application.

Exception handling in Java is about managing these errors gracefully so they do not crash your program unexpectedly.

Below is one small, runnable code + output for each core building block:

1. Proof: an unhandled exception stops the program

Without any exception handling, once an error occurs the rest of the program never runs.

2. try-catch — catching the exception so the program keeps running

Wrapping the risky code in a try block, with a matching catch block, lets the rest of the program continue even after the error.

3. finally — code that always runs, exception or not

The finally block executes whether or not an exception was thrown, and even if the catch block itself doesn't run - it's the standard place to close files, connections, or release resources.

4. Multiple catch blocks — handling different exception types differently

You can chain multiple catch blocks after one try; Java picks the first one whose type matches the exception that was actually thrown.

5. Common Runtime (Unchecked) Exceptions You'll Actually Hit

These are the exceptions beginners run into constantly. They're all unchecked (subclasses of RuntimeException), so the compiler never forces you to handle them - but real code should anyway.

ExceptionWhen it happens
ArithmeticExceptionInteger division by zero
NullPointerExceptionCalling a method/field on a null reference
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsExceptionAccessing an array index outside its valid range
NumberFormatExceptionInteger.parseInt(...) (or similar) given text that isn't a valid number
InputMismatchExceptionScanner.nextInt() (or similar) given input of the wrong type
IllegalStateExceptionCalling a method when the object isn't in the right state - e.g. Iterator.remove() before next()

Fresher Notes

  • Exception: an event that disrupts normal flow. Handle it with try, catch and finally.
  • Roles: code that may fail goes in try; catch handles specific types; finally always runs (cleanup).
  • Unhandled exceptions end the thread and print a stack trace.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Catch order: catch the most specific exception first; a multi-catch uses catch (A | B e).
  • Auto-close: use try-with-resources to close resources automatically.
  • Never swallow exceptions: at least log them with the stack trace.

8. Advanced Concepts

The Exception Class Hierarchy

Throwable sits at the top of the hierarchy and is the superclass of everything that can be thrown. Both Exception and Error extend it.

Throwable
  +-- Error                      (JVM/system-level problems - usually not caught)
  |     +-- OutOfMemoryError
  |     +-- StackOverflowError
  |
  +-- Exception                  (application-level problems - meant to be caught)
        +-- IOException          (checked - compiler forces you to handle it)
        +-- SQLException         (checked)
        +-- RuntimeException     (unchecked - compiler does NOT force handling)
              +-- ArithmeticException
              +-- NullPointerException
              +-- ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
ClassMeaning
ThrowableSuperclass of everything throwable/catchable
ErrorSerious problems from the environment/JVM (e.g. out of memory) - not caused by application logic, and generally not caught
ExceptionProblems an application should anticipate and handle

A full checked-vs-unchecked comparison, with more examples, is covered in the next topic in this module.

Proof: finally Runs Even When try Has a return

A return inside try doesn't skip finally - the JVM runs finally right before actually returning. This is a classic interview trap, especially when finally also has a return.

try-with-resources — Automatic Resource Cleanup (Java 7+)

Any resource implementing AutoCloseable declared in the try(...) parentheses is closed automatically, in reverse order, once the block ends - even if an exception is thrown. This replaces manually closing resources in a finally block.

Custom Exceptions

For business-specific error conditions, define your own exception class by extending Exception (checked) or RuntimeException (unchecked) - this lets calling code catch your exact error type and read a meaningful message.

Exception Chaining — Preserving the Root Cause

When you catch a low-level exception and re-throw a higher-level one, pass the original exception as the cause so the full failure chain is still visible for debugging - never swallow the original exception silently.

Catch Block Ordering — Child Must Come Before Parent

When catching a class and one of its subclasses, the more specific (child) exception's catch block must come first. If the parent's catch block came first, it would catch everything - including the child type - leaving the child's catch block unreachable, which is a compile-time error in Java.

try {
    // ...
}
catch (Exception e) {              // parent - catches everything
}
catch (ArithmeticException e1) {   // ERROR: unreachable, already caught above
}

try / catch / finally — Which Combinations Compile

try can never stand alone - it must be followed by at least one catch, a finally, or both.

CombinationAllowed?
try aloneNo - must be followed by catch and/or finally
try + catchYes
try + finally (no catch)Yes
try + catch + finallyYes
try + multiple catch (child before parent)Yes
try + multiple catch (parent before child)No - compile error, parent catch makes the child catch unreachable

Catch vs. finally

catchfinally
Runs only if the try block actually throws a matching exceptionRuns whether or not an exception occurred
A try can have multiple catch blocksOnly one finally block per try
Used to handle/recover from an exceptionUsed for cleanup (closing files, DB connections, streams), not exception handling

ConcurrentModificationException

Thrown when a collection is structurally modified (elements added/removed) directly while it's being iterated, instead of going through the iterator's own remove(). It's an unchecked subclass of RuntimeException.

Senior Notes

  • Catch where you can act (retry, fallback, translate), not everywhere; let others propagate.
  • Wrap low-level exceptions in domain exceptions with the cause: throw new ServiceException("msg", e).
  • No control flow: do not use exceptions for normal flow; they are slow and obscure logic.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Good practices:

  • Fail fast: validate input early and catch narrowly.
  • Translate and keep the cause at layer boundaries.
  • Log once at the boundary with context (ids), not at every layer.
  • Clean up in finally or try-with-resources.
  • Domain exceptions for business failures; no exceptions as flow control.
  • Use Optional or result types for expected absences.
  • Global handlers (@RestControllerAdvice, uncaught exception handler) are the last line.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

When an exception is thrown the JVM searches the current method exception table for a matching handler (by type and bytecode range); if none, it pops the frame and searches the caller. finally is compiled by duplicating its code on every exit path. The stack trace is captured in the constructor (fillInStackTrace), which is the costly part. try-with-resources closes in reverse order and adds suppressed exceptions.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Empty catch blocks, or catching Throwable.
  • Logging and rethrowing (duplicate logs).
  • Losing the cause: throw new X(e.getMessage()).
  • Returning null on error.
  • printStackTrace instead of a logger.
  • An exception in finally masking the original one.
  • Using exceptions to validate expected input.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Throwing is slow (microseconds) mainly because of stack trace capture; in hot paths use validation methods that return booleans or Optional. A try block without a thrown exception costs nothing. Pre-allocated, stackless exceptions are possible for rare control flow cases.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a service layer translating persistence failures into domain exceptions, one handler mapping them to HTTP codes, and structured logs with a correlation id.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Order of catch blocks.

Worked Example 2

Swallowed exception (bad).

Practice Exercise 1

try, catch, finally.

Practice Exercise 2

Translate and keep the cause.

11. Quick Revision

  • try, catch, finally.
  • Catch specific exceptions first.
  • Never swallow exceptions silently.
  • Wrap with cause when translating.
  • Use try-with-resources.

topics.name: Difference between Checked and Unchecked Exceptions

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Java exceptions are checked (must be handled or declared), unchecked (RuntimeException) and Errors (serious JVM problems).

2. Need of This Topic

  • Choosing the right kind decides how callers are forced to react and keeps APIs clean.

3. Advantages

  • Compiler enforces handling of checked exceptions.
  • Unchecked exceptions keep code concise.
  • Clear hierarchy.

4. Disadvantages

  • Checked exceptions clutter signatures and lambdas.
  • Wrong choice confuses callers.
  • Hierarchy knowledge needed.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Very common interview question.
  • Guides API design.
  • Helps understand Spring exception translation.

6. Basic Concepts

1. Checked Exception (Compile-Time Exception)

  • Any subclass of Exception, at any depth, that is not also a subclass of RuntimeException is a checked exception. For example IOException extends Exception, and FileNotFoundException extends IOException.
  • The compiler checks them at compile-time. You must either catch them or declare them with throws.
  • Examples: IOException, SQLException, ClassNotFoundException.

2. Unchecked Exception (Runtime Exception)

  • Classes that inherit from RuntimeException are unchecked exceptions.
  • The compiler does not check them. They show up only at runtime, and you are never forced to handle them.
  • Examples: ArithmeticException, NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, NumberFormatException.

Below is one small, runnable proof for each:
Proof: a checked exception must be handled or declared - the code won't even compile otherwise
Proof: an unchecked exception compiles fine, but can still crash at runtime

Fresher Notes

  • Checked exceptions (IOException, SQLException) must be caught or declared with throws; the compiler enforces it.
  • Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException) and need not be declared.
  • Error (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) signals serious JVM problems.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Hierarchy: Throwable splits into Exception (checked, except RuntimeException) and Error.
  • Choosing: use checked exceptions for recoverable conditions the caller must handle; use unchecked for programming errors.
  • Frameworks such as Spring prefer unchecked exceptions to avoid cluttered signatures.

8. Advanced Concepts

Checked vs Unchecked — Quick Comparison

AspectCheckedUnchecked
Checked byCompiler, at compile-timeJVM, at runtime
Parent classException (excluding RuntimeException)RuntimeException
Must handle?Yes - catch or declare with throwsNo - handling is optional
Typical causeExternal conditions (file missing, DB down, class not found)Programming mistakes (bad logic, null access, bad index)
ExamplesIOException, SQLException, ClassNotFoundExceptionArithmeticException, NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
NullPointerException — calling a method on a null reference
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException — accessing an index that doesn't exist
NumberFormatException — trying to parse text that isn't a valid number
InputMismatchException — Scanner reads a type that doesn't match what was asked for

IllegalStateException — calling a method at the wrong point in an object's lifecycle

Calling Iterator.remove() before ever calling next() is a classic example. There is nothing to remove yet.

Senior Notes

  • Lambdas and streams: checked exceptions do not compose well with them, so wrap them in unchecked ones.
  • Javadoc: document thrown exceptions with @throws.
  • Design: build exception hierarchies per module, with meaningful names and context in messages.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Choosing: use checked exceptions for recoverable failures the caller can act on (rare in modern code). Use unchecked for precondition and programming errors. Use domain exceptions with codes for APIs.
  • Bridging helpers: UncheckedIOException, functional interfaces that throw (ThrowingFunction), and CompletionException in async code.
  • Common unchecked: IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, UnsupportedOperationException, NullPointerException, ArithmeticException.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Class hierarchy: Throwable to Error and Exception; RuntimeException (unchecked) extends Exception. The compiler's checked analysis applies to Exception subclasses outside RuntimeException. Generic type erasure means exception classes cannot be generic. Sneaky throw can bypass checked rules, but is discouraged.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Throwing a generic Exception or RuntimeException.
  • Using checked exceptions for programming errors.
  • Catching NullPointerException instead of fixing the null.
  • Extending Exception when RuntimeException fits.
  • Empty messages, or mixing error codes with exceptions.

A good message says what failed, with values and context.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Checked exceptions make APIs verbose and break lambdas. Unchecked exceptions keep signatures clean but need documentation. Neither affects normal-path performance. Keep hierarchies shallow.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: Spring translates SQLException (checked) into the DataAccessException (unchecked) hierarchy, so service code is free of JDBC specifics.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Hierarchy lookup.

Worked Example 2

Compiler enforcement.

Practice Exercise 1

Checked vs unchecked.

Practice Exercise 2

Wrap in lambdas.

11. Quick Revision

  • Throwable: Error and Exception.
  • RuntimeException is unchecked.
  • IOException is checked.
  • Errors are usually not caught.
  • Wrap checked exceptions in lambdas.

topics.name: Error

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • An Error signals a serious JVM or system problem such as OutOfMemoryError or StackOverflowError that applications usually cannot recover from.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Knowing common Errors helps you find memory leaks, infinite recursion and class loading problems in production.

3. Advantages

  • Signals fatal conditions clearly.
  • Tools like heap dumps help diagnosis.
  • Prevents continuing in a broken state.

4. Disadvantages

  • Hard to recover from.
  • Root causes can be subtle (leaks).
  • Catching them may hide the real problem.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Production incidents involve Errors.
  • Interview topic: Exception vs Error.
  • Teaches memory and stack concepts.

6. Basic Concepts

An Error is a serious problem that a reasonable application should not try to catch.

It usually indicates something has gone wrong at the JVM/environment level (running out of memory, a stack that has recursed too deep, a broken class file) rather than a mistake in normal application logic.

Below is one small, runnable code + output for each core idea:

1. Error vs Exception — the basic difference

An Exception is usually caused by the application itself (bad input, dividing by zero, a null reference) and is meant to be caught and handled.

An Error is usually caused by the environment the program is running in (JVM ran out of memory, ran out of stack space) and is generally NOT meant to be caught or recovered from.

Exception Error
Caused by Application logic (bad input, null reference, bad array index) JVM / environment (out of memory, stack exhausted)
Recoverable? Usually yes Usually no
Should application code catch it? Yes, with try-catch Generally no
Example ArithmeticException, NullPointerException OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError

2. Proof: a StackOverflowError being thrown

A method that keeps calling itself with no stopping condition (infinite recursion) eventually uses up all the memory reserved for the call stack, and the JVM throws a StackOverflowError.

3. Why application code generally should NOT catch Errors

Technically, Error can be caught with catch (Error e) because it is a subclass of Throwable, just like Exception.

But in practice you should almost never do this, because:

  • An Error usually means the JVM itself is in a bad state (out of memory, corrupted stack) - there is often no safe way to keep running normally.
  • Catching it can hide a serious problem instead of letting it surface and be fixed.
  • Trying to do meaningful work (like logging to a file) right after an OutOfMemoryError can itself fail, since there may be no memory left to do it.

The standard advice: let Errors propagate and crash the application (or the specific thread) rather than trying to catch and "handle" them like a normal Exception.

Fresher Notes

  • Error means a serious JVM or environment problem: OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, NoClassDefFoundError, AssertionError.
  • Do not catch them in normal code; the program often cannot recover.
  • Errors are unchecked and extend Throwable, not Exception.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • StackOverflowError: recursion is too deep; fix with a base case or a loop.
  • OutOfMemoryError: heap, metaspace or native memory is full; analyze with a heap dump.
  • NoClassDefFoundError: the class existed at compile time but is missing at run time (classpath problem or failed static init).

8. Advanced Concepts

Where Error sits in the Throwable hierarchy

Both Error and Exception extend Throwable - the root class for anything that can be thrown with throw and caught with catch.

                java.lang.Object
                       |
                java.lang.Throwable
                    /       \
             Exception       Error
             /       \           \
   RuntimeException  Checked    VirtualMachineError, AssertionError,
   (Unchecked)       Exception  NoClassDefFoundError, ...
                      (IOException,           |
                       SQLException, ...)      +-- OutOfMemoryError
                                               +-- StackOverflowError

Key takeaway: Error and Exception are siblings under Throwable, not parent/child of each other. An Error is unchecked (like RuntimeException) - the compiler never forces you to declare or catch it, but that doesn't make it safe to ignore or catch casually.

Common Error subtypes

Error subtype When it happens
OutOfMemoryError The JVM heap (or another memory area) cannot allocate any more objects because it has run out of available memory.
StackOverflowError A thread's call stack exceeds its allowed depth - almost always caused by infinite or excessively deep recursion.
NoClassDefFoundError A class that was present at compile time is missing at runtime (e.g. a .class file was deleted, or a jar is missing from the classpath) - different from ClassNotFoundException, which is a checked Exception thrown by reflective loading APIs.
AssertionError Thrown by the assert statement when the asserted condition evaluates to false - used to signal "this should never happen" during development/testing.

Causing an OutOfMemoryError - the code pattern

Deliberately exhausting heap memory will crash whatever process runs it, so the exact output/stack trace is environment-dependent (it depends on heap size, JVM flags, and available system memory).

The pattern below shows the idea conceptually - repeatedly allocating memory and never releasing it, until the JVM cannot find enough contiguous heap space for the next allocation and throws OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space.

When is it (occasionally) acceptable to catch an Error?

The default rule is: don't catch Errors. There is one narrow, well-known exception: catching StackOverflowError in a controlled way to detect and report runaway recursion, typically in tooling, testing frameworks, or a sandboxed evaluator - where the goal is to fail gracefully with a diagnostic message instead of letting the thread die with a raw stack trace.

Why catching Errors is dangerous in general

Situation Risk of catching the Error
catch (OutOfMemoryError e) The JVM may not have enough memory left to even run your catch/finally block's logic (e.g. logging), and other threads may already be failing too.
catch (StackOverflowError e) in general application code Masks an actual bug (missing base case, unbounded recursive data) instead of surfacing it during development.
catch (Throwable t) / catch (Error e) broadly Swallows serious JVM-level failures alongside normal exceptions, making the application appear to "handle" conditions it has no real way to recover from.

Golden rule: catch Exception (and its specific subtypes) for conditions you can meaningfully recover from. Let Error propagate, log it if your framework/monitoring captures it automatically, and fix the root cause (increase heap, fix the recursion, fix the classpath) rather than papering over it with a catch block.

Senior Notes

  • Heap dump: enable -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError and analyze with Eclipse MAT or VisualVM.
  • Containers: use -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError so the orchestrator restarts the process.
  • Memory leaks often come from static collections, listeners, unbounded caches and ThreadLocal values.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Diagnostics tools:

  • Heap dump analysis in Eclipse MAT (dominator tree, leak suspects).
  • jcmd GC.heap_info, jmap -histo, -Xlog:gc, -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, and JFR memory events.
  • -Xss sets the stack size for deep recursion.

Fix leaks by bounding caches, removing listeners, clearing ThreadLocal values, closing resources and using weak references.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Error subclasses signal JVM-level problems.

  • StackOverflowError: a thread stack (default about 512 KB to 1 MB, set with -Xss) is full.
  • OutOfMemoryError variants: Java heap space, GC overhead limit exceeded, Metaspace, unable to create native thread, Direct buffer memory.
  • LinkageError family: NoClassDefFoundError (class missing at run time or failed static init), UnsatisfiedLinkError, ExceptionInInitializerError.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Catching Throwable or Error and carrying on.
  • Raising -Xmx without finding the leak.
  • Deep recursion on user input (a denial-of-service risk).
  • Unbounded thread creation (causes "unable to create native thread"), queues and caches.
  • Loading huge files into memory, and relying on finalizers.

Prefer resource limits and backpressure.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

GC tuning follows evidence: right-size the heap (-Xms equals -Xmx for stable services), choose a collector for latency goals, reduce allocation rate, avoid large object churn. In containers use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage and leave headroom for metaspace, threads and direct memory.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a service OOM-kills every few days; the heap dump shows a static map of sessions that is never evicted. Fix with a bounded Caffeine cache with expiry.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Leak through a static collection.

Worked Example 2

AssertionError.

Practice Exercise 1

StackOverflowError.

Practice Exercise 2

OOM flags.

11. Quick Revision

  • StackOverflowError: deep recursion.
  • OutOfMemoryError: heap, metaspace, threads.
  • Use HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError.
  • ExitOnOutOfMemoryError in containers.
  • Do not catch Error to continue.

interviewQA: What is the difference between Error and Exception?

Both extend Throwable. Exception represents application-level problems that are usually recoverable and should be caught; Error represents serious JVM/environment-level problems (out of memory, stack exhausted) that are generally unrecoverable and should not be caught.
Is Error checked or unchecked?
Unchecked - the compiler never requires you to declare or catch an Error, the same as RuntimeException.
Can you catch an Error in Java?
Yes, syntactically (Error extends Throwable), but it is strongly discouraged except in narrow, controlled cases like reporting a StackOverflowError from a sandboxed recursion check.
What causes a StackOverflowError?
A thread's call stack exceeds its maximum depth, almost always due to infinite or excessively deep recursion with no base case.
What causes an OutOfMemoryError?
The JVM cannot allocate more memory in a given memory area (commonly the heap) because it is exhausted and garbage collection cannot free enough space.
What is the difference between NoClassDefFoundError and ClassNotFoundException?

NoClassDefFoundError is an Error thrown when a class that was available at compile time is missing at runtime (e.g. a missing jar); ClassNotFoundException is a checked Exception thrown by reflective APIs like Class.forName() when a class cannot be found dynamically.
Where does Error sit relative to Exception in the class hierarchy?
They are siblings - both directly extend Throwable. Error is not a subclass of Exception, nor vice versa.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • This topic covers frequently asked exception handling interview questions with answers.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Exception rules (finally, throw vs throws, suppressed exceptions) are popular in interviews and often confuse developers.

3. Advantages

  • Covers the typical traps.
  • Short answers with code.
  • Good revision material.

4. Disadvantages

  • Memorizing without practice fails follow-ups.
  • Edge cases are many.
  • Real design needs more than rules.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Prepares for interviews.
  • Clarifies finally and return behavior.
  • Improves error design skills.

6. Basic Concepts

Exception Basics

QuestionAnswer
What is Exception Handling? Explain types of Exception.Exception Handling is a mechanism in Java to handle runtime errors so that the normal flow of the application is not disrupted. It is done using try, catch, finally, throw and throws. Exceptions are broadly classified into two types: Checked Exceptions (checked at compile time, e.g. IOException, SQLException) and Unchecked Exceptions (occur at runtime, e.g. NullPointerException, ArithmeticException). Errors (like OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) are a separate category representing serious problems not meant to be handled by applications.
What is the difference between Exception and Error?Exception represents a condition that a program can catch and recover from (e.g. NullPointerException, IOException); it is a subclass of java.lang.Exception. Error represents a serious problem that a normal application should not try to catch or handle (e.g. OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError); it is a subclass of java.lang.Error. Both extend java.lang.Throwable.
What is the difference between Checked and Unchecked Exceptions?Checked Exceptions are checked by the compiler at compile time; the method must either handle them with try-catch or declare them with throws (e.g. IOException, SQLException, ClassNotFoundException). Unchecked Exceptions (also called Runtime Exceptions) are not checked at compile time and occur due to programming errors; they extend RuntimeException (e.g. NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, ArithmeticException).

Keywords and finally

QuestionAnswer
Which keywords are used for handling exceptions in Java?Java provides five keywords for exception handling: try (block containing code that might throw an exception), catch (block that handles the exception thrown by the try block), finally (block that always executes, used for cleanup), throw (used to explicitly throw an exception), and throws (used in a method signature to declare the exceptions a method may throw).
Explain the finally block.The finally block is always executed after the try block, whether an exception occurs or not, and whether or not it is caught. It is typically used to release resources such as closing files, database connections or network sockets. The finally block will NOT execute only if the JVM is shut down using System.exit() inside the try block, or if the JVM crashes.
How do you handle multiple exceptions in Java?Multiple exceptions can be handled in two ways. 1) Single catch block with a common superclass: if the exceptions share a hierarchy, catching the base exception type (e.g. Exception) in one catch block handles all of them. 2) Multi-catch block: a single try can be followed by multiple catch blocks, or Java 7+ allows combining exception types in one catch clause using the pipe (|) operator, e.g. catch (IOException | SQLException e).

Custom Exceptions

QuestionAnswer
What is a custom exception? How do you create a custom exception class?A custom exception (also called a user-defined exception) is an exception class created by the programmer to represent application-specific error conditions, since the built-in exceptions (like IOException, NullPointerException) may not always fit business requirements. Steps: 1) Create a class that extends java.lang.Exception (for a checked exception) or java.lang.RuntimeException (for an unchecked exception) — unchecked is generally preferred unless callers must be forced to handle it. 2) Provide constructors, typically one that accepts a String message and calls super(message). 3) Throw an instance of it using the throw keyword where the error condition occurs.
What is ConcurrentModificationException?ConcurrentModificationException occurs when a collection is structurally modified (e.g. an element added or removed) while it is being iterated using an iterator or for-each loop, without going through the iterator's own remove() method. It is an unchecked exception and a direct subclass of RuntimeException. It is commonly avoided by using Iterator.remove() or classes from java.util.concurrent such as CopyOnWriteArrayList.

Fresher Notes

  • Common questions: checked vs unchecked, final vs finally vs finalize, throw vs throws, try-with-resources, custom exceptions.
  • Flow: know what happens when an exception is thrown in try, catch and finally.
  • Hierarchy: be able to explain Throwable, Exception, Error and how to read a stack trace.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Return in finally: finally runs even if try returns; a return inside finally overrides everything.
  • Lost exception: if both try and finally throw, the finally exception wins and the original is lost. try-with-resources avoids this by keeping it as a suppressed exception.
  • Context: rethrow with the cause, as in throw new X("msg", cause).

8. Advanced Concepts

try/catch/finally Mechanics

QuestionAnswer
What happens if both the try/catch block and the finally block return a value?If a finally block contains a return statement, it overrides any return value from the try or catch block, and any exception being propagated is suppressed. This is generally considered bad practice because it silently swallows exceptions and return values; finally should be reserved for cleanup, not for returning values.
Can a finally block prevent an exception from propagating?Yes. If the finally block itself throws an exception or executes a return/break/continue, it discards whatever exception was being propagated from the try/catch block, and only the finally block's outcome is visible to the caller. This is a common source of subtle bugs.
What is exception chaining?Exception chaining is the practice of wrapping a lower-level exception inside a higher-level, more meaningful exception while preserving the original exception as the "cause". Java supports this via the Throwable(Throwable cause) constructor and initCause() method, and the wrapped exception can be retrieved later using getCause(). This preserves the full stack trace for debugging while allowing higher-level, business-relevant exception types to be thrown.

try-with-resources & Best Practices

QuestionAnswer
What is try-with-resources and why is it preferred over a finally block for closing resources?try-with-resources (introduced in Java 7) automatically closes any resource that implements java.lang.AutoCloseable (or Closeable) when the try block exits, whether normally or via an exception. It removes the need for a manual finally block to call close(), reduces boilerplate, and correctly handles suppressed exceptions (if both the try body and the close() call throw, the close() exception is "suppressed" and attached to the primary exception, retrievable via getSuppressed()).
What is the difference between throw and throws?throw is used inside a method body to explicitly throw a single exception instance at runtime (e.g. throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad input")). throws is used in a method signature to declare that the method may propagate one or more checked exceptions to its caller, without handling them itself (e.g. public void readFile() throws IOException).
What are some best practices for exception handling in Java?Key best practices include: catch only exceptions you can meaningfully handle; avoid catching generic Exception or Throwable unless rethrowing or logging at a boundary; never leave catch blocks empty; prefer unchecked exceptions for programming errors and checked exceptions for recoverable conditions the caller must address; always clean up resources (prefer try-with-resources over manual finally); preserve the original cause when wrapping exceptions; and avoid using exceptions for normal control flow since they are relatively expensive and hurt readability.

Senior Notes

  • Strategy: fail fast, validate inputs, translate exceptions at layer boundaries, log once, never use exceptions for control flow, and design an error model for APIs (problem details, error codes).
  • Performance: capturing a stack trace is expensive; override fillInStackTrace only for hot control-flow exceptions (rare).
  • Concurrency: exceptions in tasks are captured in Future objects or handled by uncaught-exception handlers.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Interview patterns to practise: a custom checked exception, exception chaining, multi-catch (the catch variable is implicitly final), precise rethrow, and try-with-resources with two resources.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Detailed semantics:

  • If try throws and finally completes normally, the exception propagates.
  • If finally throws, it replaces the original, which is lost.
  • With try-with-resources the body exception is primary and close exceptions are suppressed (getSuppressed).
  • An exception in a static initializer becomes ExceptionInInitializerError.
  • If a constructor throws, the object is never returned, though a half-built object may have escaped.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common wrong answers to avoid:

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Logging answer: log one line for expected failures and a full stack trace only for unexpected ones. Add a correlation id to every line and rate-limit repeated errors to avoid log storms.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world answer: retry with exponential backoff only for transient exceptions, and make the operation idempotent (safe to repeat) so a retry cannot do harm.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

finally overrides exception.

Worked Example 2

Problem details response.

Practice Exercise 1

finally and return.

Practice Exercise 2

Suppressed exception.

11. Quick Revision

  • finally runs unless the JVM exits.
  • throw raises, throws declares.
  • Suppressed exceptions keep secondary failures.
  • Return in finally overrides.
  • Translate exceptions at layer boundaries.

topics.name: throw and throws in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Throw raises an exception object at a point in code and throws declares which checked exceptions a method may pass to its caller.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Methods must signal failures and tell callers what to expect.
  • Throw and throws are the two halves of that contract.

3. Advantages

  • Explicit failure signals.
  • Compiler checks declared exceptions.
  • Custom exceptions carry context.

4. Disadvantages

  • throws clauses can grow long.
  • Overriding methods cannot broaden them.
  • Unchecked exceptions are not enforced.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Needed to write validation and APIs.
  • Frequent interview question.
  • Foundation for custom exceptions.

6. Basic Concepts

throw and throws look similar but do completely different jobs - one actually raises an exception, the other just announces that a method might raise one.

Below is one small, runnable code + output for each:

1. throw — manually raising an exception

The throw keyword is used inside a method body to actually create and hand off an exception object at the exact point something goes wrong.

Syntax: throw new ArithmeticException();

2. throws — declaring that a method might throw

The throws keyword is used in a method signature to declare that the method might throw a particular (checked) exception type. It doesn't throw anything itself - it just forces any caller to either catch that exception or declare it too.

Syntax:

void readFile() throws IOException { ... }

throw vs throws — Quick Comparison

Aspect throw throws
What it isA statementA clause (keyword in a method signature)
What follows itA single exception object (throw new XException())One or more exception types, comma-separated
Where it appearsInside a method or block bodyIn the method signature, after the parameter list
EffectActually raises/hands off the exception right nowJust declares a possibility - forces the caller to handle it
Can you use multiple?No - only one exception object per throw statementYes - throws IOException, SQLException

Fresher Notes

  • Raising: throw raises an exception object, for example throw new IllegalArgumentException("age < 0");.
  • Declaring: throws lists in the method signature which checked exceptions the method may pass to its caller.
  • Position: throw is a statement inside a method; throws is part of the method declaration.
  • Allowed types: you can throw only Throwable objects.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Several exceptions: a method can declare many, such as void m() throws IOException, SQLException.
  • Overriding: an overriding method cannot throw broader checked exceptions than the parent method.
  • Rethrow: in a catch block use throw e;, or wrap it in a new exception and pass the original as the cause.

8. Advanced Concepts

Checked Exceptions Force Your Hand

If you throw a checked exception (anything extending Exception but not RuntimeException), the compiler forces you to do one of two things: catch it in a surrounding try-catch, or declare it with throws so the caller deals with it. Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its subclasses) have no such requirement.

Throwing a Custom Exception

Business-specific error conditions are usually modelled as a custom exception class, then raised with throw exactly like a built-in exception.

Re-throwing a Caught Exception

Inside a catch block you can inspect, log, wrap, or simply re-throw the same exception (or a new one) using throw - the enclosing method must then either handle it too or declare it with throws.

Multiple Exceptions in One throws Clause

A single method can declare more than one checked exception type, comma-separated, if different parts of its body can fail in different ways.

throws and Method Overriding

When overriding a method, the overriding method can declare fewer or narrower checked exceptions than the parent (or none at all) - but it can never declare a new or broader checked exception than the one declared in the overridden method. Unchecked exceptions are exempt from this rule entirely.

Parent.method() throws IOException
  |
  +-- Child A: throws IOException        -> OK (same)
  +-- Child B: throws FileNotFoundException -> OK (narrower, subclass of IOException)
  +-- Child C: throws (nothing)           -> OK (narrower still, drops it entirely)
  +-- Child D: throws SQLException        -> COMPILE ERROR (new, unrelated checked exception)
  +-- Child E: throws Exception           -> COMPILE ERROR (broader than IOException)

Senior Notes

  • Fail fast: validate arguments early with throw new IllegalArgumentException or Objects.requireNonNull.
  • Messages: include the bad value and context, but never secrets.
  • Precise rethrow (Java 7): rethrowing a caught general Exception needs to declare only the specific checked exceptions the try block can throw.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Guidelines:

  • Use IllegalArgumentException for a bad argument value, or requireNonNull for null.
  • Use IllegalStateException when the object is in the wrong state.
  • Use UnsupportedOperationException for operations a class does not support.
  • Document with @throws, keep throws clauses short, and prefer unchecked exceptions in application code.
  • Chain causes with the constructor or initCause; Throwable.addSuppressed carries secondary failures.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

throw compiles to athrow: it pops the throwable and the JVM searches the exception tables. The throws clause is metadata (an Exceptions attribute) used by the compiler only; the JVM does not enforce it. The stack trace is filled when the exception object is created, not when thrown, so creating without throwing still captures it.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes (rule of thumb: throw early, handle late):

  • throws Exception on every method hides what can really fail.
  • Throwing from finally can hide the original exception.
  • Creating exceptions without a message or context.
  • Throwing null, which becomes a NullPointerException.
  • Declaring unchecked exceptions in throws without documenting them.
  • Logging and then rethrowing, which gives duplicate noise.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Throwing is cheap relative to I/O, but in hot loops pre-validate and avoid exceptions for control flow. Reuse static, stackless exceptions only in very specialized cases (parsers) with care for correctness.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a service method validates, throws domain exceptions, and a central handler maps them to HTTP responses.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Overriding rule.

Worked Example 2

Rethrow with cause.

Practice Exercise 1

throw and throws together.

Practice Exercise 2

Fail fast.

11. Quick Revision

  • throw new X(message).
  • throws lists checked exceptions.
  • Only Throwable can be thrown.
  • Override cannot throw broader checked exceptions.
  • Fail fast with requireNonNull.

interviewQA: What is the difference between throw and throws?
throw actually raises one exception object at a specific point in code; throws is a method-signature clause that declares one or more possible checked exception types
Can you write multiple exceptions after throw?
No - throw always takes exactly one exception object; throws can list several comma-separated types
Is throws needed for unchecked exceptions?
No - RuntimeException and its subclasses can be thrown freely without any throws declaration
What happens if you throw a checked exception without catching or declaring it?
Compile error: "unreported exception ... must be caught or declared to be thrown"
Can an overriding method add a new checked exception not in the parent's throws clause?
No - it can only keep the same, narrow it (subclass), or drop it entirely; adding a new or broader checked exception is a compile error
Can throw appear more than once in the same method?
Yes - a method can have several throw statements in different branches, each raising a different exception

topics.name: Enums in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • An enum is a special class with a fixed set of named constants, which can also have fields, constructors and methods.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Values like days, status codes and roles are limited sets.
  • Enums make them type-safe instead of using loose ints or strings.

3. Advantages

  • Type safety for fixed values.
  • Can carry data and behavior.
  • Work with switch, EnumMap and EnumSet.

4. Disadvantages

  • Cannot be extended or created at runtime.
  • Adding constants later may affect stored data.
  • Overuse for dynamic data is a mistake.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used for states and configuration everywhere.
  • Best singleton implementation.
  • Interview topic.

6. Basic Concepts

What is an Enum?

An enum (enumeration) is a special Java type used to define a fixed set of named constants.

  • Declared with the enum keyword instead of class.
  • Every enum implicitly extends java.lang.Enum, so it cannot extend any other class (Java has no multiple inheritance of classes).
  • It exists so a variable can only ever hold one of a known, finite set of values - the compiler enforces this, unlike plain integers or strings.

Enum vs int Constants - Why Not Just Use int?

Before enums existed (pre-Java 5), developers used int or String constants to represent a fixed set of values. Enums fix several real problems with that approach:

  • Type safety: a method that takes a Day cannot accidentally be passed a random int like 7 or -1 - the compiler rejects it.
  • No invalid values: with int constants, int day = 999; compiles fine even though it's meaningless; with an enum, only the declared constants exist.
  • Readability: Day.MONDAY is self-documenting; 1 is not.

Enums Can Have Fields, Constructors, and Methods

An enum is not just a list of names - it is a full class. Each constant can carry data with it, set through a private constructor (enum constructors are implicitly private; they cannot be called with new from outside).

Built-in Methods: values(), valueOf(), ordinal(), name()

Every enum automatically gets these methods for free - you never write them yourself:

  • values() - returns an array of all constants, in declaration order.
  • valueOf(String) - converts an exact-matching String back into the enum constant; throws IllegalArgumentException if there's no match.
  • ordinal() - returns the constant's position (0-based) in the declaration order.
  • name() - returns the constant's exact declared name as a String.

Enums in switch Statements

Enums work naturally with switch - you use the bare constant name (no Day. prefix) inside each case, since the switch already knows the type from the variable being switched on.

Fresher Notes

  • Enum: a fixed set of named constants, such as enum Day { MON, TUE, WED }.
  • Enums are classes: they can have fields, constructors and methods, and can implement interfaces.
  • Useful methods: values(), valueOf(String), name(), ordinal(), compareTo.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Private constructor: each constant calls one, for example RED("#f00").
  • Constant-specific bodies: constants can override an abstract method for their own behavior.
  • Comparing: use ==. Enums also work in switch, EnumMap and EnumSet.

8. Advanced Concepts

Constant-Specific Class Bodies (Per-Constant Method Overrides)

An enum can declare an abstract method, and each constant is then required to supply its own implementation in a constant-specific class body. Internally, each such constant becomes an anonymous subclass of the enum.

Enums Implementing Interfaces

An enum cannot extend a class (it already implicitly extends java.lang.Enum), but it can implement one or more interfaces - a common way to give a fixed set of constants a shared, polymorphic contract.

Why Enum Constants Are Inherently Singletons

Each enum constant is created exactly once, when the enum class is first loaded by the JVM - there is no way to call new Day() from outside (the constructor is implicitly private), and the constants are public static final. This makes every enum constant a guaranteed, thread-safe singleton, which is why Effective Java recommends a single-element enum as the best way to implement the Singleton pattern.

EnumMap and EnumSet - Purpose-Built Collections

Because enum constants have a known, fixed ordinal(), the JDK provides specialized collections that are much faster and more memory-efficient than HashMap/HashSet for enum keys - internally backed by an array indexed by ordinal, not hashing.

  • EnumMap<K extends Enum<K>, V> - a Map keyed by an enum, iterates in natural (declaration) order.
  • EnumSet<E extends Enum<E>> - a Set of enum values, represented internally as a bit vector.

Common Traps

  • An enum cannot extend another class - it already extends java.lang.Enum implicitly, and Java has no multiple class inheritance.
  • Comparing enum constants with == is safe and preferred over .equals() - since every constant is a singleton, reference equality is always correct and slightly faster; it also avoids a NullPointerException if the left side happens to be null (Day.MONDAY == d is null-safe, d.equals(Day.MONDAY) is not).
  • ordinal() is fragile - it reflects declaration order, so inserting a new constant in the middle silently shifts every ordinal after it. Never persist an ordinal() value to a database; store the name() string instead.
  • valueOf() is case-sensitive and throws IllegalArgumentException on any mismatch, including whitespace.

Senior Notes

  • Persistence: do not store ordinal(). Store the name or a stable code (JPA @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)).
  • Fast collections: EnumMap and EnumSet use an array and a bit vector.
  • Singleton: a one-constant enum is the safest singleton and survives serialization.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Advanced use: state machines (each state defines transitions), strategy per constant, enums implementing interfaces, lookup maps built in a static block, EnumMap / EnumSet for flags, switch expressions with exhaustiveness, and values() caching to avoid repeated array clones. Use @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) in JPA.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The compiler turns an enum into a final class extending java.lang.Enum with a private constructor, public static final fields for each constant and a synthetic $VALUES array. values() clones that array each call. valueOf uses a name-to-constant map. Constants are created during class initialization, so enum initialization is thread-safe.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: persisting ordinal, adding constants in the middle (breaks ordinal-based data), mutable enum fields (global state), using enums with many fields as a database, valueOf without handling IllegalArgumentException, and switch statements without default that silently miss new constants. Add tests that enumerate values().

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Enum switch uses an ordinal lookup table; EnumMap is an array indexed by ordinal (O(1), tiny); EnumSet is a long bit mask (for up to 64 constants). Prefer them over HashMap/HashSet keyed by enums.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: HTTP status mappings, roles and permissions, order states with allowed transitions, and configuration modes. An enum with a code field maps to database codes safely.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

valueOf failure.

Worked Example 2

EnumSet.

Practice Exercise 1

Enum with fields and behavior.

Practice Exercise 2

Constant-specific methods and EnumMap.

11. Quick Revision

  • Constants are singletons.
  • values(), valueOf(), ordinal(), name().
  • Compare with ==.
  • Do not store ordinal.
  • EnumMap and EnumSet are fast.

interviewQA: Can an enum extend a class?
No - every enum implicitly extends java.lang.Enum, and Java doesn't allow multiple class inheritance
Can an enum implement an interface?
Yes - one or more interfaces, and constants can even provide per-constant overrides via constant-specific class bodies
Why is == safe for comparing enum constants?
Each constant is a singleton created once at class-load time, so reference equality is always correct and also null-safe when the constant is on the left side
Why shouldn't you persist ordinal() to a database?
ordinal() reflects declaration order and silently changes if a new constant is inserted in the middle - use name() instead
How does Effective Java recommend implementing a Singleton?
As a single-element enum - the JVM guarantees exactly one instance, and it's serialization-safe and reflection-attack-resistant by construction
What's the difference between EnumMap/EnumSet and HashMap/HashSet for enum keys?
EnumMap/EnumSet are backed by arrays indexed by ordinal() (no hashing needed), making them faster and more memory-efficient, and they iterate in natural declaration order

topics.name: Generics in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Generics let classes and methods work with types supplied by the caller, such as List<String>, with compile-time type checking.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Without generics, collections held Objects and needed casts that could fail at run time.

3. Advantages

  • Compile-time type safety.
  • No casting.
  • Reusable algorithms and classes.

4. Disadvantages

  • Type erasure removes type information at run time.
  • No primitives as type arguments.
  • Wildcards are hard to learn.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • All collections use generics.
  • Needed to read library signatures.
  • Frequent interview topic (erasure, PECS).

6. Basic Concepts

Why Generics Exist

Before generics (pre-Java 5), collections stored plain Object references. That meant:

  • No compile-time type checking - you could put anything into a List.
  • Every read required an explicit, unsafe cast.
  • Mistakes only surfaced at runtime as a ClassCastException, often far from where the bad value was inserted.

Generics let a class or method be parameterized by a type, so the compiler enforces correctness before the program ever runs.

Generics Fix This at Compile Time

With a generic type like List<String>, the compiler rejects an incompatible add() call outright, and no cast is needed on read - the compiler inserts the cast for you invisibly and guarantees it will succeed.

Generic Classes

A class can declare its own type parameter (conventionally a single uppercase letter like T) in angle brackets, and use it as if it were a real type throughout the class body.

Generic Methods

A single method can be generic even inside a non-generic class - the type parameter is declared right before the return type. The compiler usually infers T automatically from the argument, so you rarely need to specify it explicitly.

Bounded Type Parameters

<T extends Number> restricts T to Number or any of its subclasses (Integer, Double, etc.) - despite the keyword extends, this also works for bounding to an interface. This lets the generic code call Number methods like doubleValue() on values of type T, which plain <T> would not allow.

Fresher Notes

  • Type parameter: the caller picks the type, as in List<String> or class Box<T>.
  • Type safety: the compiler checks types and you need no casts.
  • Reference types only: use List<Integer>, not List<int>.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Generic method: static <T> T first(List<T> l).
  • Bounded type: <T extends Comparable<T>> lets you call compareTo.
  • Wildcards: ? extends T (read-only producer), ? super T (consumer), ? (unknown).
  • Diamond: new ArrayList<>() infers the type.

8. Advanced Concepts

Wildcards - ?, ? extends T, ? super T

A wildcard is used when the exact type parameter doesn't matter, only a relationship to it does. There are three forms:

  • List<?> - unbounded wildcard, "a list of some unknown type."
  • List<? extends T> - upper-bounded, "a list of T or any subtype" - you can safely read T out of it, but cannot add anything (the compiler doesn't know the exact subtype).
  • List<? super T> - lower-bounded, "a list of T or any supertype" - you can safely write T into it, but reads only guarantee an Object.

PECS - Producer Extends, Consumer Super

PECS is the standard mnemonic (from Effective Java) for choosing between extends and super:

If the parameterized type PRODUCES values you read -> use extends
If the parameterized type CONSUMES values you write -> use super
If it does both (read AND write)                    -> don't use a wildcard at all

Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) from the JDK is the textbook example: src only produces values (extends), dest only consumes them (super).

Type Erasure - The Runtime Reality

Java generics are implemented via type erasure: generic type information exists only at compile time for type-checking, and is then stripped ("erased") from the bytecode. At runtime, List<String> and List<Integer> are literally the same class: List.

This has real consequences:

  • You cannot do new T() or new T[10] inside a generic class - the JVM doesn't know what T actually is at runtime.
  • instanceof cannot check a parameterized type: obj instanceof List<String> is a compile error; only obj instanceof List<?> is allowed.
  • Two generic instantiations are equal via getClass() at runtime, even though the compiler treated them as different types.

Raw Types - Legacy Compatibility, Not Recommended

A raw type is a generic class used without its type parameter (e.g. plain List instead of List<String>). Raw types exist purely for backward compatibility with pre-Java-5 code, and using them today produces an "unchecked" compiler warning and throws away all of generics' compile-time safety.

Multiple Bounds

A type parameter can be bounded by one class and multiple interfaces at once, joined with & - the class (if any) must come first.

Senior Notes

  • Type erasure: at run time List<String> and List<Integer> are both List.
  • PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.
  • Erasure limits: no new T(), no generic arrays, no instanceof List<String>.
  • Invariance: List<Object> is not a supertype of List<String>.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Advanced topics: bounded and recursive bounds (<T extends Comparable<? super T>>), wildcard capture, generic methods with explicit type arguments (Collections.<String>emptyList()), type tokens (Class<T> to create instances), super type tokens (anonymous subclass captures the type), @SafeVarargs, and generic builders with self types.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Type erasure replaces type variables with their bound (or Object) and inserts casts and bridge methods. At run time the JVM sees raw types; generic information remains in class metadata (Signature attribute) for reflection. Reifiable types (arrays, raw types, unbounded wildcards) keep type info; List<String> does not.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: raw types (unchecked warnings, ClassCastException later), unchecked casts, heap pollution with varargs, generic arrays, assuming List<Object> accepts List<String>, overloading methods that differ only by type argument (same erasure), and exposing wildcard types in return values. Never ignore unchecked warnings without a reason.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Generics have no run-time cost beyond casts and boxing of primitive type arguments; the boxing is the real cost. Project Valhalla (specialized generics over value classes) aims to remove it. Use primitive streams and specialized collections for numeric data.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a generic repository and result type reused across the codebase.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Invariance.

Worked Example 2

Erasure.

Practice Exercise 1

Generic class and bounded method.

Practice Exercise 2

Wildcards (PECS).

11. Quick Revision

  • <T> declares a type parameter.
  • extends bounds the type.
  • Wildcards: ? extends (read), ? super (write).
  • Erasure: no new T().
  • Generics are invariant.

interviewQA: What problem do generics solve?
They move type-checking from runtime (ClassCastException) to compile time, and remove the need for manual casts
What is type erasure?
The compiler enforces generic type rules at compile time, then strips the type parameters from the bytecode - List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class at runtime
Why can't you write "new T()" inside a generic class?
Because of type erasure, the JVM has no runtime knowledge of what T actually is, so it cannot allocate an instance of it
What does PECS mean?
Producer Extends, Consumer Super - use "? extends T" for a source you only read from, "? super T" for a destination you only write to
Why can't you add to a List<? extends Number>?
The compiler only knows it's "some subtype of Number," not which one, so it can't guarantee any specific value you add would be type-compatible
What's a raw type and why avoid it?
A generic type used without its parameter (e.g. plain List) - it exists only for legacy compatibility and disables all generic type-safety, producing unchecked warnings

topics.name: Annotations in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Annotations attach metadata to code, such as @Override, @Deprecated and custom ones read by tools and frameworks.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Frameworks need configuration without code changes: dependency injection, mapping and testing are driven by annotations.

3. Advantages

  • Less boilerplate.
  • Compiler checks (@Override).
  • Enable frameworks like Spring and JPA.

4. Disadvantages

  • Hidden behavior is hard to debug.
  • Reflection-based processing costs startup time.
  • Overuse reduces clarity.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Spring, Hibernate and JUnit rely on them.
  • Needed to write custom annotations.
  • Interview topic.

6. Basic Concepts

What is an Annotation?

An annotation is metadata attached to code - a class, method, field, or parameter - using the @AnnotationName syntax.

  • Annotations do not change what the code does by themselves; the compiler, a tool, or a framework reads them and decides what to do.
  • They attach extra information that the compiler, runtime or tools can act on, without changing the actual logic.

@Override - Catching Mistakes at Compile Time

@Override tells the compiler "this method is meant to override a method from the parent class or interface." If it does not override anything (for example, a typo in the method name or signature), the compiler gives an error instead of silently creating a new, unrelated method.

Other Common Built-in Annotations

  • @Deprecated - marks an element as outdated; using it from another class gives a compiler warning.
  • @SuppressWarnings("...") - hides one category of compiler warning (for example "unchecked") for that element.
  • @FunctionalInterface - states that an interface has exactly one abstract method; the compiler gives an error if a second one is added.
  • @SafeVarargs - on a final, static or private varargs method, promises that it does nothing unsafe with its generic varargs array, which removes the related warning.

Fresher Notes

  • Metadata: annotations add extra information to code, such as @Override, @Deprecated, @FunctionalInterface and @SuppressWarnings.
  • No logic by themselves: compilers, tools and frameworks read them and act.
  • Framework driven: Spring, JPA and JUnit use @Service, @Entity and @Test.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Custom annotations: define your own with @interface, then add @Retention (SOURCE, CLASS, RUNTIME) and @Target (TYPE, METHOD, FIELD ...).
  • Elements look like methods and can have defaults: String value() default "";.
  • Reading at run time: use reflection, for example method.getAnnotation(X.class).

8. Advanced Concepts

Meta-Annotations - Annotations That Describe Annotations

When you write your own annotation, you configure it with annotations that apply to annotations themselves:

  • @Retention - how long the annotation is kept: SOURCE (discarded by the compiler, e.g. @Override), CLASS (kept in the .class file but not visible at run time; the default), or RUNTIME (kept and readable through reflection).
  • @Target - which kinds of elements it can be applied to (TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, etc.).
  • @Documented - includes the annotation in generated Javadoc.
  • @Inherited - lets a subclass pick up a class-level annotation from its parent class.
  • @Repeatable - allows the same annotation more than once on the same element.

Reading Custom Annotations at Runtime via Reflection

A RUNTIME annotation can be read back with the Reflection API. This is how frameworks like Spring and JPA find and act on your annotations without wiring code from you.

Real-World Framework Usage (Why This Matters)

Annotations are how modern Java frameworks avoid boilerplate configuration:

  • Spring: @Component, @Service and @Repository mark a class for Spring to manage as a bean; @Autowired asks Spring to inject a dependency; @RestController and @GetMapping link HTTP routes to methods.
  • JPA/Hibernate: @Entity maps a class to a database table; @Id and @Column map fields to columns.
  • JUnit: @Test marks a method as a test case for the runner to find and execute.

In every case, the framework scans your classes at startup using reflection, finds the annotations and builds its behavior around them. The annotation does nothing by itself; the framework that reads it does the work.

Senior Notes

  • Annotation processors (javax.annotation.processing) generate code at compile time (Lombok, MapStruct, Dagger).
  • Inheritance and repetition are controlled by @Inherited and @Repeatable.
  • Do not overuse annotations for logic: explicit code is easier to debug and test.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Further topics: repeatable annotations (@Repeatable), type annotations (@NonNull on types), annotation processing with AbstractProcessor (generate code or validate at compile time), composed annotations (Spring stereotypes combine others) and Bean Validation (@NotNull, @Size). Processors run in rounds and can create new source files.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Annotations compile into class file attributes (RuntimeVisibleAnnotations), and an annotation type is an interface extending java.lang.annotation.Annotation. At run time getAnnotation returns a dynamic proxy that implements the annotation interface and serves element values. Elements may be primitives, String, Class, enums, annotations and arrays of those.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes: forgetting RUNTIME retention (the annotation is invisible to reflection), expecting annotations on interfaces or methods to be inherited automatically, putting heavy logic in annotation magic, not noticing that a framework silently ignores a misplaced annotation, and calling reflection on every request instead of caching the result.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Annotation scanning at startup (classpath scanning) slows startup in large apps; build-time processing (Spring AOT, Micronaut, Quarkus) moves it to compile time. Cache annotation lookups instead of calling reflection on every request.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a tiny dependency injector. It creates a Service and fills every field marked with @Inject. A full framework would also scan a package for classes marked with @Component.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Retention matters.

Worked Example 2

Simple validation framework.

Practice Exercise 1

Custom runtime annotation and reader.

Practice Exercise 2

Built-in annotations.

11. Quick Revision

  • @Retention decides visibility.
  • @Target limits where used.
  • Read with reflection.
  • Processors generate code at compile time.
  • Built-ins: Override, Deprecated, FunctionalInterface.

interviewQA: Does an annotation change program behavior by itself?
No - it is pure metadata; only a compiler check, tool, or framework reading it (typically via reflection) decides what to do with it
What are the three RetentionPolicy values?
SOURCE (compiler-only, e.g. @Override), CLASS (kept in bytecode but not runtime-visible, the default), RUNTIME (readable via reflection)
Why must a framework annotation use RUNTIME retention?
Because frameworks like Spring/Hibernate read annotations via reflection while the application is running, which requires RUNTIME retention to still be present in the loaded class
What does @Target control?
Which kinds of program elements (class, method, field, parameter, etc.) the annotation is legal to apply to
What does @FunctionalInterface actually enforce?
That the interface has exactly one abstract method - the compiler errors if a second one is added, protecting lambda-expression compatibility
How does Spring's @Autowired actually work under the hood?
Spring scans beans via reflection at startup, finds fields/constructors annotated @Autowired, and injects a matching bean - the annotation just marks intent, Spring's container does the actual wiring

topics.name: Reflection API

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Reflection inspects and uses classes, methods and fields at run time, for example Class.forName, getDeclaredMethods and invoke.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Frameworks cannot know your classes at compile time.
  • Reflection lets them create objects and call methods by name.

3. Advantages

  • Dynamic behavior.
  • Powers frameworks (DI, ORM, JSON).
  • Inspect metadata and annotations.

4. Disadvantages

  • Slower than direct calls.
  • Breaks encapsulation and type safety.
  • Needs configuration in native images.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Explains how Spring and Hibernate work.
  • Useful for writing tools and tests.
  • Interview topic.

6. Basic Concepts

What is Reflection?

Reflection is the ability of Java code to inspect and manipulate classes, methods, fields, and constructors at runtime - even ones it did not know about at compile time.

  • Normally, you write obj.method() and the compiler resolves everything ahead of time.
  • With reflection, you can ask "what methods does this object's class have?" and call one by name, as a String, decided while the program is running.
  • It exists because frameworks (Spring, Hibernate, JUnit, JSON libraries) need to work with classes they were never compiled against - your application classes.

Getting a Class<?> Object - Three Ways

Every loaded class has exactly one Class object representing it, obtainable in three ways:

  • ClassName.class - at compile time, when you know the type.
  • object.getClass() - from an existing instance, at runtime.
  • Class.forName("fully.qualified.Name") - purely from a String, useful when the class name is only known at runtime (e.g. read from a config file).

Inspecting Fields, Methods, and Constructors

Once you have a Class object, you can list everything the class declares - names, types, and modifiers - without ever creating an instance.

Fresher Notes

  • Load a class by name: Class<?> c = Class.forName("com.acme.User");.
  • Get members with getDeclaredFields(), getDeclaredMethods(), getConstructors(); use them with invoke, newInstance, set.
  • Who uses it: Spring, Hibernate, Jackson and JUnit.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Private access: setAccessible(true) bypasses it (blocked across modules unless opened).
  • Cost: slower than direct calls, and compile-time safety is lost (errors appear at run time).
  • Checked exceptions to handle: ClassNotFoundException, NoSuchMethodException, IllegalAccessException, InvocationTargetException.

8. Advanced Concepts

Creating Objects and Invoking Methods Dynamically

Reflection can construct a new instance and call methods on it purely by name - this is how a framework creates classes it has never seen at compile time.

Accessing Private Members with setAccessible(true)

Reflection can bypass normal access-control checks (private/protected) using setAccessible(true) on a Field, Method, or Constructor. This is powerful but dangerous:

  • It breaks encapsulation - the entire point of marking something private.
  • It can be blocked by a SecurityManager in restricted environments, or by the module system's strong encapsulation (Java 9+, unless the module explicitly opens the package).
  • It should be reserved for frameworks and tools, not everyday application code.

Performance Cost - Why Reflection Isn't the Default

Reflective calls are slower than direct calls, because the JVM cannot apply the same optimizations (such as inlining) it applies to normal method calls - every reflective invocation goes through extra checks (access control, argument matching) at runtime.

This is why frameworks like Spring and Hibernate do the reflective lookup once (e.g. at startup, caching the resolved Method/Field objects) rather than on every call.

Real-World Usage - Why Frameworks Depend on Reflection

  • Spring uses reflection for dependency injection - scanning classes for @Autowired fields/constructors and injecting matching beans without you writing wiring code.
  • Hibernate/JPA uses reflection to map database rows to your entity objects - reading @Column-annotated fields and setting them, even private ones.
  • JUnit uses reflection to discover and invoke every method annotated @Test, without you registering them manually.
  • JSON libraries (Jackson, Gson) use reflection to convert Java objects to/from JSON by reading and setting fields.

The common thread: these tools work on classes they were compiled without knowing about - your application code.

Senior Notes

  • Faster calls: prefer MethodHandle/VarHandle, avoid reflection in hot paths, and cache Method objects.
  • Native image: GraalVM needs reflection configuration (reflect-config) because classes are resolved at build time.
  • Design: reflection breaks encapsulation; use it sparingly and prefer interfaces, ServiceLoader or annotation processing.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools beyond plain reflection:

  • MethodHandles.lookup().findVirtual(...) - fast dynamic invocation.
  • VarHandle - field access with memory-ordering control.
  • Proxy - dynamic proxies for interfaces (the basis of Spring AOP and Retrofit).
  • ByteBuddy and ASM - bytecode generation.
  • ServiceLoader - plugin discovery.
  • getRecordComponents - record introspection.
  • Module opens directives - allow deep reflection into a package.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Every loaded class has a Class object holding metadata: fields, methods, constructors, annotations, modifiers, generic signatures. Method.invoke checks access and argument types, boxes arguments, and since JDK 18 uses method handles internally (faster than the old native accessors). getDeclaredX returns members of that class only (any visibility); getX returns public members including inherited.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Using reflection where a plain interface would do.
  • Swallowing InvocationTargetException (the real error is its cause).
  • Accessing private members across modules (InaccessibleObjectException).
  • Relying on member order from getDeclaredMethods (it is unspecified).
  • Using user-supplied class or method names (an injection risk).
  • Breaking when an obfuscator renames members.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Reflective calls are several times slower than direct calls and block some JIT optimizations; cache lookups (Method, Field, MethodHandle in static final fields) and avoid reflection in loops. Startup scanning of many classes is the usual cost in frameworks.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a mini JSON serializer that writes the fields of any object, and how JUnit finds test methods by annotation.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

InvocationTargetException wraps the cause.

Worked Example 2

Class name lookup.

Practice Exercise 1

Inspect and call.

Practice Exercise 2

Dynamic proxy.

11. Quick Revision

  • Class objects describe types.
  • getDeclaredX includes private members.
  • setAccessible bypasses access.
  • InvocationTargetException wraps causes.
  • Cache Method objects.

interviewQA: What is reflection?
The ability to inspect and manipulate classes, fields, methods, and constructors at runtime, including ones not known at compile time
Name the three ways to obtain a Class object.
ClassName.class (compile-time), object.getClass() (from an instance), Class.forName("...") (from a String at runtime)
What does setAccessible(true) do, and why is it risky?
It bypasses private/protected access checks so reflection can read/write/invoke normally-inaccessible members - it breaks encapsulation and can be blocked by the module system or a SecurityManager
Why is reflection slower than a direct method call?
Every reflective call goes through extra runtime checks (access control, argument matching) that the JVM can't optimize away the way it does for normal, statically-resolved calls
How does Spring's @Autowired actually inject dependencies?
Spring scans bean classes via reflection at startup, finds annotated fields/constructors, and uses reflection to set matching bean instances into them
How do frameworks mitigate reflection's performance cost?
By resolving Method/Field objects once (e.g. at startup) and caching them, instead of re-looking them up on every call

topics.name: Nested & Inner Classes

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Nested classes are defined inside other classes: static nested, inner, local and anonymous classes.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Some classes only make sense in the context of another (builders, iterators, callbacks).
  • Nesting keeps them close and private.

3. Advantages

  • Better encapsulation.
  • Inner classes access outer members.
  • Anonymous classes give inline implementations.

4. Disadvantages

  • Inner classes hold a hidden outer reference (leaks).
  • More complex syntax.
  • Lambdas replace many anonymous classes.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used in builders, iterators and listeners.
  • Interview topic.
  • Needed to read library code.

6. Basic Concepts

What is a Nested Class?

A class declared inside another class is called a nested class. The class that contains it is called the outer class.

Java groups nested classes into two big families:

  • Static nested class — declared with static, behaves like a top-level class that just happens to live inside another class's namespace.
  • Inner class (non-static) — NOT declared static; every inner class instance is tied to a specific instance of the outer class.

Inner classes are further split into: member inner class, local inner class (inside a method), and anonymous inner class (no name at all).

Static Nested Class

A static nested class does not hold a reference to any outer object. It can be created directly using the outer class's name, without needing an outer instance first — just like any other class.

Inner Class (Member Inner Class)

A (non-static) inner class holds an implicit reference to the outer object that created it — that's why you must go through an outer instance to create one, using outer.new Inner().

Local Class (Defined Inside a Method)
