A class declared inside a method body is a local class. It is only visible within that method, and it can capture final/effectively-final local variables from the enclosing method.

Anonymous Inner Class

An anonymous inner class is a class with no name that is declared and instantiated in a single expression — usually to provide a one-off implementation of an interface or to override a method of an existing class.

Fresher Notes

  • Nested class: a class defined inside another class. Kinds: static nested, inner (non-static), local (inside a method) and anonymous (no name).
  • Inner instance: belongs to an outer instance, created with outer.new Inner(). It can use all outer members, even private ones.
  • Static nested: does not need an outer instance.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Static nested helpers: use them when the outer instance is not needed (Builder, Map.Entry).
  • Anonymous classes: implement an interface or extend a class inline. A lambda replaces them for functional interfaces.
  • Capture: local and anonymous classes can use effectively final local variables.

8. Advanced Concepts

Why Anonymous Classes Were the Pre-Lambda Way to Implement Functional Interfaces

Before Java 8, an anonymous inner class was the standard way to pass "a piece of behavior" as an argument (e.g. to Runnable, Comparator, or event listeners) since Java had no lambda syntax. A lambda expression is essentially syntactic sugar over exactly this pattern — for a functional interface (single abstract method), the compiler can infer everything an anonymous class needed to spell out by hand.

Memory/GC Implication: Inner Classes Hold a Reference to Their Outer Instance

Because every (non-static) inner class instance secretly stores a reference back to the outer object that created it (accessible via Outer.this), the outer object cannot be garbage collected while any of its inner class instances are still reachable — even if nothing else in the program references the outer object directly. This is a classic source of memory leaks, especially with long-lived inner class instances (e.g. event listeners, callbacks) held by something outside the outer object's own lifecycle.

A static nested class has no such hidden reference, so it does not keep its "outer" class instance alive.

Accessing the Enclosing Instance Explicitly — Outer.this

When a variable name inside an inner class is shadowed (the inner class declares a field with the same name as the outer class), you can still reach the outer field explicitly with Outer.this.fieldName.

Static Nested Class vs Inner Class — Compared

AspectStatic Nested ClassInner Class (Non-Static)
Needs an outer instance to create?No — new Outer.Nested()Yes — outer.new Inner()
Implicit reference to outer instance?NoYes (accessible as Outer.this)
Can access outer instance (non-static) members?No — only outer's static membersYes — directly
Keeps outer instance alive (GC)?NoYes, as long as the inner instance is reachable
Typical useHelper/builder classes logically scoped to the outer classClasses that genuinely need to operate on an outer instance's state

Senior Notes

  • Hidden reference: an inner object keeps its outer object alive. Leaks happen when the inner instance outlives the outer one (listeners, threads).
  • Default choice: prefer static nested classes.
  • Nestmates (Java 11): nested classes reach each other private members directly, with no synthetic accessor methods.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Common uses:

  • Static nested: builders and entries.
  • Inner: iterators over the outer collection.
  • Anonymous: callbacks and listeners.
  • Local records and enums, and helper classes private to one top-level class.

A lambda is different from an anonymous class: it does not create a new this (it keeps the enclosing one), it compiles with invokedynamic, and it captures variables directly. Use this and Outer.this to tell inner and outer members apart.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The compiler turns every nested class into a separate top-level class file (Outer$Inner.class, Outer$1.class for anonymous). An inner class constructor takes the outer instance as a hidden parameter stored in a synthetic field this$0. Local and anonymous classes copy captured effectively final variables into synthetic fields (val$name). Newer compilers (Java 18+) drop this$0 when the inner class never uses the outer instance, so the sample below uses it.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Using a non-static inner class for a helper: it keeps a hidden outer reference, which can leak and also drags the outer object into serialization.
  • Writing anonymous classes inside loops or hot code: each one is a separate class.
  • Expecting this in a lambda to be the lambda. It is the enclosing object.
  • Serializing inner classes.
  • Double-brace initialization, such as new ArrayList<>() {{ add(1); }}. It creates an anonymous subclass that holds the outer reference.
  • Calling outer methods from threads that outlive the outer object.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Memory: an inner object adds only one reference, and a lambda that does not capture is created once and reused. The real risk is the leak, not the overhead. Long-lived callbacks (timers, thread pools, static registries) that hold inner instances keep whole object graphs alive. Use static nested classes and weak references for listeners.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an LRU cache (keeps the most recently used entries) built from LinkedHashMap with an anonymous subclass that overrides removeEldestEntry.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Private access: an inner class reads the private state of its outer object.

Worked Example 2

Capture rule.

Practice Exercise 1

Static nested builder and inner class.

Practice Exercise 2

Anonymous class and local class.

11. Quick Revision

  • Static nested: no outer instance.
  • Inner: outer.new Inner().
  • Local and anonymous capture effectively final variables.
  • Prefer static nested classes.
  • this vs Outer.this.

interviewQA: What's the key difference between a static nested class and an inner class?
An inner class holds an implicit reference to its enclosing outer instance; a static nested class does not
How do you instantiate a non-static inner class from outside the outer class?
Outer outer = new Outer(); Outer.Inner inner = outer.new Inner();
Can a static nested class access the outer class's instance (non-static) fields?
No — it can only access the outer class's static members, since it has no reference to any particular outer instance
Why can inner classes cause memory leaks?
Because they secretly hold a reference to their outer instance, keeping that outer object reachable (and un-collectible) for as long as the inner instance is reachable
What variables can a local/anonymous class capture from its enclosing method?
Only final or effectively-final local variables — variables that are never reassigned after initialization
How did lambdas change the need for anonymous inner classes?

For functional interfaces (single abstract method), a lambda replaces the anonymous-class boilerplate entirely, though anonymous classes are still needed for interfaces with multiple methods or to extend a concrete class

topics.name: Interfaces in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • An interface defines a contract of methods that classes implement, with default, static and private methods in modern Java.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Different classes need a common set of capabilities without sharing implementation.
  • Interfaces provide that and support multiple inheritance of type.

3. Advantages

  • Loose coupling.
  • Multiple implementation.
  • Enable lambdas through functional interfaces.

4. Disadvantages

  • Changing a published interface breaks implementers.
  • Too many tiny interfaces add noise.
  • Default method conflicts need resolution.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Foundation of Spring and the Collections API.
  • Interview topic: interface vs abstract class.
  • Needed for testing with mocks.

6. Basic Concepts

What is an Interface?

An interface is a contract — it declares what a class must be able to do, without saying how. Any class that implements an interface promises to provide real implementations for its abstract methods.

  • Before Java 8, an interface could only have abstract methods (and constants) — 100% abstraction.
  • Since Java 8, interfaces can also have default and static methods with real bodies.
  • A class uses implements to fulfil an interface's contract; an interface uses extends to inherit from another interface.

Basic Interface and Implementation

Every abstract method declared in an interface must be overridden by the implementing class (unless the class itself is abstract).

Constants in Interfaces

Any field declared in an interface is implicitly public static final — a constant. It cannot be reassigned, and it belongs to the interface itself, not to any implementing instance.

Default Methods (Java 8+)

A default method provides a real implementation directly inside the interface. It exists so an interface can gain new methods over time without breaking every class that already implements it — old implementers simply inherit the default behavior instead of failing to compile.

Static Methods on Interfaces (Java 8+)

An interface can also declare static utility methods. They belong to the interface itself (called as InterfaceName.method()) and are not inherited by implementing classes.

Fresher Notes

  • Contract: an interface lists methods that classes implement with implements. A class can implement many interfaces.
  • Defaults: interface methods are public and abstract by default; fields are public static final constants.
  • No objects: you cannot create an object of an interface, but you can use it as a type.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Newer methods: since Java 8, default methods (with a body) and static methods; Java 9 added private methods.
  • Functional interface: exactly one abstract method, so it can be a lambda target (@FunctionalInterface).
  • Interface inheritance: an interface can extend multiple interfaces.

8. Advanced Concepts

Multiple Interface Inheritance & the Diamond Problem

A class can implement multiple interfaces — Java's answer to "multiple inheritance of type" without the classic diamond problem of multiple inheritance of state. But if two interfaces provide the same default method signature, the implementing class faces an ambiguity the compiler refuses to guess at:

interface A { default void hello() { System.out.println("A"); } }
interface B { default void hello() { System.out.println("B"); } }

class C implements A, B { }
// COMPILE ERROR: class C inherits unrelated defaults for hello() from A and B

The fix: C must explicitly override hello() and decide what to do — including optionally delegating to one parent via InterfaceName.super.method().

Functional Interfaces — the Bridge to Lambdas

A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method (it may still have any number of default/static methods). The @FunctionalInterface annotation isn't required, but it makes the compiler enforce the "single abstract method" rule and documents intent. Functional interfaces are what make lambda expressions and method references possible — a lambda is simply an inline implementation of that one abstract method.

Interface vs Abstract Class

AspectInterfaceAbstract Class
Multiple inheritanceA class can implement many interfacesA class can extend only one abstract class
State (instance fields)Only constants (public static final)Can have real instance fields with any access modifier
ConstructorsNoYes — run during subclass construction via super()
Method bodiesdefault/static methods only (Java 8+)Any mix of abstract and fully implemented methods
Best used forDefining a capability/contract across unrelated classesSharing common state + partial implementation among closely related classes

Senior Notes

  • Program to interfaces: this helps dependency injection, testing with fakes and mocks, and swapping implementations.
  • Interface segregation: many small interfaces beat one large one.
  • Evolving an API: add default methods instead of breaking implementers; sealed interfaces limit implementations.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Design: small role interfaces, functional interfaces (Function, Predicate, Supplier), generic interfaces (Repository<T>), marker interfaces, sealed interfaces for algebraic data types, and interface evolution with default methods. Test doubles and dependency inversion depend on interfaces. Avoid the constant interface anti-pattern; use a final class or enum.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Interface methods compile to invokeinterface and are dispatched through the receiver class itable (with inline caches in the JIT). Default methods are inherited into implementing classes at link time; resolution rules: a class method beats any interface default, the most specific interface wins, and conflicts must be resolved explicitly. Private interface methods share code between defaults. Fields are static constants initialized when the interface is first used.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: interfaces used as constant holders, one-implementation interfaces for everything, fat interfaces, default methods that depend on mutable state or break implementers, diamond default conflicts (compile error until resolved), and changing a published interface by adding abstract methods (breaks all implementers). Add defaults or a new interface.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Interface dispatch has negligible cost after JIT. Many tiny interfaces and lambdas are fine. Megamorphic call sites (many implementations) prevent inlining: watch hot loops over heterogeneous lists.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: the JDK collections (List, Map) and JDBC (Connection) are interfaces with many implementations; Spring injects implementations by interface type.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Constants in interfaces.

Worked Example 2

Sealed interface.

Practice Exercise 1

Interface with default and static methods.

Practice Exercise 2

Polymorphism through interfaces.

11. Quick Revision

  • Methods are public abstract by default.
  • Fields are public static final.
  • default and static methods since Java 8.
  • A class can implement many interfaces.
  • Functional interface: one abstract method.

interviewQA: Why were default methods added to interfaces in Java 8?
So existing interfaces (like those in the Collections framework) could gain new methods without breaking every class that already implemented them
Are fields in an interface mutable?
No — every interface field is implicitly public static final, i.e. a constant
What happens if a class implements two interfaces with the same default method?
Compile error unless the class explicitly overrides that method, optionally calling InterfaceName.super.method() to pick a specific parent's version
What makes an interface a "functional interface"?
It declares exactly one abstract method (default/static methods don't count), making it a valid target for a lambda expression
Can an interface have a static method inherited by implementing classes?
No — static interface methods belong to the interface itself and must be called as InterfaceName.method()
Interface vs abstract class — when do you pick which?
Interface for a capability shared across unrelated classes (multiple implementable); abstract class when related classes should share real state and partial implementation

topics.name: equals() and hashCode() Contract

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Equals defines logical equality and hashCode returns an int used by hash collections.
  • They must be consistent: equal objects have equal hash codes.

2. Need of This Topic

  • HashMap and HashSet find objects by hashCode and equals.
  • Without correct overrides, lookups fail and duplicates appear.

3. Advantages

  • Correct behavior of HashMap and HashSet.
  • Value-based equality.
  • Records generate both automatically.

4. Disadvantages

  • Easy to implement wrongly.
  • Mutable fields break hash-based collections.
  • Inheritance complicates symmetry.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Very common interview topic.
  • Needed for map keys and set elements.
  • Prevents subtle bugs.

6. Basic Concepts

The Default Behavior (from Object)

Every Java class inherits equals() and hashCode() from Object if it does not override them:

  • Object.equals(other) — compares by reference (==); true only if both variables point to the exact same object in memory.
  • Object.hashCode() — returns an identity hash, usually based on the object's identity, so two different objects almost always get different hash codes.

Why Override equals() — Value-Based Comparison

Most of the time, you want two objects to be "equal" if they represent the same value — not the same memory address. Overriding equals() lets you define exactly what "equal" means for your class.

The Rule: If You Override equals(), You MUST Override hashCode() Too

Java's contract requires: if two objects are equal according to equals(), they MUST return the same hashCode(). Hash-based collections (HashMap, HashSet, Hashtable) rely on this rule to find objects — breaking it silently corrupts lookups.

Fresher Notes

  • Logical equality: equals(Object) defines it; hashCode() returns an int used by hash-based collections.
  • Contract: if a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). Override both together.
  • Default behavior: equals compares references (==).

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Five rules: equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent and return false for null.
  • Helpers: use Objects.equals and Objects.hash, a record (generated for you), or IDE generation.
  • Mutable fields: do not use them in hashCode for objects stored in hash sets or maps.

8. Advanced Concepts

The Classic Bug: Overriding equals() WITHOUT hashCode() Breaks HashMap/HashSet

A HashMap/HashSet first uses hashCode() to find the right "bucket," and only then uses equals() to check candidates within that bucket. If equals() says two objects are equal but they land in different buckets because hashCode() wasn't overridden consistently, a lookup for an "equal" key will search the wrong bucket entirely and silently fail to find it.

The Full Contract

  • Reflexive: x.equals(x) must always be true.
  • Symmetric: x.equals(y) must equal y.equals(x).
  • Transitive: if x.equals(y) and y.equals(z), then x.equals(z) must also be true.
  • Consistent: repeated calls to x.equals(y) must keep returning the same result, as long as neither object's compared fields change.
  • Non-null: x.equals(null) must return false.
  • hashCode() agreement: equal objects (per equals()) MUST return the same hashCode(). The reverse is not required: unequal objects CAN share a hashCode (a hash collision); hash-based collections then fall back to equals() within the same bucket.

Objects.equals() and Objects.hash() — Null-Safe Helpers

Manually writing equals()/hashCode() with several fields is error-prone (null checks, combining hash values correctly). java.util.Objects provides null-safe helpers that do this correctly.

Records Auto-Generate Both Correctly (Java 16+)

A record automatically generates equals(), hashCode(), and toString() based on all of its components, already correctly consistent with each other — no manual boilerplate needed for the common case.

Senior Notes

  • Broken contract: causes duplicates in HashSet and failed lookups in HashMap.
  • Inheritance: getClass() vs instanceof and the symmetry problem; prefer final classes or composition.
  • JPA entities: base equals on a business key or id carefully, because ids may be null before persistence.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Implementation recipe (Effective Java): equals checks this == o, type with instanceof (or getClass for strict), then each significant field (primitives with ==, floats with Float.compare, objects with Objects.equals, arrays with Arrays.equals). hashCode combines the same fields (Objects.hash, or 31 * result + c). Records and Lombok @EqualsAndHashCode generate both. For entity classes use a business key or the id with careful null handling.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

HashMap.get(key) computes hashCode() to pick a bucket, then calls equals on entries in that bucket (after comparing stored hashes). If hashCode differs for equal objects, the lookup goes to the wrong bucket and fails. The contract: consistent across calls (no state change), equal objects share a hashCode, unequal objects ideally spread. Object.hashCode is typically an identity hash stored in the header.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Overriding only one of the two methods.
  • Using mutable fields in hashCode.
  • Writing equals(Foo) (an overload) instead of equals(Object). Add @Override to catch this.
  • instanceof asymmetry with subclasses.
  • Comparing floating-point fields with == (use Double.compare).
  • Calling equals on a null field (NullPointerException).
  • An expensive hashCode recalculated on every call.
  • JPA entities hashing a generated id that changes after persist.
  • Relying on the identity hash across JVM runs (it changes).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Good hash functions spread values evenly; poor ones (constant, only one field) make buckets long: lookups drop from O(1) to O(n) (or O(log n) with treeified Comparable keys). Cache the hash in immutable classes with expensive hashCode (String does). Check distribution when keys are structured.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: deduplicating events or customers by business key, caching with composite keys, and entities in sets.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Record gives both for free.

Worked Example 2

Symmetry violation.

Practice Exercise 1

Correct override.

Practice Exercise 2

Missing hashCode.

11. Quick Revision

  • Override both together.
  • Use Objects.equals and Objects.hash.
  • Do not use mutable fields in hashCode.
  • Equal objects must have equal hashCodes.
  • Records give both for free.

interviewQA: What does the default (Object) equals() do?
Reference comparison - equivalent to ==, true only if both variables point to the exact same object
Why must you override hashCode() whenever you override equals()?
Because equal objects (per equals()) MUST produce the same hashCode - otherwise HashMap/HashSet look in the wrong bucket and silently fail to find "equal" objects
Do unequal objects need different hashCodes?
No - a hash collision (unequal objects, same hashCode) is legal; hash-based collections then fall back to equals() to tell them apart within the same bucket
What are the 4 properties equals() must satisfy?
Reflexive, symmetric, transitive, and consistent
What does Objects.hash() do?
Combines multiple field hash codes into one int, null-safely, sparing you from writing that logic by hand
Do records need manual equals()/hashCode() overrides?
No - records auto-generate both based on all their components, already mutually consistent

topics.name: Comparable vs Comparator

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Comparable gives a class its natural order with compareTo, while Comparator defines other orders externally with compare.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Sorting and sorted collections need a way to order objects, by one field or several.

3. Advantages

  • Flexible sorting.
  • Composable comparators (thenComparing).
  • Works with TreeSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueue.

4. Disadvantages

  • Inconsistent compare logic causes errors.
  • Subtraction can overflow.
  • Comparable allows only one natural order.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Sorting is everywhere.
  • Interview topic.
  • Needed for sorted collections.

6. Basic Concepts

Two Ways to Sort Custom Objects

Java's Collections.sort() and List.sort() need to know how to order your objects. You use one of two interfaces:

  • Comparable<T> - the class defines its own single, natural ordering by implementing compareTo().
  • Comparator<T> - a separate object defines an ordering by implementing compare(), without touching the original class. You can write as many Comparators as you need.

Comparable — Natural Ordering

A class implements Comparable<T> and overrides compareTo(T other), returning negative/zero/positive to mean "less than / equal to / greater than". This becomes the class's one default ordering.

Comparator — External, Multiple Orderings

A Comparator<T> is written separately from the class it sorts, so you can have as many different orderings as you need without modifying the original class at all.

Fresher Notes

  • Natural vs external order: Comparable<T> gives a class one natural order with compareTo; Comparator<T> defines other orders outside the class with compare.
  • Return value: both return a negative, zero or positive int.
  • Where used: Collections.sort, list.sort, TreeSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueue.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Build comparators: Comparator.comparing(Person::name).thenComparing(Person::age), .reversed(), nullsFirst.
  • Avoid subtraction: prefer Integer.compare(a, b) to a - b, which can overflow.
  • Consistent with equals: keep compareTo returning 0 only when equals is true, when possible.

8. Advanced Concepts

Java 8+ Comparator: comparing(), reversed(), thenComparing()

Since Java 8, Comparator has static/default helper methods that let you build orderings from a key extractor lambda instead of writing a full compare() method by hand, chain a tie-breaker with thenComparing(), and flip direction with reversed().

Sorting the Same List Multiple Different Ways

Because a Comparator is decoupled from the class, the same Employee list can be re-sorted differently at different call sites, without Employee ever needing to change or implement Comparable at all.

Comparable vs Comparator — Compared

AspectComparableComparator
Packagejava.langjava.util
MethodcompareTo(T other)compare(T a, T b)
Implemented byThe class being sorted, itselfA separate class/lambda
Number of orderingsExactly one - the "natural" orderingAs many as you want
Requires modifying the sorted class?Yes - the class must implement ComparableNo - works even on classes you don't own (e.g. third-party classes)
Used viaCollections.sort(list) / list.sort(null)Collections.sort(list, comparator) / list.sort(comparator)

Senior Notes

  • Stability: sorting objects uses TimSort, which is stable, so successive sorts compose.
  • Broken comparators: a non-transitive one can throw "Comparison method violates its general contract".
  • Text order: for locale-aware sorting of text use Collator.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

More tools you will meet in real code:

  • Collator for locale-aware text order.
  • Natural comparators, so "file2" comes before "file10".
  • Collections.max/min, stream().sorted(cmp), TreeMap(cmp) and Comparator.nullsLast.
  • Top-k with a bounded PriorityQueue.
  • Multi-key sort using stability: sort by the least important key first.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Object sorting uses TimSort. It finds sorted runs and merges them. It is stable, takes O(n log n) time, and is close to O(n) on nearly sorted data. Primitive arrays use dual-pivot quicksort.

  • A comparator must be consistent: if a < b and b < c then a < c, and swapping the arguments flips the sign.
  • Comparator.comparing builds a comparator from a key extractor.
  • thenComparing adds a tie-breaker; reversed() flips the order.
  • comparing(f) boxes primitive keys; comparingInt/Long/Double avoid boxing.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Subtraction comparators (a - b) that overflow.
  • Comparing doubles by hand instead of Double.compare.
  • Inconsistent comparators, which can throw IllegalArgumentException.
  • Changing a sort key while the object is inside a TreeSet.
  • Ignoring null or mixing types.
  • A compareTo that disagrees with equals: a TreeSet treats "equal" items as duplicates, so elements vanish.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Sorting n items costs O(n log n) comparisons, so keep compare cheap and free of new objects.

  • For expensive keys, compute each key once (decorate, sort, undecorate).
  • For large primitive arrays use Arrays.parallelSort.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world uses: a leaderboard where ties go to the earlier submission, and a table sorted by user-selected columns.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

PriorityQueue by comparator.

Worked Example 2

Overflow trap.

Practice Exercise 1

Natural order and custom orders.

Practice Exercise 2

Null-safe order.

11. Quick Revision

  • compareTo: negative, zero, positive.
  • Comparator.comparing().thenComparing().
  • Use Integer.compare, not a - b.
  • Sorting is stable.
  • Keep consistent with equals.

interviewQA: What's the core difference between Comparable and Comparator?
Comparable defines a class's own single natural ordering (compareTo, in java.lang); Comparator defines an external, reusable ordering (compare, in java.util), and you can have many of them
Can you sort a class you don't own (e.g. from a third-party library) by a custom field?
Yes, using a Comparator - you can't make it implement Comparable since you don't control its source
What should compareTo()/compare() return?
A negative int if the first is "less than" the second, zero if equal, a positive int if "greater than" - the exact magnitude doesn't matter, only the sign
How do you sort by one field, then break ties with another?
Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor).thenComparing(secondKeyExtractor)
How do you reverse a Comparator's order?
Call .reversed() on it, or use Comparator.reverseOrder() / Collections.reverseOrder()
Is Comparable a functional interface?
Yes - it has exactly one abstract method (compareTo), so it can also be implemented with a lambda, though Comparator is the more common lambda target in practice

topics.name: Object Cloning

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Cloning creates a copy of an object using Cloneable and clone(), producing a shallow copy by default.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Sometimes you need an independent copy of an object, for example to keep a snapshot.

3. Advantages

  • Quick copy of flat objects.
  • Arrays have a working clone().
  • Can be customized for deep copies.

4. Disadvantages

  • Shallow by default: nested objects are shared.
  • clone is fragile and bypasses constructors.
  • Discouraged in modern Java.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Interview topic: shallow vs deep copy.
  • Teaches reference semantics.
  • Leads to copy constructors and immutability.

6. Basic Concepts

What is Object Cloning?

Object cloning means creating an exact copy of an existing object - a new object with the same field values, sitting at a different memory address from the original.

  • Java provides a built-in way to do this via Object.clone().
  • A plain assignment like Employee e2 = e1; does not clone anything - it just copies the reference, so e1 and e2 point to the same object.
  • Cloning creates a genuinely separate object in memory.

The Cloneable Interface

Cloneable is a marker interface - it declares no methods at all. Its only job is to act as a flag telling the JVM "this class is allowed to be cloned".

  • Object.clone() is a protected native method defined on every class (since every class extends Object).
  • If you call clone() on a class that does not implement Cloneable, the JVM throws CloneNotSupportedException at runtime.
  • To make a class cloneable: implement Cloneable, and override clone() as public (widening its visibility from protected).

Without Cloneable — CloneNotSupportedException

Forgetting implements Cloneable compiles fine, but calling super.clone() throws at runtime:

Fresher Notes

  • Cloning creates a copy of an object. Implement Cloneable and override clone(); the default Object.clone() makes a shallow copy.
  • Shallow: copies field values; referenced objects are shared. Deep: copies referenced objects too.
  • Missing marker: without Cloneable, super.clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Pitfalls: clone bypasses constructors and has many traps (final fields, subclassing, checked exception).
  • Alternatives: copy constructors, static factory methods (copyOf), serialization-based or library copies, or immutable objects that need no copy.
  • Arrays have a working clone(): int[] b = a.clone(); (shallow).

8. Advanced Concepts

Shallow Copy — clone()'s Default Behavior

Object.clone() performs a shallow copy:

  • Primitive fields (int, boolean, etc.) are copied by value - the clone gets its own independent copy.
  • Reference-type fields (objects, arrays) are copied by reference - the clone's field points to the same underlying object as the original. Nothing is duplicated beneath the surface.

This is fine when every field is a primitive or an immutable type, but it is a trap the moment a field is a mutable object.

Deep Copy — Fixing the Shallow-Copy Bug

A deep copy clones every mutable object reachable from the object, not just the top-level fields. The fix: explicitly clone (or reconstruct) the nested mutable field inside clone().

Why Many Teams Avoid clone() Entirely

Joshua Bloch's Effective Java recommends avoiding Object.clone() in new code, because the mechanism is fragile:

  • It bypasses the normal constructor entirely (a clone is created without calling any constructor of the class).
  • Every mutable field must be deep-copied by hand, and it is easy to forget one - the bug above compiles perfectly fine.
  • The checked CloneNotSupportedException is awkward for a mechanism that should always work once Cloneable is implemented.
  • Cloneable does not declare clone(), so the type alone cannot tell you a class is properly cloneable.

The recommended alternatives:

  • Copy constructor: Employee(Employee other) { this.name = other.name; this.address = new Address(other.address); }
  • Static factory method: static Employee copyOf(Employee other) { ... }

Both are simpler, do not throw a checked exception, and give you full control over what gets deep-copied.

clone() vs Copy Constructor

AspectObject.clone()Copy Constructor / Static Factory
Requires CloneableYesNo
Calls a constructorNo - object is created without oneYes - normal object creation
Checked exceptionCloneNotSupportedExceptionNone needed
Deep copy controlMust override clone() correctly for every mutable fieldExplicit, readable, easy to review
Can copy to a different typeNoYes (a static factory can return a different concrete type)
Effective Java recommendationAvoidPreferred

Senior Notes

  • Effective Java: avoid Cloneable; provide a copy constructor or factory instead.
  • Deep copies of object graphs: use a copy constructor chain, records with List.copyOf, or mapping libraries (MapStruct).
  • Immutable classes never need cloning; defensive copies protect mutable inputs.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Alternatives: copy constructors and copy factories; builders with toBuilder(); immutable value objects (no copy needed); records with wither methods; serialization round trip (slow, requires Serializable); libraries (MapStruct, Jackson convertValue, Apache Commons SerializationUtils.clone); and structural sharing in persistent collections. For arrays, collections and strings use their own copy APIs.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Object.clone() is a protected native method that allocates a new object of the same class and copies fields bitwise without calling any constructor. It requires Cloneable. Overriding should call super.clone(), widen visibility to public, narrow the return type (covariant) and deep-copy mutable fields. Final fields cannot be reassigned after cloning, a major flaw.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forgetting Cloneable, not deep copying mutable fields, clone with final fields, subclass not calling super.clone() (breaks the chain: getClass() of the result is wrong), public clone that throws checked exceptions, assuming collections' clone() deep copies (they are shallow), and cloning objects with identity fields (ids, locks, threads).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Clone is fast for flat objects but deep copying graphs costs proportional to size. Immutable sharing avoids copies entirely. Defensive copying on every getter can be a hot spot: return unmodifiable views instead of copies when callers only read.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: undo history snapshots using immutable state objects and a copy-on-change approach, instead of cloning large mutable documents.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

CloneNotSupportedException.

Worked Example 2

Collections copy.

Practice Exercise 1

Shallow vs deep clone.

Practice Exercise 2

Copy constructor alternative.

11. Quick Revision

  • Implement Cloneable and override clone().
  • Shallow vs deep copy.
  • Prefer copy constructors or factories.
  • CloneNotSupportedException without Cloneable.
  • Immutable objects need no cloning.

interviewQA: What does Cloneable do?
Nothing by itself - it's a marker interface with no methods, it just flags a class as "allowed to be cloned" for Object.clone()'s internal check
What happens if you call clone() without implementing Cloneable?
Object.clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException at runtime
Is Object.clone() a shallow or deep copy?
Shallow - primitives are copied by value, but reference fields still point to the same shared objects as the original
How do you get a deep copy?
Manually clone (or reconstruct) every mutable reference field inside your overridden clone() method
Does clone() call the class's constructor?
No - the JVM copies the object's memory directly, bypassing every constructor
Why do many style guides recommend against clone()?
It's error-prone (easy to miss a deep-copy field), bypasses constructors, and forces a checked exception - a copy constructor or static factory method is simpler and safer

topics.name: try-with-resources

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Try-with-resources automatically closes resources that implement AutoCloseable at the end of the try block.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Manually closing streams and connections in finally is verbose and easy to get wrong, leaking resources.

3. Advantages

  • No resource leaks.
  • Less code than try-finally.
  • Keeps the original exception and adds suppressed ones.

4. Disadvantages

  • Resources must implement AutoCloseable.
  • Using the resource after the block fails.
  • close() exceptions can be surprising.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used with files, JDBC and HTTP.
  • Interview topic.
  • Best practice for cleanup.

6. Basic Concepts

What is try-with-resources?

try-with-resources (Java 7+) is a special form of try that automatically closes any resource declared in its parentheses once the block finishes - whether it finishes normally or by throwing an exception.

  • A "resource" here means any object implementing AutoCloseable - files, database connections, sockets, streams, etc.
  • It removes the need to manually write a finally block that calls close().
  • Syntax: try (Resource r = new Resource()) { ... }

The AutoCloseable Interface

AutoCloseable declares a single method: void close() throws Exception;.

  • Any class implementing it can be used inside try (...).
  • Many familiar JDK classes already implement it: FileReader, BufferedReader, Connection (JDBC), Scanner, etc.
  • You can make your own classes work with try-with-resources by implementing it yourself.

The Old Way — Manual try/finally

Before Java 7, closing a resource safely meant a verbose, easy-to-get-wrong try/finally:

Fresher Notes

  • Automatic closing: try (var in = new FileInputStream("a.txt")) { ... } closes in for you.
  • Required type: resources must implement AutoCloseable (or Closeable).
  • No finally needed for closing; it works even if an exception is thrown.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Several resources are separated by semicolons and closed in reverse order of creation.
  • Java 9: you can use an existing effectively final variable: try (res) { ... }.
  • Suppressed exceptions: an exception from close() is added to the primary exception.

8. Advanced Concepts

Multiple Resources — Closed in Reverse Declaration Order

When several resources are declared in the same try (...), separated by semicolons, Java closes them in the opposite order they were opened - the last one opened is the first one closed, mirroring how nested try/finally blocks would behave.

Java 9+ — Effectively-Final Variable Enhancement

Originally, a resource had to be declared inside the try (...) parentheses. Since Java 9, you can instead reference an existing effectively final variable (one never reassigned after initialization) without redeclaring it - useful when the resource was created earlier or is reused.

Suppressed Exceptions — When Both the Body AND close() Throw

If an exception is thrown inside the try body and close() also throws while cleaning up, Java does NOT lose either one:

  • The exception from the try body is treated as the primary exception - it's the one that actually propagates.
  • The exception thrown by close() is attached to the primary one as a suppressed exception, retrievable via getSuppressed().

This is a major improvement over manual try/finally, where an exception thrown in finally used to completely replace (and hide) the original exception from the try body.

Senior Notes

  • Custom resources: implement AutoCloseable and make close() idempotent (safe to call twice).
  • Good uses: streams, connections, statements, lock wrappers and temporary state.
  • Null resource: it is skipped, so there is no NullPointerException on close.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Design tips for your own resources:

  • Implement AutoCloseable and document whether close() can throw.
  • Make close() idempotent and release in reverse order of acquisition.
  • Use Cleaner only as a safety net, never as the main way to release.

Common patterns: scoped transactions (commit on success, rollback on failure), lock wrappers, temporary directories, tracing spans and test fixtures. Scanner and ExecutorService (Java 19+) are also AutoCloseable.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The compiler expands try (R r = init) { body } into plain try/catch code.

  • An exception from the body is saved as the primary exception.
  • r.close() then runs in a nested try. A close failure is added with addSuppressed and does not replace the primary.
  • If a later resource fails to open, the ones already opened are closed in reverse order.
  • The resource variable is implicitly final.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Closing manually inside the try, which causes a double close.
  • Swallowing exceptions inside close().
  • Returning a resource from the try block. It is already closed on exit.
  • Forgetting that Files.lines and Files.walk must be closed.
  • Using the resource after the block.

Closing a wrapper also closes the stream inside it. A leak shows up as "too many open files".

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

try-with-resources costs no more than a correct try-finally.

  • Close (or flush) a wrapper before the stream it wraps. Closing the wrapper does this for you.
  • Create the wrapper in the try header so one close handles the whole chain.
  • A pooled connection is returned to the pool on close(). The socket stays open.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world uses: JDBC code, file processing, HTTP responses, and test resources (temporary files and servers).

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Suppressed exceptions.

Worked Example 2

Existing variable (Java 9).

Practice Exercise 1

Files and JDBC.

Practice Exercise 2

Custom resource and order.

11. Quick Revision

  • Declare resources in the try header.
  • Closed in reverse order.
  • close exceptions become suppressed.
  • Java 9 accepts existing variables.
  • Make close() idempotent.

interviewQA: What interface must a resource implement to be used in try-with-resources?
AutoCloseable (or its stricter sub-interface Closeable, used by java.io classes)
In what order are multiple resources closed?
Reverse of declaration order - the last resource opened is the first one closed
What happens if the try body AND close() both throw?
The try body's exception is primary and propagates; close()'s exception is attached to it as a "suppressed" exception, retrievable via getSuppressed()
How is this better than manual try/finally?
Old-style finally silently discarded the original exception if finally also threw; try-with-resources preserves both via suppression
Do you still need a finally block with try-with-resources?
Only for cleanup logic unrelated to closing the declared resources - the resource's close() is already guaranteed automatically
What changed in Java 9 for try-with-resources?
You can pass an existing effectively-final variable directly in the try(...) parentheses instead of always declaring a new one

topics.name: Varargs in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Varargs let a method accept zero or more arguments of one type, written as Type...
  • Name and seen as an array inside the method.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Some methods naturally take a variable number of values, such as sum or format, without writing many overloads.

3. Advantages

  • Flexible calls.
  • Cleaner APIs (printf, Arrays.asList).
  • Fewer overloads.

4. Disadvantages

  • Allocates an array on each call.
  • Ambiguity with overloads.
  • Generic varargs cause heap pollution warnings.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used throughout the JDK.
  • Interview topic on overload rules.
  • Helps write friendly APIs.

6. Basic Concepts

What are Varargs?

Varargs (variable-length arguments), written as Type... name, let a method accept zero, one, or many arguments of the same type without the caller having to build an array by hand.

  • Inside the method body, the varargs parameter behaves exactly like an array - int... nums is usable as int[] nums.
  • Introduced in Java 5, mainly to simplify APIs like String.format(...) and Arrays.asList(...).

Calling a Varargs Method

A varargs method can be called with any number of matching arguments - including none - or with an actual array.

Varargs Must Be the LAST Parameter

A method can mix normal parameters with a varargs parameter, but the varargs parameter must always come last, and only one varargs parameter is allowed per method - the compiler needs to know unambiguously where the fixed parameters end and the variable-length part begins.

Fresher Notes

  • Varargs let a method accept zero or more arguments of one type: static int sum(int... nums).
  • Array inside: the parameter is an array, so use nums.length and nums[0].
  • Position: it must be the last parameter, and a method can have only one.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Ways to call: pass separate values, an array, or nothing: sum(), sum(1, 2, 3), sum(arr).
  • Overloading: varargs is tried last. Exact and boxed matches win first.
  • JDK APIs: String.format, Arrays.asList, List.of and printf use varargs.

8. Advanced Concepts

Varargs is Just Syntactic Sugar for an Array

At the bytecode level, Type... name compiles down to exactly Type[] name - the compiler automatically wraps the passed arguments into an array before the call. This is why the parameter can be used as an array inside the method, and why passing an actual array directly also works (no double-wrapping happens).

void sum(int... nums)      compiles to      void sum(int[] nums)

sum(1, 2, 3)   -->   compiler builds new int[]{1, 2, 3}, then calls sum(that array)
sum(existingArray)  -->  the array is passed directly, no extra wrapping

Overload Resolution Trap — Specific Arity Wins Over Varargs

When a call matches both a fixed-arity overload and a varargs overload, Java always prefers the more specific, fixed-arity version. Varargs is deliberately treated as the "last resort" match.

Heap Pollution with Generic Varargs — @SafeVarargs

Combining varargs with generics (e.g. List<T>... lists) is legal but risky. Arrays keep their type at runtime, but generics are erased. So the compiler can only create a raw array underneath. A wrong type can then slip in with no ClassCastException at that point. This problem is called heap pollution.

  • The compiler warns: "unchecked generic array creation".
  • @SafeVarargs (allowed on static, final and private methods, and constructors) tells the compiler "trust me, this method does nothing unsafe with the varargs array". It suppresses the warning.
  • Use it only if the method never stores into the array or leaks it. It is a promise, not a fix.

Real-World Varargs — printf / String.format

The most familiar varargs API in the JDK is String.format(String pattern, Object... args). System.out.printf calls it, so you can pass any number of values.

Senior Notes

  • Cost: each call allocates an array, so avoid varargs in hot paths. The JDK adds fixed-arity overloads such as List.of(e1, e2).
  • Heap pollution: generic varargs give compiler warnings. @SafeVarargs on final, static or private methods says the method is safe.
  • null: f(null) passes a null array, while f((Object) null) passes one null element. This surprises many people.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Generic varargs create a generic array (T[]), which is unsafe; the compiler warns about possible heap pollution. @SafeVarargs (on static, final, private methods and constructors) suppresses it when the method only reads the array. JDK examples: Arrays.asList, List.of (fixed-arity overloads up to 10 then varargs), EnumSet.of, Stream.of.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Varargs is compile-time sugar: m(String... a) compiles to m(String[] a) with the ACC_VARARGS flag, and calls m("x", "y") become m(new String[]{"x", "y"}). Overload resolution runs in three phases: strict (no boxing, no varargs), loose (boxing), then varargs. A call that matches in an earlier phase never considers varargs methods.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: passing a primitive array to Object... (becomes one element), ambiguous overloads, mutating the varargs array that the caller passed (it is the caller's array), forgetting the null case, using varargs where a List parameter is clearer, and boxing surprises with Arrays.asList(int[]).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Every varargs call allocates an array and the JIT may not remove it if it escapes. In hot code add fixed-arity overloads for common counts (as the JDK does) or pass a pre-built array.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: logging (log.info("user {} did {}", user, action)) uses varargs and defers formatting until the level is enabled; builder helpers and test utilities accept varargs for readability.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Passing null.

Worked Example 2

Generic varargs.

Practice Exercise 1

Varargs in use.

Practice Exercise 2

Overload priority.

11. Quick Revision

  • Must be the last parameter; only one per method.
  • Inside it is an array.
  • Varargs is the last overload considered.
  • Beware of null arguments.
  • @SafeVarargs for generic varargs.

interviewQA: What type is a varargs parameter treated as inside the method?
An array of that type - int... nums behaves exactly like int[] nums inside the method body
Where must a varargs parameter be positioned?
Last in the parameter list, and a method can have at most one varargs parameter
If both a fixed-arity and varargs overload match a call, which wins?
The fixed-arity (more specific) overload - varargs is only chosen when no fixed-arity overload matches
What is heap pollution in the context of varargs?
Combining generics with varargs creates an unchecked raw array underneath, which can let incompatible types be stored without an immediate ClassCastException
What does @SafeVarargs actually do?

It suppresses the "unchecked generic array creation" compiler warning - it is a developer promise, not a runtime safety guarantee, and only applies to static, final or private methods, or constructors
Can you pass zero arguments to a varargs method?
Yes - the method receives an array of length 0, not null

topics.name: Instance and Static Initializer Blocks

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Initializer blocks run code during initialization: instance blocks per object before the constructor body, and static blocks once at class loading.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Some setup does not fit a field initializer, such as filling a lookup table or shared constructor code.

3. Advantages

  • Run complex initialization.
  • Static block runs once.
  • Shared code across constructors.

4. Disadvantages

  • Hidden execution order.
  • Exceptions in static blocks make the class unusable.
  • Rarely the clearest option.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Appears in output-prediction questions.
  • Explains class loading and initialization.
  • Helps understand singletons.

6. Basic Concepts

What are Initializer Blocks?

Java has two kinds of code blocks inside a class body (not inside any method) that run automatically, without being called:

  • Instance initializer block: { ... } - runs every time an object is created, right before the constructor body.
  • Static initializer block: static { ... } - runs exactly once, when the class is first loaded by the JVM, before any object of it is created.

Both exist to run initialization logic that is more complex than a simple one-line field assignment.

Instance Initializer Block

An instance block runs for every object created, in textual order with the field initializers, and before the rest of the constructor body.

Static Initializer Block

A static block runs once, when the class is loaded - no matter how many objects are created afterward.

Fresher Notes

  • An instance initializer block { ... } runs every time an object is created, before the constructor body.
  • A static initializer block static { ... } runs once when the class is first loaded and initialized.
  • Use them for setup that does not fit a single field initializer.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Order for one class: static blocks and static fields (top to bottom, once), then per object: instance fields and blocks (top to bottom), then the constructor body.
  • With inheritance: parent static, child static, parent instance + constructor, child instance + constructor.
  • Constructor copy: the compiler copies instance blocks into each constructor that calls super(...) (not into one that calls this(...)).

8. Advanced Concepts

Full Execution Order — Single Class, Multiple Constructors

For a single class, the order is: static block (once, on class load) -> instance field initializers + instance blocks (textual order, every object) -> constructor body. Proven below with two different constructors:

Why Use an Instance Block? — Shared Logic Across Constructors

An instance initializer block is a way to share setup logic across every constructor without constructor chaining via this(...). It always runs regardless of which overloaded constructor the caller picks - useful when several constructors need the same baseline setup but otherwise differ.

Why Use a Static Block? — One-Time Setup

A static block is the natural place for setup that must happen exactly once per class - e.g. initializing a static resource, loading configuration, or populating a lookup table that is too complex for a single-expression field initializer.

Execution Order With Inheritance

When a subclass object is created, initialization always flows top-down through the static phase first (for the whole hierarchy), then top-down through the instance phase per object:

new Child()
  |
  1. Parent static block/fields   (once, on class load)
  2. Child static block/fields    (once, on class load)
  |
  3. Parent instance fields + instance block
  4. Parent constructor body
  5. Child instance fields + instance block
  6. Child constructor body

Note that all static initialization for the whole hierarchy completes before any instance initialization begins, because loading the Child class forces the JVM to first fully initialize the Parent class.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer constructors and static factory methods; initializer blocks are rare (anonymous classes, shared setup).
  • Failures: an exception in a static block becomes ExceptionInInitializerError, and later uses give NoClassDefFoundError.
  • Class initialization lock: avoid heavy work and circular dependencies in static init (deadlock risk).

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Uses: loading lookup tables, registering drivers (Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver") used to rely on this), singletons via the holder idiom, enum constants, static final map setup, and shared instance setup in anonymous classes. Alternatives: static factory methods that build the map, Map.of, constructors, or Supplier based lazy values.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Class initialization (<clinit>) is triggered on first use: new, static method call, static field access (except compile-time constants), subclass initialization, or Class.forName. The JVM guarantees it runs once, under a per-class lock, with other threads waiting. Instance blocks are copied by the compiler into each constructor that starts with super(...), after the super call and before the rest of the body, in textual order with field initializers.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: heavy or failing work in static blocks (the class becomes unusable: NoClassDefFoundError), static initialization cycles (A needs B while B needs A: one sees default values or deadlocks across threads), reading a static field before it is initialized due to textual order, and relying on initialization order in tests.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Class initialization is serialized, so slow static blocks delay every thread that needs the class (startup stalls). Keep them light, defer expensive work to lazy holders, and avoid I/O. GraalVM native image can run initializers at build time (--initialize-at-build-time).

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: JDBC drivers used to register themselves in a static block, and logging frameworks initialize in static fields. A common production bug is a failing static initializer hiding behind later NoClassDefFoundError messages: look for the first ExceptionInInitializerError in the logs.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Failing static block.

Worked Example 2

Double-brace smell.

Practice Exercise 1

Execution order.

Practice Exercise 2

Static block loading a table.

11. Quick Revision

  • Static block: once at class init.
  • Instance block: each new object.
  • Order: parent static, child static, parent instance + constructor, child instance + constructor.
  • Static init errors become ExceptionInInitializerError.
  • Prefer constructors.

interviewQA: How many times does a static block run?
Exactly once, when the class is first loaded by the JVM - regardless of how many objects are created
How many times does an instance block run?
Once per object created - every time, right before the constructor body
What's the full order for a single class?
Static block (once, class load) -> instance field initializers + instance blocks (every object, textual order) -> constructor body
What's the order with inheritance?
Parent static -> Child static -> Parent instance (fields/blocks) -> Parent constructor -> Child instance (fields/blocks) -> Child constructor
Why use an instance block instead of just putting code in every constructor?
It guarantees the logic runs for every constructor automatically, without needing this() chaining or duplicating code across overloads
What's a typical real use of a static block?
One-time setup that's too complex for a single field initializer expression - e.g. populating a static lookup Map, loading configuration

topics.name: Custom Exceptions in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A custom exception is your own exception class extending Exception or RuntimeException to represent a domain-specific error.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Generic exceptions say little.
  • Domain exceptions such as InsufficientFundsException describe what went wrong and let callers react precisely.

3. Advantages

  • Clear, meaningful errors.
  • Carry extra data.
  • Easy mapping to HTTP responses.

4. Disadvantages

  • Too many exception classes add noise.
  • Checked custom exceptions clutter code.
  • Must keep messages free of secrets.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Common in business code.
  • Interview topic.
  • Basis of API error handling.

6. Basic Concepts

Why Create a Custom Exception?

Java ships with generic exceptions like IllegalArgumentException or RuntimeException, but they do not show domain meaning.

  • A custom exception names the exact business failure. InsufficientFundsException says far more than RuntimeException("balance too low").
  • Callers can catch that failure type separately from every other error.
  • It can carry extra domain data (an error code, an account id) that a generic exception has no field for.

A custom exception is just a normal class that extends one of Java's existing exception classes.

Extending Exception (Checked) vs RuntimeException (Unchecked)

  • Extend Exception (checked) when a caller can recover and must be forced to handle it. The compiler requires a try/catch or a throws declaration.
  • Extend RuntimeException (unchecked) for a programming error or an unrecoverable business rule violation. No throws declaration is required.
  • Always call super(message) so getMessage() works. Add a super(message, cause) constructor too, so it can wrap another exception.

A Working Custom Exception in Action

Throwing and catching a custom checked exception looks like any built-in exception. The only difference is that the type name carries real meaning.

Fresher Notes

  • Custom exception: your own class, such as class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception (checked) or extends RuntimeException (unchecked).
  • Constructors: message, message + cause, and optionally fields (error code, data).
  • Throwing: throw new InsufficientFundsException("...").

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Naming: name it for the problem and end with Exception, for example OrderNotFoundException.
  • Context: add fields (ids, amounts) with getters, and put the key facts in the message.
  • Base exception: use one per module so callers can catch the whole family.

8. Advanced Concepts

Adding Extra Fields to a Custom Exception

A plain exception only carries a message. A custom exception can carry structured data, such as an error code. Callers read it directly instead of parsing the message text.

Exception Chaining - Preserving the Original Cause

When you catch a low-level exception (for example from JDBC or file I/O) and throw a higher-level one, do not discard the original. Pass it as the cause. The root-cause stack trace then stays available for debugging.

Best Practices for Custom Exceptions

  • Name it clearly and end it with "Exception": OrderNotFoundException, not OrderError.
  • Never swallow it silently. An empty catch block hides real failures.
  • Do not overuse checked exceptions. Forcing every caller to declare throws for something they cannot fix only adds boilerplate.
  • Keep the hierarchy shallow. One or two custom types per domain is usually enough.
  • Always provide a message. A bare super() is nearly useless when reading a stack trace at 2 AM.

Senior Notes

  • Checked vs unchecked: choose deliberately; most application errors are unchecked.
  • Sensitive data: keep it out of messages that reach clients or logs.
  • Central mapping: turn exceptions into HTTP status codes and error bodies in one place (@ControllerAdvice).

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Design an error model with these parts:

  • A small, documented hierarchy: AppException with NotFound, Conflict and Validation children.
  • Stable error codes (strings or enums) for clients, and one HTTP status per type.
  • Structured details (problem+json) and correlation ids in logs.
  • Message text kept separate from codes, so it can be localized.
  • Tests that assert on type and code, not on message text.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

A custom exception inherits everything from Throwable:

  • The constructor captures the stack trace (fillInStackTrace).
  • Causes are chained with getCause, and suppressed exceptions are supported.
  • Overload the constructors (message, cause, message + cause) and consider a serialVersionUID.
  • Fields should be serializable or transient, because exceptions may be serialized (RMI, distributed caches).

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • One giant generic exception for everything, or exceptions used as return codes.
  • Leaking internal details (SQL, file paths) to clients.
  • Forgetting the cause when wrapping.
  • Deep hierarchies that nobody catches by type, or checked exceptions that force every caller to wrap.
  • Messages with no ids, which are hard to search in logs. Include identifiers and keep user-facing text separate.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Capturing the stack trace is the main cost of creating an exception. In performance-critical parsers that use exceptions for rare, expected control flow, you can create stackless exceptions with super(msg, null, false, false). Everywhere else, keep the trace. Avoid very deep cause chains in logs.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: payment exceptions carry a retryable flag, so the retry policy knows what to retry.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Mapping to HTTP.

Worked Example 2

Serialization warning.

Practice Exercise 1

Domain exception with context.

Practice Exercise 2

Hierarchy and cause.

11. Quick Revision

  • Extend RuntimeException for unchecked.
  • Provide message and cause constructors.
  • Name ends with Exception.
  • Add context fields.
  • Map centrally to responses.

interviewQA: Why create a custom exception instead of using RuntimeException directly?
It gives the failure a meaningful, catchable type name and lets it carry domain-specific data
When should a custom exception extend Exception vs RuntimeException?
Exception (checked) when callers must handle/declare a recoverable failure; RuntimeException (unchecked) for programmer errors or unrecoverable states
How do you preserve the original exception when wrapping it?
Pass it as the cause via super(message, cause); retrieve it later with getCause()
What's a common anti-pattern with custom exceptions?
Catching them and doing nothing (silently swallowing), or overusing checked exceptions everywhere
Can a custom exception carry extra fields beyond a message?
Yes - add private final fields (like an error code) with getters, set via the constructor

topics.name: Marker Interfaces in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A marker interface has no methods and only tags a class with a capability, such as Serializable or Cloneable.

2. Need of This Topic

  • The JVM or libraries need to know whether a class supports a feature, without requiring methods.

3. Advantages

  • Simple tagging mechanism.
  • Usable as a type at compile time.
  • Checked with instanceof.

4. Disadvantages

  • No data or behavior.
  • Annotations are more flexible.
  • Inherited markers can tag subclasses unintentionally.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Interview topic.
  • Explains Serializable and Cloneable.
  • Compares with annotations.

6. Basic Concepts

What Is a Marker Interface?

A marker interface (also called a "tag interface") is an interface with no methods and no fields. It exists only so a class can be tagged with a type.

  • Implementing it adds no behavior directly.
  • Other code checks instanceof SomeMarker and changes behavior based on the tag.
  • It attaches metadata to a class through the type system, which was the way before annotations existed.

Classic Built-in Marker Interfaces

  • java.io.Serializable - the class can be converted to a byte stream.
  • Cloneable - the class allows Object.clone().
  • java.rmi.Remote - the class can be called across a network via RMI.

None of these declare any methods. The JVM and standard library check for them with instanceof before doing the operation.

How the JVM Actually Uses the Tag

The classic example is serialization. ObjectOutputStream.writeObject() checks instanceof Serializable before it writes an object.

Fresher Notes

  • No methods: a marker interface only tags a class with a capability, such as Serializable, Cloneable or RandomAccess.
  • Checking the tag: code uses instanceof, for example if (obj instanceof Serializable).
  • Effect: the JVM or a library enables special behavior for tagged classes.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Built-in meanings: Serializable allows object serialization; Cloneable allows Object.clone(); RandomAccess tells algorithms that indexed access is fast.
  • Custom markers: you can write your own, e.g. interface Auditable {}.
  • Annotations are the modern alternative to marker interfaces.

8. Advanced Concepts

Writing Your Own Marker Interface

You can define a marker interface for your own checks, for example to tag entities that belong in an audit log.

Marker Interfaces vs Annotations - Which to Use Today

Since Java 5, annotations (see Annotations in Java) can do the same "tag a type" job. Modern code prefers them for new designs.

AspectMarker InterfaceAnnotation
Can carry metadata/valuesNo - it's just a typeYes - @Retention, custom fields like @Author(name="...")
Checkable viainstanceof (compile + runtime type check)Reflection (isAnnotationPresent, getAnnotation)
Enforced by the compilerYes - it's a real type in the class hierarchyNo - purely metadata unless a tool/framework enforces it
Can be applied toOnly classes (via implements)Classes, methods, fields, parameters, etc.
Typical modern usageLegacy APIs (Serializable, Cloneable) kept for compatibilityPreferred for new "tag this" designs (Spring's @Component, JPA's @Entity)

Marker interfaces remain in the JDK because changing Serializable or Cloneable now would break a huge amount of existing code. For new code, an annotation is usually the more flexible choice.

Senior Notes

  • Type advantage: a marker interface defines a type, so it works in method signatures and compile-time checks; annotations carry data and apply to methods and fields.
  • Sealed interfaces with a permits clause now express closed families better than markers.
  • Choosing: use annotations for framework metadata; use a marker interface when a method should accept only tagged classes.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Alternatives: annotations (data and tooling, but not types), sealed interfaces (closed families with exhaustive switches), capability interfaces with methods, and generic bounds (<T extends Auditable>). A marker works well with generics to restrict APIs at compile time; an annotation is better for framework scanning and for tagging methods and fields.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

A marker interface works through type checks: instanceof, Class.isAssignableFrom or generic bounds. The JDK uses them inside the runtime: ObjectOutputStream checks Serializable, Object.clone checks Cloneable (an instance check performed natively), Collections.shuffle uses RandomAccess to choose an algorithm, and EventListener tags listener types.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: marker interfaces on classes where an annotation fits better, inherited markers that tag subclasses unintentionally (a subclass of a Serializable class is Serializable), expecting markers to enforce behavior, and creating empty interfaces instead of real abstractions. The marker gives a promise, not a check of the implementation.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Marker checks are cheap instanceof tests. Reflection scans for annotations cost startup time; precompute type sets at startup or at build time (annotation processors, Spring AOT).

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: Serializable marks session and cache classes, a custom @Transactional annotation tags methods, and a PersonalData marker interface lets a logging utility mask any tagged type.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

RandomAccess.

Worked Example 2

Annotation alternative.

Practice Exercise 1

Custom marker and check.

Practice Exercise 2

Compile-time safety.

11. Quick Revision

  • No methods.
  • Examples: Serializable, Cloneable, RandomAccess.
  • Check with instanceof.
  • Annotations are the modern alternative.
  • Use a marker when you need a compile-time type.

interviewQA: What is a marker interface?
An interface with no methods or fields, used purely to tag a class with a type that other code can check via instanceof
Name two built-in marker interfaces.
Serializable and Cloneable (also Remote for RMI)
How does ObjectOutputStream use Serializable?
It checks instanceof Serializable before writing an object, throwing NotSerializableException if the check fails
Why are annotations often preferred over marker interfaces today?
Annotations can carry metadata/values, apply to more than just classes, and don't force implementing a type just to be "tagged"
Does implementing Cloneable give you a working clone() method?
No - it only enables Object.clone() to succeed without throwing CloneNotSupportedException; you still need to override clone() yourself

topics.name: The Object Class in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • The Object class is the root of all Java classes and provides toString, equals, hashCode, getClass, clone, wait and notify.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Every object needs basic behavior such as printing, comparing and locking.
  • Object supplies defaults for all.

3. Advantages

  • Common behavior for all classes.
  • Enables generic code.
  • Monitor support for synchronization.

4. Disadvantages

  • Default equals and toString are rarely useful.
  • finalize is deprecated.
  • Easy to misuse equals and hashCode.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Always asked in interviews.
  • Basis of collections and threading.
  • Helps write correct classes.

6. Basic Concepts

Object - the Root of Every Java Class

Every class you write - even one with no extends clause - implicitly extends java.lang.Object.

  • This is called a single-rooted class hierarchy: every object, of every type, is-a Object.
  • Because of this, every object automatically inherits a small set of methods defined on Object, whether you write them or not.
  • That's why a method like list.add(anything) can accept literally any object - Object is the universal type.

toString() - the Default Text Representation

The default Object.toString() returns fully.qualified.ClassName@hexHashCode. Overriding it is one of the most common things every class does.

getClass() - Runtime Type Information

getClass() returns the object's actual runtime Class<?> - and unlike toString() or equals(), it cannot be overridden (it's declared final in Object).

Fresher Notes

  • Root class: java.lang.Object is the root of every class. Key methods: toString(), equals(Object), hashCode(), getClass(), clone(), wait/notify/notifyAll.
  • Default toString: toString prints class name and hash (Student@1b6d3586); override it for readable output.
  • Default equals: equals compares references.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Override for value behavior: override toString for logging and debugging, and equals with hashCode for value equality.
  • Runtime class: getClass() returns the run-time class (obj.getClass().getName()).
  • Cleanup: finalize() is deprecated for removal; use try-with-resources or Cleaner.

8. Advanced Concepts

equals() and hashCode() - Just a Pointer Here

Object also declares equals(Object) (default: reference equality, ==) and hashCode() (default: an identity-based hash). Overriding these correctly - and together - is a big enough topic to have its own dedicated page: see equals() and hashCode() Contract for the full contract, the classic HashMap-breaking bug, and how to fix it.

clone() - Just a Pointer Here Too

Object.clone() performs a protected, low-level field-by-field copy, but it only works if the class implements the Cloneable marker interface - otherwise it throws CloneNotSupportedException. The shallow-vs-deep-copy nuance and why many teams avoid clone() entirely are covered in Object Cloning.

finalize() - Deprecated Since Java 9

Object.finalize() used to run just before an object was garbage collected, intended as a last-chance cleanup hook. It is deprecated since Java 9 and scheduled for eventual removal, because:

  • There's no guarantee when (or even if) it will run - the garbage collector decides, not your code.
  • A slow or throwing finalize() can silently degrade GC performance for the whole application.
  • It made resource leaks (unclosed files, sockets) intermittent and very hard to reproduce.

The modern replacements are try-with-resources (deterministic, immediate cleanup via AutoCloseable) and, for genuinely GC-triggered cleanup, java.lang.ref.Cleaner.

wait() / notify() / notifyAll() - Just a Pointer Here

Every object also inherits wait(), notify(), and notifyAll() because Java's built-in thread coordination is implemented on every object's own monitor. Calling any of these without holding the object's monitor (i.e. outside a synchronized block on that object) throws IllegalMonitorStateException. The full mechanics belong to multithreading - see the Synchronization in Java and Multithreading in Java topics for the complete picture.

All Object Methods at a Glance

MethodPurposeOverridable?
toString()Text representationYes - very commonly overridden
equals(Object)Logical equality checkYes - must be paired with hashCode()
hashCode()Integer hash for hash-based collectionsYes - must stay consistent with equals()
getClass()Runtime type infoNo - declared final
clone()Field-by-field copyYes, but requires implementing Cloneable
finalize()Pre-GC cleanup hookDeprecated since Java 9 - avoid
wait()/notify()/notifyAll()Thread coordination via the object's monitorNo - declared final

Senior Notes

  • Monitor methods: wait, notify and notifyAll work on an object monitor and must be called while holding its lock.
  • getClass vs instanceof: in equals, getClass() requires the exact class, while instanceof accepts subclasses.
  • Arrays and lambdas: Object methods are available on them too; Objects (plural) is the utility class.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants
