Best practice implementations: toString includes the identity-defining fields (never secrets), equals/hashCode use the same fields, no clone (use copy constructors), no finalize (use AutoCloseable and Cleaner). Records and Lombok generate the trio. getClass() is final and returns the runtime class; Class objects support reflection and generics via Class<? extends X>.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Every object has a header (mark word: identity hash, GC age, lock state; class pointer), so every class inherits Object methods. hashCode default is an identity hash generated lazily and stored in the header. toString default uses getClass().getName() + "@" + Integer.toHexString(hashCode()). wait/notify use the object monitor; calling them without owning it throws IllegalMonitorStateException. finalize is deprecated for removal.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: toString that exposes secrets or triggers lazy loading and recursion (parent and child toString calling each other), equals using getClass in frameworks with proxies (Hibernate proxies are subclasses), hashCode based on mutable state, calling wait outside synchronized, using finalize, and relying on identity hash codes for ordering.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Identity hash codes and monitors are stored in the header and cost memory only when used. Avoid synchronizing on objects you do not own. Object methods are intrinsics the JIT optimizes; the cost of equals/hashCode is the cost of your fields.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: debugging with a useful toString, and using Objects helpers to write short null-safe methods.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Objects utility.

Worked Example 2

wait needs the lock.

Practice Exercise 1

toString, equals and getClass.

Practice Exercise 2

Default toString.

11. Quick Revision

  • Every class extends Object.
  • Override toString, equals, hashCode.
  • getClass returns the runtime class.
  • wait/notify need the monitor.
  • Avoid finalize.

interviewQA: Why does every Java class implicitly extend Object?
Java uses a single-rooted class hierarchy, so every type shares a common base with a baseline set of behaviors
Can getClass() be overridden?
No - it's declared final in Object
Why is finalize() deprecated?
Its execution timing is unpredictable and it can silently hurt GC performance; try-with-resources/Cleaner replace it
What happens if you call wait() outside a synchronized block?
IllegalMonitorStateException - you must hold the object's monitor first
What's the default toString() output format?
fully.qualified.ClassName@hexHashCode

topics.name: String Formatting in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • String formatting builds text from templates with String.format, printf and formatted using specifiers like %s, %d and %.2f.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Reports, logs and user messages need aligned, localized and readable output.

3. Advantages

  • Readable templates.
  • Control width, precision, padding.
  • Locale-aware numbers and dates.

4. Disadvantages

  • Specifier mismatches fail at run time.
  • Slower than simple concatenation.
  • Injection risk if user text is used as the format.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used for logs and reports.
  • Interview topic.
  • Needed for money and date output.

6. Basic Concepts

Three Ways to Build a Display String

  • Concatenation ("x = " + x) - simplest, but awkward once you need padding, decimal precision, or many values.
  • String.valueOf(x) - converts a single value to text; still needs manual concatenation for anything more.
  • String.format(...) / System.out.printf(...) - a format string with placeholders, the most readable option once more than one or two values are involved.

Core Format Specifiers

  • %d - integer
  • %f - floating point (default 6 decimal places)
  • %.2f - floating point rounded to 2 decimal places
  • %s - any object (calls its toString())
  • %x - integer in hexadecimal
  • %n - platform-correct newline (prefer this over a literal \n)

Width, Alignment, and Thousands Separators

  • %10s - right-justify in a 10-character field.
  • %-10s - left-justify in a 10-character field (the - flips the alignment).
  • %,d - insert thousands separators automatically.

Fresher Notes

  • Template: String.format and printf build text from a template: String.format("%s is %d years", name, age).
  • Specifiers: %s string, %d integer, %f float, %n newline, %x hex, %b boolean, %% percent sign.
  • Width and precision: %8.2f, %-10s, %05d, %,d.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • formatted(): Java 15+ lets you write "%s is %d".formatted(name, age).
  • Argument index: %2$s %1$s reorders arguments.
  • Locale: pass a Locale for locale-sensitive output: String.format(Locale.US, "%,.2f", 1234.5).

8. Advanced Concepts

Locale-Aware Formatting with DecimalFormat / NumberFormat

String.format uses the JVM's default locale unless told otherwise, which can silently produce the wrong decimal/grouping symbol for a different region. NumberFormat/DecimalFormat give explicit control over currency and locale-specific formatting.

Common Formatting Bugs

  • Using \n instead of %n inside String.format/printf - \n always emits a Unix-style newline, which can look wrong in some Windows tools; %n emits the platform's actual line separator.
  • Too few arguments - passing fewer arguments than placeholders throws MissingFormatArgumentException at run time, not compile time, because the compiler does not check format strings.
  • Forgetting .2f-style precision on money values - a raw %f prints 6 decimal places by default, not 2.

Positional Arguments - Reusing a Value

You can reference the same argument more than once using an explicit index (%1$s) instead of repeating it in the argument list.

Senior Notes

  • Locale-aware tools: use NumberFormat, DecimalFormat and DateTimeFormatter for numbers, currency and dates.
  • Injection: do not build SQL or HTML with String.format; use prepared statements and escaping.
  • Type mismatch: a wrong type throws IllegalFormatException at run time (%d with a string).

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools you can pick from:

  • NumberFormat: currency, percent and compact numbers (getCompactNumberInstance).
  • DecimalFormat: custom patterns such as #,##0.00.
  • DateTimeFormatter: thread-safe, with ofPattern and ofLocalizedDate.
  • MessageFormat and ChoiceFormat: messages and plurals.
  • Text blocks with formatted, and String.join / StringJoiner for lists.
  • Logging frameworks use {} placeholders.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Formatter parses %[argument_index$][flags][width][.precision]conversion. Flags: - left align, 0 zero pad, , grouping, + sign, ( negatives in parentheses, # alternate. Conversions: s S d f e g x o c b n %, and date/time t. Formatting uses the default locale unless a Locale is passed. %f rounds HALF_UP.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Forgetting the Locale (you may get decimal commas on some machines).
  • Sharing SimpleDateFormat across threads (not thread-safe; use DateTimeFormatter).
  • Using %.2f on a double for money (it hides rounding errors; use BigDecimal).
  • Specifiers that do not match the arguments, or %d with a double (run-time exceptions).
  • Concatenating user input into the format string (format string injection).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

String.format parses the pattern on every call, so it is slower than StringBuilder or concatenation. In hot paths, build the text with StringBuilder.append. Keep thread-safe formatters (such as DateTimeFormatter) in constants. In logs, use placeholders so nothing is formatted when the level is off.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Receipts, reports and CSV exports use explicit locales, widths and rounding rules. Invoices use BigDecimal with NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Type mismatch.

Worked Example 2

Table output.

Practice Exercise 1

Formatting numbers and text.

Practice Exercise 2

Locale-aware money and dates.

11. Quick Revision

  • %s string, %d int, %f float, %n newline.
  • %.2f for two decimals.
  • Pass a Locale for consistency.
  • formatted() since Java 15.
  • Never use it to build SQL.

interviewQA: Difference between %n and \n in printf/String.format?
%n emits the platform-correct line separator; \n always emits a Unix-style newline regardless of OS
How do you round a double to 2 decimal places in a formatted string?
Use %.2f as the specifier
What happens if a format string has more placeholders than arguments?
MissingFormatArgumentException is thrown at runtime - format strings aren't compile-time checked
How do you left-justify a string in a fixed-width field?
Add a - flag before the width, e.g. %-10s
When would you use DecimalFormat/NumberFormat over String.format?
When you need explicit locale-aware or currency formatting instead of the JVM's default locale

topics.name: Immutable Classes in Java

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • An immutable class creates objects whose state never changes after construction, such as String, Integer and records.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Shared mutable state causes bugs, especially with threads.
  • Immutable objects are always safe to share.

3. Advantages

  • Thread-safe without locks.
  • Safe as map keys and cache values.
  • Simple to reason about.

4. Disadvantages

  • Changes need new objects.
  • More allocations for frequent updates.
  • Requires defensive copies.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Core of safe concurrent design.
  • Interview topic.
  • Records make it easy.

6. Basic Concepts

What Does "Immutable" Mean?

An immutable object is one whose observable state can never change after it is constructed. No method can modify its fields once new has finished running.

  • String is the most familiar example. Every "modifying" method like concat() returns a brand-new String.
  • Immutability is not automatic. A class has to be deliberately designed that way.

Why Immutability Matters

  • Thread-safe by construction: state never changes, so many threads can read the same object with no synchronization.
  • Safe as a HashMap/HashSet key: its hashCode() never changes after insertion, so it cannot get lost in the wrong bucket.
  • Safe to share and cache: no code can corrupt state that another part of the program relies on.
  • Easier to reason about: the value is always what it was when constructed.

The Recipe for a Truly Immutable Class

  1. Declare the class final (a subclass cannot add mutable behavior or override a getter).
  2. Make every field private final.
  3. Provide no setters at all.
  4. Initialize every field fully inside the constructor.
  5. If a field is a mutable type (like a List or Date), defensively copy it when it comes IN through the constructor and when it goes OUT through a getter.

Fresher Notes

  • Immutable object: cannot change after creation (String, Integer, LocalDate).
  • Recipe: declare the class final, make all fields private final, no setters, set everything in the constructor.
  • Records give immutable data carriers with little code.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Defensive copies: copy mutable inputs in the constructor and mutable outputs in getters (or return unmodifiable views).
  • Thread-safe: immutable objects can be shared and cached, and make good map keys.
  • Withers: changes create new objects, for example date.plusDays(1).

8. Advanced Concepts

The Defensive-Copy Bug - and the Fix

Marking a field final only stops the reference from being reassigned. It does not stop the object it points to from being mutated. If a constructor just stores the caller's List, the caller can still change it from outside.

The Fix - Defensive Copy on the Way In AND Out

Copy the mutable data in the constructor, so later changes to the caller's list cannot reach it. Copy it again in the getter, so a caller who changes the returned list cannot reach the internal state.

Modern Alternatives That Are Immutable by Default

  • java.time (LocalDate, LocalDateTime, Duration): every "modifying" method such as plusDays() returns a new instance, like String.
  • Records (Java 16+): record Point(int x, int y) {} generates private final fields, a canonical constructor, accessors, and equals()/hashCode()/toString(). A mutable component (like a List) still needs a defensive copy in a compact constructor.

Senior Notes

  • Cost: more allocations for frequent changes. Reduce it with builders or persistent data structures.
  • Shallow immutability is not enough: all reachable state must be immutable, or hidden behind copies.
  • Collections: List.of, List.copyOf, and Collections.unmodifiableList (a view, not a copy).

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Techniques: records, builders for many fields (toBuilder), withers, List.copyOf/Map.copyOf, persistent collections (Vavr, Eclipse), Collections.unmodifiable* views over private copies, immutable java.time types, BigDecimal, Optional, and enums. Lazily computed fields (the hash code in String) are allowed when every thread computes the same value. Records are shallowly immutable: copy collection components in the compact constructor.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Immutability is safe publication by construction: the Java Memory Model guarantees that final fields assigned in the constructor are visible to every thread that obtains the reference (the freeze action), even through a data race, provided this does not escape the constructor. All fields must be final (or effectively never changed), the class must not be extendable (or all methods final), and no mutable state may be exposed.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: non-final class with final fields (a subclass can add mutable state), returning internal arrays or collections, storing caller-supplied mutable objects without copying, letting this escape in the constructor, Date or arrays as fields, setters added later for convenience, and assuming Collections.unmodifiableList is a copy. Review every getter and constructor argument.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Trade-offs: immutability trades allocation for safety; the young-generation GC makes short-lived small objects cheap. For large structures use structural sharing (persistent trees) so updates copy only the path. Immutable keys can cache hash codes. Avoid defensive copies on every call by returning unmodifiable views over private immutable data.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: value objects (Money, Email, Address), configuration snapshots (swap a new immutable config atomically with AtomicReference), cache keys, events, DTOs and messages passed between threads or services.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

View vs copy.

Worked Example 2

Shallow immutability trap.

Practice Exercise 1

Immutable class with defensive copies.

Practice Exercise 2

Record version.

11. Quick Revision

  • final class, private final fields, no setters.
  • Copy mutable inputs and outputs.
  • List.copyOf makes immutable copies.
  • unmodifiableList is only a view.
  • Records are shallowly immutable.

interviewQA: What are the 5 steps to make a class truly immutable?
final class, private final fields, no setters, full initialization in the constructor, defensive copies of mutable fields in and out
Why is thread-safety a benefit of immutability?
Since state can never change after construction, concurrent reads from multiple threads need no synchronization at all
Does marking a field final make it immutable?
Only the reference is fixed - if the field points to a mutable object (like a List), that object's contents can still change unless defensively copied
Why declare the class itself final?
To stop a subclass from overriding a getter/adding mutator methods that would break the immutability guarantee
Are Java records immutable by default?
Yes for the record's own fields, but a mutable component (like a List) still needs a defensive copy in a compact constructor

topics.name: Multi-catch Block and the try-finally Return Trap

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Multi-catch handles several exception types in one block, and the try-finally return trap shows how return and exceptions in finally override earlier results.

2. Need of This Topic

  • These details decide program output and are common sources of subtle bugs and interview traps.

3. Advantages

  • Multi-catch removes duplicate handlers.
  • finally guarantees cleanup.
  • Precise rethrow keeps type information.

4. Disadvantages

  • return or throw in finally hides exceptions.
  • Multi-catch types cannot be related.
  • Easy to misjudge the final value.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Frequent output-prediction questions.
  • Prevents hidden bugs.
  • Reinforces exception flow.

6. Basic Concepts

Multi-catch (Java 7+)

Before Java 7, handling two unrelated exception types the same way meant either duplicating the catch block, or catching the broad Exception type and losing precision. Multi-catch lets one block handle several exception types with the | operator.

The Subtype Rule for Multi-catch

The types in a multi-catch must NOT be related by inheritance - if one is already a subtype of another, catching both together is redundant and the compiler rejects it outright.

Fresher Notes

  • Multi-catch handles several exception types in one block: catch (IOException | SQLException e).
  • The types must not be related by inheritance (no subclass and superclass in the same multi-catch).
  • In a multi-catch the variable e is implicitly final.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • finally runs after try/catch, even when try or catch return or throw.
  • A return inside finally overrides a return value or a thrown exception: this is the try-finally return trap.
  • The return value is evaluated before finally runs; changing a primitive in finally does not change it.

8. Advanced Concepts

The try-finally Return Trap

A finally block always runs - but if it contains its OWN return statement, that return completely overrides whatever the try block was doing, including silently discarding any exception that was about to propagate. The caller never even sees the exception happened.

Why This Happens

When a finally block completes via its own return (or break/continue/another throw), that abrupt completion replaces whatever completion the try/catch was already in the middle of - even an in-flight exception. The JLS is explicit about this: a finally clause that completes abruptly for reason S causes the whole try statement to complete for reason S, and the original reason is discarded, not chained (unlike the suppressed-exception mechanism in try-with-resources).

Why This Is a Serious Anti-Pattern

  • It hides real failures - calling code has no idea an exception was ever thrown; it just gets a value back as if everything succeeded.
  • It is almost never intentional - most developers write a return in finally by accident.
  • Static analysis tools (like SonarQube, Error Prone) flag return/throw/break/continue inside finally as a bug pattern.
  • The fix is simple: use finally only for cleanup (closing resources, releasing locks) - never for producing the method's result.

Senior Notes

  • Never return, break or throw from finally: it swallows exceptions and hides bugs.
  • Prefer try-with-resources to finally for cleanup.
  • If finally itself throws, the new exception replaces the original one.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Rules:

  • Multi-catch alternatives cannot be related by subclassing.
  • Rethrowing the multi-catch variable keeps precise types, so the method can declare just those exceptions.
  • A catch can also throw a different exception with the original as its cause.
  • finally is skipped by System.exit, Runtime.halt, an infinite loop or a JVM crash.
  • Daemon threads may be stopped before finally runs when the JVM exits.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The compiler inlines the finally block's code at every exit point of try and catch (normal end, return, break, continue) and adds a catch-all handler that runs finally then rethrows. For return expr it evaluates expr, stores it in a temporary, runs finally, then returns the temporary — unless finally itself returns or throws. A multi-catch parameter is final and its static type is the closest common supertype of the alternatives, so you can call only common members.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Traps:

  • return, break, continue or throw inside finally swallow earlier exceptions, even OutOfMemoryError.
  • A finally that throws replaces the original (try-with-resources keeps it as suppressed).
  • Catching Exception and rethrowing it wrapped loses the precise type.
  • Assuming finally changes an already returned primitive.

Static analyzers flag these (javac -Xlint:finally).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Exception tables make try blocks free on the normal path. Duplicated finally code slightly enlarges bytecode but costs nothing at run time. The expensive part is creating exceptions (stack trace). Keep finally blocks short and non-throwing; put resource cleanup in try-with-resources.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: cleanup must not hide the real failure. Log or add suppressed exceptions in finally, and never let cleanup failures mask the business exception.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Exception replaced by finally.

Worked Example 2

Order of output.

Practice Exercise 1

The try-finally return trap.

Practice Exercise 2

Multi-catch.

11. Quick Revision

  • catch (A | B e): unrelated types, e is final.
  • finally runs after try or catch.
  • return in finally overrides.
  • The returned primitive is evaluated before finally.
  • Never throw from finally.

interviewQA: What does multi-catch let you do?
Handle multiple unrelated exception types in a single catch block using the | operator, avoiding duplicated handling code
Can you multi-catch a type and its own supertype together?
No - it's a compile-time error since the alternatives would be redundant (related by subclassing)
What happens if finally contains a return statement while try is throwing?
The finally's return wins completely - the exception is discarded and never reaches the caller
Does a return in finally override even a normal (non-exceptional) return from try?
Yes - any abrupt completion in finally (return/break/continue/throw) always overrides whatever try/catch was doing
What's the correct way to use finally?
Only for cleanup (closing resources, releasing locks) - never to produce or override the method's actual return value

topics.name: Functional Interface

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A functional interface has exactly one abstract method and can be implemented with a lambda or method reference, for example Function, Predicate, Consumer and Supplier.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Passing behavior as a value needs a type for it.
  • Functional interfaces provide that type.

3. Advantages

  • Enable lambdas and streams.
  • Rich built-ins in java.util.function.
  • Composable behavior.

4. Disadvantages

  • Checked exceptions do not fit.
  • Many similar interfaces to learn.
  • Boxing in generic versions.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Base of Java 8 style programming.
  • Interview topic.
  • Needed for streams and CompletableFuture.

6. Basic Concepts

Functional Interface

An Interface that contains exactly one abstract method such types of interface called Functional

Interface & the method is called Functional Method or Single Abstract Method.

Ex:

  1. Runnable → It contains only run() method
  2. Comparable → It contains only compareTo() method
  3. ActionListener → It contains only actionPerformed()
  4. Callable → It contains only call() method

It can have any number of default, static methods but can contain only one abstract method.

Key Points about Functional Interfaces:

  1. Single Abstract Method: Functional interfaces have only one abstract method. This is also

known as a Single Abstract Method (SAM) interface.

  1. Default and Static Methods: Functional interfaces can have any number of default or static

methods in addition to the single abstract method.

  1. @FunctionalInterface Annotation: While not mandatory, it's a good practice to use the

@FunctionalInterface annotation to ensure that the interface conforms to the rules of a functional

interface.

  1. Use with Lambda Expressions: Functional interfaces are often used with lambda expressions,

method references, or constructor references to provide clear and concise syntax for implementing

the single abstract method.

Explanation:

  • The Test interface is a functional interface with a single abstract method getStudentName.
  • The Main class implements the Test interface and provides an implementation for the

getStudentName method.

  • In the main method of the Main class, an instance of Main is created, and the getStudentName

method is called with the argument "Pankaj".

  • This results in printing the string "ashok" to the console.

By organizing your code into 2 separate classes and ensuring they are both in the same package, you

have a functional implementation of a Java program using a functional interface.

Fresher Notes

  • Functional interface: exactly one abstract method; a lambda or method reference can implement it.
  • Annotation: mark it with @FunctionalInterface so the compiler checks the rule.
  • Built-ins in java.util.function: Function<T,R>, Predicate<T>, Consumer<T>, Supplier<T>, BiFunction, UnaryOperator, BinaryOperator.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

java.util.function - The Full Catalog

Beyond Function, Predicate, Consumer and Supplier, Java 8 ships primitive-specialized variants (to avoid autoboxing overhead) and two-argument variants. Knowing these saves you from writing custom functional interfaces.

Mid-Level Notes

  • What does not count: default and static methods are not abstract, and methods of Object (like equals) are ignored.
  • Compose behavior: f.andThen(g), f.compose(g), p.and(q), p.negate(), Comparator.thenComparing.
  • Primitive specializations avoid boxing: IntPredicate, ToIntFunction, IntBinaryOperator.

8. Advanced Concepts

Target Typing - How a Lambda "Becomes" an Interface

A lambda expression has no type of its own written in the code. The compiler infers its type entirely from the context it is assigned to - this is called target typing. The target type must always be a functional interface (an interface with exactly one abstract method).

Runnable r  = () -> System.out.println("run");   // target type: Runnable
Comparator<String> c = (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b); // target type: Comparator<String>
Callable<Integer> k = () -> 42;                   // target type: Callable<Integer>

The SAME lambda body can implement DIFFERENT interfaces
depending only on the variable/parameter type it is assigned to.

Java's Built-in Functional Interfaces (java.util.function)

Instead of writing a new functional interface for every use case, Java 8 ships a standard set - memorize these, they appear constantly in Stream/Optional APIs and interviews:

InterfaceAbstract MethodTakesReturnsTypical Use
Function<T,R>R apply(T t)1 argvaluetransform / map
Predicate<T>boolean test(T t)1 argbooleanfilter / condition
Consumer<T>void accept(T t)1 argnoneforEach / side effect
Supplier<T>T get()no argsvaluelazy value / factory
BiFunction<T,U,R>R apply(T t, U u)2 argsvaluecombine two values
UnaryOperator<T>T apply(T t)1 arg (T)T (same type)same-type transform
BinaryOperator<T>T apply(T t1, T t2)2 args (T,T)T (same type)reduce / combine

Senior Notes

  • Existing ones in the JDK: Runnable, Callable, Comparator, ActionListener.
  • API design: build around small, focused functional interfaces (strategy, callbacks).
  • Checked exceptions need your own functional interface that declares throws.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Composition builds behavior from small functions: Function.identity(), andThen/compose, Predicate.and/or/negate/not/isEqual, BinaryOperator.minBy/maxBy, Comparator chains. Currying and partial application with nested lambdas (Function<Integer, Function<Integer, Integer>>), memoization with a Map.computeIfAbsent wrapper, and strategies stored in maps replace if-else trees.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The compiler identifies a functional interface by counting abstract methods excluding those that override public methods of Object. A lambda expression targets it: type inference gives parameter and return types from the interface method (target typing). Primitive specializations exist because generics cannot use primitives: IntFunction, ToLongFunction, IntUnaryOperator, BooleanSupplier.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: functional interfaces with several abstract methods, throwing checked exceptions inside standard interfaces, stateful lambdas in parallel streams, boxing in hot paths with Function<Integer,Integer> (use IntUnaryOperator), overloaded methods taking different functional interfaces with the same shape (ambiguity: submit(Runnable) vs submit(Callable) with a lambda), and over-nested lambdas that are unreadable.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Lambdas that capture nothing are created once and reused; capturing lambdas allocate an object per evaluation. Primitive specializations avoid boxing. Passing method references versus lambdas has the same cost. Avoid creating lambdas inside tight loops when a constant would do.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: strategy and callback APIs. A retry helper, a validation chain, and event handlers are all functional interfaces.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Two abstract methods fail.

Worked Example 2

Throwing functional interface.

Practice Exercise 1

The core interfaces.

Practice Exercise 2

Custom functional interface and composition.

11. Quick Revision

  • One abstract method.
  • @FunctionalInterface checks it.
  • Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier.
  • andThen, compose, and, negate.
  • Primitive versions avoid boxing.

interviewQA: What is a functional interface?
An interface with exactly one abstract method (a SAM - Single Abstract Method); it may still have any number of default and static methods
Is @FunctionalInterface mandatory?
No - it's optional, but recommended, since the compiler then flags an error if a second abstract method is accidentally added
Can a functional interface extend another interface?
Yes, as long as the total count of abstract methods (after inheriting) stays exactly one
Name Java's 4 core built-in functional interfaces
Function<T,R> (transform), Predicate<T> (test), Consumer<T> (accept, no return), Supplier<T> (get, no args)
Why do primitive-specialized interfaces like IntPredicate exist?
To avoid the autoboxing/unboxing overhead of using Predicate<Integer> for primitive values
What is target typing?
The compiler infers a lambda's actual type purely from the context (variable/parameter/return type) it's assigned to - the lambda itself carries no type

topics.name: Lambda Expression

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A lambda is an anonymous function written as (parameters) -> expression that implements a functional interface.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Anonymous classes were verbose for simple behavior.
  • Lambdas make callbacks, sorting and stream operations concise.

3. Advantages

  • Short, readable code.
  • Enable functional style.
  • Method references shorten further.

4. Disadvantages

  • Hard to debug when long.
  • Captured variables must be effectively final.
  • Overuse reduces clarity.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used with streams and collections daily.
  • Interview topic.
  • Basis for reactive and async code.

6. Basic Concepts

Lambda Expression

A lambda expression, added in Java 8, is a short way to write a small piece of behavior. It brings functional programming to Java and replaces most anonymous inner classes.

Key Features

  • Simple syntax: less code than an anonymous class.
  • Functional interface: a lambda implements an interface that has exactly one abstract method.
  • Two forms: (parameters) -> expression or (parameters) -> { statements; }.

1. Using a Functional Interface

First define a functional interface:

@FunctionalInterface
interface MyFunctionalInterface {
    void sayHello();
}

Now implement it with a lambda:

public class LambdaExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MyFunctionalInterface greeting =
            () -> System.out.println("Hello, World!");
        greeting.sayHello();   // prints Hello, World!
    }
}

2. Parameters and Return Value

@FunctionalInterface
interface Addable {
    int add(int a, int b);
}

public class LambdaWithParameters {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Addable adder = (a, b) -> a + b;
        System.out.println("Sum: " + adder.add(10, 20));
    }
}
// OUTPUT: Sum: 30

Benefits

  • Conciseness: less boilerplate code.
  • Readability: it is clear what action is performed.
  • Functional style: code becomes modular, flexible and easier to reason about.
  • A lambda can be passed as an argument, or used wherever an object of a functional interface is expected.

Common Use Cases

Collections and Streams: filtering, mapping and reducing.

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;

public class StreamExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> names =
            Arrays.asList("Sheru", "Pankaj", "Dheeraj", "Udgir");
        names.stream()
             .filter(name -> name.startsWith("S"))
             .forEach(System.out::println);
    }
}
// OUTPUT: Sheru

Event handling: short handlers in GUI programs.

import javax.swing.JButton;
import javax.swing.JFrame;

public class LambdaEventHandling {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        JFrame frame = new JFrame("Lambda Example");
        JButton button = new JButton("Click Me");
        button.addActionListener(
            e -> System.out.println("Button clicked!"));
        frame.add(button);
        frame.setSize(200, 200);
        frame.setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);
        frame.setVisible(true);
    }
}
// OUTPUT (after each click): Button clicked!

Lambda vs Anonymous Inner Class

  • An anonymous class can extend a concrete or abstract class, or implement an interface with any number of methods.
  • A lambda can implement only a functional interface (one abstract method).
  • So a lambda can replace an anonymous class only when that class implements a functional interface.
  • An anonymous class can declare instance variables. A lambda cannot: variables inside it are plain local variables.
  • In an anonymous class, this is the anonymous object itself.
  • In a lambda, this is the enclosing class object in which the lambda is written.

Syntax Parts

General form: (argument-list) -> { body }

  • Argument list: can be empty or have one or more parameters.
  • Arrow token: -> links the argument list to the body.
  • Body: an expression or a block of statements.
() -> { /* no parameter */ }
(p1) -> { /* one parameter */ }
(p1, p2) -> { /* two parameters */ }

Fresher Notes

  • Anonymous function: (parameters) -> expression or (parameters) -> { statements; }.
  • Functional interface: a lambda implements one, for example Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("hi");.
  • Type inference: parameter types can be left out, as in (a, b) -> a + b.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Comparator.comparing() - Sorting Objects the Java 8 Way

Before Java 8, sorting a list of objects meant writing a full anonymous Comparator with an overridden compare() method. Java 8 added static/default methods on the Comparator interface - comparing(), thenComparing(), reversed() - so sorting logic can be built with method references and lambdas in a single line.

Comparator.thenComparing() - Multi-Level Sorting

thenComparing() lets you chain a secondary (and tertiary...) sort key that only kicks in when the primary key produces a tie - replacing the old nested if/else comparator logic.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Capturing: a lambda can use a local variable of the enclosing method only if it is effectively final (never changed after it is set).
  • this inside a lambda means the enclosing object, unlike in an anonymous class.
  • Method references are shorthand for a lambda that only calls one method: String::length, System.out::println, Person::new.

8. Advanced Concepts

Method References - The 4 Forms

A method reference (ClassOrInstance::methodName) is shorthand for a lambda that does nothing but call an existing method. It only works where a lambda would already be legal (i.e. the target type is a functional interface), and the referenced method's signature must be compatible with the interface's abstract method.

FormSyntaxEquivalent Lambda
1. Static methodClassName::staticMethod(args) -> ClassName.staticMethod(args)
2. Instance method of a particular objectinstance::instanceMethod(args) -> instance.instanceMethod(args)
3. Instance method of an arbitrary object of a typeClassName::instanceMethod(obj, args) -> obj.instanceMethod(args)
4. Constructor referenceClassName::new(args) -> new ClassName(args)

Senior Notes

  • Implementation: lambdas compile to invokedynamic and are created on first use through LambdaMetafactory; a non-capturing lambda is usually one shared instance.
  • Style: keep lambdas short and move longer logic into named methods.
  • Side effects: avoid shared mutable state inside lambdas used in streams.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

  • Typing: a lambda has no type of its own. The target type decides (assignment, method argument, cast or return).
  • Overloads: resolution looks at the shape of the lambda (number of parameters, void or value).
  • Method reference kinds: Class::staticMethod, obj::instanceMethod, Class::instanceMethod (first parameter is the receiver), Class::new and int[]::new.
  • Ambiguity: explicit parameter types or a cast resolve it when generics or wildcards confuse inference.
  • var in lambda parameters (Java 11) lets you add annotations.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

  • The compiler moves the lambda body into a private synthetic method (lambda$main$0) and emits an invokedynamic instruction.
  • On first execution, LambdaMetafactory.metafactory creates a hidden class that implements the interface and returns a call site. Later executions reuse it.
  • A non-capturing lambda is one shared instance. A capturing lambda allocates an instance that holds the captured values.
  • Unlike anonymous classes, no Outer$1.class file exists.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Capturing and changing a loop variable (copy it first).
  • Expecting a new instance each time a lambda is evaluated.
  • Writing large multi-line lambdas.
  • Swallowing exceptions inside a lambda.
  • Recursing through a local variable (use a field).
  • Using a lambda where state is needed (use a class).
  • Leaking memory through a captured this in a long-lived callback.
  • Serializing lambdas, which is fragile across recompiles.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

First use of a lambda pays bootstrap cost (class spinning, tens of microseconds), which matters in tiny CLIs and startup time; AppCDS archives lambda forms. After that, calls are inlined like normal methods. Prefer non-capturing lambdas in hot loops and avoid boxing with primitive specializations.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: event handling, sorting, DAO callbacks, and functional pipelines. Keep lambdas tiny and delegate to well-named methods.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Effectively final.

Worked Example 2

Recursive lambda needs a field or holder.

Practice Exercise 1

Lambdas and method references.

Practice Exercise 2

Capturing and this.

11. Quick Revision

  • Syntax: (a, b) -> a + b.
  • Target type is a functional interface.
  • Captures effectively final variables.
  • this means the enclosing object.
  • Four kinds of method references.

interviewQA: Can a lambda implement any interface?
No - only a functional interface (exactly one abstract method); more methods and the compiler rejects it
Can a lambda declare instance variables?
No - variables inside a lambda body are always local variables; a lambda has no state of its own the way an anonymous class does
What does 'this' refer to inside a lambda?
The enclosing class instance - unlike an anonymous inner class, where 'this' refers to the anonymous class object itself
Can local variables used inside a lambda be reassigned afterward?
No - a lambda can only capture effectively final local variables (never reassigned after initialization), or it's a compile-time error
What is a method reference, and when can you use one?
Shorthand (Class::method) for a lambda that does nothing but call an existing method; usable anywhere a lambda with a matching signature would be legal
Name the 4 forms of method references
Static (Class::staticMethod), bound instance (instance::method), unbound instance (Class::instanceMethod), and constructor reference (Class::new)

topics.name: Default Method

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A default method is an interface method with a body, introduced in Java 8 so interfaces can evolve without breaking implementers.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Adding a method to a widely used interface used to break every implementation.
  • Defaults solve that.

3. Advantages

  • Backward-compatible evolution.
  • Shared behavior in interfaces.
  • Enabled stream() and forEach on old types.

4. Disadvantages

  • Diamond conflicts need manual resolution.
  • No instance state.
  • Can blur interface and class roles.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Interview topic.
  • Explains how the JDK evolved.
  • Useful for API design.

6. Basic Concepts

Default methods / Defender Methods

Java 8 introduced default methods (also called defender methods). They let an interface carry method bodies.

The goal is to make interfaces flexible and keep old code working, especially in the Java Collections Framework.

A method inside an interface that is marked with default is a default method. It is not abstract.

Key Points about Default Methods

  1. Declaration:
    • A default method is declared in an interface with the default keyword.
    • It gives a default body that implementing classes can use as is.
  2. Purpose:
    • Add new methods to an interface without breaking existing implementations.
    • Share common behavior across many classes.
  3. Syntax: see the code below.

Code Explanation

  1. MyInterface.java:
    • It declares the abstract method existingMethod.
    • It also declares the default method defaultMethod with a body.
  2. MyClass.java:
    • It implements MyInterface.
    • It must implement the abstract method existingMethod.
    • The main method calls both the implemented method and the inherited default method.

Example 02 below uses only a default method, so the class needs no body at all.

Advantages of Default Methods

  1. Backward compatibility: add new methods to an interface without breaking old implementations.
  2. Multiple inheritance of behavior: a class can inherit method bodies from several interfaces.
  3. Less boilerplate: common code lives once in the interface.

Considerations

  1. Diamond problem: if two interfaces give the same default method, the class must override it to remove the ambiguity.
  2. Use with care: keep interface hierarchies simple so the code stays easy to follow.

Fresher Notes

  • Default method: a method with a body inside an interface, for example default void log(String m) { System.out.println(m); }.
  • Safe change: you can add methods to an interface without breaking existing implementing classes.
  • Inherit or override: implementing classes get it for free and may override it.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • JDK upgrade: defaults added Collection.stream(), List.sort() and Map.forEach() to old interfaces.
  • Conflict: if two interfaces give the same default method, the class must override it and may call A.super.method().
  • Functional interfaces: defaults do not count as abstract methods, so a lambda can still target the interface.

8. Advanced Concepts

Default Methods and the "Diamond Problem"

Interfaces can now carry behavior. So Java needed rules for the classic diamond problem: what happens when a class implements two interfaces that give the SAME default method?

        InterfaceA                InterfaceB
      default hello()           default hello()
             \                       /
              \                     /
               \                   /
                 class C implements A, B
                 // COMPILE ERROR unless C overrides hello()
                 // "class C inherits unrelated defaults for hello() from A and B"

Resolution Rules (in priority order)

  1. Classes always win - a method from the class itself or its superclass beats any interface default.
  2. More specific interface wins - if interface B extends A and overrides the default method, B's version wins.
  3. Explicit override required - if two unrelated interfaces give the same default method, the class MUST override it. It may delegate with InterfaceName.super.methodName(). Otherwise it is a compile-time error.

Senior Notes

  • No state: defaults cannot touch instance fields (interfaces have none); they call the abstract methods of the interface.
  • Best use: convenience and composition, such as Comparator.reversed, not shared state.
  • API evolution: add a default method instead of an abstract one to stay source- and binary-compatible.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Common patterns for defaults:

  • Mixins: behavior from several interfaces, as in the code below.
  • Decorators: Comparator.reversed() and Predicate.negate() wrap an existing object.
  • Optional methods: a sensible fallback that classes may override.

Keep defaults small and built on the abstract methods of the same interface.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Default methods are stored in the interface class file as normal, non-abstract methods. Implementing classes inherit them, and the JVM picks the method using the three rules shown earlier. A call such as Iface.super.m() is compiled to an invokespecial instruction on the interface.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Defaults that rely on hidden state or call order.
  • Unresolved diamond conflicts (compile error).
  • Adding a default whose signature matches an existing class method: the class method wins silently.
  • Expecting a default to be final. Classes can always override it.
  • Using defaults instead of an abstract class that needs state.
  • Removing a default later, which breaks binary compatibility.

Document defaults like a public contract with @implSpec.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Dispatch cost of default methods equals normal interface calls; the JIT inlines monomorphic sites. Large default hierarchies complicate method resolution and class loading slightly but are rarely a measurable problem.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a plugin interface gets a new optional capability without breaking existing plugins.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Class wins.

Worked Example 2

JDK defaults.

Practice Exercise 1

Default for API evolution.

Practice Exercise 2

Resolving a conflict.

11. Quick Revision

  • default keyword with a body.
  • Class method wins over interface default.
  • Resolve conflicts with X.super.m().
  • No fields in interfaces.
  • Use for convenience methods.

interviewQA: Why were default methods introduced in Java 8?
To let existing interfaces (like those in the Collections Framework) add new methods without breaking every class that already implements them
Can a default method be overridden?
Yes - an implementing class can override it just like a normal inherited method
What happens if a class implements two interfaces with the same default method?
Compile-time error unless the class explicitly overrides the method and resolves the conflict (optionally via InterfaceName.super.method())
Does a default method count toward the "single abstract method" rule for functional interfaces?
No - only abstract methods count; an interface can have one abstract method plus any number of default/static methods and still be a valid functional interface
If a class method and an interface default method conflict, which wins?
The class's own (or inherited superclass) method always wins over any interface default

topics.name: Static Method

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Interfaces can contain static methods with a body, called with the interface name, such as List.of and Comparator.naturalOrder.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Helper and factory methods related to an interface used to need a separate utility class.

3. Advantages

  • Keeps helpers with the interface.
  • Readable factory methods.
  • Not inherited, so no conflicts.

4. Disadvantages

  • Cannot be overridden.
  • Not callable through instances.
  • Can turn interfaces into dumping grounds.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used throughout modern JDK APIs.
  • Interview topic.
  • Good for clean API design.

6. Basic Concepts

Static Method (in Interfaces)

Java 8 lets an interface hold static methods with a body. Before Java 8, an interface could only have abstract methods. Now it can also have default and static methods. A static method is called on the interface itself, so no object is needed.

Before vs After Java 8:

AspectBefore Java 8Java 8 Update
Interface methodsInterfaces could only have abstract methods (no body)Introduced static methods in interfaces
What it means—Interfaces can now have static methods with a body (implementation)
Why it's useful—To create utility or helper methods related to the interface
How to use—Static methods are called using the interface name, not through implementing classes

Key Features of Static Methods in Interfaces:

  1. Utility methods: they hold helpers related to the interface that need no instance.
  2. Direct invocation: call them with the interface name, as in MyInterface.staticMethod().
  3. Syntax: write static before the return type and give the method a body. See the code below.

Explanation

MyInterface.java

  • It has an abstract method existingMethod and a static method staticMethod with a body.

MyClass.java

  • It implements MyInterface and gives a body to existingMethod.
  • main calls the abstract method on an instance and the static method on the interface.

Explanation

Interface (Example)

  • It has a static method x1 that prints a message.

Implementing class (MainTest)

  • It implements Example but does not inherit x1.
  • main calls x1 directly on the Example interface.

Benefits of Static Methods in Interfaces:

  1. Encapsulation: utility methods stay next to the interface they belong to.
  2. No separate utility class: helpers are defined inside the interface itself.
  3. Readability: related methods sit together in one place.

Fresher Notes

  • Static methods with a body: an interface can have static methods, such as static Shape unit() { ... }.
  • Call on the interface name: Comparator.naturalOrder(), List.of(), not on an instance.
  • Not inherited: implementing classes do not get them.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Factory methods and helpers: use them for code related to the interface (Stream.of, Predicate.not, Map.entry).
  • No overriding: a static method is not part of the object contract.
  • Java 9: private static helper methods can share code between static and default methods.

8. Advanced Concepts

Static Methods Are NOT Inherited by Implementing Classes

Unlike default methods, an interface static method belongs only to the interface. It is not inherited by implementing classes, and it cannot be called on an instance or overridden. This is the classic interview trap.

Senior Notes

  • Utility classes: Collections and Arrays existed because interfaces could not hold statics; related helpers can now live with the interface.
  • Focused API: do not turn the interface into a dumping ground for utilities.
  • Static factories: they give readable construction and hide implementations.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Common patterns:

  • Factory methods: List.of, Path.of.
  • Builders: Stream.builder().
  • Combinators: Comparator.comparing, Predicate.isEqual, Function.identity.
  • Named constructors: readable names such as Shape.circle(1).

Combine with a sealed interface so it exposes the factories while the implementations stay hidden in the same package.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Interface static methods are compiled as invokestatic on the interface. They are never inherited by implementing classes or sub-interfaces, and they cannot be reached through an instance. They do not use virtual dispatch, so they cannot be overridden. A class method with the same name is a separate, unrelated method. Java 9 added private interface methods (static and instance) for sharing code.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Calling the method through an instance or an implementing class.
  • Expecting a class static method to override it.
  • Stuffing unrelated utilities into an interface.
  • Making the interface depend on concrete implementations, which hurts decoupling.

Keep statics related to the purpose of the interface.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Static interface methods need no virtual lookup, so the JIT compiler can inline them easily. Prefer them to instance factories when no state is needed. Interface fields are already static final, so constants can be cached there.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: Comparator, Stream and JDBC-style RowMapper helpers expose static factories on interfaces so call sites read naturally.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Not inherited.

Worked Example 2

Private helper (Java 9).

Practice Exercise 1

Factory and helper.

Practice Exercise 2

JDK interface statics.

11. Quick Revision

  • Call as Interface.method().
  • Not inherited by implementers.
  • Used for factories and combinators.
  • Java 9 adds private methods.
  • Keep them related to the interface.

interviewQA: Can an interface's static method be inherited by an implementing class?
No - it belongs only to the interface and must be called via the interface name (InterfaceName.method())
Can a static interface method be overridden?
No - static methods are resolved at compile time and are not part of dynamic dispatch, so "overriding" does not apply
Why were static methods added to interfaces in Java 8?
To let related utility/helper logic (like Comparator.comparing()) live directly on the interface instead of in a separate utility companion class
Difference between a default method and a static method in an interface?
A default method is inherited and overridable by implementing classes; a static method belongs solely to the interface and is called through the interface name

topics.name: forEach Method

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • ForEach performs an action on every element of an Iterable, Map or Stream using a Consumer.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Looping with a lambda is shorter than a for loop for simple actions and fits stream pipelines.

3. Advantages

  • Concise.
  • Works with lambdas and method references.
  • forEachOrdered for ordered parallel streams.

4. Disadvantages

  • No break or continue.
  • Cannot modify the source during iteration.
  • Shared state is risky in parallel streams.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Common in Java 8 code.
  • Interview topic on forEach vs loop.
  • Leads to stream thinking.

6. Basic Concepts

forEach() Method

  • The forEach() method was added in Java 8. It runs a given action on each element of a collection, map or stream.
  • You write the action as a lambda expression, so the loop is short and easy to read.

Key Features of forEach():

  1. Iterable interface: available on every class that implements Iterable, such as List and Set.
    • Syntax: default void forEach(Consumer<? super T> action)
  2. Stream interface: available on stream objects as a terminal operation.
    • Syntax: void forEach(Consumer<? super T> action)

Explanation: Iterable interface

  • The lambda fruit -> System.out.println(fruit) is the Consumer. It receives each element of the list in turn.

Explanation: Stream interface

  • The list is converted to a stream, and forEach() prints each element.

Benefits of forEach():

  1. Conciseness: shorter and more readable than a traditional loop.
  2. Functional style: the action is passed in as a function, so the code is easy to maintain.
  3. Lambda expressions: the action for each element is defined in one line.

Fresher Notes

  • Action per element: forEach runs an action for each element, for example list.forEach(x -> System.out.println(x));.
  • Where it exists: on Iterable (lists, sets), on Map (map.forEach((k, v) -> ...)) and on streams.
  • Argument: a Consumer, which takes one value and returns nothing.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • No break or continue: use a normal loop, or a stream with takeWhile or filter.
  • Do not change the source: adding or removing inside forEach can throw ConcurrentModificationException.
  • Order: forEachOrdered keeps encounter order in parallel streams.

8. Advanced Concepts

forEach() Cannot Break, Return, or Modify the Collection Mid-Iteration

  • forEach() takes a Consumer, so there is no way to break out early.
  • return inside the lambda only ends that one call of the Consumer. It works like continue.
  • Adding or removing elements of the source collection while forEach() runs throws ConcurrentModificationException, just like a for-each loop.

Senior Notes

  • Parallel streams: parallelStream().forEach has no ordering guarantee, and shared mutable state is a bug.
  • Side effects vs results: forEach is fine for side effects. To build results use map and collect, not an external list.
  • Checked exceptions: inside forEach they need try/catch or a wrapper.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Alternatives to forEach with side effects: collect, reduce, mapToInt(...).sum(), Collectors.groupingBy, toMap. For index-based work use IntStream.range. For exceptions use a helper that wraps checked exceptions. For early exit use a loop, anyMatch, takeWhile or findFirst. For concurrent mutation use concurrent collections.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Iterable.forEach(Consumer) is a default method that loops with an iterator; ArrayList.forEach overrides it with an indexed loop and a modCount check at the end; Map.forEach(BiConsumer) iterates entries; Stream.forEach is a terminal operation. For parallel streams the action may run on many threads and in any order.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: modifying the source during iteration (ConcurrentModificationException), forEach with shared non-thread-safe collections in parallel streams (lost updates), expecting ordering from parallel forEach, trying to break or return from the lambda (return only exits the lambda), and using forEach where a simple loop is clearer. Remember return in a lambda behaves like continue.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

The overhead of forEach versus a for loop is negligible after JIT. For parallel work, splitting cost and synchronization dominate: only use parallel streams for large CPU-bound workloads, with associative non-interfering operations, and measure.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: logging all items, sending notifications and registering handlers are legitimate forEach uses (side effects); computing results should use map/collect.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Modification during iteration.

Worked Example 2

Ordered parallel.

Practice Exercise 1

forEach on collections and maps.

Practice Exercise 2

Prefer collect to side effects.

11. Quick Revision

  • Takes a Consumer.
  • No break or continue.
  • Do not modify the collection inside.
  • Prefer collect for building results.
  • forEachOrdered keeps order.

interviewQA: Can you break out of a forEach() loop early?
No. Consumer has no way to signal "stop". Use a traditional for-each loop, or a stream with a short-circuiting operation like anyMatch() or findFirst().
What happens if you remove an element from a list while iterating it with forEach()?
It throws ConcurrentModificationException, the same as in a regular for-each loop.
Which interfaces provide forEach()?
Iterable (default method, used by List and Set), Map (its own version taking a BiConsumer for key and value), and Stream (a terminal operation).
Is Map.forEach() the same signature as Iterable.forEach()?
No. Map.forEach() takes a BiConsumer<K,V>, so both key and value are available. Iterable.forEach() takes a single-argument Consumer<T>.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Optional is a container that may or may not hold a non-null value, making absence explicit.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Null returns cause NullPointerException.
  • Optional forces callers to handle the missing-value case.

3. Advantages

  • Explicit absence.
  • Functional chaining (map, flatMap, filter).
  • Fewer null checks.

4. Disadvantages

  • Extra object allocation.
  • Not for fields or parameters.
  • get() misuse throws exceptions.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used in Spring Data repositories.
  • Interview topic.
  • Teaches null-safe design.

6. Basic Concepts

Optional Class

Java 8 introduced the Optional class to handle null values more gracefully. It lowers the risk of NullPointerException and makes a missing value explicit.

It is a public final class in the java.util package, so you must import it. Its methods let you check whether a value is present.

Why? Calling a method on a null reference fails:

package com.test;
public class MapDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] str = new String[10];
        String lowercaseString = str[5].toLowerCase();
        System.out.print(lowercaseString);
    }
}
// Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException
//     at com.test.MapDemo.main(MapDemo.java:5)

Key Features of Optional Class

  1. Presence or absence: an Optional holds a value that is either present or absent (null).
  2. Methods: many methods handle the present and absent cases.

Common Methods

  • empty(): returns an empty Optional.
    Optional<String> emptyOpt = Optional.empty();
  • of(T value): returns an Optional holding the non-null value.
    Optional<String> opt = Optional.of("Hello");
  • ofNullable(T value): returns an Optional with the value, or an empty Optional if the value is null.
    Optional<String> nullableOpt = Optional.ofNullable(null);
  • isPresent(): returns true if a value is present, otherwise false.
    boolean isPresent = opt.isPresent();
  • ifPresent(Consumer<? super T> consumer): runs the action with the value if present, otherwise does nothing.
    opt.ifPresent(value -> System.out.println("Value is: " + value));
  • orElse(T other): returns the value if present, otherwise returns other.
    String value = nullableOpt.orElse("Default Value");
  • orElseGet(Supplier<? extends T> other): returns the value if present, otherwise calls the supplier and returns its result.
    String value = nullableOpt.orElseGet(() -> "Default Value from Supplier");
  • orElseThrow(Supplier<? extends X> exceptionSupplier): returns the value if present, otherwise throws the exception the supplier creates.
    nullableOpt.orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("Value is absent"));

Explanation

  1. Creating Optionals
    • Optional.of("Hello, World!") creates an Optional with a non-null value.
    • Optional.empty() creates an empty Optional.
    • Optional.ofNullable(null) creates an empty Optional here; it accepts null safely.
  2. Checking presence
    • isPresent() checks if a value is present.
    • ifPresent() performs an action if a value is present.
  3. Providing default values
    • orElse("Default Value") gives a default if the Optional is empty.
    • orElseGet(() -> "Default Value from Supplier") gives a default from a supplier if the Optional is empty.
  4. Throwing exceptions
    • orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("Value is absent")) throws if the Optional is empty.

In short, Optional handles missing values gracefully, lowers the risk of null pointer exceptions and keeps code readable.

Fresher Notes

  • Container: Optional<T> may or may not hold a non-null value, making "no value" explicit.
  • Create with Optional.of(v) (non-null), Optional.ofNullable(v), Optional.empty().
  • Read with isPresent(), get() (only after checking), orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, ifPresent.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Transform with map, flatMap, filter instead of manual null checks.
  • Eager vs lazy: orElse(x) always evaluates x; orElseGet(supplier) evaluates lazily.
  • Newer versions: Java 9+ adds ifPresentOrElse, or, stream(); Java 10+ adds orElseThrow() without arguments.

8. Advanced Concepts

Optional - Imperative Null-Checking vs Functional Chaining

Side-by-side proof of why Optional reduces bugs: a nested-null-check pyramid vs a flat, fail-safe chain that reads top-to-bottom.

Senior Notes

  • Return values only: not fields, method parameters or collections; Optional is not serializable and adds allocation.
  • Avoid get(): never call get() without a check; prefer orElseThrow.
  • Monad-like: a type whose chains (map, flatMap) replace nested null checks.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Idioms: return Optional from lookups (findById), chain map/flatMap/filter/orElseThrow, convert to streams with flatMap(Optional::stream), ifPresentOrElse, and use Objects.requireNonNullElse for plain defaults. In Spring Data, repository methods return Optional. Avoid Optional chains for collection results (return empty collections) and for boolean logic.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Optional is a value-based final class holding a nullable reference; it is immutable and intended as a return type. empty() is a singleton. Operations map to a small monad: map (functor), flatMap (bind), filter, or, stream. Primitive versions (OptionalInt, OptionalLong, OptionalDouble) avoid boxing. Value-based classes should not be synchronized on or compared by identity.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Anti-patterns: Optional.get() without checking, if (opt.isPresent()) return opt.get() (use map/orElse), Optional as a field, parameter or collection element, Optional.of(nullableValue), returning null from a method that returns Optional, wrapping in Optional only to unwrap immediately, and overusing it so code becomes noise. Optional does not remove the need for design clarity.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Optional allocates a wrapper (escape analysis often removes it when the chain inlines). In very hot paths prefer null checks or primitive Optionals. Use orElseGet for expensive defaults.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: repositories and services return Optional, controllers convert to 404, and configuration lookups provide defaults.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Optional misuse.

Worked Example 2

Stream interplay.

Practice Exercise 1

Chaining instead of null checks.

Practice Exercise 2

orElse vs orElseGet and orElseThrow.

Common Optional Anti-Patterns (Interview Traps)

Anti-PatternWhy It's WrongCorrect Approach
opt.get() without isPresent() checkThrows NoSuchElementException - defeats the purpose of OptionalUse orElse / orElseGet / orElseThrow / ifPresent
Optional<T> as a method parameterForces caller to wrap values; not idiomatic, adds overheadUse overloading or plain nullable parameter; reserve Optional for return types
Optional field in a classOptional is not Serializable and adds needless indirection to stateKeep the field nullable; expose Optional only from the getter if desired
opt.isPresent() then opt.get()Verbose, reintroduces the imperative style Optional was meant to removePrefer map/filter/ifPresent/orElse chains

11. Quick Revision

  • of, ofNullable, empty.
  • orElse vs orElseGet.
  • map and flatMap chain.
  • Use as return type only.
  • Prefer orElseThrow to get().

topics.name: String Joiner

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • StringJoiner joins strings with a delimiter, optional prefix and suffix
  • String.join and Collectors.joining do the same in other contexts.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Building comma-separated text with loops needs special handling for the last separator.
  • Joiners remove that.

3. Advantages

  • No trailing separator bugs.
  • Prefix and suffix support.
  • Works well with streams.

4. Disadvantages

  • Not thread-safe.
  • No escaping of delimiters.
  • StringBuilder may be faster for general appends.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used for CSV-like text and logs.
  • Interview topic.
  • Teaches clean string building.

6. Basic Concepts

Java String Joiner

Java 8 added the StringJoiner class to build a sequence of strings separated by a delimiter. It is a final class in the java.util package.

It handles delimiters, prefixes and suffixes for you. You pass a delimiter such as a comma (,) or hyphen (-) and add the parts.

Key Features of StringJoiner:

  1. Delimiter: separates each string you add.
  2. Optional prefix and suffix: added around the final result.

Explanation:

  1. Creating a StringJoiner:
    • new StringJoiner(",") uses a comma as the delimiter and no prefix or suffix.
    • To get brackets, use the three-argument form new StringJoiner(", ", "[", "]").
  2. Adding strings:
    • add("Sheru"), add("Dheeraj") and add("Pankaj") append each value.
  3. Generating the result:
    • System.out.println(stringJoiner) calls toString() and prints Sheru,Dheeraj,Pankaj.

Explanation:

  1. Creating and adding: two joiners (joiner1 and joiner2) are created and filled with strings.
  2. Merging: joiner1.merge(joiner2) adds the contents of joiner2 to joiner1. Only the parts are added, so joiner2 prefix and suffix are not repeated.
  3. Result: joiner1.toString() prints {Udgir, Latur, Pune, Mumbai}.

Benefits of StringJoiner:

  • Ease of use: delimiter, prefix and suffix are handled for you.
  • Readability: no manual concatenation or last-separator checks.
  • Merging: merge() combines several joiners.
  • Streams: works with Java Streams through Collectors.joining().

Limits of StringJoiner:

  • Java 8 or later: not available in older versions.
  • Overkill for simple cases: a plain + is enough for two or three parts.
  • Speed: StringBuilder is lighter for many free-form appends.

Common Uses of StringJoiner in Java 8:

1. Building delimited strings (such as CSV)
StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner(", ");
joiner.add("Anaji").add("Baji").add("Chimnaji");
System.out.println(joiner);   // Anaji, Baji, Chimnaji
2. Formatting output with prefix and suffix
StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner(", ", "[", "]");
joiner.add("Red").add("Green").add("Blue");
System.out.println(joiner);   // [Red, Green, Blue]
3. Generating SQL text (use bound parameters for user data)
StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner(", ", "SELECT ", " FROM table");
joiner.add("column1").add("column2").add("column3");
System.out.println(joiner);   // SELECT column1, column2, column3 FROM table
4. Joining collection elements
List<String> items = Arrays.asList("item1", "item2", "item3");
StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner(", ");
items.forEach(joiner::add);
System.out.println(joiner);   // item1, item2, item3
5. Logging and debugging
StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner(" | ");
joiner.add("INFO").add("2024-11-26").add("Application started");
System.out.println(joiner);   // INFO | 2024-11-26 | Application started
6. Combining multiple joiners
StringJoiner joiner1 = new StringJoiner(", ", "{", "}");
joiner1.add("Java").add("Python");
StringJoiner joiner2 = new StringJoiner(", ", "{", "}");
joiner2.add("C++").add("JavaScript");
joiner1.merge(joiner2);
System.out.println(joiner1);  // {Java, Python, C++, JavaScript}

Fresher Notes

  • Joining: StringJoiner joins strings with a delimiter, optional prefix and suffix: new StringJoiner(", ", "[", "]").
  • Use: add parts with add("x") and read the result with toString().
  • Alternatives: String.join(", ", list) and Collectors.joining(", ").

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Collectors.joining() - Building Delimited Strings from a Stream

Collectors.joining() is the Stream-API equivalent of StringJoiner - it concatenates stream elements with an optional delimiter, prefix, and suffix, replacing manual StringBuilder loops.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Empty joiner: setEmptyValue("none") controls the output when nothing was added.
  • Merging: merge combines two joiners.
  • Choosing: String.join is best for simple joins of an Iterable or varargs; Collectors.joining for streams.

8. Advanced Concepts

The "Empty Value" Trap

When a StringJoiner has a prefix/suffix but nothing was ever added, toString() returns just prefix + suffix - not an empty string. setEmptyValue() lets you override that fallback with a custom string, which only takes effect while the joiner is still empty.

Senior Notes

  • Mutable: StringJoiner changes in place and is not thread-safe.
  • Speed: for many free-form appends in loops StringBuilder may be faster; StringJoiner shines for delimiter handling without trailing separator code.
  • Safety: build CSV and SQL lists carefully: escape values and prefer parameter binding to avoid injection.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Choices: StringBuilder for loops with arbitrary appends, StringJoiner/String.join for delimited lists, Collectors.joining in stream pipelines (with prefix and suffix), String.format for templates, text blocks for multi-line SQL/JSON. For CSV with commas or quotes inside values, escape or use a CSV library; for SQL, bind parameters.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

StringJoiner keeps a String[] of parts and joins lazily on toString. String.join used it in Java 8 (newer JDKs use an optimized internal path). It tracks the delimiter, prefix, suffix and the optional empty value; length() computes the final size without building a new string. It is not synchronized.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: joining values that contain the delimiter without escaping, building SQL by concatenating user data (injection), assuming null is skipped (it prints "null"), using one joiner from several threads, and calling toString repeatedly in a loop. Filter nulls explicitly with Objects::nonNull.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Joining n strings is O(total length); avoid repeated joins in loops (use one builder). Presize StringBuilder when the final size is known. For huge outputs stream to a Writer instead of building a giant string.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: building a readable log line, a comma separated list for a report, and a dynamic IN clause with the right number of placeholders.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Null elements.

Worked Example 2

Merge.

Practice Exercise 1

StringJoiner basics.

Practice Exercise 2

Joining in other ways.

11. Quick Revision

  • new StringJoiner(delimiter, prefix, suffix).
  • setEmptyValue for no elements.
  • String.join for collections.
  • Collectors.joining in streams.
  • Escape values yourself.

interviewQA: What does StringJoiner return if nothing was ever added, with a prefix/suffix set?
Just the prefix concatenated with the suffix (e.g. "[]"), unless setEmptyValue() overrides that default
How is StringJoiner related to Collectors.joining()?
Collectors.joining() is built on top of StringJoiner internally - it's the Stream-API-friendly way to get the same delimiter/prefix/suffix behavior as a terminal collect operation
Is StringJoiner mutable?
Yes - add() and merge() mutate the same instance in place, unlike String's immutable concatenation
When would you prefer StringBuilder over StringJoiner?
When you don't need a delimiter/prefix/suffix pattern and are doing high-frequency, low-overhead concatenation - StringJoiner adds a small amount of bookkeeping for the delimiter logic

topics.name: Stream API

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • The Stream API processes sequences of elements with pipelines of operations: source, intermediate operations like filter and map, and a terminal operation like collect.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Data processing with loops is verbose and error prone.
  • Streams express what to compute declaratively and can run in parallel.

3. Advantages

  • Readable pipelines.
  • Lazy evaluation.
  • Easy parallelism.

4. Disadvantages

  • Hard to debug long chains.
  • Streams are single use.
  • Parallel streams can hurt performance.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used everywhere in modern Java.
  • Top interview topic.
  • Basis for reactive thinking.

6. Basic Concepts

Java 8 Stream

Java 8 added the package java.util.stream. It holds the classes, interfaces and enums for functional-style operations on elements. Import it to use streams.

A stream has these features:

  • No storage: a stream does not store elements. It carries them from a source (a collection, an array or an I/O channel) through a pipeline of operations.
  • Functional: operations do not change the source. Filtering a stream built from a collection gives a new stream without the filtered elements. The collection is untouched.
  • Lazy: the code runs only when a result is needed.
  • Single use: like an Iterator, a stream is visited once. Create a new stream to visit the elements again.

You can use a stream to filter, collect, print and convert one data structure into another. The examples below show these operations.

Explanation of the example above:

  1. Product class: holds the id, name and price of a product.
  2. Filtering and iterating: keeps products with a price above 300 and prints them.
  3. Filtering with a stream: filters and collects the result into a list.
  4. Filtering without a stream: the traditional way, with a for-each loop.
  5. reduce(): adds up the prices of all products.
  6. Collectors.summingDouble: sums the prices of all products.
  7. max and min: find the products with the highest and lowest price.
  8. count(): counts the products with a price above 300.
  9. List to Set: converts the list into a set. A HashSet has no fixed order, so the printed order can differ.
  10. List to Map: uses product ids as keys and product names as values.

The Streams API (Java 8) processes sequences of elements in a functional and declarative way. You can filter, map and reduce data without changing the original source.

Key Features of Java Streams

  1. Functional programming: functional-style operations give readable, short code.
  2. Lazy evaluation: intermediate operations do not run until a terminal operation is called. This avoids needless work.
  3. Pipeline processing: operations are chained into a pipeline.
  4. Parallel processing: streams can run in parallel to use multicore processors.

Stream Operations
