  1. Intermediate operations return a new stream and are lazy. Examples: filter, map, sorted.
  2. Terminal operations produce a result or a side effect and end the pipeline. Examples: forEach, collect, reduce.

Explanation:

  1. Creating a stream: names.stream() creates a stream from the list.
  2. Filtering: filter(name -> name.startsWith("S")) keeps only names that start with "S".
  3. Collecting: collect(Collectors.toList()) gathers the results into a list.
  4. Mapping: map(String::length) turns each name into its length.
  5. Reducing: reduce("", (partialString, element) -> partialString + element) joins all names into one string.

Parallel Streams

You can use a parallel stream to run the work on several cores.

Summary

The Streams API brings functional programming to Java and gives more readable, maintainable code. Lazy evaluation, pipelines and parallel execution make collections easier to work with. More examples follow.

Fresher Notes

  • A stream is a pipeline: a source, then intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted), then one terminal operation (collect, forEach, count, reduce).
  • No storage: streams do not store data and do not change the source. A stream can be used only once.
  • Lazy: intermediate operations do nothing until a terminal operation runs.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Primitive Streams - IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream

Wrapping every int in an Integer for a Stream<Integer> wastes memory and boxing/unboxing cycles. IntStream/LongStream/DoubleStream operate directly on primitives and add numeric-only operations like sum(), average(), and range()/rangeClosed().

Stream.iterate() and Stream.generate() - Infinite Streams

Streams don't have to come from a collection. iterate() builds an infinite stream by repeatedly applying a function to the previous value; generate() builds one by repeatedly calling a Supplier. Both are lazy, so they must be bounded with limit() before a terminal operation.

Stream.concat() - Merging Two Streams

Stream.concat() lazily concatenates two streams into one, in order, without materializing either stream first.

Collectors.groupingBy() with a Downstream Collector

groupingBy() alone produces a Map<Key, List<Element>>. Passing a second, "downstream" collector (counting(), mapping(), summingInt()...) lets you reduce each group to something other than a plain list - e.g. a count per group.

Collectors.partitioningBy() with a Downstream Collector

partitioningBy() is a specialized groupingBy() that always splits into exactly two groups keyed by true/false. Combined with a downstream collector it can, for example, count each partition directly instead of returning the raw lists.

Collectors.toMap() with a Merge Function

Collectors.toMap() throws IllegalStateException if two elements produce the same key. A third "merge function" argument tells it how to resolve duplicate keys instead of crashing - here we keep the higher salary.

IntSummaryStatistics - One Pass, Five Metrics

Collectors.summarizingInt() (or IntStream.summaryStatistics()) computes count, sum, min, max, and average in a single pass over the data, avoiding five separate stream traversals.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Collectors: Collectors.toList() (or Stream.toList() in Java 16+), toSet, toMap, groupingBy, partitioningBy, joining, counting, summingInt, averagingDouble.
  • Primitive streams: IntStream, LongStream and DoubleStream avoid boxing and add sum, average, range.
  • Shaping: flatMap flattens nested collections. distinct, limit and skip trim the data. peek is for debugging only.

8. Advanced Concepts

Stream Pipeline Internals - Laziness Proven

A Stream pipeline does nothing until a terminal operation is invoked. Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted, peek) are just descriptions that get fused and executed element-by-element only when a terminal operation (forEach, collect, reduce, count...) pulls elements through. Below, peek() proves this: notice the interleaved order rather than "all filters, then all maps".

Senior Notes

  • Parallel streams: parallelStream() uses the common ForkJoinPool. It helps only for CPU-heavy work on large, easily split data with no shared state.
  • Short-circuit operations: findFirst, anyMatch and limit stop early. Keep lambdas pure and stateless.
  • Order matters: filter before map and sorted to reduce work. Avoid streams for tiny loops where they hurt clarity.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful collectors and stream features:

  • groupingBy with a downstream collector: counting, mapping, summingInt, averagingDouble, maxBy, collectingAndThen.
  • Other collectors: partitioningBy, toMap (with merge function and map supplier), flatMapping, filtering, summarizingInt.
  • teeing (Java 12) runs two collectors and combines their results.
  • Java 16: Stream.toList() (unmodifiable) and mapMulti.
  • Infinite streams: iterate and generate, bounded by limit or takeWhile.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

A pipeline is a chain of stages. The terminal operation pulls elements through the stages one at a time (loop fusion), so filter and map do not create intermediate collections.

  • Stateless stages: map, filter.
  • Stateful stages: sorted, distinct. They must buffer elements.
  • Short-circuit operations: limit, findFirst, anyMatch. They can finish early.
  • Source: a Spliterator. It also splits the data for parallel runs.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Reusing a stream, or forgetting the terminal operation (nothing runs).
  • Side effects and shared mutable state inside lambdas.
  • Using peek for real logic. It is for debugging.
  • Calling sorted before filter (wasted work).
  • Using parallel() on small or blocking pipelines.
  • toMap without a merge function when keys can repeat.
  • Changing the source while the pipeline runs.
  • Calling Optional.get on findFirst without checking.
  • Using Stream<Integer> for number work. Use IntStream.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Performance tips:

  • Streams add a small cost per element. For tiny loops or hot numeric code, a plain loop or a primitive stream is faster.
  • Parallel streams help when the data is large (roughly 10,000 or more elements, times the work per element), CPU-bound, stateless and easy to split (ArrayList, arrays, ranges).
  • Avoid LinkedList and Stream.iterate sources in parallel.
  • To isolate the work, submit it to your own ForkJoinPool.
  • Measure with JMH, not with System.nanoTime alone.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world uses:

  • Reports: group, sum, sort, top N.
  • Data cleaning: filter nulls, trim, remove duplicates.
  • Mapping: convert between DTOs and entities.

The sample below assumes orders, Line and ProductDto exist.

10. Examples

Worked Example 2
