Practice Exercise 1

A typical pipeline.

Practice Exercise 2

flatMap, distinct and reduce.

11. Quick Revision

  • Source, intermediate, terminal.
  • Lazy until terminal operation.
  • map, filter, flatMap, sorted, distinct.
  • collect with groupingBy and joining.
  • parallel only for large CPU work.

interviewQA: Can a Stream be reused after a terminal operation?
No - once a terminal operation runs, the stream is considered consumed; calling another operation on it throws IllegalStateException
Are intermediate operations eager or lazy?
Lazy - filter/map/sorted just build a pipeline description; nothing executes until a terminal operation (collect/forEach/reduce/count) is invoked
Difference between map() and flatMap()?
map() transforms each element 1-to-1 (can produce a stream of streams for nested structures); flatMap() transforms each element into a stream and flattens all of them into one flat stream
Does a Stream modify its source collection?
No - stream operations like filter() produce a new stream/result; the original source collection is left untouched
What's the difference between Stream and parallelStream()?

stream() processes elements sequentially on one thread; parallelStream() splits the work across multiple threads via the common ForkJoin pool - useful for large datasets with CPU-heavy, independent per-element work

topics.name: Other Java 8 Enhancements

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

CompletableFuture - Asynchronous Programming

Java 8 introduced CompletableFuture to write non-blocking, composable asynchronous code - a big upgrade over the plain Future interface, which had no way to chain callbacks or combine multiple async results.

Base64 Encoding and Decoding (java.util.Base64)

Before Java 8, Base64 support required third-party libraries or the internal sun.misc.BASE64Encoder. Java 8 added a standard java.util.Base64 class with Basic, URL-safe, and MIME encoders/decoders.

Repeatable Annotations

Before Java 8, the same annotation could not be applied more than once to the same element. @Repeatable lets you mark an annotation as repeatable by pointing it to a "container" annotation that holds an array of it.

Type Annotations (JSR 308)

Before Java 8, annotations could only target declarations (a class, method, or field). Java 8 extended the @Target meta-annotation with TYPE_USE and TYPE_PARAMETER, so annotations can now appear anywhere a type is used - on generic type arguments, casts, and even implements/throws clauses - enabling stronger static analysis tools (like nullability checkers) to catch bugs at compile time.

Arrays.parallelSort() - Multicore Sorting

Arrays.parallelSort() splits large arrays into chunks, sorts each chunk on a different core using the ForkJoin pool, then merges them - faster than Arrays.sort() on big arrays on multicore machines.

Files.lines() - Reading a File as a Stream

java.nio.file.Files.lines() reads a file lazily, one line at a time, as a Stream<String> - so it can be filtered, mapped, and collected without loading the whole file into memory, and should always be used inside try-with-resources so the underlying file handle is closed.

PermGen Removed, Replaced by Metaspace

Java 8 removed the fixed-size PermGen space (a frequent source of java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space) and moved class metadata to Metaspace, which lives in native memory and grows automatically instead of a hard-coded limit.

Nashorn JavaScript Engine

Java 8 replaced the older, slower Rhino engine with Nashorn - a faster JavaScript engine built on invokedynamic, embedded directly in the JDK via the javax.script API. It lets Java code evaluate and call into JavaScript at runtime (Nashorn was later deprecated in Java 11 and removed in Java 15, but it shipped as a core Java 8 feature, so run this sample on Java 8 to 14).

Mid-Level Notes

  • Immutable types: java.time types are immutable and thread-safe; DateTimeFormatter replaces SimpleDateFormat.
  • Base64 output: Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(bytes), and getUrlEncoder for URL-safe output.
  • Map additions: Map gained getOrDefault, putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, merge and forEach.

8. Advanced Concepts

The New Date/Time API (java.time)

Java 8 replaced the mutable, thread-unsafe Date/Calendar classes with an immutable, thread-safe set of types modeled on ISO-8601: LocalDate (date only), LocalTime (time only), LocalDateTime (both, no time zone), Period (date-based amount) and Duration (time-based amount), plus DateTimeFormatter for parsing/formatting.

Old APIJava 8 ReplacementKey Difference
java.util.DateLocalDate / LocalDateTimeImmutable, no timezone confusion
java.util.CalendarLocalDate + Period/DurationClear separation of date-math vs time-math
SimpleDateFormatDateTimeFormatterThread-safe (SimpleDateFormat is NOT)

Senior Notes

  • Timestamps: use Instant for machine timestamps and store UTC; convert to ZonedDateTime for display.
  • Metaspace replaced PermGen (class metadata in native memory).
  • Parameter names: compile with -parameters and use type annotations to help frameworks.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Other additions in Java 8:

  • Concurrency: CompletableFuture, StampedLock, LongAdder.
  • Collections and utilities: Collectors, Map.merge, Objects helpers, String.join, Arrays.parallelPrefix and parallelSetAll, Files.lines.
  • Encoding: Base64, and unsigned integer methods such as Integer.toUnsignedString.
  • Annotations and reflection: @Repeatable, type annotations, and -parameters (keeps parameter names for reflection).
  • JVM: Metaspace replaced PermGen (cap it with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize), and HashMap handles collisions better.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The java.time model separates machine time (Instant, nanoseconds since epoch UTC) from human time (LocalDate, LocalTime, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, OffsetDateTime) and amounts (Duration, Period). All are immutable; arithmetic returns new instances; the zone rules database (tzdata) handles daylight saving time. Parsing and formatting use DateTimeFormatter (thread-safe).

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Storing local date-times without a zone for events that happen at an instant (use Instant/UTC).
  • Formatting with YYYY instead of yyyy (week-based year bug).
  • Parsing without the right pattern.
  • Using ZonedDateTime.equals (zone sensitive) instead of isEqual.
  • Using Date/Calendar in new code.
  • Treating Period and Duration as interchangeable.
  • Forgetting DST: adding days is not the same as adding 24 hours.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Metaspace removed the fixed PermGen limit. Class metadata uses native memory, so cap it with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
  • HashMap treeification (long collision chains become trees) and parallel streams also changed performance.
  • java.time objects are cheap but numerous: reuse formatters and avoid parsing the same text repeatedly.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world habits:

  • Store timestamps in UTC (Instant / TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE) and show them in the user zone.
  • Compute business days with TemporalAdjusters.
  • Measure elapsed time with Duration and System.nanoTime.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Old Date vs new API.

Worked Example 2

Parallel sort.

Practice Exercise 1

java.time.

Practice Exercise 2

Base64 and Map additions.

11. Quick Revision

  • LocalDate, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, Instant.
  • Duration vs Period.
  • DateTimeFormatter is thread-safe.
  • Base64 encoder and decoder.
  • Metaspace replaced PermGen.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Besides lambdas and streams, Java 8 added the java.time API, Base64, CompletableFuture, parallel array operations and Metaspace.

2. Need of This Topic

  • The old Date and Calendar classes were mutable and confusing, and other gaps needed modern replacements.

3. Advantages

  • Immutable, thread-safe date and time.
  • Built-in Base64.
  • Better concurrency utilities.

4. Disadvantages

  • New APIs to learn.
  • Mixing old Date with new time types needs conversion.
  • Some features were later removed (Nashorn).

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • java.time is used in every project.
  • Interview topic.
  • Helps modernize legacy code.

6. Basic Concepts

Fresher Notes

  • Besides lambdas and streams, Java 8 added the java.time API (LocalDate, LocalDateTime, Instant, Duration, Period, ZonedDateTime).
  • CompletableFuture for async code, Base64 (java.util.Base64) encoder and decoder, parallel array operations (Arrays.parallelSort), and repeating annotations.
  • The Nashorn JavaScript engine was added (and later removed in Java 15).

interviewQA: What is target typing in lambda expressions?
The process by which the compiler infers a lambda's type from the context (variable type, method parameter, return type) it is assigned to - the target type must be a functional interface.
What is the difference between an anonymous inner class and a lambda expression?

An anonymous class creates a new .class file, can implement multiple methods and declare its own instance state, and its 'this' refers to itself. A lambda has no separate class overhead for state, can only implement a single-method functional interface, and 'this' refers to the enclosing class.
What is the difference between map() and flatMap() in Streams?

map() transforms each element into exactly one new element (possibly producing a Stream of Streams for nested structures); flatMap() transforms each element into a Stream and then flattens all those streams into a single flat stream.
Are Stream operations lazy or eager?

Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted) are lazy - they only build a pipeline description. Nothing executes until a terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce, count) is invoked, which then pulls elements through the whole pipeline.
Can a Stream be reused/traversed twice?

No - once a terminal operation is called, the stream is considered consumed and calling another operation on it throws IllegalStateException. A new stream must be created from the source to traverse again.
What is the difference between Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier?
Predicate<T> takes T and returns boolean; Function<T,R> takes T and returns R; Consumer<T> takes T and returns nothing (side effect); Supplier<T> takes no arguments and returns T.
What are the 4 forms of method references?

Static method (Class::staticMethod), instance method of a particular object (obj::method), instance method of an arbitrary object of a type (Class::instanceMethod), and constructor reference (Class::new).
How does Java resolve the diamond problem with default methods?

A method from a class always wins over any interface default. Between interfaces, the more specific sub-interface's default wins. If two unrelated interfaces provide conflicting defaults, the implementing class must explicitly override the method (optionally calling InterfaceName.super.method()).
Why is Optional not recommended as a method parameter or class field?
It adds wrapping overhead and is not idiomatic for inputs/state (Optional is also not Serializable); it is intended mainly as a return type to signal "this method may not have a result" to callers.
Why is java.time considered better than java.util.Date/Calendar?

java.time types (LocalDate, LocalDateTime, etc.) are immutable and thread-safe, model dates/times explicitly (with/without zone), and separate date-based amounts (Period) from time-based amounts (Duration), unlike the old mutable, non-thread-safe, poorly designed Date/Calendar API.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Var lets the compiler infer the type of a local variable from its initializer, for example var list = new ArrayList<String>().

2. Need of This Topic

  • Long generic type names repeated on both sides add noise.
  • Var removes duplication while keeping static typing.

3. Advantages

  • Less boilerplate.
  • Still statically typed.
  • Helps with long generic types.

4. Disadvantages

  • Can hide the type and reduce readability.
  • Not allowed for fields or parameters.
  • Infers the exact type, not the interface.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Seen in modern code and interviews.
  • Teaches type inference.
  • Part of Java style guidelines.

6. Basic Concepts

Local Variable Type Inference (var)

Introduction

Java 10 introduced the var keyword (enhanced in Java 11) which allows local variable type inference. Instead of explicitly declaring the type of a local variable, you can use var and let the compiler infer the type from the initializer expression.

Key Features

  • var is not a keyword but a reserved type name
  • The compiler infers the type at compile time — it is NOT dynamic typing
  • Can only be used for local variables with initializers
  • Improves code readability by reducing boilerplate

Basic Syntax

  • var name = "Java"; — compiler infers String
  • var count = 10; — compiler infers int
  • var list = new ArrayList<String>(); — compiler infers ArrayList<String>

Limitations

  • Cannot be used for class fields (instance/static variables)
  • Cannot be used for method parameters
  • Cannot be used for method return types
  • Cannot be used with null initializer: var x = null; is invalid
  • Cannot be used with lambda expressions without explicit target type

Fresher Notes

  • Type inference: var (Java 10) lets the compiler work out the type of a local variable from its initializer, as in var list = new ArrayList<String>();.
  • Static typing: the type is fixed at compile time. var is not a dynamic type.
  • Where it works: local variables, for-loops and try-with-resources. It does not work for fields, method parameters or return types.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Local Variable Type Inference — Intermediate Usage

Using var in Loops

The var keyword works naturally in for-each and traditional for loops, making iteration code cleaner.

Using var with Try-With-Resources

var can simplify resource management in try-with-resources blocks.

var with Anonymous Classes

When used with anonymous classes, var captures the anonymous type, giving access to additional methods defined in the anonymous class.

Best Practices

  • Use var when the type is obvious from the right-hand side
  • Avoid var when it reduces readability
  • Use meaningful variable names when using var to maintain clarity
  • var works well with the diamond operator and factory methods
  • Prefer var in local contexts where the scope is small

Mid-Level Notes

  • Initializer required: var x; and var x = null; do not compile.
  • Readability rule: use var when the right-hand side shows the type. Write the type when it adds clarity.
  • Lambda parameters: Java 11 allows (var a, var b) -> a + b. This is useful when you need annotations on the parameters.

8. Advanced Concepts

Local Variable Type Inference — Expert Deep Dive

How var Works Internally

  • The var keyword is handled entirely at compile time
  • The compiled bytecode is identical whether you use var or an explicit type
  • The compiler infers from the STANDALONE type of the initializer. Poly expressions are rejected, which is why var f = () -> {} and var a = {1,2} are compile errors
  • var does NOT make Java dynamically typed — it is still statically typed

var vs Explicit Types — When to Choose

  • Use explicit types when working with interfaces: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
  • Using var with new ArrayList<String>() infers ArrayList, not List
  • This can inadvertently couple code to implementation details

Common Interview Questions

  • Q: Is var a keyword in Java? — No, it is a reserved type name. You can still use "var" as a variable name.
  • Q: Does var make Java dynamically typed? — No, the type is inferred at compile time and is fixed.
  • Q: Can var be used with generics? — Yes, but be careful with diamond operator inference.
  • Q: What happens with var x = null? — Compilation error, as the type cannot be inferred from null.

Senior Notes

  • Exact type: var x = new ArrayList<String>() is an ArrayList, not a List. Declare the interface type if you want it.
  • Anonymous types: with var you can call the extra methods of an anonymous class object.
  • Naming: keep names descriptive, because with var the name carries the meaning.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

OpenJDK style guideline: use var when the initializer makes the type clear, such as a constructor call, a cast or a factory method like of. Avoid it when a method call hides the type. Avoid it for literals when the exact primitive matters, because var b = 1 is an int, not a byte.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

var is a reserved type name, not a keyword. The compiler replaces it with the type inferred from the initializer. That type can even be one you cannot write by hand, such as an anonymous class or an intersection type. The bytecode is identical to writing the type yourself. Inference looks at the right-hand side only, so a bare diamond like new ArrayList<>() infers ArrayList<Object>.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Two common mistakes are shown below. First, a variable keeps its inferred type, so you cannot assign a different type later. Second, var gives ArrayList, not List, so you cannot swap the implementation. Also remember: a ternary can infer a surprising type, and var is not allowed for fields. Declare the interface type when later code depends on it.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

There is no run-time or performance difference, because var only affects the source. It cuts noise from long generic types. If it hides a type, turn on your IDE type hints.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Typical uses are loops over map entries and try-with-resources. Many teams adopt one rule: use var when the type is obvious from the right side.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Declarations that do not compile.

Worked Example 2

When var hurts readability.

Practice Exercise 1

Use var for obvious types, loops and resources.

Practice Exercise 2

var keeps the exact type, not the interface.

11. Quick Revision

  • Local variables only.
  • Needs an initializer.
  • Not dynamic typing.
  • Use when the type is obvious.
  • Allowed in lambda parameters (Java 11).

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Java 11 added String methods isBlank, strip, stripLeading, stripTrailing, repeat and lines.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Input cleaning and text generation needed Unicode-aware whitespace handling and simple repetition.

3. Advantages

  • Unicode-aware whitespace handling.
  • repeat and lines make common tasks simple.
  • Streams of lines are lazy.

4. Disadvantages

  • Only available from Java 11.
  • Small utilities, not a new capability.
  • Easy to mix up with trim.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used in validation and parsing.
  • Interview topic.
  • Shows how the String API evolved.

6. Basic Concepts

New String Methods in Java 11

Introduction

Java 11 introduced several useful methods to the String class that simplify common string operations. These methods reduce the need for external libraries like Apache Commons Lang.

New Methods Overview

  • isBlank() — Returns true if the string is empty or contains only whitespace
  • lines() — Returns a Stream of lines extracted from the string
  • strip() — Removes leading and trailing whitespace (Unicode-aware)
  • stripLeading() — Removes leading whitespace only
  • stripTrailing() — Removes trailing whitespace only
  • repeat(int n) — Returns the string repeated n times

strip() vs trim()

  • trim() removes characters with ASCII value <= 32 (space)
  • strip() removes all Unicode whitespace characters
  • strip() is the preferred modern approach

Fresher Notes

  • Six new methods: isBlank(), strip(), stripLeading(), stripTrailing(), repeat(n) and lines().
  • Blank check: isBlank() is true for an empty string or one with only whitespace.
  • strip vs trim: strip() removes Unicode whitespace, while trim() removes only characters up to the space (U+0020).

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

New String Methods — Intermediate Usage

Combining String Methods with Streams

The new String methods integrate seamlessly with the Stream API, enabling powerful text processing pipelines.

Practical Use Cases

  • Parsing multi-line text data with lines() and filtering with isBlank()
  • Building formatted output with repeat()
  • Cleaning user input with strip() variants
  • Processing CSV or log data line by line

Best Practices

  • Prefer strip() over trim() for Unicode compatibility
  • Use isBlank() instead of trim().isEmpty()
  • Use lines() instead of split("\n") for better performance with large strings

Mid-Level Notes

  • Line stream: lines() returns a Stream<String> and splits on any line terminator.
  • Repeat: repeat(3) builds repeated text, for example "-".repeat(20).
  • Later additions: indent and transform came in Java 12; formatted, stripIndent and translateEscapes in Java 15.

8. Advanced Concepts

New String Methods — Expert Deep Dive

Internal Implementation

  • strip() uses Character.isWhitespace() which handles Unicode, while trim() uses c <= ' '
  • lines() returns a lazy Stream — lines are computed on demand, making it memory-efficient for large strings
  • repeat() allocates the final array once and fills it with System.arraycopy(), so it is fast
  • isBlank() checks Character.isWhitespace() for each code point

Performance Considerations

  • lines() is lazy, while split("\n") builds the whole array of substrings at once
  • repeat() is optimized and faster than manual StringBuilder loops
  • isBlank() short-circuits on the first non-whitespace character

Quick Facts

  • repeat(0) returns an empty string ""
  • lines() is lazy, so it processes lines on demand

Senior Notes

  • Input checks: prefer strip and isBlank over trim and isEmpty. Note that a non-breaking space (U+00A0) is not whitespace for either strip or trim.
  • Lazy lines: lines() is lazy and memory friendly for large text compared with split("\n").
  • Bad count: repeat with a negative count throws IllegalArgumentException.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

The new methods combine well with streams. Here lines() feeds a pipeline that drops blank lines, strips each line and collects the words. The same sample also tries transform, translateEscapes and stripIndent, which need a newer Java than 11.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

String.isBlank uses Character.isWhitespace across the string; strip uses Character.isWhitespace (Unicode aware), whereas trim removes any code point <= U+0020. repeat allocates the final array once and uses System.arraycopy doubling. lines() returns a lazy Stream backed by a spliterator scanning for \n, \r and \r\n. Compact strings (Latin-1 vs UTF-16) keep these operations cheap.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes are listed below. Clean input once, at the point where it enters your program.

  • trim for user input: it misses Unicode spaces. Even strip misses the non-breaking space (U+00A0), so replace it first.
  • isEmpty instead of isBlank: " ".isEmpty() is false.
  • split("\n") on Windows text: it leaves a trailing \r on each line.
  • Ignoring immutability: s.strip(); alone does nothing, so keep the result.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

lines() reads the text on demand and does not build a whole split array. repeat is faster than a loop with concatenation. For heavy text work, use StringBuilder, precompile regexes used in hot loops, and stream files with Files.lines instead of reading everything.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: validating form fields, cleaning imported CSV values, and building formatted console reports.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

trim vs strip with Unicode space.

Worked Example 2

Count lines.

Practice Exercise 1

The new methods.

Practice Exercise 2

Input validation.

11. Quick Revision

  • isBlank checks whitespace-only strings.
  • strip handles Unicode spaces; trim does not.
  • repeat(n) repeats text.
  • lines() gives a Stream.
  • Negative repeat throws.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • The Java 11 HTTP Client (java.net.http) is a modern API for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 with synchronous and asynchronous requests.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Applications call REST APIs.
  • The old HttpURLConnection was clumsy and lacked HTTP/2 and async support.

3. Advantages

  • Built into the JDK.
  • HTTP/2 and async with CompletableFuture.
  • Clean builder API.

4. Disadvantages

  • Fewer features than libraries like OkHttp or Apache HttpClient.
  • You must check status codes yourself.
  • Retries and circuit breakers are manual.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Needed to call web services.
  • Interview topic.
  • Prepares for REST client work.

6. Basic Concepts

HTTP Client API (java.net.http)

Introduction

Java 11 introduced a new HTTP Client API in the java.net.http package as a standard feature. It replaces the legacy HttpURLConnection API and provides a modern, fluent interface for making HTTP requests.

Key Components

  • HttpClient — The main entry point for sending HTTP requests
  • HttpRequest — Represents an HTTP request with method, URI, headers, and body
  • HttpResponse — Represents the HTTP response with status code, headers, and body
  • HttpResponse.BodyHandlers — Predefined handlers for response body processing

Key Features

  • Supports HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2
  • Supports synchronous and asynchronous requests
  • Built-in WebSocket support
  • Immutable and thread-safe request/response objects
  • Builder pattern for creating clients and requests

Fresher Notes

  • Standard client: Java 11 added java.net.http.HttpClient with HttpRequest and HttpResponse.
  • Sync and async: it supports HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2. Use send to wait, or sendAsync to get a CompletableFuture.
  • Replaces the old HttpURLConnection.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

HTTP Client API — Intermediate Usage

POST Requests

You can send POST requests with different body types using HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.

Setting Headers and Timeouts

The builder pattern allows configuring headers, timeouts, and other request properties.

Asynchronous Requests

Use sendAsync() to send non-blocking requests that return a CompletableFuture.

Best Practices

  • Reuse HttpClient instances — they are thread-safe
  • Set appropriate timeouts to avoid hanging requests
  • Use asynchronous requests for non-blocking I/O
  • Handle response status codes appropriately

Mid-Level Notes

  • Reuse the client: build it once, for example HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build().
  • Build requests with HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(url)).header(...).POST(BodyPublishers.ofString(json)).build().
  • Body handlers pick the response type: BodyHandlers.ofString(), ofFile, ofLines, ofInputStream.

8. Advanced Concepts

HTTP Client API — Expert Deep Dive

Internal Architecture

  • The HTTP Client uses an internal SelectorManager for async I/O
  • HTTP/2 support includes multiplexing and header compression (server push is supported by the API but rarely used)
  • The client manages a connection pool internally
  • Uses Flow API (Reactive Streams) internally for body processing

Comparison with Legacy HttpURLConnection

  • HttpURLConnection: Blocking, mutable, verbose, no HTTP/2
  • New HttpClient: Non-blocking support, immutable, fluent API, HTTP/2 native

Quick Questions

  • Why was HttpClient introduced? — To replace the dated HttpURLConnection with a modern, non-blocking, HTTP/2 compatible API
  • Is HttpClient thread-safe? — Yes, it is immutable and can be shared across threads
  • How does async work internally? — Uses CompletableFuture backed by an internal executor and NIO selectors
  • Does it support WebSocket? — Yes, via HttpClient.newWebSocketBuilder()

Senior Notes

  • Timeouts and status: set connect and per-request timeouts, and check statusCode(). A 404 or 500 is not an exception.
  • Executor and redirects: the client has its own executor, so configure it for async load. Use followRedirects(Redirect.NORMAL) to follow redirects.
  • Resilience: for retries, backoff and circuit breaking use a library (Resilience4j) or a small wrapper. Send authentication headers securely.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Production usage of the client:

  • One shared client per host or service.
  • JSON with Jackson (ObjectMapper).
  • Authentication headers added in wrapper methods.
  • Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, only for idempotent calls.
  • Circuit breaker and bulkhead (Resilience4j).
  • Metrics and tracing headers.
  • Proxy and TLS setup (sslContext, proxy) and cookies (CookieManager).
  • Large bodies streamed with ofInputStream or ofFile.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

HttpClient is immutable and thread-safe. Internally it uses a selector manager thread and an executor for dispatching responses; connections are pooled and HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one connection. Requests are immutable; BodyPublisher supplies the request body (strings, files, byte arrays, streams) and a BodyHandler turns the response into a BodySubscriber consumed as a reactive stream. WebSocket support is built in via newWebSocketBuilder. The virtual-thread executor below needs Java 21.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • No timeouts. A hung server blocks forever. Set a request timeout as well as a connect timeout.
  • Creating a client per request.
  • Ignoring status codes.
  • Leaking secrets in logs, such as URLs with tokens.
  • Not closing streaming bodies.
  • Calling join() inside async chains, which blocks the common pool.
  • Retrying non-idempotent POSTs.
  • Disabling TLS verification.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Ways to improve throughput:

  • HTTP/2 multiplexing and a shared client cut connection setup.
  • Use async calls or virtual threads (Java 21) for fan-out.
  • Limit concurrency with a semaphore to protect the remote service.
  • Stream large bodies instead of buffering them.
  • Tune the connection pool with system properties such as jdk.httpclient.connectionPoolSize.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: calling a payment API with idempotency keys, a health check with short timeouts, and downloading large files with ofFile. Wrap the client in a small class so tests can replace it with a fake.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Status is not an exception.

Worked Example 2

Download to a file.

Practice Exercise 1

GET and POST.

Practice Exercise 2

Async calls in parallel.

11. Quick Revision

  • HttpClient is reusable and thread-safe.
  • Build HttpRequest, call send or sendAsync.
  • Set timeouts.
  • Check statusCode().
  • BodyHandlers choose the response type.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Java 11 adds Optional.isEmpty, and Java 9 and 10 added orElseThrow(), or, ifPresentOrElse and stream.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Everyday Optional use needed clearer methods than negating isPresent or calling get.

3. Advantages

  • More readable code.
  • Fallback chains with or.
  • Easy conversion to streams.

4. Disadvantages

  • Still not for fields and parameters.
  • Allocation overhead.
  • Versions differ in available methods.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used in modern service code.
  • Interview topic.
  • Improves null-safe style.

6. Basic Concepts

Optional Enhancements in Java 11

Introduction

Java 9, 10 and 11 each extended the Optional class - Java 9 added ifPresentOrElse(), or() and stream(), Java 10 added the no-arg orElseThrow(), and Java 11 added isEmpty(), making it more expressive for handling values that may be absent.

New Methods

  • isEmpty() — returns true if no value is present (the opposite of isPresent()); reads better in checks for absence
  • ifPresentOrElse(action, emptyAction) — runs the action if a value is present, otherwise runs emptyAction; removes if-else boilerplate
  • or(supplier) — returns this Optional if it has a value, otherwise an Optional made by the supplier; enables fallback chains
  • stream() — converts the Optional to a Stream of 0 or 1 element; plugs into Stream pipelines

Fresher Notes

  • Java 11 added Optional.isEmpty(), the opposite of isPresent().
  • Java 10 added orElseThrow() with no arguments (throws NoSuchElementException), a clearer alternative to get().
  • Java 9 added ifPresentOrElse, or and stream.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Optional Enhancements — Intermediate Usage

Chaining Optionals with or()

The or() method enables a fallback chain of Optional values, trying each supplier in sequence until a value is found.

Integrating Optional with Streams

The stream() method allows flattening a collection of Optionals into a Stream of present values using flatMap().

Best Practices

  • Use isEmpty() for guard clauses and early returns
  • Use ifPresentOrElse() instead of manual if-else blocks
  • Chain or() for cascading fallback logic
  • Use stream() with flatMap() to drop empty Optionals from collections

Mid-Level Notes

  • Readability: opt.isEmpty() reads better than !opt.isPresent().
  • Lazy fallback: opt.or(() -> other) calls the supplier only when the Optional is empty.
  • Streams: opt.stream() gives a 0 or 1 element stream (handy with flatMap).

8. Advanced Concepts

Optional Enhancements — Expert Deep Dive

Internal Implementation

  • isEmpty() simply returns value == null internally
  • or() returns this if a value is present, otherwise calls the supplier
  • stream() returns Stream.of(value) or Stream.empty()
  • ifPresentOrElse() uses a simple null check to pick which action to run

Comparison: Java 8 vs Java 11 Optional

  • Java 8: isPresent(), ifPresent(), orElse(), orElseGet(), map(), flatMap(), filter()
  • Java 9: ifPresentOrElse(), or(), stream()
  • Java 10: orElseThrow() (no-arg version)
  • Java 11: isEmpty()

Quick Q&A

  • orElse() vs or()? — orElse() returns the unwrapped value T; or() returns an Optional<T> for further chaining
  • Is Optional serializable? — No, by design. Do not use it for fields.
  • Optional as a method parameter? — No, it is designed for return types only

Senior Notes

  • Absence is a bug: use orElseThrow(); for domain errors pass a supplier, orElseThrow(() -> new X(...)).
  • Filtering empties: use Predicate.not(Optional::isEmpty) in streams.
  • Scope: Optional is a return type tool, not a field type.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Idioms combining the new methods:

  • filter(Predicate.not(Optional::isEmpty)) for streams of Optionals
  • or for layered lookups (cache, database, remote), evaluated lazily
  • ifPresentOrElse to avoid if/else
  • mapToInt in streams to get an OptionalInt
  • orElseThrow in services to map absence to domain exceptions (Spring Data repositories return Optional)

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

orElseThrow() throws NoSuchElementException("No value present") and is the clearer replacement for get(), because the name signals intent. Optional is a value-based class: do not compare it by identity, synchronize on it, or serialize it.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Calling isEmpty() then get() (use the functional style instead)
  • Mixing null checks with Optional
  • Returning null instead of an Optional
  • Using Optional parameters (use overloads)
  • Using Optional to model collections or booleans
  • Catching NoSuchElementException from orElseThrow() as control flow (throw a meaningful exception instead)

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Optional chains allocate small objects that escape analysis usually removes after inlining; in hot loops over primitives use OptionalInt or plain null checks. Optional creation in a tight loop of millions of elements is rarely a bottleneck compared with I/O. Prefer clarity unless a profiler shows otherwise.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a layered configuration lookup (command line, environment, file, default) built with or and orElse.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Fallback chain.

Worked Example 2

Empty orElseThrow.

Practice Exercise 1

The convenience methods.

Practice Exercise 2

Domain exception.

11. Quick Revision

  • isEmpty is the opposite of isPresent.
  • orElseThrow() replaces get().
  • or supplies a fallback Optional.
  • ifPresentOrElse handles both cases.
  • stream() turns it into 0 or 1 items.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Java 11 added Files.readString and Files.writeString for simple text files, and Path.of to create paths.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Reading or writing small text files used to need several lines of stream code.

3. Advantages

  • Short, readable code.
  • UTF-8 by default.
  • Works with NIO.2 Path.

4. Disadvantages

  • readString loads the whole file in memory.
  • Throws IOException.
  • No atomic write: a crash can leave a partial file.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used for configs and small files.
  • Interview topic.
  • Shows modern file I/O style.

6. Basic Concepts

Files Utility Methods in Java 11

Introduction

Java 11 added convenient methods to the java.nio.file.Files class for simple file read and write operations: readString() and writeString(). These methods eliminate the need for BufferedReader/BufferedWriter boilerplate for simple file I/O.

New Methods

  • Files.readString(Path) — Reads the whole file as a String (UTF-8 default)
  • Files.readString(Path, Charset) — Reads with the given charset
  • Files.writeString(Path, CharSequence, OpenOption...) — Writes a string to a file
  • Files.writeString(Path, CharSequence, Charset, OpenOption...) — Writes with the given charset

Key Features

  • One-line file read and write
  • Default UTF-8 encoding
  • Supports OpenOptions (CREATE, APPEND, TRUNCATE_EXISTING, etc.)

Fresher Notes

  • Simple text files: Java 11 added Files.readString(path) and Files.writeString(path, text).
  • Path.of: Path.of("a.txt") creates a path (replaces Paths.get).
  • Defaults: both use UTF-8 and throw IOException.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Files Utility Methods — Intermediate Usage

Using OpenOptions

You can control file writing behavior with StandardOpenOption values such as APPEND, CREATE_NEW, etc.

Working with Charsets

Both methods accept an explicit charset for non-UTF-8 files.

Combining with Other Java 11 Features

  • Use String.lines() for line-by-line processing
  • Use var for concise code
  • Use strip() to clean file content

Best Practices

  • Always handle IOException
  • Use readString() only for reasonably sized files
  • Pass the charset explicitly for non-UTF-8 files

Mid-Level Notes

  • Open options: writeString accepts StandardOpenOption.APPEND, CREATE, TRUNCATE_EXISTING.
  • Large files: use Files.lines(path), which streams lazily (close it).
  • Compare: Files.mismatch(a, b) (added in Java 12) returns the first differing position (-1 if equal).

8. Advanced Concepts

Files Utility Methods — Expert Deep Dive

Internal Implementation

  • readString() reads all bytes (like Files.readAllBytes()) and decodes them into a String
  • writeString() encodes the CharSequence to bytes and writes them like Files.write()
  • The default charset is UTF-8, whatever the platform default is

Comparison with Legacy Approaches

  • Legacy read: BufferedReader + FileReader + StringBuilder loop (5-10 lines)
  • Java 11 read: Files.readString(path), one line
  • Legacy write: BufferedWriter + FileWriter + write + close (5-8 lines)
  • Java 11 write: Files.writeString(path, content), one line

Missing Files and Atomic Writes

  • If the file does not exist, readString() throws NoSuchFileException
  • writeString() is not atomic: write a temp file, then move it with ATOMIC_MOVE

Senior Notes

  • Memory: readString holds the whole file in memory, so avoid it for very large files.
  • Atomic write: write a temp file, then Files.move with ATOMIC_MOVE.
  • Close streams: use try-with-resources for Files.lines, Files.list, Files.walk.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Robust file patterns: atomic replace (temp file + ATOMIC_MOVE), safe temp files (createTempFile with delete on exit or try-finally cleanup), directory walking (Files.walk, Files.find, walkFileTree), attributes (Files.getLastModifiedTime, readAttributes), permissions (POSIX) and file locking via FileChannel.lock, watching changes with WatchService, and symlink handling (NOFOLLOW_LINKS). Normalize and validate paths to prevent path traversal.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Files.readString reads all bytes and decodes them (it uses a fast path for UTF-8 and throws MalformedInputException for invalid bytes); writeString encodes and writes with the given OpenOptions (default: CREATE, TRUNCATE_EXISTING, WRITE). Files are accessed through the NIO.2 Path abstraction (file systems, including zip file systems), and operations like Files.copy and Files.move are native-assisted. Files.mismatch (Java 12 and later) compares contents efficiently.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: readString on huge files (OutOfMemoryError), forgetting to close Files.lines/walk/list streams (file handle leaks), platform default charsets in old APIs (FileReader), non-atomic overwrites (partial files after a crash), trusting user paths (path traversal), checking existence then acting (race: use the operation and handle exceptions), and string concatenation for paths (use resolve).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

I/O dominates cost: read big files by streaming (Files.newBufferedReader, Files.lines), write with buffers, use Files.copy for bulk copies, memory-map for random access, and avoid many tiny files. Large text processing should be incremental with constant memory.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a config reloader and an exporter that writes atomically so readers never see half-written files.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Missing file.

Worked Example 2

Charset.

Practice Exercise 1

Read, write, append.

Practice Exercise 2

Compare files and atomic write.

11. Quick Revision

  • readString and writeString.
  • APPEND option for appending.
  • Use Files.lines for big files.
  • Atomic write: temp file + move.
  • Path.of replaces Paths.get.

topics.name: Sealed Classes

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A sealed class or interface restricts which classes may extend or implement it using permits, with permitted subclasses being final, sealed or non-sealed.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Some domains have a fixed set of variants, such as payment types.
  • Sealing lets the compiler know all of them.

3. Advantages

  • Closed hierarchies.
  • Exhaustive switches without default.
  • Clear domain models.

4. Disadvantages

  • Less open for extension.
  • Library evolution needs care.
  • Permitted classes must be in the same module or package.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Modern Java modelling tool.
  • Interview topic for Java 17.
  • Works with records and pattern matching.

6. Basic Concepts

Sealed Classes in Java 17

Introduction

Sealed classes became a standard feature in Java 17. They let you restrict which classes or interfaces can extend or implement a given class or interface. This gives you fine-grained control over the class hierarchy.

Key Keywords

  • sealed — Declares a class or interface as sealed (restricted)
  • permits — Lists the allowed subclasses or implementations
  • non-sealed — A subclass that opens up further extension
  • final — A subclass that cannot be extended any more

Rules for Sealed Classes

  • Permitted subclasses must extend the sealed class directly
  • Each permitted subclass must be final, sealed, or non-sealed
  • Permitted subclasses must be in the same module (or the same package if there is no named module)
  • The compiler enforces the hierarchy at compile time

Fresher Notes

  • Sealed type: a class or interface that limits who may extend or implement it, for example sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {} (Java 17).
  • Subclass modifier: each permitted subclass must be final, sealed or non-sealed.
  • Location: permitted classes sit in the same module, or in the same package when there is no named module.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Sealed Classes — Intermediate Usage

Sealed Interfaces

Interfaces can also be sealed. This restricts which classes or interfaces can implement them.

Hierarchical Sealing

A permitted subclass of a sealed class can itself be sealed. This creates a controlled, multi-level hierarchy.

non-sealed Subclasses

Using non-sealed on a subclass lets anyone extend it. The hierarchy is open again at that point.

Best Practices

  • Use sealed classes for domain models with a fixed set of types (for example payment types or AST nodes)
  • Combine them with records for compact data types in the hierarchy
  • Prefer final subclasses unless extension is really needed
  • Use sealed classes to make pattern matching exhaustive

Mid-Level Notes

  • Exhaustive switch: sealed types give a closed set of subtypes, so a switch over them needs no default (pattern matching for switch is final in Java 21).
  • Algebraic data types: records plus sealed interfaces model "one of several shapes of data".
  • Omitting permits: if the permitted subclasses are in the same source file, permits may be left out.

8. Advanced Concepts

Sealed Classes — Expert Deep Dive

Internal Representation

  • The compiler stores the allowed subclasses in the PermittedSubclasses attribute of the class file
  • The JVM checks the sealed hierarchy when classes are loaded
  • Reflection API: Class.isSealed() and Class.getPermittedSubclasses()

Sealed Classes + Pattern Matching

Sealed classes allow exhaustive pattern matching in switch expressions (final in Java 21, preview in Java 17). The compiler knows all possible subtypes, so no default branch is needed.

Senior Notes

  • Domain modelling: use sealed hierarchies for states and results (Success/Failure, payment methods), interpreters and ASTs.
  • Safe change: adding a permitted subtype breaks every incomplete exhaustive switch, so you find all places to update.
  • Design choice: prefer sealed types over open inheritance when you control all variants; use non-sealed to reopen part of the hierarchy.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Sealed types plus records are called algebraic data types: a sum type (one of several variants) built from product types (records).

  • Typical models: expression trees (interpreters), commands and events, HTTP or RPC results.
  • State machines (Idle | Running | Failed) and error handling without exceptions (Result).
  • Exhaustive switches over sealed types often replace the Visitor pattern. They fail to compile when a variant is added.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The compiler records the PermittedSubclasses attribute in the class file. The JVM checks it when loading subclasses, and an unpermitted subclass fails with IncompatibleClassChangeError.

  • Permitted subclasses must be in the same module (or the same package when there is no named module).
  • They must directly extend the sealed class.
  • Each must be final, sealed or non-sealed (records and enums are implicitly final).
  • Reflection: Class.isSealed() and getPermittedSubclasses().

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Sealing a hierarchy that needs third-party extension.
  • Forgetting that permitted subclasses must be in the same module or package.
  • Making everything sealed, which makes the design rigid.
  • Leaving a default branch that hides new variants. You lose the compile-time check.
  • Adding variants to a public library type. Clients' switches break, so version carefully.
  • Mixing sealed types with proxy-based frameworks.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Sealed types add no run-time cost beyond a class-load check. Their main gain is clearer code, and the closed set of subtypes can also help the JIT. In Java 21, pattern switches compile to invokedynamic type switches, which are efficient and often better than long if-else chains.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an order lifecycle as a sealed hierarchy. Each state carries only valid data, so impossible states (shipped without an address) cannot be represented.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Unpermitted subclass.

Worked Example 2

Reopen with non-sealed.

Practice Exercise 1

Sealed hierarchy with exhaustive switch.

Practice Exercise 2

Result type.

11. Quick Revision

  • sealed ... permits A, B.
  • Subclasses: final, sealed or non-sealed.
  • Enables exhaustive switch.
  • Use for states and results.
  • Adding a variant breaks incomplete switches.

interviewQA: Why were sealed classes introduced?
To control inheritance precisely and to support exhaustive pattern matching
Can a sealed class be abstract?
Yes
What happens if a non-permitted class extends a sealed class?
Compilation error
How do sealed classes differ from final classes?
Final prevents all extension; sealed allows only the listed subclasses

topics.name: Pattern Matching for instanceof

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Pattern matching for instanceof tests a type and binds a typed variable in one step: if (o instanceof String s).

2. Need of This Topic

  • The old instanceof check followed by a cast was repetitive and error prone.

3. Advantages

  • No explicit casts.
  • Shorter equals and visitors.
  • Basis for switch patterns.

4. Disadvantages

  • Binding scope rules need care.
  • Overuse can take the place of cleaner polymorphism.
  • Generic types have restrictions.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used in modern code.
  • Interview topic.
  • Leads to switch and record patterns.

6. Basic Concepts

Pattern Matching for instanceof

Introduction

Java 16 finalized (JEP 394, after previews in Java 14 and 15) Pattern Matching for instanceof. It removes the explicit cast after an instanceof check. The type test and the cast become one expression.

Key Features

  • Combines the instanceof check and the cast into one step
  • Adds a pattern variable that is in scope when the pattern matches
  • Less boilerplate and fewer ClassCastException bugs
  • The scope of the pattern variable follows the flow of the program

Before vs After

  • Before: if (obj instanceof String) { String s = (String) obj; ... }
  • After: if (obj instanceof String s) { ... } - s is already cast.

Fresher Notes

  • Pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16) tests the type and binds a variable in one step: if (obj instanceof String s) { s.length(); }.
  • It removes the explicit cast after the check.
  • The binding variable is in scope only where the test is definitely true.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Pattern Matching for instanceof — Intermediate Usage

Scope of Pattern Variables

Pattern variables follow flow scoping. They are in scope only where the compiler can prove the pattern matched. This includes combined conditions with &&.

Using with Logical Operators

  • && - the variable is in scope in the right operand and in the if body
  • || - the variable is NOT in scope on the right side of a positive test (the match is not guaranteed)
  • ! - the variable is in scope in the else branch (and after an early return)

Simplifying equals() Method

Pattern matching makes the common equals() override much shorter.

Best Practices

  • Use pattern matching to simplify type-checking code
  • Combine with && for extra conditions
  • Use it in equals() methods for cleaner code
  • Avoid deep nesting that hurts readability

Mid-Level Notes

  • Extra conditions: if (o instanceof String s && s.length() > 3).
  • Negation with an early exit: if (!(o instanceof String s)) return; s.length(); (flow scoping).
  • equals: return o instanceof Point p && x == p.x; is short and null-safe.

8. Advanced Concepts

Pattern Matching for instanceof — Expert Deep Dive

How It Works Internally

  • The compiler generates essentially the same bytecode as a manual instanceof plus cast
  • Pattern variables are ordinary local variables in the bytecode
  • Flow scoping is a compile-time analysis only; there is no runtime overhead
  • The pattern variable is an ordinary NON-final local variable. JEP 394 dropped the implicit finality of the earlier previews, so it can be reassigned (this is discouraged)

Evolution of Pattern Matching in Java

  • Java 16: pattern matching for instanceof (JEP 394)
  • Java 17: sealed classes (JEP 409), which later allow exhaustive patterns
  • Java 21: pattern matching for switch (JEP 441) and record patterns (JEP 440)
  • Future: more kinds of deconstruction patterns

Senior Notes

  • Foundation: switch patterns and record patterns (Java 21) build on it.
  • Design: prefer polymorphism when you control the types; use patterns for sealed data and for types you cannot modify.
  • Generics: a pattern such as List<String> l compiles only when the cast is safe, for example from Collection<String>; from Object use List<?>.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Where it shines:

  • equals implementations
  • visiting unknown types (JSON values, AST nodes from libraries)
  • handling mixed collections
  • bridging into switch patterns and record patterns (Java 21: if (o instanceof Point(int x, int y)))

It complements polymorphism, it does not replace it: if you own the hierarchy, put behavior in the types.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

x instanceof T t compiles to an instanceof check plus a checked cast and assignment to the binding variable. The compiler tracks definite matching (flow scoping). The variable t is in scope:

  • in the true branch of the if
  • to the right of &&
  • after if (!(x instanceof T t)) return;
  • to the right of ||, when the left side is a negated test such as !(x instanceof T t) || t.ok()

The binding is a normal local variable (not final unless declared).

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • repeating the check and cast the old way
  • re-using the binding name in the same scope (compile error)
  • pattern variables that shadow fields
  • long instanceof chains where a switch pattern fits better
  • using patterns where an interface method would remove the type test
  • unchecked generic patterns: o instanceof List<String> l is an error unless the cast is provably safe

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

The generated code is the same as a manual instanceof plus cast, so there is no performance change. The JIT optimizes type checks well; for many alternatives, a switch pattern (Java 21) uses a type switch bootstrap that can be faster than sequential instanceof chains.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: handling events of different types from a library, and writing small null-safe equals implementations.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Scope.

Worked Example 2

Always-true pattern warning.

Practice Exercise 1

Binding and guards.

Practice Exercise 2

equals with patterns.

11. Quick Revision

  • x instanceof T t binds t.
  • Combine with &&.
  • Flow scoping after negated checks.
  • Great for equals.
  • Prefer polymorphism when you own the types.

interviewQA: What is flow scoping?
The compiler works out where a pattern variable is definitely matched, and makes it available only there.
Can pattern variables be reassigned?
Yes. They are not implicitly final.
Is there a performance difference?
No. The generated code is the same as instanceof plus a cast.
How does it work with null?
instanceof is always false for null, so the variable is never bound for null.

topics.name: Records

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A record is a concise immutable data class whose constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString are generated from its components.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Data carrier classes needed lots of boilerplate.
  • Records remove it.

3. Advantages

  • Very short code.
  • Immutable value semantics.
  • Work with pattern matching.

4. Disadvantages

  • Cannot extend classes or add instance fields.
  • Shallow immutability only.
  • Not suitable as JPA entities.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used for DTOs and keys.
  • Interview topic.
  • Core Java 17 feature.

6. Basic Concepts

Records in Java

Introduction

Records were a preview in Java 14 and final in Java 16 (so they are in the Java 17 LTS). A record is a short way to declare a class that only holds data. The data is shallowly immutable. The compiler writes the constructor, accessors, equals(), hashCode() and toString() for you.

Key Features

  • Compact syntax for data carrier classes
  • Auto-generated: canonical constructor, accessors, equals(), hashCode(), toString()
  • Implicitly final, so a record cannot be extended
  • Implicitly extends java.lang.Record
  • Components (fields) are implicitly private final
  • Immutable by default, but only shallowly (see the Mid-Level notes)

Basic Syntax

record ClassName(Type field1, Type field2) {}

This one line gives you a full class with constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString.

Fresher Notes

  • A record is a concise immutable data carrier: record Point(int x, int y) {} (final in Java 16).
  • The compiler generates the constructor, accessors (x(), y()), equals, hashCode and toString.
  • Record fields are private final; the class is implicitly final and extends java.lang.Record.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Records — Intermediate Usage

Compact Constructors

Records support compact constructors for validation. You do not write the parameter list or the field assignments. The fields are assigned automatically after the constructor body.

Custom Constructors

You can add other (non-canonical) constructors. Each one must call this(...) to reach the canonical constructor.

Records with Interfaces

Records can implement interfaces. This makes them a good fit for sealed hierarchies.

Local Records

A record can be declared inside a method to group temporary data.

Best Practices

  • Use records for DTOs and value objects
  • Use compact constructors for validation
  • Combine records with sealed interfaces
  • Prefer records over Lombok @Data for simple data classes

Mid-Level Notes

  • Add validation in a compact constructor: Point { if (x < 0) throw ...; }.
  • Allowed: extra methods, static members and interfaces. Not allowed: instance fields and extends.
  • Shallow immutability: if a component is a mutable list, copy it with List.copyOf.

8. Advanced Concepts

Records — Expert Deep Dive

Internal Implementation

  • Records compile to final classes extending java.lang.Record
  • The compiler generates equals(), hashCode() and toString() with invokedynamic (the ObjectMethods bootstrap)
  • Accessors simply return the field
  • A record is serializable only if it implements Serializable. Deserialization always calls the canonical constructor, so your validation runs again

Limitations of Records

  • Cannot extend other classes (they already extend Record)
  • Cannot declare instance fields beyond the components
  • Components are final, so there are no setters
  • Cannot be abstract
  • Cannot declare native methods

Senior Notes

  • Use for DTOs, value objects, map keys, tuples and results. Avoid for JPA entities (they need a no-arg constructor and mutability).
  • Frameworks: Jackson (2.12+), Spring and others support records.
  • Local records are handy for intermediate stream results.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Good uses

  • DTOs and API responses (Jackson 2.12+ supports records)
  • Keys in maps and sets
  • Tuples and intermediate stream results (local records)
  • Events, commands and immutable configuration
  • Record patterns such as case Point(int x, int y) (Java 21)
  • With-style copies: write withX methods yourself, because records have no built-in withers

Avoid records for entities with identity and lifecycle (JPA), classes with many optional fields (use a builder), and classes that need inheritance.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

A record compiles to a final class extending java.lang.Record. It has private final fields, a canonical constructor and accessor methods. Its equals, hashCode and toString use invokedynamic (the ObjectMethods bootstrap).

  • The compact constructor runs before the fields are assigned and may reassign the parameters.
  • Records can implement interfaces and declare static members, nested types, annotations and generic parameters.
  • Class.getRecordComponents() lists the components at run time.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes

  • Mutable components (arrays, lists) break immutability. Copy them in the compact constructor.
  • Arrays use identity in the generated equals. Override equals or use a List.
  • Overriding an accessor so it behaves differently from the field surprises callers.
  • Frameworks that expect a no-arg constructor, or JPA entities, do not work with records.
  • Sensitive fields appear in the generated toString. Override it.
  • Adding or removing components changes the serialized form (deserialization uses the canonical constructor).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

  • Records are normal objects: allocation and field access cost the same as a handwritten class.
  • The generated equals and hashCode are efficient (method handles).
  • Immutable records are safe and cheap to share between threads.
  • Project Valhalla may later allow value records without identity, for a flatter memory layout.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world uses: API layer DTOs, immutable events in an event-driven system, and cache keys with composite fields.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Cannot add instance fields.

Worked Example 2

Local record in a stream.

Practice Exercise 1

Record with validation and method.

Practice Exercise 2

Defensive copy.

11. Quick Revision

  • record Point(int x, int y) {}.
  • Compact constructor for validation.
  • Copy mutable components.
  • Implements interfaces.
  • equals and hashCode use all components.

interviewQA: Can records be mutable?
The fields cannot be reassigned, but a mutable component (for example a List) can still change. Use defensive copies.
Can records extend classes?
No. They implicitly extend java.lang.Record.
How is equals() generated?
With invokedynamic and the ObjectMethods bootstrap, comparing all components.
Are records suitable for JPA entities?
No. JPA needs a no-arg constructor and mutable fields. Records are best for DTOs.

topics.name: Switch Expressions

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A switch expression returns a value, using arrows (->) with no fall-through and yield for blocks.

2. Need of This Topic

  • The old switch statement needed breaks and temporary variables, causing bugs.

3. Advantages

  • Concise and safe.
  • Must be exhaustive.
  • Multiple labels per case.

4. Disadvantages

  • Needs default for non-enum types.
  • Mixing old and new styles is not allowed.
  • Requires Java 14 or later.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Everyday modern Java.
  • Interview topic.
  • Basis for pattern switches.

6. Basic Concepts

Switch Expressions in Java

Introduction

Switch expressions were finalized in Java 14 and are a core part of Java 17. They extend the traditional switch statement: it can return a value, use arrow syntax, and avoid fall-through bugs.

Key Features

  • Arrow syntax (->) — No fall-through, no break needed
  • Returns a value — Switch can be used as an expression
  • yield keyword — Returns a value from a block in switch expression
  • Multiple labels — Comma-separated case values
  • Exhaustiveness — Compiler ensures all cases are covered when used as expression

Old Switch vs New Switch

  • Old: switch statement with break, fall-through risk
  • New: switch expression with arrows, no fall-through, returns value

Fresher Notes

  • Switch expression (Java 14): produces a value, e.g. String s = switch (day) { case 1, 7 -> "weekend"; default -> "weekday"; };.
  • Arrow form (->): no fall-through and no break needed.
  • Multiple labels per case: case 1, 2, 3 ->.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Switch Expressions — Intermediate Usage

The yield Keyword

When a case in a switch expression needs a block of code (not just a single expression), use yield to return the value from that block.

Switch Expressions with Enums

Switch expressions work naturally with enums and can be exhaustive without a default case if all enum constants are covered.

Combining Arrows and Blocks

You can mix single-expression arrows with block arrows that use yield.

Best Practices

  • Prefer arrow syntax over colon syntax for new code
  • Use switch expressions instead of if-else chains for type mapping
  • Let the compiler check exhaustiveness — avoid unnecessary default cases with enums
  • Use yield in blocks, not break

Mid-Level Notes

  • yield: returns a value from a block, e.g. case 5 -> { log(); yield "five"; }.
  • Exhaustive: cover all values, or add default (enums and sealed types can skip it when every constant or subtype is covered).
  • Colon syntax (case X:) can also be an expression, but it needs yield and it still falls through.

8. Advanced Concepts

Switch Expressions — Expert Deep Dive

Bytecode and Internal Handling

  • Arrow-form switch compiles to the same kind of bytecode as the traditional switch (tableswitch/lookupswitch)
  • The compiler eliminates fall-through at the source level
  • yield compiles similar to a labeled break with a value assignment
  • Exhaustiveness is checked at compile time; the compiler also adds a hidden default that throws an error (IncompatibleClassChangeError, or MatchException in Java 21) if an enum changes later

Switch Expressions vs if-else Chains

  • Switch expressions use tableswitch/lookupswitch for O(1) dispatch
  • If-else chains use sequential comparison — O(n)
  • Switch expressions are more readable for multi-way branching

Senior Notes

  • Safer code: no missing-break bugs and no unassigned variables.
  • Enums: skip default so adding a constant gives a compile error where it is not handled.
  • Impossible cases: throw in the branch, e.g. default -> throw new IllegalStateException();.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Idioms:

  • Replace if-else ladders and maps of lambdas with switch expressions.
  • Return directly: return switch ....
  • Use multiple labels, and throw in the default branch.
  • Combine with enums and sealed interfaces; add guards (when) and patterns in Java 21.
  • Keep branch bodies short; delegate to methods.
  • Arrow and colon forms cannot be mixed in one switch.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

How it works inside:

  • Compiles to tableswitch or lookupswitch (enums via ordinal mapping, strings via hashCode then equals) and pushes the result on the stack.
  • Arrow cases have no fall-through; a block case must yield a value on every path.
  • The compiler checks exhaustiveness: enums and sealed types need every constant or subtype, otherwise a default is required.
  • If an enum gains a constant after compilation (separate compilation), a MatchException (Java 21) or IncompatibleClassChangeError (older) is thrown at run time.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Forgetting yield in a block.
  • Mixing colon and arrow styles in one switch.
  • Adding a default that hides a missing enum case (you lose compile-time exhaustiveness).
  • Relying on fall-through in the colon form by accident.
  • Side effects in cases that obscure the computed value.
  • A null selector throws NullPointerException. Check for null first, or use case null (Java 21).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Same as the old switch: dense int cases use a jump table, strings use hash lookups.
  • Pattern switches use a type-switch call site that caches the dispatch.
  • Prefer switch to long if-else chains for readability; the order of cases rarely matters.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: mapping HTTP status classes, parsing commands, computing prices per tier, and converting enums to display text without scattered ifs.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Not exhaustive.

Worked Example 2

Old style with yield.

Practice Exercise 1

Value-producing switch.

Practice Exercise 2

Throwing for impossible cases.

11. Quick Revision

  • case A, B -> value.
  • No break, no fall-through.
  • yield returns from blocks.
  • Exhaustive: all cases covered.
  • Throw in impossible branches.

interviewQA: Difference between yield and return?
yield returns a value from a switch expression block; return exits the method
Can switch expressions have side effects?
Yes, but the primary purpose is to produce a value
What if a new enum constant is added?
Compiler error for non-exhaustive switch expression, ensuring safety
Can null be used as a case label?
In Java 21 with pattern matching, yes. Before that, null causes NullPointerException

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • A text block is a multi-line string literal delimited by triple double quotes, with automatic indentation handling.

2. Need of This Topic

  • JSON, SQL and HTML written with escapes and concatenation are hard to read.

3. Advantages

  • Readable multi-line text.
  • No escaping of quotes.
  • Works with formatted().

4. Disadvantages

  • Indentation rules need learning.
  • SQL injection risk if values are formatted in.
  • Trailing spaces are removed.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Used for SQL, JSON and HTML.
  • Interview topic.
  • Improves test readability.

6. Basic Concepts

Text Blocks in Java

Introduction

Text blocks were introduced as a preview in Java 13 and finalized in Java 15 (so they are available in Java 17 LTS). They let you write multi-line string literals between triple double quotes ("""). This makes it easy to embed HTML, JSON, SQL, and other formatted text.

Key Features

  • Multi-line strings without concatenation or \n escape sequences
  • Automatic indentation handling
  • Triple-quote delimiters: """text"""
  • The opening """ must be followed by a line terminator
  • The closing """ position decides how much indentation is stripped

Benefits

  • Much better readability for embedded code or data
  • Less string concatenation boilerplate
  • Common indentation is removed automatically
  • All old escape sequences work, plus two new ones

Fresher Notes

  • Text block: a multi-line string literal between triple quotes, """ ... """ (final in Java 15).
  • No escapes needed: no \n and no escaped quotes, so JSON, SQL and HTML look as they are.
  • Opening delimiter: the opening """ must be followed by a newline.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Text Blocks — Intermediate Usage

Indentation Management

The position of the closing """ determines how much leading whitespace is stripped. Moving it left or right changes the indentation of the resulting string.

Escape Sequences

  • \s — keeps trailing whitespace (a space fence)
  • \ (backslash at end of line) — suppresses the newline (line continuation)
  • All traditional escapes work: \n, \t, \", \\

String Methods with Text Blocks

Text blocks produce regular String objects, so all String methods work: formatted(), replace(), indent(), stripIndent().

Best Practices

  • Align the closing """ with the content for clean output
  • Use text blocks for HTML, JSON, SQL, XML, and regex patterns
  • Use formatted() or String.format() for parameterized text blocks
  • Prefer text blocks over multi-line string concatenation

Mid-Level Notes

  • Incidental indentation is stripped, based on the least indented line and the closing delimiter position.
  • Escapes: \n and \""" work; a trailing backslash joins lines; \s keeps a trailing space.
  • Values: use .formatted(args) to insert them.

8. Advanced Concepts

Text Blocks — Expert Deep Dive

How Indentation Stripping Works

  • The compiler finds the minimum common indentation across all content lines and the closing """
  • This minimum indentation is stripped from every line
  • The same algorithm is available as String.stripIndent()
  • Trailing whitespace on each line is also removed (unless \s is used)

Compilation

  • Text blocks are compile-time constants, interned like regular string literals
  • In bytecode, a text block is a regular String constant (ldc instruction)
  • Indent stripping and escape handling happen at compile time, not runtime

Quick Questions

  • Q: Are text blocks a new type? — No, they produce regular java.lang.String objects
  • Q: How is indentation determined? — By the minimum leading whitespace common to all lines and the closing """
  • Q: Can text blocks be used in annotations? — Yes, since they are compile-time constants
  • Q: What is the \s escape? — A "space fence" that prevents trailing whitespace stripping
  • Q: Performance impact? — None at runtime; all processing is at compile time

Senior Notes

  • Good uses: embedded SQL, JSON, HTML, XML and regex-like text. For SQL values, use prepared statements, not formatted.
  • Line endings are normalized to \n.
  • Same processing is exposed for regular strings by stripIndent() and translateEscapes().

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Typical uses: embedded SQL, JSON, XML or HTML templates, GraphQL queries, shell snippets, and expected output in tests. Combine them with formatted, String.format, stripIndent and translateEscapes. Java 21 string templates were only a preview and have since been removed, so use formatted. For HTML or SQL, never concatenate untrusted data: bind parameters or escape it.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Text block processing (JLS 3.10.6) happens at compile time: line terminators are normalized to \n, incidental whitespace is removed (the smallest indentation among non-blank lines and the closing delimiter line), trailing spaces on each line are stripped, then escape sequences are interpreted. New escapes: \<newline> (line continuation) and \s (space). The result is an ordinary interned String constant.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Forgetting the newline after the opening delimiter.
  • Misjudging indentation: the closing """ position changes stripping.
  • Mixing tabs and spaces.
  • Expecting trailing spaces to stay: they are removed silently. Use \s to keep them.
  • Embedding unescaped triple quotes.
  • Building SQL with formatted from user input.
  • Relying on \r\n: it is normalized to \n.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Text blocks are compile-time constants, so they cost no more at run time than concatenation. Large embedded resources (megabytes) belong in files loaded at runtime (classpath resources), not in source.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a repository with readable multi-line SQL and prepared statement parameters, and JSON fixtures in tests.

10. Examples
