Closing delimiter controls indentation.

Worked Example 2

SQL injection warning.

Practice Exercise 1

JSON and SQL.

Practice Exercise 2

Escapes and joining.

11. Quick Revision

  • Opening delimiter then newline.
  • Common indentation is removed.
  • \s keeps a space; trailing backslash joins lines.
  • Use formatted() for values.
  • Use PreparedStatement for SQL values.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Virtual threads (Java 21) are lightweight threads managed by the JVM, so millions can run while blocking code stays simple.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Thread-per-request code scales poorly with platform threads.
  • Virtual threads keep the simple model and scale like async code.

3. Advantages

  • Massive concurrency.
  • Simple blocking code.
  • Easy migration (Spring Boot 3.2 property).

4. Disadvantages

  • No benefit for CPU-bound work.
  • Pinning with long synchronized blocks.
  • ThreadLocal usage can grow memory.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Major Java 21 feature.
  • Interview topic.
  • Changes how servers are designed.

6. Basic Concepts

Virtual Threads in Java 21

Introduction

Virtual Threads (Project Loom) are a major feature of Java 21 that introduces lightweight, JVM-managed threads. Unlike traditional platform threads (which map 1:1 to OS threads), virtual threads are cheap to create and can number in the millions, enabling massive concurrency.

Key Features

  • Lightweight — Virtual threads consume very little memory (~few KB vs ~1MB for platform threads)
  • JVM-managed — The JVM schedules virtual threads on a small pool of platform (carrier) threads
  • Massive scalability — Create millions of virtual threads without running out of resources
  • Same Thread API — Virtual threads implement java.lang.Thread, so existing code works
  • Blocking is cheap — When a virtual thread blocks (I/O, sleep), the carrier thread is freed

Creating Virtual Threads

  • Thread.ofVirtual().start(runnable) — Start a virtual thread
  • Thread.startVirtualThread(runnable) — Shorthand to start
  • Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() — Executor for virtual threads

Fresher Notes

  • Virtual threads (Java 21) are lightweight threads managed by the JVM, not the OS. You can run millions of them.
  • Create one with Thread.ofVirtual().start(runnable), Thread.startVirtualThread(r) or Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().
  • Simple code: write plain blocking code (one thread per request) that scales like asynchronous code.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Virtual Threads — Intermediate Usage

Using with ExecutorService

The Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() creates an executor that spawns a new virtual thread for each submitted task, combining the convenience of executors with virtual thread efficiency.

Virtual Threads with I/O Operations

Virtual threads excel at I/O-bound workloads. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, its carrier thread is released to run other virtual threads.

Structured Concurrency (Preview)

Java 21 also previews StructuredTaskScope for managing groups of related virtual threads as a unit.

Best Practices

  • Use virtual threads for I/O-bound tasks (HTTP calls, database queries, file I/O)
  • Don't use virtual threads for CPU-bound tasks — use platform threads or ForkJoinPool
  • Avoid thread-local variables in virtual threads (use scoped values instead)
  • Don't pool virtual threads — create new ones as needed
  • Avoid synchronized blocks in virtual thread code (use ReentrantLock instead)

Mid-Level Notes

  • Unmounting: when a virtual thread blocks on I/O, sleep or a lock, the JVM unmounts it from its carrier (platform) thread so the carrier runs other virtual threads.
  • No pooling: create one per task; limit concurrency with a Semaphore if a resource is limited.
  • I/O-bound work is the best fit; CPU-bound work gains nothing over platform threads.

8. Advanced Concepts

Virtual Threads — Expert Deep Dive

Internal Architecture

  • Virtual threads are scheduled on a ForkJoinPool of carrier threads (default: number of CPUs)
  • When a virtual thread blocks (I/O, sleep, lock), it is unmounted from the carrier thread
  • The carrier thread then picks up another virtual thread to run
  • When the blocking operation completes, the virtual thread is remounted on an available carrier
  • This is called continuation-based scheduling

Pinning

A virtual thread is pinned to its carrier thread when:

  • Inside a synchronized block/method (use ReentrantLock instead)
  • Executing a native method or foreign function

Pinning prevents the carrier from running other virtual threads, reducing throughput.

Interview Questions

  • Q: Virtual threads vs platform threads? — Virtual threads are JVM-managed, lightweight (KB not MB), designed for I/O-bound tasks at massive scale
  • Q: What is pinning? — When a virtual thread cannot be unmounted (e.g., in synchronized), blocking the carrier
  • Q: Should you pool virtual threads? — No, they are cheap to create. Pooling defeats their purpose
  • Q: Are virtual threads faster? — Not faster per-thread, but allow much higher concurrency by not wasting OS threads on blocking operations

Senior Notes

  • Pinning: avoid long synchronized blocks around blocking calls (pinning the carrier in Java 21); prefer ReentrantLock.
  • ThreadLocal works but uses memory per thread; prefer scoped values or pass context explicitly.
  • Frameworks (Spring Boot 3.2+, Tomcat, Jetty) can run requests on virtual threads with one configuration property.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

The programming model is simple: one thread per task, no pools, plain blocking code. Use try-with-resources on the executor so it waits for all tasks. For related subtasks, StructuredTaskScope (preview in Java 21) forks them together and cancels the rest if one fails. Use scoped values (preview) instead of ThreadLocal. Diagnose with jcmd Thread.dump_to_file -format=json and the JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

A virtual thread is a java.lang.Thread whose stack is stored in the heap as stack-chunk objects. The scheduler is a ForkJoinPool of carrier threads (default size = cores). On a blocking call (socket read, sleep, LockSupport.park, ReentrantLock) the JVM unmounts the virtual thread, copying its frames to the heap, and the carrier runs another one; when the operation completes the thread is rescheduled and remounted. Blocking in synchronized or native frames pins the carrier (Java 21; improved in later releases).

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and their fixes. Do not pool virtual threads. Do not use them for CPU-bound loops. Do not let unlimited threads hit one database: limit with a semaphore or connection pool. Avoid heavy ThreadLocal caches, because millions of threads multiply them. Priority and daemon status are fixed, so do not rely on them. On Java 21, replace a synchronized block that wraps I/O with ReentrantLock.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Little's Law says concurrency = rate x latency. Virtual threads let you hold 100,000 or more waiting tasks at once. They do not make code faster. They only remove the thread-count ceiling. Each one costs only its live stack (a few KB). The real limits become downstream resources such as DB connections and rate limits, so protect them explicitly. Measure with a load test.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

A web service calls two backends per request. With virtual threads each request is plain blocking code. A semaphore protects the payment gateway, and Spring Boot turns virtual threads on with one property.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Limit concurrency with a Semaphore.

Worked Example 2

Spring Boot 3.2.

Practice Exercise 1

10,000 blocking tasks.

Practice Exercise 2

Create and inspect.

11. Quick Revision

  • One virtual thread per task, no pools.
  • They unmount while blocked.
  • Limit resources with Semaphore.
  • Avoid pinning: prefer ReentrantLock.
  • Great for I/O-bound services.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Record patterns deconstruct a record in instanceof and switch, binding its components to variables, and can be nested.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Extracting fields from nested data with accessor calls is verbose.
  • Patterns do it declaratively.

3. Advantages

  • Concise data extraction.
  • Nested patterns.
  • Works with sealed types.

4. Disadvantages

  • Only for records.
  • Deep nesting can hurt readability.
  • Needs Java 21 or later.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Modern data-oriented Java.
  • Common interview topic.
  • Replaces many visitor classes.

6. Basic Concepts

Record Patterns in Java 21

Introduction

Record Patterns (finalized in Java 21, JEP 440) allow you to destructure record values directly in pattern matching. Instead of matching a record and then manually extracting its components, you can extract (deconstruct) the components inline.

Key Features

  • Destructure records directly in instanceof and switch patterns
  • Extract component values without calling accessor methods
  • Can be nested for deep destructuring
  • Works with sealed hierarchies for exhaustive matching

Basic Syntax

  • if (obj instanceof Point(var x, var y)) — extracts x and y from Point record
  • case Point(var x, var y) — same in switch
  • Components are bound to local variables for immediate use

Fresher Notes

  • Deconstruction: a record pattern (Java 21) splits a record in instanceof and switch, as in if (o instanceof Point(int x, int y)).
  • Binding: the components go into variables in one step, so you do not call accessors.
  • Nesting: patterns can contain patterns, as in Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)).

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Record Patterns — Intermediate Usage

Record Patterns in Switch

Record patterns work in switch expressions and statements, enabling powerful multi-way destructuring.

Combining with Guards

Use when guards with record patterns to add conditions on the destructured values.

Working with Sealed Hierarchies

Record patterns combined with sealed interfaces enable exhaustive, type-safe pattern matching.

Best Practices

  • Use var for type inference in record patterns when the type is obvious
  • Leverage nested patterns for deep data structures
  • Combine with sealed types for exhaustive matching
  • Use guard clauses (when) for conditional matching

Mid-Level Notes

  • Type inference: var in a pattern infers the component type.
  • Switch and guards: use case Circle(double r) -> ... and add conditions with when.
  • Matching rule: a record pattern matches only if the value has the record type and the nested patterns match. A null value never matches.

8. Advanced Concepts

Record Patterns — Expert Deep Dive

Internal Mechanism

  • Record patterns use the record's canonical deconstruction — calling accessor methods in order
  • The compiler generates instanceof checks followed by accessor calls
  • Nested patterns generate chained checks and extractions
  • Type inference (var) in patterns uses the record component's declared type

Pattern Matching Completeness

  • With sealed types, the compiler performs exhaustiveness analysis
  • Each permitted subtype's record components are known at compile time
  • No default/catch-all branch needed when all subtypes are covered

Interview Questions

  • Q: How do record patterns differ from regular pattern matching? — Record patterns add destructuring, extracting components inline rather than just binding the whole object
  • Q: Can record patterns be nested? — Yes, to any depth, for deep destructuring
  • Q: Do record patterns work with non-record classes? — No, only with records that have a well-defined canonical constructor
  • Q: Performance impact? — Minimal; compiles to normal accessor calls with type checks

Senior Notes

  • Sealed types: with sealed interfaces, record patterns give concise, exhaustive code. Visitors become switches.
  • Nested patterns: they replace chains of accessor calls and null-unsafe navigation.
  • Generic records: type arguments are inferred in patterns.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Common uses:

  • Interpreters and compilers: evaluate an expression tree (AST).
  • Transformations: simplify expressions.
  • Routing: match on command records.
  • Validation: nested checks on data.
  • Tuples: generic records such as Pair<A,B>.
  • Visitor replacement: a switch instead of visitor classes.

Combine them with guards (when) and var for brevity. Unnamed patterns (_, final in Java 22) ignore components you do not need.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Record patterns compile to calls of the record's accessor methods after a type test, with nested patterns tested recursively; if an accessor throws, the exception is wrapped in MatchException. The compiler checks that patterns are exhaustive for sealed record hierarchies, including nested ones: all combinations of component types must be covered.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes to avoid:

  • Forgetting that a custom accessor runs during matching.
  • Expecting a nested type pattern to match a null component. Only a total pattern, such as var, matches null.
  • Using patterns on non-record classes (not supported).
  • Writing huge nested patterns that are hard to read.
  • Relying on the order of accessors that have side effects.
  • Not covering every nested combination (compile error with sealed types).

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Compiled record patterns are efficient: type checks plus accessor calls, with no reflection. The switch dispatch for a sealed hierarchy uses a type switch with a cached call site. The cost is similar to hand-written instanceof chains but with exhaustiveness guarantees.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: handling domain events and commands as records and switching over them. New event types force every handler switch to be updated by the compiler.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Null does not match.

Worked Example 2

Generic record pattern.

Practice Exercise 1

Deconstruction in if and switch.

Practice Exercise 2

Sealed + record patterns.

11. Quick Revision

  • if (o instanceof Point(int x, int y)).
  • Nested record patterns.
  • var infers component types.
  • null never matches.
  • Combine with sealed interfaces.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Pattern matching for switch (Java 21) allows type patterns, guards with when, case null and exhaustive checking over sealed types.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Long instanceof chains are verbose.
  • A pattern switch handles several types in one readable construct.

3. Advantages

  • Readable multi-type handling.
  • Compiler checks exhaustiveness.
  • Guards add conditions.

4. Disadvantages

  • Case order matters (dominance).
  • Null needs explicit handling.
  • Requires Java 21.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Core Java 21 feature.
  • Interview topic.
  • Pairs with sealed and records.

6. Basic Concepts

Pattern Matching for Switch in Java 21

Introduction

Pattern Matching for Switch (JEP 441, final in Java 21) lets a switch test patterns, not just constants. You can match types, take records apart, add guards, and handle null, all inside one switch.

Key Features

  • Type patterns — match and cast in one step: case String s
  • Record patterns — take a record apart: case Point(var x, var y)
  • Guarded patterns — add a condition: case String s when s.length() > 5
  • Null handling — an explicit null case: case null
  • Exhaustiveness — with sealed types the compiler checks that every subtype is covered

Before vs After

  • Before: long if-else instanceof chains
  • After: one clean switch with type patterns

Fresher Notes

  • Type pattern: in Java 21 a case label can test a type: case String s -> ....
  • Guard: add a condition with when: case Integer i when i > 10 -> ....
  • Null and exhaustive: match null with case null. The switch must cover every possible value.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Pattern Matching for Switch — Intermediate Usage

Guarded Patterns

The when keyword adds a condition (guard) to a pattern. The case matches only if both the pattern and the guard are true.

Dominance and Order

More specific patterns must come before general ones. The compiler enforces dominance rules: a dominated case can never run, so it is a compile error.

Null Handling

A switch used to throw NullPointerException for a null selector. Now you can handle null explicitly with case null.

Best Practices

  • Order cases from most specific to most general
  • Use when guards instead of nested if statements
  • Always handle null explicitly if the input can be null
  • Use sealed types to get exhaustiveness checks

Mid-Level Notes

  • Order matters: put specific cases (with guards) before general ones, or the compiler reports a dominated label.
  • Sealed types, enums, records: no default is needed when all subtypes are covered.
  • Selector type: it can be any reference type, not just strings, enums and integers.

8. Advanced Concepts

Pattern Matching for Switch — Expert Deep Dive

Dominance Rules

  • A pattern p dominates pattern q if every value matching q also matches p
  • case Object o dominates all type patterns
  • case String s dominates case String s when ...
  • The dominating (general) case must come after the dominated (specific) one. If the general case is first, the specific case below it is unreachable and the compiler reports an error

Completeness Analysis

  • For sealed types, the compiler knows all permitted subtypes
  • For enums, all constants are known
  • The compiler adds a hidden default that throws MatchException (not IllegalStateException) if an unexpected value appears at run time

Performance

  • A pattern switch is compiled to an invokedynamic type switch, which picks the matching case at run time
  • The JVM can optimize it, and it is usually as fast as an instanceof chain

Senior Notes

  • Replaces long if-else instanceof chains and some visitor patterns.
  • Qualified enum constants can be case labels in pattern switches (case Color.RED).
  • Sealed interfaces: adding a subtype makes every non-exhaustive switch fail to compile.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax options you can combine:

  • Qualified enum constants mixed with patterns (case Status.ACTIVE), including sealed interfaces that enums implement.
  • Generic sealed hierarchies such as Result<T>, and nested record patterns.
  • yield inside block cases.

A sealed hierarchy plus a pattern switch can replace the Visitor pattern. You get the same exhaustiveness with far less code.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

A pattern switch compiles to an invokedynamic call to SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch. It returns the index of the first matching case, and is called again with a restart index when a guard fails.

  • Dominance: a label is dominated if an earlier label matches every value it could match, such as an unguarded general type before a specific one.
  • Exhaustiveness: every possible value must be covered. For sealed hierarchies that means all permitted subtypes. Otherwise add a default or a total pattern.
  • Null: a null selector throws NullPointerException unless case null exists.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • A general pattern placed before a specific one (dominance error).
  • A default on a sealed type, which turns off exhaustiveness checks.
  • Forgetting case null when null is possible (NPE).
  • Guards with side effects, because guards may be evaluated again in an unexpected order.
  • Using patterns where a polymorphic method is simpler.
  • Expecting fall-through: a pattern case cannot fall into another case that has bindings.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

The type switch call site can cache the last match and the JIT can inline it. For a few cases it is about as fast as an instanceof chain, and for many cases it can scale better. Guards run in order, so keep them cheap. Avoid allocating objects inside patterns in hot paths.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world uses: an API client mapping responses of different shapes, a rules engine, and a compiler front end. Exhaustive switches over sealed types act as compile-time checklists when new variants arrive.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Dominated label.

Worked Example 2

NullPointerException.

Practice Exercise 1

Types, guards and null.

Practice Exercise 2

Exhaustive sealed switch.

11. Quick Revision

  • case Type t when condition.
  • case null handles null.
  • Specific cases first.
  • Sealed types need no default.
  • Compiles to an efficient type switch.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • Sequenced collections (Java 21) add a common API to collections with a defined order: getFirst, getLast, addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast and reversed.

2. Need of This Topic

  • Accessing the first or last element and reversing differed for List, Deque, LinkedHashSet and others.

3. Advantages

  • Uniform API.
  • reversed() is a cheap view.
  • Less boilerplate.

4. Disadvantages

  • getFirst on empty throws.
  • HashSet and HashMap are not sequenced.
  • Custom collections may clash with new methods.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Java 21 interview topic.
  • Simplifies common code.
  • Helps LRU cache and history code.

6. Basic Concepts

Sequenced Collections in Java 21

Introduction

Java 21 introduces Sequenced Collections (JEP 431). These are new interfaces for collections that have a defined encounter order (the order in which you meet the elements). They add the same methods to get the first and last element and to get a reversed view.

New Interfaces

  • SequencedCollection<E> — extends Collection, adds first/last access and a reversed view
  • SequencedSet<E> — extends SequencedCollection and Set
  • SequencedMap<K,V> — extends Map, adds first/last entry access and a reversed view

Key Methods on SequencedCollection

  • getFirst() — get the first element
  • getLast() — get the last element
  • addFirst(E) — add an element at the beginning
  • addLast(E) — add an element at the end
  • removeFirst() — remove and return the first element
  • removeLast() — remove and return the last element
  • reversed() — return a reversed view of the collection

Fresher Notes

  • Sequenced collections (Java 21) give ordered collections one common API: first, last, add at the ends and a reversed view.
  • New interfaces: SequencedCollection, SequencedSet, SequencedMap. They are implemented by List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, LinkedHashMap, TreeSet and TreeMap.
  • Methods: getFirst(), getLast(), addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast, reversed().

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Sequenced Collections — Intermediate Usage

Interface Hierarchy

  • List and Deque now extend SequencedCollection
  • LinkedHashSet and SortedSet now implement SequencedSet
  • LinkedHashMap and SortedMap now implement SequencedMap

The Problem Solved

Before Java 21 there was no common way to:

  • get the last element of a List, a SortedSet and a LinkedHashSet
  • get a reversed view of an ordered collection

Each collection had different methods or needed workarounds.

SequencedMap Methods

  • firstEntry() / lastEntry() — get the first or last Map.Entry
  • pollFirstEntry() / pollLastEntry() — remove and return the first or last entry
  • putFirst(K, V) / putLast(K, V) — insert at the beginning or end
  • reversed() — reversed view of the map
  • sequencedKeySet() / sequencedValues() / sequencedEntrySet() — sequenced views of keys, values and entries

Mid-Level Notes

  • Live view: reversed() returns a view in reverse order, and changes show through both ways.
  • Old way: before Java 21 you wrote list.get(list.size() - 1), with different code for each collection type.
  • Map methods: SequencedMap adds firstEntry, lastEntry, pollFirstEntry, putFirst, putLast and sequencedKeySet.

8. Advanced Concepts

Sequenced Collections — Expert Deep Dive

Design Rationale

Before Java 21, getting the last element needed different code for each type:

  • List: list.get(list.size() - 1)
  • SortedSet: sortedSet.last()
  • Deque: deque.getLast()
  • LinkedHashSet: no direct method (you had to loop or copy)

Sequenced Collections unify all of these with a single getLast() method.

Implementation Details

  • reversed() returns a view, not a copy: changes to the original show in the reversed view
  • Default implementations exist in the interfaces and use existing methods
  • Specific classes (for example ArrayList) can override them for better performance
  • Unmodifiable collections return unmodifiable reversed views

Senior Notes

  • Empty collection: getFirst() on an empty list throws NoSuchElementException, so check for emptiness.
  • Immutable lists: List.of lists are sequenced, but the changing methods throw UnsupportedOperationException.
  • Not sequenced: HashSet and HashMap have no defined order.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Common use cases:

  • LRU caches (LinkedHashMap with pollFirstEntry), history (last N items), playlists and undo stacks.
  • Reverse loops without copying: for (var x : list.reversed()).
  • Streams over a reversed view: list.reversed().stream().
  • Utility code that works on any ordered collection.
  • LinkedHashMap.putFirst and putLast move entries to the ends.

Before Java 21, Collections.reverse changed the list itself, so you needed new ArrayList(list) copies.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

JEP 431 added three new interfaces and retrofitted the existing collections to use them:

  • SequencedCollection<E> extends Collection and holds reversed, addFirst/addLast, getFirst/getLast and removeFirst/removeLast.
  • SequencedSet and SequencedMap are the Set and Map versions.
  • List, Deque, LinkedHashSet and SortedSet/NavigableSet are sequenced collections.
  • LinkedHashMap and SortedMap/NavigableMap are sequenced maps.
  • reversed() returns a view, and the reversed view of an immutable collection is also immutable.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Assuming HashSet or HashMap are sequenced.
  • Calling getFirst on an empty collection without a check.
  • Changing a collection while looping over its reversed view.
  • Expecting reversed() to be a copy (use new ArrayList<>(list.reversed()) for a copy).
  • Calling addFirst on a sorted set, which is unsupported.
  • Writing your own collection with a reversed() or getFirst() that has a different return type: it fails to compile on Java 21.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

  • reversed() on ArrayList is an O(1) view, and looping through it costs the same as a normal loop.
  • Reversed views of LinkedList and ArrayDeque are also cheap.
  • getFirst/getLast are O(1) for lists and deques.
  • Prefer views to copying for large lists.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: showing the most recent activity first, and implementing an LRU cache or bounded history with first and last operations.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

View semantics.

Worked Example 2

Empty collection.

Practice Exercise 1

Uniform API.

Practice Exercise 2

SequencedMap.

11. Quick Revision

  • SequencedCollection, SequencedSet, SequencedMap.
  • reversed() returns a view.
  • List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet qualify.
  • HashSet does not.
  • Empty collections throw on getFirst.

beginner.content:
1. Introduction

  • String templates (preview in Java 21 and 22) embed expressions in strings, such as STR."Hello \{name}", with processors that can validate or transform the result.

2. Need of This Topic

  • String concatenation and format strings are error prone and can allow injection.
  • Templates aimed to make interpolation safer.

3. Advantages

  • Readable interpolation.
  • Processors can escape or bind values.
  • Works with text blocks.

4. Disadvantages

  • Preview feature; withdrawn for redesign.
  • Needs --enable-preview.
  • Not for production code.

5. Why We Learn This Topic

  • Shows the direction of the language.
  • Interview awareness.
  • Reinforces safe string building.

6. Basic Concepts

String Templates (Preview) in Java 21

Introduction

String Templates (JEP 430, preview in Java 21) introduce a new way to embed expressions directly in strings using the STR template processor. This is Java's answer to string interpolation found in languages like Kotlin, C#, and JavaScript.

Key Features

  • STR processor — built-in processor for string interpolation
  • \{expression} — embeds any Java expression in a template
  • Template processors — pluggable: STR, FMT, RAW, or your own
  • Checked at compile time — the template syntax is verified by the compiler
  • Safer — a custom processor can validate or escape embedded values

Note

WITHDRAWN FEATURE - this syntax does not compile on any current JDK. String Templates (JEP 430/459) were a preview in Java 21, re-previewed in Java 22, and then removed in JDK 23. They exist in no current release, even with --enable-preview. This page is retained for historical context only; use String.format(), formatted() or a StringBuilder instead.

Basic Syntax

  • STR."Hello \{name}" — puts the value of name into the string
  • The expression inside \{} can be any valid Java expression

Fresher Notes

  • String templates (Java 21 preview) embed expressions in strings: STR."Hello \{name}!".
  • The processor STR is built in and interpolates; others (FMT, RAW) format or defer, and you can write your own.
  • Preview feature: in Java 21 and 22 you compile and run with --enable-preview. It was removed in JDK 23, so it does not compile on current JDKs. Use formatted instead.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

String Templates — Intermediate Usage

Complex Expressions

Template expressions can contain any Java expression: method calls, ternary operators, array access, and more.

FMT Template Processor

The FMT processor supports format specifiers (like printf) inside templates, combining the convenience of templates with the precision of formatted output.

Template Processor Architecture

A StringTemplate is created from the template literal. A template processor then transforms it. STR is the standard processor; FMT adds formatting; you can create custom processors.

Best Practices

  • Use STR for simple interpolation
  • Use FMT when formatted output is needed (currency, decimals, alignment)
  • Consider custom processors for SQL, HTML, or JSON to prevent injection
  • Templates are more readable than concatenation for complex strings

Mid-Level Notes

  • Expressions inside \{ } can be any Java expression, including method calls and ternaries.
  • Text blocks work with templates for multi-line output.
  • FMT uses printf-style specifiers, for example FMT."%05d\{n}".

8. Advanced Concepts

String Templates — Expert Deep Dive

Custom Template Processors

You can create custom template processors by implementing the StringTemplate.Processor interface. This enables domain-specific processing like SQL sanitization, HTML escaping, or JSON validation.

How Templates Work Internally

  • The compiler splits the template into fragments (literal parts) and values (expression results)
  • A StringTemplate object holds both fragments and values
  • The processor's process() method receives the StringTemplate and produces the result
  • STR simply concatenates fragments and values
  • Custom processors can validate, sanitize, or transform the output

Security Benefits

  • SQL injection: a SQL processor can bind values with a PreparedStatement
  • XSS: an HTML processor can escape special characters
  • Unlike string concatenation, templates keep structure and data separate

Quick Q&A

  • Q: Are String Templates compiled differently? — Yes, the compiler creates a StringTemplate object that is processed at runtime
  • Q: Can a template processor return non-String types? — Yes, the Processor interface is generic: Processor<R, E> (R is the result type, E the exception type)

Senior Notes

  • Custom processors can validate and transform parts safely, for example producing a PreparedStatement or escaped HTML instead of a raw string, which prevents injection.
  • Production use: the feature changed during preview and was then withdrawn; String.format and formatted remain the stable tools.
  • Core idea: interpolation with safety hooks. Learn it, but do not depend on it.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Why it existed: interpolation that is safe by design. A processor receives the fixed fragments and the embedded values separately, so it can escape or bind values rather than splice them: JSON building, SQL (PreparedStatement), HTML escaping, localization. Custom processors: StringTemplate.Processor.of(...). Because the language design changed, production code should use stable approaches: String.format, formatted, text blocks, MessageFormat and prepared statements.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

A string template (JEP 430, preview in Java 21 and 22) is a StringTemplate value made of fragments and values; a template processor (an object with process) turns it into a result of any type. STR is imported implicitly and interpolates; FMT adds format specifiers; RAW returns the template unprocessed. The syntax uses \{expr} inside a string or text block. Because it is a preview, it requires --enable-preview, and the feature was withdrawn after Java 22 for a redesign, so APIs and syntax may change.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using a preview feature in production, forgetting --enable-preview at both compile and run time (class file version marks preview), building SQL, HTML or shell commands by interpolation (injection), and assuming the syntax will not change. Pin preview use to experiments and keep stable code on formatted and prepared statements.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Interpolation performance is comparable to StringBuilder/String.format alternatives: processors can be optimized by invokedynamic. Avoid expensive expressions inside templates evaluated in logging statements when the log level is disabled; use lazy logging with suppliers or placeholders.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: until the redesigned feature ships, use text blocks with formatted for emails and reports, MessageFormat or ICU for localized messages, and template engines (Thymeleaf, Mustache) for HTML.

10. Examples

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 2

Stable alternatives.

11. Quick Revision

  • Preview only: STR."...\{expr}".
  • Stable alternatives: formatted, String.format.
  • Never build SQL by interpolation.
  • Use PreparedStatement for queries.
  • Requires --enable-preview.

topics.name: Class Loader

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is a Class Loader?

Before Java code can run, the JVM must load your .class files into memory. The Class Loader

is the part of the JVM responsible for finding those .class files, reading their bytecode, and making

them usable by the running program.

Without a class loader, the JVM would have no way to turn a compiled .class file sitting on disk into

an actual, usable class inside a running program.

The Three Built-in Class Loaders

Java ships with three class loaders, arranged in a hierarchy:

  • Bootstrap Class Loader - loads core Java classes like java.lang.String and

java.lang.Object from the JDK's own libraries. Written in native code, not Java.

  • Extension (Platform) Class Loader - loads classes from Java's extension/platform libraries.
  • Application (System) Class Loader - loads the classes you write, from your project's

classpath. This is the one that loads your own Main.class, for example.

A Simple Example

When you run a Java program, the Application Class Loader is the one that loads your class first.

Loading, Linking, and Initialization

Getting a class ready to use is not a single step - the JVM does three things in order:

  • Loading - the class loader reads the .class file bytes and creates a

Class object in memory.

  • Linking - the JVM verifies the bytecode is valid, allocates memory for static fields, and

resolves references to other classes.

  • Initialization - static initializer blocks and static variable assignments actually run.

The Delegation Model (Simple View)

When a class needs to be loaded, the Application Class Loader does not just load it immediately - it first asks

its parent (Extension Class Loader), which in turn asks its parent (Bootstrap Class Loader).

Only if none of the parents can find the class does the child actually load it itself. This is called the

parent delegation model, and it stops you from accidentally overriding core classes like

java.lang.String with your own version.

ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError

These two errors sound similar but happen for different reasons:

  • ClassNotFoundException - thrown when code explicitly asks to load a class by name (e.g.

Class.forName("com.example.Foo")) and it cannot be found on the classpath.

  • NoClassDefFoundError - thrown when a class was available at compile time, but is missing at

runtime when the JVM tries to use it (for example, a JAR was removed after compiling).

Fresher Notes

  • Class loader: the JVM component that finds a .class file and turns its bytes into a Class object, lazily, on first use.
  • Three built-in loaders: bootstrap (core java.base), platform (other JDK modules) and application (your classpath).
  • Loading steps: loading, linking (verify, prepare, resolve) and initialization (static blocks run).

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Parent delegation: a loader first asks its parent, so java.lang.String always comes from the bootstrap loader and cannot be faked.
  • Class identity is the class name plus its loader, so the same bytes loaded by two loaders give two different, incompatible types.
  • Failures: ClassNotFoundException comes from an explicit lookup like Class.forName; NoClassDefFoundError means it compiled but is missing or failed to initialize at run time.

8. Advanced Concepts

Custom Class Loaders

Beyond the three built-in loaders, Java lets you write your own by extending ClassLoader and

overriding findClass(). Custom class loaders are used to:

  • Load classes from non-standard sources (a database, a network location, an encrypted JAR).
  • Implement plugin systems where each plugin gets its own isolated loader (used by application servers and IDEs

like Eclipse's OSGi).

  • Enable hot-reloading of classes without restarting the JVM.

The Delegation Model, In Detail

        Bootstrap ClassLoader   (loads java.lang.*, native, no parent)
                 ^
                 | parent
        Extension/Platform ClassLoader   (loads javax.*, JDK extensions)
                 ^
                 | parent
        Application/System ClassLoader   (loads your classpath, e.g. com.myapp.*)
                 ^
                 | parent
        Custom ClassLoader (optional, e.g. a plugin loader)

Request flow for loading a class: the request always travels up to Bootstrap first, and only if

every ancestor fails to find the class does control fall back down to the loader that was

originally asked. This is why it's called delegation - each loader delegates upward before trying itself.

Why Delegation Matters: Preventing Class Spoofing

Imagine an attacker packages their own java.lang.String class inside a malicious JAR, hoping to

replace the trusted one and intercept string operations. Because of parent delegation, when anything asks for

java.lang.String, the request bubbles up to the Bootstrap Class Loader first - which always finds

the genuine JDK version before the Application Class Loader ever gets a chance to load the fake one.

This protection is why user code cannot easily shadow java.* packages - it's a core part of the

JVM's security model, not an accident.

Namespace Isolation and "Same Class, Different Loader" Problem

A class is uniquely identified in the JVM not just by its fully qualified name, but by the combination of

(class name, class loader). This means the exact same .class file, loaded by two

different class loaders, produces two distinct Class objects that are not equal and

cannot be cast to each other - even though the source code is identical.

This is a common cause of confusing ClassCastException errors in application servers and plugin

systems, where the same library gets loaded twice by different loaders (e.g. once by the app server, once by a

deployed application's own loader).

What Happens When a Class Cannot Be Loaded

ScenarioResultWhen it typically happens
Class requested explicitly by name, not found anywhere on classpathClassNotFoundException (checked)Class.forName(), reflection, JDBC driver loading
Class was present at compile time but its .class/JAR is missing at runtimeNoClassDefFoundError (unchecked, extends Error)A dependency JAR was removed/misconfigured after build
Static initializer of a class throws an exception during initExceptionInInitializerError, then NoClassDefFoundError on later attemptsBuggy static block or static field initializer
Custom loader's classpath/source becomes unavailable at load timeNoClassDefFoundError or LinkageErrorPlugin JAR deleted while the app is running

Common Misconceptions

  • "ClassLoader loads the whole application at startup." Wrong - classes are loaded lazily, on

first use, not all upfront.

  • "There are only 3 class loaders." Wrong - there are 3 built-in loaders, but frameworks

(Tomcat, Spring Boot's fat-JAR launcher, OSGi) commonly add many more custom loaders for isolation.

  • "NoClassDefFoundError means the class was never compiled." Wrong - it usually means the class

compiled fine but its JAR/classpath entry is missing or broken at runtime.

Senior Notes

  • Custom loaders power plugin systems, app servers (Tomcat per-webapp loaders) and hot reload, but they can leak: a loader lives as long as any of its classes or instances.
  • Context class loader: Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader() lets framework code (JDBC, ServiceLoader) see application classes.
  • Diagnosis: use -verbose:class or -Xlog:class+load to see where each class came from.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to load classes and the options around them:

  • Implicit: a reference in bytecode (new, static call) loads the class.
  • Explicit: Class.forName(name) (initializes) or loader.loadClass(name) (does not initialize).
  • URLClassLoader: load from jar or directory URLs, closeable.
  • ServiceLoader: discover implementations through META-INF/services or module-info.
  • Lookup.defineClass: define a class from bytes inside an existing package.
  • Flags: -cp, --module-path, -Xlog:class+load.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Loading a class goes through fixed phases.

  • Loading: loadClass(name) asks the parent first, then findClass reads the bytes and defineClass creates the Class object.
  • Verification: the bytecode is checked for type safety and stack correctness.
  • Preparation: static fields get default values (0, null).
  • Resolution: symbolic references become direct ones, often lazily.
  • Initialization: static initializers run once, under a lock, in textual order.
  • Cache: each loader records the classes it defined, so a name is defined once per loader.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical class loading mistakes:

  • ClassCastException with the same name: the two classes came from different loaders; load the shared type from a common parent.
  • Wrong context loader: a framework cannot see your classes; set the context loader around the call.
  • Duplicate jars: two versions on the classpath, the first one wins; find it with -Xlog:class+load.
  • Unclosed URLClassLoader: keeps jar files locked and classes alive.
  • Static singletons in a shared parent: they hold references to child loader classes and leak them.
  • Catching Throwable around init: a failed static initializer gives NoClassDefFoundError on later uses and hides the first cause.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Class loading costs startup time, so tune it deliberately.

  • Fewer classes: trim dependencies and avoid reflection-heavy startup.
  • AppCDS: -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit and -XX:SharedArchiveFile map pre-parsed classes and cut startup.
  • JDK 19+: -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive creates and refreshes the archive automatically.
  • Parallel loading: loaders that register as parallel capable lock per class name instead of per loader.
  • Lazy init: keep static initializers cheap.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a servlet container redeploys a web app and memory climbs each time.

  • Cause: a library in the shared parent loader keeps a thread or static map pointing at the webapp classes.
  • Symptom: loader count and loaded class count grow after each redeploy.
  • Fix: stop threads and deregister drivers in a shutdown hook (ServletContextListener), and keep such libraries inside the webapp.

10. Examples

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Walk the loader chain.

interviewQA: What are the three built-in class loaders in order?
Bootstrap, Extension/Platform, Application/System
What is the parent delegation model?
A class loader delegates the load request to its parent first, only loading it itself if no ancestor can find the class
Why does delegation prevent core class spoofing?
Because the Bootstrap loader is asked first and always resolves java.lang.* classes from the trusted JDK before any user loader gets a chance
What's the difference between ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError?

ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception from explicitly requesting a missing class (e.g. Class.forName); NoClassDefFoundError is an unchecked Error thrown when a class available at compile time is missing at runtime
Can the same class be loaded twice in one JVM?
Yes, if loaded by two different class loaders - they produce two distinct, incompatible Class objects
What are the three phases a class goes through before use?
Loading, Linking (verify, prepare, resolve), and Initialization
Why would you write a custom class loader?
To load classes from non-standard sources, achieve plugin isolation, or support hot-reloading
Is the Bootstrap Class Loader written in Java?
No, it's implemented natively (in C/C++) as part of the JVM itself

topics.name: Runtime Data Areas

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What are Runtime Data Areas?

When a Java program runs, the JVM doesn't just execute instructions - it also needs places in memory to store

objects, method calls, variables, and class information. These memory regions are collectively called the

Runtime Data Areas.

Think of them as different "rooms" inside the JVM's memory, each with a specific job.

The Five Main Areas

  • Heap - stores all objects created with new. Shared by the whole application.
  • Stack - stores method calls and local variables. Each thread gets its own stack.
  • Method Area (Metaspace) - stores class-level information like class structure, method code,

and static variables. Shared across the application.

  • PC Register - a tiny area that tracks which instruction a thread is currently executing. Each

thread gets its own.

  • Native Method Stack - similar to the regular Stack, but for native (non-Java) method calls.

Shared vs Per-Thread Areas

This distinction is important and comes up a lot:

AreaShared or Per-Thread?
HeapShared (one per JVM)
Method Area / MetaspaceShared (one per JVM)
StackPer-Thread (one for each thread)
PC RegisterPer-Thread (one for each thread)
Native Method StackPer-Thread (one for each thread)

A Quick Mental Model

When you call a method that creates an object:

  • The method call itself (its local variables, parameters) goes on that thread's Stack.
  • The object created inside the method goes on the shared Heap.
  • The class definition for that object's type lives in the Method Area.

This is why an object can keep existing on the Heap even after the method that created it has finished and its

stack frame has been removed - as long as something else still references it.

Fresher Notes

  • Runtime data areas are the memory regions the JVM manages: heap, method area (metaspace), thread stacks, PC registers and native method stacks.
  • Shared versus per-thread: heap and method area are shared by all threads; stack, PC register and native stack belong to one thread each.
  • Objects live on the heap; local variables and call frames live on the stack; class metadata lives in metaspace.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • PC register holds the address of the bytecode instruction the thread executes next.
  • Frame contents: local variable array, operand stack and a reference to the run-time constant pool of the current class.
  • Different errors: StackOverflowError for stacks, OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space for heap, OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace for class metadata.

8. Advanced Concepts

Full Picture of the JVM Runtime Data Areas

                     JVM Process
   +-----------------------------------------------------+
   |  Shared across all threads                           |
   |   +----------------+   +--------------------------+  |
   |   |     Heap       |   |  Method Area (Metaspace)  |  |
   |   | (all objects)  |   |  (class metadata, static  |  |
   |   |                |   |   vars, runtime const pool)|  |
   |   +----------------+   +--------------------------+  |
   |                                                       |
   |  Per-Thread (one set for each running thread)         |
   |   +---------+  +---------+  +------------------+      |
   |   | Stack   |  |   PC    |  | Native Method     |      |
   |   | (frames)|  | Register|  |     Stack         |      |
   |   +---------+  +---------+  +------------------+      |
   +-----------------------------------------------------+

Comparison Table: All Five Areas at a Glance

AreaScopeStoresCan it throw OutOfMemoryError?Tuning Flag
HeapSharedObjects, instance variables, arraysYes - java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space-Xms / -Xmx
StackPer-ThreadStack frames, local variables, partial results, call chainStackOverflowError (and OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread)-Xss
Method Area / MetaspaceSharedClass metadata, static variables, runtime constant poolYes - java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace-XX:MetaspaceSize / -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize
PC RegisterPer-ThreadAddress of the currently executing JVM instructionNo - fixed tiny sizeNot tunable
Native Method StackPer-ThreadFrames for native (JNI/C/C++) method callsYes - StackOverflowError or OutOfMemoryError depending on JVM implementationJVM/OS dependent

Why the Shared/Per-Thread Split Matters in Production

This split directly explains real production behavior:

  • A memory leak from objects that are never dereferenced grows the Heap and eventually causes a

full-application OutOfMemoryError that affects every thread.

  • A single runaway recursive method only blows up that one thread's Stack

(StackOverflowError) - other threads keep running unaffected.

  • Loading thousands of dynamically generated classes (common with heavy reflection/proxy frameworks) pressures

the shared Method Area/Metaspace, which can bring down the whole JVM even though the Heap looks

perfectly healthy.

Common Misconceptions

  • "Local variables live on the Heap." Wrong - primitive local variables and object references

live on the Stack; only the actual objects they point to live on the Heap.

  • "More threads only cost Heap memory." Wrong - every new thread also claims its own Stack, PC

Register, and Native Method Stack, which is why creating unbounded threads can itself cause an

OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread, separate from Heap exhaustion.

  • "The Method Area is part of the Heap." Historically debated - the JVM spec treats it as a

logically distinct area, and since Java 8 it's physically implemented as Metaspace in native (non-heap) memory.

Senior Notes

  • Beyond the spec: real JVMs also use code cache (JIT output), direct buffers, thread stacks and GC structures that are outside the heap.
  • Footprint of a process is larger than -Xmx; plan container limits with this in mind.
  • Tools: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary shows each area.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Memory flags per area:

  • Heap: -Xms, -Xmx, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage.
  • Stack: -Xss.
  • Metaspace: -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
  • Code cache: -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize.
  • Direct buffers: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize.
  • Tracking: -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary|detail.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The specification divides memory by lifetime and sharing.

  • Per JVM: heap, method area and run-time constant pools, created at startup.
  • Per thread: PC register, Java stack and native method stack, created with the thread.
  • Frames: pushed on call, popped on return; each has locals, an operand stack and a constant pool reference.
  • Beyond the spec: HotSpot adds code cache, GC bookkeeping, symbol tables and direct memory.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Sizing container limit equal to Xmx: leave room for non-heap, often 25 to 50 percent extra.
  • Thinking all objects are on the heap: escape analysis can remove allocations.
  • Mixing up errors: each area has its own error and its own fix.
  • Raising Xmx for a leak: it only delays the failure.
  • Ignoring thread count: every platform thread costs stack memory.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Performance relevant points:

  • Stack access is very fast; heap allocation is fast but feeds the collector.
  • Reduce allocation in hot paths to cut GC work.
  • Direct memory avoids a copy for I/O but is not managed by the heap collector.
  • Fewer threads or virtual threads reduce stack footprint.
  • Measure with JFR rather than guessing.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a Spring service in Kubernetes is restarted with reason OOMKilled while heap graphs look healthy.

  • Check: heap max, metaspace, thread count, direct memory.
  • Finding: 600 threads at 1 MB stack plus Netty direct buffers filled the gap.
  • Fix: cap thread pools, set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, lower MaxRAMPercentage.

Heap, Stack, Method Area/Metaspace, PC Register, Native Method Stack
Which areas are shared across all threads?
Heap and Method Area/Metaspace

topics.name: Heap

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is the Heap?

The Heap is the area of JVM memory where all objects live - every time you write new,

the object is created on the Heap. Unlike the Stack, the Heap is shared by every thread in the application.

A Simple Example

Every object created here is placed on the Heap, no matter which method or thread creates it.

Young Generation and Old Generation

The Heap isn't one big blob of memory - it's divided into generations, based on the idea that most objects die

young:

  • Young Generation - where all new objects are created. Further split into:

  • Eden - brand new objects are born here.

  • Survivor 0 (S0) and Survivor 1 (S1) - objects that survive a

garbage collection in Eden get moved here.

  • Old Generation (Tenured) - objects that survive many garbage collections in the Young

Generation get "promoted" here, since they're likely to be long-lived.

Controlling Heap Size with -Xms and -Xmx

You can control how much memory the Heap starts with and how much it can grow to, using JVM startup flags:

  • -Xms<size> - the initial Heap size.
  • -Xmx<size> - the maximum Heap size the JVM is allowed to use.

Example: java -Xms256m -Xmx1024m MyApp starts with a 256 MB heap and allows it to grow up to 1024 MB.

What Happens When the Heap Runs Out?

If the application keeps creating objects that can't be garbage collected (because something still references

them), the Heap eventually fills up completely. When that happens, the JVM throws

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space and the application typically crashes.

Fresher Notes

  • Heap is the shared area where all objects and arrays are allocated; the garbage collector reclaims unreachable ones.
  • Sizing flags: -Xms sets the initial heap and -Xmx the maximum.
  • Generations: new objects start in the young generation and long-lived ones move to the old generation.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Young gen holds Eden plus two survivor spaces; a minor GC copies live objects out of Eden.
  • Promotion: objects that survive enough collections (the tenuring threshold) move to the old generation.
  • OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space means live data does not fit in -Xmx even after a full collection.

8. Advanced Concepts

Heap Layout in Detail

                              HEAP
   +--------------------------------------------------------+
   |          Young Generation           |   Old Generation  |
   |  +--------+  +------+  +------+     |                   |
   |  |  Eden  |  |  S0  |  |  S1  |     |     Tenured        |
   |  +--------+  +------+  +------+     |   (long-lived      |
   |  new objects  survivor  survivor    |    objects live    |
   |  born here    space 0   space 1     |    here)           |
   +--------------------------------------------------------+
        Minor GC runs here                Major/Full GC runs here
        (fast, frequent)                  (slower, less frequent)

Object Lifecycle Through the Generations

  • A new object is allocated in Eden.
  • When Eden fills up, a Minor GC runs: live objects in Eden are copied to an empty Survivor space

(say S0), and Eden is cleared.

  • On the next Minor GC, live objects from Eden AND S0 are copied to S1, and both Eden and S0 are cleared - the

Survivor spaces swap roles each cycle.

  • Each time an object survives a GC cycle, its age counter increases. Once it crosses a

threshold (default is often 15, tunable via -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold), it gets promoted

to the Old Generation.

  • Objects in the Old Generation are only cleaned up by a Major/Full GC, which is more expensive

because it scans a much larger memory region.

Heap Tuning Flags

FlagPurpose
-Xms<size>Initial Heap size at JVM startup
-Xmx<size>Maximum Heap size the JVM may grow to
-Xmn<size>Size of the Young Generation specifically
-XX:NewRatio=<n>Ratio of Old Generation size to Young Generation size
-XX:SurvivorRatio=<n>Ratio of Eden size to each Survivor space size
-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=<n>How many GC cycles an object survives in Young Gen before promotion to Old Gen

Common Pitfall: Setting -Xms and -Xmx Very Far Apart

If -Xms is much smaller than -Xmx, the JVM has to repeatedly resize (grow) the Heap as

the application's memory needs increase, which causes pauses and CPU overhead. In production, it's a common best

practice to set -Xms and -Xmx to the same value, so the Heap size is

fixed upfront and the JVM doesn't spend time resizing it under load.

Common Misconceptions

  • "All objects go straight to the Old Generation." Wrong - almost all objects start in Eden;

only long-lived objects get promoted after surviving several GC cycles.

  • "A larger Heap always means better performance." Wrong - a very large Heap can mean longer

Full GC pause times when it does eventually need cleaning, even if it's cleaned less often.

  • "Garbage Collection frees memory immediately when an object goes out of scope." Wrong - the

object simply becomes eligible for collection; the actual reclaiming happens later, whenever the GC runs.

Senior Notes

  • G1 is the default collector since Java 9; it splits the heap into regions and targets a pause goal with -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis.
  • Set Xms equal to Xmx on servers to avoid resize pauses; in containers prefer -XX:MaxRAMPercentage.
  • Evidence first: use GC logs (-Xlog:gc*) and heap dumps (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError) before changing flags.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Heap options by purpose:

  • Size: -Xms, -Xmx, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage.
  • Collector: -XX:+UseG1GC (default), -XX:+UseParallelGC (throughput), -XX:+UseZGC (low pause; generational mode with -XX:+ZGenerational in 21), -XX:+UseSerialGC (tiny apps).
  • Pause goal: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 is the G1 default.
  • Diagnostics: -Xlog:gc*, -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, -XX:HeapDumpPath.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

HotSpot heap layout (G1, the default since Java 9):

  • Regions: the heap is split into equal regions (1 to 32 MB) labeled Eden, Survivor, Old or Humongous.
  • Allocation: each thread allocates in a private buffer (TLAB) inside Eden, which needs no lock.
  • Minor GC: live objects are copied to survivor or old regions; dead ones are dropped with the region.
  • Mixed GC: after concurrent marking, old regions with most garbage are also collected.
  • Humongous: objects over half a region get dedicated regions.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical heap problems:

  • Unbounded caches: a static HashMap that only grows; use a size-bounded cache with eviction.
  • Listeners never removed: registered objects stay reachable.
  • ThreadLocal in pools: values stay as long as the pooled thread.
  • Loading whole result sets or files: stream or page instead.
  • Calling System.gc(): remove it, or disable with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning steps that work in practice:

  • Measure the live set after full or mixed GC; heap should be about 2 to 4 times that.
  • Reduce allocation rate before tuning flags.
  • Avoid boxing and temporary strings in hot loops.
  • Set Xms equal to Xmx for stable servers.
  • Change one flag at a time and compare GC logs or JFR.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order service shows steadily growing old generation and a restart every few days.

  • Step 1: dump the heap while it is high.
  • Step 2: open in MAT and check the dominator tree.
  • Finding: a static map of sessions never cleaned.
  • Fix: expire entries and add a test that checks the size stays bounded.

10. Examples

Worked Example 2

Read a GC log line.

Practice Exercise 1

Allocate and watch heap use.

Practice Exercise 2

Show the flags in use.

interviewQA: What is stored on the Heap?
All objects and arrays created with 'new', shared across all threads
What are the two main generations of the Heap?
Young Generation (Eden + S0 + S1) and Old Generation (Tenured)
What triggers a Minor GC vs a Major/Full GC?
Minor GC runs when Eden fills up; Major/Full GC runs when the Old Generation needs cleaning, and is much more expensive
What do -Xms and -Xmx control?
-Xms sets the initial Heap size, -Xmx sets the maximum Heap size the JVM may grow to
What error is thrown when the Heap is exhausted?
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Why are there two Survivor spaces instead of one?
So live objects can be copied between them each GC cycle, always leaving one Survivor space empty to copy into, which keeps memory compact
Why is it recommended to set -Xms equal to -Xmx in production?
To avoid runtime Heap resizing overhead and pauses as the application's memory usage grows
What promotes an object from Young Gen to Old Gen?
Surviving a configured number of GC cycles (tenuring threshold) without being collected

topics.name: Stack

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is the Stack?

The Stack is the area of JVM memory that keeps track of method calls. Every time a method is

called, a new block of memory called a stack frame is pushed onto the Stack; when the method

finishes, that frame is popped off.

Unlike the Heap, every thread gets its own private Stack - one thread's Stack is never visible to another thread.

What Lives in a Stack Frame?

Each stack frame holds everything a method needs while it's running:

  • Local variables (including method parameters)
  • Partial results of expressions being calculated
  • Information needed to return control to the calling method

A Simple Example

Watch how methods stack on top of each other as they call one another.

StackOverflowError

The Stack is not unlimited - if too many methods call each other without returning (most commonly from

uncontrolled recursion), the Stack runs out of space and the JVM throws a

StackOverflowError.

Controlling Stack Size with -Xss

Just like the Heap has -Xmx, the Stack has its own size flag: -Xss<size>. It sets

the maximum stack size for each thread. Example: java -Xss512k MyApp gives each thread a 512 KB

stack.

Fresher Notes

  • Thread stack: every thread has its own stack made of frames, one frame per method call.
  • Frame holds local variables, the operand stack and return information; it is removed when the method returns.
  • StackOverflowError happens when calls nest too deep, usually from missing base case in recursion.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Primitives and references are stored in the frame; the objects behind references are in the heap.
  • Thread safety: locals are private to a thread, so they need no synchronization unless a reference escapes.
  • Stack size is set with -Xss (or new Thread(group, run, name, stackSize)); the default on 64-bit Linux is typically 1 MB.

8. Advanced Concepts

Stack Frame Internals

Each stack frame the JVM pushes actually contains three logical parts:

Thread's Stack (grows downward with each call)
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  Frame: main()                                     |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  Frame: methodA()                                  |
|   - Local Variable Array  (params + local vars)    |
|   - Operand Stack (scratch space for computation)  |
|   - Frame Data (return address, reference to        |
|                 the constant pool of this class)   |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  Frame: methodB()  <-- currently executing          |
+--------------------------------------------------+

The topmost frame always corresponds to the method currently executing; when it returns, its frame is popped and

control (and any return value) goes back to the frame below it.

Stack vs Heap - Key Differences

AspectStackHeap
ScopePer-thread (private)Shared by all threads
StoresLocal variables, method call frames, referencesActual objects and arrays
Allocation speedVery fast (just move a pointer)Slower (needs GC bookkeeping)
LifetimeTied to the method call - freed automatically on returnTied to reachability - freed by Garbage Collector whenever it's no longer referenced
Failure modeStackOverflowErrorOutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Tuning flag-Xss-Xms / -Xmx

What Actually Happens on StackOverflowError

When the JVM tries to push a new frame but the thread's Stack has no room left, it throws

StackOverflowError immediately - it does not try to grow the Stack automatically

(unlike the Heap, which can grow up to -Xmx). Production causes typically fall into two buckets:

  • A genuine bug - unbounded or incorrectly-based recursion (missing/broken base case).
  • A legitimately deep call chain (e.g. deeply nested JSON/XML parsing, or a very deep object graph being

processed recursively) that simply needs more Stack space, tunable via -Xss.

Common Pitfall: Increasing -Xss to "Fix" StackOverflowError

Bumping -Xss can mask a genuine infinite-recursion bug rather than fix it - the program will still

eventually overflow, just after more iterations, and each thread now consumes more memory (which matters a lot

in high-thread-count applications, since Stack memory is per-thread and multiplies quickly). Always check for a

missing/incorrect base case in recursive code first, and only increase -Xss for algorithms that are

correctly, intentionally, deeply recursive.

Common Misconceptions

  • "Objects created inside a method live on the Stack." Wrong - only the reference variable

lives on the Stack; the actual object it points to is always on the Heap.

  • "More threads means the Heap runs out faster." Partially wrong - more threads primarily

consume more Stack memory (one Stack per thread), which is a separate, common cause of

OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread, distinct from Heap exhaustion.

  • "StackOverflowError can be safely caught and ignored like a normal exception." Risky -

by the time it's thrown, the Stack is nearly exhausted, so the catch block itself may have very little

Stack space left to execute safely.

Senior Notes

  • Escape analysis: the JIT can allocate a non-escaping object in registers or on the stack (scalar replacement), so short-lived objects may cost nothing.
  • Cost of threads: many platform threads reserve many MB of stack; Java 21 virtual threads keep stacks on the heap and grow on demand.
  • Diagnosis: jstack or jcmd Thread.print shows each stack; deep recursion or lock waits are visible there.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Controlling stack size and depth:

  • Global: -Xss512k or -XX:ThreadStackSize=512.
  • Per thread: the stackSize argument of the Thread constructor, a hint the JVM may ignore.
  • Executor threads: pass a custom ThreadFactory to set it.
  • Virtual threads (Java 21): no fixed stack size; limited by heap.
  • Main thread: stack size is set by the launcher, -Xss applies.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

How a call uses the stack:

  • Invoke: the JVM pushes a new frame sized at compile time (max locals plus max operand stack).
  • Arguments become the first local slots; this is slot 0 for instance methods.
  • Return: the result moves to the caller operand stack and the frame is popped.
  • Exceptions: unwinding pops frames until a handler matches.
  • JIT: compiled frames use machine registers and can inline callees, so the visible depth differs from bytecode.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common stack mistakes:

  • Missing base case: add it and test with small and large inputs.
  • Mutual recursion: A calls B calls A without progress.
  • Recursive toString or equals on cyclic object graphs.
  • Huge Xss for all threads: memory is reserved per thread.
  • Assuming tail-call optimization: Java does not do it, so deep recursion needs a loop.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Small methods are inlined, so call depth costs little once hot.
  • Smaller Xss lets you run more threads in the same memory.
  • Escape analysis can keep short-lived objects out of the heap.
  • Thread dumps are cheap and safe, take several 5 to 10 seconds apart.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a JSON parser endpoint crashes with StackOverflowError on deeply nested input from clients.

  • Risk: attacker-controlled depth is a denial-of-service vector.
  • Fix: enforce a maximum nesting depth in the parser and reject the request with a 400 response.
  • Backup: catch the error at the request boundary and log the input size only.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1
