Worked Example 2

Print a thread stack.

Practice Exercise 1

Trigger and measure recursion depth.

Practice Exercise 2

Locals are thread private.

interviewQA: What is stored in a stack frame?
Local variables, method parameters, the operand stack for expression evaluation, and the return address
Is the Stack shared across threads?
No - each thread has its own private Stack
What causes StackOverflowError?
Too many nested/recursive method calls exceeding the thread's Stack capacity, most commonly from unbounded recursion
What flag controls the Stack size?
-Xss
Does the Stack grow automatically like the Heap?
No - if it runs out of space, the JVM throws StackOverflowError immediately rather than growing it
Where does an object created with 'new' inside a method actually live?
On the Heap - only its reference variable lives on the Stack
Why might increasing -Xss be the wrong fix for StackOverflowError?
It can mask a genuine infinite-recursion bug and increases per-thread memory cost, which adds up quickly with many threads
What happens to a stack frame when its method returns?
It is popped off the Stack immediately and its memory is reclaimed

topics.name: Method Area

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is the Method Area?

The Method Area is the part of JVM memory that stores information about the classes

themselves, rather than the objects created from them. It is shared by all threads in the application, just

like the Heap.

What is Stored in the Method Area?

  • Class structure - the class's name, its parent class, and which interfaces it implements.
  • Method code - the actual compiled bytecode for every method in the class.
  • Static variables - fields declared with the static keyword, since they belong to

the class itself, not to any one object.

  • Runtime Constant Pool - a table of constants (literals, references) used by the class,

resolved at runtime.

A Simple Example

Static variables are a good example of something stored in the Method Area rather than on the Heap with regular

objects.

Method Area vs Heap

It's easy to confuse these two shared areas, but they store different things:

  • The Method Area stores information about the class - one copy per class, no matter

how many objects of that class exist.

  • The Heap stores the actual objects (instances) - a separate copy for every single

object created with new.

Fresher Notes

  • Method area is the shared region that stores per-class data: class structure, field and method info, method bytecode and static metadata.
  • Run-time constant pool belongs to each class and holds literals and symbolic references resolved at link time.
  • Logical area: the spec defines it; HotSpot implements it as metaspace in native memory since Java 8.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Static variables: the static field slot is tied to the class mirror, and in modern HotSpot the static object values live in the heap inside the Class object.
  • String literals are interned in the String table, which is on the heap since Java 7.
  • Per class loader: class metadata is allocated per loader and freed when the loader is collected.

8. Advanced Concepts

Method Area Contents, In Detail

                    Method Area (one region per JVM, shared)
   +------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  For each loaded class:                                     |
   |    - Fully qualified class name, superclass, interfaces      |
   |    - Access modifiers (public/final/abstract/...)            |
   |    - Method bytecode + method signatures                     |
   |    - Field information (names, types, modifiers)             |
   |    - Static variables (class-level, one copy per class)      |
   |    - Runtime Constant Pool (literals, symbolic references     |
   |      to other classes/methods/fields, resolved lazily)       |
   |    - Reference to the ClassLoader that loaded this class      |
   +------------------------------------------------------------+

Runtime Constant Pool Explained

Every compiled .class file has a constant pool - a table of numeric literals,

string literals, and symbolic references to classes/fields/methods that the code uses. When the class is loaded,

the JVM copies this into the Runtime Constant Pool inside the Method Area, and resolves symbolic

references (e.g. "call method X on class Y") into direct memory references as needed.

This is also where interned String literals conceptually tie in - the String Pool is closely

related to (and in modern JVMs physically resides in) the Heap, but its entries are referenced from constant

pools in the Method Area.

Method Area vs Heap vs Metaspace - Comparison

AspectMethod AreaHeap
What it storesClass metadata, method bytecode, static variables, runtime constant poolObject instances and arrays
Copies per classOne (shared across all instances)Many (one per object created)
Java 7 and earlier implementationPermGen (part of Heap, fixed size)Heap
Java 8+ implementationMetaspace (native memory, not part of Heap)Heap
Garbage collected?Yes, but only when the defining ClassLoader itself becomes unreachableYes, per normal GC rules for unreachable objects

Note: the Method Area is a logical concept defined by the JVM Specification; Metaspace

is simply how HotSpot (the mainstream JVM) implements that concept since Java 8. The next topic covers Metaspace

specifically.

What Happens When the Method Area Runs Out

Because static variables and class metadata for every loaded class sit in the Method Area, applications that

dynamically generate huge numbers of classes at runtime (heavy reflection, dynamic proxies, some ORM/ AOP

frameworks, or classes that are loaded but never unloaded by leaking class loaders) can exhaust it. In Java 7

and earlier this surfaced as java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space; from Java 8 onward it

surfaces as java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace.

Common Misconceptions

  • "Static variables live on the Heap with regular instance fields." Wrong - static variables

belong to the class itself and are stored in the Method Area, not per-object. Note that since JDK 7 the static field VALUES live on the heap, attached to the java.lang.Class mirror - the Method Area holds the class metadata and bytecode.

  • "The Method Area is never garbage collected." Wrong - class metadata can be collected, but

only when its entire defining ClassLoader becomes unreachable, which is much rarer than ordinary object

collection on the Heap.

  • "Method Area and Metaspace are two different things." Not quite - Method Area is the JVM

Specification's logical concept; Metaspace is HotSpot's concrete implementation of it since Java 8.

Senior Notes

  • Not the same as PermGen: PermGen was a fixed-size heap-like region removed in Java 8, which also removed -XX:MaxPermSize.
  • Code cache is separate: JIT-compiled native code is not in the method area.
  • Inspect with jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats and jcmd <pid> GC.class_stats style tools, or jmap -clstats.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to look at method area data:

  • Reflection: getDeclaredFields, getDeclaredMethods.
  • javap: -c code, -v constant pool, -p private members.
  • MXBean: ClassLoadingMXBean for counts.
  • jcmd: VM.classloader_stats, VM.metaspace, GC.class_histogram.
  • Logging: -Xlog:class+unload shows unloading.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

What the method area holds for each loaded class:

  • Class structure: name, super type, interfaces, modifiers.
  • Members: field and method descriptors, bytecode, exception tables.
  • Run-time constant pool: literals and symbolic references, resolved lazily.
  • Statics: in HotSpot the static reference values sit in the heap inside the Class mirror.
  • Vtables and itables for dispatch.
  • Implementation: metaspace in native memory, allocated per class loader.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical confusions and mistakes:

  • Calling it PermGen: PermGen no longer exists; the flag -XX:MaxPermSize is ignored with a warning.
  • Putting strings in the method area: the String table is in the heap.
  • Assuming static means immortal: statics die with their class loader.
  • Creating a class per request with dynamic proxies without caching.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Performance points:

  • Class Data Sharing keeps JDK class metadata in a shared mapped archive, so startup is faster and memory is shared between JVMs.
  • Fewer classes means less metaspace and quicker startup.
  • Cache generated classes (proxies, lambdas are fine, they are linked via invokedynamic).

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a service that uses a scripting engine for rules loads a new script class on every evaluation.

  • Symptom: loaded class count rises steadily.
  • Fix: compile each script once and cache the compiled object by script hash.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Count loaded classes.

Worked Example 2

Class loader statistics.

Practice Exercise 1

Class metadata through reflection.

Practice Exercise 2

Interned literals.

interviewQA: What does the Method Area store?
Class-level metadata: class structure, method bytecode, static variables, and the runtime constant pool
How many copies of a static variable exist for a class?
Exactly one, shared by all instances of that class
Is the Method Area shared across threads?
Yes, like the Heap, it is shared by the entire JVM/application
What is the Runtime Constant Pool?
A per-class table of literals and symbolic references, copied from the compiled .class file's constant pool and resolved at runtime
How is the Method Area implemented before vs after Java 8?
Before Java 8 it was PermGen, a fixed-size part of the Heap; from Java 8 onward it is Metaspace, allocated from native memory
Is Method Area content ever garbage collected?
Yes, but only when the ClassLoader that defined those classes becomes completely unreachable
Why do heavy reflection/proxy frameworks risk Method Area exhaustion?
They can dynamically generate very large numbers of classes at runtime, filling up the shared Method Area/Metaspace
Where do instance (non-static) fields live?
On the Heap, as part of each individual object, not in the Method Area

topics.name: Metaspace

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is Metaspace?

Metaspace is the area of memory where the JVM stores class metadata - things like class

structure, method bytecode, and static variables. It was introduced in Java 8 to replace an

older area called PermGen (Permanent Generation).

Why Did Java Replace PermGen with Metaspace?

Before Java 8, class metadata lived in PermGen, which was part of the Heap and had a fixed maximum

size set at JVM startup. Applications that loaded lots of classes at runtime (common with big frameworks

like Spring, Hibernate, and application servers) would frequently run out of PermGen space and crash with

OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space - even if there was plenty of free Heap memory otherwise.

Metaspace fixed this by moving class metadata out of the Heap entirely, into native memory

(memory managed by the operating system, outside the JVM's Heap), which can grow much more flexibly.

A Simple Example

Every class you load, including ones generated dynamically, consumes some Metaspace.

Controlling Metaspace Size

Just like the Heap has -Xms/-Xmx, Metaspace has its own flags:

  • -XX:MetaspaceSize=<size> - the initial threshold at which a garbage collection is triggered

to clean up unused class metadata.

  • -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=<size> - the maximum size Metaspace is allowed to grow to. By default,

this is unlimited (only bounded by available system memory), unless you set it explicitly.

Fresher Notes

  • Metaspace stores class metadata in native memory; it replaced PermGen in Java 8.
  • Grows by default: unlike PermGen, metaspace is not capped unless you set -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
  • Error: OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace means too many or too large classes for the limit or for the machine.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Flags: -XX:MetaspaceSize is the size at which the first metaspace GC is triggered, not a reservation.
  • Freed per loader: memory comes back only when a class loader and all its classes are unloaded.
  • Typical causes: endless generated classes (proxies, bytecode libraries, scripting) and redeploy leaks.

8. Advanced Concepts

PermGen vs Metaspace

AspectPermGen (Java 7 and earlier)Metaspace (Java 8+)
Memory locationPart of the Heap (contiguous JVM-managed memory)Native memory (managed by the OS, outside the Heap)
Default max sizeFixed at startup (small default, e.g. 64-82 MB depending on platform)Unlimited by default - grows until system memory is exhausted
ResizingCannot grow past the fixed max without a restartCan grow/shrink dynamically as classes load/unload
Common failureOutOfMemoryError: PermGen space (very common in app servers)OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace (rarer, but possible if MaxMetaspaceSize is set or system memory runs out)
GC behaviorCollected as part of Full GC, tightly coupled to Heap GC cyclesCollected somewhat independently, triggered by MetaspaceSize threshold

Metaspace Internal Layout

      JVM Process Memory
   +---------------------------------------------------+
   |   Heap (-Xms / -Xmx bounded)                        |
   |     Young Gen | Old Gen                              |
   +---------------------------------------------------+
   |   Native (non-Heap) Memory                           |
   |     +-------------------------------------------+   |
   |     |  Metaspace (-XX:MetaspaceSize /             |   |
   |     |              -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize)          |   |
   |     |    - Class metadata                          |   |
   |     |    - Method bytecode                         |   |
   |     |    - Runtime constant pools                  |   |
   |     +-------------------------------------------+   |
   |     Thread stacks, JIT compiled code cache, etc.     |
   +---------------------------------------------------+

Static variables themselves actually moved to the Heap starting in Java 8 (as part of the corresponding Class

object), while the class structure/bytecode metadata moved to Metaspace - a subtlety worth knowing beyond "it's

just PermGen renamed."

What Happens When Metaspace Runs Out

If -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize is set and reached (or, without that flag, if the OS itself runs out of

available native memory), the JVM throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. Common production

causes:

  • Classloader leaks - repeatedly redeploying an application (common in application servers)

without the old ClassLoader and its classes ever becoming eligible for collection, so metadata accumulates

release after release.

  • Frameworks that generate huge numbers of dynamic proxy/CGLIB classes at runtime without bound.
  • Leaving -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize unset on a shared/constrained host, letting Metaspace silently

consume memory that other processes on the machine needed, potentially triggering the OS's own OOM killer

instead of a clean JVM error.

Production Tip: Always Set MaxMetaspaceSize in Containers

Because Metaspace defaults to unlimited, it's easy to forget it needs a ceiling - especially in containerized

environments (Docker/Kubernetes) with a hard memory limit. Without -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize, a

classloader leak can silently grow Metaspace until the container's memory limit is hit, and the container

runtime kills the whole JVM process outright (OOMKilled) with no Java-level stack trace to debug from - far

worse than a clean OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace that at least leaves a diagnosable log entry.

Common Misconceptions

  • "Metaspace is just PermGen renamed." Wrong - it changed memory location entirely (native

memory instead of Heap) and its default sizing behavior (unbounded instead of a small fixed cap).

  • "Metaspace can never run out of memory." Wrong - it's unbounded by default but still limited

by total system memory, and can be explicitly capped with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.

  • "Static variables are stored in Metaspace." Wrong since Java 8 - static variable values live

on the Heap (attached to the Class object); Metaspace holds the class's structural metadata and bytecode.

Senior Notes

  • Always set a cap in containers, for example -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m, so a leak fails fast with a clear error instead of consuming node memory.
  • Compressed class space (-XX:CompressedClassSpaceSize, default 1 GB) holds class pointers separately and can run out first.
  • Monitor with jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace and the MXBean pool named Metaspace.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Metaspace flags:

  • -XX:MetaspaceSize: first GC threshold.
  • -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize: hard cap, unlimited by default.
  • -XX:MinMetaspaceFreeRatio and -XX:MaxMetaspaceFreeRatio: how much free space to keep after a collection.
  • -XX:CompressedClassSpaceSize: class space size.
  • -XX:+UseCompressedClassPointers: on by default for heaps under the 32 GB class limit and in general on 64-bit.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

How metaspace manages memory:

  • Native memory: memory is reserved from the OS in virtual space and committed as needed.
  • Per loader arenas: each class loader allocates metadata chunks in its own arena.
  • Release: when a loader is unloaded its arena is returned to the free lists.
  • Compressed class space: a separate region (default 1 GB reserved) for class pointers when compressed class pointers are on.
  • High-water mark: crossing MetaspaceSize triggers a GC to unload classes.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Metaspace mistakes:

  • No cap in containers: a leak eats node memory instead of failing clearly.
  • Cap too small: large apps with many frameworks need 150 to 400 MB; measure first.
  • Confusing MetaspaceSize with a limit.
  • Generating classes in a loop with CGLIB, ASM or scripting without caching.
  • Leaking loaders through threads, ThreadLocals, JDBC drivers and shutdown hooks.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Operational guidance:

  • Watch the trend of used metaspace and loaded classes, not a single number.
  • Alert when metaspace grows without a plateau after warm-up.
  • Headroom: set the cap about 1.5 to 2 times the steady value.
  • Compare class histogram snapshots to see growing class families.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an app server shows OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace after the fifth redeploy.

  • Investigate: loader stats before and after a redeploy; old webapp loaders remain.
  • Root cause: a library thread started by the webapp still runs.
  • Fix: stop the thread on undeploy, then confirm loaders drop after a GC.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Exhaust metaspace with generated classes.

Worked Example 2

Watch class count and loaders.

Practice Exercise 1

Read metaspace usage.

Practice Exercise 2

Cap metaspace.

interviewQA: What replaced PermGen, and in which Java version?
Metaspace, introduced in Java 8
Where does Metaspace physically live in memory?
In native memory, managed by the OS, outside the JVM Heap
What is the default maximum size of Metaspace?
Unlimited by default - bounded only by available system memory, unless -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize is set
Why was PermGen replaced?
Its fixed, small default size caused frequent OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space in applications that loaded many classes dynamically
What flags control Metaspace sizing?
-XX:MetaspaceSize (GC trigger threshold) and -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize (hard cap)
What commonly causes Metaspace exhaustion in production?
ClassLoader leaks from repeated hot redeployments, or frameworks generating unbounded dynamic proxy classes
Why is it risky to leave -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize unset in a Docker container?
Metaspace can grow until the container's memory limit is hit, causing an OOMKilled container crash instead of a diagnosable Java OutOfMemoryError
Did static variables also move to Metaspace in Java 8?
No - static variable values moved to live on the Heap attached to the Class object; Metaspace holds structural class metadata and bytecode

topics.name: PC Register

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is the PC Register?

The PC (Program Counter) Register is a very small piece of memory that keeps track of exactly

which instruction the JVM is currently executing for a given thread.

Think of it like a bookmark - it remembers "where we are" in the bytecode, so after finishing one instruction the

JVM knows exactly which one to execute next.

One PC Register Per Thread

Every thread running inside the JVM gets its own private PC Register. This makes sense - if two threads are

running different methods at the same time, each one needs its own separate "bookmark" to track its own

progress independently of the other.

A Simple Example

You never interact with the PC Register directly in Java code, but conceptually, it's what lets execution

resume correctly after a method call returns.

What About Native Methods?

If the current method being executed is a native method (implemented in C/C++, not Java

bytecode), the PC Register's value is undefined - because native code isn't made of JVM

bytecode instructions, there's nothing meaningful for the PC Register to point to.

Fresher Notes

  • One per thread: every Java thread has its own program counter, so threads can run different code at the same time.
  • What it holds: the address (bytecode index) of the JVM instruction the thread will run next.
  • Not for you: you cannot read or change it from Java code; the JVM updates it after each instruction.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Context switch: when the OS pauses a thread, its PC register value is saved so the thread resumes at the exact instruction.
  • Native methods: while a thread runs native code, the PC value of that thread is undefined.
  • Line numbers: stack traces show source lines because the JVM maps the bytecode index to a line using the LineNumberTable.

8. Advanced Concepts

Why the PC Register Exists

The JVM is a stack-based, bytecode-interpreting (or JIT-compiling) machine. To execute a method's bytecode

correctly, something must track "which bytecode instruction comes next" for each thread - especially since

threads can be paused and resumed by the OS scheduler at any point. The PC Register is exactly that per-thread

bookkeeping slot, holding the address of the JVM instruction currently being executed.

PC Register vs Other Runtime Data Areas

AspectPC RegisterStack
SizeTiny - holds essentially one address/valueConfigurable, can be sizable (KB to MB)
ScopePer-threadPer-thread
PurposeTracks the current bytecode instruction addressTracks method call frames, local variables
Tunable via JVM flags?NoYes (-Xss)
Can it overflow / cause OutOfMemoryError?No - it's a fixed, tiny slot, not a growable regionYes - StackOverflowError

PC Register During Context Switching

Thread T1:  PC -> instruction #42  (executing, gets paused by OS scheduler)
Thread T2:  PC -> instruction #7   (resumes, continues from its own bookmark)
...later, OS scheduler resumes T1...
Thread T1:  PC -> instruction #42  (still correctly points where T1 left off)

Because each thread has its own isolated PC Register, the JVM (and underlying OS scheduler) can freely pause and

resume threads without any thread losing track of its execution position - this is fundamental to how

multithreading works correctly at the bytecode-execution level.

Common Misconceptions

  • "The PC Register is something developers can read or modify." Wrong - it's entirely internal

to the JVM's execution engine; there's no Java API to inspect or change it directly.

  • "The PC Register can run out of memory." Wrong - it's a fixed-size, tiny piece of per-thread

state (conceptually similar to a CPU's own program counter register), not a growable memory region, so it has

no corresponding "out of memory" failure mode.

  • "Every JVM instruction execution updates the PC Register the same way for native and Java methods."

Wrong - for native methods, the PC Register's value is left undefined, since there's no JVM bytecode instruction

sequence being tracked.

Senior Notes

  • No OutOfMemoryError: the specification lists the PC register as the only runtime area with no defined out-of-memory condition.
  • Real hardware: HotSpot keeps the equivalent state in real CPU registers and thread structures, and the JIT-compiled code uses machine addresses.
  • Debugging: debuggers and profilers use bytecode index data (see javap -c -l) to place breakpoints and report lines.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools that expose the PC / bytecode index:

  • javap -c: bytecode with offsets.
  • javap -l: line and local variable tables.
  • jstack and jcmd Thread.print: show the current line of each thread.
  • -XX:+PrintAssembly: compiled code (needs the hsdis library).
  • Debuggers (JDWP): use the bci to place breakpoints.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The PC register tracks execution per thread.

  • Interpreter: after each bytecode the JVM advances the bytecode index (bci) of the current frame.
  • Frames: each frame also remembers its own return bci, so after a call returns the caller continues where it stopped.
  • JIT code: compiled methods use machine program counters, and the JVM keeps debug maps back to bytecode indexes for stack traces and deoptimization.
  • Exceptions: the exception table maps a bci range to a handler bci.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Thinking the PC is shared: it is per thread, which is why code position is never lost on a context switch.
  • Expecting OutOfMemoryError from it: it is fixed size; look at heap, metaspace or thread count instead.
  • Trusting line numbers after obfuscation: stripped debug info shows Unknown Source; keep the mapping file.
  • Reading a thread dump as a snapshot of one instant: threads are stopped at safepoints, so the line is the nearest safepoint.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

The PC register itself is never a tuning target, but its effects are:

  • Context switches: far too many runnable threads waste CPU saving and restoring state.
  • Safepoints: threads must reach a safepoint poll; long counted loops delayed this in old JVMs.
  • JIT: hot loops are compiled so the bytecode PC is no longer stepped one instruction at a time.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a production thread seems stuck. Take three thread dumps a few seconds apart.

  • If the same method and line appear each time, that thread is stuck or looping there.
  • If the line changes, the thread is working and the problem is elsewhere.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Find the line from a stack trace.

Worked Example 2

Compile without line info.

Practice Exercise 1

See bytecode offsets with javap.

Practice Exercise 2

Two threads, two positions.

Why This Matters for Interviews (Even Though It's Rarely Discussed)

The PC Register is one of the smallest and least "interesting" runtime data areas, but it's frequently used as a

quick check of whether a candidate actually understands all five JVM runtime data areas (not just Heap

and Stack), and whether they understand the per-thread vs shared distinction correctly across all of them.

interviewQA: What does the PC Register store?
The address of the JVM instruction currently being executed by that thread
Is the PC Register shared across threads?
No - each thread has its own private PC Register
What happens to the PC Register value when executing a native method?
Its value is left undefined, since native methods aren't made of JVM bytecode instructions
Can the PC Register be tuned with a JVM flag like -Xss or -Xmx?
No - it has a fixed, minimal size that isn't user-configurable
Can the PC Register overflow and throw an error?
No - unlike the Stack or Heap, it's not a growable memory region, so it has no corresponding OutOfMemoryError
Why does each thread need its own PC Register?
So the OS scheduler can pause and resume threads independently, with each thread resuming exactly where it left off in its own bytecode execution
Is the PC Register part of the Heap or Method Area?
No - it's a separate, per-thread runtime data area, distinct from both shared areas
Does application code ever read or write the PC Register directly?
No - it's managed entirely internally by the JVM's execution engine

topics.name: Native Method Stack

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is the Native Method Stack?

The Native Method Stack is a memory area very similar to the regular Stack, except it's used

specifically for native methods - methods that are implemented in a language other than Java,

usually C or C++.

Just like the regular Stack, every thread gets its own private Native Method Stack.

What is a Native Method?

A native method is declared in Java using the native keyword, but has no method body

in Java - its actual implementation lives in a compiled C/C++ library that the JVM loads and calls into. This

mechanism is called JNI (Java Native Interface).

Why Does Java Need Native Methods At All?

Most Java code never touches native methods directly, but they're used under the hood for things like:

  • Talking directly to the operating system (file I/O, low-level networking).
  • Interfacing with hardware or existing C/C++ libraries that have no Java equivalent.
  • Performance-critical operations that benefit from direct native execution.

In fact, many familiar JDK classes (like parts of java.io and java.lang.Thread) rely on

native methods behind the scenes.

Native Method Stack vs Regular Stack

The two are conceptually the same idea (tracking method calls for a thread), just for different kinds of code:

  • The regular Stack tracks calls to Java methods (bytecode).
  • The Native Method Stack tracks calls to native methods (compiled C/C++ code).

Fresher Notes

  • Native method: a method declared with native and implemented in C or C++, such as System.currentTimeMillis().
  • Native stack: the memory a thread uses while it runs native code, separate in concept from the Java stack.
  • Loading: System.loadLibrary("name") loads the library; a missing one throws UnsatisfiedLinkError.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • HotSpot uses one thread stack for both Java frames and native frames, sized by -Xss.
  • JNI (Java Native Interface) is the standard bridge between Java and native code, and it needs a header and a compiled library.
  • Crash risk: a bug in native code can kill the whole JVM with a segmentation fault and an hs_err_pid file, not a Java exception.

8. Advanced Concepts

How JNI Calls Interact with the Stacks

Thread's Memory
+------------------------------------------------+
|  Regular Stack        |  Native Method Stack     |
|  +------------------+ |  +--------------------+  |
|  | main()           | |  |                    |  |
|  +------------------+ |  |                    |  |
|  | callNative()      | |  |                    |  |
|  +------------------+ |  |                    |  |
|                        |  | native_impl()      |  |  <-- JNI transition
|                        |  | (C/C++ stack frame)|  |
|                        |  +--------------------+  |
+------------------------------------------------+
When Java code calls a native method, execution "crosses over" via JNI into
the Native Method Stack; if that native code calls back into Java, execution
crosses back onto the regular Stack.

Native Method Stack vs Regular Stack - Comparison

AspectRegular (Java) StackNative Method Stack
Used forJava bytecode method callsNative (C/C++) method calls via JNI
Defined by JVM Specification?Yes, requiredOptional - JVM Spec allows implementations to combine it with the regular Stack
ScopePer-threadPer-thread
HotSpot JVM implementationSeparate regionIn practice, HotSpot often implements it combined with the regular Stack (OS-native thread stack)
Failure modeStackOverflowErrorStackOverflowError or a native crash, depending on how the native code fails

An Important Nuance: The JVM Spec Makes This Optional

The JVM Specification does not strictly mandate a separate Native Method Stack - it explicitly allows an

implementation to combine it with the regular Stack. This is exactly what Oracle's HotSpot JVM does in practice:

Java frames and native frames for a given thread typically coexist on the same underlying OS thread stack, even

though the specification describes them as two conceptually distinct areas. Other JVM implementations are free

to keep them fully separate.

Production Relevance: Native Crashes Don't Look Like Java Errors

Because native methods run compiled C/C++ code outside the JVM's normal safety net (bounds checking, garbage

collection, exception handling), a bug in native code can crash the entire JVM process with a

native crash (segfault) rather than a clean, catchable Java exception - producing an hs_err_pidNNNN.log

crash file instead of a normal Java stack trace. This is a key reason JNI usage is treated cautiously in

production: a bug three layers deep in a native library can take down the whole application instantly, with no

chance for application-level error handling to intervene.

Common real-world native-boundary issues:

  • A misbehaving native library causing a JVM segfault under load.
  • Memory leaks in native code that don't show up in Java heap dumps at all (since they live outside the Heap

entirely).

  • JNI reference leaks (native code holding onto Java object references so they can never be garbage collected).

Common Misconceptions

  • "Every JVM has a physically separate Native Method Stack." Wrong - the JVM Spec permits

combining it with the regular Stack, and HotSpot typically does exactly that.

  • "Native method bugs always throw a normal Java exception." Wrong - native code bugs can crash

the entire JVM process outright (a native crash/segfault), bypassing Java's exception handling completely.

  • "Native methods are rare/exotic and irrelevant to typical Java apps." Wrong - many everyday

JDK operations (file I/O, threading, some java.lang.Math operations) are backed by native methods under the

hood, even if application developers never write native keywords themselves.

Senior Notes

  • Native memory (direct buffers, thread stacks, metaspace, JNI allocations) lies outside the heap, so -Xmx does not limit it.
  • Tracking: use -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.
  • Modern bridge: the Foreign Function and Memory API replaces JNI for many cases; it was preview in JDK 21 and final in JDK 22.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to call native code:

  • JNI: the classic way; a header and compiled library are needed.
  • JNA: a third-party library that avoids writing C glue.
  • Foreign Function and Memory API: java.lang.foreign, preview in JDK 21 and final in JDK 22.
  • Direct ByteBuffer: off-heap memory without native code.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

How a native call works in HotSpot.

  • Binding: the JVM looks up the symbol, for example Java_Hello_greet, in loaded libraries on the first call.
  • Transition: the thread changes state from "in Java" to "in native"; the GC may run while it is in native code.
  • Stack: native frames sit on the same OS thread stack as Java frames; there is no separate stack in HotSpot.
  • References: JNI passes handles, not raw pointers, so the GC can move objects.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong library name or path: UnsatisfiedLinkError; check -Djava.library.path.
  • Wrong signature: the C function name must match the mangled name exactly.
  • Leaking local references: in long native loops, release them with DeleteLocalRef.
  • Blaming the heap: an OOM with free heap may be native memory.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning points:

  • Call cost: a JNI call costs far more than a normal call, so batch work into one native call.
  • Direct buffers: reuse them; allocation and freeing is expensive.
  • Stack size: keep -Xss small for many threads.
  • Limit: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize caps direct buffers.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a service shows a RSS of 6 GB with an -Xmx of 2 GB.

  • Enable NMT and take a baseline, then a diff after load.
  • If Internal or Other grows, suspect direct buffers or a native library.
  • If Thread grows, suspect thread leaks.

10. Examples

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 2

interviewQA: What is the Native Method Stack used for?
Tracking method calls for native (C/C++) methods invoked via JNI, separate from Java bytecode method calls
Is the Native Method Stack per-thread or shared?
Per-thread, just like the regular Stack
Does the JVM Specification require a physically separate Native Method Stack?
No - it explicitly allows combining it with the regular Java Stack, which HotSpot typically does
What mechanism lets Java code call native code?
JNI (Java Native Interface)
What happens if native code has a serious bug?
It can crash the entire JVM process natively (e.g. a segfault), producing an hs_err crash log instead of a catchable Java exception
Can Native Method Stack usage cause a StackOverflowError?
Yes, it's possible, though native code failures can also manifest as lower-level native crashes depending on the implementation
Do JDK classes use native methods internally?
Yes - many core operations (file I/O, threading primitives, some math routines) are backed by native methods, even though most developers never see them directly
Why are JNI-related memory leaks hard to detect with a Java heap dump?
Because native memory used by native code lives outside the Java Heap entirely, so heap dumps and standard Heap-based tools don't capture it

topics.name: Object Creation

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What Happens When You Write new?

Every time you use the new keyword in Java, the JVM does a small sequence of work behind the

scenes to build you a brand-new object in memory.

Think of a class as a blueprint (like a house plan) and an object as the actual house built

from that plan. The new keyword is the construction crew that turns the plan into a real house

sitting on a real plot of land (memory).

The Object Creation Steps

When the JVM executes new Student(), it roughly performs these steps:

  • Step 1: Allocate a block of memory on the Heap large enough for the object.
  • Step 2: Set all fields to their default values (0, false, null etc).
  • Step 3: Run the constructor code to initialize the fields with real values.
  • Step 4: Return a reference (memory address) to the newly created object.

Every Object Has a Little "Header" Too

Besides your own fields (rollNumber, name), every object secretly carries a small amount of extra bookkeeping

data called the object header. It stores things like:

  • A hash code (used by hashCode()).
  • Locking information (used when the object is synchronized).
  • A pointer back to the object's class (so the JVM knows "this is a Student").

You never access the header directly - it's managed entirely by the JVM - but it's part of why even an

"empty" object still takes up some memory.

Default Values Before the Constructor Runs

A common beginner surprise: fields are NOT left "empty" or garbage before your constructor runs. The JVM

zeroes them out first (Step 2 above), then your constructor overwrites them.

Each new Creates a Separate Object

Calling new twice always produces two completely independent objects in memory, even if their

field values are identical.

Fresher Notes

  • new allocates memory for the object, sets fields to defaults (0, false, null) and then runs the constructor.
  • Where: the object lives on the heap; the variable that points to it lives on the stack (for a local).
  • Size: an object is its header plus its fields plus padding, so a small object is never zero bytes.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Order: superclass constructor, then instance field initializers and instance blocks, then the rest of the constructor body.
  • Header: with compressed class pointers, the object header is 12 bytes; objects are aligned to 8 bytes.
  • Class loading: the first new Foo() loads, links and initializes class Foo if that has not happened yet.

8. Advanced Concepts

Deep Dive: JVM-Level Object Allocation

At the bytecode level, new Student(101, "Aisha") actually compiles into two separate bytecode

instructions:

  • new - allocates raw, zeroed memory on the heap for the object and pushes a reference to it

onto the operand stack.

  • invokespecial - calls the constructor (<init>) on that freshly allocated

memory to actually initialize it.

This two-step split matters: the object technically "exists" on the heap (with all-default field values)

for a brief moment before the constructor has even started running.

Where Allocation Actually Happens: TLAB

Modern JVMs rarely allocate directly from a shared, lock-protected heap region for every single object -

that would cause heavy thread contention. Instead, each thread gets its own small private chunk of the

Young Generation called a TLAB (Thread-Local Allocation Buffer).

  • Small, short-lived objects are usually "bump allocated" inside the thread's TLAB - just moving a pointer

forward, extremely fast, no locking needed.

  • When a TLAB fills up, the thread requests a new TLAB from the shared heap (this does need a small amount

of synchronization).

  • Very large objects (bigger than a threshold) may bypass TLABs and allocate directly in the shared heap,

or even go straight to the Old Generation.

Object Layout in Memory

Heap memory for a Student object (conceptual, HotSpot-style)

+------------------------------+
|  Object Header                |
|   - Mark Word (hash, lock)    |
|   - Klass Pointer (-> Class)  |
+------------------------------+
|  Instance Fields               |
|   - int rollNumber = 101       |
|   - String name  -> "Aisha"    |
+------------------------------+
|  Padding (alignment to 8B)     |
+------------------------------+

The header typically costs 12-16 bytes (depending on JVM/compressed-oops settings) before your own fields

even start - this is why a "tiny" object is never truly free.

Allocation Strategies Compared

StrategyWhereSpeedUsed For
TLAB bump allocationThread-local slice of EdenVery fast (pointer bump)Small, short-lived objects (most objects)
Shared Eden allocationEden space, synchronizedSlower (contention)When a thread's TLAB is exhausted
Direct Old Gen / humongousOld GenerationSlowest, triggers GC pressureVery large objects, e.g. big arrays
Escape-analyzed scalar replacementStack / registers (no heap at all)Fastest possibleObjects the JIT proves never "escape" a method

Common Bugs and Misconceptions

  • "Object creation is basically free." Not true - even fast TLAB allocation still adds GC

pressure later; creating millions of short-lived objects in a hot loop (e.g. boxing primitives, building

Strings with + in a loop) is a classic performance bug.

  • Believing fields hold garbage before the constructor runs. The JVM guarantees zeroing

first - you can never see uninitialized garbage memory in Java, unlike C/C++.

  • Assuming new always hits the heap. With escape analysis and scalar

replacement, the JIT compiler can sometimes eliminate heap allocation entirely for objects proven to stay

local to a method.

  • Forgetting that constructors can throw before fully initializing an object, leaving a

half-initialized (but already heap-allocated) object referenced by nothing, ready to be garbage collected.

Senior Notes

  • TLAB: each thread allocates from its own Thread-Local Allocation Buffer, so allocation is usually a pointer bump without locking.
  • Escape analysis: the JIT can remove an allocation (scalar replacement) when the object never escapes the method.
  • Measure: use JOL (ClassLayout.parseClass) to see real object layout instead of guessing.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways an object comes into existence:

  • new: the normal way.
  • Class.newInstance / Constructor.newInstance: reflection.
  • clone(): copies without calling the constructor.
  • Deserialization: builds the object without its own constructor.
  • Factory methods and records: hide new behind a static method.
  • Array creation: new int[n] uses newarray.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

What new Foo() does inside HotSpot.

  • Bytecode: new, dup, invokespecial <init>.
  • Class check: the class must be loaded and initialized.
  • Allocation: the fast path bumps the TLAB pointer; if the TLAB is full, a new one is requested, and if the heap is full, a GC runs.
  • Zeroing: memory is cleared, then the header (mark word, class pointer) is set.
  • Constructor: <init> runs and fields get their values.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Calling an overridable method in a constructor: the subclass field is still at its default.
  • Allocating in a hot loop: new Integer or short-lived temp objects; use primitives.
  • Creating an object per call: for expensive objects like Pattern or DateTimeFormatter, make them static final.
  • Assuming zero size: an empty object still takes 16 bytes.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Allocation tuning:

  • Reduce garbage: fewer short-lived objects means fewer young collections.
  • Compressed oops: heaps under about 32 GB keep 4-byte references; crossing it makes references 8 bytes.
  • Watch allocation rate: use JFR (jdk.ObjectAllocationSample) or GC logs.
  • Layout: group fields to cut padding; use primitives over wrappers.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an API endpoint is slow under load and GC shows many young collections.

  • Record with JFR and find the top allocation sites.
  • Replace per-request regex compilation and string formatting with cached objects and StringBuilder.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Object size with JOL.

Worked Example 2

Allocation count with a quick loop.

Practice Exercise 1

Defaults before the constructor.

Practice Exercise 2

Initialization order.

interviewQA: What are the steps the JVM performs on new?
Allocate zeroed memory, set default field values, run the constructor, return a reference to the caller
What bytecode instructions does new Foo() compile to?
new (allocate memory) followed by invokespecial (call the constructor)
What is a TLAB?
Thread-Local Allocation Buffer - a small per-thread slice of Eden space used for fast, lock-free object allocation
What is stored in an object's header?
The mark word (hash code, lock state, GC age) and a pointer to the object's class (Klass pointer)
Are object fields guaranteed to be zeroed before the constructor runs?
Yes, the JVM always zeroes fields first, so Java never exposes uninitialized/garbage memory
Can the JVM avoid heap allocation entirely for some objects?
Yes, via escape analysis and scalar replacement, if the JIT proves the object never escapes the method
Why is creating millions of short-lived objects in a loop a performance concern?
Even fast TLAB allocation increases minor GC frequency and pause time due to higher allocation pressure

topics.name: References

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

A Reference Is Not the Object

In Java, when you write Student s1 = new Student();, the variable s1 does NOT

hold the actual Student object. It holds a reference - basically an address that tells the JVM

"the real object lives over there in the Heap."

Think of a reference like a house's address written on a piece of paper. The paper (variable) is

small and easy to carry around; the actual house (object) is the big thing sitting at that address.

Copying a Reference Copies the Address, Not the Object

When you assign one reference variable to another, you are copying the address - both variables now point

to the exact same object in memory. No new object is created.

A Reference Can Point to Nothing: null

A reference variable that isn't pointing to any object holds the special value null. Trying to

use a null reference to call a method throws a NullPointerException.

Two References, Two Different Objects

If instead you create two separate objects with new, each reference points to its own,

independent object - changing one never affects the other.

Reference Equality (==) vs Value Equality (equals())

== on objects checks whether two references point to the SAME object in memory, not whether

their contents look equal. Use equals() to compare the actual content.

Fresher Notes

  • Reference: a variable holds the address of an object, not the object itself; a = b copies the reference.
  • Pass by value: Java always passes a copy of the reference, so a method can change the object but cannot re-point your variable.
  • null: a reference to nothing; calling a method on it throws NullPointerException.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Strong: a normal reference; the object is never collected while one exists.
  • Soft and weak: SoftReference keeps the object until memory is short; WeakReference lets it go at the next GC.
  • == vs equals: == compares references, equals compares content when overridden.

8. Advanced Concepts

References Are Pass-by-Value Too

Java is strictly pass-by-value, even for objects. What gets copied when you pass an object

to a method is the reference (the address) itself - not the object it points to. This is a subtle but

critical distinction:

  • You CAN mutate the object's fields through the copied reference (both point to the same object).
  • You CANNOT make the caller's reference point to a different object by reassigning the parameter inside

the method - that only rebinds the local copy of the reference.

Reference Layout: Diagram

Stack (or local vars)          Heap
+----------------+             +----------------------+
| account1  ---------------->  | ReferenceCopyDemo obj |
+----------------+             |  balance = 5000       |
| account2  ---------------->  +----------------------+
+----------------+                       ^
                                          |
                    both references point to the SAME heap object

Only the arrows (addresses) live on the stack (for local variables); the object itself always lives on the

heap.

Types of References the JVM Recognizes (GC-Relevant)

Beyond ordinary "strong" references, java.lang.ref exposes weaker reference types that change

how the Garbage Collector treats the referenced object:

Reference TypeGC BehaviorTypical Use
Strong (normal)Never collected while reachableEveryday variables/fields
Soft (SoftReference)Collected only when memory is lowMemory-sensitive caches
Weak (WeakReference)Collected at the next GC cycle if no strong refs remainWeakHashMap, listener maps, avoiding leaks
Phantom (PhantomReference)Object already finalized; used only for cleanup notificationResource cleanup tracking

Common Bugs and Misconceptions

  • "Java is pass-by-reference." False - Java is always pass-by-value; what's passed for

objects is a copy of the reference value, not the object, and not a reference-to-the-reference.

  • Holding onto references longer than needed causes memory leaks. A static field or a

long-lived collection that keeps a strong reference to objects you're "done with" prevents the GC from

ever reclaiming them - a very common leak pattern in Java.

  • Confusing == with .equals() on wrapper types and Strings is

one of the most common real-world bugs, especially since small cached Integers (-128 to 127) make

== "accidentally" work sometimes.

  • Assuming setting a reference to null immediately frees memory. It only

removes one path to the object; the object is reclaimed only when the GC runs AND no other reference

exists.

Senior Notes

  • Four strengths: strong, soft, weak, phantom; they decide when the GC may reclaim an object.
  • ReferenceQueue and Cleaner: get a notification after collection; use Cleaner instead of finalize(), which is deprecated for removal since JDK 18.
  • Leaks: a long-lived map or static field holding strong references is the most common Java memory leak; WeakHashMap can help for caches keyed by identity-like objects.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Reference types and helpers:

  • SoftReference: memory-sensitive caches.
  • WeakReference / WeakHashMap: canonical maps, listener registries.
  • PhantomReference + Cleaner: run cleanup after unreachable.
  • Optional: a safer holder than null for return values.
  • Objects.requireNonNull: fail fast on null.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

How the GC treats reference strengths.

  • Strong: the object is a GC root path target and stays.
  • Soft: kept until the GC needs memory; the policy uses -XX:SoftRefLRUPolicyMSPerMB (default 1000 ms per free MB).
  • Weak: cleared when the object is only weakly reachable.
  • Phantom: enqueued after the object is finalized; get() always returns null.
  • Queues: the GC enqueues cleared references on a ReferenceQueue.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Using finalize(): slow, unpredictable and deprecated for removal; use try-with-resources and Cleaner.
  • Weak reference to a value you only hold weakly: the cache empties at once.
  • Key referenced by its own value in a WeakHashMap: the entry never goes away.
  • Static collections that only grow: a classic leak.
  • Relying on System.gc(): it is only a hint.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning notes:

  • Soft references make GC behavior harder to predict; prefer a sized cache (Caffeine) for most cases.
  • Many reference objects add reference-processing time to GC pauses.
  • Check logs: -Xlog:gc+ref=debug shows reference processing time.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: heap grows until OOM after a few days. Take a heap dump and look at the dominator tree.

  • Find the biggest retained set, then the path to GC roots.
  • A static map or a listener list holding strong references is the usual cause.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

interviewQA: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
Always pass-by-value; for objects, the value passed is a copy of the reference (address), not the object itself
What happens when you assign one reference variable to another?
The address is copied - both variables now point to the same object, no new object is created
What does a null reference mean?
The variable currently points to no object; using it to call a method throws NullPointerException
What's the difference between == and .equals() for objects?
== compares reference addresses (identity); .equals() compares logical content, as defined by the class
Can a method reassign the caller's object reference?
No - reassigning a parameter inside a method only changes the local copy of the reference, not the caller's variable
What is a WeakReference used for?
To reference an object without preventing the GC from collecting it, useful for caches and avoiding memory leaks
Does setting a reference to null immediately free the object's memory?
No - it only removes that one path to the object; actual reclamation happens later during GC if no other references exist

topics.name: Stack vs Heap

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

Two Memory Areas Every Java Program Uses

When a Java program runs, the JVM splits the memory it uses into different areas. The two you'll hear about

constantly are the Stack and the Heap.

  • Stack - stores method calls and local variables. Very fast, very short-lived.
  • Heap - stores all objects (created with new). Larger, longer-lived, shared

by the whole program.

What Goes on the Stack

Each time a method is called, the JVM pushes a new stack frame for it. That frame holds the

method's local variables and primitive values. When the method finishes, its frame is popped and everything

in it disappears automatically.

What Goes on the Heap

Every object you create with new lives on the Heap - not the Stack. Only the reference

(address) to that object sits on the Stack.

Primitives vs Objects: Where They Live

A local primitive variable (int, double, boolean, etc.) stores its actual value directly on

the Stack. An object always lives on the Heap, and the variable pointing to it (on the

Stack) only holds its address.

Why This Matters: Method Calls Are Isolated

Because each method call gets its own fresh stack frame, local variables in one method call can never

accidentally clash with local variables of another call - even recursive calls to the same method.

Fresher Notes

  • Stack: each method call pushes a frame with locals and parameters; the frame is removed when the method returns.
  • Heap: all objects and arrays live here and are shared by every thread.
  • Cleanup: stack memory is freed automatically on return; heap memory is freed by the garbage collector.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Primitives vs objects: a local int sits in the frame; a local String variable holds a reference into the heap.
  • StackOverflowError: too-deep recursion fills the stack; OutOfMemoryError: the heap is full.
  • Sizes: set with -Xss (per thread stack) and -Xms / -Xmx (heap).

8. Advanced Concepts

Stack Frame Anatomy

Each thread in Java gets its own private Stack (this is why Stack data is inherently thread-safe - no

sharing). Every stack frame pushed onto it typically contains:

  • Local variables array (primitives and object references).
  • Operand stack (used internally by the JVM to evaluate expressions/bytecode).
  • A reference to the runtime constant pool of the current class (for resolving symbols).

The Heap, in contrast, is a single shared area across ALL threads - which is exactly why object access can

require synchronization, while purely-local primitive computation never does.

Memory Layout Diagram

Thread-1 Stack        Thread-2 Stack             Shared Heap
+--------------+       +--------------+       +-------------------------+
| main() frame |       | run() frame  |       | Eden | Survivor 0/1     |
|  x = 5       |       |  local vars  |  -->  | Young Generation        |
|  obj -----------------------------------+   +-------------------------+
+--------------+       +--------------+   |   | Old Generation (Tenured)|
                                           +-> |  long-lived objects     |
                                               +-------------------------+

Notice: each thread's stack is private and small; the Heap is shared, larger, and is where the Garbage

Collector does all of its work - the Stack is never garbage collected, it just unwinds.

Stack vs Heap: Detailed Comparison

AspectStackHeap
StoresMethod frames, local vars, primitives, referencesAll objects and arrays
ScopePer-thread (private)Shared across all threads
LifetimeTied to method call (LIFO)Tied to reachability (GC-managed)
SpeedVery fast (pointer bump / pop)Slower (allocation + GC overhead)
SizeSmall, fixed per thread (-Xss)Large, configurable (-Xms/-Xmx)
Error on exhaustionStackOverflowErrorOutOfMemoryError
Thread safetyInherently thread-safe (private)Requires synchronization for shared mutable objects

Common Bugs and Misconceptions

  • "All local variables are on the stack, always." Mostly true for primitives, but a local

object variable only stores a reference on the stack - the object itself is on the heap (unless

escape analysis proves it can be scalar-replaced and avoid the heap entirely).

  • Deep/unbounded recursion causing StackOverflowError - each call pushes a

new frame; without a proper base case, thousands of frames accumulate until the (small, fixed) stack size

is exhausted.

  • Confusing "heap" (JVM heap) with "Heap" the data structure (priority queue) - same word,

completely unrelated concepts.

  • Assuming bigger Stack always helps performance. Increasing -Xss only helps

avoid StackOverflowError for deep recursion; it does nothing for heap/object performance, and consumes more

memory per thread (multiplied by thread count).

Senior Notes

  • Thread safety: locals are private to a thread, so they are safe; heap objects need synchronization when shared.
  • Escape analysis can place non-escaping objects in registers or stack-like storage, so "objects always on the heap" is a model, not a guarantee.
  • Many threads: total stack memory is threads times -Xss, which matters with thousands of platform threads; virtual threads keep stacks on the heap.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Sizing options:

  • -Xss: stack size of new threads (default 1 MB on 64-bit Linux).
  • -Xms / -Xmx: initial and maximum heap.
  • -XX:MaxRAMPercentage: heap as a share of container memory.
  • -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError: dump the heap when it fills.
  • Thread constructor: a per-thread stack size hint.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Internals of the two areas.

  • Stack frame: local variable array, operand stack and frame data, all sized at compile time.
  • Per thread: created with the thread, reserved by -Xss, and grown by the OS as needed.
  • Heap: shared, split into generations or regions by the collector, and grows between -Xms and -Xmx.
  • Reference: a frame slot holds either a primitive value or a reference into the heap.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Saying "objects are on the stack": only the reference is, unless the JIT scalar-replaces the object.
  • Raising -Xss to hide infinite recursion: fix the base case instead.
  • Large local arrays in recursion: the array is on the heap, but deep recursion still overflows with big frames.
  • Sharing a mutable heap object between threads without a lock.
  • Setting -Xmx equal to container memory: there is no room left for metaspace and thread stacks.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Prefer iteration over deep recursion; the JVM does not eliminate tail calls.
  • Small frames: fewer locals means more depth per MB.
  • Right-size the heap: too small gives frequent GC; too large gives long pauses on some collectors.
  • Many tasks: use virtual threads (JDK 21) instead of thousands of large platform stacks.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a JSON parser fails with StackOverflowError on deeply nested input.

  • Cap nesting depth and reject hostile input.
  • If the depth is legitimate, parse in a thread with a larger stack, or convert to an explicit stack on the heap.

interviewQA: What is stored on the Java Stack?
Method call frames: local primitive variables and object references (not the objects themselves)
What is stored on the Java Heap?
All objects and arrays created with new, shared across all threads
Is the Stack shared between threads?
No, each thread has its own private stack; only the Heap is shared
What error occurs when the Stack is exhausted?
StackOverflowError, typically from unbounded/deep recursion
What error occurs when the Heap is exhausted?
OutOfMemoryError
Which JVM flags control Stack and Heap size?
-Xss for per-thread stack size; -Xms/-Xmx for initial/max heap size
Why is the Stack faster than the Heap for allocation?
Stack allocation is just moving a pointer (push/pop, LIFO) with no GC involvement, while Heap allocation involves bookkeeping and eventual garbage collection
Can an object ever avoid the Heap entirely?
Yes, via JIT escape analysis and scalar replacement, if the object is proven not to escape the method

topics.name: String Pool

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

Strings Are Special in Java

Strings are used so heavily in every Java program that the JVM has a dedicated optimization for them called

the String Pool (also called the String Constant Pool or String Intern Pool). It's a special

area in memory that stores unique String literals so identical text doesn't get duplicated over and over.

String Literals Share the Same Object

When you create a String using a literal (double quotes), Java checks the pool first. If an identical String

already exists there, it reuses it instead of creating a new object.

new String() Skips the Pool

Using the new keyword with String always creates a brand-new object on the Heap, even if an

identical literal already exists in the pool.

Bringing a String Into the Pool with intern()

The intern() method looks up the String's content in the pool. If found, it returns the pooled

reference; if not, it adds the String's content to the pool and returns that reference.

Why This Saves Memory

Imagine an application that stores "India" as a city/country name a million times across different objects.

Without pooling, that could mean a million separate String objects holding identical text. With the pool,

all million literal usages share ONE object.

Fresher Notes

  • String pool: a shared table of unique string literals, so "hi" used twice is one object.
  • Literal vs new: "hi" reuses a pooled object; new String("hi") always makes a new one.
  • intern(): returns the pooled copy of a string, adding it if missing.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Compile-time constants: "a" + "b" is folded to "ab" and pooled; a runtime concatenation is not.
  • Location: since JDK 7 the pool lives in the heap, so pooled strings can be garbage collected when unreachable.
  • Why immutable: sharing is only safe because a String cannot change.

8. Advanced Concepts

Where the Pool Actually Lives

Historically (Java 6 and earlier), the String Pool lived in PermGen, a fixed-size area

prone to OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space if too many Strings were interned. Since

Java 7, the pool was moved into the main Heap itself, which lets it grow

dynamically and be garbage collected like any other heap data, drastically reducing intern-related

OutOfMemoryErrors in practice.

Compile-Time Constant Folding

The pool doesn't just apply to simple literals - the compiler also folds constant expressions at compile

time, so they resolve to the same pooled String even though the source doesn't look identical.

String Pool: Key Facts Compared

AspectString literal "x"new String("x")
LocationString Pool (in Heap since Java 7)General Heap (outside pool)
Reused if content matches?Yes, automaticallyNo, always a new object
== with identical literaltruefalse
Eligible for GCOnly if unreferenced pool-wide (rare)As soon as unreachable, like any object
Can be added to pool manually?N/A (already there)Yes, via .intern()

Common Bugs and Misconceptions

  • Comparing Strings with == instead of .equals() - works

"by accident" for literals due to pooling, then silently breaks in production once a String comes from

user input, a database, or new String(...). Always use .equals() for content

comparison.

  • "Interning everything improves performance." Over-interning large numbers of unique

runtime Strings can bloat the pool and increase lookup/GC cost - only intern Strings you know will repeat

often.

  • Assuming the pool still causes PermGen OutOfMemoryError in modern Java - since Java 7 the

pool lives in the regular Heap, so this specific historical failure mode mostly no longer applies.

  • Forgetting that StringBuilder.toString() never returns a pooled String, even

if the resulting text matches an existing literal exactly - it's a fresh Heap object unless you call

.intern() on it.

Senior Notes

  • StringTable is a native hash table; its size is -XX:StringTableSize (default 65536 since JDK 11).
  • Statistics: -XX:+PrintStringTableStatistics or jcmd <pid> VM.stringtable show size and buckets.
  • Deduplication: with G1, -XX:+UseStringDeduplication shares the char data of equal strings that are not interned.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to get a String and what each does:

  • Literal: pooled.
  • new String(s): new object, rarely needed.
  • intern(): pooled copy.
  • + with constants: folded and pooled.
  • StringBuilder.toString(): new object.
  • String.valueOf / concat: new object.
  • Text block: a literal, pooled.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

How the pool works.

  • Literals: a string literal sits in the class constant pool; the first time it is resolved, the JVM looks it up in the StringTable or adds it.
  • ldc: the bytecode that loads a constant, giving the same object each time.
  • Storage: the String objects are on the heap; the table holds weak references so unused entries can be collected.
  • Representation: since JDK 9 a String stores bytes with a coder (Latin-1 or UTF-16).

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Comparing with ==: works by accident for literals and fails for runtime strings; use equals.
  • Interning every input string: it grows the table and slows lookups.
  • Using new String(literal): it only wastes memory.
  • Concatenating in a loop: creates many temporary Strings; use StringBuilder.
  • Storing secrets as Strings: they stay in memory until collected; prefer char[] that you clear.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Table size: if you intern many strings, raise -XX:StringTableSize to a prime near the expected count to keep buckets short.
  • Dedup: try -XX:+UseStringDeduplication with G1 when heap dumps show many duplicate strings.
  • Compact strings: on by default; -XX:-CompactStrings disables them.
  • Concatenation: since JDK 9 javac uses invokedynamic (StringConcatFactory), which is fast for simple cases.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a heap dump shows 300 MB of duplicate country and status strings read from a database.

  • Intern the small, fixed set at read time, or use an enum.
  • Or enable G1 deduplication with no code change.

interviewQA: What is the String Pool?
A special memory area that stores unique String literals so identical text is shared instead of duplicated
Where does the String Pool live in modern Java?
Inside the main Heap, since Java 7 (previously in PermGen before that)
Does new String("x") use the pool?
No - it always creates a new object on the general heap, bypassing the pool
What does String.intern() do?
Returns the pooled reference for that content, adding it to the pool first if not already present
Why is == risky for comparing Strings?
It compares references, not content; it may accidentally work for pooled literals but fail for equal-content Strings from new, user input, or concatenation at runtime
Are compile-time constant expressions like "hel" + "lo" pooled?
Yes, the compiler folds them into a single literal at compile time, so they resolve to the pooled instance
Is runtime concatenation like prefix + "lo" pooled automatically?
No, it's built via StringBuilder at runtime and produces a new, non-pooled object unless .intern() is called

topics.name: Static Variables

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What Does static Mean?

Normally, every object gets its own copy of a class's fields. But mark a field static and

something different happens: instead of belonging to each object, it belongs to the class itself.

There is only ONE copy of it, no matter how many objects you create.

Static Variables Are Shared Across All Objects

Every instance of the class sees and shares the exact same static variable. Changing it through one object

is visible through every other object too.

You Don't Need an Object to Access a Static Variable

Because a static variable belongs to the class, not to any object, you can access it directly through the

class name - even before any object has been created.

Static Variables Exist Even With Zero Objects

A static variable is created once when the class is loaded by the JVM, and it keeps its value even if no

objects of that class currently exist.

Fresher Notes

  • One copy: a static field belongs to the class, so every object shares the same single value.
  • Where it lives: the value is stored with the class data in the JVM (in the Class object on the heap since Java 8), not inside each instance.
  • Access: use ClassName.field; it works without creating any object.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Initialization: statics are set once, when the class is first initialized, by field initializers and static {} blocks in order.
  • GC roots: a static reference keeps its object alive as long as the class is loaded, so large static collections can leak memory.
  • Thread visibility: a mutable static is shared by all threads, so guard it with volatile, locks or atomics.

8. Advanced Concepts

Where Static Variables Actually Live

Static variables are stored in an area of memory tied to the Class object's metadata,

managed by the Metaspace (Java 8+) or historically PermGen (Java 7 and earlier). Specifically:

  • The metadata describing the class layout lives in Metaspace.
  • The actual static variable values live as part of the class's representation on the Heap in

modern JVMs, conceptually attached to the Class object for that class.

  • They are created when the class is first loaded/initialized, and destroyed only when the class is

unloaded (which, for normal application classes, is effectively "never" until JVM shutdown).

Class Loading and Static Initialization Order

Static variables are initialized in the exact textual order they appear, interleaved with any static

initializer blocks, the very first time the class is loaded (referenced for the first time by the JVM).

Static Memory Layout Diagram

Metaspace                       Heap
+----------------------+        +---------------------------+
| Counter.class layout |        | Counter object #1          |
|  method bytecode      |        |  id = 1                    |
|  field descriptors    |        +---------------------------+
+----------------------+        | Counter object #2          |
          |                      |  id = 2                    |
          |  (Class object)      +---------------------------+
          v
  static totalCount = 3   <-- ONE value, tied to the class,
                               NOT duplicated per object above

Static vs Instance Variables: Storage Comparison

AspectStatic VariableInstance Variable
CopiesOne per classOne per object
Created whenClass is loaded/initializedEach time new runs
Destroyed whenClass unloaded (rare) / JVM shuts downObject becomes unreachable and is GC'd
AccessClassName.field (or via instance, discouraged)instance.field only
Lifetime relative to objectsCan outlive every object of the classTied strictly to its own object

Static Memory Leaks - A Real Production Hazard

Because static fields live for (almost) the entire lifetime of the application, anything you store in a

static collection and forget to remove becomes a classic, hard-to-diagnose memory leak:

  • A static List or static Map used as a "cache" that only ever grows, never

evicting old entries.

  • Static references to listeners/callbacks that outlive the objects that registered them, preventing those

objects from ever being garbage collected.

  • ThreadLocal variables stored statically in thread-pooled environments (e.g. web servers) that

are never cleared, silently accumulating request-scoped data across requests.

Because the GC sees a live static reference as a permanent GC root, none of these objects are ever

collected, no matter how much memory pressure builds up - eventually leading to

OutOfMemoryError.

Senior Notes

  • Class unloading: statics are freed only when the class loader that loaded the class is collected, which is why redeploys in app servers leak.
  • Design: avoid mutable global state; prefer dependency injection and immutable static final constants.
  • Lazy holder: use a nested holder class for thread-safe lazy singletons, since class initialization is guaranteed once by the JVM.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Static variants:

  • static: one value per class.
  • static final: a constant; a primitive or String literal is inlined by the compiler.
  • static volatile: a flag visible to all threads.
  • static block: complex one-time setup.
  • Nested holder: lazy initialization.
  • enum: a safe singleton.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

A static field is part of the class, not of any instance.

  • Linking: fields are allocated during preparation with default values.
  • Initialization: the class initializer <clinit> runs the initializers and static blocks once, in textual order.
  • Location: since Java 8 the values sit in the Class mirror on the heap; class metadata is in Metaspace.
  • Reachability: the loaded class is a GC root path, so static references keep objects alive.
  • Safety: the JVM locks class initialization, so it happens once even with many threads.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Static for instance data: all objects overwrite one value; make the field non-static.
  • Unsynchronized mutable static: data races; use atomics or locks.
  • Unbounded static cache: memory leak; use a bounded cache with eviction.
  • Static initialization order cycles: a class sees a default value of another; avoid circular statics.
  • Static holding a Context or request: blocks class loader unload.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and sizing:

  • Bound caches: a size limit or WeakHashMap or soft references.
  • Prefer constants: immutable statics add no GC cost.
  • Heap dumps: look for GC Roots of type "class" to find static retention.
  • Static init cost: heavy work delays first use; consider lazy holders.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: after each redeploy of a web app on Tomcat, Metaspace grows until OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace.

  • A shared library keeps a static reference to a webapp class.
  • The old class loader cannot be collected, so all its classes stay.
  • Fix by clearing the static in a shutdown hook or listener, and upgrading the library.
