interviewQA: What does the static keyword mean for a variable?
The variable belongs to the class itself, with a single shared copy across all instances, instead of one copy per object
Where do static variables live in modern JVMs?
Their metadata lives in Metaspace; their values are effectively part of the Class object's representation on the Heap
When are static variables initialized?
Once, the first time the class is loaded/initialized by the JVM, in textual order interleaved with static blocks
Can you access a static variable without creating an object?
Yes, directly via ClassName.field, since it doesn't belong to any specific instance
Why are static fields a common source of memory leaks?
They act as permanent GC roots for the life of the class, so anything referenced from them (e.g. a growing static cache) is never collected
What replaced PermGen for static/class metadata since Java 8?
Metaspace, which is allocated from native memory and grows dynamically instead of a fixed-size PermGen
Is a static variable shared across threads?
Yes - since it's one copy per class (not per thread), concurrent modification from multiple threads requires synchronization

topics.name: Instance Variables

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What Is an Instance Variable?

An instance variable is a field declared inside a class (without the static

keyword) that belongs to each individual object. Every time you create a new object with new,

that object gets its own separate copy of every instance variable.

Each Object Gets Its Own Copy

Unlike static variables, instance variables are NOT shared. Two objects of the same class have completely

independent values for their instance variables.

Instance Variables Live on the Heap, Inside Their Object

Because instance variables belong to an object, and every object lives on the Heap, instance variables live

on the Heap too - as part of the object's memory block.

Instance Variables Get Default Values Automatically

If you don't explicitly assign a value, an instance variable is automatically set to a default (0, false,

null, etc.) - never left undefined.

Instance Variables Disappear With Their Object

An instance variable's lifetime is tied entirely to its object. Once nothing refers to the object anymore,

the object (and every instance variable inside it) becomes eligible for garbage collection.

Fresher Notes

  • Per object: each object has its own copy of every instance variable, stored inside the object on the heap.
  • Default values: fields get 0, false or null automatically; local variables get none.
  • Lifetime: the fields live as long as the object is reachable, then the garbage collector reclaims them.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Object layout: a header (mark word and class pointer, usually 12 bytes with compressed class pointers) is followed by the fields, padded to 8 bytes.
  • References: an instance field of object type stores only a reference (4 bytes with compressed oops), not the other object.
  • Stack versus heap: the reference variable sits on the stack, while the object and its fields are on the heap.

8. Advanced Concepts

Memory Layout of Instance Variables Within an Object

Instance variables are laid out inside the object's memory block on the Heap, right after the object header

(mark word + klass pointer). The JVM (HotSpot) doesn't necessarily preserve declaration order - it commonly

reorders and groups fields by size (longs/doubles, then ints/floats, then shorts/chars, then

booleans/bytes, then references) to minimize padding and improve memory alignment, a technique called

field packing.

Instance Variable Layout Diagram

Heap: one Car object

+--------------------------------+
| Object Header (12-16 bytes)     |
|  Mark Word | Klass Pointer      |
+--------------------------------+
| Instance Fields (per-object)    |
|  int speed      = 60            |
|  String color -----------------> "Red" (separate object, own header)
+--------------------------------+
| Padding (align to 8 bytes)      |
+--------------------------------+

Another 'new Car(...)' produces an ENTIRELY separate block like this one,
with its own header and its own copy of speed/color.

Instance vs Static: Where and How Long They Live

AspectInstance VariableStatic Variable
Memory areaHeap (inside the object)Heap, attached to the Class object / Metaspace metadata
CopiesOne per objectOne per class
CreatedOn every new callOnce, at class loading
ReclaimedWhen the object becomes unreachable (GC'd)Only when the class is unloaded (rare)
Thread sharingShared only if the object itself is sharedAlways shared across all threads

Instance Fields and Garbage Collection Reachability

An instance variable's storage is only reclaimable once its owning object is unreachable - but a subtlety

often missed: if an instance variable itself references ANOTHER object, that inner object is kept alive too

(transitively), for as long as the outer object is reachable. This is why a single long-lived object with a

large collection as an instance variable can pin down a huge object graph in memory, even though most of

that graph "looks unrelated" to the leak at first glance.

Common Bugs and Misconceptions

  • Assuming instance variables are zeroed AFTER the constructor. They're zeroed BEFORE the

constructor body runs, as part of allocation - the constructor only overwrites the defaults you explicitly

set.

  • Believing field declaration order controls memory layout. The JVM is free to reorder

fields internally for alignment/packing; only the logical (source-code) view guarantees order, not the

physical memory layout.

  • Storing large objects as instance fields of a singleton/long-lived object and forgetting

they now live "forever" alongside it - a common accidental memory-leak pattern distinct from static leaks,

but with a similar root cause: an unexpectedly long-lived reference chain.

  • Confusing shadowing: a local variable or parameter with the same name as an instance

variable "hides" it inside a method unless accessed via this.fieldName - a frequent source of

subtle bugs in constructors.

Senior Notes

  • Field reordering: the JVM groups fields by size to cut padding, so declaration order does not decide the layout.
  • False sharing: hot fields of different threads on the same cache line slow each other; @Contended pads them.
  • Footprint: millions of small objects cost header overhead; use primitives, arrays or records of primitives, and measure with JOL.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Field options:

  • Modifiers: private, final, volatile, transient.
  • Initializers: inline, in an instance initializer block, or in the constructor.
  • final fields: safely published after construction.
  • Records: declare components that become private final fields.
  • Inheritance: a subclass object contains the superclass fields too.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Each object is a block on the heap: header plus fields.

  • Header: mark word (8 bytes) and class pointer (4 bytes compressed).
  • Fields: primitives stored inline; object fields store a reference.
  • Alignment: total size rounds up to a multiple of 8 bytes.
  • Allocation: fast pointer bump in a thread-local buffer (TLAB).
  • Escape analysis: the JIT may avoid heap allocation of objects that do not escape.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Public mutable fields: break encapsulation; use private and accessors.
  • Uninitialized reference: null causes NullPointerException.
  • Shared mutable field across threads: needs synchronization.
  • Calling an overridable method in a constructor: sees defaults of the subclass fields.
  • Wrong equals on == : compare objects with equals.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Footprint tips:

  • Primitives over wrappers: an Integer costs about 16 bytes versus 4.
  • Smaller types: do not use long where int is enough.
  • Lazy fields: allocate rarely used objects on demand.
  • Compressed oops: heaps under about 32 GB keep 4-byte references.
  • Measure: use JOL or a heap dump histogram.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a service keeps 5 million Tick objects with a price and time. Memory is large because of headers and boxed values.

  • Each object costs header plus fields plus padding.
  • Store prices in a double[] and times in a long[] instead.
  • Heap use drops and GC has less to scan.

interviewQA: What is an instance variable?
A non-static field declared in a class; each object created from that class gets its own independent copy
Where do instance variables live in memory?
On the Heap, stored inside the memory block of the object that owns them
When are instance variables created and destroyed?
Created each time new runs; destroyed (reclaimed) when the owning object becomes unreachable and is garbage collected
Do instance variables get default values automatically?
Yes - the JVM zeroes them during allocation, before the constructor body executes
Does the JVM preserve field declaration order in memory?
Not necessarily - HotSpot commonly reorders/packs fields by size to minimize padding, though the source-level view still shows declaration order
How do instance variables differ from static variables in lifetime?
Instance variables live and die with their specific object; static variables live for the lifetime of the class, independent of any single object
Can an instance variable cause a memory leak?
Yes, if it references a large object graph and the owning object itself is unexpectedly long-lived (e.g. held by a singleton or cache)

topics.name: GC Fundamentals

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is Garbage Collection?

Garbage Collection (GC) is the process by which the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) automatically finds objects that are

no longer being used by your program and reclaims the memory they occupy.

In languages like C or C++, the programmer must manually call free() (or delete) to release

memory. Forget to do it, and you get a memory leak. Do it too early or twice, and you get a crash.

Java removes this burden - a background process called the Garbage Collector does this cleanup for you.

Why Doesn't Java Need free()?

When you create an object with new, Java allocates memory for it on the heap. As long as

something in your program can still "reach" that object, it stays alive.

Once nothing refers to it anymore, the object becomes unreachable - and the JVM's Garbage Collector

will eventually notice this and free the memory automatically, without you writing any cleanup code.

Reachability - How the JVM Decides What's "Alive"

An object is considered reachable if it can be accessed by following references starting from a

GC Root - things like:

  • Local variables on any thread's stack
  • Active static fields of classes
  • JNI references

If you can draw an unbroken chain of references from a GC Root to an object, that object is alive. If you can't,

it's garbage - eligible for collection.

Mark and Sweep - The Basic Idea

Most Java garbage collectors are built on a simple two-step idea called Mark and Sweep:

  • Mark phase - starting from the GC Roots, the collector walks every reference chain and marks every

object it can reach as "alive".

  • Sweep phase - it then scans the whole heap and reclaims memory for every object that was

not marked - those are the unreachable ones.

Think of it like tracing string from a bulletin board (the roots) to every note connected to it. Any note with no

string reaching it gets thrown away.

You Can't Force GC, Only Suggest It

Java gives you System.gc() to request garbage collection, but it is only a hint to the JVM -

the JVM is free to ignore it entirely. Relying on it in real applications is considered bad practice; the JVM's

internal heuristics almost always make better decisions than manual triggers.

Fresher Notes

  • Automatic memory: the garbage collector frees objects that no live code can reach, so you never call free.
  • Reachability: an object is garbage when no chain of references leads to it from a GC root.
  • Not guaranteed: System.gc() is only a hint, and you cannot decide when collection happens.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • GC roots: thread stacks, static fields, JNI references and active threads are the starting points of the reachability walk.
  • Mark, sweep, compact: mark live objects, free the rest, and optionally move survivors together to remove fragmentation.
  • Stop-the-world: during some phases all application threads pause; collectors differ in how long and how often.

8. Advanced Concepts

Reachability States in Detail

The JVM specification (and java.lang.ref package) actually defines several strengths of reachability,

not just "reachable" vs "not reachable". This matters for caches, listeners, and memory-sensitive data structures.

ReachabilityReference TypeCollected When
Strongly ReachableOrdinary reference (Object o = new Object())Never, while a strong reference chain exists
Softly ReachableSoftReferenceOnly when the JVM is close to running out of heap memory
Weakly ReachableWeakReferenceAt the next GC cycle, regardless of memory pressure
Phantom ReachablePhantomReferenceAfter finalization, used to schedule cleanup actions
UnreachableNo reference chain from any GC RootImmediately eligible for collection

Mark-and-Sweep Internals

Under the hood, a naive Mark-and-Sweep collector works roughly like this:

GC Roots
  |-- Thread stacks (local variables, parameters)
  |-- Static fields
  |-- JNI handles
       |
       v
  MARK: traverse every reachable object graph
        set a "marked" bit on each visited object
       |
       v
  SWEEP: scan the entire heap linearly
         unmarked objects  -> reclaim memory, add to free list
         marked objects    -> clear mark bit for next cycle

This basic algorithm has two well-known costs in production:

  • Stop-the-World pauses - application threads are typically paused during marking so the object

graph doesn't change mid-traversal.

  • Fragmentation - plain sweep leaves free memory scattered in small holes rather than one

contiguous block, which is why most real collectors add a compaction step afterward.

Mark-Sweep vs Mark-Sweep-Compact vs Copying Collection

StrategyHow it worksFragmentationCost
Mark-SweepMark reachable objects, free the rest in placeHigh - holes left behindFast sweep, but slow future allocation
Mark-Sweep-CompactMark, sweep, then slide live objects togetherNone after compactionExtra compaction pass adds pause time
Copying CollectionCopy all live objects into a second empty space, discard the old space entirelyNone - allocation is always contiguousNeeds 2x space reserved, but very fast for short-lived objects

Java's real-world collectors combine these ideas by generation (see the "Generational GC" topic) - copying collection

for the young generation where most objects die quickly, and mark-sweep-compact for the older, longer-lived

generation.

Production Note: System.gc() in Real Systems

Calling System.gc() explicitly in application code is almost always an anti-pattern in production

services - it can trigger a full, expensive Stop-the-World collection at an unpredictable moment, causing a latency

spike for every request being served at that instant.

Some libraries (old RMI implementations, certain NIO direct-buffer cleanup paths) historically called it internally,

which surprised teams debugging periodic latency spikes. The fix in modern JVMs is the flag

-XX:+DisableExplicitGC, which makes System.gc() a no-op - useful when you can't remove the

calls from third-party code but need predictable latency.

Senior Notes

  • Trade-offs: throughput, latency and footprint cannot all be optimal; choose the collector by the goal.
  • Collectors: Serial, Parallel (throughput), G1 (default since Java 9), ZGC and Shenandoah (low pause).
  • Observe first: read GC logs with -Xlog:gc* before changing any flag.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Collectors in JDK 17 and 21:

  • Serial: -XX:+UseSerialGC, single thread, tiny heaps.
  • Parallel: -XX:+UseParallelGC, best throughput for batch jobs.
  • G1: -XX:+UseG1GC, balanced default.
  • ZGC: -XX:+UseZGC, low latency.
  • Shenandoah: -XX:+UseShenandoahGC, low pause, in OpenJDK builds that include it.
  • Epsilon: -XX:+UseEpsilonGC, no collection, for tests.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Tracing collectors find live objects, then free everything else.

  • Mark: walk references from GC roots and flag live objects.
  • Sweep: reclaim unmarked memory.
  • Compact or copy: move live objects together to avoid fragmentation.
  • Safepoints: threads stop at safe points for the stop-the-world phases.
  • Barriers: concurrent collectors use read or write barriers to track changes during marking.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Calling System.gc(): triggers a full collection; disable with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC if libraries do it.
  • Relying on finalize: deprecated; use try-with-resources or Cleaner.
  • Tuning blindly: copying flags from the internet; measure first.
  • Heap too small: constant GC; raise -Xmx.
  • Memory leak mistaken for GC problem: more heap only delays the failure.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning workflow:

  • Goal first: latency, throughput or footprint.
  • Log: -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log.
  • Reduce allocation: the cheapest GC is the one that does not run.
  • Set -Xms equal -Xmx for stable servers to avoid resize pauses.
  • Analyze with GCViewer or GCeasy.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an API shows occasional 2 second freezes.

  • The log shows Pause Full events.
  • Heap dump finds an unbounded cache.
  • Bound the cache, then re-check pause times.

interviewQA: What is Garbage Collection in Java?
The JVM's automatic process of finding and reclaiming memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable from the program
What makes an object eligible for garbage collection?
When there is no reference chain from any GC Root (stack variables, static fields, JNI handles) reaching that object
Does System.gc() guarantee an immediate garbage collection?
No - it is only a hint/request; the JVM decides whether and when to actually run GC
What are the two basic phases of Mark-and-Sweep?
Mark - traverse and flag all reachable objects; Sweep - reclaim memory for everything not marked
Why do collectors add a Compact step after Sweep?
Plain sweeping leaves fragmented free memory as scattered holes; compaction slides live objects together for contiguous free space
What is the difference between a WeakReference and a SoftReference?
A WeakReference is cleared at the next GC cycle regardless of memory pressure; a SoftReference is cleared only when the JVM is low on memory
What are GC Roots?
The starting points of reachability analysis - thread stacks, static fields, and JNI references
Why doesn't Java need a manual free() like C/C++?
The JVM's garbage collector automatically tracks reachability and reclaims memory for unreachable objects, removing the risk of manual leaks and double-frees

topics.name: Generational GC

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

Why Split the Heap into Generations?

Studies of real programs found a simple but powerful pattern: most objects die young. A temporary

string built inside a loop, a short-lived request object, a local list used once and discarded - these are created

and thrown away within milliseconds.

Very few objects (a cache, a database connection pool, a singleton service) live for the entire lifetime of the

application.

Java's Garbage Collector takes advantage of this by dividing the heap into generations and treating

young and old objects differently.

The Young Generation

Every new object is first created in the Young Generation (also called the "nursery"). It is

usually small and gets garbage collected very often, but each collection is fast because most objects in it are

already dead.

This frequent, cheap cleanup of the Young Generation is called a Minor GC.

The Old Generation

Objects that survive several Minor GC cycles are considered long-lived, and get promoted (moved) to

the Old Generation (also called Tenured Generation). This area is collected much less often, but a

collection here - called a Major GC - takes longer because the Old Generation is larger and has more

live data to examine.

Minor GC vs Major GC - Quick Comparison

  • Minor GC - cleans the Young Generation only. Fast, frequent, small pause.
  • Major GC - cleans the Old Generation (sometimes the whole heap, called a Full GC).

Slower, less frequent, bigger pause.

As a beginner, the key takeaway is: creating lots of short-lived objects is cheap in Java precisely because of this

design - the Young Generation is built to handle exactly that pattern efficiently.

Promotion in a Nutshell

Think of the Young Generation like a classroom that gets cleared out every day - most students (objects) leave after

one day (one GC cycle). A few students who keep showing up for many days in a row (surviving many Minor GCs)

eventually get "promoted" to a permanent desk in another room - the Old Generation.

Fresher Notes

  • Weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young, so collecting a small young area often is cheap.
  • Two areas: the young generation (Eden plus two survivor spaces) and the old generation.
  • Promotion: an object that survives several young collections moves to the old generation.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Minor GC cleans only the young generation and is fast; major or full GC involves the old generation and costs more.
  • Age threshold: objects get an age per survived collection; -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold caps it (15 maximum).
  • Card table: tracks old-to-young references so a minor GC does not scan the whole old generation.

8. Advanced Concepts

The Weak Generational Hypothesis

Generational GC is built entirely on one empirical observation, formally called the Weak Generational

Hypothesis:

"Most objects die young, and the ones that survive tend to live a long time."

This is "weak" (as opposed to a hard guarantee) because it's a statistical tendency, not a law - some workloads

(e.g. large in-memory caches with high churn, or object pools with unusual lifetimes) violate it and suffer worse GC

performance as a result. Understanding this hypothesis is the single most important mental model for reasoning

about GC tuning.

Young Generation Internal Layout

The Young Generation itself is subdivided further to implement an efficient copying collector:

Young Generation
 |-- Eden Space        <-- almost all new objects are allocated here
 |-- Survivor Space S0  <-- "from" space
 |-- Survivor Space S1  <-- "to" space (swaps roles with S0 each Minor GC)

Old Generation
 |-- Tenured Space      <-- objects promoted after surviving enough Minor GCs

Each Minor GC:

  • Copies all live objects from Eden into whichever Survivor space is currently empty ("to" space).
  • Copies all live objects from the other Survivor space into "to" space as well, aging them by one.
  • Clears Eden and the old "from" Survivor space entirely - they become the next "to" space.
  • Objects that have survived past a threshold (-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold, default 15) get promoted to

Tenured space instead of copied into a Survivor space again.

Minor GC vs Major GC vs Full GC

AspectMinor GCMajor GCFull GC
ScopeYoung Generation onlyOld Generation (implementation-dependent)Entire heap (Young + Old + Metaspace)
FrequencyVery frequentLess frequentRare (ideally)
Typical pauseSub-millisecond to a few msTens to hundreds of msCan be seconds on large heaps
Algorithm usedCopying collectionMark-Sweep-Compact (collector dependent)Mark-Sweep-Compact across the whole heap
Common triggerEden space fills upOld Generation occupancy crosses a thresholdAllocation failure even after Old GC, or explicit System.gc()

Production Scenario: Premature Promotion

A common production issue is premature promotion: if the Young Generation (particularly Eden and

Survivor spaces) is undersized relative to the allocation rate, objects that would normally die young get promoted

to the Old Generation before they actually die - simply because a Minor GC catches them "in transit" too many times,

or Survivor space overflows and forces early tenuring.

Symptom: Old Generation fills up faster than expected, triggering frequent, expensive Major/Full GCs even though the

application's true long-lived data set is small.

Fix: increase Young Generation size (-Xmn) or tune the survivor ratio (-XX:SurvivorRatio)

so short-lived objects have enough room and time to die inside the Young Generation before being swept along into

Old Gen.

Senior Notes

  • Sizing: -XX:NewRatio and -Xmn set the young size; too small means premature promotion.
  • Premature promotion: short-lived objects reaching old space fill it and trigger full GCs.
  • Newer collectors: ZGC became generational in JDK 21 with -XX:+ZGenerational; G1 and Parallel were always generational.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • -Xmn: fixed young size.
  • -XX:NewRatio=2: old is 2 times young.
  • -XX:SurvivorRatio=8: Eden is 8 times one survivor.
  • -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold: promotion age limit.
  • -XX:G1NewSizePercent / G1MaxNewSizePercent: young bounds for G1.
  • -XX:+ZGenerational: generational ZGC in JDK 21.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The heap is divided by object age.

  • Eden: new objects are allocated here (TLAB pointer bump).
  • Survivors S0 and S1: live objects are copied between them each minor GC and age increases.
  • Old: objects that reach the tenuring threshold, or do not fit in survivor space.
  • Remembered sets or card table: record old-to-young pointers as extra roots.
  • Young collection is copying, so cost depends on live data, not on garbage.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Tiny young generation: objects promoted too early; enlarge it.
  • Huge young generation: longer young pauses on Serial or Parallel.
  • Large temporary buffers: allocated straight to old; reuse them.
  • Caches of medium-lived objects: they survive many copies; consider an off-heap or bounded cache.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Target: keep live young survivors small.
  • Reduce allocation rate: avoid needless temporary objects in hot paths.
  • G1: do not set -Xmn; it adapts young size to the pause goal.
  • Watch: promotion rate and old occupancy after each GC.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a session service promotes sessions early.

  • Each request builds 3 MB of temporary JSON.
  • Young space is 20 MB so survivors overflow into old.
  • Raising the young size and streaming the JSON stops the full GCs.

interviewQA: What is the Weak Generational Hypothesis?
The observation that most objects die young, while a small fraction survive and live much longer - the basis for splitting the heap into generations
What is the difference between Minor GC and Major/Full GC?
Minor GC cleans only the Young Generation (fast, frequent); Major/Full GC cleans the Old Generation or the entire heap (slower, less frequent)
What are Eden and Survivor spaces?
Eden is where new objects are allocated; Survivor spaces (S0/S1) hold objects that survived at least one Minor GC, aging them before promotion
What triggers promotion of an object to the Old Generation?
Surviving a number of Minor GC cycles beyond the tenuring threshold (-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold), or Survivor space overflow
Why is copying collection used for the Young Generation specifically?
Because most objects there are dead, copying only the small number of live survivors is far cheaper than sweeping the whole space
What is premature promotion and why is it a problem?
Short-lived objects get promoted to Old Gen too early due to an undersized Young Gen, causing the Old Gen to fill up faster and trigger more expensive Major GCs
Which JVM flag controls Young Generation size directly?
-Xmn
Does every collector implement Major GC the same way?
No - the exact algorithm and even the definition of "Major GC" varies by collector (e.g. G1's mixed collections behave differently from Parallel GC's Old Gen collection)

topics.name: G1 Garbage Collector

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is G1?

G1 (short for Garbage-First) is a garbage collector built into the JVM that tries to balance two

goals at once: keeping pause times short and predictable, while still collecting garbage efficiently even on large

heaps (multiple gigabytes).

Since Java 9, G1 is the default garbage collector for most JVM configurations,

replacing the older Parallel GC as the out-of-the-box choice.

Region-Based Heap

Older collectors treat the Young and Old Generations as single large, contiguous blocks of memory. G1 instead splits

the entire heap into many small, equal-sized chunks called regions (typically 1MB to 32MB each,

chosen automatically).

Each region is dynamically labeled as Eden, Survivor, or Old at any given time - there's no fixed physical wall

between generations like in older collectors.

Why "Garbage First"?

G1 gets its name from its core strategy: during a collection, it prioritizes cleaning up the regions that contain the

most garbage first, because that gives the biggest memory reclaim for the least amount of work -

maximizing efficiency within a limited pause-time budget.

Pause-Time Goals

Unlike older collectors that just run "as needed," G1 lets you specify a target maximum pause time using

-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis. G1 then tries to pick how many regions to collect in each cycle so it stays close

to that goal, rather than collecting the whole heap in one go.

Mixed Collections - A Quick Preview

G1 doesn't only clean the Young Generation or only the Old Generation in one shot. Once Old Generation regions start

filling up, G1 runs mixed collections - a single GC cycle that collects the Young regions

plus a chosen subset of Old regions with the most garbage, all within its pause-time goal.

Fresher Notes

  • Default collector: G1 (Garbage-First) has been the default on server-class machines since Java 9.
  • Regions: the heap is split into many equal regions, each acting as Eden, Survivor, Old or Humongous.
  • Pause goal: set a target with -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis (default 200 ms).

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Garbage first: G1 evacuates the regions with the most garbage first, to get the most space for the least pause.
  • Concurrent marking: it marks old regions while the app runs, then runs mixed collections that include old regions.
  • Humongous objects: objects of half a region or more get their own regions and can cause fragmentation.

8. Advanced Concepts

G1's Region-Based Architecture in Detail

Heap (e.g. 4GB) split into ~2048 regions (region size auto-chosen, e.g. 2MB each)

[E][E][S][O][E][O][O][H][F][O][E][S][O][F][H][O] ...
 E = Eden   S = Survivor   O = Old   H = Humongous   F = Free

Humongous regions: objects larger than 50% of a region size
are allocated directly into one or more contiguous Humongous
regions, bypassing normal Eden allocation.

Because generations are just a logical label on top of physical regions, G1 can resize Young Generation capacity on

the fly each cycle - simply by reclassifying more or fewer regions as Eden - which is what lets it adapt toward the

pause-time goal dynamically instead of using a fixed generation size.

The G1 Collection Cycle

A full G1 cycle typically involves these phases:

  • Young-only collections - repeated Minor-GC-like collections of Eden/Survivor regions using

copying collection, evacuating live objects into Survivor or Old regions.

  • Initial Mark - piggybacks on a Young collection, marks GC roots.
  • Concurrent Marking - runs alongside the application threads, traces the object graph in Old

regions to compute how much garbage each Old region holds, without stopping the world.

  • Remark - a short Stop-the-World pause to finalize marking.
  • Cleanup - reclaims completely empty regions immediately, and identifies the most garbage-dense Old

regions as candidates for the next step.

  • Mixed Collections - subsequent collections that evacuate both Young regions and the

garbage-densest Old region candidates, spread across multiple cycles to respect the pause-time goal.

G1 vs Parallel GC vs CMS - Comparison

AspectParallel GCCMS (removed in Java 14)G1 GC
Heap layoutContiguous Young/OldContiguous Young/OldRegion-based
GoalMaximum throughputLow pause, no compactionBalanced throughput + predictable pause
CompactionYes, every collectionNo - suffers fragmentation over timeYes, incrementally per region during evacuation
Pause-time goal supportNo direct controlNo direct controlYes - -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis
Default sinceJava 8 and earlierDeprecated Java 9, removed Java 14Java 9+
Best fitBatch jobs, throughput-critical, few pause concernsLegacy low-latency needs (superseded by G1/ZGC)General-purpose default, medium-to-large heaps needing predictable pauses

Production Tuning Scenario

A web service on an 8GB heap was seeing occasional 800ms pauses under load, well above its 200ms SLA. Investigation

of GC logs showed large, infrequent mixed collections were pulling in too many Old regions at once.

Tuning applied:

  • Lowered -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis from the default 200ms explicitly to reinforce the target.
  • Reduced -XX:G1MixedGCCountTarget effect by tuning -XX:G1HeapWastePercent so G1 became

more willing to spread mixed collections across more cycles instead of front-loading Old region reclamation.

  • Increased heap headroom with -XX:G1ReservePercent to avoid "to-space exhaustion" fallbacks to a Full

GC, which is G1's worst-case, most expensive path.

Result: pause times stabilized under the 200ms goal, at the cost of slightly more frequent (but shorter) mixed

collections - a classic latency-vs-frequency tradeoff.

Senior Notes

  • Tuning: keep it simple, set -Xmx and a realistic pause goal; avoid fixing young size, which disables adaptation.
  • IHOP: -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent decides when concurrent marking starts.
  • Failure signs: "To-space exhausted" or Full GC in logs means G1 could not keep up; give it more headroom.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful options:

  • -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=n: soft pause goal.
  • -XX:G1HeapRegionSize: region size for many humongous objects.
  • -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=45: start of marking.
  • -XX:G1ReservePercent: free space reserve (default 10).
  • -XX:ParallelGCThreads and ConcGCThreads: worker counts.
  • -XX:+UseStringDeduplication: shares duplicate String arrays.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

G1 divides the heap into 1 MB to 32 MB regions (power of two, about 2048 of them).

  • Young pause: evacuates Eden and Survivor regions, copying live objects.
  • Concurrent cycle: snapshot-at-the-beginning marking finds live data in old regions.
  • Mixed pause: adds old regions with the most reclaimable space.
  • Remembered sets per region track incoming references.
  • Full GC: fallback, single or parallel compaction of the heap.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Pause goal too low (like 5 ms): G1 collects too little and falls behind.
  • Fixed -Xmn: removes adaptive sizing.
  • Many humongous allocations: raise region size or split the data.
  • Heap too tight: To-space exhausted; add headroom.
  • Copying old CMS flags: CMS was removed in JDK 14.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning approach:

  • Start with defaults and only set heap size and pause goal.
  • Lower IHOP if marking starts too late and Full GCs appear.
  • Check humongous counts in logs with -Xlog:gc+humongous.
  • Compare throughput against Parallel for batch jobs.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a microservice with a 4 GB heap needs p99 under 300 ms.

  • G1 with a 100 ms pause goal meets this.
  • Pauses of 30 to 80 ms are seen in logs.
  • Bulk imports of 50 MB arrays caused humongous Full GCs, so they are streamed.

interviewQA: What does G1 stand for and what is its main goal?
Garbage-First - it aims to provide predictable, configurable pause times while efficiently collecting garbage, even on large heaps
Since which Java version is G1 the default collector?
Java 9
How does G1's heap layout differ from older collectors?
G1 divides the heap into many equal-sized regions dynamically labeled Eden, Survivor, Old, or Humongous, instead of fixed contiguous generations
What is a Humongous region?
A region (or set of contiguous regions) used to allocate an object larger than 50% of the standard region size
What is a mixed collection in G1?
A GC cycle that collects Young regions together with a chosen subset of the most garbage-dense Old regions, within the pause-time goal
Which flag controls G1's target maximum pause time?
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis
Why is G1 named "Garbage-First"?
Because it prioritizes collecting the regions containing the most garbage first, to reclaim the most memory for the least work
What happens when G1 runs out of space during evacuation ("to-space exhaustion")?
It falls back to a full, Stop-the-World Full GC - the most expensive and least predictable path, which tuning tries to avoid

topics.name: ZGC

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is ZGC?

ZGC (short for Z Garbage Collector) is a scalable, low-latency garbage collector introduced as an

experimental feature in Java 11 and made production-ready in later releases. Its headline promise is

sub-millisecond pause times, even on heaps that are hundreds of gigabytes in size.

Where G1 aims for a configurable, "reasonably low" pause, ZGC aims to make Stop-the-World pauses almost

disappear entirely, regardless of how large the heap gets.

Why "Ultra-Low-Latency" Matters

Some applications - trading systems, real-time bidding platforms, large in-memory caches, latency-sensitive

APIs - cannot tolerate even a 100-200ms pause, because every request being processed at that instant freezes along

with it. ZGC is designed specifically for this class of application, where predictable, tiny pauses matter more than

maximum raw throughput.

Concurrent Collection - The Big Idea

Traditional collectors stop all application threads ("Stop-the-World") while they trace and move objects, because

moving an object while a thread is reading it is unsafe.

ZGC instead does almost all of its work concurrently - while your application threads keep running

  • including the hardest part: actually relocating (moving) live objects in memory. This is what allows it to keep

pauses so short.

How to Enable ZGC

Turning ZGC on is a single JVM flag - no code changes are needed in your application.

When Should You Reach for ZGC?

  • Your application has a strict, low latency SLA (e.g. p99 response time under 10ms).
  • You run a very large heap (many GB to TB range) and pause times with older collectors scale badly with heap size.
  • You can tolerate slightly higher CPU usage and memory overhead in exchange for near-elimination of long pauses.

If your workload is a batch job or offline data pipeline where total throughput matters more than pause time, a

throughput-oriented collector (like Parallel GC) is usually a better fit than ZGC.

Fresher Notes

  • Low latency: ZGC keeps pauses very short (typically under a millisecond in modern JDKs), almost independent of heap size.
  • Concurrent: marking, relocation and reference processing run while application threads keep working.
  • Enable: -XX:+UseZGC; since JDK 21 add -XX:+ZGenerational for the generational mode.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Colored pointers and load barriers: metadata in pointer bits and a check on each reference load let ZGC move objects concurrently.
  • Heap range: it scales from small heaps to multi-terabyte heaps (up to 16 TB).
  • Cost: it uses more CPU and some extra memory than G1, so throughput can be a little lower.

8. Advanced Concepts

Colored Pointers

ZGC's core trick for enabling concurrent relocation is a technique called colored pointers. On

64-bit systems, object references (pointers) have far more bits than are needed to address memory, so ZGC

"steals" a handful of unused high-order bits in every reference and uses them to store metadata about the object's

GC state directly in the pointer itself:

  • Whether the object has been marked as live in this GC cycle
  • Whether the object has already been relocated
  • Whether the reference still needs to be "remapped" to the object's new address

Because this metadata lives in the pointer, not in a separate side table, the JVM can inspect and update a

reference's GC status extremely cheaply, without needing to stop other threads to keep bookkeeping data consistent.

Load Barriers and Concurrent Relocation

ZGC inserts a lightweight check called a load barrier on every reference read from the heap. When a

thread reads a reference, the barrier examines its colored bits:

Thread reads reference "ref" from the heap
        |
        v
Load barrier inspects ref's color bits
        |
   +----+----------------------+
   |                           |
Good color              Bad color (object relocated / needs remap)
   |                           |
Use ref directly       Slow path: look up new address,
(fast, common case)     fix up the reference on the fly,
                         then continue using it

Result: the application thread never sees a stale
pointer to a moved object, without ever needing a
Stop-the-World pause to fix up references globally.

This is what allows ZGC to relocate (move) objects while application threads keep running - each thread fixes up

any reference it happens to touch, one reference at a time, instead of the JVM pausing everyone to fix all

references at once.

ZGC vs G1 vs Shenandoah - Comparison

AspectG1ZGCShenandoah
Typical pause targetTens to low hundreds of msSub-millisecondSub-millisecond to low single-digit ms
Core techniqueRegion-based, mostly Stop-the-World evacuationColored pointers + concurrent load barriersBrooks forwarding pointers + concurrent compaction
Scales to very large heaps?Good up to several GB, pauses grow with heapYes - pause time largely independent of heap sizeYes, similar goal to ZGC
CPU / memory overheadLowerHigher (barrier checks, extra metadata)Higher (forwarding pointer per object)
Default sinceJava 9Production-ready Java 15+ (generational ZGC in Java 21+)Not the JDK default (OpenJDK backport, Red Hat-driven)
Best fitGeneral-purpose defaultUltra-low-latency, very large heapsUltra-low-latency, similar use case to ZGC

Production Scenario: Migrating to ZGC

A real-time bidding platform running G1 on a 64GB heap was seeing occasional pauses of 300-500ms during mixed

collections, violating a strict 20ms p99 SLA for bid responses.

Steps taken:

  • Switched from -XX:+UseG1GC to -XX:+UseZGC (Java 17, then later generational ZGC on

Java 21 with -XX:+ZGenerational for better throughput on high-allocation-rate workloads).

  • Verified enough spare CPU headroom existed, since ZGC's concurrent work runs alongside application threads and

consumes extra CPU cycles that G1's Stop-the-World phases did not.

  • Monitored with GC logging (-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log) to confirm pause times dropped into the

sub-millisecond range consistently.

Result: p99 pause-related latency dropped from hundreds of ms to effectively negligible, at the cost of roughly

10-15% higher steady-state CPU usage - an acceptable tradeoff given the strict SLA.

Senior Notes

  • Generational ZGC: JDK 21 adds young and old generations, cutting allocation stalls and memory overhead; it became the default ZGC mode in JDK 23.
  • Allocation stall: if the app allocates faster than ZGC reclaims, threads wait; add heap or concurrent threads.
  • Alternatives: Shenandoah is another low-pause collector (OpenJDK builds); Parallel suits batch throughput.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Options (JDK 17 and 21):

  • -XX:+UseZGC: select ZGC.
  • -XX:+ZGenerational: JDK 21 generational mode.
  • -Xmx: leave headroom, ZGC needs free memory to relocate.
  • -XX:SoftMaxHeapSize: soft target below Xmx.
  • -XX:ConcGCThreads: concurrent worker count.
  • -XX:+UseLargePages: may cut TLB misses.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

ZGC does almost all work concurrently.

  • Colored pointers: metadata bits in 64-bit references mark state.
  • Load barrier: every reference read checks the color and fixes stale pointers.
  • Phases: short pause mark start, concurrent mark, short pause mark end, concurrent relocate.
  • Pages: small, medium and large pages are relocated to compact memory.
  • Generational (JDK 21): minor cycles for young, major cycles for old.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Heap sized exactly to live data: allocation stalls; add 20 to 30 percent.
  • Too few CPUs: concurrent threads compete with the app.
  • Expecting best throughput: Parallel is faster for batch jobs.
  • Assuming no pauses: they are tiny but exist.
  • Using non-generational ZGC on JDK 21 for high allocation rates: add -XX:+ZGenerational.
codeExamples:
// OUTPUT: (varies)
// [gc] Allocation Stall (http-1) 85.4ms    <- heap too small for the allocation rate

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Give headroom: larger -Xmx beats more flags.
  • Watch CPU: concurrent threads use cores.
  • Use generational mode on JDK 21 for typical web apps.
  • Measure p99 and p999 latency, not just average.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a trading gateway with a 64 GB heap must keep pauses under 5 ms.

  • G1 pauses grow to 200 ms with that heap.
  • ZGC pauses stay near 1 ms.
  • The cost is about 10 percent more CPU, acceptable for the latency gain.

interviewQA: What is ZGC's headline design goal?
Sub-millisecond garbage collection pause times, largely independent of heap size, even on multi-terabyte heaps
What are colored pointers?
References that use spare unused bits in a 64-bit pointer to store GC metadata (marked, relocated, remap-needed) directly in the reference itself
What is a load barrier in ZGC?
A lightweight check inserted on every heap reference read that inspects the pointer's color bits and fixes up stale references on the fly if needed
How does ZGC relocate objects without a long Stop-the-World pause?
It relocates objects concurrently while application threads run, using load barriers to transparently redirect any thread that touches a moved object's reference
What is the tradeoff of using ZGC compared to G1?
ZGC offers far shorter pauses but typically consumes more CPU and memory overhead due to barrier checks and extra per-object metadata
Which flag enables ZGC?
-XX:+UseZGC
What workload is ZGC best suited for?
Latency-sensitive applications with strict pause-time SLAs and/or very large heaps, such as trading systems or real-time bidding platforms
What is generational ZGC?
A newer mode (default in recent JDKs) that adds young/old generation separation to ZGC, improving throughput for high-allocation-rate workloads while keeping its low-pause guarantees

topics.name: Garbage Collection Cycles

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is a GC Cycle?

A GC cycle is one complete run of the garbage collector - from deciding it needs to collect, to

actually reclaiming memory, to handing control back to your application. Every GC cycle, regardless of which

collector is running, generally goes through the same three conceptual phases: Mark,

Sweep/Compact, and Promote.

Phase 1: Mark

The collector starts from the GC Roots (stack variables, static fields) and walks every reference it can find,

marking each object it reaches as "alive". Anything it never reaches during this walk is garbage.

Phase 2: Sweep / Compact

Once marking is done, the collector reclaims memory from every unmarked (garbage) object. Many collectors then also

compact - sliding the remaining live objects together - so that free memory ends up as one

large, contiguous block instead of scattered small gaps.

Phase 3: Promote

Objects that have survived several GC cycles in the Young Generation get promoted to the Old

Generation, since they've proven they are likely to stick around for a while. This ties directly into the

Generational GC design covered in the previous topic.

What is a Stop-the-World Pause?

During key parts of a GC cycle (especially marking), the collector often needs to pause every application

thread so the object graph doesn't change while it's being examined. This pause is called a

Stop-the-World (STW) event.

This is exactly why GC tuning matters in real systems - a long STW pause means your application literally freezes

for that duration, which can cause timeouts, dropped connections, or missed deadlines.

Fresher Notes

  • Young and old: new objects start in the young generation; objects that survive several collections are promoted to the old generation.
  • Minor GC cleans only the young generation and is frequent and short; a major or full GC touches the old generation too and takes longer.
  • Reachability: an object is garbage when no GC root (thread stack, static field, JNI reference) can reach it.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Stop-the-world: all application threads pause at a safepoint while the collector runs its pause phases.
  • Premature promotion: a survivor space that is too small pushes short-lived objects into the old generation and causes more full GCs.
  • Allocation rate drives minor GC frequency, while the live set drives pause time and old generation growth.

8. Advanced Concepts

Anatomy of a Full GC Cycle

1. Allocation Failure / Threshold Reached
        |
        v
2. Stop-the-World: pause all application ("mutator") threads
        |
        v
3. MARK
   - Traverse from GC Roots, mark every reachable object
   - Modern collectors do this in parallel across GC worker threads
        |
        v
4. SWEEP
   - Reclaim memory occupied by unmarked (dead) objects
        |
        v
5. COMPACT (if used)
   - Slide live objects together to eliminate fragmentation
   - Update all references to point to new object addresses
        |
        v
6. PROMOTE
   - Objects past the tenuring threshold move Young -> Old Generation
        |
        v
7. Resume application threads

Not every cycle runs every step - a Minor GC only performs steps 3-6 scoped to the Young Generation, while a Full GC

runs the entire pipeline across the whole heap.

Stop-the-World vs Concurrent Phases

Modern collectors try to move as much work as possible out of the Stop-the-World pause and into concurrent

phases that run alongside the application:

PhaseTypically STW?Why
Initial MarkYes (usually brief)Must snapshot GC roots consistently before app threads resume
Concurrent MarkingNoCan tolerate the object graph changing slightly if it re-checks (via write barriers)
RemarkYes (short)Finalizes marking, catches objects that changed during concurrent marking
SweepCollector-dependentReclaiming clearly-dead memory is often safe concurrently
Evacuation / CompactionCollector-dependent (STW in G1, mostly concurrent in ZGC/Shenandoah)Moving live objects while threads read them requires either a pause or a barrier mechanism (e.g. colored pointers)

Write Barriers - Keeping Concurrent Marking Correct

When marking happens concurrently with running application threads, there's a risk: the application could create a

new reference from an already-marked "black" object to a not-yet-marked "white" object, and if the collector never

revisits the black object, it could wrongly reclaim the white object while it's still in use.

Collectors solve this with a write barrier - a small piece of code the JVM injects on every

reference field write, which records ("remembers") that a change happened so the marking phase can re-examine

affected objects during Remark. This is what keeps concurrent marking correct.

Production Scenario: Diagnosing a Long GC Cycle

A service running Parallel GC on a 16GB heap saw a 2.5 second Full GC pause during a nightly batch job, causing a

cascade of client timeouts. GC log analysis (-Xlog:gc*,gc+heap=debug:file=gc.log) showed:

  • Old Generation occupancy climbed steadily during the batch job (a large in-memory sort operation).
  • A Full GC was triggered when Old Gen filled completely, forcing a full Mark-Sweep-Compact across the entire heap

in one Stop-the-World pause - Parallel GC has no concurrent phases at all.

Fix: switched to G1 (-XX:+UseG1GC) so Old Generation marking could run concurrently, and split the sort

operation into smaller batches to reduce peak Old Gen occupancy - cutting the worst observed pause from 2.5s to

under 150ms.

Senior Notes

  • G1 cycle: young-only collections, then a concurrent marking cycle, then mixed collections that also reclaim old regions.
  • Concurrent collectors (ZGC, Shenandoah) do marking and relocation while the application runs, so pauses stay short and mostly independent of heap size.
  • Read the log: use -Xlog:gc* and look at pause time, heap before and after, and the cause such as Allocation Failure or Humongous Allocation.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Collection kinds and the log lines you see:

  • Pause Young (Normal): routine young collection.
  • Pause Young (Concurrent Start): a young pause that also starts marking.
  • Concurrent Mark Cycle: runs beside the application.
  • Pause Young (Mixed): young plus old regions.
  • Pause Full: the fallback, single-pass compaction of the whole heap.
  • Parallel GC: generational, stop-the-world, throughput focused.
  • ZGC and Shenandoah: concurrent, short pauses.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

A tracing collector finds live objects and reclaims the rest.

  • Roots: thread stacks, statics, JNI handles and loaded classes.
  • Marking: follows references from roots; unmarked objects are garbage.
  • Generational hypothesis: most objects die young, so collecting the young generation is cheap.
  • Copying: survivors move from eden to a survivor space, and their age grows with each cycle until promotion.
  • G1: splits the heap into regions; young-only phases, a concurrent mark and mixed collections form the cycle.
  • Safepoints: pause phases begin when all threads reach a safepoint.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes with GC and the fix for each:

  • Calling System.gc(): triggers a full pause; remove it or set -XX:+DisableExplicitGC if a library calls it.
  • Relying on finalizers: they delay reclamation; use try-with-resources or Cleaner.
  • Static caches that never evict: they stay reachable; use bounded caches.
  • Unremoved listeners: the registry keeps the object alive.
  • Large temporary arrays: in G1 they become humongous allocations; reuse or split them.
  • ThreadLocal in pools: values live as long as the thread; call remove().

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Performance levers:

  • Lower allocation rate: fewer minor GCs.
  • Smaller live set: shorter marking and copying.
  • Right young size: too small promotes garbage early; too large lengthens pauses on some collectors.
  • Survivor sizing: watch the tenuring threshold in the log.
  • Avoid humongous objects (half a G1 region or larger).
  • Watch: GC time percentage, allocation rate and old generation after-GC occupancy.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an order service shows 1.5 second latency spikes every few minutes.

  • Evidence: the GC log shows Pause Full (G1 Humongous Allocation).
  • Cause: a report builder allocates a 40 MB array per request.
  • Fix: stream the data in chunks, then confirm that the full GCs disappear.

interviewQA: What are the three core phases of a GC cycle?
Mark (find live objects), Sweep/Compact (reclaim and defragment memory), Promote (move surviving objects to an older generation)
What is a Stop-the-World pause?
A pause where all application threads are frozen so the garbage collector can safely examine or move objects without the object graph changing underneath it
Why do some GC phases need to be Stop-the-World while others can be concurrent?
Phases that require a globally consistent snapshot (like finalizing marks) need a pause; phases that can tolerate ongoing changes if tracked (like concurrent marking with write barriers) don't
What is a write barrier used for in GC?
To record reference field writes during concurrent marking so the collector can revisit and correctly re-mark objects that changed mid-cycle
What's the difference between Sweep and Compact?
Sweep reclaims memory from dead objects in place, leaving fragmentation; Compact additionally slides live objects together to eliminate that fragmentation
Why does Parallel GC tend to have longer Full GC pauses than G1?
Parallel GC has no concurrent phases - the entire Mark-Sweep-Compact cycle runs Stop-the-World, unlike G1 which does most marking concurrently
What typically triggers a Full GC?
The Old Generation (or whole heap) filling up such that a Minor GC or mixed collection alone cannot free enough space, or an explicit System.gc() call
How would you diagnose a long GC pause in production?
Enable and analyze GC logs (e.g. -Xlog:gc*) to identify which phase and generation caused the pause, then correlate with allocation patterns or heap sizing

topics.name: GC Tuning

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What Does "Tuning the GC" Mean?

GC tuning means adjusting JVM startup flags so the garbage collector behaves better for your specific

application - fewer pauses, shorter pauses, less memory used, or higher throughput, depending on what you actually

need.

You don't change your Java source code to tune GC - you pass extra flags when starting the JVM.

-Xms and -Xmx: Setting Heap Size

The two most fundamental flags control how much heap memory the JVM can use:

  • -Xms - the initial heap size when the JVM starts.
  • -Xmx - the maximum heap size the JVM is allowed to grow to.

Example: java -Xms512m -Xmx2g MyApp starts with a 512MB heap and allows it to grow up to 2GB as needed.

Choosing a Collector

You can explicitly choose which garbage collector the JVM should use:

  • -XX:+UseG1GC - the general-purpose default since Java 9.
  • -XX:+UseZGC - for ultra-low-latency needs.
  • -XX:+UseParallelGC - for maximum throughput, batch-style workloads.

If you don't specify one, the JVM picks a sensible default automatically (G1 on modern JVMs).

Setting a Pause Time Goal

With G1, you can tell the collector how long you're willing to let a pause be, and it will try its best to honor

that target:

java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 MyApp

Turning On GC Logging

Before tuning anything, you need visibility into what the GC is actually doing. The modern unified logging flag is:

-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,level,tags

This writes a detailed log of every GC event - which phase ran, how long it took, and how much memory was

reclaimed - to gc.log, which you can then inspect or feed into a GC log analysis tool.

Fresher Notes

  • Measure first: turn on GC logging and tune only when pauses or throughput are a real problem.
  • Heap size is set with -Xms (initial) and -Xmx (maximum); a heap that is too small causes frequent GC.
  • Default collector: since JDK 9 G1 is the default on server-class machines; the default is fine for most applications.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Goals: low latency (short pauses), high throughput (little time in GC) and small footprint cannot all be maximized together.
  • Pause target: G1 accepts -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 as a goal, not a guarantee.
  • Containers: prefer -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 so the heap follows the container memory limit.

8. Advanced Concepts

Key JVM Flags Reference

FlagPurpose
-Xms / -XmxInitial / maximum heap size
-XmnYoung Generation size (Parallel/CMS-style collectors)
-XX:+UseG1GCEnable G1 (default since Java 9)
-XX:+UseZGCEnable ZGC for ultra-low-latency workloads
-XX:+UseParallelGCEnable throughput-oriented Parallel GC
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=NTarget maximum pause time goal (G1 and Parallel treat this as a soft goal; ZGC ignores it and bounds pauses by design)
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=NOverride G1's auto-chosen region size
-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=NOld Gen occupancy % that triggers G1's concurrent marking cycle to start
-XX:SurvivorRatio=NRatio of Eden to each Survivor space size
-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=NHow many Minor GCs an object survives before being promoted to Old Gen
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryErrorWrite a heap dump automatically on OutOfMemoryError, for post-mortem analysis
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,level,tagsUnified GC logging (Java 9+) - the starting point for any tuning effort

Reading a GC Log Line

A typical G1 GC log entry (simplified) looks like this:

[2026-08-19T10:15:42.123+0000][gc,start] GC(42) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause)
[2026-08-19T10:15:42.145+0000][gc,heap]  GC(42) Eden regions: 40->0(42)
[2026-08-19T10:15:42.145+0000][gc,heap]  GC(42) Survivor regions: 5->6(8)
[2026-08-19T10:15:42.145+0000][gc,heap]  GC(42) Old regions: 12->14
[2026-08-19T10:15:42.146+0000][gc      ] GC(42) Pause Young (Normal) 165M->98M(512M) 22.7ms

How to read it:

  • GC(42) - the sequence number of this GC event, useful for correlating across log lines.
  • 165M->98M(512M) - heap usage before GC, after GC, out of total committed heap.
  • 22.7ms - the actual pause duration for this event - the number you compare against your

MaxGCPauseMillis goal.

  • Region deltas (Eden/Survivor/Old) show exactly where memory moved, which is essential for spotting patterns like

premature promotion.

Throughput-Oriented vs Latency-Oriented Tuning

GoalRecommended CollectorKey FlagsTradeoff Accepted
Maximum throughput (batch jobs, ETL)Parallel GC-XX:+UseParallelGC, large -Xmx, tuned -XX:GCTimeRatioLonger, less predictable pauses
Balanced, general-purpose servicesG1 GC-XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200Slightly lower throughput than Parallel GC
Ultra-low-latency (trading, bidding, real-time)ZGC-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerationalHigher CPU and memory overhead
Minimize memory footprint (small containers)Serial GC-XX:+UseSerialGC, small -XmxSingle-threaded GC, longer pauses relative to heap size

Production Tuning Walkthrough: Diagnosing Frequent Full GCs

A microservice on G1 with -Xmx4g was hitting Full GCs every few minutes, each taking 1-2 seconds, and

memory usage kept climbing back to near-max after each collection - a classic sign of a memory leak, not just

under-tuning.

Diagnostic steps:

  • Enabled -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,level,tags and watched Old Gen occupancy after each cycle - it

never dropped back to baseline, confirming a leak rather than a sizing issue.

  • Added -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps to capture a heap dump automatically

when it eventually failed.

  • Analyzed the heap dump and found a static Map used as an unbounded cache, growing without eviction.

Fix: replaced the unbounded cache with a bounded, size-limited cache (eviction policy). GC frequency and pause

duration returned to normal immediately - illustrating that GC flags cannot fix an actual memory leak,

only application-level fixes can; tuning only helps when the underlying object lifetimes are legitimately what

they should be.

Senior Notes

  • Choose the collector: Parallel for batch throughput, G1 for balanced services, ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC) for very large heaps and tight latency.
  • Change one thing at a time and compare logs under a realistic load test, not a microbenchmark.
  • Fix allocation first: reducing garbage and live data beats any flag.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful flags (JDK 17 and 21):

  • Sizing: -Xms, -Xmx, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, -XX:InitialRAMPercentage.
  • Collector: -XX:+UseG1GC, -XX:+UseParallelGC, -XX:+UseZGC, -XX:+UseSerialGC.
  • G1: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, -XX:G1HeapRegionSize, -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent.
  • ZGC: -XX:+ZGenerational on JDK 21.
  • Threads: -XX:ParallelGCThreads, -XX:ConcGCThreads.
  • Logging: -Xlog:gc*.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Tuning works by trading three goals against each other.

  • Throughput: the share of time spent running application code.
  • Latency: the length of the longest pauses.
  • Footprint: heap and native memory used.
  • G1 ergonomics: sizes regions and the young generation dynamically to meet the pause goal.
  • Adaptive sizing: fixing the young size with flags disables part of that adaptation.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Huge flag lists copied from blogs: start from defaults and add one flag with evidence.
  • Tiny pause goal: MaxGCPauseMillis=10 on G1 makes young generation tiny and collections too frequent.
  • Heap larger than the container: the OOM killer ends the process; leave room for non-heap memory.
  • Fixing the young size with -Xmn and losing adaptivity.
  • Tuning when the problem is a leak: more heap only delays the failure.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Performance method:

  • Baseline: record p50, p99 and GC overhead under a realistic load.
  • Change one flag and repeat the same test.
  • Keep a change only if the numbers improve.
  • Prefer code fixes: reduce allocation and live data first.
  • Tools: GC logs with an analyzer, JFR and JMH -prof gc.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a nightly batch of 20 million rows runs 40 percent slower after moving to a container.

  • Finding: the JVM sees 1 CPU and picks Serial GC.
  • Fix: give the container 4 CPUs, or set the collector explicitly, and use a fixed heap.
  • Check: -Xlog:gc shows which collector started.

10. Examples

interviewQA: What is the difference between -Xms and -Xmx?
-Xms sets the initial heap size at JVM startup; -Xmx sets the maximum size the heap is allowed to grow to
Which flag enables G1 explicitly, and is it needed on modern JVMs?
-XX:+UseG1GC; it's usually not needed since G1 has been the default since Java 9
What does -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis actually guarantee?
It is a soft goal, not a hard guarantee - G1/ZGC try to stay within it by adjusting collection scope, but extreme conditions (e.g. allocation spikes) can still exceed it
How do you enable GC logging in modern Java (9+)?
Using the unified logging flag, e.g. -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,level,tags
In a GC log line like "165M->98M(512M) 22.7ms", what does each number mean?
Heap usage before GC, heap usage after GC, total committed heap size, and the pause duration
If Full GCs keep happening and memory never drops back down, what should you suspect first?
A memory leak (objects unintentionally kept reachable), not a heap-sizing problem - GC tuning cannot fix a genuine leak
Which collector would you choose for a batch ETL job vs a low-latency trading system?
Parallel GC for maximum throughput on the batch job; ZGC for the trading system's strict low-pause requirements
What is -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError used for?
Automatically writing a heap dump when an OutOfMemoryError occurs, enabling post-mortem analysis of what was consuming memory

topics.name: JIT Compiler

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is the JIT Compiler?

JIT stands for Just-In-Time compiler. It is a part of the JVM that converts frequently used bytecode

into native machine code while the program is running, so it can execute much faster.

Java code goes through two stages before it becomes machine instructions:

  • javac compiles .java source files into .class bytecode (platform-independent).
  • The JVM then either interprets that bytecode line by line, or JIT-compiles hot parts of

it into native code for the actual CPU.

Interpreter vs JIT-Compiled Code

When a Java program starts, the JVM's interpreter begins executing bytecode immediately - this gives fast startup but

slower execution, since every instruction is decoded and executed one at a time, every single time.

  • Interpreter - starts fast, runs slow, no upfront compilation delay.
  • JIT Compiler - takes a moment to compile, but the resulting native code runs dramatically faster on

repeated execution.

The JVM combines both: start with the interpreter for quick startup, then JIT-compile the "hot" methods that run

over and over.

What Makes a Method "Hot"?

The JVM keeps an invocation counter for every method and loop. Once a method is called (or a loop iterates) more than

a threshold number of times, the JVM marks it as hot and schedules it for JIT compilation on a

background compiler thread.

This is why the very first few runs of a Java program (or the first few iterations of a loop) are often slower than

later ones - this warm-up period is sometimes called the JIT warm-up.
codeExamples:
# Print JIT compilation activity as it happens
java -XX:+PrintCompilation MyApp

# Sample output (trimmed):
#     102    1       3       java.lang.String::hashCode (60 bytes)
#     104    2       4       java.lang.Object::<init> (1 bytes)
#     205  156       4       com.myapp.OrderProcessor::calculateTotal (48 bytes)

beginner.content:
C1 and C2 - The Two JIT Compilers

The HotSpot JVM (the standard Oracle/OpenJDK JVM) actually ships with two different JIT compilers:

  • C1 (Client Compiler) - compiles quickly with light optimizations. Good for fast startup and

short-lived programs.

  • C2 (Server Compiler) - takes longer to compile but produces highly optimized native code. Good for

long-running server applications.

Modern JVMs use both together in a strategy called Tiered Compilation, which we cover next.

Why This Matters to You

Understanding the JIT compiler explains real things you will see in production:

  • Why a server "feels slow" for the first minute after deploy and then speeds up (JIT warm-up).
  • Why microbenchmarks that don't warm up the JVM give misleading numbers.
  • Why load-testing tools often run a "warm-up phase" before taking measurements.

Fresher Notes

  • JIT means just-in-time: the JVM compiles hot bytecode to native machine code while the program runs.
  • Interpreter first: code starts interpreted, and methods or loops that run often get compiled.
  • Warm-up: a program is slower at the start, so benchmarks must warm up before measuring.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Tiered compilation: C1 compiles quickly with light optimization, then C2 recompiles the hottest code with heavy optimization.
  • Inlining replaces a small method call with its body and is the base for many other optimizations.
  • Deoptimization: if an assumption proves wrong (for example a new subclass is loaded), the JVM falls back to the interpreter.

8. Advanced Concepts

Tiered Compilation in Detail

Since Java 8, the default strategy is Tiered Compilation, which uses C1 and C2 together across

five compilation levels:

LevelCompilerDescription
0InterpreterPure bytecode interpretation, gathers profiling data
1C1Simple C1 compile, no profiling (for trivial methods)
2C1C1 compile with invocation/backedge counters only
3C1C1 compile with full profiling (branch, type profiling)
4C2Fully optimized C2 compile using profiling data from level 3

A method typically walks 0 -> 3 -> 4: it's interpreted and profiled, quickly C1-compiled with profiling to get fast

speedup sooner, and finally recompiled by C2 once it's proven hot enough to justify heavy optimization. This gives

Java both fast warm-up (like C1-only) and peak throughput (like C2-only).

Key Optimizations C2 Performs

  • Inlining - replacing a method call with the method body itself, eliminating call overhead and

opening the door to further optimizations.

  • Loop unrolling - duplicating loop bodies to reduce branch overhead.
  • Escape analysis - determining an object never leaves a method, enabling stack allocation or

elimination entirely (see the dedicated Escape Analysis topic).

  • Dead code elimination - removing code paths that profiling shows are never taken.
  • Speculative optimization with deoptimization - C2 will optimize aggressively based on assumptions

(e.g. "this call site is monomorphic") and fall back ("deoptimize") to the interpreter if that assumption is later

violated.
codeExamples:
# Inspect JIT compilation with more detail, including deoptimizations
java -XX:+PrintCompilation -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining MyApp

# A deoptimization event looks like this in -XX:+TraceDeoptimization output:
# Uncommon trap occurred in com.myapp.PaymentService::process
#   reason=class_check action=maybe_recompile

expert.content:
Sample JIT Compilation Log Walkthrough

Timestamp  ID  Attributes  Tier  Method                                Bytes
    102     1      %      3    com.myapp.Order::isValid                12
    118     1              4    com.myapp.Order::isValid                12
    340    45      %      4    com.myapp.OrderProcessor::processBatch  210
    341    45              4    com.myapp.OrderProcessor::processBatch  210 (made not entrant)
    342    46              4    com.myapp.OrderProcessor::processBatch  225

"made not entrant" means the JVM invalidated a previously compiled version - typically because a class was loaded that

invalidates an inlining assumption, or because profiling revealed the earlier compile was suboptimal, triggering a

recompile.

Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
New pods are slow for the first 60-90 seconds after every deploy, then fineJIT warm-up - code is running interpreted/C1 until C2 kicks inCompare -XX:+PrintCompilation timestamps against request latency graphs post-deployAdd a warm-up phase (synthetic traffic) before routing real traffic, or use Application Class Data Sharing / CDS to reduce startup cost
Latency spikes randomly under steady load, not just at startupC2 recompilation ("made not entrant") triggered by late class loading or megamorphic call sitesEnable -XX:+PrintCompilation and correlate recompiles with latency spike timestampsReduce polymorphism at hot call sites; avoid dynamic class loading during steady-state traffic
Short-lived batch job never seems to get fastJob finishes before C2 has a chance to compile hot methods - it never leaves the interpreter/C1 tiersCheck job duration vs typical JIT threshold (~10,000 invocations for C2)Either accept interpreted performance for short jobs, or use -Xcomp/AOT compilation for consistent latency on short-lived runs

Useful JVM Flags for JIT Tuning

  • -XX:+PrintCompilation - log every JIT compilation event.
  • -XX:CompileThreshold=10000 - invocation count before C2 compiles a method (non-tiered mode).
  • -XX:-TieredCompilation - disable tiered compilation (use C2 only, slower warm-up).
  • -Xint - force pure interpretation, useful for isolating JIT-related bugs.
  • -Xcomp - force compilation of every method before it executes (useful for testing, terrible for

production).

Senior Notes

  • See it with -XX:+PrintCompilation and, for inlining, -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining.
  • Code cache: compiled code lives in a limited area, sized by -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize.
  • Benchmark with JMH, which handles warm-up, dead-code elimination and forks for you.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • Tiered: -XX:+TieredCompilation is the default.
  • Stop at C1: -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 gives fast startup for short tools.
  • Interpreter only: -Xint, for debugging.
  • Compile everything: -Xcomp is for experiments only.
  • Threads: -XX:CICompilerCount.
  • Code cache: -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=256m.
  • Log: -XX:+PrintCompilation, or -Xlog:jit+compilation=debug.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

HotSpot profiles code while it runs and compiles what is hot.

  • Levels: 0 interpreter, 1 to 3 C1 (3 adds profiling), 4 C2.
  • Counters: method invocation and loop back-edge counters trigger compilation.
  • OSR: on-stack replacement swaps a running loop into compiled code.
  • Speculation: C2 uses profile data, such as the receiver types seen, and adds uncommon traps.
  • Background threads: compilation runs on separate compiler threads.
  • Code cache: stores the compiled code.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Timing code without warm-up: use JMH.
  • Results unused: the JIT removes dead code, so the loop measures nothing.
  • Huge methods: methods over 8000 bytecodes are not compiled by default (HugeMethodLimit); split them.
  • Code cache full: the log says CodeCache is full and compilation stops.
  • Megamorphic call sites: many receiver types stop inlining.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning for startup and peak speed:

  • Warm-up: send synthetic traffic before a node joins the load balancer.
  • Class data sharing (CDS): speeds up startup.
  • AOT and GraalVM native image: remove warm-up at the cost of peak throughput and flexibility.
  • Monitor: JFR events jdk.Compilation and jdk.Deoptimization.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: p99 latency is bad for the first minute after each deploy.

  • Cause: cold code is interpreted.
  • Fix: warm-up requests on start, readiness only after warm-up, and rolling deploys.

10. Examples

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

See methods being compiled.

Practice Exercise 2
