interviewQA: What does JIT stand for and what does it do?
Just-In-Time compiler - converts hot bytecode into native machine code at runtime for faster execution
What is the difference between C1 and C2?
C1 compiles quickly with light optimization (good for startup); C2 compiles slower but produces highly optimized code (good for long-running throughput)
What is Tiered Compilation?
A strategy (default since Java 8) that uses C1 first for fast warm-up and profiling, then C2 for peak-optimized recompilation of hot methods
Why is a Java application slower right after startup?
Because code is initially interpreted or lightly compiled; JIT needs time (and invocation counts) to identify and optimize hot methods
What is deoptimization?
When the JVM discards an aggressively optimized compiled method and falls back to the interpreter because a runtime assumption it relied on was violated
What is method inlining and why does it matter?
Replacing a call site with the callee's body; it removes call overhead and enables further optimizations like escape analysis across the inlined code
How would you force the JVM to skip JIT compilation entirely?
Run with the -Xint flag, which forces pure interpretation

topics.name: Escape Analysis

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is Escape Analysis?

Escape Analysis is a technique the JVM's JIT compiler (C2) uses to figure out whether an object created inside a

method ever "escapes" - that is, whether it becomes visible or reachable outside that method.

If the JVM proves an object never escapes, it can skip some of the normal, more expensive steps of object creation

(like allocating it on the heap), making the code run faster and reducing garbage collection pressure.

What Does "Escaping" Mean?

An object "escapes" a method if it can be accessed from outside that method after the method returns. Examples:

  • It is returned from the method.
  • It is stored in a field of another object.
  • It is passed to another method that itself lets it escape.
  • It is stored in a static variable or shared collection.

If none of these happen, the object is said to be non-escaping - it only ever lives and dies inside

that one method call.

Why Should a Beginner Care?

You don't need to write any special code to benefit from escape analysis - it happens automatically inside the JIT

compiler once a method gets hot enough. But understanding it explains:

  • Why creating small, short-lived helper objects (like a Point or a temporary wrapper) is often "free" in

modern Java, contrary to older advice to avoid object creation at all costs.

  • Why heavily optimized Java code can sometimes perform close to hand-written low-level code, even though Java is

"object heavy."

Scalar Replacement - A Quick Preview

When an object doesn't escape, the JIT compiler can go a step further and completely eliminate the object, replacing

its fields with individual local variables (like ints or references) that live only in CPU registers or the stack.

This is called scalar replacement, and it is one of the most powerful outcomes of escape analysis -

we go deeper into it in the expert section.

Fresher Notes

  • Escape analysis is a C2 JIT optimization that checks whether an object can be seen outside the method or thread that created it.
  • Scalar replacement: if the object does not escape, the JVM can drop the allocation and keep its fields in registers.
  • Result: less heap allocation and less GC work, with no change to the program output.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Escape states: no escape (stays in the method), arg escape (passed to a call) and global escape (stored in a field or returned).
  • Lock elision: a lock on an object that never escapes its thread can be removed.
  • It is automatic: it is on by default (-XX:+DoEscapeAnalysis) and applies only to hot, compiled code.

8. Advanced Concepts

Categories of Escape

The JIT compiler's escape analysis classifies every allocation site into one of three categories:

CategoryMeaningOptimization Enabled
NoEscapeObject is only used within the allocating method (and its inlined callees)Scalar replacement, stack allocation, lock elision
ArgEscapeObject is passed as an argument to another method but doesn't escape globallyLimited - depends on callee's own analysis
GlobalEscapeObject is returned, stored in a field, or otherwise reachable after the method exitsNone - must be heap-allocated normally

Scalar Replacement in Depth

When C2 proves an object is NoEscape, it doesn't just "allocate on the stack" (a common misconception) -

it can go further and eliminate the object entirely. The object's fields are "unpacked" into separate scalar values

(primitives/references) that the compiler tracks independently, often keeping them in CPU registers. No memory

allocation happens at all.

This is why the mental model "escape analysis puts objects on the stack instead of the heap" is only partially

correct - the more precise statement is: the object may never be materialized as a memory block at all.

Lock Elision (Biased/Redundant Lock Removal)

Escape analysis also enables lock elision: if a synchronized object is proven to be thread-local

(never escapes the current thread), the JIT can remove the synchronized block's locking overhead

entirely, since no other thread could ever contend for that lock.

This commonly happens with local StringBuilder usage - even though StringBuffer and older

synchronized collection wrappers have internal locks, if an instance never escapes a method, those locks are compiled

away.

Escape Analysis and Inlining Work Together

Escape analysis is far more effective when combined with method inlining. Consider a helper method that wraps an

object creation and passes it to another small method - if C2 inlines both methods into the caller, the object's

full lifecycle becomes visible within a single compiled unit, making it much more likely to be classified as

NoEscape. This is one reason very large methods (that exceed inlining size limits) can miss out on

escape analysis benefits that smaller, decomposed methods get "for free."

Diagnostic Output: JIT Escape Analysis Log

------------ EscapeAnalysis ------------
com.myapp.Vector3::length
  Allocation: new Vector3  -> NoEscape
  Eliminated: true (scalar replaced into x, y, z)

com.myapp.OrderService::createOrder
  Allocation: new Order    -> GlobalEscape (returned to caller)
  Eliminated: false (heap allocated normally)

Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
A hot method allocates heavily according to a profiler, but GC young-gen pressure is lower than expectedEscape analysis is successfully scalar-replacing most allocations - profiler "allocation counts" can be misleading vs actual heap pressureCross-check profiler allocation sampling against actual GC logs / allocation rate metricsNot a bug - confirm with -XX:+PrintEliminateAllocations that eliminations are happening as expected
Refactoring a large method into smaller ones unexpectedly improves throughputSmaller methods enabled inlining, which let escape analysis see full object lifecycles and scalar-replace allocations that previously escaped analysis boundariesCompare -XX:+PrintEscapeAnalysis output before/after refactor for the same allocation siteKeep hot-path methods small and inlinable; avoid unnecessary indirection in performance-critical code
An object expected to be scalar-replaced is not, and GC pressure stays highThe object escapes via a code path the developer didn't notice - e.g. added to a debug log statement or exception message lazilySearch for any place the object reference is stored, logged, or passed to an unfamiliar APIRemove or restructure the escaping reference (e.g. build the log message from primitives instead of passing the object)

Senior Notes

  • Not guaranteed: large methods, failed inlining or branches that leak the object can block it.
  • Not stack allocation: HotSpot does not put objects on the stack; it removes the object and keeps scalars.
  • Verify with allocation profiling or JMH -prof gc, not by guessing; do not rewrite code to chase it.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Flags (all on by default except the printing ones):

  • -XX:+DoEscapeAnalysis
  • -XX:+EliminateAllocations (scalar replacement)
  • -XX:+EliminateLocks
  • -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintEscapeAnalysis (needs a debug build)
  • Use -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis to compare behavior.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

C2 builds a connection graph of allocations and references.

  • Input: inlined code, so inlining decides how much it can see.
  • Classification: each allocation is NoEscape, ArgEscape or GlobalEscape.
  • NoEscape: eligible for scalar replacement and lock elision.
  • Limits: arrays larger than EliminateAllocationArraySizeLimit and objects used in merges are often skipped.
  • JDK 21: improved handling of objects at control-flow merges is still evolving, so results vary by version.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Believing objects go on the stack: they are removed, not stacked.
  • Hand-optimizing readable code into arrays or primitives without proof.
  • Leaking in a rare branch (for example logging the object) blocks the optimization for the whole method.
  • Benchmarks in the interpreter: escape analysis needs C2 compiled code.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Measure with JMH.

  • Profiler: -prof gc reports allocated bytes per operation.
  • Target: close to 0 B/op means allocation was removed.
  • Beware: small changes in the code or JDK can change the result.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a parser creates many small tokens per line, and young GC is busy.

  • Check: JFR allocation profile shows Token as the top allocation.
  • Action: keep the construction and use local to a small, inlinable method so C2 can remove it; if the profile does not improve, reuse a mutable cursor.

interviewQA: What is escape analysis?
A JIT compiler technique that determines whether an object's lifetime is confined to the allocating method, enabling optimizations like scalar replacement and lock elision
What does it mean for an object to "escape"?
The object becomes reachable outside the method that created it - e.g. returned, stored in a field, or assigned to a static/shared variable
What is scalar replacement?
Replacing an object's fields with individual scalar values tracked by the compiler (often in registers), avoiding heap allocation of the object entirely
Does escape analysis guarantee stack allocation?
No - the more accurate outcome is the object may never be materialized in memory at all via scalar replacement, not simply moved from heap to stack
What is lock elision?
Removing synchronization overhead from a lock proven to only ever be accessed by the current thread (thread-local, non-escaping object)
Why does method inlining improve escape analysis effectiveness?
Inlining brings an object's full usage into one compiled scope, making it far more likely the compiler can prove NoEscape
Is escape analysis something a developer configures directly?
No - it happens automatically in C2 once a method is hot enough; developers influence it indirectly via code structure (method size, avoiding unnecessary escapes)

topics.name: JVM Arguments

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What are JVM Arguments?

JVM arguments are command-line options passed to the java launcher that control how the JVM behaves -

things like how much memory it can use, which garbage collector to run, and what diagnostic output to print.

You pass them before the main class name:

java [JVM arguments] -jar myapp.jar [program arguments]
codeExamples:
# Example: run with a max heap of 512 MB and a min heap of 128 MB
java -Xms128m -Xmx512m -jar myapp.jar

beginner.content:
-X Flags (Non-Standard but Common)

Flags starting with a single -X are "non-standard" - not guaranteed identical across every JVM vendor,

but the most common ones are supported everywhere in practice. These usually control memory and basic runtime

behavior:

  • -Xms<size> - initial heap size (e.g. -Xms256m)
  • -Xmx<size> - maximum heap size (e.g. -Xmx1g)
  • -Xss<size> - thread stack size (e.g. -Xss512k)
  • -Xint - run in interpreted-only mode (no JIT)
codeExamples:
# Cap the stack size per thread to 256 KB, useful when running many threads
java -Xss256k -jar myapp.jar

beginner.content:
-XX Flags (Advanced/Non-Standard)

Flags starting with -XX: expose deeper JVM internals - garbage collector selection, JIT behavior,

diagnostics, and more. They come in a few shapes:

  • Boolean flags - toggled with + or -, e.g. -XX:+PrintGCDetails

enables it, -XX:-PrintGCDetails disables it.

  • Value flags - set with =, e.g. -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m.
codeExamples:
# Turn on detailed GC logging (older JVMs) and choose the G1 collector
java -XX:+PrintGCDetails -XX:+UseG1GC -jar myapp.jar

# Set the max Metaspace size (where class metadata lives)
java -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m -jar myapp.jar

beginner.content:
Frequently Used Flags Cheat-Sheet

  • -Xms512m -Xmx512m - set initial = max heap size (recommended in containers to avoid resize pauses).
  • -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError - automatically write a heap dump when the app crashes with

OutOfMemoryError.

  • -XX:+PrintGCDetails -Xlog:gc* - see what the garbage collector is doing.
  • -XX:+UseG1GC / -XX:+UseZGC - choose which garbage collector algorithm to use.

Why This Matters

Getting JVM arguments right is often the single biggest lever for application performance and stability in

production - more so than most code-level micro-optimizations. Setting the wrong heap size, or leaving diagnostics

off, is one of the most common causes of mysterious "it crashed in prod but not in dev" incidents.

Fresher Notes

  • Three families: standard options (-version, -cp), -X options (-Xmx512m) and -XX options (-XX:+UseG1GC).
  • Boolean flags use + to enable and - to disable, as in -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError.
  • Value flags use =, as in -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200; system properties use -Dkey=value.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Heap flags: -Xms, -Xmx, -Xss for thread stack size and -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
  • JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS adds flags through an environment variable, which is handy when you cannot edit the start command.
  • Argument files: java @args.txt reads options from a file, useful for long command lines.

8. Advanced Concepts

Standard vs Non-Standard vs Experimental/Diagnostic Flags

The JVM classifies its flags into tiers of stability, which matters for how safely you can rely on them across

versions and vendors:

CategoryPrefixStabilityExample
StandardSingle dash, no XSupported by all JVM implementations, stable across versions-cp, -jar, -D
Non-standard (X)-XHotSpot-specific but widely relied upon; can change without notice-Xms, -Xmx, -Xss
Advanced (XX)-XX:Internal tuning flags, subject to change between releases-XX:+UseG1GC
Diagnostic/Experimental-XX:+Unlock... requiredUnstable, for debugging the JVM itself; requires unlocking-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintCompilation

Discovering All Flags and Their Current Values

You rarely need to memorize every flag - the JVM can tell you what it's using and what's available.
codeExamples:
# Print every flag and its current value (including defaults you didn't set)
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -i heapsize

# Diff flags between two configurations - useful for reproducing a prod incident locally
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -Xmx512m -version > with_512m.txt
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -Xmx2g   -version > with_2g.txt
diff with_512m.txt with_2g.txt

# Inspect a running JVM's actual flags via jcmd (no restart needed)
jcmd <pid> VM.flags

expert.content:
Container-Aware Memory Flags

Before JDK 10, the JVM would read the host machine's total memory/CPU count even when running inside a

container with much tighter cgroup limits - a classic cause of containers being OOM-killed even though

-Xmx "looked fine." Since JDK 10+ (and backported to 8u191+), the JVM is container-aware by default via

-XX:+UseContainerSupport.

Instead of a fixed -Xmx, many teams now use percentage-based flags so the same image scales correctly

across different container memory limits:

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 - use up to 75% of the container's memory limit for the heap.
codeExamples:
# Recommended pattern for containerized services (Kubernetes, Docker)
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0 -XX:+UseContainerSupport -jar myapp.jar

expert.content:
Sample -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal Output

    intx CompileThreshold                        = 10000                                {pd product} {default}
   uintx InitialHeapSize                         = 268435456                             {product} {ergonomic}
   uintx MaxHeapSize                              = 4294967296                            {product} {ergonomic}
   uintx MaxMetaspaceSize                         = 18446744073709547520                  {product} {default}
     bool UseG1GC                                  = true                                  {product} {ergonomic}
     bool PrintGCDetails                           = false                                 {product} {default}

The {ergonomic} tag means the JVM chose this value automatically based on detected hardware/container

limits, not a value you explicitly set - important to check when diagnosing "why is my heap this size" issues.

Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
Container repeatedly OOM-killed despite -Xmx looking safely below the container limitHeap + Metaspace + thread stacks + native memory (direct buffers, JIT code cache) together exceed the container's total memory limit, not just the heapUse -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory to see the full memory breakdownLower -Xmx/MaxRAMPercentage to leave headroom for non-heap memory, or raise the container limit
Same JAR, same flags, but heap size differs between two serversPercentage-based/ergonomic flags (e.g. MaxRAMPercentage) resolve differently depending on detected CPU/memory of each host or containerCompare -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal output on both machines, look for {ergonomic} valuesPin explicit values (-Xmx) if strict consistency across environments is required
App runs fine locally but fails to start in CI with "Invalid initial heap size"A flag was set with a value larger than available memory in the CI runner, or with inconsistent unitsCheck the exact flags passed by the CI pipeline vs local run scriptsAlign CI resource limits with the flags, or make heap sizing percentage-based instead of hardcoded

Senior Notes

  • Inspect the real values with -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal or jcmd PID VM.flags.
  • Containers: JDK 17 and 21 are container aware; use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage instead of a fixed -Xmx.
  • Unlock carefully: experimental and diagnostic flags need -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions or -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions and may change between releases.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Common groups:

  • Memory: -Xms, -Xmx, -Xss, -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize, -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize.
  • GC: -XX:+UseG1GC, -Xlog:gc*.
  • Diagnostics: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError, -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary.
  • Modules: --add-opens, --add-modules.
  • Preview: --enable-preview.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The launcher parses arguments in a fixed order.

  • Sources: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, the command line, @argfiles, and JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS (JDK 9 and later).
  • Ergonomics: flags you do not set are chosen from CPUs and memory, including container limits.
  • Flag kinds: product, diagnostic, experimental, manageable (changeable at run time).
  • Class path: arguments after the main class or jar go to main(String[]).

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Xmx equal to container memory: no room for metaspace, stacks and buffers; use 60 to 75 percent.
  • Flag after the jar name: it becomes an application argument and is ignored by the JVM.
  • Typo in a flag: an unknown -XX flag stops the JVM; add -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions only deliberately.
  • Obsolete flags such as -XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC, removed in JDK 14.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Performance notes:

  • Xms = Xmx avoids resize pauses.
  • -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch commits memory at start for steadier latency but slows startup.
  • Xss larger stacks cost memory per thread; many threads need a small value.
  • Large pages and NUMA flags only help specific workloads; test them.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a Kubernetes pod is OOMKilled although the heap looks fine.

  • Cause: -Xmx equals the pod limit, and metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers exceed it.
  • Fix: use MaxRAMPercentage=70, and track non-heap with Native Memory Tracking.

10. Examples

Worked Example 2

interviewQA: What is the difference between -X and -XX flags?
-X flags are non-standard but common HotSpot options (like -Xmx); -XX flags expose deeper, more volatile internal tuning options, often toggled with +/- or set with =
What does -Xms and -Xmx control?
-Xms sets the initial heap size, -Xmx sets the maximum heap size the JVM is allowed to grow to
Why set -Xms equal to -Xmx in production?
To avoid runtime heap resizing pauses and ensure predictable memory behavior, especially in containers with fixed memory limits
What does -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError do?
Automatically writes a heap dump file to disk when the JVM throws an OutOfMemoryError, useful for post-mortem analysis
What is MaxRAMPercentage used for?
Sizing the heap as a percentage of the container's memory limit rather than a fixed value, so the same image scales correctly across different container sizes
How can you see all JVM flags and their actual values, including defaults?
Run java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version, or use jcmd <pid> VM.flags on a running process
Why might a container be OOM-killed even though -Xmx is well within the container limit?
Because -Xmx only bounds heap memory - Metaspace, thread stacks, JIT code cache, and native/direct memory are separate and add to total RSS

topics.name: Heap Dumps

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is a Heap Dump?

A heap dump is a snapshot of every object living in the JVM's heap memory at a single point in time - every object,

its fields, and the references between objects. It's saved to a file (usually with a .hprof extension)

that you can open later in an analysis tool.

Think of it like a photograph of your application's memory - frozen at the exact moment you took it, so you can

study it calmly instead of guessing about a moving target.

Why Do We Need Heap Dumps?

Heap dumps are the primary tool for answering questions like:

  • Why is my application running out of memory (OutOfMemoryError)?
  • Which objects are consuming the most memory right now?
  • Is there a memory leak - are objects piling up that should have been garbage collected?

Without a heap dump, you're mostly guessing from symptoms. With one, you can see exactly what's in memory.

Generating a Heap Dump Automatically on OutOfMemoryError

The easiest way to capture a heap dump exactly when it matters most is to tell the JVM to write one automatically

the moment it throws OutOfMemoryError.
codeExamples:
# Automatically dump the heap to a file when OutOfMemoryError occurs
java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps/myapp.hprof -jar myapp.jar

beginner.content:
Generating a Heap Dump On-Demand with jmap

You don't have to wait for a crash - you can trigger a heap dump manually while the application is running, using

the jmap command-line tool that ships with the JDK.
codeExamples:
# Find the process ID of your running Java app
jps -l

# Trigger a live heap dump for that process
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=myapp.hprof 12345

beginner.content:
Analyzing a Heap Dump

A raw .hprof file is not human-readable - you open it in a specialized analysis tool:

  • Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT) - the most popular free tool, shows the biggest objects, retained

size, and suspected leaks.

  • VisualVM - bundled with the JDK, simpler but useful for a quick look.
  • JMC (Java Mission Control) - can also open heap dumps alongside JFR recordings.

These tools let you browse "who is holding onto this object" (the reference chain), which is usually the key to

finding a leak.

Fresher Notes

  • Heap dump: a snapshot of every live object in the heap, saved as an .hprof file.
  • Use it to find memory leaks and see which objects take the most memory.
  • Automatic dump: start the JVM with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError so the evidence is saved when it crashes.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Manual dump: jcmd PID GC.heap_dump file.hprof or jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof PID.
  • Analyze with Eclipse MAT, VisualVM or IntelliJ; sort by retained size to find the real owners.
  • Size: the file is about as large as the used heap, so make sure the disk has room.

8. Advanced Concepts

What's Actually Inside a Heap Dump

A .hprof file contains the full object graph at capture time:

  • Every object instance, its class, and field values.
  • Every array and its contents.
  • Class metadata (static fields, class loaders).
  • Thread stacks and local variables referencing heap objects (so you can see GC roots).

From this, an analyzer computes two crucial numbers for each object:

  • Shallow size - the memory used by the object itself, not counting what it references.
  • Retained size - the total memory that would be freed if this object became unreachable, including

everything it exclusively keeps alive.

live vs Full Heap Dumps

ModeCommandWhat HappensTrade-off
Live objects onlyjmap -dump:live,...Forces a full GC first, then dumps only reachable objectsSmaller, cleaner dump; but the forced GC causes a pause and can hide short-lived garbage that might be relevant
Full heapjmap -dump:... (no live)Dumps everything currently in the heap, including garbage not yet collectedLarger file; useful for allocation-rate analysis, but noisier for leak-hunting

For leak investigations, live dumps are usually preferred since a real leak means objects survive even a

full GC.

Finding a Leak: The "Dominator Tree" Approach

In Eclipse MAT, the most effective workflow for a suspected leak is:

  1. Take two heap dumps some time apart (e.g. 30 minutes) under similar load.
  2. Run MAT's "Leak Suspects Report," which automatically flags large retained-size clusters.
  3. Use the "Dominator Tree" view, sorted by retained size, to find the single object subtree consuming the most

memory.

  1. Trace "Path to GC Roots" (excluding weak/soft references) on the suspicious object to see exactly what's still

holding a reference to it - this is usually the leak's root cause (e.g. a static Map that's never

cleared, or a listener never unregistered).
codeExamples:
# Take two dumps 30 minutes apart to compare growth
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap_t1.hprof 12345
# ... wait 30 minutes under load ...
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap_t2.hprof 12345

# In Eclipse MAT: File > Open, then use "Compare Basket" to diff heap_t1 vs heap_t2

expert.content:
Sample MAT Dominator Tree Output

Class                                   Shallow Heap   Retained Heap    %
com.myapp.cache.SessionCache            48             612,458,320    68.2%
  java.util.HashMap$Node[]              1,048,608      612,000,000    68.1%
    com.myapp.model.UserSession x 42000 -              608,100,000    67.7%
java.lang.Thread[]                      312            89,204,112     9.9%
byte[]                                  -               45,120,880    5.0%

Here, SessionCache retains 68% of the entire heap via a HashMap that has grown to 42,000

UserSession entries - a strong signal that sessions are never being evicted, a classic unbounded-cache

leak.

Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
Service memory usage climbs steadily over days until it OOMs and restartsUnbounded cache or collection (e.g. static Map) never evicting entriesTake two heap dumps hours apart, diff dominator trees, look for the class growing unboundedAdd eviction policy (TTL/size-bounded cache like Caffeine) or explicitly clear stale entries
Heap dump command hangs or times out on a large production instanceFull/live dump on a multi-GB heap under active traffic causes a long stop-the-world pause while dumpingCheck dump duration vs heap size; check if the app became unresponsive during the dumpTake dumps during low-traffic windows, or use a smaller sampling-based tool (JFR) first to narrow the suspect before a full dump
Heap dump shows plenty of free space, but OutOfMemoryError still occursThe error is not heap exhaustion but Metaspace or a native memory limit (direct byte buffers, thread stacks)Check the exact OOM message ("Java heap space" vs "Metaspace" vs "unable to create native thread")Diagnose the correct memory region (Metaspace sizing, thread count, or native memory tracking) instead of only looking at heap dumps

Senior Notes

  • Shallow vs retained size: retained size is memory freed if the object were collected, and it points to the leak root.
  • Dominator tree and path to GC roots explain why an object stays alive.
  • Security: a dump contains passwords, tokens and personal data, so protect and delete it like a secret.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to obtain a dump:

  • On OOM: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps.
  • jcmd: GC.heap_dump.
  • jmap: -dump:live,format=b,file=....
  • JMX: HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean.dumpHeap.
  • Tools: VisualVM or JConsole buttons.
  • Analysis: Eclipse MAT (Leak Suspects report), VisualVM, IntelliJ profiler.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The HPROF file stores heap structure rather than a copy of the live program.

  • Content: classes, instances, field values, arrays and GC roots.
  • Creation: the JVM stops at a safepoint and writes the heap; this pause grows with heap size.
  • live option: runs a full GC first, so the dump holds only reachable objects.
  • Compression: JDK 17 and later can write with jcmd PID GC.heap_dump -gz=5 file.hprof.gz (check your JDK build).

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • No dump path space: the dump fails because the disk is full; point HeapDumpPath to a big volume.
  • Looking at shallow size only: shallow size hides the owner; use retained size.
  • Opening a huge dump on a laptop: raise the MAT memory in MemoryAnalyzer.ini.
  • Dump after restart: the leak evidence is lost; take it before restarting.
  • Sharing dumps over chat or tickets, leaking secrets.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Performance and safety:

  • Pause: expect seconds per few GB, and take the node out of rotation first.
  • Disk: reserve about the heap size.
  • Two dumps: take one early and one later and compare the growth.
  • Lighter option: GC.class_histogram or a JFR old-object sample.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: heap grows until OOM every two days.

  • Dump: taken automatically at the OOM.
  • MAT: the dominator tree shows a static Map holding 300 MB of Session objects.
  • Path to GC roots: leads to a listener registry that is never cleared.
  • Fix: remove the listener on logout and bound the map.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Dump only live objects with jmap.

Worked Example 2

Quick histogram without a full dump.

Practice Exercise 1

Create a dump of a running process.

Practice Exercise 2

A classic leak to find.

interviewQA: What is a heap dump?
A snapshot file (.hprof) of every object, its fields, and reference graph in the JVM heap at a point in time
How do you automatically capture a heap dump on OutOfMemoryError?
Run the JVM with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=<path>
How do you take a heap dump of a running process manually?
Use jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=<file> <pid>
What is the difference between shallow size and retained size?
Shallow size is the memory of the object itself; retained size is all memory that would be freed if that object became unreachable
What does the "live" option in jmap do?
Forces a full GC before dumping, so only currently reachable objects are included, producing a smaller/cleaner dump
What tool is most commonly used to analyze a heap dump?
Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT), which offers a Leak Suspects Report and a Dominator Tree view
How would you confirm a memory leak using two heap dumps?
Take dumps at two points in time under similar load, compare dominator trees/retained sizes, and look for a class whose count/retained size grows without bound

topics.name: Thread Dumps

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is a Thread Dump?

A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread running inside the JVM at a single moment - what each thread is doing

right now, and its full call stack. It's a plain text report, not a binary file like a heap dump, so you can read it

directly in a terminal or editor.

Thread dumps are the go-to tool when an application seems stuck, hung, or unresponsive - they show

you exactly what every thread was doing at the moment things froze.

What Does a Thread Dump Show You?

For every single thread, a thread dump shows:

  • The thread's name and ID.
  • Its current state (RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, etc).
  • Its full stack trace - which method it's currently executing, and the chain of calls that got it there.
  • Any locks it holds or is waiting for.
codeExamples:
"http-nio-8080-exec-3" #45 daemon prio=5 os_prio=0 tid=0x00007f cpu=120.50ms
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
        at com.myapp.service.OrderService.calculateTotal(OrderService.java:88)
        at com.myapp.controller.OrderController.checkout(OrderController.java:41)
        at java.base/java.lang.reflect.Method.invoke(Method.java:568)

beginner.content:
Generating a Thread Dump with jstack

The simplest way to get a thread dump is with the jstack command-line tool included in the JDK.
codeExamples:
# Find the process ID
jps -l

# Capture a thread dump to a file
jstack 12345 > thread_dump.txt

beginner.content:
Generating a Thread Dump with kill -3 (Linux/Mac)

On Unix-like systems, you can also send a SIGQUIT signal (signal 3) directly to the Java process. The

JVM catches this signal and prints the thread dump to standard output/its log file, rather than terminating the

process (despite "kill" being in the command name).
codeExamples:
# Send SIGQUIT to trigger a thread dump - written to the app's stdout/log, not a separate file
kill -3 12345

beginner.content:
Common Thread States You'll See

  • RUNNABLE - actively executing code or ready to run on the CPU.
  • BLOCKED - waiting to acquire a synchronized lock held by another thread.
  • WAITING - waiting indefinitely for another thread's signal (e.g. Object.wait(),

Thread.join()).

  • TIMED_WAITING - waiting, but with a timeout (e.g. Thread.sleep()).

Seeing many threads stuck in BLOCKED state at the same spot is a strong hint of lock contention or a deadlock.

Fresher Notes

  • Thread dump: a snapshot of every thread with its state, name and stack trace at one moment.
  • How to take one: jcmd <pid> Thread.print, or Ctrl+Break on Windows and kill -3 <pid> on Linux.
  • States: read RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING and TIMED_WAITING first.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Take three dumps a few seconds apart; a thread stuck on the same frame in all of them is the suspect.
  • Deadlock: the dump ends with Found one Java-level deadlock and lists the locks each thread holds and wants.
  • Thread names: give pool threads real names, so a dump shows order-worker-3 and not pool-1-thread-3.

8. Advanced Concepts

Detecting a Deadlock in a Thread Dump

When two or more threads are each waiting for a lock the other one holds, they deadlock permanently. jstack

is smart enough to detect this pattern automatically and prints a dedicated section at the end of the dump.

Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"Thread-1":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f8a1c003f28 (object 0x000000076ac03a70, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "Thread-2"
"Thread-2":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f8a1c001a08 (object 0x000000076ac03a80, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "Thread-1"

Java stack information for the threads listed above:
===================================================
"Thread-1":
        at com.myapp.TransferService.transfer(TransferService.java:22)
        - waiting to lock <0x000000076ac03a70> (a java.lang.Object)
        - locked <0x000000076ac03a80> (a java.lang.Object)
"Thread-2":
        at com.myapp.TransferService.transfer(TransferService.java:22)
        - waiting to lock <0x000000076ac03a80> (a java.lang.Object)
        - locked <0x000000076ac03a70> (a java.lang.Object)

This is the textbook "lock ordering" deadlock: two threads acquire the same two locks in opposite order.

Reading BLOCKED vs Lock-Owner Relationships

When a thread is BLOCKED, its stack trace includes a line like

- waiting to lock <0xADDRESS> (a com.myapp.Account). Somewhere else in the same dump, another thread

will show - locked <0xADDRESS> for the same address - that's the thread currently holding the

lock you need to find.

This lets you manually trace lock-contention chains even when jstack's automatic deadlock detector

doesn't fire (e.g. contention without a true cyclic deadlock, just severe serialization on one hot lock).

Thread States - Full Reference

StateMeaningCommon Cause
NEWThread created but not yet startedRare to catch in a dump; thread object exists, start() not called
RUNNABLEExecuting or ready to execute on CPUNormal active work, or busy-spinning/CPU-bound code
BLOCKEDWaiting to enter a synchronized block/methodLock contention, potential deadlock
WAITINGWaiting indefinitely for another threadObject.wait(), Thread.join(), LockSupport.park()
TIMED_WAITINGWaiting with a timeoutThread.sleep(), wait(timeout), a connection-pool checkout with timeout
TERMINATEDThread has finished executingrun() method completed or threw an uncaught exception

Multiple Dumps Over Time - The Real Diagnostic Technique

A single thread dump only shows one instant; the real skill is taking 3-5 dumps a few seconds apart during the

incident and comparing them:

  • If the same threads are stuck at the exact same stack frame across all dumps -> genuinely stuck (deadlock,

infinite loop, or blocked on an external call with no timeout).

  • If threads are RUNNABLE but at different stack frames each time -> the app is just slow/CPU-bound, not hung.
  • If threads are BLOCKED waiting on the same lock across dumps -> strong lock contention, look at what's holding

it and why it's held so long.
codeExamples:
# Capture 5 thread dumps, 5 seconds apart, for comparison
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  jstack 12345 > dump_$i.txt
  sleep 5
done

expert.content:
Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
All request-handling threads eventually go BLOCKED and the app stops responding entirelyTrue deadlock between two locks acquired in inconsistent order (e.g. account transfer logic)jstack's "Found one Java-level deadlock" section identifies the exact threads and locksEnforce a consistent global lock ordering, or replace nested locking with a single lock / lock-free structure
Throughput degrades under load but no deadlock is reportedSevere contention on a single coarse-grained lock (e.g. a synchronized cache) - not cyclic, just serializedMultiple dumps show many threads BLOCKED waiting on the same lock address, held briefly by a rotating single ownerNarrow the synchronized scope, use a concurrent collection (ConcurrentHashMap) or finer-grained locking
App hangs specifically when calling a downstream service, never recoversA thread is TIMED_WAITING/RUNNABLE stuck inside a socket read with no timeout configured on the HTTP clientStack trace shows the thread stuck inside the HTTP client's socket read across all dumpsConfigure explicit connect/read timeouts on all outbound clients so threads never wait forever

Senior Notes

  • Virtual threads: jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json file.json includes them, while plain Thread.print does not.
  • High CPU: match the hex nid in the dump to the busiest OS thread id from top -H.
  • Automation: capture dumps on a health-check failure, and compare them with a tool such as a dump analyzer.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to get and format a dump:

  • jcmd Thread.print: add -l for locks.
  • kill -3 / Ctrl+Break: output goes to the process stdout.
  • jstack: older front end.
  • Thread.dump_to_file: text or JSON, includes virtual threads (JDK 21).
  • ThreadMXBean: dumpAllThreads from code or JMX.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

A dump is produced at a safepoint, when every thread is paused briefly.

  • Request: attach (jcmd) or SIGQUIT asks the JVM to print.
  • Per thread: name, id, nid (the OS thread id in hex), state and frames.
  • Locks: lines such as - locked and - waiting to lock show monitor ownership.
  • Deadlock check: the JVM looks for cycles in the lock graph and prints them at the end.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • One dump only: take three, a few seconds apart.
  • Reading only RUNNABLE: a thread waiting in native socket read is also shown as RUNNABLE.
  • Unnamed pools: use a ThreadFactory with names.
  • Ignoring idle pool threads: parked pool workers are normal, not a problem.
  • Dump to a file that fills the disk: rotate and compress dumps.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

A dump has a small cost, so use it with a plan.

  • Pause: grows with the thread count and stack depth.
  • Many threads: thousands of platform threads signal a pool sizing problem, and virtual threads can replace them for blocking I/O.
  • Pool saturation: all workers in the same frame, such as a JDBC call, means the dependency is slow.
  • JFR alternative: JFR records thread states over time with less manual work.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 Thread.print | grep -c "http-nio-8080-exec"
jcmd 4242 Thread.print | grep -A3 "exec-" | grep -c "SocketInputStream"

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 200
# 187      <- almost all workers wait on a slow downstream call

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a service stops answering but CPU is low.

  • Step 1: take three dumps, 5 seconds apart.
  • Step 2: count threads by state and by top frame.
  • Step 3: find the lock owner for the BLOCKED threads.
  • Step 4: fix the root cause: lock order, a timeout, or a bigger or isolated pool.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Read a blocked thread.
codeExamples:
"http-nio-8080-exec-7" #52 prio=5 os_prio=0 nid=0x2f10 waiting for monitor entry
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
        at com.shop.Cart.add(Cart.java:41)
        - waiting to lock <0x000000076b2a1c20> (a com.shop.Cart)
        - locked by "http-nio-8080-exec-3"

// OUTPUT:
// exec-7 waits on a Cart monitor that exec-3 holds: look at exec-3 next

expert.content:
Worked Example 2

Spot a deadlock.
codeExamples:
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"T1": waiting to lock monitor 0x...1 (object 0x...a, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "T2"
"T2": waiting to lock monitor 0x...2 (object 0x...b, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "T1"

// OUTPUT:
// the fix is a single global lock order, or tryLock with a timeout

expert.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Take a dump on Linux and Windows.
codeExamples:
# Linux
jcmd 4242 Thread.print > dump1.txt
kill -3 4242                     # prints to the application stdout

# Windows
jcmd 4242 Thread.print > dump1.txt
# or press Ctrl+Break in the console that runs the application

# OUTPUT: (excerpt, varies)
# "main" #1 prio=5 os_prio=0 tid=0x... nid=0x1a2c waiting on condition
#    java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (sleeping)
#         at java.lang.Thread.sleep(Native Method)

expert.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Take three dumps with a pause.
codeExamples:
for i in 1 2 3;
do
  jcmd 4242 Thread.print > dump_$i.txt
  sleep 5
done
ls dump_*.txt

# OUTPUT:
# dump_1.txt  dump_2.txt  dump_3.txt

interviewQA: What is a thread dump?
A snapshot of every thread's state and stack trace in a running JVM at a point in time
How do you generate a thread dump?
Use jstack <pid>, or send kill -3 <pid> on Unix systems to print it to the process's stdout/log
What thread states indicate a potential problem?
BLOCKED (waiting on a lock) most directly; many threads stuck at the same frame across repeated dumps in any waiting state also signals a problem
How does jstack detect a deadlock?
It analyzes the lock-wait graph across threads and reports cycles where thread A waits for a lock held by B, which waits for a lock held by A
Why take multiple thread dumps instead of just one?
A single dump only shows one instant; comparing several dumps a few seconds apart distinguishes a genuinely stuck thread from one that's just slow/CPU-bound
What's the difference between WAITING and TIMED_WAITING?
WAITING blocks indefinitely until another thread signals it; TIMED_WAITING blocks for a bounded time and resumes automatically on timeout
How would you diagnose a hang caused by a downstream call with no timeout?
Take a thread dump and look for a thread stuck inside the HTTP/socket client's read call across repeated dumps, then check if a read/connect timeout is configured

topics.name: JFR (Java Flight Recorder)

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is JFR?

Java Flight Recorder (JFR) is a profiling and event-collection tool built directly into the JVM itself. It records

detailed information about what's happening inside your application - method execution, garbage collection pauses,

lock contention, I/O, exceptions - while it runs, with very low overhead (typically under 1-2%).

It's called a "flight recorder" by analogy to an airplane's black box: it continuously records what the JVM is

doing, so if something goes wrong, you can go back and see exactly what happened.

Why JFR is Special

Before JFR, most profiling tools attached an external agent that added significant overhead, often changing the very

behavior you were trying to measure (the "observer effect"). JFR is different because:

  • It's built into the JVM itself - no external agent needed.
  • It's designed to run safely in production, continuously, with minimal performance impact.
  • It's free and included with every OpenJDK/Oracle JDK since Java 11 (and available via backport in Java 8).

Starting a JFR Recording

You can start a JFR recording right when you launch your application, or attach to one that's already running.
codeExamples:
# Start the app with a JFR recording running for its whole lifetime
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=recording.jfr,duration=60s -jar myapp.jar

# Attach to an already-running JVM and record for 60 seconds
jcmd 12345 JFR.start duration=60s filename=recording.jfr

# Check the status of an active recording
jcmd 12345 JFR.check

# Manually stop and dump a running recording
jcmd 12345 JFR.stop filename=recording.jfr

beginner.content:
What Kind of Events Does JFR Capture?

JFR organizes what it captures into "events" - each one a small, structured record of something that happened. Common

categories include:

  • CPU / Method profiling - which methods consumed the most CPU time.
  • Garbage Collection - every GC pause, its duration and cause.
  • Memory allocation - which classes are allocated most frequently.
  • Thread activity / lock contention - which locks threads waited on, and for how long.
  • I/O - file and socket read/write events.
  • Exceptions - thrown exceptions and their frequency.

Viewing a Recording

Once you have a .jfr file, you open it in JMC (Java Mission Control) - a free GUI tool

covered in the next topic - to browse the recorded events visually with charts and drill-down views.

Fresher Notes

  • JFR (Java Flight Recorder) records JVM and application events with very low overhead.
  • Start at launch with -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=app.jfr.
  • Open the .jfr file in JDK Mission Control, or print it with the jfr command.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Free: JFR is open source and free in OpenJDK 11 and later (it was commercial in Oracle JDK 8).
  • Profiles: settings=default is light, and settings=profile collects more detail with a little more cost.
  • Running JVM: use jcmd <pid> JFR.start, JFR.dump and JFR.stop.

8. Advanced Concepts

JFR Architecture: Event Streaming

Internally, JFR events are written to an in-memory circular buffer per thread, then periodically flushed to disk (or

consumed live). This design is what keeps overhead so low - most of the work is simple, lock-free buffer writes

rather than expensive synchronization or I/O on every event.

Since JDK 14, JFR also supports Event Streaming - reading events in near real-time as they're

produced, rather than only after a recording finishes, which enables live dashboards and alerting built directly on

top of JFR data.

Recording Configurations: default vs profile

JFR ships with two built-in configuration templates that trade off detail against overhead:

TemplateTypical OverheadUse Case
default< 1%Always-on continuous production monitoring
profile~2%Deep-dive performance investigation, shorter targeted recordings

You can also define a fully custom .jfc configuration file to enable/disable specific event types and

their thresholds/stack-depth precisely.
codeExamples:
# Use the deeper "profile" template for a focused investigation
jcmd 12345 JFR.start name=deepdive settings=profile duration=120s filename=deepdive.jfr

# List available/running recordings on a JVM
jcmd 12345 JFR.dump name=deepdive filename=snapshot.jfr

expert.content:
Sample JFR Text Summary (jfr print)

The JDK also ships a jfr CLI tool that can summarize or print recordings without opening a GUI - handy

for quick server-side triage or scripting.

$ jfr summary recording.jfr

 Version: 2.1
 Chunks: 3
 Start: 2026-08-14 10:02:11
 Duration: 60 s

 Event Type                          Count  Size (bytes)
 jdk.ExecutionSample                 12,904   642,180
 jdk.GarbageCollection                    8     1,920
 jdk.JavaMonitorEnter                 3,410   187,340
 jdk.SocketRead                       9,822   511,004
 jdk.ObjectAllocationSample            5,672   296,116

Continuous Production Recording Strategy

Because overhead is so low, a common production pattern is to run JFR continuously with the default

template and a rolling ring-buffer, so that whenever an incident happens (crash, latency spike, alert), you can dump

the last N minutes of recorded data retroactively - even though you didn't know in advance that you'd need it.
codeExamples:
# Start a continuous recording that keeps the last 15 minutes in a ring buffer
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=disk=true,maxage=15m,maxsize=250M,name=continuous -jar myapp.jar

# After an incident is noticed, dump what's currently buffered without stopping the recording
jcmd 12345 JFR.dump name=continuous filename=incident_$(date +%s).jfr

expert.content:
Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
Intermittent latency spikes with no clear trigger, hard to reproduceOccasional long GC pauses or lock contention that only shows up under specific traffic patternsRun continuous JFR recording; when a spike is reported, dump the ring buffer and open in JMC, filter by timestamp of the spikeIdentify and address the specific GC/lock event causing the spike (tune GC, reduce lock scope)
Team is hesitant to profile production because of past overhead problems with other toolsPrevious profiler used bytecode instrumentation/sampling with much higher overhead than JFRBenchmark JFR's actual overhead (default template, <1%) against the previous toolAdopt JFR as the standard always-on production profiler instead of ad hoc heavier tools
Need to prove a specific deploy caused a regression, but no dumps were taken beforehandNo continuous recording was configured, so historical data doesn't existN/A retroactively - this is a process gap, not a technical bugEnable always-on continuous JFR recording (ring buffer) in all environments going forward so every incident is analyzable after the fact

Senior Notes

  • Continuous recording: run with maxage and maxsize and dump on demand, so an incident always has data.
  • CLI: jfr summary, jfr print --events jdk.GCPhasePause and jfr view (JDK 21) work without a GUI.
  • Custom events: extend jdk.jfr.Event to record business timings next to JVM events.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful options:

  • duration / maxage / maxsize: bound the recording.
  • settings: default, profile or a custom .jfc path.
  • dumponexit=true: write the file when the JVM ends.
  • jfr print / summary / view: inspect on the command line.
  • jfr assemble and disassemble: split or join chunk files.
codeExamples:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=maxage=15m,maxsize=250m,dumponexit=true,filename=last.jfr ^
     -jar app.jar
jfr print --events jdk.CPULoad last.jfr

# OUTPUT: (excerpt, varies)
# jdk.CPULoad { jvmUser = 12.4 %  jvmSystem = 1.1 %  machineTotal = 35.0 % }

expert.content:
Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

JFR is built into the JVM and writes events into thread-local buffers.

  • Events: JVM (GC, JIT, locks), OS (CPU) and application ones.
  • Sampling: method samples about every 10 or 20 ms, not every call, so overhead stays low.
  • Storage: buffers flush to chunks in a repository, then to a .jfr file on dump.
  • Config: .jfc files choose events and thresholds.
codeExamples:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=app.jfr,settings=default -jar app.jar
jfr configure --help

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# Started recording 1. The result will be written to: app.jfr

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong file path: the file is written on the server, not your laptop.
  • profile in production all day: use default for continuous use.
  • No dump before restart: use dumponexit.
  • Old Java 8 flags: -XX:+UnlockCommercialFeatures is not needed in OpenJDK 11 and later.
  • Reading only CPU: check allocation, locks and GC events too.
codeExamples:
# Java 8 Oracle (old)
java -XX:+UnlockCommercialFeatures -XX:+FlightRecorder -jar app.jar
# Java 11+ OpenJDK (right)
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=app.jfr -jar app.jar

# OUTPUT:
# the second form works in OpenJDK with no unlock flag

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Overhead is usually around 1 to 2 percent with the default profile (varies by workload).

  • Reduce events: raise thresholds, for example for file and socket I/O.
  • Disk: use maxsize.
  • Stack depth: the default stack depth is 64, and deeper stacks cost more.
  • Measure: compare latency with and without recording on your load.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 JFR.start name=low settings=default maxsize=100m
jcmd 4242 JFR.check

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# Recording 1: name=low maxsize=100.0MB (running)

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: p99 latency spikes every few minutes.

  • Step 1: keep a rolling recording running.
  • Step 2: after a spike, dump the last 10 minutes.
  • Step 3: open it and compare the spike time with GC pauses, safepoints and lock waits.
  • Step 4: tune the cause: heap size, collector, or the contended lock.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 JFR.dump name=rolling filename=spike.jfr
jfr print --events jdk.GCPhasePause spike.jfr | head -8

# OUTPUT: (excerpt, varies)
# jdk.GCPhasePause { startTime = 10:15:02  duration = 145 ms  name = "GC Pause" }

expert.content:
10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Read a recording from the command line.
codeExamples:
jfr summary app.jfr
jfr print --events jdk.GarbageCollection app.jfr

# OUTPUT: (excerpt, varies)
#  Event Type                     Count  Size (bytes)
#  jdk.GarbageCollection             12           480

# Dumped recording "rec1", 3.2 MB written to: C:\temp\rec1.jfr

interviewQA: What is JFR?
Java Flight Recorder - a low-overhead, built-in JVM profiling and event-recording framework
Why is JFR considered safe for production use?
Its default configuration adds well under 1-2% overhead by writing events to lock-free per-thread ring buffers rather than doing expensive instrumentation on every call
How do you start a JFR recording on an already-running JVM?
Use jcmd <pid> JFR.start with options like duration and filename
What is the difference between the default and profile JFR templates?
default is tuned for near-zero overhead continuous monitoring; profile captures more detail (e.g. more allocation/lock events) at slightly higher (~2%) overhead
What is JFR Event Streaming?
A JDK 14+ API (RecordingStream) that lets applications consume JFR events in near real-time as they occur, enabling live dashboards/alerts
What types of events can JFR capture?
CPU/method samples, GC pauses, memory allocation, lock contention, thread activity, I/O, and exceptions, among others
What tool would you use to open and visually analyze a .jfr file?
JMC (Java Mission Control)

topics.name: JMC (Java Mission Control)

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is JMC?

Java Mission Control (JMC) is a free desktop GUI application for viewing and analyzing the data recorded by JFR

(Java Flight Recorder). While JFR does the recording inside the JVM, JMC is the tool you use to actually

look at that data - with charts, tables, and drill-down views instead of raw text.

Think of JFR as the "black box recorder" and JMC as the "playback software" investigators use to review it.

Getting JMC

JMC used to ship bundled with the JDK, but since Java 9 it's a separate free download maintained by the OpenJDK

community (and also offered by vendors like Azul and Red Hat). You download and install it once, then point it at

any .jfr recording file, or connect it live to a running JVM on your network.
codeExamples:
# Open a saved recording directly from the command line (once JMC is installed)
jmc -open recording.jfr

beginner.content:
Connecting JMC to a Live JVM

Besides opening saved .jfr files, JMC can connect directly to a running JVM (local or over the network,

via JMX) to start/stop recordings and watch live data, without needing to manually use jcmd first.

Key Views in JMC

Once a recording is open, JMC organizes the data into tabs, the most important being:

  • General - overview of the JVM, its version, flags, and system info during the recording.
  • Memory - heap usage over time, garbage collection pauses and their causes.
  • Code - "hot methods" - which methods consumed the most CPU time.
  • Threads - thread activity, lock contention (which locks caused the most blocking).
  • I/O - file and socket reads/writes, useful for spotting slow external calls.

Why Use JMC Instead of Reading Raw JFR Text?

While you can print raw event data with the jfr command-line tool, JMC's real value is visual

correlation - seeing a CPU spike, a GC pause, and a lock-contention event all lined up on the same timeline, which

makes cause-and-effect jump out in a way scrolling through text output never does.

Fresher Notes

  • JMC (JDK Mission Control) is a desktop tool to open and analyze .jfr files and monitor live JVMs.
  • Automated analysis: the rules page lists problems such as GC pauses and lock contention, with a score.
  • Separate download: JMC is not bundled with the JDK since version 9, so install it on its own.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Pages: Java Application, JVM Internals, Memory, Method Profiling, Lock Instances and Threads.
  • Flame graph: shows which methods take the most sampled time.
  • Remote JVM: connect with JMX, then start a recording from the JVM browser.

8. Advanced Concepts

The Automated Analysis Engine

JMC includes a built-in Automated Analysis Results tab that runs a rule engine over the recording

and automatically flags likely problems - similar in spirit to a linter, but for runtime behavior. It scores findings

by severity (info / warning / severe) and explains them in plain language, for example:

  • "Long garbage collection pauses detected"
  • "Class loading is a significant contributor to total time"
  • "Thread X spent a large percentage of the recording BLOCKED"

This is often the fastest way to get oriented in an unfamiliar recording before manually drilling into the Memory,

Code, or Threads tabs.

Threads Page: Lock Contention Analysis

The Threads tab's "Lock Instances" view ranks every monitor/lock by total accumulated blocking time across all

threads during the recording - directly answering "which lock is causing the most contention in production" without

manually cross-referencing multiple thread dumps by hand.

Combined with the "Hot Methods" view under Code, you can typically go from "the app feels slow under load" to "this

exact synchronized block in OrderService.reserveInventory() is the bottleneck" within a few minutes.

Memory Page: GC Pause Analysis

ChartWhat It ShowsWhat to Look For
Heap usage over timeLive heap size across the recording windowSteady sawtooth = healthy; a rising floor after each GC = possible leak
GC pause timesDuration of every individual GC pause, plotted over timeOccasional long pauses correlating with latency spike reports
Allocation by classWhich classes are allocated the most (by count and total size)Unexpectedly high allocation rate from a class you didn't expect (often a hidden autoboxing or string concatenation hot spot)

Sample Automated Analysis Output

Automated Analysis Results
============================
[SEVERE]   Garbage Collector: Frequent full GCs detected
           15 full GCs occurred, totaling 4.2s of pause time (7% of recording).
           Suggestion: Investigate the heap for a memory leak or undersized old generation.

[WARNING]  Contention: High lock contention on java.lang.Object@0x000000076b
           Thread "pool-2-thread-7" was blocked for 1.8s waiting on this lock.
           Suggestion: Review synchronized blocks guarding this object.

[INFO]     File I/O: 320 file read operations totaling 1.2s
           No action needed - within expected range for this workload.

Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
P99 latency spikes correlate loosely with "something in GC" but the team can't pinpoint itFull GCs caused by old-generation growth from a slow leak, not visible from metrics dashboards aloneOpen a JFR recording covering the spike window in JMC's Memory tab; overlay GC pause chart with the latency graph timestampsConfirmed causal link lets the team prioritize fixing the underlying allocation/leak instead of just tuning GC flags
A specific customer-facing endpoint is consistently slower than similar endpointsA synchronized block inside a shared service class is heavily contended only under that endpoint's specific call patternUse JMC's Threads > Lock Instances view sorted by total blocking time during a recording of that endpoint under loadReduce the synchronized scope or replace with a non-blocking/finer-grained concurrency structure
Team suspects a "third-party library update" caused a regression but can't reproduce it locallyThe regression only manifests under production-scale concurrency/data, which local testing doesn't replicateRun JFR in production before/after the update, compare Automated Analysis Results and Hot Methods between the two recordingsPinpoint the exact method/hot path that changed, confirming or ruling out the library update as the cause

Senior Notes

  • Allocation: use the TLAB allocation views to find the code that creates the most garbage.
  • Compare: open a good and a bad recording and compare GC, CPU and locks.
  • Security: protect JMX with authentication and TLS, and prefer copying the file from the server.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Where to look:

  • Automated Analysis: first view.
  • Method Profiling: hot methods and flame graph.
  • Memory and GC: allocation, heap use and pauses.
  • Threads and Lock Instances: contention.
  • Environment: flags, system properties, container limits.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

JMC reads the same event stream that JFR writes and adds analysis.

  • Parser: loads chunks and builds tables and graphs.
  • Rules engine: each rule reads events and produces a score from 0 to 100.
  • JMX console: reads live MBeans from a connected JVM.
  • Plugins: extra pages, such as flame graphs, come from plugins.
codeExamples:
jmc -vm "C:\Program Files\Java\jdk-21\bin"
# Linux
jmc -vm /usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk/bin

# OUTPUT:
# JMC starts using the chosen JDK as its runtime

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • JMC too old for the recording version: use a current JMC.
  • Running JMC with a JRE: it needs a JDK.
  • Trusting one rule: a rule is a hint, confirm it in the events.
  • Open JMX port without security: anyone can control the JVM.
  • Ignoring sample bias: sampling shows where time is spent, not exact call counts.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Performance tips for the tool:

  • Large files: raise the JMC heap in jmc.ini, for example -Xmx4g.
  • Time range: select a range to focus on and speed up views.
  • Filter by thread: remove idle pool threads.
  • Use the CLI for very large files.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: batch job is slower after a release.

  • Step 1: record the old and the new version with the same input.
  • Step 2: compare Automated Analysis and the flame graphs.
  • Step 3: a new hot method or more allocation shows the regression.
  • Step 4: fix, re-record, confirm.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Reading the result.

Worked Example 2

Typical workflow.

Practice Exercise 1

Open a recording.
codeExamples:
jmc -open C:\temp\rec1.jfr
# Linux
jmc -open /tmp/rec1.jfr

# OUTPUT:
# JMC opens, runs the Automated Analysis Results page first

expert.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Enable JMX for a remote connection (test only).
codeExamples:
java -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.port=9010 \
     -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.authenticate=true \
     -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.ssl=true -jar app.jar

# OUTPUT:
# JMC: File - Connect - Remote host:9010 shows the JVM

interviewQA: What is JMC and how does it relate to JFR?
JMC (Java Mission Control) is a GUI tool for visualizing and analyzing recordings produced by JFR; JFR records the data, JMC displays and interprets it
What is the Automated Analysis Results feature?
A built-in rule engine in JMC that scans a JFR recording and automatically flags likely issues (long GC pauses, lock contention, etc.) with severity ratings and suggestions
Which JMC view would you use to find the most CPU-consuming methods?
The Code tab's "Hot Methods" view
Which JMC view would you use to find lock contention bottlenecks?
The Threads tab's "Lock Instances" view, which ranks locks by total accumulated blocking time
Is JMC bundled with the JDK?
Not since Java 9 - it's a separate free download from the OpenJDK project or JDK vendors
How can JMC help confirm a memory leak?
By showing the heap usage chart's post-GC floor rising over time in the Memory tab, alongside allocation-by-class data to identify the offending class
Can JMC connect to a live running JVM, not just saved files?
Yes - it can connect via JMX to start/stop recordings and view live data on a running JVM, local or remote

topics.name: jstack

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is jstack?

jstack is a command-line tool bundled with the JDK that prints a thread dump - a

snapshot of every thread's state and stack trace - for a running Java process. It's the quickest way to check

"what is my application's threads actually doing right now?" without adding any monitoring code.

Basic Usage

You first need the process ID (PID) of the running JVM, which you can get with jps (JVM Process

Status), then pass it to jstack.
codeExamples:
# List running Java processes with their main class name
jps -l
# Sample output:
# 12345 com.myapp.Application
# 8820  sun.tools.jps.Jps

# Print a thread dump for process 12345 to the terminal
jstack 12345

# Save the thread dump to a file for later analysis
jstack 12345 > thread_dump.txt

beginner.content:
Reading a Basic jstack Entry

Each thread in the output looks like this - a header line with the thread's name/state, followed by its call stack

from the current point of execution downward.
codeExamples:
"main" #1 prio=5 os_prio=0 tid=0x00007f8ab4009800 nid=0x1a03 waiting on condition [0x00007f8ab7]
   java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (sleeping)
        at java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Native Method)
        at com.myapp.Application.main(Application.java:15)

beginner.content:
What -l and -F Options Do

  • jstack -l <pid> - adds extra information about ownable synchronizers (java.util.concurrent

locks), not just built-in synchronized monitors. Useful if your app uses ReentrantLock.

  • jstack -F <pid> - "force" mode; use this if the process is hung so badly that a normal dump

request doesn't respond.
codeExamples:
# Include java.util.concurrent lock ownership details
jstack -l 12345

# Force a dump when the process isn't responding to a normal request
jstack -F 12345

beginner.content:
Why Every Java Developer Should Know jstack

When production support asks "why is the app frozen," a thread dump from jstack is usually the fastest

and least invasive first step - it takes a fraction of a second, doesn't require restarting anything, and often

immediately reveals the culprit (a deadlock, a stuck external call, or threads piling up on one lock).

Fresher Notes

  • jstack prints the thread stacks of a running Java process: jstack <pid>.
  • Find the pid with jps or jcmd with no arguments.
  • Same user: run it as the user that owns the Java process.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Options: -l adds lock information, such as owned ownable synchronizers.
  • Save: redirect to a file, jstack -l 4242 > dump.txt, for later reading.
  • Deadlock: jstack reports Java-level deadlocks at the end of the output.

8. Advanced Concepts

Full Anatomy of a jstack Thread Entry

"http-nio-8080-exec-7" #52 daemon prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=340.10ms elapsed=612.44s tid=0x00007f allocated=48MB defined_classes=2
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
        at com.myapp.inventory.InventoryService.reserve(InventoryService.java:112)
        - waiting to lock <0x000000076bd12340> (a com.myapp.inventory.InventoryService)
        at com.myapp.order.OrderController.checkout(OrderController.java:58)
        at java.base/jdk.internal.reflect.NativeMethodAccessorImpl.invoke0(Native Method)

   Locked ownable synchronizers:
        - <0x000000076bc98a10> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync)

Key fields: daemon (whether it's a daemon thread, JVM won't wait for it to exit), cpu

(total CPU time consumed), elapsed (wall-clock lifetime), and the Thread.State line which

tells you exactly what category of wait/execution the thread is in.

jstack vs Alternatives

ToolOutputBest For
jstackPlain text thread dump, one-time snapshotFast, scriptable, works over SSH with no GUI
kill -3 (SIGQUIT)Same content, written to the app's own stdout/logWhen you don't have direct JDK tool access but can signal the process
jcmd <pid> Thread.printSame content, via the unified jcmd toolModern JDKs where jcmd is the preferred single entry point (see jcmd topic)
JFR thread/lock eventsContinuous data over a time window, not just an instantUnderstanding contention trends over time, not just "right now"

Scripting Repeated Dumps for Trend Analysis

A single dump is a snapshot; the real diagnostic power comes from taking several in quick succession and diffing

which threads remain stuck at the same frame.
codeExamples:
#!/bin/bash
# Capture 6 thread dumps, 5 seconds apart, each timestamped
PID=12345
for i in $(seq 1 6); do
  jstack $PID > "dump_$(date +%H%M%S).txt"
  sleep 5
done

# Then compare which stack frames repeat across all files (candidates for "truly stuck")
grep -A1 "java.lang.Thread.State" dump_*.txt | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

expert.content:
Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
jstack <pid> itself hangs and never prints outputThe target JVM is in a state (e.g. deep GC pause, or the target process is actually a different/zombie process) where it can't respond to the attach requestRetry with jstack -F <pid> (force mode) which reads process memory directly instead of requesting cooperation from the target JVMIf force mode also fails, the JVM may be completely wedged - consider a heap+thread dump via OS-level core dump instead
Thread count grows unbounded over days, eventually hitting OS thread limitsA thread pool is misconfigured to grow unbounded, or threads are being leaked (created but never returned to a pool / never terminate)Compare thread counts and thread name patterns across dumps taken days apart; look for a specific pool prefix growingBound the thread pool's max size and add monitoring/alerting on live thread count
App is "stuck" according to monitoring, but jstack shows all threads RUNNABLENot actually hung - likely CPU-bound (e.g. GC thrashing, inefficient algorithm) rather than blocked/deadlockedCheck CPU usage alongside the dump; take repeated dumps to see if RUNNABLE threads are progressing through different code or stuck in a tight loopProfile with JFR to find the hot method causing CPU saturation, rather than looking for a lock issue that isn't there

Senior Notes

  • Prefer jcmd: jcmd <pid> Thread.print does the same job and works with the other jcmd commands.
  • Hung JVM: if the attach fails, use kill -3 on Linux, because it needs no attach.
  • Safepoint: a dump stops the threads briefly, so avoid very frequent dumps on huge thread counts.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • jstack pid: stacks only.
  • jstack -l pid: with lock details.
  • jstack -e pid: extended info in older releases.
  • jstack -F pid: forced dump of a hung JVM, removed in recent JDKs.
  • jstack core: read a core file (older JDKs).
codeExamples:
jstack -l 4242 > dump.txt
jcmd 4242 Thread.print -l > dump2.txt

# OUTPUT:
# both files hold the same kind of data

expert.content:
Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

jstack is an attach-based client.

  • Attach: the tool connects to the target JVM through a socket file in the temp directory.
  • Command: it asks the JVM to run the thread-print diagnostic command.
  • Output: the JVM writes the dump back to jstack, which prints it.
  • Same engine: that is why jcmd Thread.print gives identical text.
codeExamples:
jstack -l 4242 | head -4

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 2026-10-07 10:15:03
# Full thread dump OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM (21.0.2+13-58 mixed mode, sharing):
#
# Threads class SMR info:

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Different user: use sudo -u appuser jstack pid.
  • Different JDK version than the target: use the matching JDK.
  • Container: run it inside the container or share the pid namespace.
  • Reading the stdout of kill -3 in the wrong place: it goes to the application log.
codeExamples:
sudo -u appuser jstack 4242 > dump.txt
docker exec shop-app jcmd 1 Thread.print

# OUTPUT:
# 1:
# Full thread dump OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM ...

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Cost and care:

  • Pause: short, grows with thread count.
  • Frequency: one dump per few seconds is fine, many per second is not.
  • Size: huge thread counts produce large files, so compress them.
codeExamples:
jstack 4242 | gzip > dump.txt.gz
ls -l dump.txt.gz

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# -rw-r--r-- 1 app app 18432 Oct  7 10:16 dump.txt.gz

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: CPU is at 100 percent.

  • Step 1: top -H -p pid finds the busiest thread id.
  • Step 2: convert it to hex.
  • Step 3: find that nid in the dump and read its stack.
codeExamples:
top -H -p 4242 -b -n 1 | head -12
printf "%x\n" 15361
jstack 4242 | grep -A8 "nid=0x3c01"

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 3c01
# "pool-2-thread-4" ... nid=0x3c01 runnable
#         at com.shop.Report.loop(Report.java:57)

expert.content:
10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Count threads by state.
codeExamples:
jstack 4242 | grep "java.lang.Thread.State" | sort | uniq -c

# OUTPUT: (varies)
#      6 java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
#     31 java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (parking)
#     12 java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (on object monitor)

expert.content:
Worked Example 2

Windows count.
codeExamples:
jstack 4242 | findstr /C:"Thread.State" > states.txt
(Get-Content states.txt | Group-Object).Count

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 4 distinct state lines

expert.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Basic use.
codeExamples:
jps -l
jstack 4242 > dump.txt
jstack -l 4242 | findstr /C:"deadlock"      # Windows
jstack -l 4242 | grep -i deadlock           # Linux

# OUTPUT: (varies)
