# Found one Java-level deadlock:

expert.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Equivalent with jcmd.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 Thread.print -l

# OUTPUT: (excerpt)
# 4242:
# 2026-10-07 10:15:03
# Full thread dump OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM (21.0.2+13 mixed mode):

interviewQA: What does jstack do?
Prints a thread dump of a running JVM process - every thread's state and stack trace at that instant
How do you find the PID needed for jstack?
Use jps -l to list running Java processes with their main class
What does the -l flag add to jstack output?
Information about java.util.concurrent ownable synchronizers (e.g. ReentrantLock), in addition to built-in synchronized monitors
When would you use jstack -F?
When the target process is unresponsive to a normal dump request; force mode reads process state directly
How does jstack report a deadlock?
It automatically detects lock-wait cycles between threads and prints a "Found one Java-level deadlock" section listing the threads and locks involved
Why take multiple jstack dumps instead of one?
A single dump is only one instant; comparing several dumps taken seconds apart distinguishes genuinely stuck threads from ones that are simply slow/progressing
What's a modern alternative to jstack for the same information?
jcmd <pid> Thread.print, part of the unified jcmd diagnostic tool

topics.name: jmap

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is jmap?

jmap is a command-line tool bundled with the JDK for inspecting a running JVM's memory -

its heap. It can print a summary of memory usage, list the object types filling up the heap, and produce a full

heap dump file for deeper analysis in a tool like Eclipse MAT.

Finding the Process to Inspect

Like other JDK diagnostic tools, jmap operates on a process ID (PID), which you find with

jps.
codeExamples:
jps -l
# 12345 com.myapp.Application
# 8820  sun.tools.jps.Jps

beginner.content:
Quick Heap Summary with -heap

This gives you a fast overview of heap configuration and current usage per generation, without producing any large

file.
codeExamples:
jmap -heap 12345

# Sample output (trimmed):
# Heap Configuration:
#    MinHeapFreeRatio = 40
#    MaxHeapSize      = 1073741824 (1024.0MB)
# Heap Usage:
# G1 Heap:
#    used     = 214748364 (204.8MB)
#    free     = 858993460 (819.2MB)
#    16.0% used

beginner.content:
Listing the Biggest Object Types with -histo

The histogram option lists every class currently in the heap, sorted by total memory used - a quick way to spot

"what's eating all my memory" without opening a full heap dump.
codeExamples:
jmap -histo 12345 | head -10

# Sample output:
#  num     #instances         #bytes  class name
#    1:        420381       40196256  [C  (char array)
#    2:        180221       28835360  com.myapp.model.UserSession
#    3:        180221       11534144  java.util.HashMap$Node
#    4:         98211        7856880  java.lang.String

beginner.content:
Producing a Full Heap Dump with -dump

When a summary or histogram isn't enough and you need to inspect the actual object graph, jmap -dump

writes a full .hprof heap dump file to disk - the same kind of file covered in the Heap Dumps topic.
codeExamples:
# Dump only live (reachable) objects, in binary format
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=myapp.hprof 12345

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • jmap inspects heap memory: jmap -histo <pid> lists classes by instance count and size.
  • Heap dump: jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid> writes an HPROF file.
  • Analyze the dump in Eclipse MAT, VisualVM or IntelliJ.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • live in the dump option runs a full GC first and keeps only reachable objects.
  • Pause: a dump stops the application, and a big heap can take many seconds and as much disk.
  • OOM dump: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps writes a dump at the failure.

8. Advanced Concepts

jmap -histo:live vs -histo

Adding :live forces a full garbage collection before generating the histogram, so only reachable

objects are counted. This gives a more accurate view of "what's actually still needed" but the forced GC causes a

pause, so it's best avoided on latency-sensitive production traffic during peak load.
codeExamples:
# Includes garbage not yet collected - no GC pause triggered
jmap -histo 12345

# Forces a full GC first, so only live/reachable objects appear - causes a pause
jmap -histo:live 12345

expert.content:
Comparing Two Histograms to Spot a Leak

A classic lightweight leak-hunting technique doesn't even require a full heap dump - just two histograms taken

minutes apart, diffed for classes whose instance count keeps growing.
codeExamples:
jmap -histo:live 12345 > histo_t1.txt
sleep 600
jmap -histo:live 12345 > histo_t2.txt

diff histo_t1.txt histo_t2.txt | grep com.myapp

# Example diff output showing a suspicious grower:
# <    2:        180221       28835360  com.myapp.model.UserSession
# ---
# >    2:        512980       82076800  com.myapp.model.UserSession

expert.content:
jmap Options Reference

OptionPurposeCaution
-heapPrint heap configuration and generation usage summarySafe, negligible overhead
-histoPrint class histogram (instance count, bytes) of the current heapCan briefly pause the JVM while iterating the heap on some collectors
-histo:liveSame as -histo but forces a full GC firstCauses a real, sometimes multi-second stop-the-world pause on a large heap
-dump:live,format=b,file=...Write a full heap dump of live objectsForces full GC and can pause the app for seconds on large heaps; large output file
-clstatsPrint class loader statisticsUseful for diagnosing Metaspace/class-loader leaks (e.g. in app servers doing hot redeploys)

Sample -clstats Output for a Class Loader Leak

$ jmap -clstats 12345

class_loader    classes bytes   parent_loader       alive?  type

<bootstrap>      724     3841004                              live    <internal>
0x00000007a1b3  1204    5230112 0x00000007a0d2      dead    org.myapp.PluginClassLoader
0x00000007a1c9  1204    5230112 0x00000007a0d2      dead    org.myapp.PluginClassLoader
0x00000007a1d5  1204    5230112 0x00000007a0d2      dead    org.myapp.PluginClassLoader
...(37 more identical dead PluginClassLoader entries)...

Many "dead" class loaders of the same type still holding classes/bytes is the textbook signature of a classloader

leak - typically caused by something (a static field, a ThreadLocal, or a registered shutdown hook) outside the

loader still referencing one of its classes, preventing the whole loader and everything it defined from being

collected.

Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
Metaspace usage keeps climbing after every hot-redeploy in an app serverOld class loaders from previous deployments are never freed because something still references their classesjmap -clstats <pid> shows growing numbers of "dead" class loaders of the same application type still holding bytesFind and remove the lingering reference (common culprits: ThreadLocal not cleared, static caches, unregistered JDBC drivers/shutdown hooks)
Running jmap -dump on a large production heap causes a multi-second outage-dump:live forces a full GC and heap dump generation is itself expensive on a multi-GB heapCompare heap size to typical dump duration; check if the app became unresponsive during the dump windowPrefer non-forced jmap -dump (no :live) if a full GC pause is unacceptable, or schedule dumps during low-traffic windows, or use JFR sampling first to narrow the investigation before a full dump
Histogram shows millions of char[]/String instances dominating memoryExcessive string creation/duplication - e.g. not using String interning for repeated values, or verbose logging building large strings unnecessarilyCross-reference the histogram with a heap dump's "Path to GC Roots" for a sample String to find where they're created/retainedIntern or deduplicate repeated strings, or reduce unnecessary string concatenation in hot paths

Senior Notes

  • Prefer jcmd: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump file and jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram replace jmap.
  • -histo:live triggers a full GC, so use it with care in production.
  • Sensitive data: a heap dump contains passwords and tokens, so store and share it with care.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • -histo: all objects.
  • -histo:live: reachable objects only.
  • -dump:live,format=b,file=f: HPROF.
  • -clstats / -finalizerinfo: classloader and finalizer data in older JDKs.
  • jcmd GC.heap_dump -all: keep unreachable objects too.
codeExamples:
jmap -dump:format=b,file=all.hprof 4242
jcmd 4242 GC.heap_dump -all all2.hprof

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# Heap dump file created

expert.content:
Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

jmap also attaches to the JVM.

  • Histogram: walks the heap and counts instances per class.
  • Dump: writes the heap in HPROF format at a safepoint, so the application pauses.
  • live: triggers a full GC before the walk.
  • Class names: [B means byte[], [C means char[], and [Ljava.lang.String; means String[].
codeExamples:
jmap -histo 4242 | head -4

# OUTPUT: (varies)
#  num     #instances         #bytes  class name (module)
#    1:        500112       40009600  [B (java.base@21.0.2)
#    2:        210554        5053296  java.lang.String (java.base@21.0.2)

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Dump to a small disk: the file is about the heap size.
  • Dump on a busy node: remove it from the load balancer first.
  • Relative file path: the file goes where the target JVM runs, not where jmap runs.
  • Sharing a dump: it holds secrets.
  • Using histo to find a leak at one time: take two and compare the growth.
codeExamples:
jmap -histo:live 4242 > h1.txt
sleep 600
jmap -histo:live 4242 > h2.txt
diff <(head -20 h1.txt) <(head -20 h2.txt)

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# < 1: 100 100002400 [B
# > 1: 300 300002400 [B       <- growing class is the leak suspect

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and cost:

  • Pause scales with heap size, so a 16 GB heap can pause for a long time.
  • Use histo first, it is cheaper than a dump.
  • Compress HPROF files for transfer.
  • Analysis memory: MAT needs a heap larger than the file for fast work.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 GC.class_histogram | head -3
gzip heap.hprof

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 4242:
#  num     #instances         #bytes  class name

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: memory grows until the pod restarts.

  • Step 1: two histograms 10 minutes apart show the growing class.
  • Step 2: take one heap dump.
  • Step 3: in MAT, open the dominator tree and path to GC roots.
  • Step 4: fix the owner, usually a static map or an unbounded cache.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 GC.heap_dump /dumps/leak.hprof
# MAT: Leak Suspects report

# OUTPUT: (example, varies)
# One instance of "com.shop.SessionCache" occupies 412 MB (64 percent)

expert.content:
10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Dump on OutOfMemoryError.
codeExamples:
java -Xmx256m -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError ^
     -XX:HeapDumpPath=C:\dumps -jar app.jar

# OUTPUT:
# java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
# Dumping heap to C:\dumps\java_pid4242.hprof ...

expert.content:
Worked Example 2

A leak that the histogram shows.

Practice Exercise 1

Histogram and dump.
codeExamples:
jmap -histo:live 4242 | head -5
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof 4242

# OUTPUT: (varies)
#  num     #instances         #bytes  class name
#    1:        812340       64987200  [B
#    2:        120004       21600720  java.lang.String
# Heap dump file created

expert.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Same with jcmd.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 GC.class_histogram | head -5
jcmd 4242 GC.heap_dump C:\dumps\heap.hprof

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 4242:
# Heap dump file created [91234567 bytes in 0.9 secs]

interviewQA: What is jmap used for?
Inspecting a running JVM's heap - printing configuration/usage summaries, class histograms, or producing full heap dumps
What does jmap -histo:live do differently from jmap -histo?
-histo:live forces a full GC first so only live/reachable objects are counted, giving a more accurate but pause-inducing snapshot
How do you generate a full heap dump with jmap?
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>
How can you spot a memory leak without taking a full heap dump?
Take two jmap -histo:live snapshots minutes apart and diff them, looking for a class whose instance count/bytes keeps growing
What does jmap -clstats help diagnose?
Class loader leaks - it lists class loaders, their classes/bytes, and whether they're still alive, revealing loaders that should have been collected but weren't
Why should jmap -dump:live be used carefully in production?
It forces a full GC and heap iteration, which can pause a large-heap application for seconds, potentially causing a visible outage
What's the difference between jmap and jstack?
jmap inspects heap/memory (histograms, heap dumps); jstack inspects threads (thread dumps, deadlock detection)

topics.name: jcmd

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is jcmd?

jcmd is the modern, unified command-line tool for sending diagnostic commands to a running JVM. Instead

of needing separate tools like jstack, jmap, and jinfo, jcmd

provides one consistent interface that can do everything those older tools do, plus more - and it's the tool the

JVM team actively adds new capabilities to first.

Basic Usage

Every jcmd command follows the same pattern: the target process ID, followed by the diagnostic command

name.
codeExamples:
# List running JVMs and their PIDs (jcmd's own built-in version of jps)
jcmd -l

# Ask a specific JVM what diagnostic commands it supports
jcmd 12345 help

beginner.content:
Getting a Thread Dump with jcmd

This replaces the older jstack command with the exact same information.
codeExamples: jcmd 12345 Thread.print

beginner.content:
Getting Heap Info with jcmd

This replaces jmap -heap for a quick heap summary.
codeExamples:
jcmd 12345 GC.heap_info

# Sample output:
#  garbage-first heap   total 1048576K, used 214823K
#   region size 1024K, 210 young (215040K), 5 survivors (5120K)
#  Metaspace       used 45210K, committed 46080K, reserved 1093632K

beginner.content:
Getting Configured Flags with jcmd

Instead of restarting a process just to check what memory/GC flags it's actually running with, you can ask the live

JVM directly.
codeExamples:
jcmd 12345 VM.flags

# Sample output:
# -XX:MaxHeapSize=1073741824 -XX:MinHeapSize=268435456 -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:+PrintGCDetails

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • jcmd sends diagnostic commands to a running JVM: jcmd <pid> help lists what it supports.
  • No arguments: jcmd lists the running Java processes, like jps.
  • One tool that replaces most uses of jstack, jmap and jinfo.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Common commands: Thread.print, GC.heap_dump, GC.class_histogram, VM.flags, VM.system_properties.
  • GC: GC.run asks for a collection, and GC.heap_info shows heap regions.
  • JFR: JFR.start, JFR.dump and JFR.stop control recordings.

8. Advanced Concepts

Why jcmd Replaced the Older Tool Family

Old Tooljcmd EquivalentAdvantage of jcmd
jstack <pid>jcmd <pid> Thread.printSame JVM attach mechanism as every other diagnostic command - one tool to learn
jmap -heap <pid>jcmd <pid> GC.heap_infoAlso exposes GC.run, GC.class_histogram, and more without switching tools
jmap -dump <pid>jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump <file>Consistent syntax; new diagnostic commands are added to jcmd first, not the legacy tools
jinfo -flags <pid>jcmd <pid> VM.flagsCan also show only non-default flags with VM.flags -all

Newer JDK diagnostic capabilities (like native memory tracking summaries, JFR control, and system property dumps) are

increasingly exposed only through jcmd, making it the tool worth standardizing on for new tooling and

runbooks.

Frequently Used jcmd Subcommands

CommandPurpose
Thread.printPrint a full thread dump, including deadlock detection
GC.heap_infoPrint heap generation sizes and usage
GC.heap_dump <file>Write a full heap dump to the given file
GC.runTrigger an explicit full garbage collection
GC.class_histogramPrint a class histogram, equivalent to jmap -histo
VM.flags [-all]Print current JVM flags (add -all to include unset defaults)
VM.system_propertiesPrint all Java system properties
VM.native_memory summaryShow a breakdown of native (non-heap) memory usage, if NMT is enabled
JFR.start / JFR.dump / JFR.stopControl a Java Flight Recorder recording without restarting the app
VM.versionPrint the exact JVM build/version running

Native Memory Tracking via jcmd

One capability that has no equivalent in the old tool family at all is Native Memory Tracking (NMT) - a way to see

exactly where the JVM's non-heap memory is going (thread stacks, code cache, GC internal structures,

Metaspace, direct buffers). This requires the JVM to be started with NMT enabled.
codeExamples:
# Start the JVM with NMT enabled (small overhead, safe for production)
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -jar myapp.jar

# Query the summary live via jcmd
jcmd 12345 VM.native_memory summary

# Sample output (trimmed):
#          Java Heap (reserved=1048576KB, committed=524288KB)
#              Class   (reserved=1114112KB, committed=48640KB)
#             Thread   (reserved=32784KB, committed=32784KB)
#               Code   (reserved=253952KB, committed=8320KB)
#                  GC   (reserved=98765KB, committed=76543KB)

expert.content:
Sample Thread.print Deadlock Output via jcmd

$ jcmd 12345 Thread.print
12345:

Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"Thread-1":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f, which is held by "Thread-2"
"Thread-2":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007e, which is held by "Thread-1"

Found 1 deadlock.

Identical detection logic to jstack, since both ultimately use the same JVM attach API under the hood -

jcmd is simply the newer, more extensible front end to it.

Production Troubleshooting Scenarios

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
Container gets OOM-killed even though -Xmx is well below the container memory limitNon-heap native memory (thread stacks, code cache, direct buffers) is consuming the remaining headroomjcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary (with NMT enabled) breaks down exactly which native region is largestRight-size the offending region (e.g. limit thread count, tune code cache size) or increase the container's memory limit to account for it
On-call engineer needs a quick health check script that covers threads, heap, and flags without SSHing in with multiple toolsLegacy workflow required separate jstack/jmap/jinfo invocations and different syntax for eachN/A - process/tooling gapStandardize a single runbook script built entirely on jcmd subcommands (Thread.print, GC.heap_info, VM.flags) for consistency
Need to start a profiling recording on a production incident without restarting the affected processTeam previously believed profiling required relaunching with -XX:StartFlightRecording at JVM startupN/A - awareness gapUse jcmd <pid> JFR.start to attach and begin recording on the already-running process, no restart needed

Senior Notes

  • Virtual threads: jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json out.json.
  • Native memory: start with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then use VM.native_memory.
  • Scripting: use -f file to run several commands, and run it as the same user as the JVM.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Command groups:

  • Thread and VM: Thread.print, VM.uptime, VM.info, VM.command_line.
  • GC: GC.run, GC.heap_info, GC.heap_dump, GC.class_histogram.
  • JFR: JFR.start, JFR.check, JFR.dump, JFR.stop.
  • Classes: VM.classloader_stats, VM.metaspace.
  • Set flags: VM.set_flag for manageable flags.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 VM.uptime
jcmd 4242 VM.set_flag MinHeapFreeRatio 20
jcmd 4242 Compiler.codecache

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 4242:
# 3612.452 s
# CodeHeap 'non-nmethods': size=5760Kb used=1200Kb max_used=1250Kb free=4560Kb

expert.content:
Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

jcmd uses the JVM attach mechanism to call built-in diagnostic commands.

  • Attach: a socket file is created in the temp directory of the target.
  • Dispatch: the JVM Attach Listener thread runs the named command.
  • Result: text is sent back to the client.
  • Reach: only the same user and the same host, or the same container.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 help VM.flags

# OUTPUT: (excerpt)
# VM.flags
# Print VM flag options and their current values.
# Impact: Medium: Depends on the flags
# Syntax : VM.flags [options]

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong user: attach fails, run as the JVM owner.
  • Relative paths: files are written by the target JVM, so use an absolute path.
  • -XX:+DisableAttachMechanism: disables jcmd, so keep it off if you need it.
  • Containers: run jcmd inside the container.
  • Many JVMs: check the pid with jcmd first.
codeExamples:
jcmd
docker exec shop-app jcmd 1 VM.command_line

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 1 com.shop.Main
# 1:
# VM Arguments:
# jvm_args: -Xmx512m

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and safety:

  • Impact: help lists the impact of each command: Low, Medium or High.
  • Avoid GC.run and heap dumps at peak.
  • NMT summary mode costs a few percent, and detail costs more.
  • Script it into a health runbook.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 -f commands.txt
# commands.txt: Thread.print / GC.heap_info / VM.uptime

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 4242:
# (output of each command, in order)

expert.content:
Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: incident runbook for a slow service.

  • Step 1: Thread.print three times.
  • Step 2: GC.heap_info and GC.class_histogram.
  • Step 3: JFR.start for two minutes with profile settings.
  • Step 4: collect the files and attach them to the ticket.
codeExamples:
PID=4242
jcmd $PID Thread.print > t1.txt
jcmd $PID GC.heap_info > heap.txt
jcmd $PID JFR.start duration=120s settings=profile filename=/dumps/inc.jfr

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# Started recording 2. The result will be written to: /dumps/inc.jfr

expert.content:
10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Dump to file, including virtual threads.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json C:\dumps\threads.json
jcmd 4242 GC.heap_dump C:\dumps\heap.hprof

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 4242:
# Created C:\dumps\threads.json

expert.content:
Worked Example 2

Native memory baseline and diff.
codeExamples:
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -jar app.jar
jcmd 4242 VM.native_memory baseline
jcmd 4242 VM.native_memory summary.diff

# OUTPUT: (excerpt, varies)
# Total: reserved=..., committed=...  (+12MB)
# - Thread (committed=...) (+2MB)

expert.content:
Practice Exercise 1

The basics.
codeExamples:
jcmd
jcmd 4242 help
jcmd 4242 VM.version

# OUTPUT: (varies)
# 4242 com.shop.Main
# 4242:
# JVM version is 21.0.2+13-58

expert.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Info commands.
codeExamples:
jcmd 4242 VM.flags
jcmd 4242 GC.heap_info

# OUTPUT: (excerpt, varies)
# -XX:InitialHeapSize=268435456 -XX:MaxHeapSize=4294967296 -XX:+UseG1GC
# garbage-first heap total 262144K, used 81920K

interviewQA: What is jcmd?
A unified command-line diagnostic tool that sends commands to a running JVM, replacing/consolidating older tools like jstack, jmap, and jinfo
How do you get a thread dump using jcmd?
jcmd <pid> Thread.print
How do you get heap usage info using jcmd?
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info
How do you discover all commands a specific JVM supports via jcmd?
jcmd <pid> help
How do you trigger a heap dump using jcmd instead of jmap?
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump <filename>
Why is jcmd generally preferred over jstack/jmap/jinfo today?
It's the single actively developed tool that new diagnostic capabilities (like NMT and JFR control) are added to first, with a consistent command syntax
How would you inspect native (non-heap) memory usage of a running JVM?
Start the JVM with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and query it live with jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary

topics.name: OutOfMemoryError

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is OutOfMemoryError?

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError is thrown by the JVM when it cannot allocate an object because it has

run out of memory in a particular area, and the Garbage Collector (GC) cannot free up enough space to continue.

It is an Error, not an Exception - it signals a serious problem that a normal application usually

cannot recover from on its own.

There isn't just one kind of OutOfMemoryError - the JVM has several memory regions, and each can run out

independently. The most common ones you will meet as a Java developer are:

  • Java heap space - too many live objects for the configured heap
  • Metaspace - too many loaded classes
  • GC overhead limit exceeded - the GC is running constantly but reclaiming almost nothing

1. Heap Space OutOfMemoryError

The heap is where all your objects (new Foo(), ArrayList entries, Strings, etc.) live. If you keep

creating objects and something keeps a reference to them (so GC can't collect them), the heap eventually fills up

completely and the JVM gives up.

2. Metaspace OutOfMemoryError

Metaspace stores class metadata (the bytecode/definitions of classes, not objects). If your application (or a

buggy framework) keeps generating and loading new classes at runtime without ever unloading them, Metaspace

fills up.

3. GC Overhead Limit Exceeded

Sometimes the heap isn't 100% full, but the JVM notices it is spending almost all its CPU time

running Garbage Collection while reclaiming very little memory each time (by default: more than 98% of time in GC,

recovering less than 2% of the heap). Rather than let the app hang forever, the JVM throws this error early.

Common Causes and Quick Fixes

  • Loading a huge file/dataset fully into memory - stream it instead (e.g. BufferedReader

line by line) rather than reading it all into one giant String or List.

  • Unbounded caches or collections - a static Map that keeps growing forever - use a

bounded cache (e.g. Caffeine with a max size) or clear it periodically.

  • Heap sized too small for the workload - increase -Xmx if the application genuinely

needs more memory.

  • Too many classes generated dynamically - increase -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize or fix the

code/library that keeps generating classes.

Fresher Notes

  • OutOfMemoryError is an Error, not an exception: the JVM could not allocate memory and the message tells you which area ran out.
  • Java heap space means the heap is full of live objects; Metaspace means too many classes are loaded.
  • Heap size is set with -Xmx, and a bigger value only delays the failure if the code has a leak.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Heap dump: start with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps so the evidence is saved at the moment of failure.
  • GC overhead limit exceeded means the JVM spends almost all its time in GC and frees almost nothing; it is a leak symptom.
  • Native thread: unable to create native thread is about OS limits and thread stacks, not the heap.

8. Advanced Concepts

How the JVM Decides "Out of Memory"

Before throwing OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space, the JVM does not give up after a single failed

allocation. Modern collectors (G1, Parallel, ZGC) will:

  • Trigger a full GC to try to reclaim space
  • If a full GC barely reclaims anything and this keeps repeating, the collector estimates the "GC overhead" ratio
  • Only after this threshold is repeatedly breached (or a single allocation genuinely cannot fit even after a full

GC) does the JVM throw the error and, optionally, dump the heap

This is why OOM often correlates with a visible GC storm in monitoring dashboards just before the

crash - CPU usage spikes because the collector is working overtime trying (and failing) to free space.

Reading the Full Error Message

The text after the colon in OutOfMemoryError tells you exactly which memory region failed - always

read it carefully before jumping to conclusions.

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
    -> The object heap itself is full. Classic memory leak or undersized heap.

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
    -> Class metadata region is full. Usually a ClassLoader leak (redeploys, dynamic proxies).

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded
    -> GC is thrashing: >98% time in GC, <2% heap reclaimed. App is effectively dying slowly.

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread
    -> Not heap at all - OS/process cannot allocate a new native thread stack.

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit
    -> A single array allocation is larger than the JVM/platform allows.

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory
    -> off-heap NIO DirectByteBuffer space (-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize) exhausted.

Diagnosing a Production Heap OOM

The standard production workflow when a service dies with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space:

  1. Capture a heap dump - ideally automatically, using

-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps so you get a .hprof file at the

moment of the crash rather than trying to reproduce it later.

  1. Open the dump in Eclipse MAT (Memory Analyzer Tool) or VisualVM and run the "Leak Suspects"

report - it clusters retained objects by dominator and flags the largest retainers.

  1. Follow the "retained size" (not just "shallow size") to find which single object graph is

holding the most memory - this is usually the actual leak, e.g. a static Map<String, Session>

with millions of stale entries.

  1. Check the GC logs (-Xlog:gc*) leading up to the crash - if old-gen occupancy climbs

steadily after every full GC instead of returning to baseline, that's the signature of a genuine leak versus just

an undersized heap.

Symptom -> Root Cause -> Diagnosis -> Fix

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
App crashes after running fine for days/weeks with heap space OOMSlow memory leak - a static/long-lived collection grows unboundedHeap dump + MAT Leak Suspects; old-gen occupancy trending upward across multiple full GCsBound the collection (LRU/TTL cache), remove entries on cleanup, or use WeakReference where appropriate
OOM appears immediately under a specific request pattern (e.g. large file uploads)A single request loads an entire large payload into memory at onceCorrelate OOM timestamp with access logs / APM traces for that endpointStream the payload (chunked reads, InputStream processing) instead of buffering it fully
Metaspace OOM after repeated hot-redeploys in an app serverClassLoader leak - old web app's classes never get garbage collected because something still references them (ThreadLocal, static field, JDBC driver registration)Heap/class histogram shows duplicate classes across multiple classloader instancesDeregister JDBC drivers, clear ThreadLocals in a shutdown hook, avoid static references to app classes from container-level singletons
GC overhead limit exceeded with CPU pegged at 100% before the crashHeap too small for live-object working set - GC runs back-to-back with tiny gainsGC logs show consecutive full GCs reclaiming under 2% of heap each timeIncrease -Xmx to match actual working set, or reduce allocation rate / retained object count
OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native threadNot heap - too many OS threads created (thread pool misconfiguration)jstack thread count vs OS ulimit -u; thread count climbing unboundedUse bounded thread pools, fix thread leak, raise ulimit only as a last resort

War Story: The Session Cache That Ate Production

A production order-processing service ran fine in staging but died with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space

roughly every 9 days in production, always around peak traffic. The on-call team's first instinct was

"just bump -Xmx" - which delayed the crash but didn't fix it.

A heap dump taken via -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError on the next crash showed a single

static ConcurrentHashMap<String, UserSession> retaining 92% of the heap, with over 4 million

entries - one for every user who had ever logged in since the last restart. The code added a session on login but

only removed it on an explicit "logout" click; most mobile users simply closed the app, so their session objects

(each holding a cached shopping cart and order history) never got removed.

Fix: replaced the unbounded map with a Caffeine cache configured with

expireAfterAccess(30, TimeUnit.MINUTES) and a hard max size, so idle sessions are evicted automatically

regardless of whether logout was ever called.

Prevention Checklist

  • Always run production JVMs with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError so you capture evidence instead of

just a restart.

  • Set -Xmx deliberately based on measured working-set size plus headroom, not by copy-pasting a

default.

  • Prefer bounded caches (Caffeine, Guava CacheBuilder with maximumSize/expireAfter) over raw

HashMap/ArrayList for anything that grows with user activity.

  • Monitor old-gen occupancy after full GC over time (not just heap %) - a rising floor across GCs is the earliest

reliable leak signal, well before an actual OOM.

  • Use -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize explicitly in containerized environments so a classloader leak fails fast

and visibly instead of silently eating host memory.

Senior Notes

  • ExitOnOutOfMemoryError: -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError kills a half-broken JVM so the orchestrator restarts a clean one.
  • Direct buffer memory is off-heap and limited by -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize; Netty and NIO code hit it.
  • Container sizing: heap plus Metaspace plus thread stacks plus direct memory must fit the container limit, otherwise the kernel OOM killer acts first.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful flags and tools:

  • -Xms / -Xmx: initial and maximum heap; equal values avoid resize pauses.
  • -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError: writes an hprof file when heap OOM occurs.
  • -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError: exits at the first OOM; -XX:+CrashOnOutOfMemoryError also writes a crash file.
  • -XX:OnOutOfMemoryError="cmd": runs a command, such as sending an alert.
  • -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary: then jcmd PID VM.native_memory summary.
  • -XX:MaxRAMPercentage: sizes the heap from the container limit.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The JVM throws OOM from several areas, and each has its own message.

  • Java heap space: an allocation failed after GC could not free enough.
  • GC overhead limit exceeded: the Parallel collector gives up when GC time is about 98 percent and recovery is under 2 percent.
  • Metaspace: class metadata lives in native memory, limited by -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
  • Direct buffer memory: ByteBuffer.allocateDirect exceeds -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize.
  • Unable to create native thread: the OS refused a thread or its stack.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Only raising -Xmx: a leak just fails later; find the retaining path.
  • Catching OutOfMemoryError and continuing: state may be corrupt; log and exit.
  • No dump path space: the volume must hold a file as large as the heap.
  • Ignoring off-heap: heap looks fine while the container is killed.
  • Loading whole files or result sets: stream or page the data.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning to prevent OOM:

  • Measure live set: heap after Full GC times 2 to 3 is a sensible heap size.
  • Cap pools and queues: unbounded structures are the usual cause.
  • Page database reads: use setFetchSize and keyset paging.
  • Pre-size collections to avoid copy spikes during growth.
  • Leave headroom: container limit above heap by 25 to 40 percent for off-heap use.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Incident: a service restarts every few hours in Kubernetes with exit code 137.

  • Symptoms: pod status OOMKilled, latency spikes before each restart, no Java exception in logs.
  • Diagnosis: kubectl describe pod, then jcmd PID VM.native_memory summary and GC logs.
  • Root cause: heap was 90 percent of the container limit; Netty direct buffers and thread stacks pushed the process past it, so the kernel killed it before Java could throw OOM.
  • Fix: heap set with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65, -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m, alerts on container working set, and -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError for real heap OOM.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Production JVM flags.
codeExamples:
java -Xms512m -Xmx512m \
  -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=192m \
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps \
  -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -jar app.jar

// OUTPUT:
// no output until a failure; then the dump is written and the JVM exits with code 3

interviewQA: What is OutOfMemoryError and is it an Exception?
It is a java.lang.Error thrown when the JVM cannot allocate memory in a given region even after GC; it is an Error, not an Exception, and generally shouldn't be caught to "recover"
What's the difference between "Java heap space" and "Metaspace" OOM?
Heap space OOM means live objects fill the object heap; Metaspace OOM means class metadata (loaded classes) fills the metaspace region - a classloader leak, not an object leak
What does "GC overhead limit exceeded" mean?
The JVM detected that GC is consuming over ~98% of CPU time while reclaiming under ~2% of the heap repeatedly, so it fails fast instead of hanging indefinitely
How do you capture a heap dump automatically on OOM?
Start the JVM with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=<dir> so a .hprof file is written the moment the error occurs
How do you find what's leaking memory from a heap dump?
Open it in Eclipse MAT or VisualVM, run the Leak Suspects report, and follow retained size (not shallow size) to the dominator object graph
Is increasing -Xmx always the right fix for OutOfMemoryError?
No - it can mask a real leak and just delay the crash; you should confirm via heap dump/GC logs whether it's a genuine capacity issue or a leak before resizing
What commonly causes Metaspace leaks in application servers?

ClassLoader leaks from repeated hot-redeploys - references left in ThreadLocals, static fields, JDBC driver registries, or shutdown hooks prevent the old classloader (and its classes) from being garbage collected
What is "OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread" and how is it different from heap OOM?

It happens when the OS refuses to allocate a new native thread stack for the process (thread count or memory limit reached) - it's unrelated to Java heap occupancy and is usually caused by unbounded thread creation

topics.name: StackOverflowError

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is StackOverflowError?

Every time a method is called, the JVM pushes a new stack frame onto that thread's call stack, to

remember local variables, parameters, and where to return to. Each thread's stack has a fixed maximum size.

java.lang.StackOverflowError is thrown when a thread's call stack grows beyond that limit - almost

always because of a method calling itself (directly or indirectly) too many times without stopping, i.e.

uncontrolled recursion.

Like OutOfMemoryError, it is a subclass of java.lang.Error, not Exception.

1. Infinite Recursion

The simplest way to trigger it: a method that calls itself with no base case (no stopping condition) at all.

2. A Base Case That's Wrong (Bug, Not Design)

More often in real code, the recursion does have a base case - but a bug means it's never actually

reached for certain inputs.

3. Mutual (Indirect) Recursion

StackOverflowError doesn't require a method to call itself - two or more methods calling each other in a

cycle produce the exact same problem.

Fixing It: Convert Recursion to Iteration

The most reliable fix for deep/unbounded recursion is to rewrite it as a loop, which uses a small, constant amount

of stack space no matter how many "steps" are performed.

Fresher Notes

  • StackOverflowError happens when the call stack of a thread is full, most often because of recursion without a stop condition.
  • Each call adds a stack frame that holds local variables and the return address, and frames are freed on return.
  • Fix the base case first; the stack trace repeats the same few lines, which shows the loop.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Stack size is set per thread with -Xss, for example -Xss1m; the default is usually 512 KB to 1 MB.
  • Hidden recursion hides in toString(), equals(), hashCode() and JPA bidirectional links that call each other.
  • Deep but valid recursion (big trees, long linked lists) is better rewritten with an explicit Deque loop.

8. Advanced Concepts

Why Java Has No Guaranteed Tail-Call Optimization

In languages like Scala or Scheme, "tail-recursive" calls (where the recursive call is the very last operation,

with nothing left to do after it returns) can be compiled into a loop by the compiler, reusing the same stack

frame.

The JVM specification does not guarantee tail-call optimization, and the HotSpot JVM does not

perform it (as of current mainstream JDKs). This means even a "clean" tail-recursive Java method still consumes one

stack frame per call - so relying on deep recursion in Java is inherently risky, unlike in TCO languages.

Manually Simulating Tail-Call Style with an Explicit Stack

When a recursive algorithm is naturally elegant but might recurse too deep (e.g. traversing a very deep tree or

long linked list), a common production technique is to replace the call stack with your own heap-allocated

Deque, which has no fixed size limit (bounded only by heap memory, which can grow far larger than a

thread stack).

Tuning Thread Stack Size with -Xss

The -Xss flag sets the stack size per thread (default is typically 512KB-1MB depending on OS

and JDK version). Increasing it lets recursion go deeper before overflowing, but it is a trade-off, not a real

fix:

java -Xss4m RecursiveApp   # 4MB stack instead of default ~512KB-1MB

Trade-off:
  Larger -Xss  -> deeper recursion survives, BUT
                  each thread now reserves more memory,
                  so max thread count for a given RAM budget goes DOWN.

  1000 threads x 512KB = ~512MB reserved for stacks
  1000 threads x 4MB   = ~4GB reserved for stacks (may itself cause native OOM)

In server applications running hundreds of threads, bumping -Xss globally to fix one bad

recursive path can quietly push the JVM toward

OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread instead - so treat it as a stopgap, and fix the

recursion (or convert it to iteration) as the real solution.

Reading a StackOverflowError Stack Trace

The key diagnostic signal is repetition: the same one or two method frames repeating hundreds or

thousands of times is the fingerprint of runaway recursion, as opposed to a normal deep-but-varied call chain.

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.StackOverflowError
    at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.applyRule(DiscountEngine.java:42)
    at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.applyRule(DiscountEngine.java:42)
    at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.applyRule(DiscountEngine.java:42)
    at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.applyRule(DiscountEngine.java:42)
    ... (repeats thousands of times) ...
    at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.applyRule(DiscountEngine.java:42)
    at com.shop.pricing.OrderService.calculateTotal(OrderService.java:88)
    at com.shop.web.CheckoutController.checkout(CheckoutController.java:31)

Line 42 in DiscountEngine.applyRule is where to look first - that's the recursive call site, and the

bug is almost always in its base/stopping condition.

Symptom -> Root Cause -> Diagnosis -> Fix

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
StackOverflowError on a specific "rule engine" / tree-walking code path only for certain inputsRecursive base case never reached for those inputs (e.g. cyclic data structure, off-by-one termination bug)Trace repeating frame in the stack trace to find the exact recursive method and inspect its termination conditionFix the base case / add a cycle-detection guard (visited set) before recursing further
StackOverflowError only in production, never locallyProduction data is deeper/larger than test fixtures (e.g. a genuinely deep category tree, deeply nested JSON)Reproduce with production-sized/shaped input in a test; measure actual recursion depth reachedConvert to an iterative algorithm with an explicit Deque, which scales with heap, not stack
Two mutually-recursive methods (e.g. Parser/Evaluator) overflow on complex expressionsIndirect/mutual recursion with no depth limit, common in recursive-descent parsersLook for alternating method names in the repeating stack framesAdd an explicit maximum nesting-depth check, or rewrite using an explicit stack-based parser
Increasing -Xss "fixes" it temporarily, then OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread appears under loadLarger per-thread stacks multiplied across many concurrent threads exhaust native/process memoryCompare thread count x -Xss against available process memory; check ulimit -uRevert -Xss increase; fix the underlying unbounded recursion instead of masking it

War Story: The Self-Referencing Category Tree

An e-commerce catalog service exposed a "breadcrumb" feature that recursively walked up a product category's

parent chain to build a path like Electronics > Laptops > Gaming Laptops. It had worked in

production for two years.

A data-migration script introduced a bug that, under a rare merge-conflict scenario, set a category's

parentId to point to one of its own descendants - creating a cycle. The very next time a customer

viewed a product in that category, the breadcrumb-building recursion walked up the "parent" chain forever

(A -> B -> C -> A -> B -> C ...) until StackOverflowError crashed that request thread.

Because the cycle only affected one category, it looked like a random, hard-to-reproduce crash for days.

Fix: the recursive breadcrumb builder was rewritten iteratively with an explicit

Set<Long> visitedIds, so that if a cycle is ever encountered again, the code detects it and

throws a clear, catchable IllegalStateException("Cyclic category detected") instead of crashing the

thread with StackOverflowError.

Senior Notes

  • No tail call optimization exists in Java, so tail-recursive code still uses one frame per call.
  • Raising -Xss costs memory for every thread, so raise it only for a known deep workload or use a dedicated thread with a custom stack size.
  • Serialization and JSON libraries recurse on object graphs; a cycle gives a StackOverflowError, so break cycles with @JsonIgnore or @JsonManagedReference.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Options and variants:

  • -Xss: -Xss512k, -Xss2m; applies to new Java threads.
  • Thread constructor: the fourth argument sets a stack size hint for one thread.
  • -XX:ThreadStackSize: same effect in KB.
  • Trace length: the trace is capped by -XX:MaxJavaStackTraceDepth (default 1024).
  • Explicit stack: ArrayDeque for DFS, tree walks, flood fill.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Every thread has its own stack, created with a fixed size.

  • Frame: each call pushes a frame with locals, operand stack and a return address.
  • Limit: when the next frame does not fit, the JVM throws StackOverflowError at that call.
  • Frame size: methods with many locals use bigger frames, so the maximum depth varies.
  • JIT: compiled code can use smaller frames or inline calls, so depth differs between runs.
  • Heap: objects are not on the stack, only references.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Missing base case: add and unit test the stop condition.
  • Base case never reached: for example the argument moves away from zero.
  • Cyclic data: track visited nodes in a Set.
  • Mutual toString/equals/hashCode: exclude the back reference.
  • Catching the Error: hides the bug; fix the cause.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning notes:

  • Memory cost: stack memory is reserved per thread, so 500 threads at 2 MB reserve about 1 GB virtual.
  • Shrink for many threads: lower -Xss only if you have measured the depth you need.
  • Memoize: dynamic programming turns deep recursion into loops.
  • Avoid deep recursion in request threads because the web container stack is small.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Incident: a JSON endpoint returns HTTP 500 for some customers only.

  • Symptoms: StackOverflowError with a repeating trace of BeanSerializer frames.
  • Diagnosis: read the repeating lines of the trace; they list Order.getCustomer then Customer.getOrders.
  • Root cause: a bidirectional JPA relation serialized directly; customers with orders loop forever.
  • Fix: return a DTO, or mark the back reference with @JsonIgnore or use @JsonManagedReference and @JsonBackReference; add a test with a linked pair.

10. Examples

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

interviewQA: What causes StackOverflowError?
A thread's call stack exceeds its maximum size, almost always due to recursion (direct, indirect, or via a cyclic data structure) without a properly reached base case
Is StackOverflowError an Exception or an Error?
It is a java.lang.Error (subclass of Throwable, sibling of Exception) - it signals a serious JVM-level condition, not an ordinary recoverable exception
Does Java optimize tail-recursive calls into loops?
No - the JVM spec does not require tail-call optimization and mainstream HotSpot JVMs do not perform it, so every recursive call, even tail-recursive ones, consumes a stack frame
How does -Xss relate to StackOverflowError?
-Xss sets the per-thread stack size; increasing it lets recursion go deeper before overflowing, but increases memory reserved per thread, reducing how many threads a given memory budget supports
How would you fix a recursive method that risks StackOverflowError on deep input?
Rewrite it iteratively using an explicit Deque/stack on the heap, since heap-based structures aren't bound by the fixed thread stack size
How do you recognize StackOverflowError from a stack trace at a glance?
The same one or two method frames repeat an unusually large number of times consecutively, unlike a normal varied deep call chain
Can mutual recursion between two methods cause StackOverflowError?
Yes - Method A calling Method B calling Method A in a cycle with no terminating condition overflows the stack exactly like direct self-recursion
Why is simply increasing -Xss risky as a fix in a high-concurrency server app?
Multiplying a larger stack size across hundreds/thousands of threads can exhaust native process memory, potentially trading StackOverflowError for OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread

topics.name: High CPU

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What Does "High CPU" Mean for a Java App?

A Java process is said to have a "high CPU" problem when it consumes an unusually large, sustained share of the

machine's CPU - often 100% of one or more cores - even though the actual useful work being done doesn't justify

it.

This isn't a single exception you can catch. It's a symptom you observe from outside the JVM (via

the OS) and then have to trace back inside the JVM to find which thread(s) and which line(s) of code are

responsible.

Cause 1: A Busy (Spinning) Loop

The simplest way to cause high CPU is a loop that keeps running without ever pausing or blocking - e.g. waiting

for a condition by spinning instead of using proper thread coordination.

Cause 2: Catastrophic Regex Backtracking

Certain regular expressions can take exponential time on specific "evil" inputs due to backtracking - a single

matches() call can peg a CPU core for minutes on a moderately long string.

Cause 3: GC Thrashing

When the JVM is allocating objects faster than it can safely reclaim memory, the Garbage Collector runs almost

continuously, consuming large amounts of CPU just to keep the app barely alive (see the "High GC" and

"OutOfMemoryError" topics for the full picture).

How to Start Investigating High CPU

On any OS, the basic workflow is the same two-step process:

  • Find which OS thread is hot - use top -H -p <pid> (Linux) or Task Manager's

per-thread view to find the native thread ID (TID/LWP) consuming the most CPU.

  • Map that OS thread to a Java thread - take a thread dump with jstack <pid> and

match the hex-converted TID to the nid=0x... field in the dump to see exactly which Java method that

thread is stuck executing.

Fresher Notes

  • High CPU means the process uses most cores; first decide whether the work is useful (real load) or wasted (spin loop, GC, regex).
  • top shows the busy process, and top -H -p PID shows the busy thread inside it.
  • Thread dump with jstack PID shows what the busy threads are executing.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Hex conversion: the thread id in top is decimal, but jstack shows nid=0x..., so convert with printf "%x" TID.
  • Common causes: infinite loops, busy waiting without sleep, catastrophic regex backtracking, and a HashMap corrupted by threads.
  • GC threads can be the busy ones; check with jstat -gcutil before blaming application code.

8. Advanced Concepts

The top -H + jstack Correlation Technique

This is the single most important production skill for high-CPU Java diagnosis - correlating an OS-level thread ID

with a JVM-level stack trace.

  1. Identify the process: top -p <pid> confirms the Java process itself is the CPU hog.
  2. Break it down by thread: top -H -p <pid> shows individual native threads (LWPs) and their

individual CPU%. Note the TID of the hottest thread(s), e.g. 18452.

  1. Convert to hex: printf "%x\n" 18452 gives 4814.
  2. Take a thread dump: jstack <pid> > dump.txt (or kill -3 <pid> to print it

to stdout/log).

  1. Search the dump for nid=0x4814 - that block of the dump is exactly what that hot native thread was

executing in Java at that moment.

"pool-3-thread-7" #47 prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=48213.45ms elapsed=612.09s tid=0x00007f2c productive
   nid=0x4814 runnable [0x00007f2b1a1fe000]
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
        at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.matchPromoCode(DiscountEngine.java:118)
        at com.shop.pricing.DiscountEngine.applyRule(DiscountEngine.java:64)
        at com.shop.pricing.OrderService.calculateTotal(OrderService.java:88)

Taking 2-3 thread dumps a few seconds apart and seeing the same line repeatedly is strong evidence

of a genuine hot loop (as opposed to normal, varying activity) at that exact line.

Async-Profiler / JFR for Flame Graphs

For CPU problems that are spread across many methods rather than one obvious hot loop, sampling profilers give a

much clearer picture than manual thread-dump correlation:

  • Java Flight Recorder (JFR) - built into the JDK, low overhead, can even be run continuously in

production: java -XX:+FlightRecorder -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=recording.jfr MyApp,

then open the recording in JDK Mission Control to see a flame graph of where CPU time was actually spent.

  • async-profiler - an external agent that samples native + Java stacks with very low overhead,

commonly attached on demand: ./profiler.sh -d 30 -e cpu -f flamegraph.html <pid>.

Flame graphs let you see, at a glance, which method call trees consume the widest share of total CPU samples -

far faster than manually diffing multiple jstack dumps.

Symptom -> Root Cause -> Diagnosis -> Fix

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
One core pegged at 100% constantly, even at low trafficBusy-wait / spin loop instead of proper blocking wait (e.g. polling a flag instead of using wait/notify or a BlockingQueue)top -H shows one thread consistently hot; jstack repeatedly shows same RUNNABLE frame in a tight loopReplace polling with proper synchronization primitives (wait/notify, CountDownLatch, BlockingQueue, CompletableFuture)
CPU spikes to 100% on specific user input (e.g. certain search strings)Catastrophic regex backtracking (evil regex pattern with nested quantifiers)Correlate the hot thread's stack trace with java.util.regex.Pattern$Matcher frames; test the exact input against the regex in isolationRewrite the regex to avoid nested quantifiers/ambiguous alternation, or use a regex engine/library with backtracking limits (e.g. RE2J)
High CPU across many GC threads, correlates with high allocation rateGC thrashing due to excessive allocation rate or undersized heapGC logs show frequent full GCs with low reclaim %; correlate CPU spikes with GC log timestampsReduce allocation rate (avoid unnecessary object creation, reuse buffers), tune heap size/GC algorithm
High CPU with no single obviously hot thread - spread across many threadsInefficient algorithm (e.g. O(n^2) logic) run at scale, or excessive serialization/deserializationJFR/async-profiler flame graph shows a wide, flat top spread across a specific method call treeOptimize the hot algorithm (better data structure, caching, batching), or parallelize/offload it appropriately
CPU high only right after deployment, settles after a few minutesJIT warm-up - code is running in interpreted/C1 mode before hitting C2 optimization thresholdCompare CPU trend against JIT compilation logs (-XX:+PrintCompilation) and request latency trend post-deployUsually expected/benign - consider a warm-up phase before routing production traffic (readiness gating)

War Story: The Promo Code Regex That Cost 40% of the Fleet

A retail checkout service began throwing timeouts across roughly 40% of instances during a flash sale, while the

rest of the fleet looked healthy. CPU graphs showed the affected instances pinned at 100% on exactly one core each,

while overall request rate hadn't grown dramatically.

Running top -H plus jstack on an affected instance repeatedly showed the same hot thread

stuck inside DiscountEngine.matchPromoCode, which validated promo codes using a hand-written regex

containing a nested quantifier: ^(PROMO-[A-Z0-9]+)+$. A marketing campaign had, that day, started

generating promo codes with an unusual trailing suffix that didn't cleanly match - triggering catastrophic

backtracking on every validation attempt for those specific codes, and each affected instance happened to be one

that had recently received a request containing one of the problem codes.

Fix: the regex was replaced with a simple, linear-time manual prefix/character-class check

(no nested quantifiers), and a CPU-time watchdog was added around promo validation as a safety net for future

regex-related regressions.

Prevention Checklist

  • Avoid regex patterns with nested or overlapping quantifiers on untrusted/variable-length input; test regexes

against long adversarial strings before shipping.

  • Never busy-wait; always use blocking coordination primitives (wait/notify,

BlockingQueue, CompletableFuture, CountDownLatch).

  • Bake top -H + jstack correlation (or an equivalent APM CPU profiler) into your standard

incident runbook so responders don't waste time guessing.

  • Run continuous low-overhead JFR recording in production so a CPU spike can be analyzed retroactively without

needing to reproduce it live.

  • Load-test with realistic, occasionally adversarial input data (not just "happy path" fixtures) to catch

algorithmic complexity issues before production.

Senior Notes

  • Sampling profiler: async-profiler or JFR gives hot methods with low overhead, which is safe in production.
  • Take 3 dumps a few seconds apart; a thread in the same frame each time is the suspect.
  • JIT compiler threads burn CPU during warm-up, so a spike right after start is often normal.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Diagnosis toolbox:

  • top -H -p PID: per-thread CPU.
  • jstack PID / jcmd PID Thread.print: thread dump with nid.
  • jcmd PID JFR.start duration=60s filename=a.jfr: Flight Recorder.
  • async-profiler: asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f flame.html PID.
  • jstat -gcutil: rules GC in or out.
  • ThreadMXBean: in-process per-thread CPU time.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

CPU time in a JVM is spent in a few places.

  • Application threads: your code and libraries.
  • GC threads: marking and copying; busy when memory is tight.
  • JIT compiler threads: compile hot methods; heavy at startup.
  • Safepoint and VM thread: pauses for GC and deopt.
  • Runnable but blocked in native I/O: shows RUNNABLE but uses little CPU, so confirm with top.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Guessing: changing code before taking a dump.
  • One dump only: a single sample can be unlucky; take three.
  • Spin on a flag: use a latch, a condition or a blocking queue.
  • Regex on user input: avoid nested quantifiers and bound input length.
  • Unsynchronized HashMap: concurrent resize can create a loop in old JDKs; use ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Logging in a hot loop: string formatting costs CPU even when the level is off, unless you use parameters.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning approach:

  • Profile first: optimize the top frame in the flame graph only.
  • Algorithm: a better data structure beats micro tuning.
  • Cache pure results with a bounded cache.
  • Batch work to reduce per-call overhead.
  • Size pools to cores for CPU-bound work: about availableProcessors() threads.
  • Warm-up: expect higher CPU for the first minutes while the JIT compiles.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Incident: CPU of one pod sits at 800 percent after a deployment, other pods are fine.

  • Symptoms: p99 latency up, load average high, no errors in the log.
  • Diagnosis: top -H shows 6 threads near 100 percent; converted ids match http-nio-exec threads; three dumps show the same Pattern.matcher frames.
  • Root cause: a new validation regex with nested quantifiers hit a long malformed input from one client.
  • Fix: rewrite the regex without nesting, limit input length to 256, use a timeout wrapper, and add a test with a hostile string.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

Safer polling with a deadline.

Practice Exercise 1

Busy spin loop.

Practice Exercise 2

Find the thread with top and jstack.

interviewQA: How do you diagnose which Java thread is causing high CPU on a server?
Use "top -H -p <pid>" to find the hot native thread ID (TID), convert it to hex, then match it against the nid field in a jstack thread dump to see exactly what that thread was executing
What is a "busy-wait" loop and why is it bad?
A loop that repeatedly checks a condition without blocking/sleeping, consuming 100% CPU on that core; it should be replaced with proper blocking coordination like wait/notify or a BlockingQueue
What is catastrophic regex backtracking?
A regex with ambiguous nested/overlapping quantifiers can require exponential time to fail to match certain inputs, because the engine tries an exponential number of backtracking paths, pegging CPU
How can GC cause high CPU?
If allocation rate is too high or the heap is undersized, the GC runs very frequently or continuously trying to reclaim space, consuming large amounts of CPU with little useful application progress
What's the difference between jstack and a profiler like async-profiler/JFR for CPU issues?

jstack gives point-in-time snapshots useful for finding one obviously hot, repeating stack frame; a sampling profiler aggregates over time into a flame graph, better for CPU spread across many methods
Why might taking multiple jstack dumps a few seconds apart be more useful than just one?
Seeing the same stack frame repeat across multiple dumps is strong evidence of a genuine hot loop, distinguishing it from normal varying thread activity captured in a single snapshot
Can high CPU happen right after a deployment even with no bug?
Yes - JIT warm-up means new code runs interpreted/less-optimized initially, causing temporarily elevated CPU until hot methods are compiled by C2; this is usually benign and settles quickly

topics.name: High GC

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is "High GC"?

Garbage Collection (GC) is the JVM automatically reclaiming memory used by objects that are no longer reachable.

Some GC activity is normal and healthy - it's how Java manages memory without manual free() calls.

"High GC" describes a situation where GC runs too often or takes too long

relative to the actual work the application is doing - so much of the app's time is spent pausing for GC instead

of serving requests. This shows up to users as slow response times, timeouts, or stutter, even though there's no

crash (yet).

Simulating High GC Frequency

Allocating lots of short-lived objects very rapidly forces the JVM's young generation to fill up and collect over

and over again, which you can literally watch happen with GC logging enabled.

Simulating Long, Painful GC Pauses

Filling the heap close to its limit with objects that survive (are retained) forces expensive, longer full GCs

instead of quick young-gen collections.

Simple Fixes at the Beginner Level

  • Reduce unnecessary allocation - avoid creating throwaway objects inside hot loops (e.g. building

Strings with + in a loop instead of StringBuilder).

  • Reuse objects/buffers where safe, instead of allocating a new one every call.
  • Right-size the heap - a heap that's too small forces the JVM to collect constantly just to make

room for normal traffic.

Fresher Notes

  • High GC means the JVM spends a large share of time collecting garbage, so the application slows down or pauses.
  • GC logs are switched on with -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log in Java 9 and later.
  • Young versus old: short-lived objects die in the young generation cheaply; objects that survive move to the old generation.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Allocation rate: creating many temporary objects (strings in loops, boxing) triggers frequent young collections.
  • Full GC that frees little means the live set is too big for the heap; this is a leak or an undersized heap.
  • jstat: jstat -gcutil PID 1000 prints occupancy and counts every second.

8. Advanced Concepts

Reading GC Logs Like an Engineer

Modern JVMs (9+) use unified logging (-Xlog:gc*). A single Young GC log line carries several important

numbers worth learning to read at a glance:

[12.451s][info][gc] GC(142) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 812M->210M(1024M) 45.223ms
   |          |     |                                         |     |      |
   timestamp  GC#   pause type / cause                     before after total-heap  duration

Key ratios to track over time, not just single lines:
  - Frequency:  how many GC(#) events per minute -> allocation rate proxy
  - Reclaim %:  (before - after) / before        -> how effective each GC is
  - Pause time: duration in ms                    -> user-facing latency impact
  - Post-GC floor: "after" value trending UP over successive GCs -> leak signal

A healthy young-gen GC reclaims 80-95% of the young generation in a few milliseconds. When reclaim percentage drops

and pause duration climbs together, that's the classic signature of a heap under real memory pressure, not just

routine collection.

Throughput vs Latency: Choosing (and Tuning) a Collector

"High GC" often isn't really about a bug - it's about a collector mismatched to the workload's goals.

  • G1 GC (default since JDK 9) - balances throughput and pause time; tunable target pause via

-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200. Good general-purpose default.

  • Parallel GC - maximizes throughput, accepts longer/less predictable pauses; suited for batch

jobs where total runtime matters more than individual pause length.

  • ZGC / Shenandoah - designed for very low pause times (sub-millisecond to a few ms) even on

huge heaps (100s of GB), at some throughput/CPU cost; ideal for latency-sensitive services with big heaps.

A common production mistake is running a latency-sensitive API on Parallel GC's default settings (tuned for

throughput) and being surprised by occasional multi-second pauses under load - the fix is often just switching

collector or its goals, not rewriting application code.

Symptom -> Root Cause -> Diagnosis -> Fix

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
Frequent short Young GC pauses (many per second) under normal loadHigh allocation rate - too many short-lived objects created per requestGC logs show high GC(#) frequency; profiler (JFR Allocation Profiling) shows top allocating call sitesReduce allocations in hot paths (avoid boxing, reuse buffers, use StringBuilder, avoid unnecessary intermediate collections)
Occasional very long Full GC pauses (seconds) causing request timeoutsOld generation filling up, forcing expensive Full/Mixed GC compactionGC logs show "Pause Full" events with large before->after deltas and long duration; correlate with request timeout spikesInvestigate for a leak first (see Memory Leak topic); if genuinely legitimate live-set, increase heap or switch to a low-pause collector (G1/ZGC) with tuned targets
Reclaim percentage steadily dropping across successive GCs over hoursSlow memory leak - live set growing, less to reclaim each cyclePlot post-GC heap occupancy over time; a rising floor (not returning to baseline) confirms a leak, not just loadHeap dump + MAT to find and fix the leak (see Memory Leak topic)
High GC CPU usage with small heap even at low trafficHeap sized too small for the working set, forcing constant collection just to fit normal live dataCompare -Xmx to observed steady-state old-gen occupancy after GCIncrease -Xmx to comfortably exceed the real working set with headroom
Latency-sensitive service has rare multi-second pause spikes despite low average GC timeWrong collector for the goal - e.g. Parallel/throughput-tuned GC used for a latency-critical APICheck configured collector (-XX flags) and its pause-time targets against SLA requirementsSwitch to G1 with -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, or ZGC/Shenandoah for very tight pause SLAs on large heaps

War Story: The Nightly Batch Job That Broke the Live API

An order-analytics service shared its JVM heap between two workloads: a customer-facing REST API and a nightly

batch aggregation job. After a new "real-time trending" feature was added to the batch job, on-call started

getting paged for API p99 latency spiking to 4-6 seconds every night at 2 AM - always exactly when the batch job

ran.

GC logs during the incident window showed a burst of large "Pause Full" events instead of the usual quick Young

GCs - the batch job's new trending logic built several large intermediate HashMaps that lived just

long enough to get promoted into old generation, filling it and triggering expensive full compactions, which

stopped-the-world for every thread including the ones serving live API traffic.

Fix: the batch workload was moved to a separate JVM process entirely (different heap, different

GC tuning profile suited to throughput), fully isolating its allocation behavior from the latency-sensitive API

process - a textbook case of "one JVM, two very different workloads" being the real root cause, not a code bug.

Prevention Checklist

  • Enable GC logging permanently in production (-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=10,filesize=50m)
  • the overhead is negligible and the historical data is invaluable during incidents.
  • Track GC pause time and frequency as first-class dashboard metrics (via JMX/Micrometer), not just heap

percentage.

  • Separate workloads with very different allocation profiles (batch vs. real-time) into different JVM

processes/pods rather than sharing one heap.

  • Choose the collector based on stated latency vs throughput goals, and revisit that choice as heap size or SLA

requirements change.

  • Load-test with production-realistic allocation patterns, not just request volume, since GC pressure depends on

what each request allocates, not just how many requests arrive.

Senior Notes

  • Collector choice: G1 balances throughput and pauses; ZGC and Shenandoah give very short pauses on large heaps.
  • Pause target: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 is a goal for G1, not a guarantee.
  • Tune last: reduce allocation and fix leaks first, then size the heap, and only then change collector flags.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Flags and views:

  • -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=20m: rotating GC logs.
  • -XX:+UseG1GC / -XX:+UseZGC / -XX:+UseParallelGC: choose the collector.
  • -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis: G1 pause goal.
  • -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent: when G1 starts concurrent marking.
  • -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch: touches heap pages at start for stable latency.
  • Tools: GCeasy, GCViewer, JFR, jcmd PID GC.heap_info.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

How the generational collectors work in outline.

  • Eden: new objects are allocated here by fast pointer bumping.
  • Young GC: live objects are copied to survivor spaces; dead ones cost nothing.
  • Promotion: objects that survive several collections move to the old generation.
  • Old collection: G1 does concurrent marking and mixed collections; a Full GC is the fallback.
  • Safepoint: application threads stop while the collector works in a pause.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • System.gc() calls: forces a Full GC; remove or add -XX:+DisableExplicitGC.
  • Heap too small: frequent collections; raise -Xmx after measuring the live set.
  • Heap too large with default pauses: long Full GCs; consider ZGC.
  • Large temporary arrays: humongous allocations in G1; stream data.
  • Copying tuning flags from blogs: test each flag against your own GC log.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning order:

  • 1. Cut allocation: avoid boxing, reuse buffers, avoid needless copies.
  • 2. Fix leaks: a rising floor cannot be tuned away.
  • 3. Size the heap: about 2 to 3 times the live set.
  • 4. Pick a collector for the goal: throughput or latency.
  • 5. Compare pause p99 and GC time percentage before and after.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Incident: an API has 5 second pauses every few minutes.

  • Symptoms: timeouts in bursts, CPU spikes, GC pause metric high.
  • Diagnosis: GC log shows Pause Full (Allocation Failure) every 3 minutes; the heap after Full GC is 90 percent of 2 GB.
  • Root cause: a report job loaded a million rows into a list; the live set filled the heap.
  • Fix: stream rows with a fetch size, move the job off the API pod, set heap to 4 GB with a heap-usage alert, and watch the floor after Full GC.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

Choose a collector.

Practice Exercise 1
