Practice Exercise 2

Watch GC with jstat.

interviewQA: What does "high GC" mean and what user-facing symptom does it usually cause?
GC running too frequently or taking too long relative to actual work, causing elevated latency, timeouts, or throughput drops even without a crash
What's the difference between a Young GC pause and a Full GC pause?
Young GC only collects the young generation (fast, frequent, usually a few ms); Full GC collects the entire heap including old gen (slower, less frequent, can pause for hundreds of ms to seconds)
How do you tell from GC logs whether you have a leak versus just high load?
Track post-GC heap occupancy over time - if it returns to roughly the same baseline after each GC, it's load; if the floor keeps rising across successive GCs, it's a leak
What does -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis do?
Sets a soft target maximum pause time for G1 GC; G1 adapts region sizing and collection scheduling to try to meet it, though it's a goal, not a hard guarantee
When would you choose ZGC or Shenandoah over G1?
When the application needs very low, consistent pause times (sub-millisecond to a few ms) even with a very large heap, and can accept somewhat higher CPU/throughput overhead in exchange
Why might running a batch job and a latency-sensitive API in the same JVM cause GC problems?

Their very different allocation patterns (large batch intermediate structures vs small request-scoped objects) share one heap, so the batch job's allocations can trigger costly full GCs that pause the API's threads too
What's the first thing to check if GC frequency suddenly increases after a deploy?
What changed in allocation behavior - new code creating more objects per request, larger cached objects, or a new dependency with heavier allocation patterns

topics.name: Memory Leak (JVM)

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

Can Java Even Have Memory Leaks?

Java has automatic Garbage Collection (GC), so many beginners assume "memory leaks" are a C/C++ problem that

simply can't happen in Java. That's not true.

A memory leak in Java happens when objects are no longer needed by the application, but

something still holds a reference to them - so the GC considers them "reachable" and correctly

refuses to collect them. The objects are technically alive but functionally garbage; over time they accumulate and

can eventually cause OutOfMemoryError.

In short: Java prevents dangling pointer bugs, but it cannot prevent you from forgetting to let

go of a reference you no longer need.

Cause 1: An Unbounded Static Collection

A static field lives for the entire lifetime of the application. If you keep adding to a static

collection and never remove old entries, it grows forever.

Cause 2: Unclosed Resources

Streams, database connections, and file handles hold onto native/off-heap resources. Forgetting to close them

leaks memory (and OS handles) even though the Java object itself is small.

Cause 3: Listener / Callback Leaks

Registering a listener (observer/callback) on a long-lived object, but never unregistering it, keeps the listener

  • and everything it references - alive forever, even after the "real" owner is done with it.

The Beginner-Level Fix Pattern

  • Always pair "register" with "unregister", "open" with "close" (prefer try-with-resources).
  • Don't put request-scoped or session-scoped data into static fields.
  • If you need a cache, use one with a maximum size and/or expiry, never a plain growing

List/Map.

Fresher Notes

  • Memory leak in Java means objects that are no longer needed are still reachable, so the GC cannot free them.
  • Symptom: heap use after each GC grows slowly until an OutOfMemoryError appears after hours or days.
  • Static collections such as a static Map used as a cache are the most common leak source.

expert.content:
7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Listeners: registering a listener or callback and never removing it keeps the whole owner object alive.
  • ThreadLocal values in a thread pool stay for the life of the pooled thread unless you call remove() in a finally block.
  • Unclosed resources: streams, connections and executors that are not closed keep buffers and threads alive.

8. Advanced Concepts

The GC Roots Model: Why "Reachable" Isn't Always "Needed"

The JVM's GC works purely on reachability from a set of "GC Roots" (local variables on active

stacks, static fields, JNI references, etc.) - not on whether a human thinks an object is "still useful." An

object graph is kept alive as long as any chain of references connects it back to a GC root, no matter how

irrelevant that chain has become to the application's actual logic.

GC Roots (static fields, thread stacks, JNI refs)
        |
        v
  EventBus.listeners (static singleton, always reachable)
        |
        v
  Listener lambda  --references-->  Widget.this
                                          |
                                          v
                                    byte[1MB] bigData

Even though 'Widget' has gone completely out of scope in main(),
it is still reachable via EventBus -> listeners -> lambda -> Widget.this
so the GC correctly (but unhelpfully) keeps it alive forever.

This is the core mental model every "memory leak" investigation comes back to: find the unexpected path from a

GC root to the object that shouldn't still be alive.

ThreadLocal Leaks in Pooled-Thread Environments

ThreadLocal is a particularly sneaky leak source in server applications that use thread pools (which

is essentially all of them - servlet containers, executor services). Because pooled threads are reused

indefinitely, a ThreadLocal value set during one request and never explicitly removed stays attached

to that pooled thread and leaks into - or just wastes memory across - every future task that thread executes.

Diagnosing a Leak with a Heap Dump: Dominator Tree and Retained Size

The professional workflow for confirming and pinpointing a leak:

  1. Capture two heap dumps some time apart under steady load (e.g. via

jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=dump1.hprof <pid>), then compare object counts/sizes between them

in Eclipse MAT's "Compare Basket" - classes whose instance count grows roughly linearly with time/traffic and never

shrinks are your leak suspects.

  1. Run the Leak Suspects report - MAT clusters the dominator tree and highlights the single

biggest retained-size object graphs automatically.

  1. Inspect "Path to GC Roots" on the suspect object, excluding weak/soft references - this shows

you the exact reference chain (e.g. Thread -> ThreadLocalMap -> Entry -> YourObject) keeping

it alive, which tells you precisely which piece of code to fix.

  1. Distinguish shallow vs retained size - shallow size is just that one object; retained size is

everything that would be freed if that object became unreachable. Sort by retained size, not shallow size, to find

the real culprit.

Symptom -> Root Cause -> Diagnosis -> Fix

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
Old-gen heap occupancy climbs steadily over days, eventually OOMsUnbounded static/singleton collection accumulating entries foreverTwo heap dumps compared in MAT; instance count of one class grows roughly linearly with uptimeBound the collection with a max size and/or TTL (e.g. Caffeine cache) instead of a raw growing Map/List
Memory grows specifically correlated with thread-pool task count, not request countThreadLocal values set but never removed on pooled threadsHeap dump "Path to GC Roots" from suspect object shows Thread -> ThreadLocalMap -> Entry chainAlways call ThreadLocal.remove() in a finally block after use, especially in pooled-thread environments
File descriptor / socket count grows until "Too many open files" errors, alongside memory growthStreams/connections opened without try-with-resources, never explicitly closedOS-level: lsof -p <pid> shows growing open file/socket count over time correlated with memory growthUse try-with-resources (or explicit close() in finally) for every Closeable resource
Memory grows after a UI/component library is used heavily, even though components are discardedListener/observer registered on a long-lived event bus/singleton, never unregistered when the component is donePath to GC Roots shows EventBus/listener list -> lambda/inner class -> the "discarded" objectAlways pair register() with unregister(), or use weak listener references where the framework supports it
Memory grows specifically after cache lookups for keys that should have expiredCache implemented with plain HashMap and manual/buggy eviction logic instead of a proper cache libraryInspect cache entry count vs configured max/TTL; check eviction code path for bugsReplace hand-rolled caching with a battle-tested library (Caffeine, Guava Cache) with built-in size/time eviction

War Story: The Executor Service That Remembered Every User

A support-ticketing platform started seeing gradual memory growth over about two weeks per deployment, always

eventually requiring a restart. The team initially suspected the newest feature (file attachments) since memory

growth "felt" proportional to ticket volume.

A heap dump comparison in MAT told a different story: the fastest-growing class was

java.lang.ThreadLocal$ThreadLocalMap$Entry, retained by the application's fixed-size

ExecutorService thread pool. A "current user" ThreadLocal, set at the start of each

ticket-processing task to make the acting user's ID conveniently available deep in the call stack (avoiding having

to pass it as a parameter everywhere), was never removed at the end of the task. Because the executor's threads were

long-lived and reused for years, each thread's ThreadLocalMap silently accumulated stale entries -

technically the map does replace the value on the next set() for the same ThreadLocal instance, but the

real leak was several different ThreadLocal instances (one per feature team, added over years) each

accumulating separately, and some of those held large per-user context objects that outlived their usefulness.

Fix: every ThreadLocal.set() in the codebase was audited and paired with a matching

remove() in a finally block, and a code-review checklist item was added specifically for

ThreadLocal usage going forward.

Senior Notes

  • Diagnose with two heap dumps (jcmd PID GC.heap_dump file.hprof) taken some time apart and compare the growing classes in MAT.
  • Dominator tree and path to GC roots show which static field or thread holds the memory.
  • Bounded caches: use Caffeine or a size-limited LinkedHashMap, and use WeakHashMap only when you understand its key semantics.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools and commands:

  • jcmd PID GC.class_histogram: counts per class; run twice and compare.
  • jcmd PID GC.heap_dump: full dump for MAT or VisualVM.
  • JFR with OldObjectSample: finds leak candidates with low overhead.
  • jmap -histo:live PID: forces a GC then lists live objects.
  • Weak and soft references: WeakReference for listeners, SoftReference only for simple memory-sensitive caches.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

The GC frees what is unreachable from GC roots, so a leak is a reachable but useless object.

  • GC roots: thread stacks, static fields, JNI references and class loaders.
  • Retained size: memory that would be freed if an object was removed.
  • Class loader leaks: in app servers, a leftover reference keeps the whole old webapp and its Metaspace.
  • Saw-tooth shape: heap use falls after each GC but the minimum rises, which is the leak signature.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Cache without limit or TTL: use Caffeine with maximumSize and expireAfterWrite.
  • Mutable key without equals/hashCode: entries pile up.
  • Inner class holding the outer: a non-static inner class or lambda keeps this alive.
  • Not closing resources: use try-with-resources.
  • Not shutting down executors: idle pool threads keep class loaders alive.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and prevention:

  • Monitor the floor: alert on heap after GC trend, not on peak usage.
  • Load test long: leaks need hours; run a soak test.
  • Size limits everywhere: queues, caches, maps, sessions.
  • Prefer weak listeners or explicit unregister in lifecycle callbacks.
  • Dump on OOM: keep the flag always on.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Incident: heap grows 40 MB per hour and the service dies after 2 days.

  • Symptoms: old generation floor rises on every Full GC; OOM at the weekend.
  • Diagnosis: two class histograms 1 hour apart show com.shop.AuditEvent growing; MAT path to roots ends at a static List in AuditBuffer.
  • Root cause: the flusher thread died after a network error and the buffer was never drained.
  • Fix: use a bounded queue, restart the flusher on error, drop or spill oldest events when full, and alert on queue size.

10. Examples

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

Bounded cache with LinkedHashMap.

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Listener leak.

interviewQA: Can a garbage-collected language like Java still have memory leaks? How?

Yes - a leak occurs when an object is no longer logically needed but a reference chain from a GC root (static field, active thread stack, etc.) still exists, so the GC correctly but unhelpfully keeps it reachable and alive
What is a "GC root" and why does it matter for leak analysis?

A GC root is a starting point the collector considers inherently reachable (static fields, local variables on live stacks, JNI references); leak analysis works backward from a suspect object to find the unexpected reference path connecting it to a GC root
Why are ThreadLocal variables a common leak source in server applications?

Pooled threads are long-lived and reused across many tasks; if a ThreadLocal value is set but never removed, it stays attached to that thread's ThreadLocalMap indefinitely, silently retaining memory across unrelated future tasks
What is the difference between "shallow size" and "retained size" in a heap dump?

Shallow size is the memory of just that one object; retained size is the total memory that would become collectible if that object were made unreachable - retained size is what matters for finding the real leak culprit
How would you confirm a suspected memory leak before spending time fixing it?

Capture two heap dumps under steady load some time apart and compare class instance counts/retained sizes - a class growing roughly linearly with time/traffic that never shrinks is strong evidence of a real leak versus normal fluctuation
Why do unclosed resources (streams, connections) count as a memory/resource leak even if the Java object is small?

Closeable resources often wrap native/OS-level handles (file descriptors, sockets, native memory buffers); failing to close them leaks those underlying OS resources even though the Java wrapper object itself is tiny
What's the standard fix pattern to prevent listener/observer leaks?

Always pair every register()/addListener() call with a corresponding unregister()/removeListener() call, ideally tied to the listening object's own lifecycle end, or use weak references where the framework supports them
What tool would you use to find the exact reference chain keeping a leaked object alive?
Eclipse MAT's "Path to GC Roots" (excluding weak/soft references) on the suspect object in a heap dump, which shows the precise chain of references from a GC root down to that object

topics.name: Thread Exhaustion

beginner.content:
6. Basic Concepts

What is Thread Exhaustion?

Every Java thread you create consumes real operating-system resources: a native memory stack (default roughly

512KB-1MB), kernel scheduling structures, and a slot against the OS's per-process thread limit.

Thread exhaustion happens when an application creates far more threads than it should (usually

unintentionally) - either running out of memory to back them, or hitting the OS's hard limit on threads per

process. Unlike heap OOM, this isn't about your objects; it's about the JVM itself running out of room to create

new threads.

Cause 1: Creating a New Thread Per Task, Unbounded

The classic beginner mistake is calling new Thread(...).start() for every incoming task instead of

using a bounded thread pool. Under enough load, this creates thousands of threads simultaneously.

Cause 2: An Unbounded Thread Pool (CachedThreadPool)

Executors.newCachedThreadPool() creates a new thread for every submitted task if none are

idle, with no upper bound on pool size. If tasks arrive faster than they complete (e.g. they're all

blocked waiting on something slow), the pool will keep growing without limit - same problem as Cause 1, just

hidden behind an innocent-looking API.

The Beginner-Level Fix: Always Use a Bounded Pool

Use a thread pool with an explicit, sensible maximum size for the kind of work being done, instead of an unbounded

pool or raw new Thread() per task.

Fresher Notes

  • Thread exhaustion means no thread is free (pool full) or the JVM cannot create more threads.
  • Platform threads are mapped to OS threads and each reserves a stack, so thousands of them are costly.
  • Symptom: requests wait in a queue, latency rises, and the log may show unable to create native thread.

7. Intermediate Concepts

Mid-Level Notes

  • Pool sizing: an unbounded Executors.newCachedThreadPool() can create thousands of threads under load.
  • Blocking calls: threads waiting for a slow database or HTTP call are held, so a slow dependency exhausts the pool.
  • Thread dump shows many threads in the same WAITING or BLOCKED frame, which names the bottleneck.

8. Advanced Concepts

Anatomy of "unable to create new native thread"

This specific OutOfMemoryError message is misleading to newcomers because it says "OutOfMemoryError" but usually

has nothing to do with the Java heap. It occurs when the JVM asks the OS to create a new native thread (via

pthread_create on Linux) and the OS refuses. That refusal has two common underlying causes:

  • Native memory exhaustion - each thread reserves a stack (-Xss, default

~512KB-1MB); with thousands of threads, that alone can exhaust available process/native memory, especially in a

memory-constrained container.

  • OS thread-count limits - Linux's ulimit -u (max user processes/threads) or

/proc/sys/kernel/threads-max, and inside containers, resource limits (cgroups) can cap the number of

threads far below what raw memory would allow.

Exception in thread "pool-4-thread-8231" java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread
    at java.base/java.lang.Thread.start0(Native Method)
    at java.base/java.lang.Thread.start(Thread.java:803)
    at java.base/java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.addWorker(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:957)
    at java.base/java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.execute(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:1378)
    at java.base/java.util.concurrent.AbstractExecutorService.submit(AbstractExecutorService.java:145)
    at com.shop.orders.OrderNotifier.notifyAsync(OrderNotifier.java:52)

Diagnostic checklist:
  $ ps -eLf | grep  | wc -l        # actual current thread count for the process
  $ cat /proc//limits | grep processes    # ulimit -u as seen by the process
  $ jstack  | grep 'nid=' | wc -l         # cross-check via JVM's own thread list

Thread Pool Sizing: CPU-Bound vs I/O-Bound Work

Choosing a pool size isn't arbitrary - it should be driven by what the tasks actually spend their time doing:

  • CPU-bound tasks (pure computation, no blocking) - optimal pool size is roughly

number of CPU cores (+1). More threads than cores just adds context-switching overhead with no

throughput gain.

  • I/O-bound tasks (waiting on network calls, DB queries, disk) - threads spend most of their time

blocked, not computing, so a much larger pool can improve throughput. A common starting formula:

threads = cores x (1 + wait_time / compute_time) - e.g. if a task waits 90ms for every 10ms of actual

CPU work, that's a wait/compute ratio of 9, suggesting roughly 10x the core count.

In practice, teams tune this empirically with load tests rather than trusting the formula blindly, but the formula

gives a sane starting point instead of guessing "100 sounds fine."

Bounding Cached Pools and Rejecting Overload Gracefully

The real production fix for thread exhaustion is rarely "just use a fixed pool" alone - it's combining a bounded

pool with a bounded queue and an explicit rejection policy, so the system fails predictably under overload instead

of unboundedly consuming resources.

Symptom -> Root Cause -> Diagnosis -> Fix

War Story: The Retry Storm That Multiplied Threads

A payments-notification service used Executors.newCachedThreadPool() to fire outbound webhook calls

to merchant endpoints asynchronously - reasonable when merchant endpoints usually respond in under 200ms. During a

partial outage of one large merchant's endpoint, its webhook URL started timing out after the client's default

60-second socket timeout instead of failing fast.

Because the cached pool has no upper bound, and webhook volume didn't slow down, the service kept spinning up a

brand-new thread for every notification, each of which sat blocked for up to 60 seconds waiting on that one

unresponsive merchant. Within about 12 minutes, the process had accumulated over 30,000 threads and crashed with

OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread - taking down webhook delivery for

every merchant, not just the one that was actually having problems.

Fix: the cached pool was replaced with a bounded ThreadPoolExecutor (max 200 threads,

bounded queue, CallerRunsPolicy), and the HTTP client's socket timeout was reduced to 5 seconds with a

per-merchant circuit breaker, so one slow merchant could no longer starve threads needed for everyone else.

Prevention Checklist

  • Never use Executors.newCachedThreadPool() or raw new Thread() per task in production

code that handles untrusted/variable load - always define an explicit maximum.

  • Pair a bounded pool with a bounded queue and a deliberate rejection policy (

CallerRunsPolicy, AbortPolicy with monitoring, or a custom handler) so overload is

handled predictably.

  • Set aggressive timeouts on any blocking call made from within a pooled task - a thread blocked forever on a

downstream dependency is a thread that can never be reused.

  • Monitor thread count (via JMX/Micrometer jvm.threads.live) as a first-class metric with alerting,

the same way you'd monitor heap usage.

  • Size pools deliberately using the CPU-bound vs I/O-bound distinction, and validate under realistic load tests

rather than trusting a guessed constant.

Senior Notes

  • OS limits: check ulimit -u, /proc/sys/kernel/threads-max and container pid limits; each thread also uses -Xss of native memory.
  • Virtual threads (Java 21) are cheap and block without holding an OS thread, so use Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() for blocking I/O.
  • Protect dependencies with timeouts, bulkheads and bounded queues, and limit concurrency with a Semaphore when a downstream cannot take more.

9. Code for Each Concept

Basic Code: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and options:

  • Fixed pool: newFixedThreadPool(n) with an unbounded queue; safe thread count, unsafe queue.
  • Cached pool: unbounded threads; risky under load.
  • ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, bounded queue and a rejection policy (AbortPolicy, CallerRunsPolicy).
  • Virtual threads: Thread.ofVirtual().start(r) or the per-task executor.
  • Tomcat: server.tomcat.threads.max.
  • Stack size: -Xss.

Intermediate Code: How It Works Internally

Why threads run out.

  • Platform thread: a thin wrapper over an OS thread with its own stack (about 1 MB reserved).
  • Pool saturation: all workers are busy, new tasks wait in the queue or are rejected.
  • Blocking: threads waiting on slow I/O are not doing useful work but still occupy the pool.
  • Virtual thread: a JVM-managed thread that mounts on a carrier, and unmounts when it blocks.
  • Little's law: needed threads = request rate times average latency.

Advanced Code: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Pool per request: creating an executor in each call leaks threads; share one and shut it down.
  • Forgetting shutdown: non-daemon workers keep the JVM alive.
  • Waiting for a task in the same pool (nested submit and get) causes deadlock.
  • No timeouts: a hung dependency holds threads forever.
  • Huge ThreadLocals with virtual threads: millions of copies; prefer scoped values or pass parameters.

Advanced Code: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • CPU-bound: pool near the core count.
  • I/O-bound: more threads, or virtual threads, sized by the downstream limit.
  • Bulkheads: separate pools per dependency so one slow service cannot take all threads.
  • Timeouts everywhere: connect, read and queue wait.
  • Lower -Xss only after measuring depth.
  • Monitor: active threads, queue size and rejection count.

Advanced Code: Real-World Scenario

Incident: the checkout API stops answering although CPU is near zero.

  • Symptoms: requests time out, load balancer marks pods unhealthy, CPU 3 percent.
  • Diagnosis: jstack shows all 200 http-nio-exec threads in SocketInputStream.socketRead0 inside the payment client; ls /proc/PID/task | wc -l shows 260 threads.
  • Root cause: the payment provider became slow and the HTTP client had no read timeout, so every Tomcat thread waited.
  • Fix: 2 second read timeout, a separate bounded pool with a circuit breaker for payments, return a clear error when full; consider virtual threads for the blocking calls.

interviewQA: What does "OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread" actually mean?

The JVM asked the OS to create a new native thread and it was refused - usually due to native memory exhaustion (thread stacks) or hitting an OS/cgroup thread-count limit, not the Java heap being full
Why is Executors.newCachedThreadPool() dangerous in production?
It has no maximum pool size, so if tasks arrive faster than they complete (e.g. they block on a slow dependency), it will keep creating new threads without bound, risking thread exhaustion
How do you size a thread pool for CPU-bound work versus I/O-bound work?
CPU-bound: roughly the number of CPU cores (+1); I/O-bound: a larger pool since threads spend most time blocked, often estimated as cores x (1 + wait_time/compute_time)
What's the role of a bounded queue and rejection policy in a ThreadPoolExecutor?

They provide backpressure - once the pool and queue are both saturated, the rejection policy (e.g. CallerRunsPolicy) determines what happens next instead of letting the pool grow unboundedly or silently dropping work
How would you diagnose which threads are causing thread exhaustion in a running process?
Compare ps -eLf thread count and /proc/<pid>/limits against expectations, then use jstack to see what the accumulated threads are doing (often BLOCKED/WAITING on the same downstream call)
Why can a slow downstream dependency cause thread exhaustion even with reasonable traffic volume?

If each task blocks waiting on the slow dependency for a long time, worker threads accumulate faster than they're freed, especially with an unbounded pool, eventually exhausting native thread capacity
What's the trade-off of reducing -Xss to allow more threads within the same memory budget?
Smaller per-thread stacks let more threads fit in a given memory budget, but increase the risk of StackOverflowError for any code with deep recursion or large stack frames
